en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
In the Vinaya Piṭaka,
the Commentary by Vajirabuddhi.
The Introduction to the Composition:
By him through whom all beings to be trained were liberated for the sake of the purification of wisdom and compassion;
Bowing my head to that one who has become vision,
who has reached the end of the world, and to the Dhamma for the sake of the world,
and to the Saṅgha endowed with virtues such as moral discipline—
Having extracted the essence from all these locations,
with the intention of providing a concise summary for my sake,
and being urged on by the sight of the welfare of the bhikkhus;
I shall write, in brief, the words that were spoken by the teacher Buddhaghosa,
which are known as the *Samantapāsādikā* and are composed in a style free from obscurity.
In brief, it is written in the section on "Lapsed Terms" (līnapada):
"The designation, the characteristic mark, the agent, the measure, and the purpose—
all these must be stated beforehand for anyone who wishes to speak."
By way of its verbal expression, it is known by the designation *Samantapāsādikā*. Because it does not suffice for the needs of the community of monks in other lands, this is its purpose (*nimitta*).
It is the work of one whose name, Buddhaghosa, was adopted by his teachers; thus, he is the author (*kattā*). Its extent is approximately twenty-seven thousand verses;
thus, it is the measure (*parimāṇa*). For the sake of the long endurance of the Dhamma, this is its motive (*payojana*).
Regarding this, he asks: "As for what was stated—that one 'desires to speak what ought to be spoken'—what kind of speaker is that?

It is said: One who is learned in the meaning of the text, steadfast, a speaker who is pure and free from avarice, who does not abandon the fourfold [assembly], and who is eager for the welfare of the teacher.

In this context, "it should be recited" refers to the *pāṭha* (the text). For that is of many kinds: that which conforms to the meaning (*atthānurūpa*) and that which conforms to the words (*byañjanānurūpa*). How so?

It is spoken with intentional reference (*sandhāyabhāsita*), spoken according to the literal expression (*byañjanabhāsita*), a recitation with remainder (*sāvasesapāṭha*), a recitation without remainder (*niravasesapāṭha*), the definitive (*nīta*), and the interpretable (*neyya*).

Among these, that which possesses multiple meanings is called "spoken with intentional reference," such as: "Having killed mother and father," and so forth. That which possesses a single meaning is "spoken according to the literal expression."
The "nominal" (nāma) refers to such passages as, “Phenomena are preceded by the mind. The "incomplete" (sāvaseso) refers to such passages as, “Everything, monks, is aflame.
The "contrary" (viparīto), which is "complete" (niravaseso), refers to such passages as, “All phenomena in every aspect come within the range of the knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One.
The "direct" (nīto) is to be understood exactly according to the words, such as, “Impermanent, suffering, non-self,” and so forth.
That which is to be recollected through reasoning is called "that which is to be understood" (*neyya*), such as the passage beginning, "Bhikkhus, there is one person...

The meaning (*attha*) is also of many kinds: the literal meaning (*pāṭhattha*), the essential nature of the meaning (*sabhāvattha*), the meaning of what is to be known (*ñeyyattha*), the meaning conforming to the text (*pāṭhānurūpa*), the meaning not conforming to the text (*pāṭhānanurūpa*), the meaning with remainder (*sāvasesattha*), the meaning without remainder (*niravasesattha*), the explicit meaning (*nītattha*), the implicit meaning (*neyyattha*), and so forth.
Among these, that which is uttered for the purpose of making known this or that specific designation—
The word *pāṭha* (text) refers to the meaning of the text, as in the phrase “possessing the meaning and the phrasing” (*sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ*), and so forth.

The word *sabhāva* (intrinsic nature) refers to the characteristic, function, and so on, of material and immaterial phenomena, as in the phrase “he develops right view” (*sammādiṭṭhiṃ bhāveti*), and so forth.

That which, when known, leads to welfare is called the object of knowledge (*ñeyyattha*) because it is worthy of being known, as in the phrases “one who speaks of the goal” (*atthavādī*) and “one who speaks of the Dhamma” (*dhammavādī*), and so forth. That which is spoken according to the text is conformable to the text (*pāṭhānurūpa*).
“Bhikkhus, the eye is past karma,” so it was said by the Blessed One; therefore, even the eye is karma.

This was stated by one who, while obstructing the meaning through the mere shadow of the phrasing, followed the literal reading. That which is stated by leaving nothing out to be excluded and thus making a complete enumeration has a residual meaning, as in:
“Dependent on the eye and forms, [visual consciousness] arises,” and “All tremble...”
The opposite of this is the sense of being exhaustive (*niravasesa*), as in: "All are afraid of death, including the wielder of the rod" (*daṇḍassa*, *sabbe bhāyanti maccuno*).

The sense that is to be understood through the words themselves is the explicit meaning (*nītattha*), as in: "I have wandered and transmigrated, both I and you. In this regard, monks, who is the thinker? Who is the believer?... except for those who have seen the state" (*sandhāvitaṃ saṃsaritaṃ mamañceva tumhākañca.

Tatra, bhikkhave, ko mantā ko saddhātā... aññatra diṭṭhapadehi*). Furthermore, the explicit meaning is illustrated by: "Forms, sounds, tastes, odors, tangibles... (*rūpā saddā rasā gandhā, phoṭṭhabbā*).

...as in the passage beginning, “and it is delightful,” and so forth. The meaning that is to be inferred (neyyattha) is to be understood by way of conventional designation (sammuti), as in the passage beginning, “Bhikkhus, there are these four persons who are like clouds,” and so forth. And it has been said:
“That meaning which is to be known from the words, the wise know that to be the explicit meaning (nītattha).”
“The convergence of the meaning itself is called the 'meaning that is to be understood' (neyyattha).

Thus, one who understands the meaning of the text when it has been analyzed in this way is "one who knows the meaning of the text" (pāṭhatthavidū). One who is not shaken by the arguments of opponents because of dwelling in a [spiritual] refuge for a long time is "unshakeable" (asaṃhīra).
One who is able to speak because of being perfected in cultivation, scripture, and realization is "an eloquent speaker" (vattā), according to the method of both concise and detailed exposition.
The meaning is "one capable of making [others] understand by means of reasons, examples, and so forth. It is called *suci* (pure) because it "purifies" both oneself and others;

the meaning is that it is free from the stains of immorality (*dussīlya*) and wrong view (*duddiṭṭhi*). For an immoral person harms himself and becomes one whose words are not to be trusted, like a physician who is constantly ill due to his improper diet and conduct.
One with wrong view harms others and does not become a refuge for them, like a cluster of lotuses infested by venomous snakes.
One who has failed in both respects is in every way unfit for veneration, like a firebrand smeared with excrement or a black snake dwelling in excrement.
But one who is accomplished in both is pure and in every way fit for veneration and service by the wise, like a treasure-mine free from danger.
He is not stingy; that is to say, he is not one whose teacher’s fist is closed.
The meaning is that he does not abandon the tetrad known as the Sutta, the *Suttānuloma*, the *Ācariyavāda*, and *Attanomati*, and he is an expounder of its very purpose.
Alternatively, he does not abandon the fourfold epistemic criteria (*pamāṇacatukka*) divided into direct perception, inference, verbal testimony, and implication.
"One is the categorical statement, the other is the analytical statement..."
“One should question the third, but set aside the fourth.

Thus, one who does not abandon the aforementioned tetrad is called *hitussuka*. This means he is eager (*ussuka*) for the welfare (*hita*) of his listeners, in the sense that he desires their awakening.
He is thus “dear even to the well-disposed” (*sucittā piyo*). Because he does not abandon the tetrad, he is “venerable” (*garu*); because he cannot be shaken, he is “steadfast” (*asaṃhīra*).

He should be cultivated: because he knows the proper place, he speaks appropriately; because he desires their welfare, he is patient with their words; because he is skilled in the meaning of what is recited, he delivers profound discourse;
and because he is free from stinginess, he does not lead them toward what is improper.
Thus: "He is dear, respected, and worthy of cultivation; he speaks appropriately and is patient with their words."
“He shall deliver profound discourse, yet he does not lead one astray into what is improper”—
thus has the teacher been described;
now the listener is being defined.

One who honors the Teacher of the Dhamma, adorned with the jewels of qualities such as faith and wisdom, free from deceit and hypocrisy, possessing a stream [of virtue], wise, and facing the door to the Deathless—
therein, through reverence for the Dhamma, he does not despise the teaching; through reverence for the Teacher, he does not despise the speaker.
Because he is adorned with qualities such as faith and wisdom, he does not despise himself; because he is free from deceit and guile and is oriented toward the Deathless, his mind is undistracted;
and because he is well-endowed (sumedha), he attends to things thoroughly—this is the meaning. For it has been said:
"Bhikkhus, one who possesses five qualities, while hearing the True Dhamma, is capable of entering upon the fixed course of rightness."
"Rightness regarding wholesome states. By what five [qualities]? He does not despise the discourse, he does not despise the speaker, he does not despise himself;
with an undistracted mind he listens to the Dhamma with a one-pointed mind, and he attends to it wisely.
Because it has attained those characteristics, cultivation belongs to listening; thus it is called "hearing" (*sota*).
Commentary on the Introduction to the Work:
Now follows the commencement of this undertaking. In this context, the term "he" (*yo*) is an indefinite designation;

by it, the author demonstrates that no specific reason—such as being of pure birth, lineage, or clan, or having been purified from the stains of defilements, or being worthy of honor—is required, but rather anyone at all may undertake this work for the sake of the quality of "Lord of the World" (*lokanāthatā*) described in the opening verse of this *Samantapāsādikā*.
Having made [the mind] firmer and immovable by means of the root-cause as previously described, and fulfilling the time for that aforementioned cause to its ultimate extent,
one finally accomplishes the fruit of the aforementioned cause and thereby achieves the purpose of that aforementioned causal fruit;
such a person alone is determined to be worthy of the highest veneration.
To this extent—
this salutation is not in every way [a result of] fear, delusion,
or wrong view; it is shown that this salutation has wisdom as its forerunner.
In this context, "causes" refers to the meritorious deeds comprised of the thirty perfections (*pāramitā*), which are exceedingly difficult to perform.
Indeed, they are called "exceedingly difficult" because they are carried out with extreme hardship, great effort, and a power that transcends the path of words.
Precisely because they are so exceedingly difficult, their fruit—known as the state of a Protector (*nāthatva*)—is extremely rare in the world and not shared by others.
They bear fruit; that is the cause-and-effect therein. What is called the "root-cause" is the Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā) capable of producing the aforementioned cause.

From the initial aspiration onwards, according to the method beginning with "I shall liberate those who are not liberated," it proceeds uninterruptedly until the purpose of the cause-and-effect is fulfilled. With reference to this, it was said:
“Many times this earth, together with its forests, its mountain peaks, and its oceans,
has gone to destruction at the time of the end of an eon,
by water, fire, and wind.”

“How could there be great asceticism for a Bodhisatta?”—it is because he was endowed with this [compassion] that he said, “Homage to him, the Great Compassionate One. The so-called “time of the cause” refers to the divisions of time such as four, eight, sixteen, and incalculable *asaṅkhyeyya* aeons;
it is with reference to this that he said, “a time immeasurable even by tens of millions of eons (*kappakoṭīhi*). In this context, the sense is one of absolute connection (*accantasaṃyoga*).
The usage of the word should be understood as in such examples as "he studies for a month" or "he walks for a day.

Granted that this duration can be measured and understood by way of incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyya*), nevertheless, with reference to its being unintelligible even by way of ten million eons (*kappakoṭi*), he said:
"a duration immeasurable even by ten million eons. In this context, it is called *kāla* because it measures (*kālayati*), that is, it casts away or destroys.

The meaning is "the life of beings. *Kala* means "dispersion. In this context, it is called a *kappa* because it is calculated (*kappīyati*) and conceptualized (*saṃkappīyati*) by way of similes such as the mustard seed and the mountain;

it is not reckoned by the calculation of human days, months, or years. It is called a "limit" (*koṭi*) because it constitutes the ultimate limit of the path of counting, beginning with "one" and so forth.
Thus, "ends of *kappas*" (*kappakoṭiyo*) refers to the limits of those *kappas*. By means of these...
It is called "immeasurable" (*appameyya*) because it cannot be measured; that which is immeasurable is *taṃ appameyyaṃ*.

"Practicing" (*karonto*)—since verbal roots have various meanings—means giving gifts, guarding moral virtue, emerging from the mass of greed, understanding this or that Dhamma distinguished by its own welfare, the welfare of others, and so forth, striving and exerting oneself with various efforts, or forgiving the various offenses of sentient beings.
The meaning is: considering the truths of conventional designation, mutual agreement, and ultimate reality; resolving upon the welfare of various beings;
suffusing the entire world with loving-kindness; and maintaining equanimity toward each being while abandoning partiality based on distinctions such as friend or enemy.
"Attained exhaustion" means having reached, in the sense of experiencing, the great suffering of saṃsāra which has infinite divisions.
This is the meaning of *sampatto*. For the suffering of *saṃsāra* is called "weariness" (*kheda*) because it exhausts and causes one to fall away from both physical and mental happiness.

The phrase "for the benefit of the world" (*lokahitāya*) is an indication of the aforementioned cause, fruit, and purpose; some also say it is an indication of the reason for experiencing the suffering of *saṃsāra*:
"Though he was capable of going to Nibbāna from the sufferings of birth and *saṃsāra*..."
And as for the statement, "Even though he has long wandered in saṃsāra, it was solely out of compassion," that is incorrect.
For the Blessed One does not experience the suffering of saṃsāra for the sake of the world’s welfare.
Indeed, the experiencing of suffering by anyone does not bring benefit to the world. Rather, this is said to show [his practice of] the thirtyfold classification of the pāramīs.
The cause, and the fruit known as lordship (*nāthatta*), which is the result of the perfections. As he said:

"For it is by relying on me, Ānanda, as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitta*), that beings subject to birth are liberated from birth," and so forth. In this context, the Blessed One sowed the seeds of wisdom—the means for developing the state of being those to be trained—among sentient beings through the aforementioned causes;
and by means of the cause and fruit, [he did so] through the state of having matured faculties.
The meaning is that he trained beings who were fully prepared to be trained, and liberated them from the suffering of *saṃsāra*.

It was not by means of the suffering of *saṃsāra* that he rendered any assistance to the world; therefore, the connection is: "performing deeds exceedingly difficult for the sake of the world's welfare.
According to this interpretation, [the text refers] to the Bodhisatta starting from the time of the very first arising of a Bodhisatta.
The attainment of the cause and fruit known as the perfection of being a protector (*nāthatta-pāramitā*) should be understood. For the intended connection is:
"He who is the Protector. Regarding this matter:
"That very first thought which arose for your enlightenment..."
“You yourself have dwelt as the one worthy of worship in this very world.
This statement is the proof. The fact that the first thought constitutes a perfection (pāramitā) must be established by the analogy of a tree’s growth beginning from its sprout.
Here it may be asked: “Is the statement ‘he experienced weariness’ pointless, since it is impossible to establish the presence of such qualities according to the method already described?”

No; because it illustrates the state of not turning back midway. It shows that while performing difficult tasks, one simply becomes weary, but does not turn back midway because of being unable to endure the weariness.
Alternatively, it demonstrates the Blessed One’s capacity to personally experience suffering for one who desires to remove the suffering of the world.
“Whatever excellent gift or fault there may be, until I have awakened like a lotus,
[I shall endure] all the sufferings of all beings at all times throughout the aeon”—
for one with such an intention, the very capacity to experience even one’s own suffering is itself the supreme meaning.
The meaning is "he shows. Alternatively, the meaning "one who has reached exhaustion" (*khedaṃ gata*) may also be understood as "one who has reached proficiency in activity" (*byāpāra-paricaya*).
Having seen a person engaged in activity regarding work and so forth, there are indeed speakers in the world who say, "This one is exhausted by work; this one is exhausted by beings," and so on.
According to this interpretation, by the word *nātha* (Protector), the state of being a Protector that has reached the ultimate limit—established through the attainment of Buddhahood—is indicated.
It should be understood that the period of remaining [in the world] after attaining [enlightenment] is being shown here. Some write:

"By saying 'of the Greatly Compassionate One,' he shows [him] as one who has become a Buddha"; however, that does not seem correct, because that designation was still in use even during the time of the Bodhisatta.
Therefore, while performing such difficult deeds for this long a time, at the end, through the fulfillment of those perfections of difficult deeds—[he attained] their...
The meaning demonstrated here is that, having attained the state of a Protector which is the fruit [of his practice], he has engaged in activity for the benefit of the world.
Even when it is said, "He went to enlightenment" (*bodhiṃ gato*), the complete causal process and its fruit are shown.
Furthermore, because of the presence of a specific term, the homage is paid to the Protector who has already attained the state of Buddhahood, not to the Bodhisattva. This being so:
The subject matter intended here is that of the Vinaya. And this [discipline] extends from the time of going forth until the time of death.

Who indeed would not attain the happiness of transcending this world and the next, by fulfilling—even for their own benefit and with the sole intention of removing their own suffering—this extremely brief period of mere virtue, which is so easy to practice, while being possessed of shame?
For did not the Blessed One act with the intention of removing the suffering of the entire world?

The Teacher praises his own virtue by means of a pretext, saying that even after passing away for an immeasurable period of ten million eons, he had reached exhaustion through suffering that was exceedingly difficult to endure. Regarding the phrase "for the welfare of the world" (*lokahitāya*):
here, "world" (*loka*) refers to that wherein suffering is found, or it is that which is worn away (*luyate*) by the sufferings of birth, aging, and death.
By the word "world" (loko), he includes both the world of sentient beings (sattaloka) and the world of birth (jātiloka).

Therefore, having combined for the sake of the world—the welfare of those sentient beings in this world and the next, or the welfare of worlds that have transcended the next world or whose worldly origination has been cut off—namely, the welfare known as a happy dwelling in the present life (diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra) in this world of birth or in the world of space (okāsaloka); [he speaks] for the world, for worlds, or in the world.

Having formed a collective singular compound (*sarūpa-ekadeseka-sesa*) from the word *hita*, he says "for the welfare of the world" (*lokahita*). He is called the "Protector" (*nātha*) because of his capacity to teach the Dhamma in accordance with the inclinations, latent tendencies, conduct, and dispositions of all beings;
thus, by virtue of his role as one who entreats them—saying, "Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the Dhamma... listen to it"—he is the Protector.
Furthermore, by laying down training rules (*sikkhāpada*) appropriate to the transgressions of the bhikkhus, [he protects them] regarding both the present life and the future life.

And it "shines" (tapati) by approaching with compassion; or, according to the Suttanta method, it shines by approaching all those beings with both compassion and wisdom regarding their latent defilements;

or, according to the Abhidhamma method, it shines in the sense of "heating" because, having examined various formations through their characteristics such as impermanence, one approaches and delimits one's own defilements with wisdom. Thus, it is so called in the sense of heating.

He is called the Protector (*nātha*) because he protects. He is called the Protector also in the sense of sovereignty, because he is without a rival in the world including the devas, because his teaching of the Dhamma is unopposed by anyone, and because he exercises supreme mastery over the mind.
This is according to the statement: "With a discourse on the Dhamma, he instructed, urged, roused, and gladdened [them]," which refers to what is known as gladdening.

He should be understood as the "Protector" (*nātha*) in the sense of aspiration—that is, from the time of his initial resolve onwards, in the manner of aspiring, "How indeed might I, having been liberated myself, liberate others?

and so forth; he is the Perfectly Enlightened One (*Sammāsambuddha*). All the qualities of a Buddha, such as the four grounds of self-confidence (*vesārajja*), the four analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), and so on, should be connected with all four aspects of being a protector;
however, they have not been connected here for fear of excessive prolixity.

*Namoti* is, in the ultimate sense, a bending of the mind characterized by an overwhelming abundance of reverence for the qualities of the Buddha; and from that bending of the mind arise the bending of speech and body.
This is connected with the elliptical reading *atthu me*. Regarding the term *mahākāruṇikassa*:

here, because it has all sentient beings as its object and because it arises from great exertion, this great compassion is called *mahākaruṇā*. In this regard, it extends from the initial aspiration until the entry into the city of *nirvāṇa* without residue.
"Engaged" means the Blessed One is one of great compassion (*mahākāruṇika*). Here, by the phrase "of one of great compassion," he shows the root cause as previously stated.
For one who lacks compassion and is indifferent toward the suffering of others would consider even the mere aspiration for Buddhahood to be too burdensome;

thus, having fulfilled over an immeasurable time that cause which is extremely difficult to perform—the state of being a protector (*nāthatta*), which consists of both the cause and its fruit—[he becomes so].
"How will he bring about the welfare of the world? Therefore, praising the quality of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) alone because it is the root of all virtues, he said:

"Homage to the Greatly Compassionate One. By this much, the following meaning has been shown: the fruit corresponding to the cause, the cause corresponding to the fruit, the root corresponding to both, and the purpose corresponding to all three.
Thus is the wonderful person, the Protector, established in the qualities of a protector;
homage to the one who is a refuge for the helpless and who bestows the attainment of those who seek a protector.
Here it might be asked: "Since many qualities of the Blessed One exist, why is only the single quality of 'being greatly compassionate' mentioned? It is said in reply:
"In a teacher who is free from fault, there is no ground for censure;
and in a teacher who is possessed of fault, censure is therefore appropriate.
"I have not offered censure, but rather a question. Furthermore—
“Even when a tree is laden with fruit, the fruit does not fall unless it is shaken;
yet the great fruit of the Teacher’s admonitions and questions is indeed attained.
One does not properly lift up what has not been lowered, nor grasp a jar that has not been set down.”
For when an objection has been raised, there is the binding of the intellect by the desire for a reply:
"Just as one who has fallen into snow wakes up by means of a fragrant ointment,
so too does one whose meaning is shattered awaken by means of the ointment of the Teacher’s purpose."—
And thus it is said:
"Even a proper admonition is indeed censurable for teachers who have grown arrogant;
yet you, a disciple, have been struck down by their words—protect yourself further with such speech."
"Saravatī is defiled by her teacher; therefore, she should release herself.
The teacher conquers himself, just as Sadasa does his chariot.
To this, it is replied:
For even one who has a thousand tongues, with a hundred tongues for every single word,
would not be able to speak the names of the qualities of the One Possessing Ten Powers, even in an entire eon—
for example:
Even if a Buddha were to speak the praises of another Buddha for an entire eon,
without speaking of anything else,
that eon would be exhausted while the time remaining would still be very long.
"The praise of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted."—
Because of their vastness, it is impossible to state the remaining qualities of the Blessed One.
Moreover:
“O Ten-Powered One, just as you possess both wisdom and compassion for beings, so too are these two supreme qualities;
indeed, your multitude of virtues is threefold.

This is stated as one because they are the most excellent of all virtues and because they are the root. Alternatively, it is because [compassion] is one of the six unique knowledges (*asādhāraṇañāṇa*).
They say that by the mention of one [term], the others are also included by virtue of their characteristic of association.
Moreover, because the Abhidhamma deals exclusively with the domain of wisdom (*paññā*), at the commencement of the *Abhidhamma-aṭṭhakathā*, the Master praised the quality of wisdom in the verse:

"As compassion [is directed] toward beings, so is the wisdom of that Great Sage. This refers to the wisdom that discerns, in accordance with the differences in the inclinations, latent tendencies, dispositions, and resolutions of various beings.

And because of his preeminence in great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) toward sentient beings. At the beginning of the commentaries on the Suttantas, both of the Blessed One’s qualities—wisdom and compassion—are praised: “His heart is cooled by compassion; the darkness of delusion is dispelled by the lamp of wisdom.
However, here in the Vinaya, regardless of their disposition or other factors, even one who hears what ought not to be heard from an ordinary person out of mere compassion [is subject to censure].

It should be understood that the quality of compassion alone is praised here, insofar as he established the training rule by questioning those who ought to be questioned and speaking to those who ought to be spoken to.
Wisdom and the other [qualities] are for the sake of one’s own and others’ welfare.
All virtues of the Victor are consequent upon that;
therefore, both these types of virtues have been described here by the preeminent teacher for him who is an ocean of virtues.
To this extent, the verses from the commentaries and so forth,
and the beauty of the word-meanings as stated in brief—
this too, I say, is the method of detailed exposition.
I shall summarize for you what follows from this.
In the second verse, "not understanding" (*asambudhaṃ*) means not awakening to the true nature (*yathāsabhāva*) of phenomena.

"Practiced by the Buddhas" (*buddhanisevitaṃ*) means practiced, as appropriate, through the sphere of activity, cultivation, and service of the Buddhas, the Paccekabuddhas who awakened after the Buddha, and so forth. "Existences" (*bhavā*) refers to the various states of existence.
The meaning is that it goes to, approaches, or proceeds toward an existence other than the present existence (*vattamānabhava*).

Alternatively, "existence" (*bhava*) refers to the view of eternalism (*sassatadiṭṭhi*); because it is the opposite of that, "non-existence" (*abhava*) refers to the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*). Or, "existence" is increase; "non-existence" is decrease.

Or, "existence" is an unhappy destination (*duggati*); "non-existence" is a happy destination (*sugati*). [This is seen] in such passages as "immeasurable states" (*appamāṇā dhammā*) and "states of one beyond training" (*asekkhā dhammā*).

For [the prefix] *a-* has the sense of growth (*vuddhi*), as in the case of the letter *a*. "Becoming" (*bhava*) means that which causes to become; it is birth. Or, "becoming" (*bhava*) is that which comes to be.

Thus, the arising of various aggregates (*khandha*) accompanied by change is illustrated. "Non-becoming" (*abhava*) means destruction; what is meant is that one goes from the state of birth to the state of death.
Here, even the death of Arahants should be understood in terms of momentariness. [The phrase] "non-existence in states of becoming" (*bhavesu abhava*)...
"Becoming and non-becoming" (*bhavābhava*): the meaning is that it proceeds toward the designation of non-existence (*abhāva*) within the realms of becoming (*bhava*).

"The world of living beings" (*jīvaloka*) refers to the world of sentient beings (*sattaloka*); since it is impossible for the world of formations (*saṅkhāraloka*) or the world of space (*okāsaloka*) to undergo becoming and non-becoming, he specifies the world of sentient beings as "the world of living beings.
"Destroyer of the net of defilements such as ignorance": here, all nine supramundane states (*lokuttaradhamma*) are included.
For "leading to diminution" (*apacayagāmitā*) refers to the specific destruction of the net of defilements such as ignorance by means of the four paths;

this [quality] belongs to that [path], and it also applies to Nibbāna because it becomes its object and thereby functions as its companion. As it is said: "That which, friend, is the destruction of lust...
this is called Nibbāna. The same applies to Arahantship, because of the presence of the expression "destruction of lust and so forth" in its description.
Because the commonality of the fruit exists for all three fruits, this ninefold [path] is called "the destroyer of the web of defilements beginning with ignorance.
Alternatively, by way of the causality characterized by concomitance, there is the grasping of the object as an antidote.

For it is said that even if a state (dhamma) is not explicitly mentioned therein, it should be understood as being mentioned there; thus, by the grasping of the object as a cause, all four [truths] are [implied].
The fruits have been grasped. It is called *dhamma* because it sustains one from falling into the hells and other lower realms by causing rebirth in a happy destination (*sugati*).
Furthermore, it is called *dhamma* because, having restrained unwholesome states that would prevent rebirth in a happy destination, it nourishes, maintains, and increases [wholesome states].

Moreover, it is threefold—divided into the realms of sense-desire, form, and formlessness—and because it brings about ultimate happiness and is the most excellent even among those, it is the "supreme *dhamma*" (*dhammavara*).
Here it is said: "Bhikkhus, through non-comprehension and non-penetration of the Four Noble Truths, this long course has been run and wandered through.
From this statement, it is established that the world of living beings goes from existence to existence without having awakened to the Dhamma of the Four Truths.
Therefore, that which goes while unawakened is referred to by the demonstrative pronoun "tassa" (of that) at the end, by way of a specific designation for it.
By way of restriction, even the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths, which destroys the web of defilements such as ignorance, comes to be designated as the "excellent Dhamma. Otherwise,
the use of a case-ending identical to that of the description— namely, "Homage to that excellent Dhamma which destroys the web of defilements such as ignorance"—
would not be logical due to the risk of over-extension (*atippasaṅga*), [if it were not restricted] to "the excellent Dhamma which destroys the web of defilements such as ignorance."

If it is argued that the word [in question] is a qualifying term, and therefore there is no possibility of those two truths being included within the truth of suffering or the truth of the origin, we say:
No, because they are not distinguished in a place where they share the same grammatical case as their respective definitions.

Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with the statement that nine supramundane states are included, since the fruits are not comprised within the truth of the path or the truth of cessation. As for the fruits...

In the commentary on the Verañjakaṇḍa of the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, it is stated: "It is not only the Noble Path and Nibbāna, but also the Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti-dhamma) together with the Dhammas of the Noble Fruits.
For this has been said: 'Come for refuge to this Dhamma, which is the fading away of lust, unshakable, and sorrowless...'.
Thus, there is a contradiction in the statement that this verse contradicts what precedes and follows it, and is contrary to the Dispensation. To this it is replied: All of this is inappropriate.
Because of not knowing the meaning of the verses stated [in the commentary]. For here, the Teacher has shown the analysis of occurrence, the cause of occurrence, and the object.

How so? Therein, "not understanding" (*asambudha*) means non-understanding (*asambodha*); in terms of its referent, this is ignorance (*avijjā*). By that [ignorance], craving and clinging are included.

These three factors together constitute the truth of origination (*samudayasacca*). "Becoming this or that" (*bhavābhava*) expresses the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*), which is distinguished by the categories of happy and miserable destinies.
For, in its essential meaning, existence (*bhava*) consists of the five aggregates of clinging.

Because of the statement, "Thus there is the origin of this entire mass of suffering," the manifestation of suffering is called "occurrence" (*pavatti*), and the origin of suffering is called the "cause of occurrence.
And by including what was not previously mentioned, the two truths of cessation and the path—which are the antidotes to ignorance, the cause of occurrence—are [also included].

This is what is called the "object. For it has been said: "In this context, what is ignorance? It is non-knowledge regarding suffering... [and so on] ...non-knowledge regarding the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.

And herein, the truth of cessation was cultivated by the Buddha through the cultivation of the resorting to the objective field, while the truth of the path was cultivated through the cultivation of development.

To this extent, the meaning of the verse is as follows: "Homage to the excellent Dhamma"—that is, to that object consisting of cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*magga*), which has reached its full utility and is frequented by the Buddhas, yet remains unawakened [by others], and which destroys the aforementioned triple net of defilements such as ignorance (*avijjā*).

Furthermore, the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*) also serves as a decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for the destruction of defilements according to the method of the Suttas.
Because his nature is to destroy the defilements, it is possible to say that he is "the destroyer of the net of defilements such as ignorance.
For this being the case, the meaning of the verse—"He teaches the Dhamma which leads to the fading away of lust"—as well as the meaning of the Sutta—"He teaches the Dhamma...
he proclaims the holy life"—is grasped in its entirety. Alternatively, by this verse, only the Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti) is grasped.
With reference to this, it was said: “He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning... [and so on]... he reveals the holy life.
This too, though not yet fully awakened by others, has been practiced by the Buddhas alone; it is a practice of the range of experience not practiced by anyone else. As it was said:

“Venerable sir, our teachings have the Blessed One as their root, the Blessed One as their guide, the Blessed One as their resort... having heard them from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember them.”
In the third verse, although the qualities beginning with virtue (sīla) may be either mundane or supramundane according to their occurrence,

nevertheless, because of the expression "the Noble Saṅgha" at the end, these four aggregates of the Dhamma (dhammakkhandha)— virtue and so forth— are exclusively supramundane. And here, although one should have said "by means of virtue,
concentration, wisdom, liberation, knowledge and vision of liberation, and so forth," the form is constructed by applying the grammatical rule of single-remainder elision (sarūpekasesa).

It is said, “beginning with the knowledge of liberation. And here, although by the term “liberation” only the dhammas that constitute the fruit are intended in the Sutta, nevertheless, according to the statement:
“Having emerged from the path, one reviews the path; one reviews the defilements abandoned;
one reviews the fruit; one reviews Nibbāna,” there is also the knowledge that reviews the path and so forth.
It should be understood as "knowledge of liberation. For liberation (*vimutti*), release (*vimokkha*), and destruction (*khaya*) are one in meaning.

As it is stated in the Sutta: "Knowledge of destruction and knowledge of non-arising; here 'destruction' refers to the Path, while 'the destruction of lust' and 'the destruction of hatred' are designations for the Fruition and Nibbāna.
The destruction of defilements that have been abandoned is simply their literal destruction. By the word "beginning" (*pabhuti*)...
Virtues such as the three types of higher knowledge (*tisso vijjā*), the six direct knowledges (*cha abhiññā*), and the four analytical insights (*catasso paṭisambhidā*) are included herein.

He is endowed with these in the sense of possessing them and in the sense of not having fallen away from them. He is a "field for people seeking the wholesome" because, according to the Sutta, he is "the unsurpassed field of merit for the world," being the place where the wholesome grows and, according to the method of the Suttas, serving as a decisive support-condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*).
If it is argued that the Saṅgha is indeed a field for the wholesome, but not for people who seek the wholesome—and therefore this [claim] is not tenable—[we reply]:
No, because the meaning of the Sutta is possible. For it is stated in the Sutta: "The unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
For whom in the world? For one who seeks merit; the Saṅgha is a field because it is a field of merit due to being a supporting condition for merit.

The Saṅgha is also called "those who seek the wholesome. For even in the world, Devadatta’s field and Yaññadatta’s field are called a "rice-field" and a "barley-field" respectively because they serve as the basis for planting rice and barley.

It is called the "Noble Saṅgha" (ariyasaṅgha) because it is noble (ariya)—that is, free from defilements and pure—or because it has attained the state of a Noble One (ariyabhāva) through the commonality of virtue and view.
“Because it is a collection (saṅgha), [he pays homage] to the Saṅgha. Some write: “By the word ‘noble’ (ariya), he excludes the conventional Saṅgha (sammuti-saṅgha)”;
that is not correct, because [the Saṅgha] is distinguished by the inclusion of the qualities of the knowledge of liberation (vimutti-ñāṇa-guṇa).

By the word “with my head” (sirasā), he certainly indicates a bowing of the body; nevertheless, pointing specifically to the highest limb out of reverence for the supreme Saṅgha, he says, “I bow with my head.”
Furthermore, the head’s preeminence is due to its being the support for the supreme faculties of sight and hearing;
and their preeminence should be understood as being caused by the unsurpassed vision and the unsurpassed hearing. Here it is said by one skilled in the connections [of the text]:
“The introduction, the word, the meaning of the word, and the analysis of the word;”
"An explanation of the injunctions and prohibitions is sixfold for that [text].
Why was the homage to the Triple Gem stated first instead of saying this? It is said: because it is the conduct of the virtuous (*satācārattā*).

Indeed, it is the conduct of noble persons (*sappurisānaṃ*) to perform the rite of worshiping the Triple Gem at the commencement of a commentary. Therefore, "because it is the conduct of the virtuous..."

"May we not be defeated! Thus it is done. Furthermore, for one who possesses clarity of wisdom and desires to comment upon the Vinaya Piṭaka—which is endowed with four profound characteristics—there arises a great fear, as if plunging into the great ocean.
Yet this performance of prostration and worship, born from recollecting the virtues of the Triple Gem, brings about the destruction of that fear. As it has been said:

“Thus for those who recollect the Buddha,” and so forth. Furthermore, by means of this method of honoring the Teacher, the Master causes the world—which, in the absence of a Teacher, has a misplaced adherence toward one who is not a Teacher—to generate a true appreciation for the Teacher, the Fully Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha), and to abandon its appreciation for one who is not a Teacher;
thus, it makes the world take the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata as its own.

He avoids the aforementioned fault. Because the continuity of the aggregates is prone to many interruptions, and because there is the possibility that his own lifespan, complexion, happiness, and strength might be exhausted during the unfinished commentary on the Vinaya, he aspires for the benefits stated in the passage beginning, “For one whose nature is to pay homage...
[his] lifespan, complexion, happiness, and strength [increase],” until the conclusion of the commentary. Moreover, in this context:

The ritual of homage and worship to the Buddha, the Blessed One, generates enthusiasm in those who are practicing the Buddha-vehicle for the sake of attaining the state of a Perfectly Enlightened Buddha.
The ritual of worship to the True Dhamma— whether distinguished as mundane and supramundane,
or as exclusively supramundane— generates enthusiasm in those who are practicing the Pacceka-buddha vehicle for the sake of attaining the state of a Pacceka-buddha.

It generates [zeal]. For those who merely desire the penetration of the True Dhamma, this procedure for worshipping the Ultimate Saṅgha generates enthusiasm in those practicing the Disciple Vehicle (Sāvakayāna) for the sake of attaining the state of the Ultimate Saṅgha;

or, it is for the purpose of satisfying the minds of those who hold the view that auspicious rites and the like are meaningful, free from obstacles, long-lasting, and highly esteemed—thus [it says] "worship."

And he performs the auspicious rite praised by the Blessed One: "The Blessed Buddha is an auspicious sign, and the Dhamma and the Saṅgha are auspicious signs; those who begin with auspicious signs achieve all their goals swiftly. It is said:
"The Blessed Buddha is an auspicious sign, the Dhamma and the Saṅgha are auspicious signs;
those who begin with auspicious signs achieve all their goals swiftly."
“Knowing that ‘By means of the methods for honoring the Teacher, one obtains many such virtues as these,’ one should be intent upon honoring the Teacher.

And here, because the Dhamma and the Saṅgha are centered upon the Teacher, the method for honoring the Dhamma and the Saṅgha should be understood as the “method for honoring the Teacher,” both according to the Dispensation and according to worldly convention. Therefore, this is said:
“The Teacher” (satthā) is the Dhamma spoken by the Sugata;
at the time of his Parinibbāna, he was the Teacher because of his self-restraint;
in the *Suvatthi-gāthā*, he is called the “Tathāgata.”
And because the Teacher has said that the Saṅgha is restrained by self-control,
what more need be said?
Since the Teacher is the embodiment of the Dhamma, therefore the Dhamma is considered the Teacher.
That Saṅgha, established in the Dhamma, attains the status of a Teacher.

For there are those in the world who, when a man stands holding a sword sheathed in its scabbard, do not touch him separately but say, "This man is standing holding a sword. Therefore he said in the Cariyāpiṭaka:
"Homage to the Jewel of the Buddha; homage to you, the Jewel of the Dhamma."
“Homage be to the Jewel of the Saṅgha, who has brought together the Three Jewels.

Furthermore, if one designates as “Buddha” the continuum of aggregates (khandhasantāna) characterized by the manifestation of the supreme liberation through unimpeded knowledge regarding all phenomena, then the Dhamma is certainly worthy of homage; what need is there to mention the Saṅgha? In the Saṅgha...
He indicates that it is a vessel because of the statement: "Gotamī, give [it]; when it is given to the Saṅgha, both I and the Saṅgha will be honored.

Alternatively, he indicates the Saṅgha [as the vessel] because: "The Dhamma, well-awakened by the Buddha, has been brought down to our ears—even those such as mine—without any loss, like oil poured into a golden vessel, through the succession of teachers until the present day."
The teacher pays homage with extreme reverence, saying, "I bow my head.

Thus they speak of the various purposes for prostration; however, the purpose intended by the teacher himself is stated by him alone in the fourth verse, beginning with "Thus, one who is to be worshipped forever," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "Thus" (*iccevaṃ*) here:
The word *iti* signifies the completion of the procedure for worshipping the Triple Gem.

If it were thought that the Triple Gem is worthy of worship only by the procedure exactly as prescribed, and not by anything beyond that—lest one fall into the undesirable consequence [of over-extension]—the author says, "Thus, eternally worthy of homage.
In this context, the word *evaṃ* (thus) indicates the aforementioned method; [it means] by the aforementioned method, or otherwise...
The meaning is that for one who constantly, uninterruptedly, and regularly pays homage to such a being—
who is worthy of homage— it brings benefit and produces great fruit, even if one does not remain [in that state] for more than a moment. Thus, while paying homage to the Triple Gem—
which has established its status as a "gem" in the sense of being difficult to find and in the sense of producing great fruit— I obtained, that is, received, this flood of merit (*puññābhisanda*).
It is called *puñña* because it purifies by abandoning unwholesome stains through methods such as "abandoning by way of its factors" (*tadaṅgappahāna*).

It is called *abhisanda* because it moistens the mind due to its coolness resulting from the subsiding of the distress of the defilements. Thus, it is a "flood of merit" (*puññābhisanda*) because it is both merit and a flood; that is, "that flood of merit.
However, in the *Gaṇṭhipada*, they say it means "greatness of merit"; yet, because of the word "vast" (*vipula*), that meaning is not tenable.
"Teacher. Alternatively, "overflowing of merit" (*puññābhisanda*) means an abundance of merit; the verbal root is *sanda*, meaning "to flow.
Therefore, the sense that it is a "stream of merit" or a "support of merit" is appropriate. Furthermore, by the word "vast" (*vipula*), it is shown that this [merit] is extensive, not limited.

The fifth verse: In that Vinaya Piṭaka, which stands complete in both text and meaning for those modest individuals in the sense of being put into practice, the entire threefold Dispensation is established among those very persons.

If one asks, "Whose Dispensation?"—it is the Dispensation of the Blessed One who is "unestablished" (aṭṭhita). For the Blessed One is "unestablished" by virtue of the absence of annihilationism (ucchedadiṭṭhi), which is a cause for establishment.
It is said: For one who holds the view of annihilationism remains indifferent to the next world, devoting himself solely to the pursuit of sensual pleasure;
he does not exert himself to perform meritorious deeds for the sake of the next world.
One who holds the view of eternalism, however, strives to perform them. But the Blessed One, neither standing in that way nor striving in that way, follows the Middle Way.
He himself crossed the flood and caused others to cross it as well. As it is said: "Friends, I have crossed the flood without a foothold and without an effort.
Or, in terms of its purpose: because he is well-established among beings by way of the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), he is "well-situated" (*susaṇṭhita*).
Indeed, because he is well-situated, he desires only to remove the suffering of beings and to provide them with their welfare.
Delighting in prosperity and remaining impartial, he teaches the Vinaya; therefore, in this section on the commentary on the Vinaya, praising him with appropriate verses, it says:
“Of one well-established. However, in the *Gaṇṭhipada*, [it refers] to the sutta:
“But when, monks, a desirable result of karma has appeared,” and to the sutta: “Well-proportionedness is beautiful form.”
The meaning stated as "by way of being well-established" is not in accordance with the intended subject matter.
[Regarding the word] *amissaṃ*: is it "unmixed with the Vinaya," or rather "the power of the ancient teachers"? It is neither of these two. For the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā* is indeed unmixed (*amissā*).
Therefore, the connection is: "they will explain that which is unmixed (*amissaṃ*) by means of the neuter gerundive. [As for] "the power of the ancient teachers":
Regarding the *aṭṭhakathā* (commentary): because of the statement, "Since they composed the *aṭṭhakathā* in the past," there is indeed what is called their "power" (*ānubhāva*).
For when people see something unprecedented, there are those in the world who ask, "Whose power is this?
Alternatively, having followed the Blessed One’s intention (*adhippāya*), one develops and clarifies the meaning in various passages; or rather, it is the development of that respective meaning.
"Vibhāvanā" refers to the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), which is called "the power.
Since the power of the former teachers already exists, why would they need to describe it again with this undertaking? Therefore, the sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth verses are stated.
Therein, [they are described] by those whose clear vision is purified because the stains have been washed away by the water of the knowledge of the Noble Path (*ariyamaggañāṇa*).
The construction should be understood as follows: "Because of having washed away the taints by that very [knowledge], they are purified in the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā);

and because of being purified in the analytical knowledges, they are skilled in describing the True Dhamma. Some say: "When 'former teachers' (pubbācariya) is mentioned, both the teachers of the world and those such as Rāhula within the Dispensation are included;
therefore, the words 'and wishing to exclude them,' etc., were spoken. This is because it was stated, "I shall describe that."
If it is argued that the deficiency of the ancient commentary (pubbaṭṭhakathā) has been shown [by this], we say no;

rather, the words beginning with "kāmañca" were spoken to show that it was "commented upon by means of various methods. [The term] "saddhammasaṃvaṇṇanakovidehi" refers to those who are skilled in commenting on the True Dhamma, or those who are skilled in that particular commentary.
"Sallekhiya" means that which scrapes away (sallikhati) or makes thin the multitude of defilements; thus it is "effacement" (sallekho).

The state of effacement is "effacement-ness" (sallekhiya); in that state of effacement. "Nosulabhūpamehi" means by those who are not easily comparable. "Of the Mahāvihāra" means of the lineage of the Mahāvihāra.
They are called "flag-comparable" (dhajūpamā) because they have the flag as their simile in the sense of being pre-eminent through wisdom.
"By those who follow the likeness of the banner. The intended meaning is "by those who have followed the lineage of the Supreme Buddha, having followed the intention of the Buddha.
Here, because of the statement, "He is a 'Sambuddha' because he has awakened to the truths by himself," the term *vara* (supreme) includes Pratyekabuddhas as well.
Therefore, it was stated [in the commentary] in order to exclude them.
Having shown that the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) was incomplete, he now says "The Exegesis" (*saṃvaṇṇanā*) and so forth, in order to show his own specific work and its purpose.
"It does not accomplish any purpose" means it does not achieve any purpose, fruit, or benefit;
this is like [the usage] in such passages as "that brings no purpose whatsoever to that bhikkhu. *Ajjhesanaṃ* (entreaty).

"Buddhasirivhayassa" means: since the Blessed One taught the Dhamma when requested by Sahampati Brahmā, and the Vinaya was established based on the request of Sāriputta, this teacher, honoring that duty toward his teachers, indicates that he composed this commentary based on the request of the elder Buddhasiri. "Samanussaranto" means...
This demonstrates the non-existence [of that] and shows due respect.

Following that, two verses are spoken for the purpose of showing the procedure to be performed. By means of this, one dispels doubts regarding the conditions and the explanations set forth in those commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*);
or, regarding what is wholesome in a single commentary, one avoids the rejection [of it] by saying, "This method does not exist in the commentary."
It prevents [wrong views]; by abandoning what is unreasonable, it causes those who are attached to it to relinquish that attachment;
by demonstrating the Theravāda, it shows the method of reasoning and deliberation (*ūhāpoha*) among the holders of the Vinaya regarding the adjudication of the Vinaya;
and by refuting an unreasonable Theravāda, it rejects the notion that the authority of a person is the measure [of truth]. These are the benefits.
They are shown by the demonstration of the procedures that ought to be performed.
And commencing this commentary, I shall undertake it making the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* its body;
likewise, whatever exposition is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*, as well as the exposition stated in the world-renowned commentaries such as the *Kuṇḍī* and others—I shall proceed from those as well.

I shall begin by grasping the most appropriate meaning—whether according to the method of the *Mahā-ṭīkā* (Great Commentary) through its analysis, or through the logic of the Vinaya—as if it were an ornament for that very body [of the text].
The inclusion of the word "commentary" (*saṃvaṇṇanā*) once again is for the purpose of showing that it is not merely a commentary, but something else as well.
Alternatively, it means: "Having composed a commentary that includes the Theravāda within itself, I shall begin."

The interpretation should be understood as follows. For the Theravādins wander outside of the *Aṭṭhakathā*. Here, by the word "etcetera," the *Cūḷapaccarī*, *Andhaka-ariya-aṭṭhakathā*, *Paṇṇavāra*, and others are also included.
In that context, it is said that *paccarī* is the name for a boat in the Sinhalese language; because [the work] was composed while sitting in one, it received that very name.
There is a monastery called Kurundīvallivihāra; because [the work] was composed there, it became known as the *Kurundī*.

"Having prepared the rites that ought to be performed, I stand ready; therefore, let them listen to me"—this is the commentary on the verse. "That [commentary] of mine" (*taṃ me*) means "by me" (*mayā*);
the words "being spoken by me" (*vuccamāna*) are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

"Let them listen" (*nisāmentu*) means let them see with the eye of wisdom (*paññācakkhu*), or let them hear by means of the mental formations of faith, energy, rapture, and gladness, while honoring [the teaching].
"Reverently [listen to] the Dhamma. Whose Dhamma? The Dhamma of the Tathāgata, the lamp of the Dhamma. What does this show?

It shows that the Dhamma stands in the place of a lamp because it reveals what is beneficial and what is harmful, while the Tathāgata, the bearer of the Dhamma, stands in the place of one who holds a lamp;
therefore, even though that Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna, he shows that they should listen with attention, honoring the Dhamma reverently without grieving over him there.
Alternatively, because of the statement, "The Tathāgatas are the Dhamma-body," he is the Lamp of Dhamma (Dhammapadīpa), that is, the Blessed One.

That which is the Dhamma and Vinaya exactly as spoken by the Buddha was likewise known and realized by the sons of the Buddha, the disciples—those who grasp it without remainder, not exceeding the intellect or intention of those sons of the Buddha. "In the past" (pure)—
"Of old" means the ancient elders (*porāṇattherā*). "Commentaries" (*aṭṭhakathā*) refers to the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathāyo*), using the plural form of the accusative case.
Whatever subject matter has been stated in the commentaries, all of that—excluding only those instances which are merely the errors of careless scribes—is [to be accepted].
Is this authoritative for everyone? No; rather, it is for those who possess reverence for the trainings (*sikkhā*) here in the Vinaya.
In the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is stated that for the wise, there is indeed an offense (*dukkaṭa*) whether in truth or in falsehood;
this should be understood as a scribal error (*pamādalekha*). The connection is: "Excluding the scribal error, it will be authoritative.

From that—that is, from the various meanings stated in the commentaries—the sequence of the system (*tantikkama*) is the sequence of the Canon (*pāḷikkama*). The *suttantas* are the constituent parts of the discourses.
*Anto* is seen here in the sense of the inclusion of internal components and so forth. *Suttantika* means "pertaining to the Suttantas";

the meaning is "of those pertaining to the Suttantas," that is, of the words contained within the Suttanta texts. Alternatively, it is called *anto* because it is measured (*amīyati*), which is to say, it is established (*sādhīyati*).
By what is it established? By the *sutta*. The end (*anto*) of the *sutta* is the *suttanta*. What is that? It is...
Thus there are eight alternatives. The words contained in that Sutta are "Suttantika" (pertaining to the Suttas).
It elucidates, in accordance with each respective Āgama-Sutta and Abhidhamma-Vinaya-Sutta, the meaning of those Suttantika words.
This, then, is the brief exposition of the meaning here regarding the Suttantika passages beginning with: “Itipi so Bhagavā.”

The meaning of the words is in accordance with the *āgama* suttas. [For example: "A legal issue arising from dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*) may be wholesome, may be unwholesome, or may be indeterminate"—the meaning of such words from the Abhidhamma and Suttanta is in accordance with the Abhidhamma and Suttanta, and so forth.
"Hessati" means "it will be"; the intention is that it will be performed. Regarding the phrase "vaṇṇanāpi," here the word "api" (also/even) [indicates inclusion].
The meaning is "collectively," and it should be connected with the word "therefore" (*tasmā*).

How? Because it is an authority for the wise, because it summarizes the detailed path, because it leaves no part of the analysis unexplained, because it does not deviate from the sequence of the treatise (*tantra*), and because it explains the words of the Suttas in accordance with the Sutta-commentaries—therefore, one should train diligently. Here, "the sequence of the treatise..."
Although this was already established by the statement "having descended," it is said that the phrase "of the Suttantikas" was included to show:

"The masters of the commentaries (Aṭṭhakathācariyas) have departed [on this task] under the heading 'the burden of the Suttantikas' in the Verañjakaṇḍa and other sections; however, we shall depart only after having spoken [our own views].
The commentary on the introductory discourse for the commencement of the book is finished.
Commentary on the Narrative of the External Introduction:
First, the Vinaya must be defined, as it is manifold through its divisions such as *tadaṅgavinaya* (restraint by means of that very factor). If it is argued:

"Since it was previously stated that 'the Dhamma and the Vinaya were spoken by the Buddha,' it should not now be asked 'by whom it was spoken,'" [we reply: that is not so. [The text continues: ...of that...
The connection is that [the statement] was spoken with reference to such words as these.
"By whom it was borne and brought" and "wherein this word is established"—this entire statement was spoken with reference to the entire Vinaya Piṭaka.

"It is not a statement of personal direct experience" means that it was not spoken as a direct assertion; for there is nothing whatsoever in the past and so forth that is not directly experienced by the Blessed One.
If it is argued that if a statement were not based on personal direct experience (*attapaccakkha*), it would not give rise to an offense of reciting the words (*padasodhammāpatti*), we say no;

for even what was spoken by a disciple gives rise to an offense of reciting the words. If it is argued that this leads to an over-extension (*atippasaṅga*) due to the absence of a restrictive rule, we say no;

because in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) on the training rule regarding the recitation of words, it is specifically qualified as "that which has been entered into the three councils" (*saṅgītittayaṃ āruḷho*). Likewise, in the commentary, because it has been entered into the council, [the phrase] "of the aggregates" (*khandhānañca*)...

"Succession... [and so on] ...is called saṃsāra"—such statements, as well as those that follow the sequence established in the formal recitation (saṅgīti), produce the offense of violating the textual integrity (padaso dhammaṃ).
Thus says the Venerable Upatissa. Commentary on the First Great Council (Paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā)
Regarding the phrase "and what is called the First Great Council," the word *ca* (and) here has the sense of "moreover"; by it, he indicates that there are others as well.
It is said that because [the monks] went to that Sālavana grove, took leave of their friends and kinsmen, and then returned, it became known as "Upavattana" (the Place of Return).
As for "of the twin Sāla trees," it is said that one row of Sāla trees was at the head [of the bed] and one at the foot; therein also—

One young *sāla* tree was near the upper part [of the mountain], and one was near the lower part; it is also said that they stood with their roots, trunks, branches, and leaves interwoven with one another.

In the phrase "in the element of Nibbāna without residue" (*anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā*), the instrumental case is used in the sense of a characteristic of a state (*itthambhūtalakkhaṇe*), as in such examples as "one who has performed his duty, having brought a bowl filled with food by way of a face free from hatred, joy, laughter, and mental distress."
At his final Nibbāna, for the sake of his final Nibbāna, do not grieve there with your mind, nor lament with your speech, because of the statement: "Lamentation is wailing.
In the phrase "by the Great Samana," the instrumental case is used in the sense of the ablative (nissakka), as in the example:
"The rays of the sun are the refuge for one whose light has become feeble. And as for that favor of the Blessed One—its...
"Anuggahassa" means "of one who has been assisted," according to the teachers. However, some say it means "since I have been assisted.
"Nibbasanāni" means those whose function as clothing is finished; they were removed after being used by me. He asks, "If you will wear them well-fitted":
these are hemp garments resembling armor. The nine successive dwellings and so forth are like sovereignty. The eight attainments [are like the royal insignia].
And the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is called an "attainment of successive dwelling" (*anupubbavihāra*) by way of the order of its acquisition.
The word *purā* is employed by poets in two times: when the future is near and when the past is long ago.

The Teacher’s dispensation itself is the *pariyatti* (the doctrine); thus it is the "Teacher’s dispensation as *pariyatti*. This consists of nine divisions by way of the discourses (*sutta*), verses (*geyya*), and so forth.

Because they uphold the entire classification of the *pariyatti* contained within the Three Pitakas, they are called "those who uphold the entire classification of the *pariyatti* of the Three Pitakas.
It should not be said that [the dispensation] cannot exist without them, because of the statement: "those who uphold the entire classification of the *pariyatti* of the Three Pitakas."

Even though this is so, there is a distinction: they heard [the teachings] both in the presence of [the Buddha] and in his absence, whereas for the Elder, there is nothing that was not received in his presence.
*Na vāyanti* means "they do not blow" (*vāti*); thus, according to the analysis (*vibhāsā*), the meaning is "he knew" or "he did not know.

In that context, it refers to selecting. The word *bahu* has the sense of abundance, just as in the passage: "The boundless, shoreless, and vast should be understood. Previously, [it was said]: "He who holds the entire three-piṭaka, with its various divisions..."
If it is argued that because this has been stated, the phrase "much learning... [and] mastery" is not appropriate, we say no. This is because the Tipiṭaka is infinite;
therefore, the intended meaning is that, relative to us, he possessed much learning. Otherwise, it would follow that the Elder Ānanda was of little learning, which would contradict the statement:
"There is nothing that was not received in his presence. Furthermore, [the phrase] "half a month had passed" [is explained as follows]:
Here, one day was lost; that was the first-day-of-the-month (pāṭipada), known as the day of tumultuous noise, and therefore it was not included here.
Having proclaimed the grounds for spiritual urgency, "playing well" refers to playing from a state of agitation. In the phrase "on the following day," the word *api* implies a concessive permission.
Because the Subha Sutta states, "not long after the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna," [this refers to] among the eighty-four thousand aggregates of the Dhamma.
If it is asked, "Is it not included?"—no, because it was obtained during the time of the Blessed One, like the *Kathāvatthu*.
"Discarded, fallen, and filthy" means discarded, fallen, and filthy. "The wheel of command" (*āṇācakkam*) means that the command itself is the wheel in the sense of being unimpeded.
"Falling together here" means falling together in one place. "Having come through the air, he sat down"—this refers to the second occasion.

The Venerable Upatissa said this with reference to his mode of arrival. Either he first traveled through the air and, upon reaching the assembly, showed himself at his seat by sinking into the earth without displacing the row of monks;
or else, having arrived at the sight of the assembly in both ways, both [explanations] are appropriate, for otherwise one of the two would become false.
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa questioned the Venerable Upāli... [as before] ...the Elder Venerable Upāli answered.
This passage, which summarizes the questions and answers previously stated in the words "First, friend Upāli," etc., was recorded by the compilers of the Council and written in the *Gaṇṭhipada*.
Let it be so; but for what purpose was the "Introduction" (*nidāna*) also questioned here?

Why was the sequence not stated as previously shown—namely, “he asked about the person, he asked about the matter”—but instead the sequence made as “he asked about the matter, he asked about the source, he asked about the person”? Some say:
“It was stated out of order because the formulation of the training rule (sikkhāpada) is rooted in the matter. However, the investigation on this point is found in the Verañjakaṇḍa.
It is performed when [the assembly] has arrived. "In Rājagāraka" means in the park named after that. Indeed, even the royal residence (rājagāra) is worthy of being enjoyed.

Therein, [the Sangītikāras] show, by way of abbreviation, what was previously stated in detail beginning with "the Venerable Mahākassapa," etc., by means of the group of masters (vasīs). If this is so, then as for the Nidāna as well...

If it is asked: "In the passage 'he questioned [the Buddha] and he questioned the person,' the sequence of the questions is shown; why then is the sequence of the Venerable Ānanda’s answers not also shown?
It is for the purpose of showing that, according to this sequence, the compilation of all five Nikāyas has not been recorded. But how have they been recorded?
The Venerable Mahākassapa questioned [the Buddha] on all five Nikāyas in their proper sequence, and the Venerable Ānanda [replied].

However, whether questioned or unasked, he answered by inserting appropriate statements—such as the intrinsic nature of each respective sutta, the background story that arose in the interim, the sequence of the summary and the exposition, and the sequence of the matrix and the commentary—and thus it was said:
"By this very method, he questioned [the Buddha] regarding all five Nikāyas. Alternatively: "At Ambalaṭṭhikā..."
Although one should say "at the royal palace" (*rājāgārake*), he illustrates this meaning even with the inverted expression "at Ambalaṭṭhikā at the royal palace.
For it is said: "He dwelt at Ambalaṭṭhikā at the royal palace.
Seeking the builder of this house of the self-existence—the mason of craving—he, by means of which knowledge...

It is possible to see him; the meaning is that for his sake, having made the resolution at the feet of Dīpaṅkara, one wanders through many births in the cycle of existence for such a long time without finding that knowledge.
"Birth is suffering again and again" is the statement of the reason for seeking the builder of the house.
"All your rafters have been broken"—all your rafters of the defilements without exception have been shattered by me.
The "house-top" (gahakūṭa) is ignorance. Knowledge accompanied by joy is "consisting of joy.
For knowledge consisting of joy does not [perceive] the distinct nature of the aggregates. The statement that its purpose is "to loosen what has been made firm" is said by way of general tendency;
however, we shall clarify that point in various places. [This applies to] the Dhamma and the Vinaya, which are free from mutual confusion.

In this context, regarding such statements as "the taking of life is unwholesome" (*akusala*), it is the volition (*cetanā*) that originates the application which cuts off the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) in one who intends death that is unwholesome; it is not the act of taking away (*atipāta*), defined as the cutting off of the life-faculty known as a living being.

Likewise, the intimation (*viññatti*) consisting of the seizing of what is not given—the property of another—is an indeterminate (*abyākata*) phenomenon; [it is] the volition that originates that intimation...
He is capable of instructing on phenomena that are free from mutual confusion, such as by saying, "The volition of theft is an unwholesome phenomenon.
For one who takes another's property belonging to others with a thieving mind, there is one of the following—*pārājika*, *thullaccaya*, or *dukkaṭa*—according to the specific case;
for one who takes what is being given under the pretext of being the storekeeper’s portion, there is a *pācittiya*; and for one who takes it for his own benefit...
[In the case of] an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya), there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who takes [it] out of mere greed;
there is no offense for one appointed as a money-disposer (rūpiya-chaḍḍaka). Thus, the meaning is that he is capable of training even in the Vinaya which is free from such mutual confusion.
"He develops" means he increases; by this, he shows the growth of the mind by way of its fruit and its impulsion (javana). "Undistinguished" (avisittaṃ).
The meaning is that it is common to both the recitation and the teaching.
Here, by way of the one who teaches, the "teaching" refers to the Three Piṭakas;
by way of those to be trained, this is also called the "dispensation."
“By way of the meaning to be told, and also by way of the telling”;
thus, *desanā*, *sāsanā*, and *kathā* should be understood as synonyms.
Because the word *sāsana* is neuter, it is stated: “…pe… dhammasāsanāni. [The term] *duccarita-saṃkileso* means...
In terms of its meaning, it is volition, or else a mental state that proceeds in such a manner.

Because they proceed after having penetrated the characteristics of impermanence and so forth, the insight-minds are mundane in terms of their object; however, in terms of non-delusion, they are supramundane.

Or rather, the supramundane itself is the "clear realization" (*abhisamaya*) in terms of its object—the reality known as Nibbāna—and also in terms of non-delusion regarding the other [realities] such as the Path.

Some [say this]. Here, what is called "penetration" (paṭivedha) is knowledge; if it is asked how that is profound, some say: "At the time of measuring deep water, there must be a long measure; 'now' is said for the purpose of showing that such a state is unobtainable.
For the sake of which: for the sake of the path and the fruit. And they do not experience, they do not attain, that goal.
Something intended by himself, as well as the "Exposition of Itivuttaka. Why? Because [the meaning] was grasped without having been thoroughly investigated.

Because he has attained the fruit, he is one who has penetrated the unshakable. Again, by the mention of "one whose taints are destroyed" (khīṇāsava), he shows specifically the Arahant, not the trainee (sekha).
For just as a treasurer, having guarded the king’s bracelets, crowns, and so forth, [provides them] at whatever moment is desired—
He brings [them] near; thus he taught the Dhamma for the sake of the path and fruit to beings who possess causes.

Because those very [three knowledges] are explained there in detail within the Vinaya Piṭaka, the teachers say that by striving, one attains those very ones. For what purpose are only three knowledges analyzed there?
Because they constitute the ultimate proximate support (*upanissaya*) for the perfection of virtue (*sīla*). "By means of seven other factors..."
“Endowed with this, a bhikkhu is an expert in the Vinaya. He knows what is an offense and what is not an offense; he knows what is a light offense and what is a heavy offense.
He recollects his manifold past lives... with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, he sees beings...
through the destruction of the taints... he enters and dwells in [the state of liberation].”

The Sutta is the proof for this. Having mastered the Vinaya, by relying on the perfection of virtue, one acquires the knowledge of the divine eye and the knowledge of recollecting past lives simultaneously with the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhayañāṇa).

Some say that the phrase "of those very [knowledges]" was stated in order to show that there is no separate preparatory work required for these two. However, in the Abhidhamma, there are three types of clear-knowledge (tevijjā).
The six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), the four analytical insights (*paṭisambhidā*), and other specific qualities such as the right efforts (*sammappadhāna*) have been analyzed.
Although they have been analyzed, nevertheless, because they are of the nature of wisdom (*paññājātika*), the four analytical insights are specifically attained;

it is for the purpose of showing this that the reversal of the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa-vipallāsa*) was made by stating "right there" (*tattheva*). [The phrase] "by means of a Dhamma wrongly grasped by oneself" refers to...
This is a remainder of the recitation. Here, the instrumental case is used in the sense of the agent and in the sense of the cause; the intended meaning is "by one who has wrongly grasped the causes.
But why [is it called so]? This explains the meaning stated as "conformable" (*anulomika*).
This is the method of the commentary on the account of the First Great Council (*Paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanānaya*).
Commentary on the Second Council Discussion:

*Pannabhārā* means those who have laid down the burden of the aggregates (*khandha*). For it is said: "The five aggregates are indeed burdens. They are those who say, "We shall be present" or "We shall not be present. Among them, it is said, the younger ones were indeed [so]. *Jammaṃ* means base or wretched.
This is the method for the commentary on the discussion of the Second Council.

In the commentary on the Third Council, regarding the phrase "having passed away from the Brahma-world," it is stated that only these are fixed: the four paths, the five deeds of immediate retribution, and fixed wrong view;
the sublime states (mahaggata) are not fixed. Therefore, by way of aspiration, there can also be rebirth in a lower plane. *Aticchatha* means having passed beyond.
The intention is: "Do you wish [to go]? Go and seek alms. *Keṭubha* is a treatise connected with the rules for composing poetry (*kāvya*).
