Some say it refers to *kiriyākappa*; others say it is a treatise characterized by the analysis of verbal roots, agents, and so forth.
*Asandhimittā* is her name; it is said that no joints (*sandhi*) were discernible in her body, as her body was as if made of honey-cakes.
Therefore, they also say, "A daughter named so-and-so was born. Four *pattha* by the Magadhan measure make one *āḷhaka*;
four *āḷhakas* make one *doṇa*; four *doṇas* make one *mānikā*; four *mānikās* make one *khārikā*; and twenty *khārikās* make one *vāha*.
Regarding the "garland of ketaka flowers," they say it is "a mass of radiance arising from the head. This [was mentioned] in connection with the power of the king's majesty.

The subject matter has been stated, but not in its proper sequence. Now, illustrating the subject matter that carries the burden of the Buddha’s dispensation in its correct sequence, he said, “It is said that the king,” and so forth.
“Tamed” means tamed by the subduing of the defilements (*kilesa*). “Guarded” means guarded by body and speech. There is also a reading, “facing the east.
Because he was the eldest brother previously, he displays the gesture of taking the alms-bowl out of that very habituation.
"Abhāsī" means he thought, "I shall speak. Others say that even though it was said "having understood," he spoke everything [therein].
"Amata" (the Deathless) is a designation for the virtues of cessation, which is synonymous with Nibbāna; heedfulness is its footing and its path.
"Maccu" (Death) is a designation for the faults of the process of existence (pavatti); heedlessness is its footing and its path. Thus, the four Truths [are explained].
They have been demonstrated. Because it has gone for refuge to the Saṅgha, the going forth is dependent upon the Saṅgha; or rather, because the shaving of the head is dependent upon that [Saṅgha].
Since this is an occasion for praising the power of the Elder Nigrodha, he spoke by combining what was said previously with what is to be said later:
"Again, King [Asoka], having caused the great monastery named Asokārāma to be built, [provided] sixty thousand... and so on.

“He had eighty-four thousand monasteries built. Because of the statement, “Even for an ordinary person (puthujjana) who is virtuous, there is enjoyment [of merit] through reflection,” it is only those in training (sekkhā) who are heirs in the ultimate sense;

nevertheless, for the sake of Prince Mahinda’s ordination, the Elder spoke thus by way of a conventional expression established according to worldly usage: “Whoever, O Great King... [is] a legitimate son. For it is said in the Vedas:
“From limb by limb you are produced, from the heart you are born;
you are indeed one’s own self, O son, live for a hundred autumns.
Therefore, in this manner, if a biological son (orasa-putta) has gone forth under his parents, in substance he himself has gone forth.

They appear as such. Why do the preachers of the Dhamma not announce it? The king dispatched his ministers, saying, "Go and bring the Elder," and the preachers were sent for the purpose of forming an escort when the Elder arrived; that is why they did not speak.

Furthermore, they speak according to the very method stated by him because of his ferocity, and his ferocious nature was [evident] from [his command]: "Cut down the mango tree and make a fence of bamboo!"
It should be explained by means of the account of Vutta-āmacca. But why do the preachers of the Dhamma issue a royal command?
Because it has been stated: "One who is capable of upholding the Dispensation. The "island partridge" is a decoy partridge.
Although this man was appointed to the task of using a decoy partridge, he was pure in heart; therefore, he questioned the ascetic. "Sāṇipākāraṃ" means with a fence of hemp-cloth.
One who speaks by analyzing is a *vibhajjavādī*, as in the passage beginning, "There is, O Brahmin, this method.
Furthermore, the Blessed One is an eternalist (*sassatavādī*) because of such statements as, "Monks, there is that which is unborn, unbecome, and unconditioned.

He is also a partial-eternalist (*ekaccasassatiko*) because of the statement, "Phenomena with conditions; phenomena without conditions. And he is a proponent of the finite and infinite (*antānantiko*).
“The end of the world can never be reached by traveling;
yet without reaching the end of the world, there is no release from suffering.
This is because of the statement: “Monks, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning; its prior limit is not known. Furthermore, regarding the position of the Eel-Wrigglers (*amarāvikkhepika*):

The Blessed One partially adopts [the position] by way of illustrating the undeclared points (avyākata-vatthu), such as: "Whether the world is eternal—this is undeclared; whether the world is non-eternal—this is undeclared," and so forth, and by way of illustrating conventional truth (sammuti-sacca).
For that [state] cannot be described in terms of internal or external, etc., as it is said: "The base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana) is not to be described as having an internal object," and so on.
Likewise, he also partially adopts the side of those who maintain the doctrine of fortuitous origination (adhiccasamuppattika-pakka).
This is because of the statement: “Enjoying extinction (nibbāna) obtained for nothing. For in that context, “for nothing” (mudhā) is a synonym for arising by chance (adhiccasamuppanna).

Furthermore, the Blessed One [refuted] the proponent of consciousness (saññīvāda) and others by way of existence with perception, existence without perception, and existence with neither-perception-nor-non-perception. And he refuted the annihilationist (ucchedavāda), as seen in the statement:
“For I, brahmin, preach the annihilation of lust. He also refuted the proponent of Nibbāna in this very life (diṭṭhadhammanibbānavāda).

And because of the statement, “Birth is exhausted; the holy life has been lived,” because of the statement, “There is now no further becoming,” and because of the illumination of the attainment of cessation in this very life,
the Blessed One is called a Vibhajjavādī— one who speaks by way of analysis— since he explains in such various ways according to the dispositions of those to be trained.
The method of explaining the narrative of the Third Council.
The elder named Sumana was called Puppha; some say he was Mahāpaduma. They say the province of Mahiṃsa was the Andhra kingdom.
The "Dhammacakkhu" refers to the three paths; some say it refers to the path of stream-entry. There were also five kingdoms.
There are five regions called Cīna. "In Rājagaha" refers to the monastery built for the Queen. "On Silakūṭa" means on a mountain peak. "Vaḍḍhamāna" is a cosmetic powder;
it is said to be highly esteemed in the Noble Land (Ariyadesa). "Those who make [others] their masters with a single flavor" refers to the Damilas.

"Sārapāmaṅga" means an excellent waist-belt. Having inspired a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) by means of the *Petavatthu* and other texts, [he spoke] for the sake of realization (*abhisamaya*).
And the *Saccasaṃyutta*. The great monastery site named Meghavana Uyyāna. The reading is “in sixty-two caves.
“The ten brothers” refers to the ten beginning with Prince Abhaya; they are not mentioned here.

“Having completed the rains retreat and performed the *pavāraṇā*” means by way of the four-month *pavāraṇā*. Or, having performed the *pavāraṇā* on the first occasion, [he stayed] there for one month.
Having stayed [there], he spoke on the full-moon day of Kattika; otherwise, it could not be understood because it is stated [elsewhere] that "on the full-moon day, the Great Hero [spoke].
By the term "Great Hero," he refers to the relics by way of metaphorical designation for the Buddha. "The height of the leg" (jaṅghappamāṇa) is what they call "the height of the base of the stupa.
Cūḷodara and Mahodara were the nephew and maternal uncle. The radiance while the Buddha was still living is the "fresh radiance" (sarasarasmi).
He sent a written message to the king and spoke these words as a verbal message: "It is said to be a measure of a *doṇa* according to the Magadhan *nāḷī*, or twelve *nāḷīs*.

‘Having been cut at a restricted place’ is the reading. Having caused five rays to revolve from all directions means that there are five because they emerge from the five fruits, and those are indeed six-colored. On the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kattika..."
The meaning is: on the first day of the bright fortnight. The families of *nāgas*, *yakṣas*, and other deities who stood surrounding the site of the Great Bodhi tree.
Some say that "Gopaka" refers to royal attendants whose duty was to perform such tasks; others say it is the name of those families themselves.
The *Kāliṅgas* are those who carry water and so forth. Some say that a family born in the *Kāliṅga* country and endowed with noble birth is called a *Kāliṅga* family.
"On the first day of the month" means on the first day of the second *uposatha* period.
Because the ocean was seen by those staying there, that place is called "the site of the Ocean Sal-tree. There were sixteen clans of noble birth and eight clans of brahmin ministers.
The Elder Mahā-Ariṭṭha went forth at Cetiya-giri. "In the vicinity of the minister's residence."
He spoke by way of the appropriate time. The Elder Mahinda arrived at the island of Tambapaṇṇi when he was twelve years old;
having resided there for two years, he established the Vinaya. He passed away (parinibbuto) when he was sixty-two years old.
"The Vinaya is for the purpose of restraint" refers to the Vinaya Piṭaka or its mastery. It is the knowledge and vision according to reality.

It is the discernment of name-and-form together with its conditions. In the absence of reviewing the path and so forth, there is no such thing as "attaining final nibbāna in the interval" for a trainee;
rather, there is only death. Therefore, it says "knowledge and vision of liberation.
"For the sake of final nibbāna through non-clinging" means for the sake of final nibbāna by not clinging to, not grasping at, or not retaining even the slightest trace of any phenomenon whatsoever.
In the *Upanisads*, the sequence of reasons begins with: “The Vinaya is for the sake of restraint,” and so forth.

Having thus far demonstrated the accomplishment of one’s own welfare, he now says, “For this purpose, lend an ear,” in order to demonstrate the accomplishment of the welfare of others. Its meaning is as follows:
“Lending an ear” (*sotāvadhāna*) refers to the act of lending one’s ear to others in order to learn the teaching of the Vinaya and the deliberations on the Vinaya for oneself.

Therefore, it should be understood that for those who have mastered the discourse on the Vinaya, the sequence of causes as previously stated is already established as its proximate cause (*upanisā*), and thus it need not be shown again.

Otherwise, since the phrase "its proximate cause" would already include *parinibbāna* without clinging by that very statement, there would be no possibility of applying the ear beyond *parinibbāna* without clinging; hence, the phrase "applying the ear for this purpose" [would be redundant].

It would be purposeless if it were not possible [to apply] here; yet it should be understood that it is not purposeless, because its aim is to show the fundamental cause for the accomplishment of the welfare of others.
Thus, in whatever way and whatever term may be applicable here;
"The wise one should employ all things in such and such a manner.
The commentary on the introductory narrative (Bāhiranidānakathā) is finished.
The commentary on the Pārājika section begins.
The Verañjā Chapter:
Commentary on the Verañjā Chapter.
“At that time the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall. At that time...”
"But at that time, not far from Vesālī, there was a village named Kalandagāma. If it is asked:
"What is the purpose of beginning the Verañjakaṇḍa when the Vinayanidāna ought to have been begun [first]? It is said: It is in order to show the source of the Vinayanidāna from its very beginning.
If this is so, then by the statement: "Friend Upāli, where was the first Pārājika rule laid down? In Vesālī," [the source is shown].
If it is asked, "Is there a contradiction?"—there is no contradiction. Why? Because the question regarding the source (*nidāna*) is: "Wherein is it prescribed?
Even so, when it is asked, "What is the source of the first *pārājika*?", is not the reply with the common Great Source (*mahānidāna*) inappropriate? It is not inappropriate;
for since the sources of all the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) were asked about individually, each of them must be answered accordingly.
And first, he stated the Great Introduction (Mahānidāna), which is common to all. The offenses such as the Pārājikas were compiled entirely according to the sequence of questions and answers.

If one asks how they were compiled: the Venerable Mahākassapa questioned the entire Vinaya in successive order, and the Elder Upāli, being questioned, answered continuously and appropriately as each point arose.

It should be understood that even those cases such as the Vinītavatthu, when they are appropriate, were included and recited by way of the sequence of the responses; otherwise, the Verañjakaṇḍa would either be the introduction to the first Pārājika itself, or it would be irrelevant, or purposeless,
or it would have to be recited separately immediately after the inquiry into the introduction to each training rule.

Or rather, [the offense] is incurred by one who abandons [the training]; therefore, beginning from the outset, the section "At that time" and so forth was commenced in order to show the source of the discipline (*vinaya-nidāna*).
Now we shall explain the purpose of stating this source: first, it demonstrates that the Blessed One is worthy of being obeyed, since the discipline is taught as his command;

second, it demonstrates that the discipline, being of the nature of a command, has no other scope [than his authority]; and third, it demonstrates the great power of those disciples who abide by the command.

His purpose is threefold. How so? For the Blessed One is worthy of commands and instructions because he has abandoned the defilements, because he has attained distinguished qualities, because he is the eldest and most excellent in the world, and because he has reached the state of equanimity (*tādibhāva*).

The Blessed One’s attainment of the state of equanimity should be understood by his being unshakable even by the eight grounds of abuse, such as being "lacking in flavor" and so forth; for even regarding those eight grounds of abuse...
The abandonment of defilements is to be understood from the canonical text that explains the manner of their arising within oneself.
The excellence of the qualities attained is to be understood through the demonstration of the realization of the four jhānas and the three true knowledges (vijjās). This is shown by such passages as:
"O Brahmin, I do not see anyone in the world with its devas... [who could reproach me]—his head would surely split apart," and "He is the eldest and the best in the world."
The status of being the eldest and most excellent is to be understood from his speech; this has the purpose of illustrating the Blessed One’s fitness to issue commands.
The words, “Wait, Sāriputta, wait, Sāriputta; the Tathāgata himself will know the time for that,” illustrate that this matter is not within the domain of others.
And [the statement], “Very well, Bhante, I could even turn the earth upside down.”
By these three lion-roars of the Elder— “Venerable sir, I shall manifest a hand for one day,” and “Venerable sir, it would be well if the entire Saṅgha of bhikkhus were to go to Uttarakuru for alms”—
one should understand that this demonstrates the great power of the disciples who stand under his command. Why did the Blessed One not dwell in places such as Sāvatthī, but instead [go elsewhere]?

If you ask why he was dwelling right there in Verañjā at that time: it was for the purpose of generating joy in Naḷeruyakka; for the purpose of ensuring the Saṅgha of bhikkhus did not suffer from lack of alms;
for the purpose of generating faith in the brahmin of Verañjā; because it was a place that manifested the majesty of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna;
and because it was a place where the Elder Sāriputta engaged in reflection that served as the cause for requesting the formal establishment of the Vinaya rules.
Among these, the last is the powerful cause; therefore it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “At that time means at whatever time [the Venerable...

was present... at that time. Among the first four causes for non-inclusion, by the first, the Blessed One inspires respect in the monks through his protection of their minds from non-human beings by means of the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettā*) and so forth. By the second...
This shows that a monk who frequents assemblies should gather a following in this way, and should likewise be one of few desires and contented.
By the third [instruction], it is shown that he should benefit families while remaining indifferent to material requisites.
By the fourth, it is shown that even though he possesses such great power, he should not be greedy for the sake of requisites, but should live solely dependent on what is given by others.
It shows that [the word] "it must be" (bhavitabbaṃ) is required. Because of the statement, “...of the passage beginning with ‘Therefore’...

the commentary on the meaning of the Vinaya,” it follows that the passage beginning with “Therefore” is one thing, and the Vinaya is another. “From the passage beginning with ‘Therefore,’ what other Vinaya is there here?”
"Showing its meaning, I shall compose a commentary on the Vinaya. One might ask:
"Was it not already stated previously that 'this is not a word from the direct personal experience of the Buddha, the Blessed One,' and so forth?
Therefore, while demonstrating in various ways the meaning of the reading beginning with 'by him' (tena) as spoken by the Elder Upāli, I shall proceed..."

The meaning here should be understood as follows: it is a commentary on the meaning of the Vinaya, which consists of the words of the Blessed One that are based on his own direct personal realization.

If this is so, does it not contradict such statements as, "By whom was the Vinaya Piṭaka, adorned with introductory narratives (nidāna) such as 'At that time the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Verañjā,' preserved? regarding the phrase "At that time," and so forth?

If it is argued that this is because it demonstrates its inclusion within the Vinaya Piṭaka, we say no; for that designation is established even in other contexts, as in the expression, "a man whose clothing was adorned with various kinds of wall-paintings," and so forth.
Furthermore, its inclusion in the Vinaya is also logical, since the compilers of the Council authorized it as being of primary importance to the Vinaya.
Here it is asked: just as in the Sutta Piṭaka there is the phrase "at one time," and in the Abhidhamma...
And why, instead of stating it indefinitely as "at whatever time," is the specific designation "at that time" stated here first?

It is said: because the Blessed One dwelt in various places for the sake of the occasion of the proclamation of each respective training rule, or for the sake of the occasion that served as the cause for the proclamation of that training rule.
And because those compilers of the Council were masters who had thoroughly understood the time that had passed.

How so? From such statements as, "Those monks who were of few desires complained," and "Then those monks reported this matter to the Blessed One," and "Then the Blessed One, having caused them to assemble on account of this cause," and "Of the monks..."

Because of the statements in the Khandhakas: "It is suitable for that, it conforms to that... [omission] ...for ten reasons, for the welfare of the Saṅgha," and "And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule (sikkhāpada)," and because of the sequence of the Vinaya beginning with:
"I allow, monks, the going forth by means of the threefold taking of refuge"—this refers to the time when that training rule was laid down.
That specific occasion for the establishment of each respective rule of discipline was well known to those five hundred bhikkhus who were upholders of the Dhamma;

however, this method does not occur in the Suttantas or the Abhidhamma. Therefore, because it is well known, and because of its connection with the word "dwells" (*viharati*)—on account of that time serving as the cause—the [explanation] begins with the first person singular (*yam-niddesa*), and so forth.
And because [the former] is impossible, in the Vinaya Piṭaka, the description by means of *taṃ* (that) is stated first. How so?
Because here, due to the impossibility of saying either "At one time, not far from Vesālī, there was a village named Kalandagāma" or "At one time, [going] to Vesālī...
[there was]," and because it is possible to use the description by means of *taṃ*, it is not expressed by the description by means of *yaṃ* (which).

Regarding the statement, “At that time... there was a village named Kalandagāma,” it is said either because [the location] was well known, or because it is a description given without specific limitation.

Although this is indeed a description with specific limitation according to the method already stated, since it refers specifically to that [village], nevertheless, it is called a “description without specific limitation” because at that particular time, it was unknown to other monks.
It has been said. As for what was stated, "For this is the principle (yutti) throughout the entire Vinaya," that should be understood as having been said by way of its predominance.

If the word *tena* were an indefinite demonstrative expression, then in the passage, "Therefore, monks, [this is] the training rule (sikkhāpada) for the bhikkhus," this word *tena*—which already has its meaning established by the preceding context—would likewise have to be an indefinite demonstrative expression.

In such passages as, “At that time the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Uruvelā,” the word *tena* (by that) would be a term expressing an indefinite indication (*aniyamaniddesa*), yet it is not so;
therefore, with reference to those for whom the meaning indicated by that [word] is unknown, he says:
“This is a term expressing an indefinite indication. Alternatively, because its meaning was not shown prior to that, even later...
Because it shows a designation [of time] through that connection, it is said: "This is a statement of an indefinite designation.
Alternatively, since the word *samaya* (time) indicates time without specifying "this is the name for the morning and so forth," it is likewise appropriate to say:
"That is to say, this is a statement of an indefinite designation. Or else, when it is said "by that" (*tenā*), by that...
With the words "by a pot" and "by a cloth," he establishes a restriction with the phrase "by occasion" (*samayena*) in order to exclude all such unwanted applications.
But by what occasion? By the occasion of Sāriputta’s reflection, which is established in its meaning as occurring at a later time. Here it may be asked:
if the occasion of reflection is intended here, [then how is this so]? For in the subsequent passage, both the sense of cause and the sense of instrument are possible.

"Does this not contradict such statements as: 'For that time when the training rules were laid down was difficult to understand even for Sāriputta and others; by reason of that time, and by way of that cause'?

No, because it is stated in a general sense. For why is there a description here in the Vinaya Piṭaka using the instrumental case (*karaṇavacana*), instead of stating it as in the Suttantas and Abhidhamma? To this, [the answer is: therefore, of that...

Desiring to state the purpose of the instrumental case (*karaṇavacana*) in the context of this exposition by way of its general application, the Teacher said: "The time when that formulation of the training rule [occurred]," and so forth.
He did not intend to state the purpose of the instrumental case being used here and now; rather, for this [term], only the sense of cause (*hetu*) is possible, not the sense of instrument (*karaṇa*).
Therefore, he said: "By means of that which is established in meaning at a later time," and so forth. And "the occasion" (*samayañca*).

The meaning is: "having taken into account the convergence of the conditions for arrival and the time appropriate thereto. The intention is: "Having obtained both the completeness of the conditions and the time of arrival, we shall know [the answer].
Here it is asked: Just as in the passage, "Monks, there is indeed one moment and one occasion," where the moment (*khaṇa*) and the occasion (*samaya*) are one—
"Meaning" (*attha*) and likewise "time" (*kāla*) and "occasion" (*samaya*): thus, "time" and "occasion" might have the same meaning.
Furthermore, here "occasion" (*samaya*) refers to the concurrence of conditions for arrival; since time itself is also a condition for arrival, it is included by the very mention of "occasion.
Why, then, is "time" mentioned separately? It is said: because time was first delimited [by the phrase] "perhaps even tomorrow" (*appeva nāma svepi*).

"Samaya" does not mean time. In the phrase "at that [time]," it indicates that one should approach depending on the convergence of the other conditions for arrival during the specifically determined time;
and even within that determined time, it refers to the specific occasion such as morning and so forth, according to the aforementioned convergence.
Thus, by the word "sva" (one's own), it shows the state of being fixed to a specific time, such as morning, within the delimited day. Therefore...
It should be understood that because "time" (*kāla*) and "occasion" (*samaya*) do not have the same meaning, the separate mention of "time" is purposeful.
Since the word "moment" (*khaṇa*) has multiple meanings— as in "O Bhikkhu, moment by moment you are born, you live,
and you die," "he goes frequently to the presence of the Bhikkhunī," and "moment by moment he speaks the Teacher’s instruction"— so it is likewise here.
And as for the word *samaya*, in order to specify it individually [from *khaṇa*], he said: "Bhikkhus, there is indeed only one moment (*khaṇa*) and one occasion (*samaya*).
The meaning of *khaṇa* and *samaya* is identical; *khaṇa* means the obtaining of an opportunity, the sense being the ninth moment, excluding the eight inopportune moments.
They propound their respective views—such as annihilationism and so forth—within this occasion (*samaya*), which is reckoned as a position of speculative view (*diṭṭhigata*).
A proponent of the doctrine. It is called *Tindukācīra* because it was surrounded by a row of *timbaru* trees known as *tindukācīra*.
*Ekasālaka* means a single *sāla* tree; some also call it a *kuṭikā*. *Atthābhisamaya* means the attainment of one’s own welfare.
*Dhīra* refers to a wise person, and no other. *Sammā mānābhisamaya* means [the realization] thoroughly...
"By the abandoning of conceit" means by the thorough abandoning of conceit through its total eradication.

In such passages as "the meaning of suffering is oppression," and in such passages as "the penetration of the four truths by way of four aspects," the meaning is the state of being the aspect of suffering belonging to suffering, which is comprised of the five aggregates.
The meaning of "conditioned" is the sense of arising from causes; the meaning of "suffering" is the sense of torment, referring to painful feeling.
The meaning of "the state of change" regarding pleasant feeling should be understood as the meaning of "clear realization" (abhisamaya), beginning with the sense of oppression.
The time of the descent into the womb and so forth was manifest among gods and humans through such events as the shaking of the earth and the appearance of light.
The time of his performing difficult austerities was also manifest by such reports as, "The ascetic Gotama is dark, not fair. And for seven weeks...
And there are other occasions for dwelling in happiness in this very life.
He dwells "at all times" in that occasion, from the beginning of the undertaking until the attainment of its final conclusion;
thus, by way of constant association, he dwells at that time through the dwelling in compassion—that is, through the dwelling in the function of compassion.
The meaning [is as follows]. For that occasion is an occasion for the function of compassion (*karuṇākicca*). There are two functions of the Blessed One:

the function of knowledge (*ñāṇakicca*) and the function of compassion. Full enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*) is the function of knowledge; having entered the attainment of great compassion (*mahākaruṇāsamāpatti*), surveying those beings who are ready to be trained and performing what is appropriate for them is the function of compassion.
[As it is said: “Bhikkhus, when you have assembled, two things are to be done.”
For it has been said that even the Blessed One does exactly that. Alternatively, there is the connection with the instruction given by visiting monks.
In that context, showing the dwelling as an act of compassion, he said, "He dwelt in the dwelling of compassion.

In the phrase *adhikaraṇañhi kālattho*, the particle *hi* has the sense of a reason (*kāraṇattho*). Therein, in the Abhidhamma, [the term *adhikaraṇa*] is reckoned in terms of time, collection, moment, coincidence, and cause.
The meaning of "occasion" (*samaya*) should be understood as fivefold. How does the occasion, in the sense of time and collection, become a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*)?
Just as one says, "He was born at the time of the forenoon," where the time is the place of origin, so too should the word "occasion" be understood in the sense of time.
How [is it] in the sense of a heap? Just as one says, "He was born in a heap of barley. Therefore, at whatever time or in whatever heap the mind has arisen, at that time or in that heap...
It is meant that contact and the other [mental factors] arise. Regarding the phrase "for the locus" (*adhikaraṇaṃ hi*):

here, in the Abhidhamma, the locus is defined as the sense of time (*kālaṭṭho*) and the sense of collection (*samūhaṭṭho*). It should be understood that this was said with reference to the locus expressed by the words "at which time" (*yasmiṃ samaye*).
Now, demonstrating the characteristic of one state by means of another state (*bhāvena bhāvalakkhaṇaṃ*), he says: "of those mentioned therein," and so forth.
In that regard, what is meant by the "state" (bhāva) of those things taught in the Abhidhamma? It is their arising and their existence;
this [existence] belongs to those phenomena such as contact (phassa) and so forth taught therein. Furthermore, that state is characterized and known by means of the state of the occasion (samaya).
Therefore, it is said that the locative case designation is employed there.
In this context, "moment" (*khaṇa*) refers to the ninth moment, which is free from the eight unfavorable moments; when that exists, [the dhammas] arise.

"Concurrence" (*samavāya*) refers to the completeness of causes such as the eye-faculty and so forth; when that exists, they arise. "Cause" (*hetu*) refers to the object of perception, such as visible form and so forth.
Therefore, when these three—the moment, the cause, and the concurrence—exist, there is the existence and presence of those [dhammas] such as contact (*phassa*).

"It happens" (hoti) is what is said. However, since both the sense of cause (*hetu*) and the sense of instrument (*karaṇa*) are possible here—meaning that two meanings are possible for a single word—the third case ending is applied to the word *samaya* as used in this Vinaya in the senses of agent (*kattā*) and instrument (*karaṇa*), and also in the sense of cause (*hetu*).
It is said to be "difficult to understand" because it was stated: "The Tathāgata alone will know the proper time for that."

[The word] *hoti*. Regarding the phrase *tena samayena*: for the sake of that occasion, just as in the expressions “he dwells for food” or “he dwells for knowledge,” the meaning is that he dwells for the purpose of obtaining either food or knowledge. Thus, when it is said “he dwells at that time,” the instrumental case (*tatiyā*) should be understood in the sense of cause (*hetvatthe*);
therefore, [it refers to] both the occasion for the formulation of the training rule (*sikkhāpada-paññatti*) and the transgression (*vītikkama*).
It is said that he dwelt here and there while looking about. This should be understood from such passages as the third *pārājika* rule and others:

“Bhikkhus, I wish to retire into seclusion for half a month. Therefore, since the second case (*dvitīyā*) occurs here in the sense of absolute connection (*accantasaṃyoga*) regarding time and distance—as in “he studies for a month” or “he studies for a day”—but here it has the sense of cause (*hetu*) or instrument (*karaṇa*).

And because it is possible [to use the instrumental case here]: at that time when the sense of cause (*hetu*) is possible for a word in the instrumental case, the Blessed One dwelt in various places while depending upon that which has become the cause—namely, either the transgression of this or that matter, or what is termed the "time of transgression," as well as the cause for the promulgation of the training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
When the sense of instrument (*karaṇa*) is possible, he did so by means of that which has become the instrument.
The intended meaning is that the Blessed One dwelt here and there, enacting the training rules (sikkhāpada) as each occasion arose.
However, in the *Gaṇṭhipada*, it is stated: "The transgression by Sudinna and others is indeed the cause;
but the time, which constitutes its fixed condition, is the instrument itself, because the training rule must be enacted without exceeding that specific time. This [is the view].

It is faultless. As for what was said—that "this instrumental case (karaṇa), although it should have been mentioned first because it belongs to the preliminary stage, was mentioned later"—that is poorly stated.
For, from the perspective of the sense of cause (hetu), just as the instrumental sense is applied later, it enters into connection precisely in that sequence;
and thus it has been so applied. As for this instrumental sense which the commentator (Aṭṭhakathācariya) mentioned later...
The Teacher has written that one should understand that which was first stated—the meaning of the reason—to have been joined later after having first been joined;

this is called "the ease of the joining. From here onwards, wherever it is said "written by the Teacher" (*ācariyena likhita*) or "the Teacher’s conjecture" (*ācariyassa takka*), there the "Teacher" should be understood as the Teacher Ānanda, a resident of Kalasapura.
Here it is asked: Just as it is said in the Suttanta, "At one time the Blessed One," so too should it be said, "At that time the Blessed One was at Verañjā.
If the Elder intends to state a synonym, then terms such as "the Tathāgata" or "the Sugata" should also have been mentioned.
Or, if there is some specific purpose for employing these two particular terms, then that should be stated.
It is said: for some who do not understand the supremely profound disposition and course of the Buddha, the Blessed One, [the following passages are cited]:
“While the training rule had not yet been laid down, he did not see the danger... [and so forth]... he made it known”;
and “Then the Blessed One questioned the Venerable Sudinna,” followed by “‘Did you consent, bhikkhu? ‘I did not consent, Blessed One’,” and so forth.

Likewise, having seen the mastery of the Vinaya—such as the questioning of the monk Purāṇavohārika and the establishment of the second Pārājika rule according to the limit stated by him, as well as the granting of the going-forth to Devadatta—one might, based on the Buddha’s perfect enlightenment, conceive a doubt, thinking:
"But how could such things apply to you, a wretched fellow who eats spittle? and so forth.

It should be understood that the Venerable Elder Upāli took up these very two phrases in every instance in order to dispel both types of doubt: the doubt that might arise based on the mastery of the Vinaya concerning harsh speech, and the doubt regarding his state of having destroyed the taints (*khīṇāsava*).
By this he demonstrates: "Granted, he is indeed a Buddha because of his omniscience regarding all that is to be known; yet, because all faults have been shattered..."

“The Blessed One is indeed the Teacher. It is also stated elsewhere: “The Tathāgatas ask even though they know... [omission] ...for the Tathāgatas there is the demolition of the bridge regarding what is unbeneficial.
And it is said in the Suttanta: “I guide Kesī with gentleness, and also with harshness,” and so forth.

Regarding the phrase “in the case of a non-common cause”: herein, the roots of wholesomeness never become the roots of unwholesomeness, nor likewise do the roots of unwholesomeness [become the roots of wholesomeness].
The indeterminate roots are never wholesome; this is the only way [of classification] that applies.

Because wholesome roots are a condition by way of root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*) for the material phenomena co-arising with them, the method beginning with "wholesome [roots] are conditions only for wholesome [phenomena]" does not apply here.

It is called *pucimanda* because it is said that *pucci* are leprosy, and it "softens" (*mandayati*) or destroys them. It is characterized by its inclination toward the accomplishment of the welfare and happiness of sentient beings.
In this context, in order to show the beings mentioned in general by dividing them into two categories, it is said:

“Because of the great helpfulness toward human beings,” and so forth. “For the welfare of many people” means for the sake of the benefit of many people; for the Blessed One is the teacher of benefit pertaining both to the present life and to future lives through the perfection of wisdom.
“For happiness” means for the sake of happiness; for he is the bestower of the attainment of happiness that assists others through the perfection of generosity.
Through his perfection of loving-kindness and compassion, out of sympathy for the world, he is like a mother and father; indeed, he is the protector and guardian of the world.
Regarding the phrase "of gods and humans," this refers specifically to those capable individuals who are susceptible to instruction (veneyya-satta);

it shows that his own appearance in the world was for their attainment of the path and fruit of Nibbāna. For when it is said "for their welfare" (*atthāya*), it means for the ultimate goal, which is Nibbāna; and when it is said "for their benefit" (*hitāya*)...
When it is said [“for the sake of the path leading to that”], it means for the purpose of reaching that [Nibbāna] via the path; for there is no benefit superior to the path.
“For happiness” means for the sake of the bliss of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), because there is no happiness higher than that.

Regarding the phrase “by means of what is comprised by view and virtue,” here only view and virtue are mentioned without including concentration and wisdom, because this applies in common to all those in training (*sekha*) and those beyond training (*asekha*).
In the *Kosambakassutta* as well, it is said: "He dwells having attained commonality in virtue; he dwells having attained commonality in view.

If you argue that wisdom (*paññā*) is also included by the mention of "view" (*diṭṭhi*), we say no; for this would entail the undesirable consequence that even stream-enterers and others possess the state of fulfilling wisdom.

Therefore, although wisdom and view share the same characteristic, there exists a distinction between their different states, just as there is between the faculties of resolve (*dhiti*), concentration (*samādhi*), and right concentration (*sammāsamādhi*).
"Knew" (*aññāsi*): here it means "known" by way of the ear-door;
for meanings are called "heard" (*suta*), as in such passages as, "Venerable Gotama, this has been heard by me: evil conduct is both seen and heard.
Or, it may be used in the sense of emphasis, as in, "Upāli, a bhikkhu indeed causes a schism in the Saṅgha. "Existing" (*vijjamāna*) means being present in Verañjā.

"Of one who has become thus, of one who has come to be thus. How has he become thus? "Of the Son of the Sakyans, who went forth from the Sakyan clan"—the meaning is that when used in conjunction with the word *abhi* (towards), the accusative case endings are employed, as in the phrase "thus having become, he stands; his fame has spread abroad.

By the statement, "One develops loving-kindness conditioned by the clinging to sensual pleasures and is reborn in the Brahma-world," [it is shown] by means of this clinging to sensual pleasures as the cause.
They say that the doctrine of those who maintain that one is reborn only in the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) after having performed karma is refuted.

Having heard that "the sensual pleasures in the Brahma-world are sublime," or having formed such a conception, one subsequently performs karma leading to that state with the condition of sensual clinging (*kāmupādāna*), thinking, "I shall enjoy the excellence there.

Thus, even in the Brahma-world, things are called "sensual pleasures" (*kāma*) in the sense of being desirable; and because craving has that as its object, it is called "sensual clinging" (*kāmupādāna*).
And they say, "It has been so stated," but this must be investigated. Furthermore, karma is the productive cause of the eye, while craving is the root cause of karma;

therefore, that which is a root cause is not itself the producer. Craving for form and so forth constitute the truth of suffering because they are included within the aggregates, and also because of the statement:
"Not to obtain what one desires is also suffering. Thus, they are called "originators" by virtue of being its root causes.
It should be connected thus: "the originator of this fivefold aggregate which has become its cause.
Because of the statement, "With the arising of the taints, there is the arising of ignorance," it is also appropriate to say that it is the cause of that [ignorance] alone.

Furthermore, because of the statement, "Just as form and so forth, craving too is the locus for the arising and abandoning of craving," craving—just like form and so forth—is the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*).
It has been said. For this was stated: “In the world, craving for form is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing;
it is here that this craving, when arising, arises,” and “it is here that this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned.
And because of the statement in the *Visuddhimagga*: “But in every way, the pentad of the aggregates of clinging is suffering and a noble truth, with the exception of craving.”
If it is argued that this contradicts the statement that craving for form and so forth constitute the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*), we say no;

for those [cravings] are spoken of in various places in order to demonstrate their mutual non-confusion. If craving were not included within the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*), then in the *Saccavibhaṅga* it would not have been said:
"In that regard, what are the five aggregates of clinging, in brief, which are suffering? Namely: [and so on].

Regarding the passage, “The aggregate of clinging to form... pe... the aggregate of clinging to consciousness,” should it not have been stated here that “the aggregate of clinging to volitional formations [is] craving, with the exception of craving itself”?
And yet it was not so stated. Therefore, does this imply that craving is included within the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*)? No; for that would entail the fault of confusing cause and fruit.

If you argue that there is no fault of confusion, [we reply that] in the *Saccavibhaṅga* (Analysis of the Truths) of the Pāḷi, the truth of origin (*samudayasacca*) is defined by way of five categories.
How so? "Craving" is the first section; "craving and the remaining defilements" is the second;
"craving and the remaining defilements and the remaining unwholesome states" is the third;

"craving and the remaining defilements and the remaining unwholesome states and the three wholesome roots associated with the outflows" is the fourth; [and] "craving and the remaining defilements... [is the fifth].
"The remaining unwholesome states, the three wholesome roots associated with the outflows (*sāsava*), and the remaining wholesome states associated with the outflows"—this is the fifth section.
Yes, it has been pointed out, but only in the *Abhidhammabhājaniya*, not elsewhere;
and that method is not found in the exposition of the Noble Truths (*ariyasacca-niddesa*). For there, he says simply, "the four truths."
In the *Suttantabhājaniya* and *Pañhapucchaka*, it is not stated as "the four noble truths" [as it is in the Abhidhamma]. Therefore, the *Suttantabhājaniya* alone is the authority there;
and since craving (*taṇhā*) is mentioned therein, it is as he said: "Therein, what is the noble truth of the origin of suffering?
It is this craving that leads to renewed existence... namely, craving for sensual pleasures," and so forth. Also: "What is impermanent, that is suffering."

Since it is stated in this manner, what is said therein is indeed authoritative. From the statement, "He dwells having attained the first jhāna by means of the earth-kasiṇa," the jhānas are referred to as "kasiṇas.

Some say that this was said with reference to the learning-sign (*uggahanimitta*) and the counterpart-sign (*paṭibhāganimitta*); however, that is not correct. Even the thirty-two aspects (*dvattiṃsākāra*), having set aside their conventional designations (*paṇṇatti*),...
From the statement, "Mindfulness should be established [on them] as repulsive," it should be understood that form and the other [sense objects] are the domains of mindfulness.
These seven true states (saddhamma) are: faith, moral shame, moral dread, erudition, the arousal of energy, established mindfulness, and clear comprehension.
"By way of intrinsic nature" means by way of suffering. "Does not fall away" refers to the devas. "To be known" (ñāteyya) means that which is to be known. "To be seen" (daṭṭheyya) means...
It is to be seen. Or alternatively, the meaning is: "I do not say that the end of the world is to be known by going.

rather, it is said that only by reaching the end of the world through the noble path (*ariyagamana*) is there liberation from suffering. "One who has attained peace" (*samitāvī*).
"One whose defilements have been stilled. "Subsisting by nutriment" means subsisting by way of conditions (*paccaya*).
The intention is that whatever subsists by way of conditions, all that constitutes "one world" in the sense of being subject to breaking up and falling apart.

For conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) are called "beings" (*satta*), "clinging beings" (*visatta*), and "attached beings" (*satta*) because they are dependent upon their respective conditions. They "surround" and "attend. "Disā" is the plural accusative case. "Bhanti" [means they shine].
They appear. Which ones? Those very same moon and sun, radiant and luminous. The eight worldly conditions are merely conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*).
Because of the statement, "all around Sineru," they say that Yugandhara and the other mountains stand surrounding Sineru in a circular form.
This world-system rises up having surrounded [it]. [In the phrase *parikkhipitvā*,] the letter *m* serves as a phonetic conjunction (*padasandhikara*).
