the world of beings (satta-loka) by way of the distinctions of latent tendencies and underlying dispositions; and the world of space (okāsa-loka) by way of the dimensions of the world-systems (cakkavāḷa) and so forth.
But how does the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimutti-ñāṇadassana)—which belongs to the sense sphere, is limited, and is mundane—overcome the entire world?
It is like omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) because its power is incomparable.

For, within its own domain, it follows the course of the Blessed One’s omniscient knowledge, and its occurrence is more rapid due to arising immediately after two moments of the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*).
No one else’s consciousness arises with such rapidity, even that of the Venerable Sāriputta; it is said that for him, this mental cycle occurs immediately after fifteen moments of the life-continuum.
It is said that in the island of Siṅghala there are the Nāgas Aggisikha and Dhūmasikha. An "atthapada" (word of meaning) is a word that illuminates a meaning;

the sense is that all these words which illuminate a single meaning constitute a sentence. The "eight directions" refer to the eight liberations (aṭṭha vimokkhā) or the meditative attainments (samāpattiyo).

The term "satthavāho" (caravan leader) is a conventional designation for "sattha" (caravan), just as "pisitāsa" (flesh-eater) is a designation for a "pisāca" (demon). "I was a frog in the water, not on land."
“Maṇḍūka, my domain is only water; while I was listening to your Dhamma, [you] pressed down on my head with a staff”—this is the remainder of the reading.
Or, the genitive case is used in the sense of disregard. Having smiled, thinking, “Even by this much such a supernormal power (iddhi) will arise,” he said:
“And here, ‘liberation’ (vimokkha) means the Path; the knowledge immediately following that is called the fruit-knowledge (phala-ñāṇa). At that moment...”
"Buddho" means "one who has awakened. It is used in the sense of the agent for "the awakening of all. It is used in the sense of the causal agent for "awakening [others].
A word that indicates the state of being supreme is called "seṭṭha," and likewise "uttama.

"Sacchikāpaññatti" refers to the designation of self-existence (sayambhutā) by virtue of having realized all phenomena; or, it is a "realization-designation" because they have been known and realized by oneself alone. "Bhagī" means "possessor of fortune"; thus, he is "Bhagavā."

[He was] one who partook of robes, alms-food, and so forth. He frequented remote lodgings in forest groves and jungle thickets. He was a partaker of the essence of the goal, the Dhamma, and liberation.

He brought about the destruction of the host of defilements such as lust. Having developed himself, he was one whose body was developed. Because he had gone to the end of existence—that is, Nibbāna—by means of the attainment of the Path, he was "one who has reached the end of becoming" (*bhavantago*).
“Abandon the single state of greed, monks,” and so forth—having taken up these [teachings] according to the method of the single [dhammas] and so on, he speaks.

There are perversions such as perceiving the impermanent as permanent, suffering as happiness, the non-self as self, and the foul as beautiful, by way of the defilements of craving and views and the defilement of misconduct.
Or, monks, craving arises in a bhikkhu for the sake of robes; it arises for the sake of almsfood, lodgings, and for the sake of existence and non-existence.
Or: there are five "mental obstructions" (*cetokhila*) that have come down as being characterized by anger toward the Teacher, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, the training, and one's fellow practitioners.
There are five "fetters" (*vinibandha*) that have come down as follows: one is not free from lust for sensual pleasures... [and so on] ...toward the body and form;
and having eaten until full, even to the point of distending the belly, one leads the holy life with the aspiration for some order of devas. These are the roots of dispute.
Anger, enmity, hypocrisy, spite, envy, avarice, deceit, craftiness, obstinacy, aggression, adherence to one's own views, being tenacious in grasping, and being difficult to let go.
However, in the *Vibhaṅga*, it is stated as: "anger, hypocrisy, envy, craftiness, evil desire, and adherence to one's own views.
Dependent upon craving comes seeking; dependent upon seeking comes gain.
"Depending on gain, there arises evaluation; thus there arise desire and lust, attachment, possessiveness, stinginess, guarding, and for the sake of guarding, the taking up of sticks and weapons...
[and so forth]... unwholesome states come into being"—this is what was said. There are six types of craving for the phenomena of visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects;
these occur specifically by way of craving for sensual pleasure (*kāmataṇhā*), craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*), and craving for non-existence (*vibhavataṇhā*).
There are eighteen; taking those same [eighteen] with respect to the internal [bases], there are eighteen, and with respect to the external [bases], eighteen—thus thirty-six.
Those [thirty-six] in the past, thirty-six in the future, and thirty-six in the present—thus there are one hundred and eight modes of craving’s wandering (*taṇhāvicarita*).
It is called *Māra* because it kills; for it is said, "Heedlessness is the path of death. Alternatively, it is so called because it destroys right livelihood.
The defilements (*kilesa*) are called "Māra" because they are like murderers; the aggregates (*khandha*) themselves are Māras because they are like executioners.

Volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*) are Māras because they bring about the production of the suffering of birth, and because aging and so forth arise for one who is born. Death-Māra (*maccu-māra*) is so called because it slays the life-span included within a single existence.
*Aṇimā* is the attainment of invisibility, like an atom. *Laghimā* is the swift movement of the body or the mind.
Mastery (*mahimattā*) is such things as touching even the moon, the sun, and so forth with one's hand. Attainment (*patti*) means reaching whatever place one desires.
Manifestation (*pākamma*) is the accomplishment of whatever purpose one seeks to gain. Lordship (*īsatta*) means self-mastery. Sovereignty (*vasitta*) means mastery over others.
The power of determining according to one’s wish (*yatthakāmāvasāyitā*) means wherever one wishes, whatever one wishes, and for as long as one wishes.

In that context, first, there is the establishment of the meaning. Regarding the passage beginning "The Noble Truth of Suffering is suffering in the sense of oppression, being conditioned, burning, and change," this is the answer to the question preceded by an objection:

"If there are other meanings of suffering such as form-craving and so forth, why are only four [truths] mentioned? [The answer is: Because they are manifested by way of the vision of the other truths.

Therein, knowledge of the truths is also described by way of each individual truth as its object, according to the method beginning: “In this context, what is knowledge of suffering? It is the wisdom that arises with reference to suffering.

Furthermore, it is described by way of accomplishing the function regarding the remaining truths while taking one truth as the object, according to the method beginning: “Bhikkhus, he who sees suffering also sees the origin of suffering.”

It has been said. In that context, when one takes each truth as an object, first, regarding suffering—which has the characteristic of oppression by its own nature—through the vision of its origin, because it is accumulated and conditioned by that origin which has the characteristic of accumulation, its aspect of being conditioned (*saṅkhata*) becomes manifest.
Furthermore, because the Path removes the torment of the defilements and is perfectly cool, [its aspect of peace becomes manifest].
Therefore, by the vision of the Path, the sense of "torment" becomes manifest in it, just as the ugliness of Sundarī became manifest to Nanda upon seeing his celestial nymph.
However, there is no need to say that the sense of "changeability" becomes manifest in cessation by the vision of cessation—which is by nature unchanging.
Likewise, although origination has the characteristic of accumulation by its own nature, [the sense of "torment"] becomes manifest in it through the vision of suffering.
The meaning of "source" (nidāna) becomes manifest through the demonstration of the disease arising from unwholesome food, just as food is seen to be the source of that disease.

The meaning of "bondage" (saṃyoga) is shown by the demonstration of cessation (nirodha), which is disjunction. And the meaning of "impediment" (palibodha) is shown by the demonstration of the path (magga), which is the means of escape.
Likewise, [the meaning of "origin"] is shown by the demonstration of origination (samudaya), which is non-separation from that very cessation which is the escape.
Through the vision of [the truth of] suffering, the meaning of seclusion (*viveka*) becomes manifest. Through the vision of the path, the meaning of the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*) becomes manifest;

for in this beginningless saṃsāra, the path has never been seen before, and since it too is conditioned by causes, the unconditioned nature of that which is free from conditions becomes exceedingly clear.
Furthermore, through the vision of suffering, its meaning of the deathless (*amata*) becomes manifest.

For suffering is poison, and Nibbāna is the deathless. Likewise, by seeing the origin [of the path], the meaning of "cause" is revealed regarding the path characterized by deliverance, such that one understands:
"This is not the cause for attaining Nibbāna; this is the cause.
By seeing cessation, the meaning of "seeing" is revealed, just as one who perceives extremely subtle forms thinks of his eye: "How clear my eye is!"

It is like the state of being serene. Through the vision of suffering, the sense of predominance is like the exalted status of a lordly person upon seeing a multitude of wretched people afflicted by many diseases.

Thus, here, four meanings are stated for each [truth] by way of its characteristic and because the other three are manifested through the vision of one of them. "Seclusion from the substrata" (upadhiviveka) is the state of being free from defilements (nikkilesatā).
They are "enemies" (paccatthikā) because they obstruct [one's] welfare. They are "adversaries" (paccāmittā) because they are hostile enemies.
By the phrase "having realized, he proclaimed," he demonstrates the Blessed One’s omniscience to this extent.

Having thus demonstrated his perfection of knowledge, he now says, "He taught the Dhamma," and so forth, in order to demonstrate his perfection of compassion. Alternatively, what was it that he proclaimed?
That knowledge is entirely for the benefit of the three worlds. What kind of Dhamma did he teach? "Virtuous in the beginning," and so forth.
By this statement, he illuminates his fitness to speak. The "Dhamma of the Dispensation" refers to the instruction and the scriptures.
"Purification of duty" means purification of duty regarding the abandonment of defilements and the object of Nibbāna. The "holy life of the Dispensation" refers to the Three Trainings.
Or [the phrase] beginning with "nine thousand koṭis," and so forth. The path itself is the holy life; thus it is "path-holy-life" (*maggabrahmacariya*).

The three Pitakas that elucidate this are here called "with meaning and with phrasing" (*sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ*). Briefly explaining [the Dhamma] by means of the six bases of meaning is "manifestation" (*saṅkāsana*).
Explaining from the beginning is "elucidation" (*pakāsana*). Expounding both of these in detail is "exposition" (*vivaraṇa*). Again...
*Vibhajana* (analysis) is the act of dividing. *Uttānīkaraṇa* (making plain) is making [the meaning] clear through similes and so forth.

It should be understood as "establishing" (*paññāpana*) by means of generating satisfaction in the minds of the listeners and by means of their attentive focus. Regarding the terms for "phoneme" (*akkhara*): it is called a phoneme because it does not perish (*akkhaṇato*).

Some say, "A single-syllable word is a phoneme. A word (*pada*) is that which ends in a case-ending. Regarding "syllable" (*byañjana*): it is called a syllable because it manifests (*byañjayati*), namely, a sentence (*vākya*). Alternatively, a sentence is a collection of words.
The "manifestation of analysis" (*vibhāgapakāsa*) is called the "aspect" (*ākāra*). The etymological derivation such as "it touches, therefore it is contact" (*phusati ti phasso*) is "nirukti";

the designation of that which has been pointed out by nirukti is called "description" (*niddesa*). "It touches, therefore it is contact"; that [contact] is threefold: to-be-experienced-as-pleasant, to-be-experienced-as-painful, and to-be-experienced-as-neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
Among these, this is the application: one collects [the meaning] by means of syllables (*akkhara*), and one manifests it by means of phrases (*pada*).
He reveals it through phonemes, analyzes it through modes, clarifies it through etymologies, and makes it known through definitions.
Or, having condensed it through syllables, he elucidates it through phrases; having revealed it through phonemes, he analyzes it through modes;
having clarified it through etymologies, he makes it known through definitions. Or, having opened it up through syllables, he leads [the student] through phrases.
It should be understood that one who gains knowledge through a condensed statement (*ugghaṭitaññū*) is guided by means of the syllables and led by means of the characteristics;

one who gains knowledge through an elaboration (*vipañcitaññū*) is led by means of the terminology and guided by means of the definitions; and one who is to be led (*neyya*) is likewise guided. "Meaning" (*attha*) refers to the meaning of what has been spoken.

The penetration of the specific nature of that very meaning is called "penetration" (*paṭivedha*). Both of these are termed "meaning. Therefore it was said: "By way of profundity of meaning and profundity of penetration..."
"‘With its meaning’ (sātthaṃ): whether it be ‘the Dhamma’ or ‘the teaching,’ this refers merely to the phrasing (byañjana).

The holy life of the Dispensation (sāsanabrahmacariya), which is pure by virtue of being free from defilement, and the Path comprised within the three trainings—both are included under the term ‘holy life’ (brahmacariya).

‘By way of practice’ means for the sake of practice. ‘Through proficiency in the scriptures’: as one studies the aggregates and so forth again and again, they become clear. [This applies even to] poorly recited texts."
If these [questions] were recited, they would only lead to confusion.
2–3. "Is it endurable? refers to cold, heat, and so forth. "Is it sustainable? means whether life can be maintained with whatever means for sustaining life one has obtained.

"Little affliction" (*appābādha*) means having few calamities; "little illness" (*appātaṅka*) means being free from disease. "Is there lightness in the bodily functions? asks whether the body is agile in its activities.

"Is your strength sufficient for the duties of a recluse? Is your dwelling comfortable according to the manner previously described, by way of being free from illness or by way of freedom from longing?
From the age of sixty-seven onwards is the final stage of life; thus it is said, "facing north.

When the revelation of the world had occurred, why did he look back here? He replied, "In this world, there is not even one equal to you," saying, "You are the foremost in the world with its devas," and so forth.

"Pre-eminent and supreme. By way of rebirth, they are "devas. Because they arise in accordance with the experience of forms—either through the enjoyment of forms or by way of aspiration—and because they arise as feelings of joy associated with lust, warming the heart like the juices of mangoes and other fruits, they are called "the flavors of form" (*rūparasā*).
He says, "They have been abandoned even by the Tathāgata," by way of emphasizing the subject at hand. [This applies] to the Tathāgata as well.
Indeed, they have been rendered like a palm tree with its crown cut off, in that they have been abandoned by anyone.
How so? By the mention of "the taste of form" and so forth, those things subject to ripening (*vipākadhammadhamma*) are included;

although these still exist, because craving and ignorance—which are like the crown [of the tree]—have been severed by the army of the Path, they have become incapable of producing future aggregates of ripening (*vipākakkhandha*), which are like a row of palm trees. Therefore...
They have been made like a palmyra stump. They say that wholesome joy is also included here.

Those things corresponding to the path of action that were abandoned by the first path have their roots cut off by the second; those corresponding to sensual lust have been made like a palmyra stump by the third;
and those corresponding to the lust for form and the lust for the formless have been rendered non-existent by the fourth. This is the state of being subject to no further decline.

But when explaining [the state of their cessation], he said, "they are of a nature not to arise again in the future. They are abandoned through abandonment by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgappahāna*) at the moment of insight or at the preliminary stage of jhāna;
they have their roots cut off through suppression (*vikkhambhanappahāna*) at the moment of jhāna, as it is said: "quite secluded from sensual pleasures";
and they are rendered like a palmyra stump through abandonment by eradication (*samucchedappahāna*) at the moment of attaining the third true knowledge (*tatiyavijjā*).
But when those forms, tastes, and so forth have been rendered non-existent and are of a nature not to arise again in the future, this is one and the same point. Or rather:
by the first breakthrough they are abandoned; by the second, their roots are cut; by the third, they are made like a palmyra stump.
Since they have thus been rendered non-existent, they should be understood as being of a nature not to arise in the future.

Alternatively, it should be understood that [craving] has been abandoned by the knowledge of suffering, its root cut off by the knowledge of the origin, rendered like a palm stump by the knowledge of cessation,
brought to non-existence by the knowledge of the path, and made subject to non-arising in the future by the knowledge of reviewing.
Or else, it has been abandoned by the mundane path, its root cut off by the path of seeing, and rendered like a palm stump by the threefold path of development, and so forth.
Because it was not within the brahmin’s sphere of experience, the flavor of the Dhamma was not extracted for him.
(11) Regarding the phrase "the element of the Dhamma" (*dhammadhātu*): here, omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) is called the "element of the Dhamma.

The expression "like the full moon" is used in accordance with the word "compassion" (*anukampā*); the reference to the sun is in accordance with the word "thoroughly penetrated" (*suppaṭividdha*); and [the comparison to] the earth is due to his mind being equal to the earth.

They say that the cause [of this] is "the expansion of compassion" (*karuṇā-vipphāra*). For when he reveals his own qualities—which ought to be concealed—by saying, "Vigour has indeed been aroused by me," and so forth, it should be understood that he is revealing the expansion of his own compassion. "Varabhūrimedhaso" means one of excellent and vast wisdom;
or alternatively, *bhūrī* is "ground" (*bhūmi*), thus the meaning is: one whose excellent wisdom is spread out like the earth. He awakened (*abujjhi*).
In this context, "bodhi" refers to a tree as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). It is "bodhi" because one awakens by oneself, or because those possessing it awaken through it;
thus, the path is also *bodhi*. Likewise, omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) is also *bodhi*. Nibbāna is *bodhi* because it is that which is awakened to.

The three types of clear knowledge (*vijjā*) should be understood according to their occurrence for one who possesses the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the three knowledges. Its state of sharpness is due to one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*).
Some arrows, though sharp, become blunt upon hitting the target; this is not so. Through the power of the faculty of mindfulness, its hardness is to be understood;

through the power of the faculty of faith, its clarity; and through the power of the faculty of energy, its courage, owing to its thorough overcoming of the enemies that are the defilements without faltering along the way—for the purpose of giving birth to the Path.
The time of conception occurs because it follows immediately after equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) and is in conformity with it (*anuloma*).
"Desire" (*chanda*) and "intention" (*saṅkappa*) are both nothing but lust (*rāga*), distinguished by their different states—
just as one says, "He approaches the elephant's trunk."
“With a heart stained by passion,
one approaches a lover who has gone astray;
fallen into sensual desire, one does not know moderation regarding the world.”
Just as in the case of the *Ādi* [sections], regarding the statement "even though the meaning has already been stated in the *Vibhaṅga* itself," this is the intended meaning:
even if it were brought here from the *Vibhaṅga* text, it would not be of benefit to everyone; therefore, I shall clarify it according to the method of the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
"By these" means by sensual pleasures. Among bodily seclusion and the rest, seclusion from acquisitions (*upadhiviveka*) is the third;

therefore, having set aside the third and taken the other two, and having taken suppression-seclusion (*vikkhambhanaviveka*) among "seclusion by way of its constituent part" (*tadaṅga*) and so forth, it is said, "only three.

If it is argued that this being so, there would be no distinction because "suppression of the mind" and "seclusion of the mind" are identical in meaning, it should not be viewed thus, because this belongs to the section on absorption (*appanā*). By the inclusion of "bodily seclusion,"...

The inclusion of the preliminary stage is understood; therefore, "seclusion of mind" refers to seclusion by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgaviveka*), which should be taken as occurring at the time of absorption through suppression, so that there is no confusion.

Alternatively, it is also appropriate to hold that by "seclusion of mind" both seclusion by substitution of opposites and suppression are included, while by the other term [seclusion of body] only seclusion by suppression is meant.
Or else, because they pertain to the two types of sensual desire (*kilesakāma*), they are subsumed under two distinct functions.

It is like a man. Just as in the world one says, “The tree bears fruit,” by way of designating what is non-existent through what is non-existent, so too in the Dispensation one says, “Jhāna with applied thought and sustained thought,” by way of designating what is existent through what is existent;
this is the intended meaning.
Regarding the term "stilling" (*vūpasama*): here, of what is there stilling? Is it of those [factors] belonging to the first jhāna, or rather of those belonging to the second jhāna?
If it were of those belonging to the first jhāna, there would be no stilling of them; for there is no first jhāna that is devoid of applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).

If it were of those belonging to the second jhāna, there is indeed no stilling there because of their absence—if this is the objection, then this is said in reply: tenetaṃ vuccati: This is stated as follows: [text continues]
Regarding the term “having surmounted”: the surmounting does not refer to those [factors] alone.
If it is asked, “Does it then refer to the entire mass of factors of the first jhāna?”—it is for this reason that it is said, “but by surmounting the gross,” and so forth.

If it is asked, “Are all factors of the first jhāna indeed gross in comparison to the second jhāna, and not merely the pair of applied thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra)?”—it is not only applied and sustained thought [that are gross].

"Because of their grossness in relation to those [states] associated with them": through the seeing of the disadvantage in those very [states], there is an absence of them at the moment of the second jhāna.
Therefore it is said: "because of their non-manifestation at the moment of the second jhāna.
This is stated for the purpose of showing that factor by whose power or application this jhāna is called "tranquilizing" (*sampasādana*) and "unification" (*ekodibhāva*).

Faith and concentration are explained in the Vibhaṅga. This commentary on the meaning is not inconsistent with what was stated regarding ghee and so forth in the training rule concerning superior food.

"He sees evenly" means that for one whose taints are destroyed, having abandoned laxity and restlessness, there is equanimity toward the occurrence of the six desirable and undesirable objects at the six sense doors, which consists in the state of not abandoning one's naturally pure condition.

Equanimity with regard to the sixfold base (*chaḷaṅgupekkhā*). Equanimity that has become neutral during the apprehension of the settling [of the mind] through the reflection on the hindrances and so forth is called equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*).
Equanimity that has become neutral during the process of investigating is called equanimity of insight (*vipassanupekkhā*).

Among these, there is equanimity as a divine abiding (*brahmavihārupekkhā*), equanimity as a factor of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅgupekkhā*), equanimity as neutrality (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*), and equanimity of jhāna (*jhānupekkhā*).
Purity-equanimity (*pārisuddhupekkhā*) and equanimity as the middle state (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*) are identical in actual meaning; their distinction is merely according to their different states.

Likewise, the unity of equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) and equanimity of insight (*vipassanupekkhā*) is to be understood by way of wisdom (*paññā*), while their twofold nature is to be understood by way of function (*kicca*).

Furthermore, the sixfold equanimity (*chaḷaṅgupekkhā*) belongs to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), while the equanimity of the divine abodes (*brahmavihārupekkhā*) belongs to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), and so forth, according to their respective planes (*bhūmi*). Thus ends the section on the sixfold equanimity.

Equanimity as a divine abode (brahmavihārupekkhā) belongs only to one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), whereas equanimity as a divine abode belongs to all three types of persons—worldlings, those in training, and those beyond training; thus it is according to the person (puggala).
Equanimity with six factors is associated with a consciousness accompanied by joy, while equanimity as a divine abode is associated with a consciousness accompanied by equanimity;
thus it is according to the mind (citta). Equanimity with six factors has six objects, while equanimity as a divine abode has mental phenomena (dhamma) as its object.
By way of object: equanimity regarding feeling is included in the aggregate of feeling, while the other nine are included in the aggregate of mental formations;

thus, by way of inclusion in the aggregates. The sixfold equanimity—the equanimity of the divine abodes, the enlightenment factor of equanimity, the equanimity of jhāna, the equanimity of purification, and the equanimity of neutrality—are identical in meaning;
therefore, at a single moment, only one of these can occur, not the others. The same applies to equanimity regarding formations and equanimity in insight.

"Feeling, energy, and equanimity may arise at one and the same moment. Six-factored equanimity is indeterminate; the divine abiding of equanimity is both wholesome and indeterminate, as are the others.
However, equanimity of feeling may also be unwholesome.
Thus, according to the wholesome triad, these ten—when condensed—are indeed four factors, by way of energy, feeling, neutrality, and knowledge. "Of pain, grief, pleasure, and joy..."
If it is asked: why are these stated according to the method explained in the *Vibhaṅga* rather than by way of the sequence of abandoning?

It is for the purpose of preserving the Sutta. Regarding the phrase "the contrary of the desirable and undesirable," they say that it should be understood as "it experiences [them] in the manner of the contrary of the desirable and undesirable, without taking them by way of their objective support.
Why? Because all [these types of contact] proceed by taking a single kasiṇa as their object.
Starting from the third jhāna, it is taught under the heading of mindfulness (*sati*) because it has arrived acting as an aid.
Although the night possesses clarity due to the absence of clouds and the like, it does not become unhelpful—as it might be during the day—even when there is turbidity caused by clouds and so forth;
therefore, it is said: "Or, by way of its being helpful to itself. [And: "Because of the overpowering of the sun's radiance, there is no gain of the night."
"These two causes are the reasons for impurity; these two—being gentle and being helpful to oneself—are the reasons for similarity," they say.
This refers to that birth which is impure; therefore, some say it is a statement regarding the cause.
The commentary on the Discourse on Jhāna is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on Past Lives: 12.
Because jhānas share the characteristic of one-pointedness of mind, he said, "for some, it is the state of one-pointedness of mind. Of the wholesome [states]...
Because they share the same nature as the emergence from existence (*bhavokkamana*), [the text] says, "for some, they are the bases for the emergence from existence.
Because they do not share that same nature in the remaining cases, he does not say "bases for the feet" (*pādakaṭṭhānī*) in those other places, but says "the feet" (*pādakāni*).

By this, he illustrates that even for those things that have become the "feet," concentration of mind (*citt’ekaggatā*) brings about the emergence from existence as far as possible, while for the others, it brings about the state of being the "feet" as far as possible. Because they do not share that same nature, [the text specifies] the "feet" for access and insight [concentration].
It shows that they are common to both as bases for direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) and as bases for insight (*vipassanā*);
likewise, it demonstrates their absence as bases [for one another]. For among these, only the fourth is a basis for direct knowledge, not the others.
Among those, the third is the basis for the fourth, the second for the third, and the first for the second. Alternatively, [it may be explained as follows:]
The phrase "the four jhānas" was stated according to what was available.
Because of the origin of the Vinaya and the establishment of residence at Verañjā,
the Blessed One therefore taught the threefold clear knowledge at Verañjā.
For this has been said: “A bhikkhu who is well-practiced in the Vinaya, by relying on the perfection of virtue,” and so forth.

Indeed, for one possessed of virtue, when sitting in the night or day quarters for the purpose of reviewing his virtue, from the very moment he sits down, because of his great frequency in recollecting his own past deeds, the knowledge of the recollection of past lives (*pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa*) is accomplished without difficulty. Likewise...
Through the habit of discerning the passing away of beings in dependence upon oneself, the knowledge of death and rebirth (*cutūpapāta-ñāṇa*) is easily accomplished;
through the habit of seeing subtle forms in water and so forth, the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*) is accomplished.

Since the holy life (*brahmacariya*) reaches the state of being unbroken and so forth by avoiding the sevenfold bond of sexual intercourse, or by avoiding the taints of sensual desire and the rest, therefore for him there arises the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "it succeeds without difficulty," here in the *Vinayanidāna*, only the threefold knowledge (*vijjattaya*) is shown;

therefore, he says, "showing a portion of those qualities which he was the giver of. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of it being merely the attainment of the threefold knowledge.
By the words "he was thus," although the preliminary practice for the four meditations (*jhāna*) is also included, [the text]...

It is not only the preceding triad of jhānas; nevertheless, by taking only the preceding triad of jhānas, he said, "Thus is the demonstration of the sequence of the fourth jhāna," meaning that "having attained the fourth jhāna by this sequence beginning with the attainment of the first jhāna.
If one asks why that is, it is because they constitute the plane of requisites (sambhāra-bhūmi).

For this is said in the Commentary: "And here, because one attains psychic power by means of the first three jhānas—having entered upon the perception of bliss and the perception of lightness through the pervasion of rapture and the pervasion of bliss, and having become a body that is light, soft, and wieldy—one reaches psychic power;
therefore, in this sense, they are called 'stages of equipment' because they lead to the acquisition of psychic power."
[The first three jhānas] are to be understood [as such]. But the fourth jhāna is the natural ground for the attainment of supernormal powers (iddhi).
It was with reference to this very meaning that it was said: "Previously, these four jhānas were the bases of direct knowledge (abhiññā) for some.

If that is so, why was it not stated as "these" including the fourth jhāna as well? If you say that it is because that [fourth jhāna] is the natural ground, it should not be so stated; for from the fourth jhāna...
Because there is the possibility of the existence of another’s mind that has attained states such as concentration;
since it is said, "He directed his mind toward the knowledge of recollecting past lives" when a certain state exists, therefore, when that fourth-jhāna consciousness—

which serves as the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā)— has arisen and reached its natural plane, the preliminary-work consciousness (*parikamma-citta*) [is directed] toward the knowledge of recollecting past lives.

"He directed it" (abhininnāmesi), he said. Regarding the phrase "it becomes capable of being directed": here, one directs that preparatory consciousness (*parikamma-citta*) for the purpose of attaining the various supernormal powers (*iddhividha*).
Having withdrawn it from the kasiṇa object, one sends it forth toward the supernormal powers.

However, since it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* that this is "for the purpose of bringing forth the knowledge of the various supernormal powers and so on from the jhāna that serves as the basis for direct knowledge (*abhiññā-pādaka-jhāna*)," [the meaning is as follows].
The meaning intended is that it is "capable of the resolution.

In the second alternative, the construction should be understood as: "when he is thus concentrated, thus attained to imperturbability," because this includes the functions of the first jhāna and so forth by means of the removal of the hindrances and the surmounting of applied thought (*vitakka*) and the rest. This is the construction in the first alternative.
It is not possible [to apply the word "thus" here], because by the statement "but in the case of 'pure,' etc.," the connection of the word "thus" (*eva*) is precluded.
For that very reason, he said: "pure by way of the state of purity of equanimity and mindfulness," and so forth.
"Of those within the range of desire" means by way of the desire arisen in such a manner as: "O, may I indeed fall into an offense, yet may the monks not know of me."
The meaning of *anaṅgaṇa* is "without blemish" due to the absence of causes for anger that have arisen.

Furthermore, in this context, even the aforementioned types of desire are obstacles to the attainment of the first jhāna and so forth, because it has been said: "Venerable sirs, deliberate lying is an obstructive state," let alone the causes for anger that fall within the sphere of desire; therefore, it is said: "Of the opposites to the acquisition of jhāna..."
"...of evil desires" and so forth. However, in some manuscripts the reading "of desires conditioned by the attainment of jhāna" is seen; that is a scribal error.

Furthermore, in the *Gaṇṭhipada*, the meaning written as "O, may the Teacher teach the Dhamma to me alone after questioning me" is poorly expressed. For [desires] are not conditioned by the attainment of jhāna.
The teacher says that anger and the rest are mentioned in the Anaṅgaṇa Sutta, yet they cannot logically occur for one who has attained jhāna because of their absence;

this should be investigated. Here, it should be understood that the eight factors are demonstrated again and again with the words, “When his mind is thus concentrated,” etc., for the purpose of showing the progressive distinction of the three true knowledges (vijjā).
Furthermore, these [knowledges] should be understood as progressively more distinguished because they demonstrate one’s own suffering,
the suffering of others, and the pacification of both. For the Blessed One, having seen his own boundless suffering in saṃsāra through the knowledge of recollecting past lives,

and having seen the suffering of other worlds through the knowledge of death and rebirth, as well as the pacification of both through the knowledge of the destruction of the taints, he teaches that [Dhamma].

Alternatively, by the first [verse], he illustrates the relinquishing of attachment to self through the vision of one's own suffering; by the second, the relinquishing of anger toward others through the vision of their suffering;
and by the third, the relinquishing of delusion through the vision of the Noble Path.
Thus, it should be understood that these two types of mundane higher knowledge (*lokīya-abhiññā*) alone are included here because they illustrate such various distinguished qualities.
If it is argued that because one’s dwelling (*nivāsa*) is indeed only in past births, therefore it should not be said "in past births" (*atītajātīsū*), [the answer is:

No, because it is shown that the conventional designation of "dwelling" is established even for a single portion of a birth. Although in the Pāḷi, by such statements as "one birth, two births," and so forth, the recollection of the entirety of a birth appears to be like the recollection of past dwellings (*pubbenivāsānussati*), it should not be viewed in that way.

The locative case is used both to show that even the recollection of a single part [of a past life] is indeed "recollection of past lives" (*pubbenivāsānussati*), and for the purpose of including the location and so forth.

By the word "etc. in the phrase "in the recollection of those who have cut off the cycle of rebirth (*chinnavaṭumaka*) and so forth," it should be understood that the worlds not yet inhabited, the continents, kingdoms, cities, villages, and so on are included.
However, in the *Gaṇṭhipada*, it is stated: "The supramundane virtue (*lokuttara-sīla*) and other qualities of those who have cut off the cycle of rebirth were not [taught] by the Blessed One..."
It is said: "They were known during his time as a Bodhisatta. From the implication of the context, one might conclude that these were mundane knowledges;
however, this appears inconsistent with the statement "those who revile the Noble Ones" made in the section on the knowledge of the divine eye.

For such a thought does not occur to one who does not see a Noble One. But for what purpose is *anussati* (recollection) mentioned here? Is it not the case that this is a section concerning *vijjā* (clear vision)?
Why? Because it is produced through the mindfulness of a beginner, and because mindfulness of past phenomena holds a preeminent role.
For it is said: "I recollect.
"He remembers those things that were known while they were present in the past; [he does not remember them as if they were currently existing]."
"Regarding future phenomena, the wise one remembers his aspiration.
Thus was the verse spoken by the teacher’s son.

In that regard, when passion (*rāga*) is predominant, there is a fire-dissolution; when hatred (*dosa*) is predominant, there is a water-dissolution; when delusion (*moha*) is predominant, there is a wind-dissolution. Some say, "In hatred..."
They say: "In the case of greed, there is a fire-conflagration; in the case of hatred, a water-conflagration; in the case of delusion, a wind-conflagration.
Because the mind or speech in that [state] occurs according to the determination of existence and so forth, it says "or in existence" and so on.

By the two phrases "of such a name" and "of such a clan," he illustrates the dwelling-place of the range, which is designated based on the internal and external. [He is] one who eats the fruit that has come forth.

He subsisted on food consisting of fruits that had fallen of their own accord. The phrase "with a maximum lifespan of eighty-four thousand kappas" refers to the period prior to his making the aspiration.
For one who is turning back, there is no reviewing of past lives through the knowledge of recollecting past existences (*pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa*).

However, it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* (The Knot-Book): "This is a demonstration of the majesty of those who have attained the knowledge of recollecting past existences. Regarding the word "amutra" (there), in the first interpretation:
Recollection was described by way of the "lion's leap," and that indeed was by way of direct order (*anuloma*).
Some also write "by way of reverse order" (*paṭiloma*), but that is difficult to understand. To demonstrate the lion's leap, it was said, "In many millions of eons," and so forth.
By means of this scriptural citation, showing the commonality of the fruit through the commonality of practice, [the Buddha spoke] to the brahmin...

The phrase "he generates respect" precludes the statement that he exalts himself alone. The words "It is indeed good to see such Arahants" direct him toward the very thought that had previously arisen in him.

By the expression "the first breaking forth," it shows that the shell of the egg of ignorance has many layers; by this, it indicates that there was no breaking forth through the eightfold mastery and so forth.
The commentary on the Discourse on Past Lives is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Knowledge of the Divine Eye: 13.

The phrase “for the knowledge of passing away and rebirth” is stated by way of a metaphorical designation for the fruit. For this divine-eye knowledge, because it has visible form as its object, [is so designated].
It has as its object that which is limited, present, internal, and external. It does not take either death or rebirth-linking as its object.
Therefore, it should be understood that the statement, "I know beings according to their kamma," is spoken by way of a metaphorical designation of the fruit.
Because it is based on the divine abiding (*dibbavihāra*), it is called "divine" by way of a metaphorical designation of the cause. However, by this [statement], some teachers—
Those who claim that "the wholesome and unwholesome eyes, the divine eye, and those belonging to the sense-sphere" are intended here are refuted;

for it is the wisdom of the fourth jhāna that is intended here. Regarding the phrases "because of its great radiance" and "because of its great range," it is stated: "according to the rules of grammar.
Thus should be understood the sequence of the arising and the nature of the eleven defilements of the Great Being.
Having increased his light and seen various kinds of forms with the divine eye, the doubt arose in him, "What indeed is this?
This defilement is mentioned in the *Upakkilesa Sutta* in the passage: "And because of my doubt, my concentration fell away;
when concentration had fallen away, the radiance disappeared and the vision of forms vanished. Then, [regarding] the forms...
As he thought, “Doubt arose in me while I was looking; now I shall attend to nothing at all,” he practiced non-attention.
Then, as he attended to nothing at all, sloth and torpor arose. Thereafter, for the sake of abandoning those, he increased the perception of light and looked at forms;
as he looked at the great gifts and rākṣasas in the Himalayas and other places, terror arose.
Then, for the sake of abandoning that [fear], as he reflected, "The danger seen by me does not exist when looked at in its true nature;
what indeed is there to fear in the unseen?", a state of elation arose. In the *Gaṇṭhipada*, however, it is stated:
"Elation arises from seeing divine forms. But that is poorly said, because the meaning is established later by the mention of "longing" (*abhijappā*).

The teacher says: Then, for the sake of abandoning that state of agitation, as he slackened his energy—thinking, "I have exerted firm energy, and because of that this elation arose in me"—bodily coarseness, bodily distress, and bodily lethargy arose.
Then, as he abandoned that [exertion], over-exerted energy arose; therein he saw the fault.

As he looked, excessive laxity of energy arose; then, having abandoned that, with energy proceeding with evenness, and having abandoned the place such as the Himavat mountains out of fear of trepidation, he increased his light toward the world of the gods.
As he looked upon the host of gods, an eager longing termed craving arose. Then, [he thought]: "While I am attending to the form of a single birth, this eager longing..."
“Since this diversity has arisen, I shall now attend to various kinds of forms.
Thus, at times increasing his light toward the world of the devas and at times toward the world of humans, as he attended to various kinds of forms, the perception of diversity arose in him.
Then [he thought]: “As I was attending to various kinds of forms, the perception of diversity arose in me; therefore, now...”
Thinking, "Abandoning the grasping of desirable signs and so forth out of fear of longing and the like, I shall attend only to a single type of form," he did accordingly;
yet, because he had not resolved [his mind] despite having abandoned the defilements, a state of intense contemplation (*abhinijjhāyitatta*) toward forms arose. Thus, the thought occurred:
"I indeed know the radiance, but I do not see the forms," and so forth.

The meaning of this is as follows: "When I attend only to the preliminary illumination, then I perceive the illumination, but I do not see forms with the divine eye; and at the time of seeing forms, I do not perceive the illumination.

Why was this said? Is it not because this [attainment] belongs to the stage of the special qualities (*upakkilesa*)? It is not merely the abandoning of the defilements (*upakkilesa*) that must be accomplished here.
This is for the purpose of showing that although this [mind] has become purified, there is still something further to be done.
Regarding such passages as "doubt is a defilement of the mind," some say: "I abandoned these states by seeing their disadvantage as 'defilements,' not because they had arisen in me at that time.
By the phrase "human [state]," he shows the transcendence of one's natural condition.
"By means of the fleshly eye" refers here to the acquisition of the scriptures (pariyatti); this is compared to [the eye] having color alone as its object.
For here, the word "beings" (satta) refers to color alone, not to all conditioned phenomena as in the phrase "all beings subsist on nutriment.
Low birth and so forth are the outflow and result of delusion. Those endowed with bodily misconduct in a previous past existence...
The connection should be understood through the ellipsis of the text as follows: "They existed [in the past], but now they have been reborn in hell.
For it is stated according to the functions of both: "Knowledge of the destination according to karma has exclusively the past as its object, while the divine eye has the present as its object.
He is called "elderly" because he was spoken of with the intention that he did not know what is appropriate or inappropriate for recluses, or the conduct of the world.

It should be understood that he reviles by means of disparaging their virtues. Some say: "If a noble person (ariyapuggala), who is described as 'fixed and destined for full enlightenment,' were to speak harsh words capable of obstructing the path, he would thereby create a karma leading to the states of misery (apāya) and would thus himself fall into those states;
therefore, [the matter] must be investigated. "Do not exert effort," [it is said].
They say: "Because it was spoken by the Elder, it creates an obstruction to the Path. Previously, the door to the states of misery was closed by the stream-enterer;
therefore, for him there is no obstruction to heaven. They say: "'As before' means that the fruition of the process [of rebirth] occurred as it had been.
For it is said: "This, monks, is growth in the discipline of the Noble One: that one who, seeing a transgression as a transgression, makes amends in accordance with the Dhamma."

Some say that it became normal again through his word. If it is said, "If he does not endure," this is stated with reference to his lack of endurance due to the weakness of the quality of patience possessed by stream-enterers and others, or for the sake of ensuring his future restraint.
Or, because of the absence of a source of happiness such as an object of perception, they become *kālakañcika* asuras. [He says: "O sirs, go from here to a happy destination."

According to the wording, it also pertains to the human realm. "The science of the knowledge of the divine eye" means that the divine eye itself is "knowledge" (*ñāṇa*) in the sense of seeing, and it is "science" (*vijjā*) in the sense of finding out the meaning of this or that matter.
The commentary on the discussion of the knowledge of the divine eye is concluded.

Commentary on the Discourse on the Knowledge of the Destruction of the Taints (Āsavakkhayañāṇakathāvaṇṇanā): 14. Regarding the phrase "When his mind is thus concentrated," does this refer to that very same [state] previously mentioned, or rather to another fourth jhāna consciousness?
In the Commentary as well, it is stated that having emerged from that [state], the first two types of clear knowledge were attained; then, by way of re-entering that very same state...

In order to show that it has been made new and fresh, it is said: "‘So with his mind thus concentrated’—here the fourth-jhāna consciousness that serves as the basis for insight (vipassanā) is to be understood. Here it may be asked:

if that same [consciousness] has been made new by way of re-attainment, then why is it not—as before—described as "the basis for insight, the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā), and the basis for cessation (nirodha)"?

Without stating, "Here, the fourth jhāna consciousness should be understood as that which accomplishes all tasks and bestows all mundane and supramundane qualities," it is merely said, "Here, the fourth jhāna consciousness based on insight (vipassanā) should be understood.
Is it not the case that this very point is stated here because [the fourth jhāna] produces all qualities together with the path of Arahantship?
Is it not the case that [the path] does not arise merely from the production of the first two types of knowledge? It is said:

It should be understood that the "basis for insight" (vipassanā-pādaka) is mentioned here for the purpose of showing that the specific determination of the factors of enlightenment, the path-factors, the jhāna-factors, the modes of progress, and the liberations of the Noble Path occurred by way of the necessary condition of the preliminary-stage insight known as equanimity regarding formations (saṅkhārupekkhā), which leads to emergence.
In this context, [the path arises] because it is included therein, and not merely by having that [insight] as its object.
“By way of a method” means by another manner as well. For what purpose is this section, “These are the taints,” undertaken?
It is for the sake of conforming to the context [of the statement]: “for the sake of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. For at the moment of the path, the mind is being liberated;
at the moment of the fruit, it has been liberated—this is stated according to the principle of identity. For that which is being liberated is itself, at a later time, the liberated one.
That which is liberated is precisely what is called "being liberated" during the prior stage.

For it is only while one is actually eating that, at the conclusion of the meal, one is called a "feeder. "By this, he shows the knowledge of reviewing"—and regarding the knowledge of reviewing, in the *Paṭṭhāna* it is said:
"Having emerged from the path, one reviews the path, the fruit, Nibbāna, and the defilements abandoned..."

"He reviews [it]"—this is stated as the order of arising (*uppattikkama*). However, the order of occurrence (*pavattikkama*) here is stated in two ways: by way of its literal form (*sarūpato*) and by way of its meaning (*atthato*).
Therein, "the knowledge 'it is liberated' arose" is the demonstration of the order of occurrence of the fourfold reviewing-knowledge by way of its literal form.
"Birth is destroyed," and so forth, is by way of its meaning. For that very reason, at the end, it says "he has directly known," which refers to the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*).
He gave this instruction because the knowledge of reviewing does not function in that same way.

Knowing "it is without rebirth-linking," one is said to know "birth is exhausted. As for the statement, "The knowledge of the future through the divine eye is the knowledge of the future limit," this is said because the knowledge of the future limit is dependent upon the divine eye.
The commentary on the discussion of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhayañāṇakathā*) is finished.
Commentary on the discussion of the declaration of lay discipleship (*upāsakattapaṭivedanākathā*): 15.
"From being pleasant to the ear to reaching the heart" is said with reference specifically to the words. "By not exalting oneself," and so forth.

With respect to the person (*puggalavasena*), "pleasing to the ear" refers to the faculty of hearing (*sotindriya*). "Delightful to the range of perception" means delightful to the range of knowledge (*ñāṇāpātha*).
It is either naturally facing downwards, or else the path is free from sorrow (*asoka*); for at that time, sorrow is being abandoned.
It is "not disagreeable" because it is conducive to one's temperament and so forth. Because of the statement "this sweet [Dhamma]," the expression "this Dhamma" appears somewhat redundant.
Therefore, having joined the phrases individually as "this fading away of lust" (*rāgavirāgam imam*), one should then join them collectively as "approach this Dhamma" (*dhammam imam upehi*).
This indicates that some recite it as, "approach the Dhamma itself for the sake of refuge" (*dhammam eva saraṇattham upehi*).
For those who have gone for refuge, by that very act of going for refuge, the Three Jewels destroy fear, terror, miserable rebirths, defilement, suffering, and harm.

"Refuge" (saraṇa) is the name. Going for refuge is a mental state that has dispelled defilements through faith, reverence, and so forth, and which proceeds in the mode of taking that [state] as its ultimate resort.
A sentient being possessing that state goes for refuge. By way of classification, going for refuge is twofold:

supramundane (lokuttara) and mundane (lokiya). Therein, the supramundane occurs at the moment of the path for those who have seen the Truths, through the total eradication of the defilements of going for refuge.
By having Nibbāna as its object, it succeeds in all three Jewels by way of its function.

The mundane [going for refuge] of worldlings succeeds by way of its object—having the qualities of the Buddha and so forth as its object—through the temporary suppression (*tadaṅga-vikkhambhana*) of the defilements that obstruct going for refuge.
In terms of meaning, this is the acquisition of faith in the Three Jewels and the right view rooted in that faith. As for the supramundane [refuge]...
The four fruits of asceticism (*sāmaññaphala*) are the fruit of karmic result (*vipākaphala*); the destruction of all suffering is the fruit of benefit (*ānisaṃsaphala*).
For it is said: “Whoever [takes refuge] in the Buddha and the Dhamma... is liberated from all suffering. Worldly [refuge] is the attainment of existence and enjoyments.
For it is said: “Whoever has gone for refuge to the Buddha. Worldly going for refuge [is characterized] by ignorance, doubt, wrong knowledge, and so forth, regarding the three objects [of refuge].
It becomes defiled; it does not possess great radiance, nor does it have great expansion. For that which is supramundane, there is no defilement.

That which is mundane is twofold, divided into the blameworthy and the blameless. Among these, with respect to other teachers and so forth, it is blameworthy through such acts as surrendering oneself;
that has an undesirable fruit. It is blameless at the time of death; because it is without karmic ripening, it is fruitless. As for the supramundane...
There is no division [among them]. For even in another existence, a noble disciple (ariyasāvaka) does not designate another teacher.
Any lay follower (gahaṭṭha-upāsaka) who has gone for refuge is an upāsaka because of his attendance upon the Triple Gem. His virtue (sīla) consists of the five abstinences (veramaṇi).

His livelihood (ājīva) is a life lived according to the Dhamma, free from the trade of weapons, living beings, meat, liquor, and poisons. The failure of the aforementioned virtue and livelihood constitutes a transgression.
"Failure" means the opposite of success. "Shall we indeed obtain?
is said with reference to those who are destitute; "Shall we indeed be able? is said with reference to those who are prosperous. Therein, "at Verañjā":
it is held up, thus it is the bowl-hold (*paggaha*); the meaning is "by that bowl-hold, by means of the bowl. "Having taken up" means...
This is an illustration. "And it is not allowable" means that although cooked food is generally allowable, it is stated here because it is not well-cooked;
the commentary’s statement, "Even if one receives rice with the grains still visible, it is not allowable to cover it," is the proof for this point.
By the words, "Or I shall lay down a training rule for the disciples," the virtue of purity of livelihood is indicated.

it is a compound meaning "long" (*cira*) with respect to time (*kāla*), and "long-lasting" (*ciratthiti*) with respect to duration (*ṭhiti*).

The meaning has been clarified in the *Gaṇṭhipada*. If "being without taints" (*anāsavatā*) were due to the taints having been ceased by means of the Noble Path, then even minds in the world would be without taints.
For it is not the case that ceased minds take objects; therefore, they [the worldlings' minds] would be "with taints" (*sāsava*) by virtue of the taints that have not yet been ceased.
If this is argued, [the answer is: the path-consciousness of a stream-enterer is [without taints] by virtue of the taints to be abandoned by the higher paths.

it is said that this Venerable One, having attained Arahantship by discerning through hundreds of thousands of methods even a single verse of the Dhamma discourse he had received from the Elder Assaji, and being established in the knowledge of the perfection of a disciple, thought: “Oh, how truly majestic is this True Dhamma!...”

Reflecting, "How wonderful it would be if this True Dhamma were to endure for a long time—even though he has produced in me a great distinction of virtue merely by hearing it from another's mouth, even without the Master of Dhamma being present," he considered that matter and its cause through the knowledge of his own chief disciple: "Of which Blessed Buddhas... She made her request. Then the Blessed One, demonstrating that he had accepted her request, that the time mentioned by her as "this, O Blessed One, is the time" was not actually the right time, and that the [proper] time has no other scope, said, "Wait, you," and so forth.

"Being without teachers and not being exhorted," and so forth—relying on this method regarding their vastness and greatness, the Teacher prescribed for his disciples the Vinaya procedures such as the duties toward preceptors (upajjhāya-vatta) and the training rules (sikkhāpada) corresponding thereto.
Thereafter, he dwelt in Verañjā for twelve years in succession. At that time, the Venerable Sāriputta [was concerned] with the causes for long endurance pointed out by the Teacher.

It exists, because there was the intention to authorize the recitation of the Pātimokkha for the sake of instruction.

he who quickly penetrates the means to that cessation—

Regarding that, the classification according to order will be made clear later in the section on the training rules (*sikkhāpada*). As for the classification according to nature, it begins with the condition of following one who has been suspended (*ukkhepanīyakamma*).

Up to this point, the Elder Venerable Upāli has demonstrated the introduction (*nidāna*) for the entire Vinaya Piṭaka, adorned with seven factors:
reflection, request, time, knowledge of the proper occasion, cause, fruit, and purpose. Therein:

The Elder’s reflection that served as the cause for requesting the formulation of the Vinaya is called *vitakka* (reflection). His actual request, expressed through the words “Now is the time for this, Blessed One,” and so forth, is called *yācanā* (request).
The attainment of seniority, abundance, excellence, great learning, and greatness is called *kāla* (the right time). Only an Omniscient One is truly called *kālaññū* (one who knows the right time).

From the statement, "for the warding off of states [conducive to defilement]," the fruit is known as the warding off of those states that are the basis for the taints (*āsava*).

From the statement, "so that this holy life may endure for a long time," it should be understood that the purpose is the long endurance of the holy life of the Dispensation (*sāsana-brahmacariya*). And there is a verse on this point:
“Reflection, request, time, one who knows the time, the cause, the fruit, and the purpose—these seven factors are the foundation of the Vinaya. 22.
“The inner circle” means the interior circle. For that is inside the others; it is the small circle.
Or: having given [the gift] to those monks by way of granting permission. Those beings who are to be disciplined (*vinetabba*) through the wandering of those Buddhas.

Peaceful happiness (*santaṃ sukhaṃ*), not the happiness of sensation (*vedanāsukhaṃ*).
As if vibrating with movement. "In the ten-thousandfold world-system" is said from the perspective of the devas;

It is stated in the *Anugaṇṭhipada*: "From where did you obtain that? However, some say: "The first [term] looks toward the action;
the second, the object to be given. But the Teacher says: "In the first construction, whatever merit of giving there is..."
"How could it be obtained? For household life is full of obstacles to merit. By this second interpretation, he shows:

nevertheless, he acquiesced because it served as a cause for inspiring faith in Upagutta later on. In this regard—

The resolve of Upagutta should be stated. If it is asked: "What is the purpose of the Buddhas' habit [of appearing as birds]?"—the purpose is that, because of Māra’s transformation, there would have been an obstacle to the Brahmin’s merit.

he gave as an offering every variety of permissible goods without exception.
"How is it that the Blessed One, together with his disciples, went away having set aside such a vast quantity of allowable goods in a heap?

Otherwise, Māra’s desire alone would be fulfilled,
and not that of the twice-born bird;
he might even encounter great evil.
Because of his false pride toward the Tathāgata,
the Blessed One— accepting that gift and not refusing it, thereby using a skillful means to increase the Brahmin’s merit while thwarting Māra’s intention—
departed. This method [is understood] even without the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).

"It is indeed fitting to contemplate the proper method. Now, the Venerable Elder Upāli, having shown the common introductory cause (*nidāna*) for the formulation of the Vinaya,

begins with the individual introductory causes (*nidāna*) known as the specific formulations of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*), and proceeds to explain the classification of persons, subsequent formulations (*anupaññatti*), divisions of offenses, intermediate offenses, and so forth.
In order to demonstrate the various methods after having rendered them free from tangles and obscurities, he said:
"Then the Blessed One, having dwelt at Verañjā for as long as he pleased," and so forth.
Standing here, one should explain the classification of the sequence of all the training rules (sikkhāpada).
Once that is established, the sequence of the causal origins (nidāna) can then be established.

In this regard, for all the training rules (sikkhāpada), four kinds of sequence are obtainable according to their occurrence: the sequence of teaching (desanā-krama), the sequence of abandonment (pahāna-krama), the sequence of practice (paṭipatti-krama), and the sequence of arising (uppatti-krama).
Among these, when the Blessed One was permitting the recitation of the Pātimokkha to the bhikkhus at Rājagaha—
Following the sequence of recitation that had been authorized for the recitation of the Pātimokkha, the Venerable Mahākassapa first asked about the recitation of the Pārājika rules;
immediately after that, he asked about the recitation of the Saṅghādisesa rules;
then, having asked about the recitation of the Aniyata rules and the detailed recitation, he subsequently asked about the Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga in that very same order.
And for the purpose of questioning those matters included within the *Nidāna-uddesa* that had not been specifically enumerated by way of their own form, he also questioned them in the *Khandhaka*.

By this, the *thullaccaya* offenses prescribed in the *Khandhaka* are included. Following the very order in which they were questioned, the Elder Upāli, while teaching all of that—including the classification of the offenses—illuminated the *thullaccaya*, the *dubbhāsita*, the origins of the offenses (*āpatti-samutthāna*), and so forth.

Having included [the material], he taught it; this is the sequence of the teaching here. Furthermore, having selected [material] from both the *Vibhaṅgas* and the *Khandhakas*, the *Parivāra* text was then compiled separately.
It is with reference to this very method that it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
“By this same method, he also incorporated [it] into the *Khandhakas* and the *Parivāra*,” and so forth. Moreover, according to the *Pāḷi*: “By this same method, in both Vinayas...”
"He asked. Being asked again and again, the Venerable Upāli answered"—this much alone was stated; therefore, Mahākassapa questioned him only regarding the two Vibhaṅgas.
But when answering, the Venerable Upāli, while teaching the Nissaggiya offenses, included them within the Khandhaka and Parivāra and taught them as such.
At that time, the textual tradition of the Khandhaka and Parivāra had not yet been separated [into independent sections]; this is the sequence of the teaching. If...
If it is argued that the introduction to the origin (*nidānuddesa*) should be taught first, we say no, because it is impossible.

For since it proceeds according to the method beginning with "For whomsoever there may be an offense," it is not possible [to recite it] until the offenses included in the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) have first been shown.
[As the Buddha said: "Those training rules which have been laid down by me for the monks, I authorize you to recite the Pātimokkha for them."
According to the sequence of the words, it follows that the training rules themselves must be taught first; thus, the order of the recitation of the *pārājika* rules is possible.

Furthermore, because the unwholesome offenses included in the recitation of the *pārājikas* and so forth must be abandoned according to their relative gravity, the order of abandonment is also possible here.

so too the sequence of their arising is possible for these training rules according to their respective occurrence among these three orders. For indeed, whatever is common [to all],...
Regarding that very same matter which had arisen concerning a particular monk, it was laid down for the nuns as well:

placed the rule immediately after the phrase "There [it was] at Vesālī," thus bringing it to Vesālī. Otherwise, for those rules laid down at Bārāṇasī, such as "Monks, [you should not...]"...

1. The Section on Defeat (Pārājikakaṇḍa) 1. The First Defeat:
Commentary on the Recitation-Section of Sudinna (Sudinnabhāṇavāravaṇṇanā)
Here, regarding the first source, one should understand the offense of defeat (*pārājika*) by way of the method for avoiding accusations,
specifically through the elucidation of the person and the subject matter.
In that regard, the Blessed One, having spent the rains retreat at Verañjā, while wandering on tour in due course during the bright fortnight of the month of Kattika—

Thus, having reached Vesālī, the sequence of the text appears as if he remained in Vesālī for eight years until the promulgation of the first *pārājika* training rule; yet the Blessed One did not dwell there for that entire duration.
For after he had authorized Sudinna’s going-forth and full ordination in the presence of his disciples...

was stated not only to show that [the offense] is established by the rule of specific designation (*suddesa-sikkhāpada*) alone, but also to show that it is established by the rule of general designation (*anuddesa-sikkhāpada*) as well, namely, that there is a *pārājika* offense even in the case of animals and so forth.
Alternatively, if he had prescribed the rule of specific designation as being with remainder (*sāvasesa*), then by this rule of general designation...
It is stated for the purpose of showing that they are not established [as offenses]. “In that case, monks, I shall lay down a training rule (sikkhāpada) for the monks”—the meaning is:
“I shall lay down that very same training rule which was first laid down, having made room for those who are innocent despite having a slight fault, and having made it an emphatic repetition.
Otherwise, [in rules] such as “there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for one who speaks otherwise or harasses,” etc., [it would be inconsistent].
The meaning—that by means of two objects one incurs two offenses, or does not incur them—is well-expounded by this other statement as well;
the intention is that it has been made even more firm by way of making it perfectly clear. In the third proclamation and in others as well, he is thus purified.
First, the method for resolving the difficult points (*gaṇṭhipada-naya*) regarding the section beginning with "In the case of that which has a mental basis" (*yassa sacittakapakkhe*) shall be stated.

The phrase "in the case of that which has a mental basis" (*sacittakapakkhe*) is said with reference to drinking intoxicants and so forth when performed without a conscious intent (*acittaka*). However, among those actions with a mental basis, that which is produced exclusively by what is unwholesome (*akusala*)—both of these are called "worldly offenses" (*lokavajja*).
For in the case of drinking intoxicants, having known it as "intoxicant" (*surā*) or "it is not permitted to drink," [one drinks].
In the case of drinking, it is indeed unwholesome; likewise, for nuns, there is no fault in applying ointments for the sake of fragrance or color, nor in applying them for medicinal purposes.
Because of this lack of fault, it is stated merely that [the former] is "not to be considered.

In that context, the statement "it is not permitted, having known" would be inconsistent, because it would entail the undesirable consequence that even a formal offense (*paṇṇattivajja*) could be classified as a worldly offense (*lokavajja*). To avoid this undesirable consequence...
With the desire to avoid [misunderstanding], it is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* of the Vajirabuddhi Thera:

"In this context, the investigation as to whether something is 'with consciousness' (*sacittaka*) or 'without consciousness' (*acittaka*) pertains only to the knowledge of the object (*vatthu*), not to the knowledge of the formal rule (*paññatti*).
If it pertained to the knowledge of the formal rule, all training rules (*sikkhāpada*) would be offenses by nature (*lokavajja*); however, not all training rules are offenses by nature."

"Therefore, it is only in the knowing of the site that [an offense occurs]"—this is logical. Why? Because among the training rules (*sekhiya*), the knowledge of the formal rule (*paññatti*) alone is the criterion, not the mere knowledge of the site.

Furthermore, as it was stated in that very same context: "If someone were to pour liquor into the mouth of one who is fast asleep, and it should enter within, there is an offense; in that case, just as for a nun below the collarbone..."

Regarding the statement, "When one touches another person above the knee, for her who consents through the mind alone without moving the body, the offense is said to be 'merely an act' (kiriyāva) because an act generally arises [therein];
likewise, this too is merely an act at that time," that has not been well-considered, because it fails to establish the state of being exclusively unwholesome.
However, the offense of drinking liquor is indeed exclusively unwholesome.
It is stated with the understanding that even one who perceives [the substance] as marrow incurs [an offense] by drinking it once through a single act.

This, however, is the meaning here: taking the offense under the heading of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*), that training rule for which the mind is exclusively unwholesome (*akusala*) is a "worldly offense" (*lokavajja*).
As for that which is reckoned as "with-mind" (*sacittaka*) or "without-mind" (*acittaka*), [it is the latter].
And in the case of those involving the mind, the mind is exclusively unwholesome; furthermore, that [unwholesomeness] such as drinking liquor and so forth is a worldly offense (*lokavajja*).
Summarizing this point, it is said: "That for which, in the case involving the mind, the mind is exclusively unwholesome, that is a worldly offense.

For this statement, "in the case involving the mind," was spoken with reference to that which is mindless (*acittaka*). Indeed, it is not necessarily [the case] for one who possesses a mind (*sacittaka*).
There is a purpose for the qualification "on the side of being with consciousness" (sacittakapakkhe).

For in this context, on the side of being with consciousness through the mind that knows the formal rule (*paññatti*)—excluding the transgression of the rule—the mind is exclusively unwholesome (*akusala*);

whereas on the side of being with consciousness through the mind that knows the underlying matter (*vatthu*), the mind may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate. Therefore, it is said: "On the side of being with consciousness, his mind is exclusively unwholesome."
"It is not so called" means that it was stated: "The remainder is [governed by] conventional rule (paṇṇatti-vajja).

Because there is no transgression in the case of overweening pride (adhimāna), and because it is not subject to formal designation in a dream—meaning that even if a shadow of transgression exists in a dream, it is said to be of a non-designatable nature.
Furthermore, this statement was made for the purpose of both strengthening and loosening [the rules]; therefore, as for what was stated...

Regarding the section on the external introductory narrative, it should be understood that the statement beginning with, "The purpose of making firm what was loose is stated as being for the most part," is indeed well-said.
The commentary on the Story of the Female Monkey is finished.

Those who dwell in the Vajjī country are called Vajjins; their sons are the Vajjiputtas.
"As much as required" means as much as is needed according to one's purpose or intention. In this regard, it was said: "without having renounced the training or disclosed one's weakness."
That [rule] is appropriate when the renunciation of training and the failure to disclose weakness—which are associated with it—have been laid down, and not otherwise.
Nevertheless, this was said with reference to what must now be prescribed:
"How indeed can the group-of-six monks keep extra robes? The monks of Āḷavī are having huts built that are of improper size."

Or if he claims superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*), he must not be ordained when he arrives. For a subsequent rule (*anupaññatti*) has the purpose of strengthening what has been established and loosening what has been made restrictive.

Indeed, it has the purpose of showing the restriction for one who has committed a *pārājika* offense or another offense, because it functions as a subsequent rule characterized by an extension of the original definition.
Thus, rather than being stated at the end, it is stated at the beginning—just like the subsequent rule "whether from a village or from the forest"—when [the candidate] is complete.
Regarding this training rule:
"The introduction, the analysis of the matrix, and the detailed exposition which determines it;
thereafter, the classification of offenses, and non-offense in other cases."

This method should be understood. In this regard, the threefold basis—namely, the case of Sudinna, the case of the monkey, and the case of the Vajjiputta monks—is called the *nidāna* (origin) of this training rule. From that origin, the analysis of this *mātikā* (matrix) arose: "Whosoever, monk, having entered upon the training and the way of life of the monks...
[as above] ...is not in communion. For therein, even down to...

Regarding the phrase "to one who is an animal," by using the feminine gender and case-ending, [it implies]: "Friend, it is true that a training rule was laid down by the Blessed One, but that was for a woman, not for a man, not for a paṇḍaka, nor for a hermaphrodite.

Just as in the case of the *makkaṭi-pārājika* (the monkey-offense), another person might likewise cast a deceptive pretext; therefore, this [text] is intended to show such an opportunity for the absence of deception.

It is said. Regarding the introduction (nidāna) concerning the story of the monkey, the division of the matrix (mātikā) statement as “even with one who is an animal” is not made merely to show the accomplishment of sexual intercourse with a woman;
therefore, the commentary (vibhaṅga) is its regulator—the commentary that regulates the intended meaning of that matrix.
For in the commentary it says: “Three kinds of women. Three kinds of hermaphrodites.”
