"Three types of paṇḍakas; three types of men; three paths for a human woman...
[and so on] ...two paths for a male animal"—in this manner, the rule was established by closing off every possible occasion for fault.
Here it is asked: If that is so, then not only by way of a common training rule (*sādhāraṇasikkhāpada*) or by way of a change of gender (*liṅgaparivattanavasena*), but—
In the Vibhaṅga, it would have to be stated for both monks and nuns that they are "one who has entered upon the training and the way of life.
By not stating this, a nun who remains in the status of a monk due to the manifestation of the male organ might say:

"At the time of my full ordination, I did not enter upon the training and the way of life of the monks; therefore, even though I have not formally renounced the training, [I am not excluded] by means of sexual intercourse..."
"Am I one who has committed a *pārājika* offense? It is said: it should not be stated in that way, because it would lead to an undesirable consequence (*aniṭṭha*).
If it were said that "one who has entered upon the training and the mode of life" applies to nuns as well, it would follow that there is also a renunciation of the training for nuns;
and that is undesirable. This is another undesirable consequence: [the conclusion that] "all training rules (*sikkhāpada*) are indeed common, not uncommon."
Furthermore, it was stated, "I allow you, monks, that very same upajjhāya," and so forth, for the purpose of showing that this person has entered upon the training and way of life of the monks;
moreover, one who, having made such a pretext, engages in sexual intercourse becomes one defeated (pārājika), just like the Vajjiputtakas.
For, in the absence of the statement "one who has entered upon the training and way of life of the monks," they [would not have been considered defeated].

When it was said by the Blessed One, "Bhikkhus, you have fallen into an offense entailing defeat (pārājika)," it should be understood that some who were addressed as "bhikkhus" remained within the marks of a bhikkhu,

while others had disrobed (vibbhanta), as evidenced by their statement: "Venerable Ānanda, if we were now to receive the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One, we would receive the full ordination."

"Then, there is a distinction regarding the offense (*āpatti-bheda*). This means that from the *Vibhaṅga*, there is a distinction regarding the offense, such as: "If the body is visible, it is a *pārājika*; if it is mostly visible, it is a *thullaccaya*," and so forth. "There is no offense in another way than that.

This means that from that very same *Vibhaṅga*, there is indeed a distinction regarding non-offense (*anāpatti-bheda*) in a manner other than the way the offense was described. "If one consents, it is an offense."
"For if the Vibhaṅga did not exist, it would not be known that there is no offense when one does not consent to an act involving a Pārājika.
Thus far, the meaning of the verse has been stated in brief. And here:
"The origin, the analysis of the matrix, and the purpose of the Vibhaṅga;"
"And the manner of non-offense; first, that which is purposeless.
Having shown this method, the meaning of all training rules (sikkhāpada) should be explained. How so?
By the manner in which each training rule was laid down by the Blessed One, one must consider whether that manner is capable or incapable [of being fulfilled].

The introduction (nidāna) is twofold; this is the classification of the introduction. The matrix (mātikā) is also twofold: that which depends on an introduction and that which does not depend on an introduction.
Among these, the training rules (sikkhāpada) beginning with the fourth pārājika depend on an introduction.

For it was not the case that the monks from the banks of the Vaggumudā themselves brought about for themselves the non-existent superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma) characterized by false speech and then proclaimed it.
For they praised the superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma) to householders one after another, yet that alone did not constitute a matter of defeat (pārājika).

In this regard, the Blessed One, using that as a pretext, established the rule of defeat by making that incident the formal cause (nidāna); therefore it is said, "dependent on the cause" (nidānāpekkha).
Having understood the training rules (sikkhāpada) that depend on a cause in this manner, one should likewise understand those that are the opposite.
They should be understood as being independent of their specific causes;

this is the classification of the matrix (mātikā). This is for the purpose of illustrating the manner of dividing the matrix by way of showing the various types of objects, applications, intentions, and constraints sufficient for a root-offense, or for the purpose of showing the distinctions among offenses when there is a transgression due to the insufficiency of those factors or the absence of one or another of them.

And because it is for the purpose of showing that there is no offense when [the conditions] are absent—it should be understood that the Vibhaṅga (Analysis) is undertaken throughout as a detailed exposition of the Mātikā (Summary), based upon these three purposes.
Herein, however, the term "bhikkhu" is used merely to illustrate the meaning of the word through its various etymologies:
"one who begs is a bhikkhu," "one who has entered upon the practice of begging is a bhikkhu," and "one who wears torn robes is a bhikkhu."

Or it is used as a conventional designation (*samaññā*), occurring merely to indicate the locus of the application of the term "bhikkhu" without regard for the actual attainment of the state of a bhikkhu;
or it occurs in connection with the formal ordination (*upasampadā*), as in: "Come, bhikkhu!"—thus one is a bhikkhu; "one who is ordained through the going for refuge"—thus one is a bhikkhu;
"one who is ordained by a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations"—thus one is a bhikkhu.

Or, the analysis (*vibhaṅga*) is observed with equanimity because it possesses all the terms of asceticism (*sāmañña*), whether it proceeds by way of illustrating the accomplishment of the state of a bhikkhu— such as "a bhikkhu who is excellent," "a bhikkhu who is essential," "a bhikkhu in training" (*sekkha*),
or "an adept" (*asekkha*)— or by way of illustrating a bhikkhu endowed with those qualities that constitute a bhikkhu,
such as in the case of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) concerning other matters.

It should be understood that [the term] "equanimity" (ajjhupekkhitā) refers to that which proceeds by way of the six doors and by way of observing the legal case (*adhikaraṇa*) and so forth, because such [observation] is absent in the other cases.

Among those, the passage beginning with "three women" is intended to show the restriction regarding the object (*vatthu*), while the passage beginning with "for one who engages in sexual intercourse with a human woman on the three paths,
there is an offense of defeat" (*pārājika*) is intended to show the restriction regarding the application (*payoga*).

The passage beginning with "when it has occurred, if a bhikkhu’s intention to engage [in sexual intercourse] is present" and so forth proceeds by way of demonstrating the determination of the mind (*cittaniyama*).

The passage beginning with "if he consents, there is an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*); if he does not consent, there is no offense" and so forth proceeds for the purpose of showing the presence or absence of an offense based on the existence or non-existence of the determination of the mind, given that the determination of the physical act and the object (*vatthupayoganiyama*) is already established.
The passage beginning with "if most of the corpse has been devoured, there is an offense of serious transgression (*thullaccaya*)" and so forth...
It proceeds for the purpose of showing the classification of offenses in the event of transgression due to the inadequacy of the object;
it proceeds for the purpose of showing non-offense because there is no transgression when the mind’s determination is deficient, even if one does not consent.
Thus, in the other training rules as well, the *vibhaṅga* (analysis) serves as the method according to what is applicable; this is its purpose.
The section on non-offenses (*anāpattivāra*), however, is threefold by way of illustrating non-offenses: from the root offense, from a portion other than that, and from all offenses.
Among these, the first proceeds in reliance upon three purposes, just like the *Vibhaṅga*. What are the three?

To illustrate the state of being purposeful or purposeless through the extraction or non-extraction of the matrix-terms (*mātikāpada*)—both those with meaning and those without meaning—in a manner other than [the usual], for the sake of showing their utility or lack thereof.
This is for the purpose of showing the sequence of practice otherwise than that, and also for the purpose of providing an answer regarding the capacity for an offense.

How so? In the *eḷakaloma-sikkhāpada*, the words "If wool should arise for a monk who has set out on a journey, it may be accepted by that monk if he so desires" are merely words intended to illustrate the basic case (*vatthu*).
Regarding those called "meaningless," there is no offense for them.

By such methods as, "There is no offense when wool has arisen for one who has not set out on a journey, provided it is accepted by one who desires it," the fact that [other cases] are purposeless due to not being removed otherwise is illustrated;
namely, in the matrix (mātikā), the phrase "one should engage in sexual intercourse" is meaningful.
In order to demonstrate that this [offense] possesses a specific purpose, it is stated: "There is no offense for one who does not know and does not consent.

Since there is an offense through the state of knowing and consenting, whereas there is no offense for one who does not practice [the act], therefore the intention of the *mātikā*—which states, "Whosoever, a bhikkhu, should practice sexual intercourse, he is defeated and no longer in communion"—is thus established.

Regarding the five factors stated as: "another’s possession, the perception that it is another’s possession, valuable property, the intention to steal, and the act of taking away"—in order to explain the exemption from offense even when these factors are fulfilled in the case of property belonging to ghosts or animals, provided the value is sufficient for an offense, it was said:
"There is no offense if it belongs to a ghost," and so forth. There is no offense if one knows: "This [is not mine]," "This..."

However, statements such as "Give this," "Bring that," "There is need for this," or "Make this allowable" (kappiya) should be understood as being spoken for the purpose of demonstrating the sequence of practice other than that [previously mentioned]. Up to this point,
the meaning of the verse beginning with "The analysis of the nidāna and the mātikā" has been elucidated.

In this regard, first, the initial promulgation was established after the First Enlightenment had passed, and because it was established during the time when the Venerable Sudinna was eight years old, it was established at a time when he had attained the greatness of seniority by years.

The second supplementary promulgation arose at a time when he had attained the greatness of great learning. For that Venerable One, having committed the offense of defeat regarding a female monkey, [acted] as he did with those matters connected to women...
Thinking that female animals were not intended in the training rules (*sikkhāpada*), just as they were not intended here [in this case], he said:
"It is true, friend, that a training rule was laid down by the Blessed One; however, it was for a human woman, not for a female animal.

This third supplementary rule (*anupaññatti*) arose at a time when [the Vajjiputtakas] had attained the pinnacle of gain and greatness. For those Vajjiputtakas had indeed reached the height of wealth and influence.
Having become ordained, they ate as much as they desired, bathed, and lay upon excellent couches; thus they provided the basis for the third supplementary rule (anupaññatti).
Since these [offenses] arose within the Saṅgha that had reached vastness and magnitude, and since they themselves had also reached vastness and magnitude, it is said:
"Herein, vastness and magnitude are also found. This is the first Pārājika training rule (sikkhāpada).
It should be understood that this [offense] is designated based on three kinds of objects and four kinds of times.
In this context, "anyone who" (*yo pana*) is the term for exhaustive inclusion. "A monk" (*bhikkhu*) is the term for restricting the excessive application of that [inclusion].

"One who has entered upon the training and livelihood of monks" (*bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno*) is its qualifying statement; for not everyone who merely bears the name "monk" [is necessarily subject to this rule].

Whatever training has been prescribed by the Blessed One as the minimum to be trained in by bhikkhus ordained by any form of ordination, and whatever livelihood has been declared therein as "living together"—he indeed fulfills both of these.
But when did he fulfill them? Immediately upon being ordained by any form of ordination whatsoever.
Whether one knows both of these or does not know them, by virtue of having accepted them, one is said to have "entered" (samāpanna) into that state.
"Living together" means as long as one has not renounced the training and has not reached the state of a *pārājika*. As for what was stated in the Andhaka-ṭīkā:
"One who fulfills the training has entered the training; one who does not transgress the livelihood has entered the livelihood."

That was stated by way of the highest limit. For one who does not fulfill the training, or who is full of sensual thoughts and the like, or who transgresses even a single remaining rule of right livelihood, is certainly not called "one who has entered upon the training and the right livelihood.
However, by way of the highest limit, the fourfold combination is obtained: there is a bhikkhu who has entered upon the training and possesses the virtues...
Reflecting thus: there is one who has not entered upon the livelihood but transgresses a training rule while being without consciousness;
there is one who has not entered upon the training but has entered upon the livelihood, being full of sensual thoughts and the like, yet remains free from offense;

there is one who has neither entered upon the training nor entered upon the livelihood, having fallen into an offense without remainder; and there is one who has both entered upon the training and entered upon the livelihood, fulfilling the training.

If it is argued that this very fourth type of bhikkhu—one who does not transgress even while living—is intended here as the "excellent" (ukkaṭṭha) one, for it is not fitting for the Blessed One to speak of one who is not excellent; [we reply: No, because that would contradict the statement:
“In this context, that which is the training in higher virtue is the training intended. If the intention were to include only the excellent, then [the word] “training”...
The intention is that only this much should be stated: "the three trainings. For one who has attained the three trainings is the most excellent of all.
If it is argued that only the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*) is mentioned because of the subsequent statement, "he might engage in sexual intercourse," we say no;
for even he is incapable of such an act. Indeed, one who fulfills the training in higher virtue and does not transgress the rules of conduct (*sājīva*)—
The intention is that one who is capable of engaging in sexual intercourse would indeed engage in it only while failing to fulfill that training and transgressing the way of life (*sājīva*);
therefore, the meaning here should be understood in this way.

Since the way of life, which consists of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*), includes only the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*) and not the other two—the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-sikkhā*) or the training in higher wisdom (*adhipaññā-sikkhā*)—[the former alone is intended].
Therefore it is said: “In this context, that which is the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*) is the training intended here.
Consequently, the way of life (*sājīva*) that encompasses the training in higher virtue is called the “training in way of life” (*sikkhāsājīva*).

Thus, the term “training” (*sikkhā*) was employed for the purpose of specifying the way of life. For the very purpose of illustrating that meaning, the *Vibhaṅga* does not refer to the training itself, but [speaks] regarding that...
"Because he trains, he is said to have entered upon the right mode of livelihood. By this it is shown that this is indeed a single point of meaning.
And because the training begins immediately after the attainment of full ordination (*upasampadā*), one is said both "to train" and "to have entered [the mode of livelihood].
One who has thus come to be reckoned as "one who has entered upon the training and the right mode of livelihood"—such a person...

The meaning that "depending on such a condition, at a later time, one might engage in sexual intercourse without having renounced the training known as livelihood and without having disclosed one's weakness in that very matter" is logical; however, this contradicts the method of the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
Since that [contradiction] cannot be a reason for rejection, one must proceed in accordance with it.
But here the underlying intention must be sought, which is now stated:
in all the training rules, this alone is the common characteristic of a bhikkhu, namely, "one who has entered upon the training and the mode of life of bhikkhus.

Even a disciple whose taints are destroyed (an arahant) incurs an offense that is unintentional, as does one still in training (a sekha). But an ordinary person (a puthujjana) incurs even those that are intentional; therefore—

Considering that this characteristic of a bhikkhu is common to both those in training (sekha), those beyond training (asekha), and ordinary worldlings (puthujjana) bhikkhus, the term "one who has entered upon the training and the mode of livelihood" (*sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno*) is formed by combining them through the grammatical method of retaining only one part of a compound with identical initial sounds (*sarūpa-ekadesekasesa-naya*).
This is because, by employing a superior term (*ukkaṭṭha*), the inclusion of non-superior instances is established; thus, in the Aṭṭhakathā, only the superior [category] is mentioned.
It has been stated. To ensure that very [practice] is accomplished, after providing the resolution for the absence of a formal training rule (*sikkhāpada*) in the passage, "He trains in that;
therefore he is said to have entered upon the mode of livelihood," it is further stated:

"Since he has also entered upon that which is not a training, he should be understood by way of meaning as one who has entered upon the training. And: "Without renouncing that training which he has entered upon, and that mode of livelihood..."
This is the intended meaning of the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) when it says, "having entered [the meditative attainment], without having manifested weakness therein.

However, within this intended meaning, it should be understood that only the training in higher virtue (*adhisīlasikkhā*) is mentioned because it is universally beneficial and because the Vinaya deals primarily with virtue.
And just as one who undertakes a training rule (*sikkhāpada*) is said to undertake virtue, so too is it here.
Thus, it is appropriate to say that one who renounces the training rules renounces the training known as virtue (*sīla*);
therefore, it is stated therein: "without having renounced that training which he has undertaken.
One who, having renounced the training, engages in sexual intercourse does not indeed "abolish" [the status of a monk]. For he is no longer a bhikkhu.

Having offered it, he consumed it; thus was the rule laid down: "Whosoever, however, is a bhikkhu... Up to this point, what needs to be said regarding the phrase "one who shares the training and the livelihood" has been stated in brief.
What is the purpose of this specific expression? Is it not already established that "whosoever, however, is a bhikkhu who, without having renounced the training, [declares] his weakness..."?

If it is argued that one should say only this much—"Because he has not made himself known... [and so on]... there is no communal living"—that should not be said, because it leads to an undesirable consequence.

However, even for one who has entered upon the training and the mode of livelihood, but who is a "living-in-theft" (theyyasaṃvāsa) bhikkhu or the like by mere designation or mere profession, there is indeed a renunciation of the training.
And without having renounced the training, [to engage in] sexual intercourse...

For one who partakes [of the act], there is an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika). Or, in the case of one who has subsequently fallen into an offense entailing expulsion and is no longer endowed with the training and the way of life (sikkhāsājīva), that offense applies to him;

or in the case of one who, due to being a "half-impotent" (pakkhapaṇḍaka), is no longer endowed with the training and the way of life because he has entered into the state of impotence, that same offense applies to him as well.
Regarding both of these: "And in the case of the side of the state of impotence, the half-impotent [is considered] for the purpose of full ordination (upasampadā)..."
It is stated that "it is not a basis" (*na vatthu*); therefore, it is established that in the other case it *is* a basis.
In that case, one who is ordained while in the state of being a paṇḍaka does not possess the training and the mode of livelihood because of his paṇḍaka-nature;

thus, due to the absence of any training to be relinquished, he—without having formally renounced the training—performs sexual intercourse with another by means of the mouth, such as grasping the genitals, and so forth.
The intention is: "If he were to enjoy [it], how could there be for him an offense involving defeat (pārājika)? This method applies later only to one who does not obtain the side of the non-paṇḍaka;

however, for one who does obtain it, just as there is no death even when the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is interrupted during the moment of attaining wholesome states of formless beings, so too the state of being a bhikkhu exists on the side of the paṇḍaka condition. Or, for one who consents to co-residence...
There is no state of living in communion by theft for one who has committed the ultimate offense, as there is for one who has committed the ultimate offense;
nor does he cause [the Sangha] to share a sleeping place and so forth. However, unlike one who has committed the ultimate offense, he does not serve to complete the quorum of a chapter;

he has not attained the training and the common way of life, yet he belongs to the other side. This is his distinction from that [other person]. Is he possessed of a root-cause (sahetuka), or is he without a root-cause (ahetuka)?

It is not without cause. For since full ordination (*upasampadā*) was permitted for him on the side of those who are not paṇḍakas, it is because he possesses a rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) with a cause.
If it is asked, "Why was it not permitted even on the side of his being a paṇḍaka?"—it is because he is a paḍaka, just like an *opakkamika-paṇḍaka* (one who becomes a paṇḍaka through external means).

Furthermore, by the phrase "one who has entered upon the training and the mode of livelihood" (*sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno*), his undertaking of the training (*sikkhāsamādāna*) is indicated; and that undertaken training...
It is appropriate to say, "without having renounced [the training] there and without having manifested one's weakness," and not otherwise;

for this reason, to avoid the aforementioned undesirable consequence, it was said: "Whatever bhikkhu, having undertaken the training and the way of life of the bhikkhus, without having renounced the training...
and so forth. And as it is here, so too [in the case of]: "Whatever bhikkhu... [and so on].

"Having undertaken the training and the mode of livelihood, and without having renounced the training or disclosed one's weakness, if one should take what is not given—reckoned as theft—from a village or from the forest;
or if one should have a robe made the size of the Sugata’s robe or larger;
[or] if one should cut [it], it is a *pācittiya*," and so on—in this manner it should be applied in all cases. "Even down to [taking from] an animal," etc.
This is stated with reference to a human woman; for it would not be appropriate to say, "let alone a eunuch or a male.
The remainder follows the method explained in various other places.
This, then, is the exposition of the first *pārājika* in the *mātikā*.
Commentary on the Fourfold Discussion of Discipline (Catubbidhavinayakathāvaṇṇanā) 45.

Regarding the word "having extracted" (*nīharitvā*): here the meaning is "having extracted from the Dispensation" (*sāsanato*). [As it is said: "Upananda, a bhikkhu endowed with five factors should not be subjected to interrogation.
Which five? He does not know the Sutta; he does not know what is in accordance with the Sutta... and so forth.
Thus, having extracted and proclaimed the Sutta and that which is in accordance with the Sutta from the beginning of the formal teaching (pariyatti-sāsana), they said: "There is no offense;

such is the learning and the inquiry of our teachers. Thus, having extracted and proclaimed the Teachers' Tradition (ācariya-vāda) from the beginning of the formal teaching, in the case of the Bhārukacchaka incident, they said: "The Venerable Upāli spoke thus..."
“There is no offense, friend, if it was in a dream,” they declared, having drawn their own conclusion from the very beginning of the formal teaching (pariyatti-sāsana).
It was by virtue of that personal judgment (*attanomati*) that the Elder attained the rank of foremost among those who possess such wisdom. Moreover, this was said by the Blessed One:
“If one, being spoken to by one who is not fully ordained—whether by one for whom a rule has been laid down or by one for whom one has not—disregards him... [there is] an offense.”
"Regarding the *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing). For therein, the Sutta is called "that which is laid down" (*paññatta*). The remaining three [parts of the Vinaya] are called "not laid down" (*apaññatta*).
Therefore, this verse, "The Vinaya is fourfold, O Great Elders," is well-spoken. With reference to this, it was said by the Elder Nāgasena:
"By the 'directly spoken word' (*āhaccapada*) means by the collection of words spoken directly concerning the eight grounds for censure; that is, by what has been uttered."

The intended meaning is: "by means of a collection of words uttered from the throat. "By its essence" (rasena) means by the essence of that which was spoken directly [by the Buddha], that is, by the analytical determination extracted therefrom; for the *suttānuloma* is like the shadow of the *sutta*.

The "Teacher's Statement" (*ācariyavāda*)—which is called the "Teacher's Lineage" (*ācariyavaṃsa*)—is authoritative only as it has been handed down through the succession of teachers mentioned in the Canon (*pāḷi*).

For the purpose of seeing. *Adhippāya* (intention) is that which proceeds by way of reasoning and deliberation, established through logical justification, and which serves as a substitute for direct perception and other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Regarding the term *adhippāya*, some explain its meaning as "one's own opinion.
Although it is stated here in the *Parivāra-aṭṭhakathā* that "what is called 'in accordance with the Suttas' refers to the four Great Authorities" (*mahāpadesa*), [it is nevertheless accepted].

Thus, what is meant by way of meaning is that which is established by the method of the great authorities (*mahāpadesa*), namely: what is rejected and what is not rejected, what is permitted and what is not permitted, and what is allowable and what is unallowable.

In this context, since "place" (*ṭhāna*), "occasion" (*okāsa*), and "authority" (*padesa*) are synonyms for "cause," as seen in the Teaching such as, "Ānanda, it is impossible, it is out of the question," and likewise "the ground for censure" and "the ground for lack of right view."

And because it is said, “Furthermore, ‘not having seen’ is one portion,” they are called *mahāpadesā* (great authorities) from the worldly perspective; thus, the meaning is that they are great reasons (*mahākāraṇāni*).
Here, what is intended by “reason” is an indicative cause (*ñāpaka-hetu*). Their greatness, however, is due to their vast scope, just like the great primary elements (*mahābhūtāni*).
They are of two kinds: the great authorities of the Vinaya and the great authorities of the Sutta. Among these, the great authorities of the Vinaya...
They apply themselves to the Vinaya; the others apply themselves to both. For that very reason, in the *Parivāra* and the *Anuyogavatta*, it is said:
"He does not know the Dhamma; he does not know what is in accordance with the Dhamma. Therein, "Dhamma" refers to the two remaining Piṭakas, setting aside the Vinaya Piṭaka.
"What is in accordance with the Dhamma" refers to the four Great Authorities (*mahāpadesa*) among the Suttantas. Among those, as for the one who [does not know] the Dhamma...

If one knows the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, but does not know the Vinaya or what is in accordance with the Vinaya, he thinks, "I am protecting the Dhamma," and thus makes the Vinaya contrary to the Vinaya;
another, thinking, "I am protecting the Vinaya," makes the Dhamma contrary to the Dhamma. One who knows both fulfills both.
Herein, this is merely the introduction: regarding that, the first [case] is where one misbehaves in the sense of:
"If he consents to the insertion, and consents to what has been inserted, to its remaining, and to its withdrawal, there is an offense; if he does not consent, there is no offense.
This venerable one, when there is the conjunction of a tactile object to be experienced as pleasant and the body-faculty, being clearly aware of it—
Having delimited that one is said to "consent" merely by the arising of a bodily pleasant feeling,
he [the author] implies that there would be an offense of *pārājika* even for one who lacks the intention to repeat the act; likewise, this applies to one who—

whether due to the nature of the bedding or a defect in the womb— experiences neither a painful, unpleasant feeling nor a bodily sensation at all because their body has been struck by wind (flatulence), regardless of whether they know it or not.

Having cited the Sutta passage, “There is no offense for one who does not consent,” he creates the contingency that there would be no offense even for one whose intention is to engage in sexual intercourse;

likewise, by taking the case of a *dukkaṭa* offense—wherein a *saṅghādisesa* occurs if emission happens through an effort made with lust for emission, let alone with lust for sexual intercourse—he turns a point of *dukkaṭa* into a point of *saṅghādisesa*.
In this way, he renders the Vinaya contrary to the Vinaya.

The other says, "Since it is stated that 'there is no offense for one who does not know,' then for one who knows, whether or not there is pleasant feeling, there is consent (sādiyanā) simply by virtue of knowing.
Thus, even for one who does not intend repeated practice, he commits an offense in a situation where there is no offense;
he turns what is blameless into what is blameworthy, and in this way, he perverts the Dhamma. However, one who knows both [cases]—[for a monk...]
"Because of the statement, 'the mind of service is established,' here the mind of service alone is the criterion;
through its presence there is an offense of *pārājika*, and through its absence there is no offense. Having said this, one protects and fulfills both.
In this manner, a purposeful application should be made for all training rules (*sikkhāpada*) as far as possible.

Because it was established by being excluded from the Canon (pāḷi) after having been included in the Council (saṅgīti), it is "excluded from the Canon" in terms of its meaning, method, and conformity;
the sense is that it proceeds by way of a decision that has entered into the Canon and proceeds by way of a decision that has not yet entered [into the formal Canon].
Although the Blessed One knew, "He will not uproot it," he spoke merely so that future generations might know their opinion.
And for the purpose of showing that [the Sangha] should take my word as authoritative, at the time of his Parinibbāna he said:
"If it so desires, Ānanda, after my passing away, let the Sangha abolish the minor and lesser training rules.
By this, it is established that even a training rule that has been laid down may be abolished by whichever Sangha has been authorized by the Blessed One to do so.
“His [the teacher’s] exposition is in accordance with the established rules and clarifies what is additional; it was certainly already permitted by the Blessed One.
Furthermore, this is for the purpose of showing that among the families of teachers regarding the training rules on what is deficient or excessive, no mutual dispute should be raised.
Why is the Saṅgha not to be abolished? Because it shows the danger of mutual dispute. And by the Blessed One: “By all of you…”
It is said: "One should train with those who are united, harmonious, and non-contentious. In this regard, because some elders spoke thus, it appeared as if they were speaking of something else;

therefore, [the Buddha] acted so that one should train only with those who are non-contentious, having announced the motion consisting of a second proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*) even in the absence of such [dispute].
The undertaking [of this work] is also for the purpose of making it clear according to one’s own understanding.

In that regard, because of the statement, “In the commentaries on the Sutta, Abhidhamma, and Vinaya,” it should be understood that this exposition is common to all three Piṭakas; however, the passage beginning with “Now, furthermore, this is allowable” (atha panāyaṃ kappiyaṃ) pertains only to the Vinaya.
“Similar to the Saṅgha of the makers” means similar to the Saṅgha of those who performed the recitation. “Without setting aside the fourfold set beginning with the Sutta...”
In the *Gaṇṭhipada* of the Elder Dhammasiri, it is stated: "It is like a Saṅgha of performers for an action that is not contrary [to the Sutta].
That is incorrect, because those words—"The Sutta alone is more powerful; for the Sutta is irrefutable, being like a Saṅgha of performers"—are inconsistent with them.
However, in the *Pākatika Gaṇṭhipada*, it says: "Having determined that matter, it is like a Saṅgha of performers for that."
It has been stated. "An opponent" (paravādī) means one who understands our own system but belongs to another school; this is what is meant.
How is it that an opponent [asserts] something in accordance with the Sutta? The Sutta passage, "Except for water and tooth-wood," belongs to our own school (sakavādī);
because it is in accordance with that, even the water inside a coconut fruit is indeed water—this is the position of the opponent as well.
“When the water of a coconut is old, it binds bile;
that same water, when fresh, subdues bile and strengthens the bodily tissues.
When the opponent had spoken thus, the proponent, because he was an expert in the nature of grain-fruits and because of the pervasiveness of their nutritive function, [replied]:
Saying, “That is only for the time being,” he rejects it.

Regarding the opponent’s claim that it is the Teacher’s doctrine—that “even though one avoids the toll by entering the vicinity, it is still theft”—when the opponent states, “One who acts in such a way incurs a *pārājika* offense,” the proponent replies: “He avoids the toll; there is an offense...”
Having shown the sutta "of a dukkaṭa" together with the words from the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā found in that very place, he refutes [the opponent's view], stating:
"For one who acts in such a way, it is indeed a dukkaṭa. Regarding the phrase "another person’s own intention," here [it means]:

for one who exerts effort thinking, "I will steal another's property before the meal," or "I will take it before the meal," even though it becomes after the meal, it is only the preliminary effort (*payoga*) of the "before-the-meal" [act].

When the opponent says, "Therefore, because you are of the Theravāda school, one who stands as the owner of the original value (mūlaṭṭha) is indeed guilty of a pārājika offense," the proponent refutes this by showing the Sutta:
"If he steals that property either before or after that agreement, there is no offense for the one standing as the owner of the original value.
Thus he rejects [the opponent's position].

Regarding the phrase "Paro suttaṃ": having shown that the sutta written in the *Paṭṭhāna*—"A state with an indeterminate cause is a condition, by way of object-condition, for a state with a cause fixed in the rightness"—the proponent of his own school (sakavādī) rejects the opponent's (paravādin) assertion that "Nirvana alone is not the object of the Noble Path," on the grounds that it does not conform to such suttas as those concerning the triad of objects (*ārammaṇattika*). This concludes the section on conformity to the suttas.
For it is only that which is actually included in the discourse (sutta) that is called [a canonical text], and nothing else.

Therefore, although it is established by the mere statement "it is known to have come down in the Pāḷi," the Master [Buddhaghosa] says, "it is known to have come down in the Pāḷi as it was entered into the three councils (saṅgīti)," and so forth. For such a thing is a careless scribal error, according to the Teacher.
And because of the saying, "Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless; heedlessness is the path of death," having eaten what was given as food...
"Having avoided dangers and dwelling with mindfulness established, one is permanent.
A discourse that has ascended to such a meaning should not be accepted; therefore it was said:

"If it is not so understood," which implies that even when [the meaning] is established, "if it is not so understood, it does not descend [into the text], it does not coincide [with it]. This is because of what was stated: "or a non-Buddhist discourse."
Even one’s own Sutta should not be accepted if it does not accord with the meaning.

Regarding the two methods—“one’s own teacher’s doctrine” (*ācariyavāda*) and so forth—one should understand the words of the *Aṭṭhakathā* found here and there as resulting from scribal errors, by correlating them with the doctrines of the Elders (*theravāda*).
Furthermore, this "teacher’s doctrine" refers to the doctrine of another; for instance, when an opponent says: “Root-seed means turmeric and ginger.”

"Regarding the passage: 'If one cuts, or causes to be cut, or breaks [vacā]... pe ... a seed while perceiving it as a seed, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya),' since you have recited this, for one who cuts a turmeric root, there is an offense of expiation.

When this was said, the proponent of the opposing view, having shown the passage beginning with "or whatever other things there are that grow from roots," [refuted it] by means of the teacher's opinion (ācariyavāda) known as the commentary (aṭṭhakathā).

He rejects it. For a knot does not arise from a knot. "In accordance with the Sutta" means that the opponent [says]: "There is no offense, because it accords with the statement, 'This is how our teachers have learned it.
Our ancient bhikkhus, having closed off a room in a single-story building, came back after sleeping with one who was not fully ordained; therefore, for us..."

When it was said, "If you yourselves, being a certain group, say 'it is permissible,' nothing can be said against you," the proponent refutes this by citing the commentarial statement beginning with, "For those who have mastered the Suttas and that which is in conformity with the Suttas, the mastery of their own teachers is the authority. The opponent then states his own opinion:
"In the case of those who have lain down without asking permission after opening the door..."
Regarding the phrase "they are released," here both persons are released: namely, the one possessed by a *yakkha* and the one who was bound and laid down.
Because you belong to the Theravāda school, [the opponent] refutes [your position] by stating that all others—whether lying down in such-and-such a manner or otherwise—are also released.
Now, this is his own opinion (*attanomati*). As for the statement "another's sutta": when the proponent of another school says "they incur an offense," the proponent of our own school [responds].

Having shown the commentary’s statement beginning with, “If one who is weary from the day sits on a couch and falls asleep through the influence of drowsiness without having lifted his feet from the ground, there is no offense,” it refutes the notion that those who lie down in a single position (ekabhaṅga) and so forth are exempt.
Then, [the author presents] his own opinion, while the other [author] cites what is in accordance with the Sutta: “O Lord of Devas, I say that mental distress is twofold... [and so on].
Because it is consistent with such statements as “I say that there is what should be cultivated and what should not be cultivated,” you have no fault in maintaining a wife;

therefore, when the opponent says, “there is the support of children and wife,” the proponent—though he may not be very learned—rejects this, asserting that unwholesome action must necessarily be accompanied by lust. This same principle applies to the remaining cases as well.
This should also be applied in other ways according to what is appropriate by means of this method. All of this was said by the Elder Upatissa and others.
However, the Elder Dhammasiri says: "In this context, the 'other' mentioned refers to one belonging to another school (nikāya); he brings forward his own suttas and so forth.
The proponent of his own position, having compared those with his own suttas and so forth, accepts them if they agree, but rejects them if they do not."
The commentary on the fourfold exposition of the Vinaya is finished. Regarding the word-by-word analysis (*padabhājanīya*) in the *Sikkhāpadavibhaṅga*:
although the phrase "but whoever" (*yo pana*) is a term used for exhaustive inclusion, nevertheless, [the subject] is "a monk" (*bhikkhu*).
Because this subsequent term stands in grammatical apposition [with the preceding], its analytical terms (*vibhaṅgapada*) are stated accordingly.
Although the three terms expressing the word "bhikkhunī" are common to any renunciant— whether they possess the status of a bhikkhu or lack it—
they nonetheless refer to the case where "a person is impure, having committed one or another offense involving defeat (*pārājika-dhamma*)."
“If one who possesses pure view, having had no opportunity granted, speaks with the intention of causing [the other] to fall away, there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa* and *dukkaṭa*” —

such a sutta was stated for the purpose of showing that the person whose meaning is consistent with the literal explanation is the basis for the phrase “there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa* and *dukkaṭa*,” and not the other who has become a householder; this applies to the entire Vinaya Piṭaka.

For the Blessed One undertook the subject matter concerning the common characteristics of a monk. However, one who, being pure, stands in the guise of a householder for some reason, is a subject matter precisely because of his own status as a monk;
likewise, even one who is impure is a subject matter because he stands in the guise of a monk—this is the meaning shown.
Even one who is impure [is a subject matter] when [he is approached] by relatives or enemies...

Or, due to causes such as fear of the king, one who has diligently removed his saffron robes—even though he is merely the physical substrate—is not considered to have entered into the state of living in communion by theft (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*) because of his subsequent taking up of the saffron robes again;
this is said because he has not abandoned his commitment to the meaning of the term "bhikkhu.
However, one who possesses the marks [of a monk] and has himself accepted the meaning of the term "bhikkhunī," while living in communion by theft—
If one who possesses pure view, having had no opportunity granted, speaks with the intention of causing [the other] to fall away, there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa* and *dukkaṭa*;
this meaning also has been shown.
The two expressions, "a monk by convention" and "a monk by admission," reinforce the aforementioned meaning.

This explains the additional meaning: that one whose roots of merit have been severed by the arising of a fixed wrong view in the interim is called a "bhikkhu" solely by way of conventional designation and self-claim, but not in the ultimate sense.
What is meant? "Monks, I do not see even a single other thing that is so greatly blameworthy... [as stated in the Sutta].
“Bhikkhus, it is just as with this wrong view. Bhikkhus, wrong view is the foremost among great offenses.
This was spoken by the Buddha and entered into the three councils; and regarding this, the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) also states:
“Those for which wrong view is the foremost are ‘foremost in wrong view’ (*micchādiṭṭhiparamāni*). The five deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantariya-kamma*) are great offenses, [and] wrong view...
"But the intention is that [the latter] is more blameworthy. Why? Because for those [other unwholesome states], there is a limit;
even when they are extremely powerful, they last only for an eon (*kappa*). However, for fixed wrong view (*niyatamicchādiṭṭhi*), there is no limit;
for one possessed of it, there is no emergence from existence (*bhava*). Therefore, [it is said]: "In this person, wholesome states (*kusalā dhammā*) conducive to being a monk are still present."

Nor can it be said that he is "pure. Because it is stated, "On account of failure in view, one incurs two offenses," it cannot be said that he is "impure" or that "he has committed some offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
For he belongs to neither side; therefore it is said: "He is a bhikkhu by convention and by admission, but not in the ultimate sense."
But for what purpose did the Blessed One not prescribe a *pārājika* offense for such a definitely wrong view (*niyatamicchādiṭṭhi*), which is so greatly blameworthy?
Because it is difficult to discern. By its very nature, this kind of view is difficult to distinguish as either "right" or "wrong," let alone as "definite" or "indefinite.
In that regard, if an offense of defeat (*pārājikāpatti*) were prescribed, monks would [be unable to determine their status] toward one another...
Thinking that a *pārājika* offense had not been committed, they would fail to perform the Uposatha and other duties,
thereby destroying the Dispensation before long and generating demerit for themselves by acting with misconduct even toward pure monks. Therefore, out of skill in means,
without prescribing a *pārājika*, he prescribed for him the act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) and the proper conduct (*sammāvatta*).
The Saṅgha has rendered him one who is not to share in the community and not to dwell together with it.
For if this view of his were indefinite, then by fulfilling the proper conduct and receiving reinstatement, he would become a regular monk.
But if it is definite, there is no possibility, no occasion, for one who holds a definite wrong view to fulfill the proper conduct, receive reinstatement, and become a regular monk.

He saw this principle: that such a person would merely bear the name of a "monk by convention" and a "monk by profession," and after death, like Ariṭṭha, would become nothing more than a mere splinter in the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).

Among the eight ways of receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), only three are mentioned here; the others are not included because they are individual cases and do not constitute the true nature of monks.
In that context, the acceptance of advice, answering questions, and full ordination (*upasampadā*) belong to the two elders alone;
the remaining three [modes of ordination] belong to the bhikkhunīs and are therefore not intended here.
Among the three types of ordination, the four phrases beginning with "a noble bhikkhu" are stated because they are common to all three. By way of the "Come, bhikkhu" (*ehibhikkhu*) formula...
Indeed, one who is ordained—whether by the three-refuge formula or by the motion followed by the fourth proclamation—becomes noble, essential, a trainee (sekha), and one beyond training (asekha).
However, the mention of "ordination" for them is for the purpose of indicating their status as disciples;
for it is only these [disciples] who incur offenses, not the Perfectly Enlightened Ones nor the Pacceka-buddhas.

Regarding the phrase "this is intended in this sense," here it refers to one who is capable of incurring an offense and has been fully ordained by a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha-kamma*). For others—who have been ordained through the "Come, monk!

formula (*ehibhikkhu*), the going for refuge, the acceptance of instruction (*ovāda*), or the answering of questions—are not capable of incurring an offense; therefore, having excluded those cases, "this is intended in this sense."
Regarding the word "bhikkhū" (monks), it is said that the Elder Dhammasiri maintained that this was the final [category] mentioned;

however, that is incorrect. For only this much was stated: "Two types of persons are incapable of committing an offense: Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas. Otherwise, those such as the "Come, monk" (ehibhikkhu) and others would also have had to be mentioned.
Furthermore, it continues: "Two types of persons are capable of committing an offense: monks and nuns."
And because it is stated generally with the word “and,” and furthermore, because it demonstrates the grounds for fear regarding offenses.
How so? The Venerable Sāriputta did not accept alms-food from a public rest-house out of scruple;

and Mahākassapa was swept away by the river while crossing, having taken all three robes with him out of fear of being separated from his robes. And what [is the purpose] of the going for refuge and full admission?

Regarding one who has received full ordination (*upasampanna*), rules concerning the duties toward a co-resident (*saddhivihārika*) and so forth are seen to have been laid down for those who do not conduct themselves properly;

therefore, this [interpretation] is ill-considered. The Elder Upatissa says that "a monk" is intended here in this sense because of the fear of an unintended consequence regarding the admission [to the order] through the going for refuge (*saraṇagamana*), which had been rejected on account of an offense (*āpatti*).

With reference to those who are capable, even though that [permission] was previously refused, when it is stated [here], a false apprehension or doubt may arise among the bhikkhus that it has been permitted again by one speaking thus; therefore, it is said that it was not [previously] stated. This accords with the statement:
"A 'bhikkhunī' is one fully ordained in both Saṅghas. For this refers to the permission for the ordination of the Sākiyan women and others.
This was said out of fear of an endless proliferation.

However, this is our own position here: because this is a description of the bhikkhu’s path, we include as much as is subsumed under that term and whatever appears here and there in the Vinaya Piṭaka in the sense of the actual occurrence of an offense.

Or, in the sense of causing others to incur offenses such as by announcing or concealing grave matters (*duṭṭhulla*), having shown all of those [definitions], now, with reference to that subsequent phrase stated for the purpose of qualifying the term "bhikkhu"—namely, "one who has entered upon the training and the way of life" (*sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno*)—this is said:
"This is the 'bhikkhu' intended in this context. For it is he alone who, immediately after the formal ritual proclamation (*kammavācā*),...

He has entered upon the training and the mode of livelihood; for from that point onward, the origin of the training rules with specific designations is shown, and the renunciation of those very rules is seen, not that of the other.
Furthermore, the renunciation of those very rules is possible because they were undertaken after saying, "Venerable sir, let the Saṅgha lift me up out of compassion. And of him alone...
Because immediately upon full ordination (upasampadā), there is the instruction and demonstration of what is not to be done and the reliance [on the precepts],
and because it fulfills the characteristic of renouncing the training— such as saying, "I renounce the recitation of the Vinaya Pātimokkha"—
it is said that, with respect to the renunciation of the training, that very [ordination] is intended here.
Since, however, the renunciation of training is appropriate in every respect, it is therefore appropriate to say:
"For one who has renounced the training and transgresses this or that matter, there is no offense regarding those respective offenses; for the other, there is an offense.
Therefore, "in whatever instance there is a proclamation of what is blameworthy, or a proclamation of what is blameless, this [is the case] in this..."
It should be understood that it is appropriate to say: "The term *bhikkhu* is intended here in the sense of one who has transgressed [the rule] in various instances;
specifically, it refers to one who has received full ordination (*upasampanna*) by means of the formal motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha*).

This being the case, as for what was stated—"By whatever kind of full ordination this person has been ordained, having engaged in sexual intercourse, he becomes one defeated (*pārājika*)"—it is [to be understood accordingly].
“‘Bhikkhu’ here is intended to mean ‘one who possesses the goal (attha)’”—this too must not be said. Why? Because the fault of contradiction is thereby avoided.

How so? If one who has been fully ordained (*upasampanna*) by a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha*) is indeed what is intended here by both “bhikkhu” and “fully ordained,” then one who has not been fully ordained is called “not fully ordained” (*anupasampanna*); thus, those who have been fully ordained in a manner other than by a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations [are excluded].
The Teacher explains that by this [definition], such defects of contradiction as "the Elder Mahākassapa and others, by standing in the place of those who are not fully ordained,
would incur the offense of *sahaseyya* (sharing a sleeping place) and *padasodhamma* (reciting the Dhamma together)," and "at the time of reviling and so forth,
they would incur only a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing)"— are all avoided. "Maṅguracchavi" means a dark-skinned person.
Because the intoxication with birth overwhelms your minds to such a great extent, you must train yourselves in my teaching in this way:
"Accompanied by zest, accompanied by the bliss of the first jhāna, [one should practice] regarding the foul and regarding mindfulness of breathing.
This is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada*. "Perception of the bloated" means the perception of the first jhāna obtained through the sign of the bloated corpse. "Perception of form" means...
The perception of the fine-material-sphere jhānas, such as the earth-kasiṇa and so forth. He explained this:

"Venerable sir, the perception of the bloated corpse is not clear because the foulness [meditations] are not to be expanded; venerable sir, the perception of form is clear because the kasiṇas are to be expanded.
The sequence for the fivefold higher ordination has been taken from the Mahāvagga. Regarding the phrase "by a motion followed by a fourth [proclamation]," although the motion (*ñatti*) comes first...

It is called "fourth by motion" (*ñatticatuttha*) because, although there is no difference in meaning or phrasing among the three proclamations (*anussāvana*), the motion itself is distinct in both meaning and phrasing;
thus, taking it as the fourth [element], it is termed "fourth by motion. In accordance with the literal phrasing, the Commentary states:
"by three proclamations and one motion. However, according to the sequence of the presentation of the meaning, it is stated by way of the words: "by one..."
It should be stated: "by means of a motion (ñatti) and three proclamations (anussāvana). However, because it is said here, "Monks, there are these four formal acts (kamma);

monks, there are these six formal acts that are illegal formal acts (adhamma-kamma) and factional formal acts (vagga-kamma)," a formal act that is subject to subversion is also in some instances called simply a "formal act.
Therefore, it is specified as "by one that is not subject to subversion" (akuppena).

Since even some who are unshakable (*akuppa*) are not worthy of their status, and one who has not yet attained restoration is nevertheless called "restored" (*sosārita*) in the Campeyya Khandhaka, it is therefore said, "by one worthy of his status.
If this is so, one might argue that only the phrase "by one worthy of his status" should be stated, as the unshakable state is established by this very term, and thus the preceding word is redundant.
That is not so; for [the rule applies to] one ordained by means of an unshakable state that is unworthy of its status.
"In this context, it is not intended" means because it would lead to an undesirable consequence (*aniṭṭha-pasaṅga*). However, when these two are stated together, this meaning is understood:
"One who is fully ordained by that which is unshakeable (*akuppa*) is also intended here as a 'bhikkhu';
one who is fully ordained by what is worthy of standing [in its place] (*ṭhānāraha*) is also intended here as a 'bhikkhu'; and one who is fully ordained by what is shakeable (*kuppa*)."

[This] is not intended. Therefore, this point is also established: because of the statement, “Whosoever, O Bhikkhu, knowingly ordains a person under twenty years of age, that person is unordained,” as long as it is not known [that he is actually under twenty], even though one has entered into the state of being a Bhikkhu by name and by profession, such a person is not a Bhikkhu by name and by profession in the sense previously shown.
Unlike other bhikkhus, it does not constitute an offense such as *omasanapācittiya* when standing in the position of one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*);

rather, it remains solely an occasion for an offense when standing in the position of one who is not fully ordained, such as: "If one recites the Dhamma word by word to one who is not fully ordained, perceiving them as fully ordained, there is an offense of *pācittiya*. However, one who is fully ordained with an unshakable [ordination]...
Even one who has subsequently committed a *pārājika* offense remains in the position of one who is ordained by virtue of his lineage;
however, among the persons to be avoided mentioned in such passages as, “Monks, a paṇḍaka who is unordained should not be ordained,

and one who is ordained should be expelled,” it should be understood that some individuals are called “ordained,” yet do not remain in the position of one who is ordained, while others do remain there.

In this context, however, one should understand this fourfold classification: there is action that is both unshakable and worthy of its fruit; there is action that is worthy of its fruit but not unshakable;
there is action that is both unshakable and not worthy of its fruit; and there is action that is neither unshakable nor worthy of its fruit.

Among these, the first has already been explained, while the third and fourth are evident. As for the second, it refers to [action] performed toward the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs by way of a particular sequence.
It is obtained when there is a change of gender for one who has been fully ordained on one side.

For although the formal act of full ordination consisting of a motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatutthakamma*) received by that person previously during the time of being a trainee (*sikkhamānā*) remains indeed unshakable and worthy of standing, nevertheless, when the male gender appears, it is said here:
"I allow you, monks, that very same preceptor and that very same full ordination."

Because that person has not yet entered the [higher] stages, it is said that the formal act (*kamma*) now becomes subject to invalidation due solely to his falling back into the state of a novice (*sāmaṇera*).

It should be understood that, through the change of gender, there is a relinquishing of the full ordination (*upasampadā*) conferred upon that person by the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha— just as there is a relinquishing of the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) of robes— otherwise, that person...
One who is fully ordained is called a *bhikkhu*. Alternatively, even when there is no change of gender (*liṅgaparivatta*), that act of ordination on one side is invalidated;
it does not remain in its proper place. Therefore, for the time being, she does not receive the designation "bhikkhunī.
This is because, whether or not she has committed any particular *pārājika* offense, out of a desire to disrobe, she assumes the lay appearance.
Furthermore, for one who consents [to the change of sex], full ordination (upasampadā) is obtained from both Saṅghas;
therefore, by that method, it is called "changeable" (kuppa), yet because of the absence of the aforementioned defects in the formal act (kamma), it is called "fitting the occasion" (ṭhānāraha).
However, when a bhikkhunī consents to the female characteristic (gihiliṅga) and the male characteristic (purisaliṅga) appears, she does not obtain full ordination among the bhikkhus.
The teacher [Dhammapāla] says: "Some say that if one has renounced the training and left the order, the grounds for the offense are not seen;
however, that is incorrect because a nun does not have the possibility of renouncing the training. This is our position.
In the *Gaṇṭhipada*, it is stated: "Just as it is said 'it must be done,' so too, considering that an offense arises when it is not done, the performance [of the duty] is the Teacher’s instruction."
It has been stated. Wherever the term "Gaṇṭhipada" is mentioned, it should be understood as referring to "the Gaṇṭhipada of the Elder Dhammasiri.
This concludes the commentary on the analysis of the *Sājīva* section.
“‘The Mahābodhisattas are fixed’—this is stated in the *Anugaṇṭhipada*. Where it says ‘in the *Anugaṇṭhipada*,’ there it should be understood as [the work] of the Elder Vajirabuddhi.

Alternatively, among the three types of enlightenment—namely, the enlightenment of a disciple (*sāvakabodhi*), the enlightenment of a paccekabuddha (*paccekabodhi*), and the perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*)*—those beings who are intent upon perfect enlightenment are called ‘bodhisattas’ or ‘mahābodhisattas. This is because they possess abundant virtue of the *pātimokkha*. *Sammāsambodhi*: Perfect enlightenment; the supreme, complete awakening of a Buddha. *Bodhisatta*: A being intent on enlightenment; one who has set out for awakening. *Mahābodhisatta*: A great being intent on enlightenment; a bodhisatta destined for supreme, perfect enlightenment. *Pātimokkhasīla*: The moral discipline of the *pātimokkha*; the code of monastic rules. *Anugaṇṭhipada*: A sub-commentary (a commentary on a commentary). *Vajirabuddhi*: The name of a renowned Theravāda commentator. *Sāvakabodhi*: The enlightenment of a disciple; the awakening attained by a *sāvaka* (hearer). *Paccekabodhi*: The enlightenment of a paccekabuddha; the awakening attained by one who attains Buddhahood independently but does not teach the path to others. *Tīsu bodhīsu*: Among the three types of enlightenment. *Sattā*: Beings; those who are intent upon or devoted to. The provided text is already in English. Here it is: "Mahābodhisattvas are fixed," so it is stated in the Anugaṇṭhipada. Where it says "in the Anugaṇṭhipada," there it should be understood as [the work] of the Elder Vajirabuddhi. Among the three types of enlightenment—namely, the enlightenment of disciples, the enlightenment of paccekabuddhas, and right self-enlightenment—it is those beings intent upon right self-enlightenment who are called Bodhisattvas or Mahābodhisattvas. This is because of their abundance of the morality of the Pātimokkha.

In a certain *gaṇṭhipada* (commentary on difficult points), it is stated that [the bhikkhu-sīla] is "superior" (*adhika*) because it is practiced for the purpose of burning away the defilements (*kilesa*), and because it was prescribed by the Supreme One, the Blessed One; and it is "supreme" (*uttama*) because it occurs only when a Buddha has appeared.

Although even Paccekabuddhas are indeed endowed with the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha by way of natural law (*dhammatā*), nevertheless, [it is said] "only when a Buddha has appeared..."
It has been determined by that method [of explanation] that [the training precepts] proceed. Therefore he said, "For it is not by setting aside that designation," and so forth.
Furthermore, even from the perspective of the restraint of the Pātimokkha, only virtue associated with the Path and its Fruits is "higher virtue" (adhisīla); however, that is not intended here.
For that is not included within the recitation of the Pātimokkha. This is a statement of the complete and excellent reason.
Since all training rules (sikkhāpada) share a common characteristic, it has been established that noble persons (ariyapuggala) may incur certain offenses due to this subsequent rule (anupaññatti).

Therefore, does the statement in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), “For one who has attained [that state] does not engage in sexual intercourse,” appear as if it were untenable? It is not untenable; it is indeed tenable in every respect.
The investigation regarding the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) proceeds according to each specific case as set forth in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).

For instance, in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*, under the section on the water-boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*), it is stated: "for a nun who is crossing [the river] having covered the three circles but not having thrown out her inner robe (*antaravāsaka*)," because this is recorded in the *Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga*.
This same method applies to other similar cases as well. What is the purpose?
What is this? It is for the purpose of following the sequence of the Canon and demonstrating the sequence of the Canon. Herein, this is a brief explanation of the underlying intention:
regarding the training rule on the recitation of the words (*padasodhamma*), when one has been fully ordained and perceives oneself as fully ordained, there is no offense;

however, according to the training rule on not performing the *anuddhamma* (formal acts), there may be an offense in the case of one who has been suspended (*ukkhitaka*) despite being fully ordained, and likewise in the case of the training rule on sleeping together (*sahaseyya*).
And so forth. The meaning here, however, will be made clear later.
As it was stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “Even beyond that, the consciousness of the path and fruit is itself ‘higher mind’ (*adhicitta*), yet that is not intended here”;
and: “Even beyond that, the wisdom of the path and fruit is itself ‘higher wisdom’ (*adhipaññā*), yet that is not intended here.”
"For a bhikkhu who has entered that attainment does not engage in sexual intercourse. This contradicts the scriptural passage:

"In this context, it is this training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā) which is intended by the term 'training' (sikkhā). For this scriptural passage demonstrates that it is specifically the training in higher virtue that is intended here, and not the others.
Furthermore, the words of the Commentary [indicate] that all three of those mundane [trainings] are intended.
He illuminates [this]. Herein, this is the intention of the Commentary: all three mundane trainings are possible in this first *pārājika*.

For even a monk who has attained higher mind (*adhicitta*) and higher wisdom (*adhipaññā*) might, depending on such an unsuitable condition, turn away from that higher mind and higher wisdom and reach a breach of virtue; such a possibility exists.

He exists, yet he has not attained supramundane consciousness and wisdom; this same principle applies to all other offenses involving volition, such as taking what is not given, while for those lacking volition, the other [type of person] also exists.

Nevertheless, because it encompasses the Vinaya Piṭaka and the morality of the Pātimokkha, it is only the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*) that is eligible for renunciation in this subsequent phrase: "without having renounced the training."

It should be understood that for the sake of showing what is mundane (*lokiya*), it is stated in the Canon: "In this context, that which is the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*) is the training intended here.
Here, "training" (*sikkhā*) should be understood as both abstention from bodily and verbal misconduct and volition (*cetanā*); however, elsewhere it should be understood as volition alone.
"Training rule" (*sikkhāpada*) refers to both a training rule that is explicitly stated (*suddesa*) and certain training rules that are not explicitly stated (*anuddesa*).

"Making it the basis for the mind" (*cittassa adhikaraṇaṃ katvā*) is stated for the purpose of showing that the locative case is used in the sense of a basis (*adhikaraṇatthe bhummam*), meaning "one trains in that.
"According to the training rule" (*yathāsikkhāpadaṃ*) is stated by way of reflection; for even the reflection on virtue is itself virtue. Therefore...
Even one who engages in a volition dissociated from abstinence regarding conduct such as well-covered [behavior] is nonetheless reckoned as fulfilling the training.

One who does not transgress the boundary stated in the rule, “An intentional lie is an offense of expiation” (Pācittiya), is said to “train in that training precept. However, it is stated in a certain *gaṇṭhipada* (commentary): “‘Training’ (sikkhā)…”
The arising of consciousness that occurs through the state of training in that training rule (*sikkhāpada*) is [the training]. "That livelihood" (*sājīva*) is the formal designation (*paññatti*).
To demonstrate its meaning, it was previously stated that this is a synonym for restraint from sexual intercourse.

Because there is no lack of strength in the world due to the absence of that tradition—which is esteemed for its virtue and esteemed for its merit—through the training, the disclosure of weakness does not occur therein. For that [tradition] is indeed desirable.
Therefore, it is said: "And whatever livelihood he has entered upon, having not disclosed his weakness therein.
For weakness can only arise through an order, says the Venerable Upatissa.
Commentary on the Discussion of Renouncing the Training (Sikkhāpaccakkhāna-kathā-vaṇṇanā)
"Here I go" means to such-and-such a shrine or dwelling place, or to a house and so forth.

"In the manner of conceiving a state" means because of the expression "may I become this," it refers to the manner of conceiving whatever state one wishes to become; the intended meaning is: by way of conceiving a state other than the state of a monk.

46. "With the hand" refers to speech alone. By the phrases "desiring the state of a householder," etc., he demonstrates the restriction of the mind (*cittaniyama*). The renunciation of the training occurs by means of a single act of consciousness (*citta*), not in its absence.
51. By the phrases "the Buddha, the Dhamma," etc., he demonstrates the restriction of the field (*khetta-niyama*).

Therein, by the first fourteen phrases, the relinquishing of one's own nature (*sabhāvapariccāga*) is shown, and by the final eight, the undertaking of another state (*bhāvantarādāna*) is demonstrated. "I renounce... [is the formula].
By "dhārehi" (hold), he shows the restriction of time. By the word "vadati" (speaks), he shows the restriction of the formal act (*payoga*).

By "viññāpeti" (makes known), he shows the restriction of understanding. By phrases such as "one who is insane renounces the training" and "one renounces the training in the presence of one who is insane," he shows the restriction of the person. [And] by an Ariyan [renouncing it] to a non-Ariyan...

However, by means of such statements as "one renounces the training in the presence [of the Saṅgha]," he shows that even when there is a restriction regarding the person and so forth, a restriction regarding the time [of the act] is impossible to determine.

Regarding this, the Teacher says: "It is our opinion that even if the time-restriction is not present in a barbarian language (*milakkhabhāsā*), the renunciation of the training is still valid provided that the meaning of the time-restriction is clearly expressed in that language.
By means of such terms as "for the sake of sport" (*davāya*), there is a restriction regarding the field (*khetta*) and so forth.
It shows that even when there is truth, it does not take root due to the absence of mental determination (*cittaniyama*).
"He wishes to announce but does not announce" shows that even when there is mental determination, it does not take root due to the absence of determination regarding the application (*payoga*).

"He announces to one who does not understand, but does not announce to one who understands" shows that even when there is determination regarding the mind, the field, the time, the application, and the person's discernment, [it fails] for the very person toward whom he announces.
It is stated for the purpose of showing that [the training] does not take root in another; therefore it is said in the Aṭṭhakathā:
"If one specifies a single person, thinking 'let this one alone know,' and informs them, and if he alone knows it, the training is renounced.
But if he does not know it... [etc. ...the training is not renounced. Or, if one does not announce it at all, it is not renounced.
“The training has been discarded” is stated for the purpose of showing that the training is discarded solely through the restriction of the mind and so forth, and not otherwise.
Up to this point, the word-commentary for the phrase “without having made known one’s weakness regarding the training... has been shown by way of three modes.
Therein, it should be understood that two are unmixed and the last one is mixed. For that very reason, [it is said] “by a breach of speech.”
The meaning is that by merely hearing the words intended to illuminate that matter, one makes it known through that very verbal expression.
"Associated with the mind" means associated with the state of mind desiring to renounce. One is called "knowing the occasion" simply by knowing the intention behind it.

53. The *Vaṇṇapaṭṭhāna* is a discourse illuminating the qualities of the Buddha. It is said that the *Upāli-gāthā* was spoken by the householder Upāli. "Knowledge" (*paññāṇa*) and "recognition" (*saññāṇa*) are one in meaning; therefore, "knowledge of enlightenment" (*bodhipaññāṇa*) means the recognition of enlightenment (*bodhisaññāṇa*), which is to say, the seed of enlightenment (*bodhibīja*).
Regarding the phrase "having determined both," it is stated in one of the *Gaṇṭhipadas* (commentaries on difficult points):
"Even when both know [the renunciation], if it is said with the intention 'I renounce,' and only one among them knows [it], the renunciation has not been made.
However, this does not accord with the *Aṭṭhakathā*. For whether one says "I am a householder" (*gihī homi*) or "in a householder" (*gihimhi*), although it is a verb in the present tense...

It does not occur [as a separate word]. Because there is no sense of "hold" (*dhārehi*) in that context, and because when "hold" is spoken, it moves above the *parassapada* [ending], therefore it does not occur.
The term "dhamma" is stated in all instances as "the directly visible Dhamma" (*sandiṭṭhikaṃ dhammaṃ*); this is said in order to reveal that which he intends by saying "directly visible.
Otherwise, if it were simply said, "I renounce victory over victory," it would also apply to universal monarchs (*cakkavatti*) and so forth.
By association with that, the word "Buddha" should also be mentioned at the end.

Among the synonyms for "teacher," however, the phrase "he who ordained me," and so forth, was spoken either without having taken formal dependence (*upajjhā*) or referring to one who had gone forth under another.
"Okallaka" is a synonym for a pauper. "Moḷibaddha" means one whose topknot is tied, or one who has removed his crown. "Cellaka" refers to a novice.

Ceṭaka was of middle standing; Moḷigalla was a great novice (mahāsāmaṇera). [The recitation was made] in the presence of humans, or of beings such as nāgas who had assumed human form, or of kinnaras and others who understand speech.
It is said that the reading is "devatā nāma mahāpaññā" (the deities are indeed of great wisdom).
"Davāya" means suddenly. "Ravābhaññena" means by way of faltering recitation; for it is due to a lack of mastery over the phonemes and their combinations, or over the articulations.

Or there is a failure of speech due to lack of clarity. Because his faculties are not under control, it is said that he is "like a painted figure"—that is, one who is dull-witted and of slow intelligence.
If it is asked, "In what respect is one dull-witted? it is because of a lack of skill regarding the proper occasion.
The commentary on the discussion of renouncing the training is finished.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Root Formulation (Mūlapaññattikathāvaṇṇanā) 55.
The phrase “known as ‘practicing’” does not exist in the matrix (mātikā); therefore, he said: “‘He should practice’—in this context,” and so forth.
In all manuscript copies of the Canon (pāḷi), it says: “This is what is called sexual intercourse”; however, in the Commentary (aṭṭhakathā), it says: “This is called sexual intercourse.”
The names have been extracted. By means of a woman’s characteristic, one’s own characteristic—this is shown as being difficult to discern.
By means of one’s own characteristic, a woman’s characteristic is not shown because it is easy to discern.

Regarding the phrase “having released from four places,” this is said with reference to that which actually touches the inner surface; there is no offense for one who removes [the object] without touching it.
"Middle" refers to the central portion. "The middle of the upper part" refers to the central portion of the upper part.

If it is argued that an offense occurs here as well because an offense can arise for one whose physical sensitivity (*kāyappasāda*) is impaired—since the phrase "one whose body-sensitivity is destroyed" implies this—[the answer is] no;
