it is to demonstrate this that the words "or dead skin" and so forth are stated. For dead skin is non-clung-to (*anupādinna*); an offense of defeat (*pārājika*) occurs only with respect to what is clung-to (*upādinna*). "Having covered" means without concealing [it].
The intention is that one should sit so as to conceal [the teeth] such that they are not visible.
A *gonasa* is a circular snake (*maṇḍala-sappa*) with a cow-like back, on whose back red circles are seen.

Although, by catching fish while moving through the water in the mud, they are able to swallow even the body of a large elephant in a single gulp in the ocean—being larger than that—[they are still small].

And since they have been taken [as objects], sexual intercourse is not possible in their mouths and so forth; therefore, some say there is no delimitation of location (*ṭhānapariccheda*) therein—this must be examined.

The phrase "for this very reason" (*etameva hi*) refers to what follows immediately after. "Together with the application" (*saddhiṃ yojanāya*) means together with the application of the words (*akkharayojanāya*).
"But the training rule (*sikkhāpada*), having been laid down, is to be trained in equally by all modest persons (*lajjīpuggala*)."
In his *Gaṇṭhipada*, it is stated: "Because it is said, 'those who train equally,' every training precept must be trained in by all bhikkhus;
for there is nothing deficient or superfluous for anyone. However, in the *Parivāra*:
"Neither one who has been suspended, nor one who is on probation..."
"He is neither a schismatic in the Saṅgha nor has he gone over to another faction;
standing on the ground of common affiliation,
how indeed could he be one who does not share in the training?"
It has been stated. And in the commentary on that passage, it is said: "This question was asked with reference to one who previously worked as a barber.
For he is not permitted to carry a barber’s kit, whereas others are; therefore, he is excluded from the training.
All of this should be understood in such a way that it is consistent and harmonious. Furthermore, there are training rules (sikkhāpada) common only to the bhikkhunīs.
“A bhikkhu trains; likewise, another bhikkhu who has not previously been bathed also trains in that training rule.

This is said with the intention that, for the sake of proficiency in its meaning, every single training rule is indeed what is called "training equally. This connects to the phrase "that which was stated.
The section beginning with "three women" is for the purpose of defining the basis [of the offense], because it serves as the specific determiner and the characteristic [of the offense].
It has been stated. By that, one rejects [objects] made of gold, silver, and so forth, which were produced with the possibility of non-human females.
From this point onward, those "three reasons for the existence of the analysis" (vibhaṅga) previously mentioned should be understood by applying them as appropriate.
Commentary on the Explanation of the First Tetrad.

57. Regarding the phrase "there would be an offense involving defeat (pārājika)": because that unwholesome offense overcomes the arising of virtue (sīla) in that bhikkhu, it is called "defeat" (pārājika) due to its overcoming by passion;
having overcome and destroyed the offenses such as dukkaṭa and thullaccaya committed previously, it remains alone by itself.
This is so whether the [other] offenses are similar or dissimilar to the basis (vatthu).
Some say that he is not himself overcome by other offenses of the same class as the *pārājika* offenses.
That has already been examined previously. However, when all four *pārājika* offenses occur together, they then overcome his status as a monk;
they make him a non-monk and render him one who is no longer fully ordained (*anupasampanna*).
Even by common designation, he is not a bhikkhu. Some say that he does not incur an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for abusive speech.

Because the second interpretation of the meaning includes the attainment, achievement, and transgression of an offense involving defeat (pārājika), it is included among those who speak of the attainment of an offense;
and this dependence on another is appropriate. Such a person is indeed called a bhikkhu who has committed an offense; otherwise...
By reason of its momentary destruction, he would be without offense, yet it does not cease to exist. When, then, does it exist?
When he passes away, and when, having renounced the training, he stands on the level of a novice (sāmaṇera) and so forth.
If this is so, then when the training has been renounced, both the offense of defeat (pārājika) and the training itself have been renounced; thus, both exist for him simultaneously.
Why are offenses such as *saṅghādisesa* not relinquished by the relinquishing of the training? They must be confessed again once one has been re-ordained.

The relinquishing of the training constitutes an emergence from the offense; however, it is not a monk who emerges from the offense, but a householder who emerges, or a novice who emerges. Therefore, because of the contradiction with the Vinaya, one does not emerge [from the offense]. But if indeed a householder emerges...
Or a novice (sāmaṇera) might be endowed with virtue and an attainer of jhāna, or an attainer of the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) or the fruit of arhatship (arahatta-phala);
or one who has committed a pārājika offense and is thus guilty of an offense might be an arhat.

Or one who has been suspended (ukkhitaka), or one who has left the order (uppabbajita), or one deserving probation (parivāsāraha), or one deserving penance (mānattāraha), or one who has left the order, might be endowed with virtue and an attainer of jhāna, or an attainer of the fruit of stream-entry or the fruit of arhatship.

Or if he were one who has attained [the goal], yet being guilty of an offense and obstructed from being an Arahant, he would have to be given probation or the *mānatta* penance again after being re-ordained, or—if he is one who has been suspended—he would have to be reinstated; such a person is found here.
Now, this is the analysis: one who has committed an offense involving defeat (*pārājika*) remains so as long as he continues to claim the status of a monk.

He consents to co-residence; because it constitutes an obstacle, even for one who personally undertakes the precepts on Uposatha days and other occasions—just as a householder does—the undertaking of the precepts does not take root, let alone the attainment of jhāna and so forth.

If he does not consent to the state of a bhikkhu, does not claim it, and does not consent to co-residence, but merely discloses his status to the bhikkhus out of fear of kings, enemies, thieves, and the like...

One does not abandon the saffron robe; one remains as if unordained, yet incurs [the offense of] sharing a sleeping place and so forth; and one partakes in virtue, meditative absorption (jhāna), and the rest.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
"When one has fallen into an offense and seeks purification, the offense should be disclosed. For when it is disclosed, there is ease for the attainment of the first jhāna," and so forth.
In this context, "there are offenses" refers to all offenses whatsoever, categorized as those with remainder (*sāvasesa*) and those without remainder (*anavasesa*), which have been committed.
Even so, one who stands upon the plane of a householder or similar status might well partake of the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and so forth because of standing in the pure state;

however, one who has been suspended (*ukkhitaka*) and not reinstated, or who has fallen into a heavy offense (*garudhamma*) and not undergone the formal rehabilitation (*avuṭṭhita*), or who has renounced the training (*sikkhā-paccakkhāya*)—[none of these may partake].

One who remains on the plane of a householder and so forth does not partake of the jhānas and other such states, because he stands at the extreme limit of purity and because he still has duties to perform;
for this very reason, the Blessed One stated, "He must be ordained again and reinstated.
Therefore, for that person, those obstructive factors (antarāyika-dhamma) incurred during his time as a monk, having generated remorse, lead to [the attainment of] the roots of non-remorse.
They prevent the arising of joy and so forth, but not only in relation to themselves. If they do not prevent it, then [joy] arises.

If, having committed a grave offense (*garuka-āpatti*), one has disrobed after confessing it to the monks—considering that one has disrobed while remaining a regular monk (*pakatatta*)—one would be a partaker of the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and so on, because it is said:
"For one who has confessed, there is ease. How much more so during the time when one was still a monk!
"However, some say that one who has been suspended (ukkhitaka) is not [excluded] because he still has duties to perform. But one who follows him may share in that [status] after abandoning that view.

Regarding the phrase, 'Monks, it is not [permissible] for an assembly including householders where one who has renounced the training and committed an ultimate offense is seated,' here 'householder' (gahaṭṭha) refers to one who naturally remains in the marks of a layperson. The training..."
Having renounced the marks of a bhikkhu, he stands as one who has renounced the training.
Because he still has regard for his own robes and, desiring the status of a sāmaṇera, he becomes a sāmaṇera by means of those very same marks through the threefold going for refuge.

Even one who, having committed the ultimate offense, was consenting to living in communion, later—by the sequence previously described—not consenting and desiring the status of a sāmaṇera [becomes so].
One becomes a novice (sāmaṇera) through the three goings for refuge, like one who has renounced the training;

he need not have the yellow robe received from the monks again, because he remains established in the very same signs (liṅga) previously given by them. However, if one who has committed a pārājika offense, when being accused, says after being defeated, "Come, venerable sir, let me be a novice;
give me the refuges," and [the monks] say, "Very well, take them," [he does not become a novice].
It should be said: having set him aside from the layman’s dress, he should be made to receive the saffron robes again and then be ordained.
“However, all of this must be understood after careful consideration, as it has been stated according to my own judgment,” says the teacher.
“Insertion” means the contact of the penis with [the female organ] by one who is inserting it. “Having inserted” means by one who inserts it as far as the base.

The time of effort is the period when [the emission] has not yet occurred. At the moment of the emission of semen, the male organ is said to be "stationed. "Extraction" refers to the time of bringing it out.
However, in the *Gaṇṭhipada*, it is stated that "stationed" means remaining after ceasing from the effort;
this was said for the purpose of showing the distinction between the states without confusion. Indeed, the emission of semen occurs even during the times of insertion, being inserted, and extraction.
The commentary on the first tetrad is finished.
Commentary on the two hundred and sixty-nine tetrads, [59–60]:
Because of the statement, "A corpse is for the most part unexposed," even one that is for the most part exposed constitutes a ground for defeat (*pārājika*).
This shows that what is entirely gnawed or torn away constitutes an offense of Thullaccaya.
Likewise, because of the statement "mostly gnawed," it shows that what is dead and entirely gnawed or torn away constitutes an offense of Dukkaṭa.

And they do not prescribe [the offense] as having a remainder. For what reason? Because this training rule concerns what is forbidden by the world (lokavajja), not what is forbidden by formal precept (paṇṇattivajja).
In this context, "training rule" (*sikkhāpada*) refers to a *pārājika*.

For even a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) therein is a transgression by nature (*lokavajja*), not a transgression by formal precept (*paṇṇattivajja*). Alternatively, both are prescribed without exception.

For when the lower limit has been established within the domain of a *pārājika*, it is precisely that which follows beyond it that is prescribed as a *thullaccaya*. In that regard, the domain of the *thullaccaya* also...
It should be understood that this is stated as the lower limit, just like the field for a *pārājika* offense. Regarding "an offense of serious transgression (*thullaccaya*) when half is carved":
that place where the sign (*nimitta*) has been carved should be understood as the basis for an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Here it is asked:
Does the Blessed One prescribe an offense of formal rule (*paṇṇattivajja*) only as something with a remainder? No; rather, it is categorically according to what is possible in each respective case.

"We shall explain [this]. But for what purpose did the Blessed One not prescribe a *pārājika* offense for half-eaten [flesh]?"—this first question arises because the formulation of the Vinaya is within the domain of the Buddha.
However, the following is merely a semblance of a reason: "Because the state of being 'half' is difficult to determine.
For that which is "mostly eaten" refers to the four parts of the anus, the urinary tract, and the mouth.
Having passed two sections among the body parts, eating up to the end of the third section is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);
having passed the third section, eating up to the end of the fourth section is a matter of wrong-doing.
Even if it is said that "the sign has been entirely devoured," they explain that this was stated with reference specifically to a living body.

Having examined it, one should take [the decision]. Regarding "a whole body": in the case of a fresh, uncorrupted human body while still alive, there is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) for inserting [the organ] into the eyes, nose, and so forth.
For animals such as elephants and horses, there is a *thullaccaya* for inserting it into the nose or the sheath of the penis.
This is according to this canonical text: "If he inserts what is not the way into what is not the way, there is an offense of *thullaccaya*."
This is stated here by way of a specific distinction of meaning: there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in the case of the armpits and so forth;
for all animals, there is an offense of wrong-doing in the eyes, ears, and wounds; and for the rest of the body as well, there is likewise only an offense of wrong-doing.

This is established in the Vinaya account concerning the incident where [the monk] said, "Come, venerable sir, engage in sexual intercourse," and [the other] replied, "Enough, sister, this is not allowable. By this, first of all, the absence of lust for sexual intercourse is shown.
The enjoyment of release (*mocanassāda*) is demonstrated by the passage: “Come, venerable sir, touch [her] between the thighs...
that bhikkhu did so. For this reason, the Blessed One said: “There is an offense entailing formal meeting of the Saṅgha (*saṅghādisesa*).

However, it is stated on the basis of the established principle that: “But for one who touches [her] between the thighs with lust for sexual intercourse, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).”
The eyes, ears, wounds, and so forth of human beings constitute the basis for a *thullaccaya* offense, whereas those of animals constitute the basis for a *dukkaṭa* offense;
here, the textual trace (*pāḷileso*) is difficult to discern. Therefore, based on the statement: "Monks, one should not touch the private parts with a lustful mind;
whoever should touch them, there is an offense of *thullaccaya*," [the rule applies] to one who touches the eyes, ears, or wounds with a lustful mind.
“It is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); this is established”—this should be understood as the reading of the text (pāḷilesa) in the Chapter on Leather (Cammakkhandhaka).
Regarding the statement, “‘Of a living person’—the word ‘living’ is stated for the purpose of making it known that there is no need to speak of one who is dead,” so they say.
As for the phrase “In the Great Commentary (Mahā-aṭṭhakathā), however,” although it is said, “Having made the body of the Great Commentary,” nevertheless, in the other commentaries...

This is stated for the purpose of showing that, because there is no explicit statement [in the Vinaya] such as "by means of the mouth" regarding sexual desire (*methunarāga*), that statement exists precisely therein;
thus, it is spoken in order to correlate it with the wording of the Pāḷi. However, in the *Anugaṇṭhipada*, it is said: "All of that refers to the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* itself:
'If, out of sexual desire, one touches the female organ without inserting [the penis], it is a serious offense (*thullaccaya*)'; and: 'Out of sexual desire...'"
In some places it is stated even by way of the mouth; however, in the Canon (Pāḷi) it is stated without distinction: "And, monks, with a lustful mind, the private parts must not be touched.

Therefore, it is said: "all that. They praise the former because, according to the method already explained regarding animals (*tiracchānagati*) and so forth, there is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) [for touching] and an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) due to the lust for physical contact, as established by the words of the Commentaries (*Aṭṭhakathā*).

“‘All that... [as before] ...they praise the former’”—this is stated as a determination made by later teachers on the island of Sīhaḷa, having compared the words spoken in the *Pāḷi* and the *Aṭṭhakathā* following the communal recitation (*saṅgīti*).
Here, the phrase “otherwise” (*itarathā hi*) refers to the ordinary perspective.
Why is it an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)? Because it is said: “For one who inserts fingers, seeds, and so forth, there is an offense of wrong-doing.”
Because it has been so stated, it is logical. Regarding the phrase "the anus of a female animal":
here, since the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* previously referred to it as the "organ" (*nimitta*) and now refers to it as the "anus," it appears logical that a *dukkaṭa* offense occurs for any remaining organ.

"In the manner already stated" means by way of the lust for sexual intercourse. And regarding the *thullaccaya*: because it is mentioned in the *Khandhaka* specifically by way of the anus as the organ.
It should be accepted after investigation.
The commentary on the discussion of the sixty-nine sets of four is finished.
The commentary on the discussion of the classification of the fourfold set on spread-out rugs.

61-2. "Having made the female sign into a post": having inserted a post inside the female sign and either leveled it or left the post protruding, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who touches [the organ] against the protruding post, because of the absence of insertion.

If he touches the post itself—which was only slightly inserted—against the generative organ, it is an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*). Also: "The scent of the lotus is from the state of the lotus."
It seems those dwelling on Dīpa recite it as *sutta-bhikkhumhi*, just as in the passage where [it says] "when a mind of intimacy has arisen toward a monk who is asleep" (*sevanacittaṃ upaṭṭhite*).
They also recite it as *suttabhikkhumhi*, which is indeed the straightforward reading.
The commentary on the section concerning the fourfold breaking of the spread (*santhata*) is finished.
The commentary on the word-by-word analysis (*padabhājanīya*) is finished. Regarding the commentary on the miscellaneous discussion (*pakiṇṇakakathā*):
by way of those training rules (*sikkhāpada*) which are called "active" (*kiriyā*), [the offenses] involving both body and speech [are explained].
It is to be understood by means of intimation (*viññatti*). It is to be understood even without intimation by way of non-action (*akiriyā*);

however, in this context, the mind is immeasurable because the origination from the disclosure of the elements (*bhūtārocanasamuṭṭhāna*) is action (*kiriyā*), and because it is without mind (*acittaka*). Therein, action should be understood as originating from the immediately preceding moment of consciousness (*anantaracitta*) regarding an offense.
Even that which does not produce intimation is, for the most part, termed "action" according to the method of general usage (*bāhullanaya*).

It is said thus: even in the absence of an explicit solicitation (*viññatti*) in the first *pārājika* offense, it is stated, "If he consents, there is an offense of defeat (*pārājika*)," and "If he does not consent, there is no offense.

Even the action designated as solicitation does not occur without the intention to engage in sexual intercourse, because it is produced by the mind, because it is a form of mental modification, and because it follows the movement of the mind. Therefore...
This intimation-form, known as *kiriyā*, does not persist without its originating mind, just like other mind-born material phenomena (*cittaja-rūpa*);

however, the other [type of form], the sound-base (*saddāyatana*), does persist. Therefore, since one concludes that when there is *kiriyā*, the mind of sexual intercourse that produced it must necessarily exist, the claim that "there is no offense because one did not consent" is untenable. This is because, although it is indeed the producer of intimation...
The mind of service does not produce an intimation (*viññatti*) at all times; therefore, since it arises spontaneously even without an intimation, it is said:
"If he consents, there is an offense of defeat (*pārājika*). If it does not arise, it is called "not consenting," and for him there is no offense.
For this very reason, the Blessed One delimited the offense by means of the mind itself, asking: "With what state of mind were you, monk?"

It should be understood that this does not refer to a formal act (*kiriya*). Up to this point, the six origins of offenses (*āpatti-samudāna*), which are themselves called the "factors that cause an offense," as well as the four ways of incurring an offense—namely, by body, by speech, by both body and speech, and by a formal motion (*kammavācā*)—are consistent with these scriptural passages;
otherwise, they would be inconsistent. How so? For regarding whatever offense...
One commits [an offense] by means of the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*), yet the body and so forth are not present therein as that which has committed it;

therefore, one commits [the offense] through seven factors including the formal proclamation that cause the offense, and thus even there the body and so forth are found either collectively or individually.
Consequently, the statement "in four ways" is not tenable, and it should rather be said, "one commits an offense in three ways"—thus [the two statements] are contradictory.
...they exist. How are they non-conflicting? Because the body and so forth are divided into the categories of being with intimation (*saviññattika*) and without intimation (*aviññattika*).

Whatever offense is an act of commission (*kiriyā*), one commits some by means of the body with intimation, some by means of speech with intimation, and some by means of both body and speech with intimation.
However, whatever offense is an act of non-commission (*akiriyā*), one commits some by means of the formal ritual statement (*kammavācā*).
One incurs it, and that indeed is only by means of residual non-intimating bodily or vocal actions, not without them;
for there is the statement: "If one does not relinquish it by body or speech, at the conclusion of the formal act (kammavācā), there is an offense of Saṅghādisesa.
Or, without distinction, one incurs a certain offense by body, a certain one by speech, and a certain one by both body and speech. As for what is here...

The meaning should be understood as follows: "By means of body and speech" means that some offenses are incurred solely by means of body and speech, while others are incurred by means of the formal ritual utterance (*kammavācā*). Thus they are non-contradictory. Herein, this is the concise explanation of the meaning:
"One incurs [an offense] by means of the body" means by means of the body together with informative intimation (*saviññattika*), regarding that which should not be done.

Having performed one thing, one commits an offense; having failed to perform what ought to be done by means of an intimation (*aviññatti*), one commits an offense—both of these are called bodily action (*kāyakamma*).

For even that which is not actually done is called "done" in common worldly usage, as in such expressions as, "This was a misdeed (*dukkaṭa*) committed by me," or "The merit (*puñña*) that I did not do," and so forth.
And in the Teaching, it is said: "Friend Ānanda, this is a misdeed for you, in that you [did not do] to the Blessed One..."
In passages such as "he did not ask," and likewise here in the Vinaya method, even that which is not to be done by the body is called "bodily action" (*kāyakamma*);

this same principle applies to phrases such as "one falls into [an offense] through speech. In this context, the inclusion of the term "origination" (*samuṭṭhāna*) is for the purpose of showing that one incurs an offense only by means of the bodily and other divisions—whether it be something to be done or not to be done—and not otherwise. The inclusion of the term "action" (*kiriyā*)...
[This is] for the purpose of showing the distinction between the body and so forth as being with intimation (*saviññatti*) or without intimation (*aviññatti*).

The inclusion of "perception" (*saññā*) is for the purpose of showing the distinction in the state of mind regarding what constitutes a factor (*aṅga*) or a non-factor (*anaṅga*) of an offense; therefore, that state of mind which is present at the moment of an action-characteristic (*kiriyālakkhaṇa*) or a non-action-characteristic (*akiriyālakkhaṇa*), or from which an action or non-action arises, does not constitute a factor or a non-factor of an offense indiscriminately; rather, it is by means of whatever perception...

It is called "liberation through perception" (*saññāvimokkha*); thus it is shown that the consciousness associated with that [perception] is a factor (*aṅga*), while the other is a non-factor (*anaṅga*).

Now, because a training rule (*sikkhāpada*) is "with mind" (*sacittaka*) by means of whatever consciousness [is present], and "without mind" (*acittaka*) due to the absence of that [consciousness], its state as a "worldly offense" (*lokavajja*) is stated without distinction because of its blameworthy nature (*sāvajjatā*). However, even while being equally blameworthy, some [offenses]...
The term "worldly offense" (*lokavajja*) is included for the purpose of showing that some offenses are "offenses by rule" (*paṇṇattivajja*).

Since it is the mind itself that is called "worldly offense," the term "action" (*kamma*) is included to prevent the undesirable consequence that mental action (*manokamma*) might also be considered an "offense.
Furthermore, as for the action here characterized by non-doing (*akiriyālakkhaṇa*), it might otherwise be excluded from the triad of wholesome states (*kusalattika*).
The inclusion of the "wholesome triad" (kusalattika) is for the purpose of preventing an undesirable consequence. Furthermore, regarding the indeterminate offense (abyākatā āpatti) mentioned here,
since one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling (saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpanna) incurs it even though there is no feeling (avedana),
it should be understood that the inclusion of the "feeling triad" (vedanāttika) was made to prevent the undesirable consequence that this [offense] would not be found within the feeling triad.

For a training rule (sikkhāpada), even when committed by one who is without consciousness—though it is conventionally designated as "three minds, three feelings" with reference to persons possessing consciousness—is nevertheless called "three minds, three feelings. In this regard, there is this scriptural passage:

"There is an offense that one commits without consciousness and emerges from without consciousness; there is an offense that one commits with a wholesome mind and emerges from with a wholesome mind," and so forth. (Anugaṇṭhipada)

However, it is said: "Perception always brings about non-offense, while the mind brings about offense; that which is called 'without mind' (acittaka) is the non-cognition of the object, whereas 'non-release through perception' (no-saññā-vimokkha) is the cognition of the transgression—this is the distinction between them.
"By way of including all" means by way of including all training rules (sikkhāpada). [This refers to] the giving of robes and so forth to a bhikkhunī.
From the perspective of action (*kiriyā*) and non-action (*akiriyā*): the acceptance of gold, silver, and so forth may be from action;
the refusal of what has been set down [as a deposit] may be from non-action; the construction of a hut on a site that has been designated and exceeds the prescribed measure may be from action;

the construction of one on a site not designated or exceeding the measure may be from both action and non-action. "Whatever mental factor it obtains" refers to the mental state of the body or the mental state of speech; thus it is. Even without...
Regarding the phrase "by mind": here the intended meaning is both "even without mind" and "together with mind.
That which was described as the body—both informative (*saviññatti*) and non-informative (*aviññatti*)—its action is bodily action (*kāyakamma*); likewise for verbal action (*vacīkamma*).

In this context, the informative body accomplishes action through its arising, while the other does so through its non-arising. It should be understood that the same applies to speech; thus it is called a training rule (*sikkhāpada*).

It is stated that [this] applies to transgression because of the statement: "Whatever there is therein, the mental body and the verbal body. It is said in the *Anugaṇṭhipada*: "The laughter-arousing [consciousness] and the determining consciousnesses (*voṭṭhabbanāni*) are also minds that originate an offense.
When one sees while laughing, 'This too was not delimited by me,' then the determining consciousness follows the course of the impulsion (*javana*).
The superknowledge-consciousnesses (*abhiññācittāni*), however, do not know the formal designation (*paññatti*).
These [cases] are to be understood at the time of performing miracles through psychic power (*iddhi-vikubbanā*) and so forth.
Here, however, regarding the rule: "Whatever monk, having undertaken the training and the way of life of the monks...

[etc. ...while engaging in sexual intercourse, some become one who has committed a *pārājika* offense and is no longer in communion; some do not become one who has committed a *pārājika* offense and is no longer in communion."

Among the bases for an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) or a grave offense (*thullaccaya*), there is someone who, while engaging in [sexual intercourse], is not one who has committed a defeat (*pārājika*).

A *pakkhapandaka* (one who is impotent during certain phases) who was ordained during the phase when he is not impotent, yet engages in sexual intercourse during the phase when he is impotent—he does not incur an offense of defeat;
thus, he is called "one who is not defeated. For there is no such thing as an offense for one who is not a monk. Because he is without offense, during the phase when he is not impotent...
Has one who has returned [to the laity] lost his status as one who lives in communion (*asaṃvāsa*), or not?

He has. For it is said: "He is incapable [of being ordained again] with that same bodily bond. Because it is stated: "But whichever bhikkhu, bhikkhus... [is found guilty], he is one who lives outside of communion," it is only he who, by means of his status as a bhikkhu, engages in sexual intercourse who is incapable [of re-ordination].
If you argue that this does not constitute a defeat (*pārājika*) for him, we say no; for it is said: "By a competent bhikkhu..."

In the passage stating, "The Saṅgha should be informed by one who is capable," this should be understood in the same way as when a formal act (*kamma*) succeeds even though the proclamation (*kammavācā*) was recited by one who was not a bhikkhu, because a failure of the formal act is impossible. Herein is the reasoning:
if he who recites the proclamation has previously been fully ordained (*upasampanna*), and the Saṅgha perceives him as such, then it is so.

"The teacher says: 'We have patience [that] the action succeeds and not otherwise. If a householder, a member of another sect, or a paṇḍaka, perceiving himself as one who has not yet been ordained, utters the formal act (kammavācā), the formal act has not been pronounced by the Saṅgha;
for according to the statement, 'The Saṅgha should ordain, the Saṅgha ordains, he is ordained by the Saṅgha,' it must be by the Saṅgha."

When the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*) is being recited, it should be understood that if it is uttered by one who is included within the Saṅgha—or even by one who is merely perceived as being included within the Saṅgha—it is indeed as if it were uttered by the Saṅgha; this is the principle that applies to all formal acts (*kamma*).
Likewise, there is the case of one who commits sexual intercourse and must be expelled; for it has been stated: "He who violates a bhikkhunī—this one is to be expelled."

In this way, even though he is not yet fully ordained (*anupasampanna*), he incurs offenses such as sharing a sleeping place; furthermore, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for insulting him.
One who practices sexual intercourse with a non-nun is not to be expelled, because of the absence of a textual passage stating:

"Monks, one who has committed the ultimate offense (*antimavatthu*) who is not fully ordained... [is] to be expelled. For that very reason, he is included in the category of those who are fully ordained.

He goes [into exile], yet he does not incur an offense such as sleeping together; rather, being considered one who is no longer in communion (*asaṃvāsa*), he does not count toward completing the quorum for a formal act.
For "communion" (*saṃvāsa*) is said to consist of performing formal acts together and receiving the same recitation of the scriptures.

Furthermore, considering "shared training" (*samasikkhatā*) also to be communion, the shadow of the underlying reason is seen in the fact that because he lacks it with him, he incurs an offense of "learning the words" (*padasodhamma*). This is just as in the case of a nun...

Because there is no communal living characterized by shared formal acts (*ekakamma*) with the Saṅgha of monks, a nun is not in communion with a monk, and likewise a monk is not in communion with a nun;
however, she does incur an offense involving the loss of status (*padasodhammāpatti*).

Similarly, by the illustration that "even one who has committed a final offense (*antimavatthu*) is not said to be one who must be expelled," this shadow of the reason does not fall within the scope of the rule.

Furthermore, because of the statements: “If a monk misbehaves with a sleeping monk, and the awakened one consents, both are to be expelled,” and “In that case, monks, you must expel the nun Mettiyā,” it follows that even one who has entered the midst of the Saṅgha and been defeated while being investigated by an investigator is likewise not one who is fully ordained;
thus, there is no offense of expiation for abusive speech [against such a person].

It should be understood that [the offense] arises from speaking thus. Although there is no text stating, "Perceiving one who is fully ordained as fully ordained, desiring to revile him," nevertheless, in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*, it is stated:
"The fact that he is reviled refers to his status as one who is fully ordained; the reviling by way of birth and so forth under some other pretext;
the awareness, 'He reviles me'; and the absence of any prior intention for a specific purpose—these are the factors here."

Although it is stated that there are "four factors," nevertheless, regarding the training rule on abusive speech (*duṭṭhadosa-sikkhāpada*), because of the statement: "If a person is impure, having committed one of the *pārājika* offenses, and another who perceives him as pure, having asked for permission, speaks with the intention of reviling him,

there is an offense of abusive speech (*omasavāda*)," it follows that for one who reviles [the other] specifically while perceiving him as ordained (*upasampanna*) despite his impurity, [there is an offense].
[If one speaks] with the view that [the person] is impure, it is a dukkaṭa offense.

However, because of the statement in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī: “A person is pure, having not committed any pārājika offense; if one who likewise views him as pure, having asked for permission, speaks with the intention of reviling him, there is an offense of abusive speech,” it follows that [in this case] there is the status of being ordained and the perception that he is ordained.
It should be understood that this was not stated because that factor is not definitive.

Furthermore, in this context, the fourfold classification regarding the renunciation of training should be understood: there is a person who has renounced the training but has not entered upon the mode of livelihood of training;
there is one who has entered upon the mode of livelihood of training but has not renounced the training; and there is...

There is one who has both renounced the training and entered into a life-style contrary to the training, and there is one who has neither renounced the training nor entered into a life-style contrary to the training.
In this context, the third type should be understood as one who has renounced the training of a bhikkhunī.

For as long as she does not discard the distinctive marks, while still having zeal for the saffron robes and desiring to fall away from the state of asceticism, she [remains] regarding the training...
Even when she renounces the training, a bhikkhunī remains one who has entered upon the training and the way of life. For it was said by the Blessed One:
"Bhikkhus, there is no renunciation of the training for a bhikkhunī. But when does she cease to be a bhikkhunī?
When, desiring to fall away from the state of a recluse, she puts on the dress of a householder, she is reckoned as "one who has gone over" (vibbhantā). For it was said by the Blessed One:
“As soon as she has disrobed, at that very moment she is no longer a bhikkhunī. To what extent, then, is one said to have disrobed?

When, desiring to fall away from the state of a recluse, she shows no attachment to the saffron robes—either she removes the saffron robe, or she goes about naked, or she goes about having covered herself with grass, leaves, and so forth, or she wears the saffron robe itself in the manner of a householder’s dress, or [she wears] white...
When she puts on a [lay] garment, or enters among the heretics together with her own religious insignia and undertakes such vows as the plucking out of hair,

or adopts the insignia of a heretic, then she is said to have "left the order" (vibbhantā). In that regard, one who, while still remaining within the insignia of a bhikkhunī, undertakes the vows of a heretic—
like a monk who has gone over to the faction of the heretics— even if she later undergoes the formal going-forth (pabbajjā) again...
She does not receive it; the others receive only the going-forth (*pabbajjā*), but not the full ordination (*upasampadā*).

Although in the Canon it is stated, "Monks, that nun who, while still wearing the saffron robe, has gone over to another religious order—if she returns, she is not to be ordained," this implies that one who first disrobes and subsequently goes over to another religious order may, upon her return, be ordained.
It appears as if it were permitted. However, because the teachers of the Council (Saṅgīti-ācariyas) stated, "There are twenty-four pārājikas," she cannot be ordained again;
therefore, the renunciation of the training was not permitted by the Blessed One. A bhikkhunī who has committed an ultimate offense (antimavatthu) is indeed a bhikkhunī.
A bhikkhunī who is a "pakkhapaṇḍaka" is also indeed a bhikkhunī. This is the inquiry: "How so?"

**Commentary on the Section on Settled Cases (Vinītavatthu) 67.** "Settled cases" (*vinītavatthu*) refers to those cases that have been settled and adjudicated. Having extracted the individual names and counts for each of these cases— beginning with "Now at that time,
a certain monk"— in order to clear away the defects of deficiency or excess, [the following is stated].

Because they are both summaries (*uddāna*) and verses (*gāthā*) characterized by the rules of prosody (*chandovicitilakkhaṇa*) through the attainment of mantras and so forth, they are called “summary-verses” (*uddānagāthā*).

It should be understood that the form *uddānā* is derived from the verbal root *sudh* (to cleanse). Furthermore, these summary-verses were established by the Elders of the Dhamma-Saṅgaha at the time of the Council;
if one asks where, it was at the conclusion of the Word-Commentary (*Padabhājanīya*). [The following are] the “Context Verses” (*vatthugāthā*).
In the *Gaṇṭhipada*, it is stated: "The names 'Then at that time, a certain monk' and so forth are the introductory narratives (*nidāna*) for these cases of disciplinary training (*vinītavatthu*).
Therefore, it should be understood that the cases of disciplinary training themselves are called "story-verses" (*vatthugāthā*) according to the method explained therein.
This is a brief indication of the intended meaning here: "Monk, you have fallen into an offense..."

The "cases of discipline" (vinītavatthu) are those matters that have been settled and adjudicated by way of showing a root-offense, such as: "Bhikkhu, there is no offense of pārājika; there is an offense of saṅghādisesa and dukkaṭa";
or by way of showing a classification of offenses, such as: "Bhikkhu, there is no offense for one who does not consent";
or by way of showing non-offenses, such as: "Bhikkhu, there is no offense for one who does not consent. These are the cases of discipline. Of those cases of discipline...
The discourse that illuminates the source and the basis is called the *vatthugāthā* (basis-verses). Some say that the *uddānagāthā* (summary-verses) themselves are called "basis-verses.
This contradicts the statement: "By means of this characteristic, those who uphold the Vinaya will decide upon the Vinaya in the future.
For not even a single characteristic of decision-making is seen in the summary-verses; [this is because] of the summary-verses...
The specific purpose has been stated as: "The holders of the Vinaya will easily learn it. Therefore, this diversity should be understood as being due to the diversity of the purposes.
Herein, this is the analysis of the compound: *vatthūni* (bases) themselves are the *gāthā* (verses), thus *vatthugāthā*.

The inclusion of the word *gāthā* here is for the purpose of distinguishing them from the *vinītavatthu* (cases of discipline). It should be understood that the inclusion of the word *vatthu* is for the purpose of distinguishing them from the *uddānagāthā* (summary verses).
Some, however, say: "Where 'the grounds for the verses' (*gāthānaṃ vatthūni*) should have been said, it is stated as 'the verses on the grounds' (*vatthugāthā*).

Regarding the Monkey Story (*makkaṭivatthu*), other monks related it there, whereas here he relates it himself. In that case, because it was stated that "the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) was laid down by the Blessed One," the Vajjiputtakas were indeed others. "In that case it was the Elder Ānanda; here, they themselves."
It is stated in a certain commentary (*gaṇṭhipada*). The intention of the Master has been explained previously;
therefore, it should be examined. 67–8. *Ñatvā* means having known by oneself without asking. *Pokkharaṃ* refers to the body, which is like the head of a drum (*bheripokkhara*).
Worldly people call that which is complete "beautiful"; therefore, by the first meaning, "due to the beauty of the complexion" means due to the excellence of the skin of the body.
The purpose [of the first epithet] is [to show her excellence], while by the second, her beauty of complexion is shown. It is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* (Commentary on Difficult Points):

“Because she has the color of the interior of a blue lotus, she is ‘golden-colored’; therefore, she received the name Uppalavaṇṇā. However, the statement that her bodily skin is the color of a blue lotus indicates that her skin is smooth (*sāma*).

In the world, however, from the expression “a woman equal to a blue lotus, a praised dark-complexioned one,” it follows: “She who is *sāmā*, of dark complexion, with a waist thin like a *sāma* [lotus].”
Because of the statement, "That service is my dwelling in heaven," service to women is praised. There is also a reading: "As long as there is darkness for her.
He who is not smeared by the objects of sensual desire (vatthukāma) through the defilements of sensual desire (kilesakāma). 69.
"The female characteristic has appeared" means the female form has appeared; and that, moreover, [occurs] when the male faculty (*purisindriya*)...
By means of disappearance, through the manifestation of the female faculty (*itthindriya*). The same applies to the manifestation of the male faculty (*purisindriya*).
By this it is shown that the male faculty does not arise in Brahmās, but only the male physical form arises;
and just as in the case of certain eunuchs (*paṇḍaka*) where the male physical form arises even without the male faculty, it is not so for them [the Brahmās].

That has been shown; moreover, that femininity-faculty or masculinity-faculty disappears starting from the seventeenth moment of consciousness in reverse order, like those who are dying when the faculty vanishes.
When the present faculty has ceased, the other dissimilar faculty becomes manifest. For this is the case for one who has entered a deep sleep.
A faculty discordant with that [state] becomes manifest; therefore, it is said, "of one who has fallen asleep during the middle of the night.
Because of the statement, "Monks, I allow that very same person as the preceptor, that very same person as the one for full ordination," the preceptor is indeed the one who conducts the ceremony;
and since the teacher for full ordination is a bhikkhunī, considering her to be the teacher, the duties toward the preceptor apply to her.

Regarding the duties toward the teacher (*ācariyavatta*): must this bhikkhu go to the nuns’ residence every morning to perform these duties, and must those nuns come to his dwelling to perform the duties toward a co-resident student (*saddhivihārikavatta*) and so forth? No;

for by the statement, "I allow you, bhikkhus, to associate with the bhikkhunīs," it is shown that there is no separation [between them], and thus it is not merely the case that [the duties] are again [performed by] the preceptor (*upajjhāya*).

It should be understood that the passage beginning with "I allow you, monks, that very same preceptor" was spoken for the purpose of showing that [the candidate] is to be received [into the order], but the full ordination (upasampadā) is not to be performed.
In this context, "to be associated with the nuns" means I allow her to be in the company of the nuns alone, being without the monks; therefore, according to this reading of the text...
“The commentary’s statement that ‘there is no offense for her because of [the distance of] another village and so forth’ is established;
since it is possible to come and have intercourse, and since the going was permitted by the Blessed One, how could there be an offense based on the conditions of ‘another village’ and so forth?
For the Blessed One does not enjoin one to an offense—this is indeed logical; otherwise, [regarding] those offenses which belong to the bhikkhus...”

Because of the scriptural statement, "There is no offense for those offenses that are not shared with the bhikkhunīs," it does not follow that there is no offense regarding [crossing] village boundaries and so forth.

Rather, the fact that they are shared means it is indeed an offense; for it is said: "Those offenses which are not shared by bhikkhunīs with bhikkhus, and those offenses involving crossing a village boundary, crossing a river, staying apart at night, or withdrawing from a group with a bhikkhunī—[these are shared]."

If it is argued that [the offense] is not an offense regarding those specific offenses because it was not so stated, we say no; for it was not so stated because it would lead to an undesirable consequence (*aniṭṭha-pasaṅga*).

The meaning is that it was not stated in that way because it would lead to the undesirable consequence that even when she has gone over to the nuns, if they abandon her and associate with others, there would be no offense at all for her regarding going from one village to another and so forth at any time. In this regard, the case of the offense regarding going between villages, etc., is as follows:
Even if she intentionally commits an offense at that time, because she does not incur an offense due to the cause of the manifestation of her gender, it is a non-offense (*anāpatti*).

It should be understood that she is said to "emerge" precisely in the sense of not having incurred an offense. Likewise, the yogi brings about the cessation of defilements even before they have arisen.
Even a bowl that has not been tied [with the full number of stitches] is called "one with fewer than five ties," or alternatively, one that has not been formally announced is called "unconfessed."
There is training; thus it should be understood that even here, although she has not committed an offense, the offense is said to be "cleared.

However, because she is able to associate with the bhikkhunīs even while not committing the offense of lying down in the same bed as a man, it is therefore considered a non-offense, and so it is stated in the Commentary:
"The offense of lying down in the same bed applies to both. For this has been said:

In the *Parivāra*, it is said: "One incurs an offense in four other ways: in the midst of the Saṅgha, in the midst of a group, in the presence of an individual, and by the manifestation of sexual characteristics. Furthermore, regarding what was stated in the *Parivāra*:

"There is an offense such that one emerges while incurring it, and incurs it while emerging"—this refers to the fact that one incurs [an offense] such as sleeping together [with a woman], while one emerges from offenses that are not shared [with others].
It should be understood that this was said with reference to both cases. "The monastery is distant" means it is at least five hundred bow-lengths away;
the meaning is that for one entering the village starting from the monastery, there is an interval between villages (*gāmantara*).

"Having avoided the appointment" means having not made an appointment for traveling on the road. "Having abandoned them" means having renounced them. "Even by a novice who has completed his years of training."
From the wording, it appears as though there is no taking of formal preceptors for one whose years [of seniority] are not yet complete.

"Having performed a formal act of the Vinaya and set aside" means having set aside by means of a formal resolution (*vikappa*). It should be understood that for those items not so resolved, there is forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) upon the lapse of ten days.
However, after receiving them again, it is permissible for seven days; thus [the Buddha said], "Monks, I allow the storage of goods for monks."
This is stated because of the words: "having had it accepted by the bhikkhunīs, one may consume it. By "giving away without regard" is meant:
either by giving away the object without regard for it, or by accepting it [again] with the thought, "I will accept and consume it again.
If, during the period of the pakkhamānatta penance, the gender changes once more, then only the six-night *mānatta* penance itself should be granted.
The Teacher says that [the rule] "at the time of being a bhikkhu" refers to an offense not concealed, and not to one concealed;
however, it should be understood that this is stated because concealment is impossible for a bhikkhunī, and thus there is no granting of *parivāsa*.
If a bhikkhunī, having committed an *asādhāraṇa* (unshared) *pārājika* offense, acquires the male gender (*purisaliṅga*), [she reappears] among the bhikkhus.

One does not obtain full ordination (*upasampadā*), but one obtains the going-forth (*pabbajjā*); having gone forth, while remaining in the state of a monk, one does not incur an offense for sharing a sleeping place.
When a nun who has disrobed manifests the male characteristic, she does not obtain full ordination among the monks;
[if she commits an act], it is a *pārājika*. If, while still being a householder who has not disrobed, he violates a nun—provided that...
The female gender manifests; she does not receive full ordination among the bhikkhunīs, nor again when the change of gender occurs does she receive it among the bhikkhus.
When a bhikkhunī undergoes a change of gender and becomes a bhikkhu, if he should renounce the training, disrobe, and regain the female gender, he receives full ordination among the bhikkhunīs.

Because in both cases he had not previously attained the status of one defeated (*pārājika*). However, if a nun who has completed twelve years of seniority should acquire the male characteristic, she is indeed a fully ordained monk (*upasampanna*).
If he returns after having renounced the training again, he must not be ordained because he is less than twenty years of age.
Furthermore, if there is a change of gender, [he should be ordained] among the nuns.

She receives full ordination (*upasampadā*). Thus, if a girl who has completed the twelve years of the preparatory period undergoes a change of sex, she becomes a woman who has entered the household life; it is said that if she is now fully twelve years old, she may be ordained.

Should a nun lose her female characteristics, or a monk lose his male characteristics, such that they become a *pakkha-paṇḍaka* (one who is impotent for part of the time), she [the former nun] is no longer a nun.
A nun is to be expelled by the nuns, while a monk may be [expelled] by the monks, because of the possibility of returning to his original status.
However, with reference to the "natural eunuch" (*pakati-paṇḍaka*), it is said: "The eunuch is to be expelled.

For the "periodic eunuch" (*pakkha-paṇḍaka*) is to be expelled through suspension from communal living, whereas the other is subject to both forms of expulsion; this is the meaning. If they were to return to their original state again, [the Buddha said]: "Monks, I allow you..."
"The procedure is possible thus: 'With that very same preceptor, with that very same full ordination, and for those very same years, one may associate with the bhikkhunīs.

If their gender were to change, then regarding those offenses which are common to both bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs, they must be cleared in the presence of the bhikkhunīs; however, those offenses which are not common [to both] are non-offenses."
This procedure is also possible. As for what is stated in the *Parivāra*: "Simultaneously with its acquisition, one abandons the former and establishes oneself in the latter;
the intimations (*viññatti*) subside and the formal rules (*paññatti*) cease;
simultaneously with its acquisition, one abandons the latter and establishes oneself in the former; the intimations... and so forth—that refers to the procedure as already described.
"‘It is said’ means ‘our patience,’ says the Teacher. Regarding the disappearance of either the female or male characteristic:
does it disappear by taking the entire body with it, or does it disappear of its own accord? What of this?
If, first of all, it disappears by taking the entire body with it, then this person would be one who has passed away. Therefore, he would have passed away from his state as a recluse."
Furthermore, one who is being reborn would be subject to spontaneous birth (*opapātika*). Then, if [the faculties] themselves simply vanish, that state of theirs is also contradicted.
For the female faculty and the others are established having pervaded the entire body;
thus, their disappearance should be understood as occurring like momentary cessation. Therefore, it should be understood that there is no occurrence of the aforementioned fault.

It should be understood that just as when the light of lamps that are mutually interconnected ceases, the place of the remaining body persists even though the light of one has ceased, so too it is with the remaining parts of the body. 71–2.
"Whether he is released or not, there is only misconduct" is said because of the absence of lust for release. "Not an object" means non-acceptance.

"If, having lain down at night without closing the door, one thinks, 'I will rise during the day,' there is an offense of *dukkaṭa* due to disrespect.
Here too, because the word "having lain down" (*nipanno*) is used, [the offense applies] when dawn has risen.

And it should be understood that this is because [the Buddha] did not say, "Get up. Some say: "In the *Mahāpaccarī*, this was stated with reference only to the *dukkaṭa* offense of disrespect (*anādariya*), and not to the *dukkaṭa* mentioned in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. It is said that there is no offense for him because, in fact, he has not actually lain down.
However, if he has restrained himself during the night and is lying down, and someone opens the door at the time of dawn, [he is not at fault regarding] the maintenance of the doors and so forth.
They say: "For one who lies down without having performed [the formal act], there is indeed an offense.

Why? Because it is the field for an offense. Since even one possessed by a *yakkha* is called "deranged in mind" (*khittacitta*) as if unconscious, there is no offense for him regarding a *pārājika* offense, let alone another; therefore, it is said: "Even one who has become unconscious like one possessed by a *yakkha* is not released [from the offense]."

That which is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī* was said with the underlying intention that one who previously slept during the day intentionally is not released later even if seized by a *yakkha* or rendered unconscious, because the offense was incurred at the very moment of the act of lying down. One is released only when having been bound and made to lie down;
this applies not only to those seized by *yakkhas* and the like, but also to anyone who, until the very end, still intends to sleep themselves.

As long as it does not exist, one is released. When, having become weary, one has the intention to lie down due to a desire for sleep, then one should sleep only after having had [the companion] restrained, or kept awake, or made to attend; otherwise there is an offense.
If there is no companion, or if one does not see [a companion], or if one is unable to go, then even after waiting for a long time, afterwards—
Being overwhelmed by pain, one sleeps without volition; for him, there is no offense because of the statement, "There is no offense for one overwhelmed by pain.

Since that [state] is not within the scope of that [rule], no offense is seen. For one sleeping while unconscious, no offense is seen because of the statement, "There is no offense for one whose mind is deranged.
However, since the teachers do not speak thus, [the phrase] "no offense is seen" is used without distinction.
They say: "If one sleeps without regaining consciousness, no offense is seen because of the lack of mastery over oneself;

however, if one regains consciousness but, due to physical exhaustion, consents to lying down and falls asleep, since the lack of mastery over oneself is not evident in that case, therefore an offense does indeed exist"—this is the intended meaning of their statement.
In the opinion of the Elder Mahāpaduma, one possessed by a *yakkha* or one whose mind is deranged is released.
The intention is that one who has been bound and laid down is released because they lack the intention to lie down and because they are overwhelmed by pain.
This being so, the Pāḷi, the Commentary, and the Elder’s opinion are in agreement; therefore, this alone is the intended meaning of those respective determinations, and we accept it as such.
The Teacher [states] that, according to the *Anugaṇṭhipada*, even one seized by a spirit or one who has lost consciousness is not said to be "freed";
the intention is that he is capable of incurring a *pārājika* offense because he regains consciousness from time to time.
If it is argued that, based on the *Kurundi* statement, "or having been bound and made to lie down," one is not freed even if lying down in a single position, [the answer is: he is indeed freed. Why?

Because it is not so designated in terms of its meaning (*atthato*). According to the *Kurundi* tradition, this accords with the doctrine of the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*. Why? Because they share the common characteristic of being subject to no one’s authority (*avasavatta-sāmaññato*).
Although it does indeed accord, the teachers do not speak in this way. To show that it is not only they [the teachers], but also the Elder Mahāpaduma who holds this view, it is stated:
“by the Elder Mahāpaduma. In the doctrine of the Elder Mahāpaduma, regarding the committing of a *pārājika* offense...
It is said, "One who is seized by a *yakkha* is incapable [of such an act]"; however, regarding this, the teachers say as follows:

therefore, for one who falls and lies down right there without rising, there is an offense whether he knows it intermittently or does not know it."
To show the statements found in all the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) collected together, it was said: "In this case, who is released and who is not released?
One possessed by a spirit (*yakkha*) or one who has lost consciousness is not only capable of committing a *pārājika* offense;
indeed, everyone commits it. Thus, by the statement "only one who is bound and laid down is released," even for that person—
Because he is not subject to his own will, they do not say, "No offense is seen.

2. The second *pārājika*.
Commentary on the Story of Dhaniya (84):

Regarding the second [verse], the intention is that he dwelt in four monasteries on Mount Gijjhakūṭa, which— because it was surrounded by kings— is named "Rājagaha," and which possesses the locative case ending in the sense of proximity and as the locus of action.

The connection for this should be understood as: "They entered the rains residence. For it is only three [monks] who, having established the motion (*ñatti*), perform a formal act of the community (*gaṇakamma*);

fewer than that or more than that do not, because such acts would not be accomplished. In this regard, for the sake of proficiency in the formal acts of the Saṅgha, the Gaṇa, and the individual (*puggala*) according to the method of the Vinaya, this supplementary explanation should be understood:
there is a Saṅgha formal act which the Saṅgha alone performs, neither the Gaṇa nor the individual.
Setting aside that one part of the characteristics of an act which consists of a formal resolution (*apalokanakamma*), the other fourfold types of acts should also be understood.
There is a Saṅgha-act which the Saṅgha performs, the group performs, and the individual performs. What is this?
It is that which was previously set aside. For this has been stated in the *Parivāra-aṭṭhakathā*: "In whatever monastery there are two or three persons..."
Those who dwell there, having sat down [in that place], perform even what they themselves have done as if it were done by the Saṅgha.

Furthermore, in a monastery where there is only one bhikkhu, whatever formal agreement (katikavatta) is made by that bhikkhu while sitting after having performed the preliminary duties and preliminary tasks on the Uposatha day, it becomes exactly the same as if it were done by the Saṅgha. It is also stated: "In a monastery with only one bhikkhu..."
"Even when recited by one person alone, the previous formal act is indeed pacified.

There are formal acts of a group that the Saṅgha performs, the group performs, or an individual performs; these are to be understood according to the three types of *pārisuddhi-uposatha*, which are performed in the presence of others.
There are also formal acts of a group that only the group performs, neither the Saṅgha nor an individual. These...
The *pārisuddhi-uposatha* (uposatha by means of mutual declaration of purity) is performed by way of announcing it to one another; it should be understood according to that [method].

There is the *puggala-kamma* (an act performed by an individual), which is done by an individual alone, neither by the Saṅgha nor by a group (*gaṇa*); that should be understood by way of the *adhiṭṭhāna-uposatha* (uposatha by formal determination).
There is the *gaṇa-kamma* (an act performed by a group), where only a certain group performs it while another does not; in that case, there are two types of non-triads.
They perform [the formal act], not three [or fewer]. Only three perform the *saññatti* (motion), neither fewer nor more; therefore it is said:
"Only three, having established the motion (*ñatti*), perform the formal act of the assembly (*gaṇakamma*); neither fewer nor more, because [fewer] would fail to accomplish it.
Therefore, it should be understood that only three are considered a quorum according to the method of the Vinaya, and not more than that. However, in the *Anugaṇṭhipada*, it says:
"Although only three people perform the characteristic act of a formal legal procedure (*kamma*), it has been stated that what they have performed is equivalent to what is performed by a *saṅgha*;
thus, in one sense, even three individuals are a *saṅgha* according to the Vinaya method. This entire statement is made with reference to formal legal procedures of the Vinaya;
however, with reference to the acquisition [of requisites], even a single person—even one who is not fully ordained—is called a "saṅgha."
It is said that they "enter into reckoning. Immediately upon the rising of the dawn on the day of the *pavāraṇā*, they are called "those who have completed the rains" (*vutthavassa*);

this is stated according to the method of maximum inclusion as "starting from the first day of the month" (*pāṭipadadivasa*). For this very reason, it is said, "they have performed the *pavāraṇā* at the Great *Pavāraṇā*.
Otherwise, it would follow that those who did not perform the *pavāraṇā* due to an obstacle could not be called "those who have completed the rains."

85. By means of this training rule concerning the prohibition against giving orders— “Let not future generations fall into the habit of slaughtering living beings”—
wherever there is the baking of bricks, the cooking of rice, the building of huts, the construction of monasteries, the performance of new work, the repair of what is broken or dilapidated,
the sweeping of monasteries, the setting fire to grass, or the excavation of wells and lotus ponds, a monk who knows that such slaughter is taking place [must intervene].
This shows that even a "permissible statement" (*kappiyavacana*) should not be uttered;
for that very reason, without stating the alternative method, it is said in the sections on non-offenses for those training rules: "There is no offense for one who is mindless or unaware.

It is thus established that for those dwelling there as well, it is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). For otherwise, the Blessed One would not have ordered them to be torn down.

This same principle applies here to the terms "tearing down," "cutting down," and "stripping away"; these too are simply distinctions of offenses. For this very reason, as in the training rules concerning tearing down and so forth, it is stated:

Furthermore, when there is a corruption of the Canon (*pāḷi*), how can there be no corruption of the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*)?
Regarding the statement, "It is permitted to build a dwelling in the form of a house of bricks (*giñjakāvasatha*)," this refers to a dwelling that must be constructed by piling up natural bricks.
Regarding the term *giñjakāvasatha*: it is not called "made of clay" (*mattikāmaya*), but rather it is called a "brick hut" (*iṭṭhakakuṭikā*).

Therefore, the Teacher [Vasubandhu] maintains that even if it contains husks, cow dung, grass, or straw, and even if it is made of unrefined clay, it is nevertheless called "entirely made of clay" (*sabbamattikāmaya*);
for ashes and such things are taken up only for the purpose of strengthening the clay.
Even one made of unburnt clay does not count as a "brick house" (*giñjakāvasatha*);
furthermore, the Venerable Dhaniya did not complete that hut all at once like a potter making a jar, but rather finished it by gradually piling up lumps of clay after each had dried.
A hut made entirely of clay is like a hut made of unburnt clay.
Some say that it is permissible because it is constructed as a single solid unit and not made of separate bricks; therefore, it is allowable.
However, if one lives inside a hut made entirely of clay after constructing a grass hut or similar structure outside it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

If, however, one makes openings here and there, fastens them together, and thus makes it a single solid unit, it is permissible. If one lives inside after constructing a grass hut or similar structure within [the clay structure], [it is likewise an offense].
It is permissible. If only the builder resides there, he incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense on account of the act of building, not on account of residing.

"for the purpose of protecting the bowl and robes. Commentary on the Decisions Outside the Text:

—“I allow you, monks, all metal ware except for a hammer;

Therefore, this scriptural passage proceeds by way of genus, stating "except for a weapon," while the scriptural passage as it has been shown proceeds by way of prohibiting modifications such as coloring or polishing; thus, both are not contradictory. Therefore...
It is exactly as previously stated. "By the tip of the awl" means by the point of the needle; it refers to the method described in the passage, "Like a mustard seed on the tip of an awl.

"Gomuttaka" refers to lines shaped like cow's urine. Because a key is an accessory for lodgings, it is permissible even if made of gold or silver; thus its luster is visible.

These include such items as "the fan and the palm-leaf fan," as stated in the text. In the *Gaṇṭhipada*, however, it is said:

"Polishing with color and making a glossy finish on oil containers is permitted because they are requisites for lodgings (*senāsana*). "Royal favorites" refers to those who are dependents of the royal family.

"Boundary" here means the land intended by the context, as well as a formally established boundary (*baddhasīmā*). Regarding this, the *Anugaṇṭhipada* states: "The boundary belongs to those to whom it belongs; others must not act there."
It has been stated: "The earth and the boundary belong to those [who own it], and therefore they alone may prohibit [the establishment of a boundary].

86–7. There was [the intention] to have a wooden shed built, and there was also [the intention] to build one. "In pieces" should be understood as being like fruit that has been broken into bits.

88. Regarding the reading, “Having spoken such words,” [the meaning is as follows]: “You have been released because of your greed; do not do such a thing again.

"Is it possible that one should generate excessive joy and gladness after having made the invitation, 'By this there is purpose'? "This is true;

It should be understood that he speaks thus. Regarding the phrase "in such places as these":

they reproached him. That which is called a *rudradāmaka* is produced from *rudra-dāmaka* and other such [sources].

In cities such as Bārāṇasī, blue coins (*nīla-kahāpaṇa*) endowed with the [proper] characteristics were produced by various kings in accordance with ancient treatises. It is said that a *rudradāmaka* is worth one-third of those.
Therefore, for him, a quarter [of a coin] constitutes the basis for a *thullaccaya* offense. However, in this context, a *māsaka* is not the fixed measure.
