For they [hold that] after attaining the first jhāna, while sitting in various postures and striving for the second [jhāna], at the time when the coarse activity of consciousness occurs due to initial application (vitakka) and sustained application (vicāra) in the access concentration (upacāra)—"
“They say [the breath] is gross by way of the occurrence of inhalation and exhalation.

It is written: “The Majjhimabhāṇakas say that for one who has attained jhāna, at the time of entering it and upon obtaining a single sitting, the second [breath] is more subtle than the first due to the state of tranquility in the successive occurrences of consciousness during the access stage.”
However, regarding "in insight," this sequence is for one who has become intent upon the analysis of the four elements;

it should be understood that it is also for others. The phrase "in the grasping of the whole of materiality" is said with reference to the vision that "this much is materiality, and there is nothing other than this.
Regarding the phrase "in the grasping of both materiality and immateriality," from the contemplation of dissolution—which takes the characteristics such as impermanence as its object—onwards...
Insight is powerful. "By the method stated previously" means by the method beginning with "at a time when nothing has been grasped," according to the opinion of all [the masters].
"Purification" (sodhanā) means answering. "Of this" refers to the phrase "tranquilizing the bodily formation.
"Bowing forward" is *ānamanā*. "Bowing sideways" is *vinamanā*. "Bowing well" is *sannamanā*. "Bowing backward" is...

*Bāṇamanā* (bending): It should be understood that the word *uttā* is used for the purpose of revealing the meanings of *ānamana* (bending), *iñjana* (moving), and so forth—just as one stands having grasped the knees.
The connection is: "In whatever manner there is bending and so forth, or shaking and so forth, in that same manner they cause [the body] to become tranquil (*passambhayanti*).
*Iti kira* means "if it is thus. *Evaṃ sante* means "even if it is already peaceful and subtle, if it becomes further tranquil. *Pabhāvanā* means "production" or "arousing."

Because the in-breaths and out-breaths have subsided, there is no development of the concentration of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassatisamādhi*). Since that is absent, one does not attain [jhāna];
and due to the absence of attainment, one does not emerge from it. "It is said thus" (*iti kira*) means: first of all, this is the statement;
that is to say, sound itself is the sign of sound, as in the phrases "mindfully he breathes in, mindfully he breathes out."
Having established this, thirty-two steps consisting of four tetrads should be understood.

Regarding "non-oppression": although practices such as the observance of duties on the shrine terrace (*cetiyāṅgaṇa*) are included in meaning within the morality of restraint by the Pātimokkha—due to the statement, "for whomsoever there may be an offense"—nevertheless...
“Sāriputta, the Teacher does not lay down a training rule or recite the Pātimokkha for his disciples as long as certain things that are bases for the taints do not appear among the Saṅgha.

Because this was not intended [in the previous context], it is called “pertaining to higher conduct. Furthermore, it is said: “But whatever here is not a basis for an offense is entirely unmixed [with them].”
"As stated" means because it is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for the practice of yoga and application. "Living simply" means possessing eight requisites.

Regarding the "fivefold meditation subject": here, both the jhāna, the sign (*nimitta*), the scripture that illuminates their meaning, and the lodging endowed with qualities such as being suitable for coming and going, as well as the washing of soiled robes and so forth, are called "meditation subjects."
Minor impediments: he wavers, thinking, "Has it not fallen in between?

"With the mind distracted internally" means with the mind distracted within one's own internal domain. "Agitated" means due to lack of concentration. The "base of the post for the tethering rope" refers to the tip of the nose or the sign of the face.
"Right there" means at the sign such as the tip of the nose. "Like the plank of a swing..."
“They say that one sees both ends and the middle on a single side.

Here, however, refers to the Simile of the Saw. “From the place of contact” means from the location where there is touching. “The sign should be established” is said in the sense that it should be established when the sign exists.
It is called “weighty development” because it is to be developed by the venerable ones. “Some say” means some meditators say.
Because of the statement, "Due to the diversity of perception," even what has been stated by some is indeed authoritative;

however, it was stated in that way because it does not appear in the commentary from the time of the recitation onwards. Even though there is no such conceptualization as "Does the form of a star appear to me?
and so forth, these elements appear in various ways to one who simply meditates upon them, just as these elements arise through the diversity of the primary elements (*dhātu*).
"It is not permissible to say 'it is not the sign' because it would be a deliberate lie," so it was said.
"The meditation subject" here refers specifically to the counterpart sign mentioned.
"In the sign" means in the counterpart sign. "Various forms" refers to the manifold variety described as "four colors occur. They discern this.
"Making known while understanding. "In-breath and out-breath" refers to the sign produced from those [breaths], or it refers to the various aspects of the in-breath and out-breath.
For it is said that one who fixes the mind on the sign also discerns its various aspects, or else binds one's own mind to the in-breath and out-breath.
[One observes them] by way of the color of the stars and so forth, and by way of their characteristics such as hardness and so forth.
"It is rejected in the Commentaries" means that it is rejected in the Sinhalese Commentaries after stating the reason: "because it is too close to the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
Why? Because when absorption (appanā) occurs in the sixth or seventh consciousness-moment, there is no opportunity for the fruit (phala) within the cognitive process of the Path (magga-vīthi).

If one asks, "Let it occur here [in the fifth moment]?"—no; for even mundane absorption (lokiya-appanā) shares the same destiny as supramundane absorption within the cognitive process of absorption (appanā-vīthi).

Even a bhikkhu who has attained jhāna, desiring to sit for seven days after entering jhāna for the sake of dwelling in happiness in this very life (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra*), enters and sits in either the fourth or the fifth [jhāna], but not the sixth or the seventh.
For absorption (*appanā*) occurs there; beyond that, it no longer serves as a basis for absorption. Because it is close to the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), the fourth [jhāna]—
The Master says that it goes to the fifth [consciousness] because it stands between the impulsions, like a pot placed on dry land;
this is called mastery over adverting (*āvajjanavasī*), which is the adverting only to the factors of jhāna without adverting to diverse objects.
Thereafter, the arising of four or five reviewing consciousnesses is called mastery over reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇavasī*).
For this very reason it was said: "But mastery in reviewing is indeed included within mastery in adverting.
Mastery in attainment (samāpajjanavasī) means entering into attainment for as long a duration as one desires; it is the capacity to establish that desired limit of time.
The difference between mastery in resolution (adhiṭṭhānavasī) and mastery in emergence (vuṭṭhānavasī) lies in the power of resolution.
They say as well: "The impulsion (javana) runs; but by the power of emergence (vuṭṭhāna), it runs even more intensely than intended.
Furthermore, having adverted to an object such as the earth-kasiṇa and having performed the impulsion, one adverts again, and thereafter the fifth jhāna consciousness arises;
this, they say, is the highest limit. But for the Blessed One, it occurs immediately after the adverting [consciousness].
That "there is jhāna" is stated in its entirety in the *Anugaṇṭhipada*.
It is written: "The 'basis' (*vatthu*) is the heart-basis; the 'door' (*dvāra*) is the eye and so forth; the 'object' (*ārammaṇa*) is visible form and so forth.
Or, consciousness sees the object of visible form as it has been apprehended, or it sees it otherwise. How? "As the basis, door, and object of the visible form have been apprehended..."

It is said: “or. My conjecture is that one should examine and then accept this: that for whichever consciousness there are bases, doors, and objects among the forms as they have been delimited, that consciousness sees those very forms, bases, doors, and objects as they have been delimited;
or else, it should be understood that there is the elision of one instance of the word "object" (*ārammaṇa*).
Beyond that, in the three tetrads, one should count by taking two words at a time as each single unit.

Here, the "experience of rapture" (pīti-paṭisaṃvedana) should be understood from the perspective of the object through serenity (samatha), and from the perspective of non-delusion through insight (vipassanā).

However, regarding the passage beginning with "This knowledge is painful," where it was stated [in the previous tetrad] "from the perspective of the object and from the perspective of non-delusion," what is stated here is expressed in the reverse order of that previously mentioned method.
For in that state, because the delusion by which that suffering was concealed no longer manifests,
or because of the capacity to review it at will whenever one desires during such an occurrence of knowledge,
knowledge is said to exist due to non-delusion regarding the three— suffering and the rest. Regarding cessation, there is the experience of joy associated with it as its object.
It does not arise from non-delusion because there would be no abandonment of delusion, and because it would contradict the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*.

In that context, the passage beginning with “by way of long inhalation,” etc., is stated to show [the jhāna] by way of its object. The intended meaning here is: “By means of that mindfulness and that knowledge, that joy is clearly experienced (*paṭisaṃviditā*) because its object is clearly experienced.
The passage beginning with “for one who adverts,” etc., refers to non-delusion.
This was said in order to show the experience of rapture (*pīti*). It applies to one who knows, sees, and reviews [the object] by way of its impermanence and so forth;
to one who resolves and becomes intent upon it by way of being directed toward that; and likewise to one who exerts energy and so forth through momentary concentration (*khaṇika-samādhi*).

"To be directly known" (*abhiññeyya*) is by way of full understanding as the known (*ñāta-pariññā*); "to be fully understood" (*pariññeyya*) is by way of full understanding as investigation (*tīraṇa-pariññā*). For the entire truth of suffering (*dukkha-sacca*) is [both].
It is that which is to be directly known (*abhiññeyya*) and that which is to be fully understood (*pariññeyya*). Regarding this, it is written: "And herein, there is this joy.

It is stated that the passage beginning with "that which is to be directly known" refers to the moment of the Path (*magga*). Because the function of insight (*vipassanā*), characterized by non-delusion, is accomplished by means of the Path, the Path itself is described as if it were making the objects—beginning with "that which is to be directly known"—its own objective support.
The statement that bodily pleasure is absent in the stage of serenity (*samatha*) was made for the purpose of showing the plane of insight.
"In the two passages concerning the mental formations": this refers to "experiencing the mental formations... training" and "training while tranquilizing the mental formations... experiencing.

All terms such as "gladdening" (modanā) are synonyms for rapture (pīti). "Contemplation of impermanence" (aniccānupassanā) and so forth refer to the defilements and the formative activities (abhisaṅkhāra) of the aggregates rooted in those defilements.
"Developed in this way" does not mean developed by the production of the fourfold or fivefold jhānas. Thus...

Having brought it to fulfillment in every aspect, it was developed. Even at the times of reviewing the path of insight, everything was shown by the Blessed One, who is skilled in means, precisely through the inhalation that occurs.
Why is this said? The intention is: "by us."
172. Regarding the phrase *ussukkavacanaṃ*:
it is said that this is a designation for a word that is well-known; thus, it is called a "corresponding word" (*samānakapada*).

Just as in the expression “having heard, they eat,” the word *sañcicca* (intentionally) is the *ussukka* (the preparatory or qualifying term) for the word *voropeti* (to deprive of life), so too here [the former is the qualifier] for the latter.
It is said that both the volitional intent (*sañcetanā*) and the taking of life belong to one and the same person.

According to the Elder Upatissa, these [terms] were stated to show that it is not merely by means of the mental factor (*cetasika*) alone that the offense occurs, but that the preliminary effort (*payoga*) must also be intended.

Thus, although one should have said, "having known, having perceived, having willed, and having deliberated," he said, "knowing... [and so on]... transgression," including even the act of taking life.
It has been shown; therefore, the meaning has been demonstrated without regard for the literal phrasing (*byañjana*).

For it is the preceding volition that accomplishes the meaning, since the meaning consists in the accomplishment of transgression. "Every most subtle personal existence" is said with reference to form (*rūpa*), not the formless (*arūpa*).
For in this context, as in the *Khandhavibhaṅga*, there is no distinction between grossness and subtlety regarding those aggregates classified as "self" that are formless.

[The phrase] "not intended" [is used]. "In the mother's womb" is a statement made in reference to the majority of cases; yet even for spontaneously born (*opapātika*) humans, it is indeed a *pārājika* offense.

If one asks why that [womb] is mentioned, given that there is no physical effort (*upakkama*) in a formless body (*arūpakāya*), it is because the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) arises for that very same material body (*rūpakāya*) together with the immaterial aggregates (*arūpakkhandha*).
By this, it is established that even a human being (*manussaviggaha*) is indeed "possessing life" (*sajīvaka*). Herein...
“In the mother’s womb” means in the womb of either a human mother or an animal mother. For it is said in the *Parivāra*:
“One might kill a woman who is one’s mother, and one might kill a man who is one’s father;
having killed both mother and father, one would not thereby incur an immediate retribution.”
“This question has been thought out by the wise.
Here, “first” refers specifically to the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*).

For within the continuum of consciousness comprised within a single existence, the rebirth-linking consciousness is called the first consciousness, and the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*) is called the last. Otherwise, in the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), there would be no first consciousness.
There is no such thing [as a "first" human body], because there is an absence of the arising of consciousness without the conditions of immediate contiguity, absence, and disappearance;
or else, if it did exist, there would follow the fault of the manifestation of a new being (*sattapātubhāva*).
Although it is impossible to deprive this very first human body of life, starting from that as the beginning, among all those human bodies that arise in the continuum until death—
In the case of immeasurable [beings], one is seen as "the very first.

However, when a human form has reached a continuity (*santati*) by way of preceding and succeeding moments, it is then possible to deprive it of life. For it is by disrupting the continuity that one is said to take life.
And here, if the principle of diversity (*nānattanaya*) is intended, the expression "the very first" is appropriate.

But is it not the case that [the first moment] is not the "very first" because of the unity of the continuity (*santati*) within the principle of unity (*ekattanaya*), and since the principle of unity is intended here—as indicated by the statement "it disrupts the continuity"—therefore the expression "the very first" is not tenable? No;

because there is a multiplicity of present moments within the continuity. Since what is called "continuity" refers to the successive arising of many [moments], therefore [one can say]: "This is the very first."
Thus, in this context, both methods are included; otherwise, the statement "it disrupts the continuity" would not be established.

Although here, because of the expression "it disrupts the continuity," only the present of continuity (*santati-paccuppanna*) is intended and it does not appear as the present of duration (*addhā-paccuppanna*), nevertheless, when the present of continuity is disrupted...

The temporal present (*addhā-paccuppanna*) is indeed already destroyed; however, there is no need to state here that when the temporal present is destroyed, the continuous present (*santati-paccuppanna*) is also destroyed.
Therefore, the Commentary says: "Both of these can be deprived [of life];
thus it should be understood that this statement, 'he destroys the continuity,' was made with reference to that very [temporal present]."

Because of the statement, “He disrupts the continuity,” there is no offense on account of transgression when a being who is naturally destined to die at the end of his lifespan dies while a transgression has occurred,
since the continuity has not been disrupted by that transgression. If, however, there were an offense on account of transgression and one were bound by karma for a being who dies prematurely—
before reaching the end of his lifespan— due to a transgression occurring in the interim, that would not be logical.
The Teacher [states]: "Whether one should praise the beauty of death, or incite another toward death—this too is a *pārājika* offense, and one is no longer in communion.

From this statement, it should be understood that at the very moment of the volition (*cetanā*), there is a *pārājika* offense because it is exclusively unwholesome, because it is associated with painful feeling, and because it is a bodily action, a verbal action, and a functional act (*kiriyā*).
"Merely seven or eight impulsion-moments" is stated by way of a homogeneous object; for that very reason, it is said, "by way of a homogeneous continuity," and so forth.

Because it is endowed with its own opposite, the condition for the immediately preceding [consciousness] becomes weak, as if it were no longer as it was before. "That" refers to the disruption of the life-faculty.
*Īti* refers to the seven kinds of insects and the like that, having stung in battle, are released for the purpose of killing.
*Pajjaraka* refers to the burning of the body. *Sūci* refers to a spear. *Visūcikā* refers to dry dysentery. *Pakkhandikā* refers to bloody dysentery.
Having manifested a massive body measuring two or three hundred *vyāmas*, he stood there; [this is] the extraction of the nāga, having become enraged.
"Observing the body of another" refers to the practice of causing an untimely death or inducing a burning sensation [in them].
"Some" refers to the Mahāsaṅghikas. "This woman"—[referring to] the womb (*kulumba*).
How does she [affect] the other? If one approaches with a corrupted mind, both that embryo and that psychic power perish together.
The breaking [of the pot] and the extinguishing [of the fire] occur at one and the same moment, like the shattering of a jar and the extinction of its fire.
It is written that "this does not accord with what is practiced among the Suttantikas. Having adopted their view, it is said:

"When it is stated that 'this also applies to stationary things,' others say it should be refuted on the basis of the triad [of factors]. Regarding the volition of final determination (*sanniṭṭhāpaka-cetanā*) in the acts of taking by hand (*sāhatthika*) or by relinquishing (*nissaggiya*):
By means of the seventh, co-arisen bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*), the "by one's own hand" (*sāhatthika*) nature is to be understood.

However, in the case of verbal intimation (*vacīviññatti*), because it arises simultaneously with all seven types of volition (*cetanā*), the seven sounds come together and attain the state of each individual syllable;
then, by as many syllables as it makes its intention known, [the action is completed] by the intimation produced by the final syllable.

The status of being an instigator (*āṇattikata*) should be understood through verbal intimation (*vacī-viññatti*) that arises simultaneously with the seventh consciousness (*sattama-cetanā*). The same applies to practices involving knowledge (*vijjāmaya-payoga*).
However, regarding instigation by means of the body (*kāyena-āṇattiya*), the method is exactly as stated for direct physical action (*sāhatthika*).

In the case of stationary mechanisms (*thāvara-payoga*), one is bound by the kamma and incurs an offense for as long as the death of another occurs; beyond that, if there is excessive wandering [of the mechanism], there is an abundance of kamma-binding.
It should be understood that [this applies] after death. Herein, there is one offense of defeat (*pārājika*).
Since the volition that accomplishes the purpose is found here and in the second *pārājika*, but not elsewhere, these verses are common to both:
“Those phenomena which are subject to the fixed order of real things, those phenomena are considered fixed;”
Those which are the fixed laws of future phenomena are here called "undetermined.
For those which are the fixed laws of past phenomena, that status of conditionality remains constant;
for those which are the fixed laws of future phenomena, the status of conditionality is dependent.
“Therefore, there is certainty regarding the cause; that too is the fixed order of phenomena (*dhammaniyāmatā*).
Its fruit is uncertain, yet the expectation of the fruit is certain.
Thus indeed is the fixed order of phenomena established for all things.”
The volition that accomplishes a purpose is that which follows the fixed order of what has been acquired.
Because it precedes the accomplishment of the purpose and because the purpose is accomplished after it,
all six types of volition are, without distinction, accomplishers of purpose.
“Since it is possible to clarify an injunction by way of its distinctions,
therefore that very injunction is stated as being effective for achieving the goal.
Whether in the case of wrongness or rightness, they are considered to be fixed or unfixed.”
In the Abhidhamma, not everything exists [as a fixed category]; therein, that [intention] may be determinate.
Whatever intention of theft there is—whether by one’s own hand or by command—it is, according to the method of the Abhidhamma, exclusively determinate.
“Based on the destruction of life, there are [the factors] such as ‘by one’s own hand’ and ‘by command,’ etc.;
according to the method of the Abhidhamma, these should each be combined with that dyad.
The cutting off of the life-faculty and volition—these two together [constitute the act].”
Not by manual action is it equal to even a command;
the severance of the life-faculty and the volition—
these two are not [equal] by manual action, much less by a command.
“At the moment the life-faculty is cut off, there is the volition of the killer.
What phenomenon, having long endured, determines the offense?
If one were the killer at the very moment the life-faculty is cut off;”
Whether dead, asleep, or awake, the killer may be skilled.
"The classification of the triad of the skilled, and also the classification of the triad of feeling;
likewise, the one who has gone [to that state] is established [as the agent], along with the volition to kill by one's own hand."

Furthermore, regarding those five—the seed, the inclination, karma, the dhamma, and the fixed course—which are brought forward and illustrated in the Commentary, I think that among them this volition that accomplishes the purpose enters into conjunction;

for if one were to say, "This fixed course of volition that accomplishes the purpose does not exist," there would follow the undesirable consequence that even the rightness and wrongness of volitions would be non-existent. This is because [the factors] are being analyzed.
It should be understood that by this [path], all [beings] likewise, according to their capacity, partake of and proceed toward the determinations of karma and consciousness (*kamma-citta-niyāma*).
The danger in life was not yet analyzed in the description of the praise of death;

however, here, in the word "intention" (*saṅkappa*), it is analyzed because it has become manifest through its meaning as "one who perceives death, whose volition is death, whose purpose is death," and because it has been made clear and is no longer subtle.
Or it is made indivisible. This is not the name for *vitakka* alone; rather, it should be understood as the name for both *saññā* and *cetanā* as well.
It is stated exactly thus in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*. 174.

Because it was stated as "from the body" (*kāyato*), although one should have said "by the spear and arrow" (*satti-isa*), the phrase "by the arrow, spear, etc. (*usu-satti-ādinā*) is used for the sake of euphony (*vacana-siliṭṭha*).
It has been stated. Regarding the object of the action in the case of an unspecified [offense], it is either that person or someone else.
As for the phrase "by both": although the first blow was not capable by itself, yet having obtained the second, it became the cause for the destruction of life;
for it was given by the killer precisely for that purpose. However, the second blow was given with a different intention. Therefore, it is well said: "by the first blow alone."
“The volition called ‘dāruṇa’ (terrible) is the prior-stage volition that has arisen with reference to a grave object; it is a volition that is a killer by its very nature.
It is not [the volition] that is terrible,” so it was written by the Teacher. “The prior-stage volition is merely an accompaniment; the killer-volition alone is terrible.
Thus it is said. Regarding “according to intention”: one penetrates both [aspects]; for even one who acts with his own hand is not exempt because of the agreement.

The specific details of the action are not found in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*). They say: "The Master [Buddhaghosa] included it because it accords with the Canon (*pāḷi*), which says: ‘Pierce thus, strike thus, kill thus.
Phrases such as "having struck in front" are merely conventional designations for the object (*vatthuvisaṅketa*).
By saying "standing in the village," the person alone is specified. However, by way of gender, it is said: "Long... pe... kill."
He commands without specifying. Others say that if he were to speak by specifying, he might say, "Kill this long one.
However, the Teachers (Ācariyas) say: "When 'long' is said, it is already specified; thus he speaks without specifying.
But the intention of the commander is not, 'Kill whichever one among the long and so forth. Furthermore, "the meaning [of the command] refers to one [individual] even when [spoken] by the mind..."

It is written: "He commands without having specified [the victim]. It is stated that "the other kills someone else of a similar kind, yet the commander is released," because [the act] did not proceed according to his intention.

In a certain *gaṇṭhipada* (commentary), it is written: "Thus, even by way of length and so forth, it appears as if it is logical that [the offense applies] only to one who has not been specifically identified by the mind.
One should accept everything only after thorough investigation.

Regarding the phrase "because the location has been restricted": here, while specifying the restriction of the location, one intends only to kill someone sitting in that place, yet one is not oneself present there at that time.
Therefore, one's own life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) does not become the object (*ārammaṇa*) together with the location;
thus, it is another person who is killed by means of oneself. How so? One is oneself short...
Having become attenuated, in the prior stage it refers to oneself;

yet at the moment of the command, when one issues the order, "Kill him who is tall, short, stout, or strong," the mind proceeds by taking as its object the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) of another such person, because that specific form does not exist within oneself.
Therefore, the one who is the root-cause is bound by the kamma. It should be understood that this case is exactly like that.

In the *Dūtaparamparāniddesa* (Exposition on the Succession of Messengers), it says: "If he commands [the first messenger], there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). If he informs the other [the second messenger], there is an offense of wrong-doing.
This is stated with reference to the wrong-doing incurred in both the reporting and the acceptance by the teacher and the pupil as the case may be.
It is established that the executioner does not accept [the order], yet for him there is an offense of wrong-doing; however, that [offense] does not arise because of the absence of opportunity.
It has been said: because the scope for the offense to be incurred in the sense of being the "root" (mūla) is not delimited, a grave offense (thullaccaya) is stated for him in that scope.
If the murderer accepts [the order], the teacher, as the root, incurs a grave offense together with the previous offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Why? Because by him the great multitude has been incited to evil. But this—
If the murderer does not communicate that matter [to the victim], one incurs a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) and a *thullaccaya* (grave offense).

If he does communicate it, one incurs a *pārājika* (defeat) itself. Why? Because of the absence of the volition (*cetanā*) that accomplishes the purpose. However, in the *Anugaṇṭhipada*, it says: "If he accepts [the task], that is a *dukkaṭa*. If one asks:
'If this is so, why is it not stated in the text?'—it is because the murderer, having accepted [the task] thinking, 'I shall do well,'..."

He does not do that. For, when such a restriction has been made, in order to clarify the meaning for those who have developed doubt as to what constitutes the offense for the one who is at the root (the instigator) and whether there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for him, it is said: "For the one who is at the root, there is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya). And:
"The murderer accepts [the gift], there is an offense of wrong-doing; and for the one who is at the root, there is an offense of serious transgression."

It is said that "it does not adhere," because the purpose here is to show the offense incurred in the sense of being the root; thus it is said, "the murderer accepts it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
In the exposition of the verse on the messenger of Visākka, it says: "Because of the desire to speak, having spoken here with difficulty, there is no further purpose."

It was stated that this was not spoken by the Blessed One. However, as for what was stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*—namely, "there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who stands at the root"—this is the analysis thereof:

even though Saṅgharakkhita was informed of the matter by Buddharakkhita, who had been instructed by the teacher, and although he accepted it saying, "Very well," nevertheless, this offense of wrong-doing belongs to the teacher alone, because of the failure of the agreement (*visaṅketatta*).
It does not apply to Buddharakkhita; why? Because he has committed the offense through an intention aimed at accomplishing a purpose. For this very reason, it is stated in the Pāḷi:

"There is an offense of pārājika for both the commander and the executioner. However, that dukkaṭa which must be incurred in the sense of being the root [agent] was not mentioned under the rule "there is no offense for the one who is the root," because the scope [of that exemption] was not defined there.

Since it is stated that "in the case of one who does not communicate [the intent], there is a grave offense (thullaccaya) for the one who is at the root," it should be understood that it is established that in the case of one who does communicate, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Furthermore, regarding the statement, "If the executioner accepts [it], there is an offense of wrong-doing," this offense of wrong-doing belongs to the executioner alone;
for he, having first caused the instigator, Buddharakkhita, to incur an offense involving defeat (pārājika), himself...

Regarding the statement, "Having deprived him of life, he will incur [an offense]," although it is not explicitly stated in the Pāḷi that "he deprives him of life, and for both the commander and the executioner there is an offense of pārājika," nevertheless, this is indeed stated by implication.
Furthermore, it was not stated because of the method previously explained in the passage, "from which point the pārājika was prescribed. "He deprives him of life..."
For it was stated previously: "If one causes [another] to forfeit [the robe], there is an offense of *pārājika* for all.
Here, the offenses of *dukkaṭa* and *thullaccaya* mentioned previously for the teacher and the pupil have not yet been incurred; rather, they have already incurred an offense of *pārājika*.
Nevertheless, considering that the murderer's state of *pārājika* became manifest through the pupil's offense of *pārājika*, it is said: "There is an offense of *pārājika* for all."
In the case of the *pārājika* offense, it is stated [that both parties incur the same offense] as one; it is not so stated here in the passage:
"The instructor and the executioner incur a *pārājika* offense. Why? Because the executioner incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
For he first incurs an offense of wrong-doing and only afterwards incurs the *pārājika*. However, if the pupil [acts] solely out of respect for the teacher’s instruction...
If they announce it themselves while intending not to die, there is no offense of *pārājika*.
However, there is indeed an offense of *dukkaṭa* on account of conveying an improper message.
To establish this point, some cite the example of the hunter’s wife, who was a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*), giving him a bow, arrows, and a stake; this is [refuted] by the *Tittira-jātaka*.
"It accords with that; therefore, it conforms to both the Sutta and the Aṭṭhakathā, and thus it is not mere reasoning," says the Teacher.
Here, however, because it is stated without distinction in the sequence of messengers—namely, "Speak to such-and-such a person;
let such-and-such a person speak to such-and-such a person"—one may announce it by speech, or by hand gestures, or by letter, or by messenger; there is no discrepancy.
If the meaning of the root term is specified and an intermediary messenger speaks, it should be understood that once that [time] has passed, it is a breach of the agreement (*visaṅketa*).
Now, regarding these same two sections, the method stated in the *Anugaṇṭhipada* is as follows: "The murderer accepts [the order];
there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). This offense belongs to the murderer alone, not to the instigator, Buddharakkhita. However, if...

Thus, among the deaths resulting from execution or natural death, he will inevitably undergo one or the other; at the very moment of Buddha-rakkhita’s command, there may be either a *pārājika* or a *dukkaṭa* offense.

Just as the word "iti" functions by virtue of the context in the phrase "thus with thought and mind," so too does it function here in the phrase "thought-intention" (*cittasaṅkappo*), as seen in the passage:
"The killer accepts [the order]; for the one who was at the root [of the plot], there is an offense of serious transgression (*thullaccaya*)."
By way of context, it is already stated that "for one who is the root-offender, there is an offense of wrong-doing" (*dukkaṭa*).
If one asks why it is not stated explicitly [in this case], it is for the purpose of providing a guiding principle for what follows.

For when it is said, "for one who is the root-offender, there is an offense of wrong-doing," because it is restricted solely by way of the root-offender, it is not understood that "there is a wrong-doing for the one who receives. [This is illustrated by: "The murderer receives..."
For when it is stated, "there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," without specifying [which party], it is possible to apply the dukkaṭa to both parties.
Therefore, taking this very point as the basis, the commentators of the Aṭṭhakathā said:

"When Saṅgharakkhita has accepted [the gift], it should be understood that the offense of wrong-doing belongs to the one who offered it. For the one who receives, neither [the gift] was permitted, nor...
It is rejected; however, it is rejected solely because Buddhārakkhita was not designated as the recipient, and thus for him it would constitute either a *pārājika* or a *dukkaṭa*.

This is the meaning illustrated; therefore, that too is well-stated. Since it is possible to apply [the rule] by way of both [the giver and the receiver], the teachers have stated: "This *dukkaṭa* applies only to the one who accepts. In this regard:

The status of being the "original owner" (mūlaṭṭha) is neither permitted—because there is no statement saying "of the original owner"—nor is it prohibited—because there is no textual passage stating "for the one receiving [it], there is an offense of wrong-doing" (dukkaṭa).

Since the phrase "of the original owner" is not mentioned in the Canon (pāḷi), it would give rise to the principle that the murderer might incur a dukkaṭa by reason of the act of receiving; therefore, [the text specifies] "this dukkaṭa is for the one who receives it."
What was said there is well-said. For in that case, it was prohibited for Buddharakkhita;
however, according to the method already stated, his offense is *aniyata* (undetermined).

But why, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, instead of stating that the murderer incurs a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) due to the act of accepting [the gift], is the *dukkaṭa* stated solely from the perspective of the one who provided the basis (*mūlaṭṭha*)? It is for the purpose of preventing what is undesirable.

For when it is said, “If Saṅgharakkhita accepts [it], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) on account of the acceptance,” since this is stated in its own form according to the immediately preceding method,
it follows that here too, the grave offense (thullaccaya) for the one who is the root-cause is indeed what was stated in the Aṭṭhakathā.
Thus, not mentioning that very grave offense which has thus been incurred because it is obvious, [the text speaks] of the one who accepts...

An offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) has been mentioned. To prevent the assumption that this refers to an undesirable case—on the grounds that it was not explicitly stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*—it was said: "This wrong-doing applies only to one who [accepts] the root [offense]. For according to the method explained by the Master, even for one who accepts [the gift] in the manner described, the wrong-doing is indeed explicit (*uttāna*). If it is asked: "Why is it said that what is explicit is acceptable to us? It is for the purpose of illustrating the practice (*paṭipatti*). [As stated] in the *Piṭakattaya*, etc.: ... [text continues] ... In the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā*, it is said: "If he accepts it with his own hand, there is an offense of wrong-doing. In the *Vinayagaṇṭhiṭīkā-ṭīkā-ṭīkā-ṭīkā-ṭīkā-ṭīkā*, it is said: "If he accepts it with his own hand, there is an offense of wrong-doing. In the *Vinayagaṇṭhiṭīkā-ṭīkā-ṭīkā-ṭīkā-ṭīkā-ṭīkā-ṭīkā-ṭīkā-ṭīkā-ṭīkā-ṭīkā*, it is said: "If he accepts it with his own hand, there is an offense of wrong-doing. In the *Vinayagaṇṭhiṭīkā-ṭīkā-ṭīkā-ṭīkā-ṭīkā-ṭīkā-ṭīkā-ṭīkā-ṭīkā-ṭīkā-ṭīkā-ṭīkā*, it is said: "If he accepts it with his own hand, there is an offense of wrong-doing. In the *Vinayagaṇṭhiṭīkā-ṭīkā-ṭīkā-ṭīkā-ṭīkā-ṭīkā-ṭīkā-ṭīkā-ṭīkā-ṭīkā-ṭīkā-ṭīkā-ṭīkā*, it is said:

In the *Vinayagaṇṭhiṭīkā-
"Even teachers of unimpeded intelligence, because [the matter] is not explicitly stated in the Canon or the Commentary in its own form,
proceed in such instances in this manner; how much more so, then, should well-disposed sons of good family—
who do not overstep the method set forth for the future, who avoid the fault of confusion, and who do not transgress the boundaries of the commentary— proceed accordingly?"

And it has been stated by others. However, because this [passage] was not mentioned in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, and because such a reading was inserted later by the Teacher, it is not found in some manuscripts;
therefore, we shall write down everything. This being so, there would be no offense in the act of receiving [the message], nor even in the cases of receiving a go-between or rejoicing at death.
There is an offense; how could there not be one in the case of accepting [the means] for killing? Therefore, this is a *dukkaṭa* offense for the one who accepts it;
for that very reason, the phrase "of the one who possesses the root" (*mūlaṭṭhassa*) is not stated here.

Furthermore, in the previous method as well, this should be understood as applying to the one who accepts; however, it was not stated because there was no occasion [to mention it]. Therefore, whosoever accepts it, for each of them there is indeed an offense on account of that act.
This is our position in this matter. And as it is here, so it is also in the case of taking what is not given.

175. Although in the Pāḷi and in the Aṭṭhakathā, only a dukkaṭa offense is mentioned in the sections concerning one who is alone and perceives oneself as being alone, nevertheless, for one who speaks with the intention, "Let him die," provided there is an indication [of the person], there is an offense for that which was indicated.
By the death [of the intended victim], there is an offense of defeat (pārājika); even if no one dies, by the death of anyone at all, there is an offense of defeat.

When one designates someone, saying, "Let such-and-such a person, having heard [this], report it to my victim," the lack of a fixed appointment (*visaṅketa*) should be understood because it is spoken through a succession of messengers. If, however, one says, "Let whoever hears it speak," and the victim hears it himself—
If [the person] dies because of a lack of mutual agreement, it is not a *pārājika* offense. If anyone, having heard [the command], speaks [to another] and that person dies, it is a *pārājika*.
If one utters the words, "Let anyone who hears my speech kill him," and someone else, having heard it, kills him, it is a *pārājika*;
but if one kills him oneself after having heard it, because there is no mutual agreement, it is not a *pārājika*. This should be understood according to the circumstances as they arise.

176. Regarding the phrase "one is released by giving the price": here, it is stated by implication that one is released even before [the act of] breaking, crushing, falling away, pulverizing, or throwing into fire.
"From whose hand the price was received" means from the hands of those relatives and attendants from whom the price was taken by that bhikkhu, or from the hand of the owner of the book.
If he takes back the price previously given and gives it to those very relatives and others, he is released;
thus, it becomes the property of the owner of the manuscript itself. However, in the *Anugaṇṭhipada*, it is stated:
"Even if he, having become remorseful, quickly gives them the price, he is released"; this refers to the wealth with which the manuscript was purchased.

It has been stated [that one is not freed from the offense]. Why? Because even if the book is not returned when the money has been taken from the hand of the owner of the book, one is released [from the offense].
If it is said with reference to other wealth, that is not tenable, because the book has not been relinquished due to its state of being owned by oneself.
If, after giving the book back to the owners, one does not take the price, one is not released, because it has not been relinquished due to its state of being owned by oneself.
If a book, when being given as a root-asset, is applied with the thought, "Let it be yours alone," one is released from the state of ownership because of having been freed from it.

Herein, this is the investigation: just as even if a shrine, an image, a lotus pond, or a bridge is taken after having been purchased, the merit belongs only to the maker and not to the one who took it by purchase; so too, regarding the evil [kamma] by which the book [was acquired].
If it is argued that this [offense] applies only to one who has written [the letter] himself and not to another, we say no;

for there is the statement: "Or he should seek out a weapon-bearer for him. Thus, it is established that it is a *pārājika* offense for one who, having obtained a weapon made by another, deposits it [with the victim].
Likewise, even if one obtains a manuscript written by another, if he deposits it in such a way that the person condemned to death sees it and dies, [the same offense applies].

"Pārājika is established": regarding the phrase "such as a cetiya," the teacher has analyzed this by taking it as an instrumental condition (*karaṇapaccaya*), meaning that the action is the cause for death in this very life.
However, it occurs to me that this matter should rather be established by taking "such as a cetiya" as a locative condition (*nidassanapaccaya*).

Regarding the phrase "as many as those living beings" (*tattakā pāṇātipātā*): it is written that even a single volition is called "as many" by virtue of its function, just as the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) and the right efforts (*sammappadhāna*) are each fourfold.
"Having fixed the measure" means having fixed the measure intended by oneself.
With the intention, "Once such a pit has been dug by me, let him fall into it and die," the killer fixes the measure of the pit.
If [the Teacher] had intended [the pit] to be dug, he would have said, "In this pit," with reference to that.
However, since the size to be dug was not specified, he said, "Even with a single stroke of the spade," and so forth;
for although this was suggested by the Suttantika Theras, the Master [Ācariya] maintains that the volition of determination (*sanniṭṭhāpaka-cetanā*) exists in both cases. Of many...

If it is asked how there is a fixed object (ārammaṇa-niyama) regarding death: when the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) of one among those to be slain is taken as an object, it is indeed taken as an object by all of them.
Even when one dies, it is not possible to take his entire life as an object;

for the volition of killing (pāṇātipāta-cetanā), whether in the process of arising, already arisen, in the process of ceasing, or in its state of existence, has only the present as its object and the pre-arisen as its object.

Therefore, that too is logical. At the very last moment, when only a single thought-moment remains, that life-faculty (jīvitindriya), having existed as a pre-arisen state, serves as the object (ārammaṇa).

When the volition included within the seventh impulsion performs its function, in actual fact, the entire life-faculty of that being has been taken as the object and has been destroyed; it cannot be otherwise than this.
In the same way, having first thought, "I shall kill many beings," at the time of making a firm resolve,
one who accomplishes one of the methods such as administering poison gives rise to a volition of the aforementioned kind by taking the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) of one among them as its object.
When it has arisen in this manner, all of them are killed by that very [volition].
Because death is inevitable for all, it is otherwise impossible to deprive them of life or to take hold of them.

If it is asked, "How can there be a mass of unwholesome karma when many die by means of a single volition?"—it is because each volition that arises toward their individual deaths performs its own specific function. How so?

All those volitions are indeed to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapajjavedanīya*); therefore, by whichever one among them the rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) is bestowed, [that volition alone determines the result].
All other [karma], being obstructed by more powerful wholesome karma, falls into the category of "ahosi-kamma" (karma that has been) and so forth;

they are unable to produce a result again. Just as with *aparāpariya-vedanīya* (karma to be experienced in subsequent lives), the wholesome volition, having obstructed that [unwholesome karma], bestows rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*);
likewise, this volition also [functions] by way of bestowing rebirth-linking and so on in the very next existence for those [other karmas].

Because it performs a function that is difficult to accomplish, even though it is singular, it is called a "heap" (*rāsi*). Furthermore, the rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) produced by that [kamma] results in an extremely intense fruition (*vipāka*).
This is the distinction here; such details have been elaborated upon in the *Anugaṇṭhipada*.

Because of the underlying intention of "not wishing to die," there is an offense even in the case of death by spontaneous birth (*opapātika*). [This is so] because of the statement, "having been reborn."
If it is argued that "falling is not seen," [the response is] written: "Spontaneous birth (opapātika) and falling are one and the same.

Alternatively, because of the statement "in every respect, indeed, he is not seen," and because the intention "let him die here" is possible, it is well said: "If he dies being unable to cross over, it is indeed a pārājika offense.
If, however, it has been dug with the specific restriction "let him die after falling," then he is a spontaneously born human being (opapātikamanussa).
And having been reborn, thinking "it is impossible to cross" due to the fixed nature of his state, he dies;
thus the shadow of a *pārājika* offense is not seen. Therefore it is said, "being unable to cross. For he, being unable to cross, falls again and again and dies;
thus the meaning is that his downfall is established even by that. In this regard, it might be asked: "But what about one who..."
When it is said, "One who is unable to cross over dies," at the moment of digging the pit, that person still lives in the immaterial world (*arūpaloka*).
Furthermore, the volition of killing is a condition for a state of fixed wrongness (*micchattaniyata-dhamma*) by way of the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*);
and the material life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvitindriya*) is a condition for the kamma of matricide, patricide, the murder of an arahant, and the shedding of blood by way of the object-condition.

Because of the statement "it is a condition," it has the material life-faculty (*rūpajīvitindriya*) as its object; yet that [material life-faculty] does not exist for a being of the formless realm (*arūpāvacara*), nor is that volition (*cetanā*) present.
Thus, an indeterminate state (*aniyata-dhamma*) is a pre-arising condition (*purejāta-paccaya*) for a state fixed in falsehood (*micchattaniyata-dhamma*);

namely, as an object-pre-arising condition (*ārammaṇa-purejāta*), as a basis-pre-arising condition (*vatthu-purejāta*), and as an object-pre-arising condition. The material life-faculty is [the condition] for the karma of matricide.
Because of the statement, “It is a condition by way of the prenascence condition,” it has a future object. There is no other being here who, having fallen [into the water], is about to die;
this being the case, what is the object of the murderous volition? The object is the present life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) of whichever living being is currently alive here.
Even though that being does not die, nevertheless there is the taking of life (*pāṇātipāta*).

It is just so. For example, suppose a man first thinks, "I shall kill seven people standing in a row by piercing them with a single arrow," and at the moment of his resolve, he discharges the arrow making the life of one among them the object;
even though the arrow misses that person and kills the other six, he is still considered a killer of living beings (*pāṇātipātī*). So it is here as well.
Regarding the phrase “whosoever,” when one intends to kill, the murderous volition proceeds by taking anyone at all as its object;

thus, even if that person is an *amata* (one who cannot die), one becomes a killer of living beings (*pāṇātipātī*) by virtue of the other [the victim]. If [the victim], having become an *arahant*, passes away into final *nibbāna*, then [the assailant] is indeed a murderer of an *arahant*.
This same method applies everywhere in such cases. It is said that this alone is the reasoned exposition of the determination handed down through the succession of teachers.

Regarding the phrase "the state of falling is the measure": here, just as when a mother dies after having fallen and changed her sex, one becomes a matricide rather than merely a murderer of a man, therefore the offense occurs by way of the falling itself. Why? Because the state of falling and the state of death belong to a single continuum;
for that very life-faculty (jīvitindriya) has no change of sex, whereas only the female and male faculties (itthi-purisa-indriya) do.

In the course of its occurrence, there are moments of ceasing and arising; the terms "woman" and "man" are merely conventional designations used therein. Therefore, he is indeed a matricide and not a murderer of a man.

Just as there is an offense by way of the form of falling [into hell] for him, so too here there is a thullaccaya by way of the form of falling, because they belong to a single continuum (*ekasantāna*). This is the reasoning in the first Elder’s position. In the second...
Even though he is a *peta* and a *yakkha*, because his rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) is without root-cause (*ahetuka*) due to unwholesome kamma-result,
and because— as stated in the passage "on the left side he becomes a pig"— the form is common to all types of materiality, and because he belongs to the class of non-human beings (*amanussa*),
there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for killing him in the form of an animal; this is determined by the nature of the death-form (*maraṇarūpa*) and the basis (*vatthu*).

There is indeed a transformation of a light offense, just like the transformation of the *pācittiya* offense involving the cutting down of trees and so forth growing there. This [latter] alone is more appropriate, and therefore it was mentioned later.
