thus, it is said, the Elder Upatissa speaks.

Because it is certain that what has fallen from its place necessarily enters the stream of water, it is said: "The offense here should be understood as occurring by the mere act of falling from its place. The offense occurs only when it has entered the stream of water. For Sukka’s entire body was his "place";

one should consider that as long as it has not entered [the water], it cannot be said to have "fallen from its place. Because the Elder was an Abhidhammika, [he held that] there is no emission of semen...
Because it is stated in the *Kathāvatthu-aṭṭhakathā* that "it arises from lust," its origin is mental (*cittasamuṭṭhāna*).
Furthermore, because of the statement, "He took a portion of that impurity with his mouth and placed a portion in the organ of generation," its origin is seen to be seasonal (*utusamuṭṭhāna*).
And this [occurrence] belongs only to one who is not free from lust; for it is said: "Bhikkhus, it is impossible, it is out of the question, that an Arahant..."
Because of the statement, "the impurity may be emitted. In the commentary on the *Parūpāhāra* [Sutta], it says: "He has a receptacle (*āsaya*);
that is, there is a place for that semen to settle, just as there is for feces and urine. Thus, its "receptacle" is established.

Because it is not mixed with the material form produced by ordinary consciousness (*pākatika-citta-samuṭṭhāna-rūpa*), and because it issues forth from it, the location of the semen is threefold: the head of the penis, the waist, and the body.
The teachers prescribe [these methods]. That should be regarded as being like snake venom;

and just as there is no fixed rule for the location of the venom, which occurs when one is touched by the power of anger, so too for this [passion], there is no fixed rule for its location, as it occurs when one acts out of the power of lust—this is the reasoning.
The "condition that causes agitation" refers to conditions such as medicine, lodging, food, and so forth. "Also from the breaking of association" means: among these...
[It occurs] by means of two or even three [perceptions]. Regarding the phrase "one whose perversions have been abandoned":

here, one would fall into the position that whatever the trainees (sekkha) and worldlings see, even in a dream, all of it is perverted and entirely unreal. Consequently, this would contradict the statement:
"But what one sees from a prognostic sign (pubbanimitta) is exclusively true. Therefore, this was not said with reference to the object.
For if it were made on the grounds that [the vision] is either true or false, then with reference to that, one might have to say:
"The Asekhas, because they have abandoned the perversions, see only what is true, not what is untrue. However, this was said with reference to the act of seeing itself;
for that [vision] is unreal, since even though they do not see, they are as if seeing; even though they do not hear, they are as if hearing; and even though they do not know, they are as if knowing.
"It is as if it were so; yet, because one also sees with insight (vipassati), it is not mere reasoning (takka)," says the Teacher.
That [object] is not the sign of form (rūpanimitta) and so forth; this was said with reference to adventitious, present signs of form and so forth.

For signs of form and so forth that have become the sign of kamma (kamma-nimitta) or the sign of destiny (gati-nimitta) certainly do serve as objects for the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). Among these, the sign of kamma is exclusively past.
The sign of movement may be present for a short time.
"Such as these" means objects such as the signs of forms that have been directly experienced, previously experienced, or imagined, as well as those that are adventitious and presently arisen;
and it also includes those associated with lust and other defilements. A monkey’s sleep is characterized by rapid shifting; for he [jumps] from the branch of a tree...

Out of fear of falling, they frequently open their eyes and fall asleep. Although people open their eyes again and again and see quite clearly as if fully awake, nevertheless, just as those who have awakened repeatedly enter the *bhavaṅga* (life-continuum), so too during sleep they enter the *bhavaṅga*;
it is because of this that they are said to "sleep. [It is] by means of the *bhavaṅga*-consciousness...

Because of the statement, "Indeed, one sleeps well," it is called "sleep" (niddā) since it serves as the necessary condition for the physical body to enter a state of effortless tranquility beyond the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).

Due to the weakness of the physical body, even though there is a crossing over from the life-continuum at the time of seeing a dream, it is said that [the dream] "occurs" because of the attainment of a state of effortless tranquility; hence, beings are said to be "awakened."
They are not so called because the body born of kamma has reached a state of feebleness and tranquility;
consequently, the heart-base (hadayavatthu) supported by it does not become very clear, and thus the mental activity supported by that base is like the light of a lamp resting on an unsteady wick.
For this very reason, it is said in the Commentary: "Because this volition has a weak basis, it is unable to draw forth rebirth-linking..."
"‘Incapable,’ etc., has been stated.
However, in the *Gaṇṭhipada*, it is written: ‘Because of having a weak basis, even the sign that appears in a dream is weak.
That [statement] is ambiguous; for every sign exists, and volition does not [become weak] simply because its objective basis is weak. By that...
The occurrence of consciousness is weak when it has a past or future object, or an object that is a mere conceptual designation (paññatti), because it is not weak when it has a present basis.
It is not logical for a volition lacking a basis to be weak, because such a volition possesses an exceeding power derived from the influence of mental cultivation (bhāvanā).
For consciousness endowed with the power of cultivation, even though it is formless, takes up the extremely heavy physical body.
It establishes [the body] in the Brahma-world in a single moment of consciousness.
A sense-sphere consciousness (kāmāvacara-citta) similar to that—even if it is not intensified—renders the material body capable of leaping through the air, let alone one that is otherwise.

What, then, is the inferential reason here by which the power belongs to the consciousness itself? It is because we see the production of specific actions, such as those resulting from repeated practice, brought about by the power of consciousness.
Therefore, the Teacher’s conjecture is that it is called "having a weak physical basis" because it has a weak heart as its physical basis.

If the heart-basis were capable of producing the state of dullness or sharpness in the consciousness dependent upon it—just as the bases of the eye, ear, and so forth are faculties by virtue of their own dull or sharp nature—then it would be a faculty;
but this is not a faculty. For this reason, in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, within the text on derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*), [it is not included among the faculties].
It was not included in the formal enumeration (uddesa). For, because it is not a faculty (anindriya), it was not enumerated immediately after the body-faculty (kāyindriya);
and because it is a physical basis (vatthurūpa), it was not enumerated even immediately after the life-faculty (jīvitindriya), which is not a physical basis.
Therefore, the statement that "because of its lack of clarity, the mental process dependent upon it is also unclear" is not established.
Why is this so? Because it is established even for those without sense faculties through the conjunction of conditions such as suitable or unsuitable climate and food;
because a change in the occurrence of consciousness is observed [in them]; and because it is directly evident. For even one who has not awakened imagines himself to be awake.
To this extent, sleep is the specific state of the coarse physical body being devoid of effort and remaining in a state of tranquility.
This [state] occurs through a specific mode of the mind’s transition from the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).

A sentient being endowed with that [state] has emerged from the life-continuum and sees a dream; he is called "overcome by monkey-sleep" (*kapimiddhapareta*), and thus the meaning that he is asleep and not yet awakened is established.
Because one is said to be "utterly asleep" due to the uninterrupted continuity of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), it was stated:
"If he sees while asleep, it would entail a contradiction with the Abhidhamma," and so forth. Because, however, at the moment of sleep one is not called "awake," it was stated:
"If he sees while awake, it would entail a contradiction with the Vinaya," and so forth; and because his sleep has not yet been exhausted.
Furthermore, there exists a state where the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) has not yet submerged; therefore it is said, "Overcome by monkey-sleep, he sees.
Otherwise, this person would be neither asleep nor awakened, and even while not having entered that sleep himself, he would fall into it.
At this point, the Abhidhamma, the Vinaya, the words of the Elder Nāgasena, and logical reasoning—all are mutually consistent. In this regard:
"Overcome by monkey-sleep" (*kapimiddhapareto*) means overcome by sleep that has emerged from the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
For here, this is what is called "monkey-sleep. It is defined as follows: "In that regard, what is sleep (*middha*)? That which is the body’s lack of health, lack of fitness for work...

[etc]... falling asleep; this is called sleep. This is indeed non-material (*arūpa*); it is the lack of health and the state of nodding in the physical body (*karajakāya*), which is the result of that [sleep].
A particular kind of sleep is called "monkey-slumber" (*kapimiddha*) by way of figurative designation (*kāraṇopacārena*).
And as for what was said: "Great King, one who is overcome by monkey-slumber sees a dream.
Regarding the phrase "that which is the emergence from an offense": herein, that disciplinary act (*vinayakamma*) by which there is emergence from it is intended here.

"Emergence from an offense" (āpattivuṭṭhāna) means: regarding the phrase "by means of applying the term for the whole to its parts," examples such as "one who cuts branches is called 'one who cuts trees'" are given;
and "the aggregate of feeling" (vedanākkhandha), etc., are examples of conventional (ruḷhi) terminology.

Furthermore, the words "and not by me" refer to the action of the verb "to investigate" (vīmaṃsana); and regarding "liberation" (mocane), it is stated with reference to the determination (sanniṭṭhāna) and the natural tendency toward liberation (muñcanapakati).
240. "They go" refers to the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*). "Like a forest-clearing" refers to what is brought as a load.
Lust itself is called the "savor" (*assāda*) by way of the associated pleasant feeling. As for the phrase "and while sleeping," this should be examined;

it is said with reference to one who sleeps without interrupting the continuity of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), like one overcome by drowsiness. "For the sake of watching over" means for the sake of cleansing.

266. They say: "There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) even for the contemplation of the private parts of those [images] made of wood, clay, plaster, or painting. They record: "[It is an offense] when passion has arisen, born from the desire to emit.

Or, as in the case of sand, where it says "the elephant's desire will perish," the reading everywhere is "there is an offense" (āpatti). [And also]: "Come, friend novice, take hold of my private part."

Because it has been performed, it appears as though it would be appropriate to call it "vocal action" (*vacīkamma*). This being the case, there would be a confusion [of categories], as a transgression might also arise from another instance, such as an order saying, "Do this.
Therefore, some hold that it should not be stated [as vocal action]. 267.
Regarding the phrase "a row of flowers" and "a row of salt," it is said there are two kinds.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the emission of semen is finished.
2. Commentary on the training rule concerning physical contact: 270.
By the word "immersed" (*otiṇṇo*), his state of intent for sexual intercourse is shown. "With a mind affected by lust, with a woman..."
By the word "together" (*saddhiṃ*), his exertion is shown. For the term "together" (*saddhiṃ*) illuminates conjunction;
and that application is meeting, coming together, or adhering. With what kind of mind? With a perverted mind, not with the intention of receiving the bowl, and so forth—this is the intended meaning.
By the phrase "should enter into physical contact," the perception of touch on the part of one who exerts himself is shown.
...there is. For it is by making an effort that one who discerns contact is said to "attain.
Thus, his accomplishment of the three factors is shown. Alternatively: "descended" (*otiṇṇo*). By what? By a transformed mind, like a being [descended] into a *yakkha* or similar entity.
Or, this instrumental case is used in the sense of the accusative: "descended into a transformed mind," as a being [falls] into a well or similar pit. Alternatively: "from lust..."
Thinking, “I shall emerge,” he entered the state of a bhikkhu;
then, with a mind transformed from that intention to emerge, and with that as the cause, he sank back into that very same passion.
Whether a woman has come near him or whether he has approached her—whether she is impassioned or dispassionate toward him, that is irrelevant here.
As in the case of bodily contact with a nun, there is no requirement for mutual passion on the part of both.
"Bodily contact" (*kāyasaṃsagga*) refers to the joining of the bodies of both. In the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), however, it is stated:

"‘Should enter upon’ (*samāpajjeyya*) refers to transgression (*ajjhācāra*). This refers to the act of entering upon [the transgression], not to the bodily contact itself. [The phrase] "the entering upon of bodily contact" [is used].
For [this] is called "misconduct" (*ajjhācāra*). However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā* it is stated: "That which is called bodily contact is, in its actual meaning, misconduct.

This contradicts the definition given later in the *Pāḷi*: "If one has the intention to engage [in sexual intercourse], but does not exert oneself with the body and perceives contact, there is no offense. This is because of the perception of contact.
For bodily contact has been explained [as such]. If that is indeed a transgression (*ajjhācāra*), how can there be no offense? This has been well stated;

however, having extracted the phrase "should engage in bodily contact" and because both phrases—"transgression is said to be" and "should engage"—are common to the general exposition (*sāmaññabhājanīya*), in the absence of the act to be engaged in, there is an absence of engagement. Thus, in terms of its actual meaning, it is a transgression.
It might be said: "Or by taking the hand.

Here, by the phrase "taking the hand," the entire body that is clung-to (*upādinnaka*) is included, but not external ornaments of the hand and so forth which belong to a different continuity (*bhinnasantāna*) though connected to it.
By the mention of "seizing the guild" (*veṇiggahaṇa*), those things not clung-to (*anupādinnaka*) that belong to an undivided continuity, such as hair, body hair, nails, and teeth, are included.
It should be understood that what is grasped is that which is produced by temperature conditioned by kamma. For this very reason, it is said in the Commentary:
"Even one who touches something clung-to or not clung-to with some hair or other [part] that is not clung-to incurs a *saṅghādisesa* offense.

By this, it should be understood that even hairs, body-hairs, and so forth, though not clung-to, constitute a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the offense. Even so, regarding the phrase "he acknowledges the contact":
If it is argued that this contradicts the method of the Pāḷi and its commentaries, which state: "With the fulfillment of three factors, there is a *saṅghādisesa*;
because of not discerning the contact, with the fulfillment of two factors, there is a *dukkaṭa*," we say no, because the meaning of that passage is understood as follows:
for even one who discerns the state of being touched is said to "discern the contact"—this is one sense of the term. Therefore, [regarding] a woman and oneself...
And having touched the state of mutual contact among the head-hairs and other parts included in the body, one discerns the contact that relishes it;
this does not occur solely through the arising of body-consciousness (*kāyaviññāṇa*). In this regard, body-consciousness is not a decisive factor.

When the body of a monk—whether by the woman’s acquired body (*upādinnaka*) or her unacquired body—is touched upon his own acquired body, if his body-faculty (*kāyindriya*) is clear, [he discerns the contact].
When that [body] exists, body-consciousness arises in it; by means of that, one is said to "discern contact.

However, in the case of a body not subject to grasping (*anupādinnaka*), or one that is lustful with a lack of confidence in its faculty of the body, or a body afflicted by a cataract-like wind (*timiravāta*), body-consciousness does not arise.
And by means of that, one is not said to discern contact; it is merely with the intention of seeking pleasure.
One who, having made an effort, enters into physical contact perceives that touch by means of mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*);
therefore it is said: “By the phrase ‘should enter into physical contact,’ his perception of the touch while making an effort is shown.
Furthermore, another monk, touched by something connected to or released from the body of a woman, [experiences] body-consciousness (*kāyaviññāṇa*).
One who arouses [the mind] indeed discerns contact; therefore it is said: "In this case, body-consciousness is not of one-sided certainty.
Furthermore, a man, having donned a garment while sleeping with a woman, might touch the upper part of her garment slowly out of lust for physical contact;
even though he does not discern the contact of the hair emerging from between the garments, he still possesses the intention for sexual intercourse.
Having exerted oneself with the body, one is said to "perceive contact" (*phassa-paṭivijānāti*), and thus incurs a *saṅghādisesa* offense.
For it is stated: "If one touches the body [of another] thinking, 'I will touch blue,' it is a *saṅghādisesa*. This is the second meaning.

Thus, because of its manifold meanings and because its intended sense is difficult to discern, in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*, the perception of contact is not treated as a mere constituent factor (*aṅga*).

It has been stated. For when that [phrase] is stated, there is the possibility that a monk, even after having committed a *saṅghādisesa* offense, might perceive himself as not having committed it, thinking:

"I was seen by [her] touching with a fingernail or a hair; yet no body-consciousness arose in me from the brushing of the hair, and because my limbs were stiffened by blurred vision and wind, I did not perceive the contact.
Therefore, it is not stated [that he must perceive himself as not having committed it], but rather: "he perceives the contact."
And having shown the method stated in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) for these phrases, including "nor does one discern contact," he [the opponent] is to be informed.
Up to this point, the reason for [the claim] "not by knowing the meaning of those words" has been explained in detail.
This concludes the commentary on the word-analysis (*padabhājanīya*).

271. Although it is stated in general terms that "a lustful mind" (*rattaṃ cittaṃ*) in this context means "one that has undergone change" (*vipariṇataṃ*), it should be understood as "lustful" specifically through the desire for physical contact, because in the *Vinītavatthu* it is said:
"If he touches [a woman] out of motherly affection for his mother... [etc.]... there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Likewise, although it is stated without distinction that "a woman" (*mātugāmo*) means "a human female," [it is specified further].
Rather, it is human women with unimpaired faculties who are intended here, because it is stated: “If she is a dead woman and he engages in bodily contact...

[etc. ...there is an offense of thullaccaya. Since the term “human woman” is already established by that much alone, the statement “not a yakkhinī, not a petī, not a female animal” indicates that even among those with unimpaired faculties, not all beings with a human form are considered women.

"Here, 'human woman' is meant. This is stated for the purpose of showing that even female *yakkhas* and others, who achieve their success through a specific supernormal power (*iddhi*) inherent to their own birth, may also possess human forms.

Among them, the female *yakkha* constitutes the basis for a grave offense (*thullaccaya*), because a grave offense is prescribed for physical contact with a female *yakkha* among the cases explained in the Vinaya. The female *peti* follows the same principle.

A divine woman is an object for a *thullaccaya* offense. An animal woman is an object for a *dukkaṭa* offense. Some say that an animal woman who has assumed human form is likewise an object for a *thullaccaya* offense.

However, since the *Vibhaṅga* lacks the scriptural passage stating, "It is a human woman and one perceives her as a human woman," whereas there are statements such as, "It is a woman and one perceives her as a *yakkhinī*," it follows that *yakkhinīs* and the like do not fall under the category of "woman" (*itthī*).

In the passage beginning with “if she is a woman and he perceives her as a woman,” it should be understood that *yakkhis* and so forth are not mentioned because, were they included therein, it would follow that they too would constitute grounds for a *saṅghādisesa* offense.
However, some maintain that in the Vinaya rule—“A certain bhikkhu [had sexual intercourse] with the body of a female animal...
[resulting in] an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)”—the term “female animal” refers to non-human beings (*amanussa*), while ordinary female animals are excluded.

This is what is intended; therefore, a *dukkaṭa* offense is stated. In the sections beginning with “she is a woman and perceives her as an animal,” and “she is an animal and perceives her as a woman,” only an ordinary animal is intended, and that too is specifically an animal male.
For this very reason, in the training rules concerning wicked speech, one’s own body, and sexual service, the sections connected with human males [are excluded].
They say that likewise, the section concerning animals has not been included. Similarly, "eunuch" here refers only to a human eunuch, and "male" here refers only to a human male;
therefore, non-human females, non-human eunuchs, non-human males, female animals, eunuch animals, male animals, and hermaphrodites belonging to humans, non-humans, or animals [are not included].

Thus, these eight persons have not come here; by way of them, the determination of the classification and non-classification of offenses—according to the distinctions of the basis (*vatthu*), perception (*saññā*), and doubt (*vematika*)—as well as the calculation of the exclusion of those who have not arrived, should be understood without confusion.
Likewise, their sections on the combination of pairs (*dukamissaka*) and so forth, and the determination of the classification of offenses and non-offenses [should be understood].
In that regard: "non-human, paṇḍaka, non-human male, animal female, and animal paṇḍaka..."
There are four cases involving an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*):

non-human females, human females, and hermaphrodites (both sexes) constitute cases of a grave offense (*thullaccaya*); non-human hermaphrodites and animal hermaphrodites constitute cases of wrong-doing.
However, since the female non-human is not mentioned in the text (*pāḷi*), male non-humans, eunuchs, and males who are hermaphrodites are not included there.
They say: "The animals, hermaphrodites, and eunuchs are not included because they share the same destiny as animals;
the human hermaphrodite is not included because he shares the same destiny as a human eunuch. However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā* it says:
"Even for a female nāga maiden, a female supaṇṇa maiden, a kinnarī, or a cow, there is only an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)."
Because it has been so stated, that alone must be accepted as the authoritative measure.
Herein is this investigation: regarding the passage, "Monks, the Pātimokkha is not to be recited in an assembly where a being of the animal realm is seated," the commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) states:
"'A being of the animal realm' means one for whom full ordination (*upasampadā*) is prohibited."
Because it is stated [in this way], the classification of animals and humans is distinguished from ordinary animals;

likewise, because the classifications of *yakkhas*, *petas*, animals, and humans are specified here by the statement, "In the case of an animal’s arising of suffering, there is only a *dukkaṭa* offense";
and because of the specific statement regarding the offense here that "the form of falling away is the measure, not the form of death"; and [because of the statement] "from both sides..."

And because it is stated in general terms: "If one, with a lustful mind, touches with his body the body—below the collarbone and above the knees—of a *yakkha*, a *peta*, a *paṇḍaka*, or a human form belonging to the animal realm, there is an offense of *thullaccaya*," it is established that he [the human] is distinct [from these].
And because of this distinction, [the rule regarding] a female human form belonging to the animal realm...
There is a distinction in the case of one who enters into physical contact; therefore, there must be a corresponding distinction in the offense.

If, in the training rule on physical contact, a female being belonging to the animal realm or a human female were also intended, then—since the absence of perception due to the commonality of form would be impossible—she would have to be mentioned in the training rules on wicked speech and on personal service as well.
It would exist, and it would be in the future. If you argue that it is not included because it was omitted from the abbreviated section (*saṃkhittavāra*) in its specific form, [we reply:
since the phrase "she is a woman and a female animal, and she perceives both as women" is included here, the description of the male characteristic (*purisaliṅga*) is not applicable here;

therefore, the male animal is also included here, and for a human female disguised as a female animal, even though she is not explicitly mentioned in the text (*pāḷi*), there is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
The intention behind the statement, "because it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*," is that the underlying reason for this word must be sought.
This [interpretation] is not tenable. Why? Because when women and men are mentioned together, the masculine gender is present.
Here, however, the three categories—animals, male *paṇḍakas*, and women—are all combined together and referred to as "animal" (*tiracchānagata*).
In that context, among human and non-human beings, the designations of female, eunuch, and male should be understood according to what is applicable.
Because the sections [of the rule] were abbreviated in the two training rules concerning indecent speech and so forth, humans, animals, and others are not explicitly mentioned.
As there is an offense in the cases already described, so it is here as well. Otherwise, for one who merely makes light of a male, there is no offense.
In the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated that there is a *thullaccaya* offense for one who makes light of a paṇḍaka. Therefore, those [other] cases are understood to be abbreviated.
Furthermore, there is a distinction regarding a paṇḍaka, a human male, and an animal when one perceives them as a female;
nevertheless, since a *dukkaṭa* is stated in those instances, what is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* alone is the authoritative standard for these two.
The commentators state that where a logical connection (*yutti*) or a reason (*kāraṇa*) is seen to be superfluous in the discourses, one should examine that and then accept [the reading].
In such instances, one must speak only after having investigated thoroughly.
Regarding this, the enumeration of the sections (*vāra*) as they appear in the Canon should first be understood in brief as follows: five based on women.
The five cases rooted in a woman, a paṇḍaka, a male, an animal, and a root [offense] make twenty cases with a single root;
likewise, there are twenty with two roots, and twenty with mixed roots—thus there are sixty cases, which constitute three sets of twenty.
In each set of twenty, taking one case for each root, three cases involving the body and what is connected to the body have been stated. The remaining...
The fifty-seven sections were abbreviated; likewise, three sections on "connected with the body" (*kāyapaṭibaddha*) were stated, while the rest were abbreviated.

In this way, regarding the section on "connected with the body," the section on "body-connected," the section on "formal relinquishment" (*nissaggiya*), the section on "body and formal relinquishment," and the section on "formal relinquishment and formal relinquishment," three sections each were stated, while the rest were abbreviated. Thus, of the six...
The eighteen permutations are stated explicitly by way of the three [factors]; the remaining three hundred and forty-two permutations are abbreviated.
Following that, for the case of a woman who is lustful, the eighteen permutations previously mentioned are arrived at by adding "body to body" to each one;
thus, twenty-one permutations are stated explicitly, and [the rest] amount to nine hundred and ninety-nine...

The three hundred and twenty [rules] have been condensed. Following that, two tetrads are presented: one consisting of four rules illustrating offenses and non-offenses, and another consisting of four rules based on the intention to use and the intention to release.
In this regard, the distinction is as follows: because the term "touching" (*parāmasana*) in the matrix (*mātikā*) includes everything from touching up to the final stage of pressing (*chupana*).
All twelve terms have been included; therefore, without extracting the individual words, he says: "touching, stroking, and contact.
One should understand that "stroking" is synonymous with "touching," for if "contact" were mentioned alone, it might be thought that stroking is a separate entity.
In this first section, "she is a woman and she perceives her as a woman," all twelve [terms] apply.
The acts of touching and so forth have been shown by way of application. Beyond that, four phrases—consisting of two phrases at the beginning—are presented;

it should be understood that the others are abbreviated. However, in the section on the body among the *nissaggiya* rules, because [the other acts] cannot occur in every manner, only "touching" (*āmasana*) is mentioned, and not the others.
The reading is "he causes to move and he takes away" (*sañcopeti harati*), meaning "he causes to move and [he takes away]. [This is stated] in the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries.

However, it has been written: "‘In the same manner as before’ refers to surrounding with ropes, cloth, and so forth"; later, "‘In the same manner as before’ means there is a comprehension [of the body]";
"Because an offense was prescribed for grasping a braid, there is a *saṅghādisesa* even when touching body hair";
and "The phrase ‘by means of what is clung-to (*upādinnaka*)’ and so forth was stated in order to explain that."
"In the exposition according to what has been specified" means in this very exposition as it was specified.

When it is said, "He took hold of something similar," the meaning is that he took hold of something of that same kind; thus one should regard that [act] as grave. This refers to the analysis of bodily contact (*kāyasaṃsagga-vibhaṅga*).
The other [type of offense] is also the touching of what is connected to the body. "And in taking hold" means either "taking hold. "In having failed" means in having missed [the mark].
*“Sāratta”* means colored by lust for physical contact; the meaning is that she is intended by oneself.
If one thinks, “I will take one who is dispassionate [toward me],” and takes her out of affection for a relative—such as a mother or a sister—a *dukkaṭa* offense is appropriate here.

If one thinks, “I will take one who is dispassionate [toward me] because she is colored by lust for physical contact,” and takes a mother, one has taken someone unintended. Regarding this, according to the opinion of the Elder Mahāsumma:
If one takes hold of something connected to the body with the intention, "I will take hold of the body," it is a *thullaccaya*;

this is because such a view has been established. Furthermore, because of the statement, "If there is a woman, and he perceives her as a woman, and he is lustful, and the monk touches the body of that woman with his body, it is an offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*)," it appears that it would also be a *saṅghādisesa*. [If one thinks,] "I will take hold of what is detached..."

He takes hold of one who is impassioned; here too, it appears to be a *saṅghādisesa* offense, because of the statement: "If he touches his body with the thought, 'I will touch the blue [robe],' it is a *saṅghādisesa*.
Regarding this, however, the reason is stated in the *Anugaṇṭhipada*: "It is not so in the prior stage, because of the lust for bodily contact. Some, however, say:
"One who exerts effort with the thought, 'I will touch only the blue [robe],' out of fear of a grave offense..."

They say that if one touches the body, since at the prior stage [of intention] the thought "I shall touch what is connected to his body" has occurred, there must be an *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) offense.
It is said that the Elder Dhammasiri says, "In such a case, it is a *saṅghādisesa*.

Regarding a hermaphrodite woman (*itthi-ubhatobyañjanaka*) and a hermaphrodite man (*purisa-ubhatobyañjanaka*), the classification of offenses is according to the method already stated; even when the female characteristic (*itthiliṅga*) is concealed...
They say that the offense occurs only through the agency of a woman.
281. Regarding the commentary on the cases of discipline (*vinītavatthu*):
"A *tiṇaṇḍupaka*" is something to be made by taking roots such as those of the *hirivera* plant. A "seal-ring of palm-leaf" (*tālapaṇṇamuddikā*) is one made of palm leaf.
It is established that finger-rings, palm-leaf mats made by him, waist-bands, earrings, and so forth—all these are not permitted.
It is said that those dwelling in Tambapaṇṇi do not touch depictions of female forms or hip-cloths; this is merely a matter of local custom.
"Mixed with gems" means that which has been fashioned for the purpose of ornamentation, such as being entwined with golden vines and the like.
"Having combined with gold and cooked" means having added gold-essence and cooked it. "From the seed," meaning starting from the mineral ore.

"It is not allowable for the Elder" because it was said, "It has been sent for you. It is said that if one says, "Perform an offering to the cetiya," it is permissible. A bubble is a speck. Even brass is of the same category as gold.
For this has been stated in the Andhakaṭṭhakathā:
“Spurious gold (ārakūṭaloha) is exactly like real gold; it resembles gold, yet it is not to be handled.

However, because of the statement, “But it is permissible for medicinal purposes,” even a portion of the method explained in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā is authorized. Therefore, having understood the underlying intention in each respective case, one should clarify the matter accordingly.
The commentary on the training rule concerning physical contact is finished.
3. Commentary on the training rule concerning indecent speech: 283.
In the third [training rule], there are three sections on *saṅghādisesa*, three sections on *thullaccaya*, three sections on *dukkaṭa*, and three sections on what is connected to the body.
Twelve sections have come down in their original form. Among them, the three *saṅghādisesa* sections are stated in the second training rule (*sikkhāpada*);

thus, they should be understood as one root-section for each of the three [offenses] involving those who have reached twenty years of age. Therefore, fifty specific sections are condensed here; otherwise, [the full list would include cases such as:
"it is a woman, he is doubtful, and he is lustful," and "the monk [inserts his organ] into the woman's anus..."
If he speaks in praise with reference to the anus or the urinary passage... [as before] ...it is a *thullaccaya* offense.

If there is a woman, and the monk perceives her as a eunuch, or perceives her as a male, or perceives her as an animal, yet he is lustful and speaks in praise with reference to that woman’s anus or urinary passage, and also reviles her, it is a *thullaccaya* offense. If there is a eunuch, and he perceives him as a eunuch... [as before] ...it is a *thullaccaya* offense.
If one were lustful and, with reference to a paṇḍaka’s anus, spoke in praise [of it], there would be an offense of thullaccaya;
thus, for such bases of offenses, one might fall into the state of non-offense. But that does not occur.
To show that for one who perceives a paṇḍaka as a woman, there is an offense of dukkaṭa, [the text says]: "If both a woman and a paṇḍaka are perceived by both as women..."

Because it is stated, "there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa* and *dukkaṭa*," it follows that it has already been stated, "if [the object] is a paṇḍaka and one perceives him as such, there is a *thullaccaya*.

Therefore, it should be understood that in all abbreviated sections, wherever there is a case for *thullaccaya*, a *thullaccaya* is indeed stated, and wherever there is a case for *dukkaṭa*, a *dukkaṭa* is likewise stated.
Likewise: "If she is a woman, but he is doubtful, and he is lustful..."
And if a bhikkhu, excluding the female organ and the urinary tract, speaks in praise [of her body] with reference to the area below the collarbone and above the knees...
[and so on], according to this method, the grounds for a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) should also be extracted as applicable.
Likewise: "The woman is present, but the bhikkhu is uncertain [about her sex], yet he is lustful; and the bhikkhu [touches] what is connected to the woman's body..."

The section on items connected to the body (*kāyapaṭibaddhavāra*) should also be extracted according to the circumstances, following the method beginning with: “He speaks in praise of it specifically… [and so forth]… there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

Although a triad of sections on relinquishment (*nissaggiyavāra*) is obtainable—just like the triad of sections on items connected to the body—it has not been extracted because there is no distinction in the nature of the offenses.
However, since that [section] follows the same method as the triad of sections on items connected to the body, its corresponding sections should also be understood accordingly.
[The offense] is to be extracted. In all cases, it should be understood that an ignorant girl, an elderly woman, a madwoman, and so forth, are not intended;
this is even more so for ordinary female animals, as well as for eunuchs and the like. The remainder should be understood according to the method stated in the second [offense].

Commentary on the Word-by-Word Analysis (Padabhājanīyavaṇṇanā) 285. "In the same manner as stated" refers to what was written as: "In the case of physical contact, by means of a female characteristic. It is said that "by means of a female characteristic" is the reading of the Great Commentary (Mahā-aṭṭhakathā).
"It does not apply to the head" means that there is no verbal abuse; however, it does apply when [the body] is touched. In this regard, the following...

The distinction is this: only when combined with these three [factors] is it called a *saṅghādisesa*, because of the definitive application of the terms "vagina" (*vacca-magga*) and "anus" (*passāva-magga*), or because of their extreme coarseness;
it is not so by means of the other eight, such as "one who has no genitals" (*animittāsi*) and so forth.

Among those, "you have no blood," "you have constant blood," "you have constant rags," "you are a discharger," "you are a female eunuch," and "you are a man-like woman"—these six are indefinite terms regarding the [sexual] organs.

The two phrases "you are signless" (*animittāsi*) and "you are a mere sign" (*nimittamattāsī*) are not gross; since it is stated that eight such phrases do not give rise to a *saṅghādisesa* offense, they are therefore grounds for a *thullaccaya*.
Some say they are grounds for a *dukkaṭa* because they are merely insults, as in the case of the Paribbājaka-vatthu.
The phrases "you are a woman-eunuch" (*itthipaṇḍakāsi*) and "you are a man-eunuch" (*vepurisikāsī*) refer to these very same phrases.
Those [defilements] that indicate the specific shape of the entire body are pure and do not give rise to a *saṅghādisesa* offense because they possess the commonality of the entire body;
the others do give rise to it because they lack that commonality. For those [others] indicate only the urinary passage, like the word "summit" (*sikharaṇī*).
However, the expression "one who possesses both sexual organs" (*ubhatobyañjanā*) is a statement mixed with a basis for a *saṅghādisesa* offense due to the male characteristic.
In the case of a hermaphrodite (purisobhato-byañjanaka), the female characteristic is concealed while the male characteristic is manifest.
If one were to arouse that [desire] as well, some ask: "How is it that the phrases 'you are without characteristics' (*animittāsi*) and so forth do not give rise to a *saṅghādisesa* offense?

That is not correct, because even for a man there is a designation for the characteristic, as seen in the summary table (*mātikā*): "A *saṅghādisesa* [offense] occurs in connection with sexual intercourse."

Because the characteristic has been stated, some say that when one makes an overture even by means of references to sexual intercourse, there is a *saṅghādisesa* offense for one who understands it, and a *thullaccaya* for one who does not understand;
for making an overture by other means, there is a *thullaccaya* for one who understands, and a *dukkaṭa* for one who does not understand.
All of this must be accepted only after careful deliberation.
287. Regarding the phrase "Hasanto" (Laughing): if she to whom he speaks understands him, it is a *saṅghādisesa*.
Commentary on the Subject Matter (Vinītavatthu-vaṇṇanā) 289.

The reading is "paṭivuttaṃ nāma. The word "no" is redundant. They say, "It also occurs by means of writing letters"; if that accords with the procedure immediately following the mental advertence (*āvajjana*), it should be accepted.
The commentary on the training rule concerning indecent speech is finished.
4. Commentary on the training rule concerning personal service according to one’s desire:
In the fourth [training rule], three sections on *saṅghādisesa* offenses are presented; the remaining fifty-seven sections consist of *thullaccaya*, *dukkaṭa*, and *pācittiya* offenses.
It should be understood as abbreviated; because another [version] is impossible, it has not been cited here.
The sequence for the remaining connections should be understood according to the method already stated. "By the city's requisites" means by the city's surroundings, such as walls and moats.
"White-requisite" means white adornment; the meaning is "adornment of virtue" (*sīla*). "Wheel of energy" means the wheel of effort (*vīriya-cakka*). "Vasala" means foul-smelling.
He spoke with reference to the sign (*nimitta*); it was with reference to that very thing that it was said: "What evil is mine? What foul odor is mine? (291).

"In the presence" (*santike*) means where one stands while making the request. "If one joins [the first section] according to the text (*pāḷi*), then the meaning is the service for the sake of sensual pleasure.

As for "the rest," the word "intention" (*adhippāyo*) is the phrasing (*byañjana*), because of the absence of a [separate] meaning. In the second [section], according to the text, there are the words "for the sake of sensual pleasure."

"The phonemes [are mentioned] because their meaning is absent therein. Thus, others say that the four phrases have been joined according to two types of grammatical analysis (*viggaha*). It is said. 295.

Among these training rules (*sikkhāpada*), if there is a transgression through lust for sexual intercourse, there is no offense (*anāpatti*) involving a formal meeting of the Saṅgha (*saṅghādisesa*). Therefore...

“What, venerable sir, is the ‘foremost gift’? “Sexual intercourse. This should be understood as spoken solely for the purpose of praising sexual intercourse, and not as spoken with the intention of sexual intercourse or for its sake;
there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in praising the service of sensual desires to another bhikkhu. [For example: “Give the foremost gift to whoever dwells in your monastery.”
There is also an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) by way of figurative speech. Some say this is because it is stated: "One should speak in praise of serving one's own desires;
[praising] one such as me who is virtuous. Others say that because all five factors are present, it is a formal offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*).

This should be determined after careful consideration. However, in the *Gaṇṭhipada*, it is said: "In these two training rules, just as in the case of physical contact, there is no grave offense (*duṭṭhulla*) in speaking of desire regarding female spirits (*yakkhinī*) and so forth."

They say it is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense). However, it is recorded that this does not appear in the *Aṭṭhakathās* (Commentaries). Furthermore, they say that one who possesses both sexual organs belongs to the category of the *paṇḍaka* (eunuch).
The commentary on the training rule regarding sexual intercourse at one’s own request is finished.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule on Acting as a Matchmaker (Sañcaritta-sikkhāpada) 297.
*Ahamhi duggatā* means "I am in distress. In the phrase *aham khvayyo*, the word *ayyo* is used in the plural sense.

298. *Oyācantī* means they beg the gods by lowering their voices. *Āyācantī* means they beg with reverence by raising their voices. "Adorned" refers to being decorated with ornaments and the like; "well-groomed" refers to being beautified through the arrangement of hair and so forth. They say that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in the act of adorning [the woman].
Commentary on the Word-by-Word Analysis (Padabhājanīyavaṇṇanā) 303.

“Together with the formal act” means occurring along with the *paridaṇḍa* (the formal censure). “A woman who dwells according to her will” (*chandavāsinī*)—the canonical text says, “The beloved dwells with the beloved,” but the intended meaning is that she dwells with a man. The commentary says, “The beloved dwells with the beloved.
“She will accomplish that action” means that if she reports it, she must certainly report it to both parents. Of the two parents...

Regarding the statement, "If one reports this, it is a *saṅghādisesa*," it is said in the *Vinayavinicchaya*: "The subject matter (*vatthu*) must be examined. And regarding that subject matter, it is stated:
"The Elder Udāyī reported [this] to a courtesan. That [statement] is purposeless, because of the commentary’s (*aṭṭhakathā*) remark:
"There is no discrepancy even when reporting to one's mother and so forth. However, the phrase "But that" is the teacher’s own statement. [The term is] *māturakkhitam*.

When one who has been sent with the command "Speak" goes and speaks of her as being protected by both mother and father—even though she is indeed protected by her mother alone—that is still a breach of the agreement (*visaṅketa*).
Why? Because it is stated that "speaking of her as being protected by the father or any other [guardian] constitutes a breach of the agreement";
otherwise, the word "or any other" (*ādi*) would be meaningless. Having joined one decade with the other decade, [the text continues] regarding the previous emission of semen...
Because it is stated in the aforementioned manner, it should be understood that the mother sends her own daughter to the presence of one protected by her mother. 338.
"Without having welcomed" is a mere expression; even if she does welcome her, as long as she has not yet announced the message, she is not said to have been "examined.
At the time of announcing the message means at the moment the messenger utters the words of the command.

"By the method stated in the third clause" means that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) due to the fulfillment of one factor. "A formal meeting of the Saṅgha offense (*saṅghādisesa*) by counting the objects" refers, it is said, to counting both types of objects. 339.
Regarding the fourth case, "there is no offense": here, however, [it is said] that "if one accepts [the gift], does not examine it, and does not return it, there is no offense."

They say that this was stated for the purpose of showing that there should also be a textual basis for non-offense (anāpatti-pāḷi) in the case where "one who is going does not fulfill [the promise], while one who is coming fulfills it";
in some manuscripts, the word "atthi" (there is) also appears. [End of] Commentary on the Basis for Discipline (Vinītavatthu-vaṇṇanā).
341. *Alaṃvacanīyā* means "not to be spoken to"; here the word *alaṃ* is used in the sense of prohibition. *Therapitā vadati* means "the old father speaks.
Although there is no explicit definition here stating, "A woman is a human female, not a *yakkhī*, not a *petī*, nor one belonging to the animal realm;
a man is a human male, not a *yakkha*," and so forth, nevertheless, in the context of physical contact and other such matters, the term "human female" (*manussitthī*) is understood.

Because the definition of "woman" has been established, here too it is understood as a human woman. Since it is a preliminary stage to sexual intercourse, a human hermaphrodite (*ubhatobyañjanaka*) constitutes a grave offense (*thullaccaya*);

it should be understood that all others—human eunuchs (*paṇḍaka*), hermaphrodites, animals, males, and so forth—constitute an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*), because they arise from a factor of the teaching on sexual misconduct (*micchācāra*). However, according to what is possible:

The days must be calculated. Just as in the case of not knowing the formal rule (paññatti), it should be understood that there is no lack of intention (acittakatā) even in the case of not knowing the state of being one who is to be spoken to.
Regarding "in cases such as lewdness," the phrase "in this case too" is already implied.

They say: "Even for one who, having delivered a letter, reports the reply, there is no acting as a go-between (sañcaritta) if they are unaware of the state of being a go-between"; this should be accepted after investigation.
The commentary on the training rule concerning matchmaking is finished.
6. Commentary on the training rule concerning building a hut (Kuṭikāra-sikkhāpada).
342. "Soliciting" means urging, saying, "Give! Give! "Requesting" means making known one's need, saying, "We have this requirement. "Manual labor" (hatthakamma)...
If one asks for requisites [thinking], "He will give me the price," it is not permitted. Some say it is permitted when one receives light or a discourse while staying in a lodging.

"Not inhabited" means ownerless. "It should not be used if it has not been brought [to the monastery]" refers to what was stated: "There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for requesting soup or rice.
Although it was stated, "Even if they are worth heavy goods," nevertheless, regarding that object...
They say that although it is small in quantity, it is great by way of its value, such as yellow orpiment, vermilion, and so forth; therefore, it is not permissible to ask for it.
"So kira" refers to the seer (isi). "Tadā ajjhagamā" means he then obtained it.

"Na hi sakkā yācanāya kātuṃ" means it is indeed not possible to do so by means of begging; therefore, the intended meaning is that [the Buddha] himself used requisites that had been requested [for him].
The phrasing is consistent, but not the meaning. Why? Because both [meanings] are intended here; showing this, he said, "But because... and so forth.
"By the method stated here" means by the method stated in this analysis of the training rule (*sikkhāpada-vibhaṅga*).

Because of the expression "by means of a request," it must be practiced by one who builds himself; and because of the expression "having others complete it," it must also be practiced by one who has it built by others.

Both of these are the agent and the instigator. The phrasing would be inverted; for the phrasing "by one who causes to be done" (kārayamānena) becomes inverted when stated as "by one who does" (karontena), because it does not have that meaning.
For one who is causing [another] to do is not [simply] called "one who does.
"By the method stated here" means by the method concerning the measure of the subject matter taught. This being so, [the phrase] "by one who does or by one who causes to be done..."
If it is argued that, based on the word "or" (*vā*), one who is building [a hut] may also say that it was built by others, the *Anugaṇṭhipada* states:

"The words beginning with ‘if, however’ (*yadi pana*) were spoken in order to answer that point. This is stated by way of the expression "one building a hut by means of begging" (*saññācikāya kuṭiṃ karonto*).
Because the particle "or" (*vā*) is taken here in the sense of an alternative (*vikappa*), rather than stating "in length and in breadth," [the rule applies].
If it is increased on even one side, there is likewise an offense. It is said that a bed of standard measure is nine *vidatthi*s.

By the statement "four cubits in width," the expression "or three cubits across" is also consistent, because a definitive statement such as "where it conforms to the measure" would otherwise be impossible.
Even if it is smaller than the standard measure—meaning even if it is four or five cubits in width, provided it does not exceed [the limit] in length.
The subject matter taught is exactly the prescribed measurement. For one who constructs a subject matter that has not been so taught, there is an offense.
This is because it is stated: "One should construct a hut that exceeds the measurement as 'a hut exceeding the measurement'. The reading is "thambhatulā" (the pillar and the beam).
Regarding the phrase "by way of the formal proclamation," they say that even the Tamil language is permissible here.
353. *Cārabhūmi* (the ground for wandering) and *gocarabhūmi* (the ground for the range of activity). "Not taken" means not prohibited. In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is written:
"For the sake of [punishment], a prison with secure bonds, or a place of non-action; those who sell perfumes, those who cut off hands and feet, and perfume-sellers.
Regarding "with two oxen," since it is said that this refers to the minimum limit, they cannot be driven away because their access has been cut off; this also applies to the exit.
It should be understood that this was said for the purpose of explaining the meaning. "Pācina" refers to the site or the foundation.
"Tadatthāya" means for the purpose of roofing it. "Paṇṇasālam-pi" means even a leaf-roofed hut that has been plastered inside and out;

by this very [statement], it is said to have "walls and a roof," for indeed, everything that is unplastered is permitted. Having previously set aside a small amount, one increases it again. In that...

Whether it has been placed at the door-bolt or at the window-lattice. Regarding the phrase "right at the outset," the Elder Dhammasiri says this means "at the very time [of the offense]," while the Elder Upatissa says it means "at the time of placing [the bowl].

Since the first [condition] does not involve the application of plaster (*lepasa aghaṭittattā*) and the second was done under the heading of a formal duty (*vattasīsa*), there is no offense for either.
If it was done by one who was commanded, it falls under the statement: "he does it himself or causes it to be done."

The offense applies to both [the builder and the supervisor] when there is a self-assignment (*attuddesikatā*); when there is none, it applies only to the one who possesses the original site (*mūlaṭṭha*).

When the lower measurement is possible, for one building a hut made entirely of clay, the teacher’s opinion is that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) followed by an offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*).
354. The "Thirty-Six Tetrads" consist of: the tetrad on the site not being declared, the tetrad on the site being declared, and the tetrad on exceeding the measurement.
There are six tetrads: the tetrad on measurements, the tetrad on exceeding the measurement when the site has not been designated, and the tetrad on measurements when the site has been designated.
Likewise, there are five [tetrads] for each of the sections beginning with "if he should so command," making thirty-six in total.

Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of showing the classification of offenses": here, because of the *mātikā* (matrix) which states, "If, O Bhikkhu, on a site that is encroached upon and lacks space... [etc. ... it is a *saṅghādisesa*."

Because it was stated without distinction, the classification of offenses is shown in order to avoid the wrong apprehension that there is a *saṅghādisesa* offense even in the case of a site with living beings (*sārambha*) or one lacking a space for circumambulation (*aparikkamana*).

Therefore, the intention is that they have been "stated" [in this context]. If it is asked: why is the matter of an *dukkaṭa* offense stated in the *mātikā* instead of being stated thus in the *vibhaṅga*?
[It is because] monks must be brought along for the designation of the site; by those monks, the site...
It must be designated. Of what kind? One that is free from harm (*anārambha*) and has a space for circumambulation (*saparikkamana*);

not the other. Regarding the other, it is stated [in the rule] by way of its disadvantage: "If a monk, on a site that is harmful and lacks a space for circumambulation... Since there are sites that are harmful and those that are free from harm, and there are those with a space for circumambulation and those without, [the former is required].

"There is [a site] with harm and with space for walking around; there is [a site] with harm and without space for walking around; there is [a site] without harm and with space for walking around; there is [a site] without harm and without space for walking around.

Because of this manifold variety, it must be taught that "the site without harm and with space for walking around" is what is intended, and not the others. If one asks, "What is the purpose of this teaching? it is for the purpose of providing the means for avoiding the causes for the establishment of grave offenses.
For, because it is the cause for the establishment of a grave offense (*garukāpatti*), the failure to make a formal request (*akataviññatti*),
and because the state of having a site under construction (*sārambhabhāva*) is a cause for one’s own suffering and the suffering of others by causing distress to householders—

these are avoided by means of the pretext of "indicating the site. Indeed, a monk does not [indicate a site] for the purpose of building an improper hut (*akappiyakuṭi*) nor as a sign of causing distress to householders.
The site for a building undertaking: it has already been established that they point out a site for the purpose of building a hut.
"Mixed offenses" refers to offenses mixed with *dukkaṭa* and *saṅghādisesa*. 355.

In this context, where one should say "with two *saṅghādisesas*," it is stated as "by means of two *saṅghādisesas*" due to a change in grammatical case and a change in number. There is also a reading: "an offense of two *saṅghādisesas*."
364. It does not constitute a roof because of the absence of plastering; thus there is no offense, for that [roof] is established by what follows.
It is with reference specifically to the roofing that the state of being "plastered inside and outside" is stated.

Having said, "A house with a cock’s comb is permissible," those who subsequently demonstrate this by way of the method beginning with "the roof by means of rafters" and so forth, are speaking only of small huts with roofs of grass and leaves. In that context, the roofing—
It is appropriate [to say] that the state of being "plastered" (*ullitta*) and so forth refers specifically to the act of covering after binding it with poles lengthwise and crosswise like a net,
and then covering it with grass or leaves. Therefore, even without [the specific mention of] plastering,
there is indeed an offense for one who causes a wall made of clay to be built and then has it plastered on top, or whitewashed, or both joined together upon the wall.
“By plastering the wall,” it is written. “And ‘this refers only to the roof-covering’ is said by way of emphasis;

it does not exclude the lower part,” they say—this should be investigated. “In this case” means in the grass hut. “According to the instruction given” means in the manner already described; such is the intention.
Regarding the passage beginning with “the craftsmen incur three offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),” he hears even that group of six.
It is obtained. Since it was authorized in both cases, there is no offense for the one who gave the command.

For the one who was commanded, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) due to not acting in accordance with what was commanded by the one who gave the command. If he also makes a personal dedication, saying, "I too shall dwell here," it is a formal offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*).
However, in a case where it was stated without qualification, "Build a hut," even for the one who gave the command...
The *saṅghādisesa* offense is unintentional because the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) is so constituted.

Regarding the phrase "and I shall dwell [there]," since there is an absence of anyone else to whom one has assigned [the task], there is indeed an offense for one who acts [in that way], as this is specifically determined by the words "or while doing";
however, there is no offense for one who does not assign [the task], because it was not so designated. "In this case, 'intention' consists merely in the knowledge of the formal rule (*paññatti*)."
And it is so written. However, in the *Anugaṇṭhipada*, regarding the phrase "I shall dwell [there]," it states that an offense applies to one who desires, "There will be a dwelling place for me";
but for one who desires an *uposatha* hall, there is no offense.

Therefore, having stated, "Both [conditions] coincide," and because of the statement, "When a serious matter arises in the Vinaya adjudication, one must remain firm," according to the *Mahāpaccarivāda*...
If it is argued that the other [offense] should be mentioned later, we say no, because of its greater force.
Since there is the statement, “Except for the dwelling-house, there is no offense anywhere,” confusion arises because this [act] was performed for the sake of the dining hall and so forth as well.
It is just as when two or three people act with the thought, “We shall dwell together,” and for that time, one is still protected; likewise, [one thinks], “This place will be the dwelling-house.”
Even if one has analyzed [the matter] by saying, "This is the Uposatha hall," there is still an offense. The tradition of the Mahāpaccari is strong regarding these two cases;
therefore, there has been excessive elaboration [in the commentary] with such phrases as "stated later" and so forth. What is the use of that?
Having applied other tetrads according to their possibility in the manner of "one brings to completion what was begun by oneself, both by oneself and by others," and so on—

These [cases] must be shown: although there is no offense of *saṅghādisesa* regarding such things as caves, if there is a formal request (*viññatti*) for them to be built, there is indeed an offense on that account.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the building of a hut (*kuṭikāra-sikkhāpada*) is finished.
