380. "To be attained by a disciple" is said with reference to an ordinary disciple (*pakatisāvaka*), not to a chief disciple (*aggasāvaka*). According to the specific supporting conditions (*upanissaya*) and the particular individual, it is stated as "the three knowledges" (*tisso vijjā*) and so forth.

By one disciple the three knowledges are attained, by another the four analytical insights (*catasso paṭisambhidā*), by another the six direct knowledges (*cha abhiññā*), and by another the entire nine supramundane states (*navalokuttaradhamma*); thus, each is attained separately according to what is possible.
It should be understood that this has been stated.
From the words, "Those monks who are experts in the Suttas," and so forth, it is established that even while the Blessed One was still living, the division of the Tipiṭaka already existed.
"Dhamma-preachers" refers to those learned in the Abhidhamma; "they will remain for their pleasure," and so forth, [is said] by the Venerable Dabba.

It appears as if he were being incited toward a delight in frivolous talk (*tiracchānakathā*); however, it should not be viewed in that way. Rather, it should be understood that he thought thus while avoiding the following:
the obstruction to the comfortable dwelling of those versed in the Suttas and so forth due to their association with him;
the state of discontent for them as well, owing to his lack of delight in frivolous talk; and, consequently, their falling away from the life of a recluse (*sāmañña*).
They say: “The nature of created things (nimmitānaṃ dhammatā) refers only to those created by disciples, not by Buddhas.

When it is stated that “the most effective instrument is the instrument (sādhakatamaṃ karaṇaṃ),” the meaning is that the third case ending occurs only in the sense of the instrument. 383–4. *Yaṃ* means *yena*.
“*Kattā*—is he an agent (*kattā*) or not an agent (*na kattā*)? so it is written. “He behaves toward me as if I were his wife.”
The accusation of one who speaks with force is powerful. Regarding the phrase "for this reason" (*tena hi*):

here it should be understood that just as he prescribed a *saṅghādisesa* offense even without asking, in the case of the matter concerning remorse over a mere touch—where lust for physical contact had arisen—so too was it spoken because he already knew her state of immorality beforehand. If she had been expelled based on a confession of what actually occurred, the Elder...
He is the one who acts. Now, if she were innocent, it would not have been said by the Blessed One, "Expel her," yet it was indeed said; therefore it is stated:
"If she was expelled on the basis of her own admission, then the Elder is the one who acted.
Now, as for "without her admission": this refers to her state of natural depravity even without that specific admission, namely, "Venerable sir, I have been defiled by you."
Having made a secret agreement, he was expelled; thus, the Elder is not the one who committed the act. The residents of Abhayagiri, too, having cited their own sūtra, say:
"In your doctrine, the Elder is the perpetrator. Why? Because a *dukkaṭa* offense does not warrant expulsion by way of shaving the head (*liṅganāsanā*);
for only those guilty of a *pārājika* offense are to be expelled by shaving the head. And since it was said, "Expel him," they became *pārājika* offenders.

With what intention did he say this? From that [statement], the Elder becomes the perpetrator. However, when it is said, "Destroy her by means of her own admission," the intended meaning is that even one who has not committed a *pārājika* offense may be destroyed by her own word.
The Mahāvihāravāsins also, having stated their own Sutta, say, "In your doctrine, the Elder is the perpetrator. Why? Because of the phrase, "By means of her own admission..."
For when it is said, "Annul it," the truthfulness of the admission is established by the very words "Annul it.
The intention is that only what is true should be annulled through an admission, not what is untrue. "In the former manner" refers to the statement regarding the *dukkaṭa* offense.
It should be understood that the former proceeds by way of logical reasoning (*yutti*), while the latter proceeds by way of the actual wording of the Canon (*pāḷi*).

385–6. Regarding the phrase "with rapture and pleasure" (*pītisukhehi*): here, although one should have said "with pleasure," the inclusion of "rapture" is stated in order to exclude the pleasure of the third jhāna and bodily pleasure, referring instead to the rapture associated with the mind.

If what was done on account of the accused were called "groundless," and one were to say, "It was not committed, it was not done," thinking, "These people will do it," then, having perceived such a thing as seen...
The reading is "codeti. The reading is: "In this same manner, those things heard, suspected, or anticipated should also be understood in detail.
The phrase "by one of the four" is stated by taking what has come down specifically in the recitation of the Pātimokkha;

however, the Teacher [Ācariya] holds that there is no such restriction, for even for one who does not accuse by means of one of the other [three], it is a *saṅghādisesa* offense. For from the state of being a bhikkhu...

Because it is capable of causing one to fall away. From the statement "standing nearby," it follows that for one who accuses or causes another to be accused in the absence [of the person], the offense does not reach its head.

If one accuses or causes another to be accused based on what was seen through what was heard or suspected, or if one accuses or causes another to be accused based on what was heard or suspected through what was seen and so forth, the offense certainly reaches its head because of accusing on grounds that are unfounded (*amūlaka*). For this has been said:
“If one sees another committing an offense entailing defeat (pārājika), and he accuses him, saying: ‘I have heard… [etc.
… he has committed a saṅghādisesa offense,’ then that person is impure for having committed a particular offense entailing defeat.

If, while maintaining the view that he is impure, he speaks with the intention of causing the other to leave the community without having asked for permission, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). If, however, he asks for permission…”
“...if one speaks with the intention of causing [the other] to fall away, there is no offense”—by this, it appears as if it were not the same [case].
How so? One who has seen another committing an offense entailing defeat (pārājika) is indeed an impure person;
thus, if one who holds such an impure view accuses the other, saying, “I have heard that you have committed an offense entailing defeat,” there is an offense for every single word spoken.
Because of the statement, "It is a *saṅghādisesa* offense," there is an offense according to the former method;

because of the statement, "If one speaks with the intention of causing [the nun] to fall away, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa* according to the latter method.
Thus, two methods of the Canon appear as if they contradict each other. However, the Buddhas do not speak what is contradictory; therefore, the underlying reasoning must be sought here.
The commentators of the *Aṭṭhakathā* say: "There is no offense for one who accuses based on what is rooted, or based on perception being rooted;
however, there is an offense for one who accuses based on what is unrooted, or based on perception being unrooted. The meaning of this is as follows:

there is no offense for one who accuses based on what is "rooted"—meaning by way of seeing, hearing, or suspicion—or even by what is "unrooted" due to the absence of those [grounds], or by what is "perception-rooted"; whereas there is an offense when there is an absence of the roots such as seeing and so forth.
There is an offense for one who accuses [another] with what is groundless, or even with what has a basis, or by means of a perception that is groundless; therefore, it is said: "it is seen.

When accusing someone of having committed an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika-dhamma*), etc., whether one does so on the basis of seeing—which is a basis—or even with words such as "I have heard it," which do not constitute a basis, or by means of a perception that lacks a basis, there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*. This is stated in order to clarify the meaning of that [term].
It should be understood that the sections beginning with “one who is doubtful about what has been seen” have been stated.
However, in the case of the first section and those following, because the person is impure due to being accused on the basis of a root-offense or on the basis of a perception, there is no offense.
Nevertheless, those sections were stated for the purpose of illustrating that meaning. For therein, the sections beginning with “there is one who has not seen it” [are found].
It is stated for the purpose of showing that there is an offense for one who accuses [another] on groundless charges.

The passage beginning with “one who is doubtful about what has been seen” is stated for the purpose of showing that there is an offense for one who accuses [another] on the basis of perception despite the lack of a foundation. Otherwise, the sections beginning with “there is what has been seen” and “one who is doubtful about what has been seen” would be indistinguishable from one another.
However, this is the definitive conclusion here: just as in the case of an impure person who has not granted leave...

For one who, having caused [the matter] to be investigated, then accuses [another], there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); and for one whose intention is to revile, there is an offense of wrong-doing by way of abusive speech.
Likewise, even one with impure views who accuses another of impure views on groundless grounds incurs an offense;

however, if he accuses them on a grounded basis, there is no offense—this is the determination, just as it was stated: "There is no offense when one with impure views accuses a pure person regarding what is impure."
This accords with the phrase "of one with impure views," and it should be understood accordingly. Otherwise, a different logical connection must be sought.
Regarding the term "one endowed with virtue" (*sīlasampanna*): "The word of one who is immoral is not authoritative. For a bhikkhunī has no authority over a bhikkhu;
therefore, the Elder spoke thus with reference to the procedure according to the stricter rule. By the second Elder, even though the bhikkhunī did not know..."

"Others say: 'If one reproaches [another], or if trainee nuns (sikkhamānā) and others reproach them, and having heard them, the monks themselves investigate and act upon his admission—what fault is there in this?
It was with reference to this that it was said. By the third [case], even after hearing the words of the heretics (titthiya), the monks themselves investigate;
therefore, no one fails to obtain [the verdict]. Thus everything is consistent. So it is said.
"Thirty" means thirty in number. "Anuyoga" means a response. "Ehi" means he will come. "By way of what has been seen" (diṭṭhasantānena) means by the method seen;
the intention is "by the manner seen. "Having established" (patiṭṭhāya) means having obtained a footing. "In the place" (ṭhāne) means in a place where one feels shame.

"Taking up" (gāhaṃ) refers to the act of taking up a formal charge, thinking, "I shall accuse him. "Intention" (cetanā) refers to the volition of taking up that formal charge. "Discourse" (vohāra) refers to...
Having understood [the object] from this and that, there is its manifestation. "Designation" (paññatti) refers to name-designation (nāmapaññatti).

That which is cognized by the mind-door consciousness—arising immediately after the stream of ear-door consciousness that has sound as its object, and which has previously grasped the conventional sign—is that through the cognition of which the meaning of that designation, whether ultimate or non-ultimate, is then cognized for a third time by the mind-consciousness.

That which is revealed in the Pāḷi through the six designations beginning with "name" (nāma) is shown by the teachers to be sixfold, such as "designation of what exists" (vijjamāna-paññatti) and "designation of what does not exist" (avijjamāna-paññatti).
The state of belonging to that category (tabbhāgiya-bhāva) and the state of not belonging to that category (atabbhāgiya-bhāva) apply only to a dhamma that has been produced (nipphanna-dhamma),
and not to a designation (paññatti), because a designation is a basis for a legal question (adhikaraṇīya-vatthu) and because it functions with respect to a locus (adhikaraṇa).

And it is said: "It is like the designation 'bed' applied to one who is on a bed. Furthermore, it is written: "'By way of a synonym' means that there is no such thing as a designation (paññatti) that is without a basis.

It is merely a synonym; it does not exist by way of intrinsic nature (sabhāva). It is merely a name (abhidhāna); there is no corresponding referent (abhidheyya). "In this very [case]" means in this very training rule (sikkhāpada).

"Not in all cases" means not in the case of legal issues arising from disputes (vivādādhikaraṇa) and so forth. Why? Because of the passage beginning with "For it is not," etc., which establishes the existence of legal issues arising from disputes and the rest.

“There is no groundless legal issue (adhikaraṇa) as such. By “by means of the methods of settling previously mentioned,” the intended meaning is: “by means of those methods of settling with reference to which the methods of settling operate.

Furthermore, it is said that [the groundless issue] does not exist by way of its own nature because it has not attained a specific nature, like consciousness and so forth when they have not yet arisen. For the designation (paṇṇatti) of disputes and so on is not the actual sense of a legal issue; thus, [it is called groundless] with respect to the designation.

Because the *samatha* (methods of settling) do not proceed when there is an *adhikicca* (an improper act), it is therefore not subject to formal legal procedure (*adhikaraṇīya*). Thus, the intention is that the designation of disputes and so forth as "legal matters" (*adhikaraṇa*) does not apply here.
And in this regard, there is [the following verse]:
"If an offense of defeat (*pārājika*) is groundless..."
The fruits and path-states are mere designations;
likewise, those things that constitute the basis for the fourth pārājika would likewise be mere designations.
“Then the phenomena such as the paths and fruits would be twofold— namely, past and future—
or else the sixfold designation would not exist.”
"By way of a method, they speak the conventional discourse. "Anuvadanti" means they revile.

"Kiccayatā" means the state of being a duty. If one asks, "What is that? it is the *apalokana-kamma* (act of notification), and so forth. "Kicca" refers, it is said, to the mind that originates the formal communication (*viññatti*).
387. Regarding "being groundless due to the absence of what was seen and so forth": herein, one who, even having seen [the offense], is unable to say, "I have seen you," [is considered groundless].
He says, "I have heard it," according to his own settled view. Because he holds an impure view regarding that matter, there is an offense for him.
However, this refers to one who previously heard it and was without offense, but later, having forgotten it, speaks while still possessing a pure view;
it is said with reference to such a person. "This principle applies everywhere," say others. (Jeṭṭhabbatika)

"Acceptable to crows" (kākekappa). "Yadaggena" means "as far as" or "at which time. He shows that the phrase beginning with "it is not allowable" was stated solely for the purpose of clarifying the state of being doubtful.
By that [phrase], one might fall into the error of thinking that one who is merely doubtful is called "one who has forgotten" because he does not remember;
however, that is not correct, because [the state of doubt] occurs immediately prior [to the act]. Therefore, the statement of the second Elder was spoken later.
389. "In all" means in all the Aṭṭhakathās. "Okāsakamma" means making room. It is written as "okāsena kammaṃ okāsakammaṃ.

Just as in the phrase "a maiden sees no sun," it is understood that the maiden does not see the sun, so too when it is said "having made no room (anokāsaṃ kāretvā)," it is understood as "not having made room."
The commentary on the first training rule concerning corrupting faults is finished.
9. Commentary on the second training rule concerning corrupting faults: 391.
"In Veḷuvana itself" was said with reference to the time they spoke. "Previously, friend, we heard..."
This was said with reference to the statement beginning, "We said [this]; she was incited by us who were angry and displeased.

"Of another portion" (*aññabhāgassa*) means: this legal case concerning a goat, which is of a different portion from the state of being a human monk—that is, the portion consisting of a beast, a goat.
Or, it is that which possesses another portion; thus, it is designated as the portion consisting of a beast, a goat.
"Another part belongs to this goat"—this goat is called an *aññabhāgiya* (heterogeneous) legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*).
In that context, "the body of a statue" and "the body of a stone child" are illustrations.

Here, however, the first etymological explanation is stated according to the opinion of those who maintain that the meaning of the word is the genus (*jāti*). For that [genus] is primary because of its status as the owner and its permanence.

It should be understood that the second derivation was stated according to this sutta: "The meaning of the word is 'births' (jātiyo) that are distinct (byattā) due to being the opposite of that [nature], while remaining in their own essential nature (sattisabhāve).
Regarding the phrase "the locus for the designation of naming" (nāmakaraṇasaññāya ādhāro): here, "naming" (nāmakaraṇa) is simply the name itself.
The "designation of naming" (nāmakaraṇasaññā) is the designation for those who perform the naming; it belongs to that [designation]. A human birth is the locus for the birth of a goat.
The meaning is that this name does not lack a basis, unlike the hair of a tortoise. However, the name "dabba" given to the goat is called the "region" (desa).

Therefore, by means of the phrase "the elder with what is groundless," etc., another matter is attached to or clings to the elder merely through conventional usage and not in actual fact; it adheres slightly, hence it is called a *lesa*.

This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). Since the "lesas" (stains) mentioned in the *desa* (the introductory narrative) are not different in substance from those in the *attha* (the formal explanation), it should be understood that after extracting the phrase "taking some portion, a mere lesa," the passage beginning with "ten lesas: the stain of birth" and so forth was stated.

Just as in the *nidāna*, so too in the laying down of the training rule (*sikkhāpada-panñatti*) and in the *mātikā* (summary table), this is the very same meaning. Because "of another class of legal issue" (*aññabhāgiyassa adhikaraṇassa*) refers to the goat. "Some portion" (*kañcidesaṃ*)...

"Taking the mere mention of them" means taking the name "Dabba"; this meaning is already evident through the context of the origin story (*aṭṭhuppatti*), and therefore it has not been analyzed separately.
Furthermore, because it is unspecified: for not everyone has a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) concerning another that is exclusively a goat, as was the case with Mettiya and Bhūmajaka;
there may also be others involving cows, buffaloes, and so forth, and yet it is not...

Just like Mettiya and Bhūmajaka, all [those who commit offenses] take on what is merely a semblance (*nāmalesa*). They also take on other semblances, such as those pertaining to caste (*jātilesa*) and so forth;
therefore, because of this lack of restriction, it was not analyzed according to the method previously stated.

Furthermore, if it were stated in that way, the status of being "connected with another case" (*aññabhāgiyatā*) would apply only to a goat, not to anything else, which is why only that [goat] was shown. And as for what is called a "semblance" (*lesa*), it is indeed a semblance, not...
Nor was it analyzed in that way because of the risk of the false assumption that "he" [the accuser] is shown by his birth and so forth.

393. Regarding the phrase "of another case": it refers to one other than the person being accused. Regarding the phrase "of the legal issue": it should be stated as "whether of a human, or a non-human, or an animal.
For if it were stated thus, then the stains of birth and so forth would apply only to humans and the like.

If it is argued that they are indeed so stated, otherwise they would fall into the four types of legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*), because the genitive case in the phrase "some part or mere trace of a legal issue" (*adhikaraṇassa kañci desaṃ lesamattam*) was taught as being primary;

[the answer is] no, because—just as with names—it is possible for there to be a fixed rule regarding the status of humans and so forth as the substratum (*ādhāra*) of universals (*jāti*) and so on, whereas there is no such fixed rule regarding their status as the locus of a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*). This is what is meant.
And when there is a fixed rule (niyama), birth is the basis for caste, gender is the basis for sex, and one who has committed [an offense] is the basis for the offense;
furthermore, the owner of even conflicting or unaccepted bowls and robes is the basis.

Since it would reach the status of a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) by means of that [basis], the word "of the legal issue" (*adhikaraṇassa*)—meaning "one commits"—should indeed not be divided and thus should not be omitted.
It may be [that it] should be extracted. Therefore, everything beginning with “*Adhikaraṇan’ti vacanasāmaññato*” must be stated.

[The term is] not evident because there is no other place where it has been shown besides this. And it must be understood by those who uphold the Vinaya (*vinayadhara*), since otherwise [the Parivāra states]:
“A legal issue arising from a dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*) belongs to the category of the four legal issues as a legal issue arising from a dispute,” and so forth.
According to this method, if one were to ask "Why? regarding a case that does not belong to the future category, no reason would be apparent;

therefore, the Vinaya-holders must understand both the inclusion within that category (*tabbhāgiyatā*) and the exclusion from it (*aññabhāgiyatā*). For when these are understood, a legal issue arising from dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*) is correctly classified as a legal issue arising from dispute.
Why? Because of its inclusion within that category. The other [legal issues] are not so classified because of their exclusion from it; thus they are known through the ease of the reasoning.
Therefore, [the phrase] "relying on a legal issue (adhikaraṇa) obtained through the commonality of the term," and so forth, is used.

In that regard, because the *āpattāññabhāgiya* has a wide scope and its designation is unlike the others, it is stated separately—even though it is likewise included within the category of legal issues—as "or it is an *āpattāññabhāgiya*. And because it is included within the category of legal issues, it is called an *adhikaraṇāññabhāgiya*.

It should be understood that this is what is stated here by the word "or. Furthermore, it should be understood that among those two, "belonging to another case" (*aññabhāgiyatā*) is mentioned first because its scope is broader and because it has been included in the *mātikā*, whereas "belonging to that same case" (*tabbhāgiyatā*) follows later.

In this regard, since the fact that a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) belongs to that same case is established through the method of implication (*atthāpatti-naya*) by the statement "a legal issue belonging to another case," therefore [the text says]: "A legal issue belongs to that same case."

Instead of providing a mere summary by saying "it becomes so," this exposition is preceded by a question: "In what way does one legal issue (adhikaraṇa) belong to the same category as another legal issue?

Even therein, although the fact that a legal issue arising from an offense (āpattādhikaraṇa) belongs to a different category is stated specifically in terms of the Pārājika offenses—because the context concerns those who have been charged with a Pārājika—it nevertheless applies also to the remaining classes of offenses.

It should be understood as follows: regarding that formal accusation such as, "The monk named so-and-so was seen committing a *saṅghādisesa* offense," one should understand that statements therein such as,
"He holds the view that it is a *thullaccaya* when it is a *saṅghādisesa*,

or he holds the view that it is a *saṅghādisesa* when it is a *dubbhāsita*," are spoken either because of his lack of knowledge regarding the Vinaya or because of the similarity between the respective cases.
In all instances, it is not stated that "there is a view of a *pārājika* offense," because there is no offense for one who perceives it as such.
It is stated [in the text] because, in the explanation of the term *tabbhāgiya*, it is also described as being *aññabhāgiya*.
"By way of similarity of the subject matter" means by way of similarity of the subject matter of the accusation. Otherwise, [it would have been called] "the four failures."
The statement would be contradicted. "By way of similarity and dissimilarity of intrinsic nature" means by way of being similar or dissimilar in their essential character (*sabhāva*).

In that regard, even when there is a difference in the objective basis (*vatthu*) such as the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and so forth, because of the similarity of intrinsic nature, an offense of defeat (*pārājika*) regarding superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*) belongs to that very category for that person.

this is established as having been mentioned separately in their respective introductory narratives (*nidāna*). The meaning is: "there is no offense for first-time offenders. (From the *Anugaṇṭhipada*)

Furthermore, it is said: "In accordance with the rule regarding a seat concealed by a bush in the Acelaka-vagga, which states, 'A wise man is his companion,' it is declared that even [with] a hundred women, no offense is committed. And:

"Regarding the rule for a companion, stating 'both a woman and a man,' this refers to the closing training rule in the Bhikkhunī-vagga and the rule regarding an unconcealed seat in the Acelaka-vagga."
And in the section on non-offenses, it is said: "Any intelligent man whatsoever as a companion. It should be understood that this was stated in accordance with these [cases].
The commentary on the second indeterminate training rule is finished.
Commentary on the Miscellaneous:
Furthermore, regarding this miscellaneous section—namely, this "Indeterminate Chapter" (Aniyata-khaṇḍa)—if it is argued that it is purposeless because its content is not new, we say no;
for it serves the purpose of illuminating the characteristics of the imposition and non-imposition of offenses, which are distinguished by their gravity and lightness. Herein...

For indeed, by the passage beginning, "If she should say, 'I have seen the venerable one sitting and engaging in sexual intercourse with a woman,' and he admits it, he is to be dealt with according to the offense...
[etc. ...he is to be dealt with for sitting," the characteristic of a formal charge (*āropanakamalakkaṇa*) regarding both heavy and light offenses is shown;
and by the term "he is to be dealt with" (*kāretabbo*), the characteristic of the non-charge (*anāropanakamalakkaṇa*) is also shown.

It has been shown. If it is argued that it should be listed either at the beginning or at the end for the purpose of illustrating the characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*), no; because that is impossible. How so?
First, it is not possible at the beginning, because those training rules (*sikkhāpada*) for which this is the characteristic have not yet been shown.
Nor is it possible at the end, because of the mixture with heavy [offenses]. Therefore, it deserves to be listed precisely in the middle of the heavy and light [rules].

Because they are mixed together. Whatever light offense is shown therein, that too is [included among] the heavy ones and so forth. For this very reason, it says: "by means of the secret delight known as the defilement dependent on sexual intercourse," and so on;
therefore, some say it was recited immediately after the heavy offenses. If this is so, one might ask:

"Is the first [recitation] not sufficient, since the definition is established by that much alone? What is the purpose of the second? No, because its purpose is to restrict the scope and to prevent the grasping of an incorrect condition.

Regarding the phrase, "In a concealed seat that is not suitable for action": because this characteristic is prescribed by way of restricting the location, it would be a misconception to think that it does not apply to a location contrary to that;
thus, the intention is that the second [qualification] is indeed purposeful for the sake of precluding such a misconception. Why?

Because it distinguishes the types of locations, demonstrates the distinctions of privacy, and demonstrates the distinctions of delighting in secluded sitting. This is so in the case of the restriction of the location.
Furthermore, a distinction arises from the pleasure derived from sitting in private.
There may also be a difference between the two training rules concerning sitting in private, because they illustrate a distinction regarding bodily contact.

For even in a place unfit for formal acts—whether it be uncovered or covered—if one sits there, bodily contact is established by the grasping of hair and so forth that have emerged through the windows, door-panels, or cracks.
These and other methods should also be understood in detail. Some say: "Because it follows the method established in the *Bhikkhu-pātimokkha*, this section is omitted in the *Bhikkhunī-pātimokkha*.
Others say: "It is because it did not arise there due to the specific occasion (*atthuppatti*).
That [second view] is incorrect, as it fails to demonstrate the manifold significance [of the rule]. For at all times during the dispensation of every Buddha, there are five [classes] of monks...

There are four recitations for the bhikkhunīs. Some say that this refers to the *saṅghādisesa* and *pācittiya* offenses specified therein because the formal proclamation of the recitation of the *Pātimokkha* is not common [to both orders].

For those bhikkhunīs, a specific form of bodily contact—by way of the "above-the-knee" rule (*ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalika*) and the eight bases (*aṭṭhavatthuka*)—is the basis for a *pārājika* offense: "If she should consent to the grasping of the hand, or the body for that purpose..."
From the words "one might consent," there is consent; from the words "one might stand together," there is standing;
from the words "one might go to an appointment," there is going; and from the words "one might enter a concealed place," there is entering a hidden location.
Likewise, [it refers to] if one were to stand together with, or converse with, another person in a concealed place at night in the dark without a lamp.
Their intention is that because of the statement “or,” even indecent speech (*duṭṭhullavācā*) constitutes an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*);
therefore, since it would result in those [offenses] being improperly included in the section on undetermined offenses (*aniyata-kaṇḍa*), they were not mentioned there.
The commentary on miscellaneous matters is concluded.
The Section on Indeterminate Offenses is finished.
4. The Section on Forfeiture. 1.
The Chapter on Robes.
1. Commentary on the First Kathina Training Rule 459. *Samitāvinā*:

One by whom the defilements have been stilled is a *samitāvī*; [the rule refers to] "by that *samitāvī*. Where "three robes" (*tīṇi cīvarāni*) should have been said, "the triple robe" (*ticīvara*) is used.
Here, the grammatical rule—that a numeral preceding a word ending in *u* or *e* takes the singular—is to be understood as the characteristic feature.

Furthermore, that name applies both to what has been determined and to what has not been determined. In such passages as, "If a bhikkhu should be separated from his three robes even for a single night," it refers to what has been determined by the determination of the three robes.
In the passage, "I allow you, bhikkhus, to determine the three robes," it refers to what has not been determined; here, however, both cases are possible.
In the passage, “The triple robe was authorized by the Blessed One for the bhikkhus,” it refers specifically to what has been formally resolved (*adhiṭṭhita*).

In the passage, “They enter the village with another triple robe,” it refers to what has not been formally resolved. For the formal resolution of a triple robe is effective only upon a single robe, and not upon the other [extra robes], as is the case with the formal resolution of a bowl;
therefore, the other [extra robes] remain in the state of being surplus. By that...
It was said: “How indeed can the group-of-six monks wear an extra robe? and so forth.
Regarding the first formulation here, it is stated that if one should wear an extra robe for even a single night, it constitutes an offense of expiation (nissaggiya);
beyond that, [the Buddha] declared: “Monks, I allow you to wear an extra robe for a maximum of ten days.”
"And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule thus: 'An extra robe may be kept for at most ten days;
for one who keeps it beyond that, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya). Thus the Blessed One established the training rule in its complete form.
Then, during the time of Ajātasattu, following his final enlightenment, the Kathina ceremony was authorized."
Starting from this point, the monks recite this training rule: “When a robe has been finished and the *kathina* has been suspended, for a monk...
[ten days] ...it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). This same method applies to the second and third *kathina* rules as well. Nevertheless, in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*, it is stated only thus:
“‘At most ten days’—this is the supplementary rule (*anupaññatti*) here. Therefore, “when the robe has been finished... [and so forth].
It is established that the statement, "by a bhikkhu when the kaṭhina has been removed," is neither an original rule (paññatti) nor a supplementary rule (anupaññatti).

For the section concerning the kaṭhina is not seen in the context of the original rule or the context of the supplementary rule; therefore, one must conclude here that the method already stated is the essential point.
Furthermore, it might be argued: "From the time of the arising of the kaṭhina, for the Blessed One..."
"The statement was spoken as being an *anupaññatti* (subsequent rule). If this were so, there would be two *anupaññattis*;

consequently, there would be a contradiction with the statement in the *Parivāra* that "there is one *anupaññatti*. Furthermore, for the purpose of illustrating the method already described, that statement was spoken here later rather than at the time of the first *paññatti*.
Because it has been established here, [it applies] subsequently to the second and third [rules].
It is stated thus among the "first promulgations" (paṭhamapaññatti) already mentioned. Otherwise, even there, that statement would have had to be made later.

However, in the *Anugaṇṭhipada*, it is said: "With reference to the fact that they were stated later, [the rules] such as 'when the robe has been finished' are subsequent promulgations" (*anupaññatti*).
Regarding "the affection of trainees and worldlings, the reverence of arahants": whether it be the tenth or the ninth.
The locative case is used in the sense of the ground (bhummatthe). 462–3.
Regarding the phrase "when the robe is finished" (*niṭṭhitacīvare*): this is stated solely for the purpose of indicating the mere absence of the obstacle (*palibodha*) regarding the robe;
therefore, it is said, "the robe is lost, or ruined, or burnt, or the expectation of a robe has been cut off. If...
It may have been stated for the purpose of showing that a robe should be kept for a maximum of ten days;
he [the monk] may keep one that has been lost or otherwise damaged. Here, "keeping" means either storing or using. Both of these apply whether the robe has been made up or not;

therefore, it should not be said that it must "have been made up. For it is not the case that an offense involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) occurs only when one exceeds the limit with something that has already been made up.

Therefore, regarding the robe with reference to which it is said, "when the robe is finished," one must not understand the meaning to be that it may be kept for a period of ten days at most once the kaṭhina has been removed.
For if that robe exists while the kaṭhina has been removed, no exemption is granted even for a single day. Moreover, "a robe" is defined as "the last [robe] that is subject to formal assignment."

It has been stated. And therein, it is said that [the robe] has been "made" (kata); therefore, it should be understood that this was not stated with reference to that [case], because it is impossible.
However, in the *Anugaṇṭhipada*, this is stated: "In that regard, it might be thought: 'If for that bhikkhu the robe has met with any one of the conditions such as being lost...'"
If there were [such a robe], what kind of robe would one be permitted to wear for a maximum of ten days?

Since there is no robe to be worn [in this case], the phrases beginning with “lost” (*naṭṭhaṃ*) and so forth are stated in order to show the restriction on its acquisition by way of its removal from the inventory.
This meaning, however, is that when none of the robes mentioned in the sequence beginning with “lost” is present...
It should be accepted; if one lets it exceed ten days, it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment (*nissaggiya*). This same principle applies everywhere.
When it is said, "it has been made," only a robe that has already been fashioned is intended. If one asks: why is it not explicitly stated that a "made" robe is intended in this context?
Because it is obvious. How so? Because there is no possibility of wearing robes that have been lost, destroyed, or otherwise ruined.

It is clear that only the robe made [of rags] is intended here. How so? Just as in the first *niyata* offense, because only sexual intercourse, physical contact, and sitting in private are mentioned, the "privacy" (*raho*) of the ear is stated by way of extracting the essential meaning; therefore, it was not said that "the privacy of the eye is intended in the other sense.
It should be understood that this case is exactly the same. Furthermore, the phrase "or it has been made" should not have been stated.

Why? Because even for one who lets the time for what has not been made pass, it is an offense of expiation (*nissaggiya*); although it is indeed an offense of expiation, here the intended meaning is the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) of the three robes.

Regarding that determination of the three robes, it is not permissible to determine what has not been made, what has not been dyed, or what has not been made fit by saying, "I determine this outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*)," and so forth.
To illustrate this point, it is said, "or it has been made. Otherwise, [the rule would be redundant].

If it is said, “When the robe has been finished and obtained,” how is it understood that, such being the case, the forfeiture offense (nissaggiya) applies to one who lets the three robes exceed ten days?

It is by the authority of the word. Because it was stated, “Monks, I allow you to determine (adhiṭṭhātuṃ) the three robes, but not to assign them to another (na vikappetuṃ),” it follows here as well that “extra robe-cloth is that which has not been determined.”

Only this much need be said. Because, by the statement "or it has been made," he permits that even the remainder [of cloth] other than the robe intended here may not be kept for more than ten days, he says:
"An extra robe (atirekacīvara) is one that is neither formally determined (anadhiṭṭhita) nor assigned to another (avikappita).
In this regard, it might be asked: just as "not assigned" (avikappita) is stated by way of defining the meaning...

It is stated thus, and likewise: “The last [allowance] is subject to alteration. Why? Because, by way of the subsequent rule beginning with “when the robe is finished,” only the three robes may be worn for a period of up to ten days.

Otherwise, even if one day is exceeded, it becomes an offense of forfeiture, according to the statement: “Whosoever, monk, should wear an extra robe, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.”
One may not keep any robe other than the three robes for more than ten days; beyond that, it is subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*), because it is stated [in the rule] as "within ten days.
As it is said: "There is no offense if one determines or designates [the robe] within ten days"; otherwise, the statement would have been merely "one determines [it] within ten days.
Therefore, the meaning should be understood according to the method explained in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
"Others say all this. Herein, as for the statement:

"If a robe has arisen within the *kathina* period, it should be kept for at most ten days"—this statement, which was spoken for the purpose of establishing that [position], contradicts both the subsequent discussion given right here and the reasoning already stated; therefore, it should not be accepted.

Right here, the discussion is stated as follows: "If one thinks, 'The Kathina suspension will take place tomorrow,' and does not formally determine (adhiṭṭheti) a robe-cloth that arose on that very day, it is an offense involving forfeiture (nissaggiya) at the rising of the dawn. Why?

Because the training rule (sikkhāpada) was stated with the words, 'When the robe-cloth is finished,' and so forth. Within the period of the Kathina, one receives the privilege [to keep it] even for more than ten days, because of the Kathina."

One does not obtain [the benefit] even for a single day beyond that. How so? Just as the Saṅgha, having performed the Kathina ceremony, obtains the benefit of the Kathina-removal (kathinubbhāra) from the day it was performed until its removal—even if there is only one day remaining—but does not obtain it on the following day.
If, through forgetfulness, the cloth to be distributed (bhājanīyacīvara) has not been distributed, then on the following day, even for those who have not performed the Kathina ceremony...
It is common property. If there are days remaining, it accrues to the Saṅgha for whom the kaṭhina has been spread;
likewise, from the day it was spread until its removal, it is permissible—whether not formally resolved upon or not assigned—as it falls within the period authorized.
The day of the kaṭhina ceremony is included in the count; from the day of its removal, any robe-cloth that arises must be kept for a maximum of ten days.
One obtains the exemption [from forfeiture] up to that point, but beyond that, one does not. Why? Because of the statement: "Monks, I allow you to keep an extra robe for a maximum of ten days.

Even within the period of the Kathina, the possibility of an offense involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) upon the rising of the sun on the eleventh day is prevented by this supplementary rule (*anupaññatti*): "When the robe is finished and the Kathina has been suspended. And it is not...
"They made it on that day or another day. Likewise, regarding the third *kathina* rule, it was deliberated upon by the Blessed One when he said:
"When a monk's robe is finished and the *kathina* has been removed, if an out-of-season robe (*akālacīvara*) should arise for that monk...
[He then added: "That which I previously permitted in the first training rule—'an extra robe may be kept for at most ten days'—[applies here as well]."
And by the statement, "That too arises only outside of the *kathina* month, not within it," it is demonstrated that [the robe] does not fall within the period.

Furthermore, from the statement, "'Even if given at the proper time, if it is assigned specifically, this is an out-of-season robe (*akālacīvara*)', it is demonstrated that after the suspension of the *kathina*, one does not receive the ten-day exemption;
however, along with those [other cases], one may again receive it for five days after the suspension of the *kathina*—this is the implication."

"Because it was stated—after defining the time of the arising of an out-of-season robe (akālacīvara)—that 'the robe must be finished... [and] must be made as quickly as possible,' it is thereby prohibited.

By both of these [rules], it is established that a robe which arises within the period of the kaṭhina is not permitted to remain [unused] for even a single day after the dismantling of the kaṭhina. Therefore, this is of two kinds.

It should be understood that we have stated this by way of investigation, thinking: "This must not be accepted, as it contradicts the investigation already set forth here and the reasoning already explained.
Here one might ask: "In the phrase 'when the robe is finished and the kaṭhina has been removed,' what is the basis for the locative case regarding the arising of the robe?"
Does it restrict the arising [of the robe], or does it restrict the wearing, or does it restrict both? What follows from this?
If it restricts the arising, then even if the Kathina has been suspended only in the last month of Kattika, a robe that arises [afterward] must be worn for ten days starting from that point;

thus, one incurs an offense even if that month has not yet ended. If, on the other hand, it restricts the wearing, then a robe that arises while the Kathina is still in place—even if it has been suspended—[must be worn for ten days].

"One may keep [it] for at most ten days"—this constitutes an offense. Now, if both [conditions] are restricted, should it not be stated with a specific qualification, as in the case of the third *kathina*?
It is replied: Granted, both are restricted, yet there is no purpose in a specific qualification.

That which was stated as "when the robe is finished" refers to the robe-material that arose while the *kathina* was still in place; it does not refer to that [robe-material arising after the *kathina* has been removed].
It is said, “it must be kept,” for this has already been established. Since the phrase “or it has been made” and so forth establishes that meaning, there is no further purpose in the qualification;
for one does not make something forfeitable merely by making it, nor is it possible to keep what has been lost and so on.
Or rather, whatever was the intention with which the Blessed One laid down this training rule, that is the intended meaning.
It should be understood that [the robe] is explained in the third *kathina* rule. Why is it explained there? Because of the intention to show a specific provision.
For the specific provision is expressed by the words, "But if there is no completion," and so forth.

Furthermore, by not saying "a robe might arise" but rather using the qualification "an out-of-season robe (*akālacīvara*) might arise," it indicates that even when the *kathina* has been dismantled, a robe for the proper season (*kālacīvara*) may still exist.

What is this? It is robe-cloth obtained in the month of Kattika during the last [period]. For that very reason, it is stated there: "obtained in the eleventh month when the kaṭhina has not been spread.
Therefore, the absence of the faults mentioned regarding the restriction of the time of acquisition is established. Furthermore, as for what is stated there:

"Even if given at the proper time, if it is given specifically [for oneself], this is called 'out-of-season robe-cloth' (akālacīvara)," there are two alternative interpretations of its meaning. According to the interpretation based on specific designation (ādesa):...

Regarding the term "out-of-season robe" (*akālacīvara*): even though it has received that designation, because it arose at a [permitted] time, it receives the exemption of being considered a "seasonal" robe;
how much more so, then, when it is not designated as such? This first alternative merely reinforces the absence of the fault mentioned in the rule regarding the determination of its origin.

Likewise, a robe that has reached the status of an "out-of-season robe" by way of designation, because it arose during the robe season, receives the exemption of ten days from the end of the robe season.
"He does not obtain it, let alone designate it"—this second [statement] merely supports the absence of the fault mentioned in the rule for the storage [of robes]. If this is so, one might ask:
"What is the purpose of the 'out-of-season robe' (akālacīvara) being designated as such by way of designation?

It should be understood that its purpose is to ensure that it remains common property even for the Saṅgha of monks who have already performed the Kathina ceremony, provided they are designated by the Saṅgha.
Furthermore, for an individual, even the days [of the Kathina period] are simply days.

Thus, because it does not fall within the reckoning [of the period], and because it is not subject to forfeiture due to its dependence on the expression "when the Kathina has been dismantled" by virtue of obtaining what is designated as out-of-season robe-cloth, and because it conforms to that [rule], it is said: "and also of seasonable robe-cloth.
In this way, it should be understood that there are four kinds of statements here in every respect. Moreover, there is a certain dismantling of the Kathina by a particular person.
When the *kathina* has been dismantled, a certain monk receives a robe at a time when it is the proper season for robes, while another receives one when it is not the proper season.

That [robe] belongs to him once he has crossed the boundary; it has not yet entered the state of being "dismantled" (*ubbhāra*). Excluding those two cases where it arises when the *kathina* has been dismantled, it should be understood that in all other instances it arises when the *kathina* has been dismantled.
For indeed, for the one for whom it was dismantled, it is a robe received outside the proper season.
For another, it is out-of-season robe-cloth (*akālacīvara*). Likewise, there is that which arises when the kaṭhina has been suspended by some means of suspension;
for everyone in that case, it is indeed out-of-season robe-cloth. That should be understood as it was laid down.

Likewise, there is that which arises after the kaṭhina has been suspended, excluding what arises during the last month of the rainy season. Likewise, there is that which arises [after the kaṭhina has been suspended]...
An out-of-season robe-cloth (*akālacīvara*) that arises during the *kathina* period should be understood as having arisen either in the winter or the summer.

Thus, because there are many varieties according to the distinction between the individual and the time, it should be understood that when [a robe] has arisen, it is not stated [in the rule] as "arisen when the *kathina* has been dismantled" (*ubbhatasmiṃ kathine*).
To show this alternative meaning (*atthavikappa*), because it is not one-sided (*anekamsikattā*), [the text says]: "When the *kathina* has been dismantled for the monk..."
"The kaṭhina has been dismantled. Although this much suffices for the point to be established, the phrase "one of the eight headings" and so forth is stated [to provide detail].
It should be said that the words "I maintain" appear in the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga. By the word "thus," it is meant that there is no difference in the wording there.
The phrase “the last is that which reaches the point of assignment” (vikappanupaga) is stated as a comprehensive inclusion of all [robes].

The phrase “the last is that which reaches the point of determination” (adhiṭṭhānupaga), however, is not a comprehensive inclusion. For it is not the case that whatever portion of the outer cloak (saṅghāṭi) is the last to reach the point of determination, that same portion of the inner robe (antaravāsaka) and so forth is the last to reach the point of determination, because determination is of many kinds. There is no such division for assignment.

Its "single state" (ekavidhattā) should be understood as follows: excluding the last [instance], the meaning should be understood as "it becomes an offense involving forfeiture (nissaggiya) upon the rising of the sun on the eleventh [day] from that point. The "last" refers to the first dawn of the following Kattika month;
for that does not constitute an offense involving forfeiture by virtue of the time. For this very reason, it was said in the commentary on the Accekacīvara-sikkhāpada:
“However, from the sixth day onwards, even a robe that has arisen which was not designated as urgent, as well as a robe that has been set aside, indeed receives this same exemption.
It is with reference to this very principle that it is said:
“For a robe designated as urgent, when the Kathina has not been spread, there is one month plus eleven days; when the Kathina has been spread, there are five months plus eleven days; beyond that...”

"But there is no exemption even for a single day," he said right there. When this principle is established, it follows as a matter of course that one does not obtain a non-urgent robe after twelve days have passed.

From that, it is established that in the rule "there is no offense if one perceives a non-urgent robe as a non-urgent robe," the term refers to something other than an urgent robe that is similar to one, provided it has not been formally determined (adhiṭṭhita). In that regard:

However, the phrase "five months" is a statement of the maximum limit. It should be understood that once a rain-cloth (*vassikasāṭikā*) has reached the status of a non-seasonal cloth (*avassikasāṭikā*), it receives dispensation for eleven months.

Regarding the rule "that which exceeds ten days is an offense involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*)," there is a distinction in the wording for emerging from the offense, such as: "concealed for ten days," "concealed for more than a half-month," "concealed for more than a month," and so forth.
Just as there is no difference in the wording here, so too, even that which exceeds a year is said to exceed ten days;

likewise, in the case of the second *kathina*, even staying away for a year is said to be staying away for a night. In the third case, it should be understood that even exceeding a year is said to be exceeding a month.
"If one perceives [the robe] as determined when it is not determined, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*)."
This is the illustration of the initial phrase for one triad-offense of *pācittiya*. This same method applies to [the terms] "unauthorized" (*avikappita*) and so forth;
therefore, having explained one in detail among the eight triad-breaks here, one should explain the initial phrase for each of the others.
Since two [triads] have been condensed by the Blessed One himself, even though many triad-breaks are possible, only one is stated: "This..."

They say, "This is the nature of the Vinaya. Regarding the sections on offenses of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*), however, one *dukkaṭa* is explained in detail, while the remaining seven are likewise abbreviated.
In the same way, each successive final section should be understood as a category of non-offense (*anāpatti*).
The phrase "there is no offense within ten days" has this concise meaning: that [extra robe] may be kept for a maximum of ten days. That is the extra robe (*atirekacīvara*).
If one resolves, designates, or relinquishes it within ten days according to one's own determination;
or if, by its very nature, it is lost, destroyed, burnt, or another person takes it away by force or takes it with confidence;
there is no offense regarding the *pācittiya*. However, regarding the *dukkaṭa*, there may be an offense or there may be no offense, depending on whether there was a change in perception.
Furthermore, regarding the last [offense] here, by way of two phrases, it should be understood that the two triplets of *pācittiya* offenses— namely,
"perceiving as cut what is not cut" (*anacchinne acchinnasaññī*) and "perceiving as trusted what is not trusted" (*avissāsaggāhe vissāsaggāhasaññī*)—
as well as the two *dukkaṭa* offenses, are condensed. For in this context, if one formally determines [the robe] within ten days, it remains for at most ten days.
It should be understood that he resolves [the robe] during the portion of the day after dawn has passed. This, first of all, is the determination according to the Pāḷi.
However, in the Aṭṭhakathā, regarding the passage beginning with "heavier than this," there is this determination preceded by an objection:

"In the Gaṇṭhipada, however, even though it is heavier than the giving away of the robe from here, they perform the formal act consisting of a motion and a second proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*) just as they do by means of a mere announcement (*apalokana*)."
Thus, although this [formal act] is to be performed by means of a motion (*ñatti*), it is also permissible to do so by means of a formal statement (*pakativacana*).

If this were so, it would contradict what is stated in the commentary on the *Kammavagga* of the *Parivāra*: “Even a formal act consisting of a motion (*ñattikamma*) must be performed by establishing only a single motion;
it should not be performed by way of a formal act consisting of obtaining permission (*apalokanakamma*), etc. Therefore, it is said: “This is in conformity with those [other acts].”

Therefore, that was stated according to the direct order (*anulomanaya*). However, we say that the rule is such that just as the *pārisuddhi-uposatha* for two people occurs without a formal motion (*ñatti*), so too does the giving of a robe relinquished by two people;
therefore, it is permissible to say, "We give to the Venerable One. How, then, is this to be known?
Because it conforms to that [rule]. This formal act of motion (*ñattikamma*) is indeed one and the same.

The Teacher [Vajirabuddhi] states that it should be understood as a "means of accomplishment" (sādhana) because it is permissible to perform [the formal act] even by means of a mere motion (apalokana). However, in the *Anugaṇṭhipada*, having raised an objection here, it is stated:
"This has been established. A formal act consisting of a motion (ñattikamma) must be performed by setting forth only one motion.
This was said with reference to what is found in the Canon (pāḷi); however, this particular point is not actually found in the Canon, but was stated by bringing it forward through implication (lesa).
"This is permissible even by means of a formal announcement.
This is the method: when other robes have been eaten by termites and so forth, one says, "Mine too have been eaten," and so on.

Because of the statement, "That which was made by another... [is] a maker," it is established that a third *kathina* robe—being of the same kind and of the same purpose as the first—is identical to the first.
469. Regarding the phrase “to determine the three robes” (*ticīvaraṃ adhiṭṭhātun*): here, the “three robes” refers to those suitable to be determined by means of the determination of the three robes;
or rather, I authorize that which may be determined as the three robes and not assigned to another.

Because there is no limit to the time for such determination, I authorize that one who desires them at all times should determine them precisely; however, having fixed a time limit, one may assign them [to another].
I do not permit it. However, when there is a requisite, it is allowable to relinquish it and then make a formal assignment (vikappa) at any time;
this is established by the statement, "There is no offense if one determines [the robe] within ten days or assigns it," as has been said.

As for the rain-cloak (vassikasāṭikā), after that period, one may only assign it and not determine it. For a cloth that has been finished is, within four months, on the day of the commencement of the rains—
The meaning is: "I authorize [you] to determine [the robe] within ten days starting from the beginning;

I authorize you to assign it [to another] if you wish to keep it as your own possession after four months have passed. Regarding "less than the Sugata’s robe," this is the maximum limit for all three robes.
However, in the argument stating, "It is permissible to determine a requisites-cloth as a triple-robe (ticīvara),"...

It is permissible provided there is such a requisite condition. Just as it has been established that it is permissible to designate [an item] when a condition exists, it goes without saying that it is permissible to resolve upon it by means of another resolution.

Since it is stated without specific restriction that "one resolves or designates within ten days," this applies equally to both those robes that have been resolved upon—namely, the outer cloak (*saṅghāṭi*), the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*), and the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*)—and those that have not yet been resolved upon.

[This refers to] the name. For in such cases as "this is the *saṅghāṭī*," it is stated as being unformalized (*anadhiṭṭhita*). In the passage "one might be separated from the three robes" (*ticīvarena vippavaseyya*), it is stated as being formalized (*adhiṭṭhita*).
Regarding the phrase "in a neighboring monastery" (*sāmantavihāre*), the Elder Dhammasiri says it means "in a monastery [near] the alms-village.
The Teacher says it can indeed be obtained even in one further away. In the *Anugaṇṭhipada* as well, it says: "'In a neighboring monastery' is merely the heading of the teaching..."
Therefore, it is said: "Having observed a designated spot, one should determine [the robe] even if it is standing at a distance.
A "neighboring monastery" (*sāmantavihāra*) is one where it is possible to go and return on that very same day.

For one who wishes to avoid being separated from the robe overnight, it is not permitted to determine [the robe] as being at a distance from there; for thus it is stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*. Some say: "In the *Cīvaravaṃsa*..."

They say: "If another person, having moved it, places it on a peg, then even for one who makes a formal determination (adhiṭṭhāti) without knowing that [the robe has been moved], the determination succeeds because the robe has been clearly identified.

Regarding the phrase "having made a determination," this refers to [determining] it as a requisite cloth (parikkhāracola) and so forth. The passage beginning with "only larger" and so forth describes the characteristics common to all formal determinations.
In that context, the phrase "must again be determined" refers to a robe that has already been determined.
Because it constitutes a single part. If it is not resolved (*anadhiṭṭhita*), then by virtue of its being a part of that which is resolved, it enters into the category of the resolved.
Likewise, if it is resolved, by virtue of its being a part of that which is not resolved, it enters into the category of the non-resolved;
such is the characteristic. And herein, it is not only the second layer (*paṭṭa*) [that is meant], but also the third layer and so forth. As it has been said:
“I allow... [as before] ...a saṅghāṭi robe made of four folds from cloth that has been removed during the season... [as before] ...as much as needed of rag-robes.
“The remaining monks” refers to the monks who were seated at the time when this will be spoken. Therefore, it is permissible;
just as it was said, “Monks, I allow you to determine the three robes, but not to assign them,” so too is the requisite cloth.
It has been stated, but neither an upper limit nor a numerical limit for that has been specified;
therefore, the meaning is that it is permissible to relinquish even all three robes and, having determined them with the words, “I determine these robes as requisites-cloths,” to use them.
If it is asked, “How is it known that ‘this is the opening for a hoard’? [it is because] by that...

Furthermore, on that occasion, when the monks possessed a complete set of the three robes (ticīvara) and there was a need for water-strainers (parissāvana) and bags (thavikā), it was permitted by the statement: "Monks, I allow requisites-cloth (parikkhāracoḷa).
Since there is no prohibition against monks having only one water-strainer or bag, rather than two or three, [the allowance stands].
It is established that requisites such as water-strainers, whether they are of the last permissible size for alteration or exceed that size, are allowable.

If it is argued that this contradicts the statement, "What if I were to establish a boundary and set a limit for the robes of the bhikkhus?", the answer is no, because of a failure to understand the context and because of the contradiction itself. What has been said?
Is it so? In the *Cīvarakkhandhaka*, first the householder’s robe was permitted; thereafter, the *pāvāra*, silk, *kojava*, woolen blankets, and so forth.
Then, at that time, various kinds of robes had arisen for the Saṅgha.
Thereupon, the thought occurred to the bhikkhus: “What kind of robe has been permitted by the Blessed One, and what has not been permitted?”
In this matter, by the words beginning with, “Monks, I allow six kinds of robes: linen,” etc., the types of allowable robes were authorized;

however, no specific number or measure was prescribed. Then, [the Blessed One] saw many monks burdened by their robes—having made a cushion of robes on their heads, having made a cushion of robes on their shoulders, and having made a cushion of robes on their hips.
As they were returning, having seen them, it occurred to the Blessed One:
“…Even those sons of good family who are sensitive to cold and afraid of cold in this Dhamma and Discipline are able to subsist with the three robes.
What if I were to establish a boundary for the robes of the monks, set a limit, and allow the three robes? Thus the robe was allowed.
And yet, that was only one. However, the group of six (Chabbaggiyā) took it up wrongly and kept many of them.
Those [robes] remained in their possession beyond the permitted limit. Therefore, it was authorized: "Monks, I allow you to keep an extra robe for a maximum of ten days.
From this it is understood that they were keeping many extra robes.

By saying, "I allow you to keep them for no more than ten days, not just that one alone," he has shown—even while there is a boundary established and a limit set for robes known as the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) of the three robes—the method for avoiding an excess of the three robes by way of a daily restriction.
Beyond that, [he says]: "Monks, I allow an extra robe."
By permitting [the robe] "to be determined" (*vikappetuṃ*), the procedure for keeping an extra robe even without a fixed limit of days is shown;
thus, it is established that these two are also modes of storage (*nidhānamukha*). Likewise, there may be the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) of requisites-cloth (*parikkhāracoḷa*);

otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the permission for the determination of other robes, due to the contradiction with the establishment of the boundary limits (*sīmāmariyāda*). It is precisely the laying down of the rule for the determination of the three robes (*ticīvara*) [that is intended].

The triple robe is the noble standard. Therefore it is said: "This is a separate mode of storage. It is further stated: "First, the triple robe must be formally determined (adhiṭṭhātabba) by means of the determination for the triple robe;
if one is unable to carry it about, one must relinquish it (paccuddharitvā) and determine it as a requisite cloth (parikkhāracoḷa).
However, this was not said from the very beginning [regarding the requisites]. "Just as the triple robe is to be carried about..."

Permission for a sick person who is unable [to remain] to live apart from their robes was authorized; for one who is not sick, the placing of them within a house was authorized under the rule concerning suspicious circumstances;
furthermore, when there is a valid reason, living apart for six nights was authorized; for one who is unable even after that, relinquishment was authorized;
and even when relinquished, it was authorized to determine [the robe] within ten days, and for one who is unable even to do that, the act of assigning [the robe to another] was authorized.

"In the same way, since both [types of] designations—whether in the presence of another or in their absence—involve the property of another, it might be that the Blessed One permitted its use after resolving upon it as 'requisite-cloth' (*parikkhāra-coḷa*) in the absence of a formal designation;
for it is with this intention that those who know the meaning say so," thus it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*. "In the past," and so forth, refers to "the separate mode of storage."
This was stated for the purpose of showing the application (*payoga*) of what has been said. Regarding the phrase "difficult to maintain within an unbounded boundary" (*abaddhasīmāyaṃ dupparihāraṃ*):
it is because it is possible to go beyond the vicinity (*upacāra*) even for the sake of making a formal assignment (*vikappanā*) and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "the rain-cloak is not of excessive measure": this was stated because the maximum limit for its size has been specified. This also applies to a bed-covering (*paccattharaṇa*).

“Only that which is to be formally resolved upon (adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ) [is valid]”: the meaning is that what is given with words such as, “Venerable sir, this must be spread over our lodging,” should not be resolved upon;
rather, only that which is given with the words, “This is for you,” and is intended by oneself, should be resolved upon.
“Once resolved upon, it remains resolved upon; it is not relinquished again because there is no limit of time.”

It is written: "Others say it is also permissible with a single statement. Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of medicine, robes, parents, and so forth," one who sets aside [the funds] thinking, "By means of this I will purchase medicine;
I will give this to my mother," must perform the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
Others say, "There is no need for the act of formal determination for one who distinguishes them by saying, 'This is for medicine; this is for my mother.'"
It was said: "This was written with reference to the laying down [of the robe] after releasing its own nature.
It was further stated: "'It must be resolved upon again'—this is the tradition of the Aṭṭhakathā (Commentary) as it has come down from the Saṅgīti;
beyond that are the various reasoned investigations of the teachers on this point. "Of a robe of standard measure" means of the lower (pacchima) measure. Two...
"Robes" means together with the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*). "This method" refers to the same principle as "wherever [the measurement] is suitable," and so forth.
Because of the statement, "For one who exceeds that, it is subject to cutting off," exceeding it is prohibited;
since it is not prohibited below that limit, it is permissible. Herein, it might be argued: "The minimum measurement for the triple robe is not found separately in the Sutta. This should not be said.
Because they are accomplished through the trainings that ought to be practiced. What is meant by this? It should be said:

"From the statements, 'I shall wear my lower robe evenly all around,' 'I shall put on my upper robe,' and 'I shall go well-covered within an inhabited area,' it must be understood that to whatever extent 'evenness all around' and 'being well-covered' are achieved according to the sequence explained in the Aṭṭhakathā, [the training is fulfilled] by means of those. By way of these:
The "final measure" is established; and that indeed is said to be exactly as previously stated, such as the five-fist measure and so forth. For this very reason he says:
"Apart from a mere hint (lesa), there is nothing separate in the Sutta.
Furthermore, the meaning here is: "Even if it were intended [there], it would still not coincide"; therefore, the connection with the words "if" (yadi) and so forth is certain.
It is said: "Because it is delimited and it accords. However, in the case of the other [robes], according to some teachers' views, there is no delimitation;

according to others, it does not accord with what precedes and follows—this is the connection. A formal resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna*) is indeed a formal resolve; however, at the time of use, that which has not been resolved is not permitted.
All of this applies only to the three robes (*ticīvara*). Now, regarding this training rule (*sikkhāpada*), this...

The brief analysis: With reference to robes that arise from the first day of the winter season when the *kaṭhina* has not been spread, and from the first day of the summer season when the *kaṭhina* has been spread, it is stated, “when the robe is finished,” and so forth.
Here it is asked: “Even for one who has had dyers wash [the cloth] and have it made white, the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) is indeed a formal determination.”
Is it not the case that, according to the words [of the Vinaya], even when one has not dyed [the robe], the determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) takes effect;
and therefore, after performing the needlework, dyeing it, and applying the *kappa-bindu*, there should be no rule that it must be determined? It is said:

it must indeed be done, for it is determined just like a bowl (*patta*). Just as a bowl, once determined, does not lose its determination whether it returns to a white state or a copper-colored state, nor is it otherwise.
One approaches the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*), thinking, "It should be viewed in this way.
They say: "From the moment that using [the robe] and so forth becomes permissible, from that point onward it must be determined within ten days.
Since the statement was made without qualification, one determines what is to be determined and assigns what is to be assigned; thus it is said.
Having made this distinction, the statement "one should not assign it" appears as if it were contradictory [to the previous rule].
Now, this section of the Khandhaka and Parivāra, which is connected to the methods of formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) and assignment (*vikappana*), is spoken of as miscellaneous (*pakiṇṇaka*).
First, in the Khandhaka: "Monks, I allow you to formally determine the three robes (*ticīvara*), but not to assign them; [I allow] the rainy-season robe (*vassikasāṭika*)."
It is stated: "One may determine [the robes] for the four months of the rains, but beyond that, one must assign them. Furthermore, in the *Parivāra*, it is said many times:
"Nine robes are not to be determined; nine robes are not to be assigned"; and "In a set of ten, ten robes are to be determined;
in a set of eleven, eleven robes are to be determined; they are not to be assigned."
By means of a formal declaration (*vacana*), it is stated that "all robes must be formally determined (*adhiṭṭhātabba*) and must not be assigned to another (*vikappetabba*).
Therefore, these two [statements] appear to be contradictory; however, in the Khandhaka itself, it is stated:
"The rainy-season robe (*vassikasāṭikā*) may be determined for the four months of the rains, and after that, it may be assigned. Regarding this, in its commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*):

It is stated: “A rain-season robe (*vassikasāṭikā*) that is not of excessive size must be formally determined (*adhiṭṭhātabba*) for the four months of the rains after taking its name according to the method already described;
beyond that, it must be relinquished (*paccuddharitvā*) and then assigned (*vikappetabba*) to another.
However, this appears somewhat contradictory, because mutual relinquishment is possible during the winter, whereas assignment is impossible during the rainy season.

Furthermore, here, based on the authority of the statement, “There is no offense if one determines or designates [the robe] within ten days,” it should be understood that designation is not prohibited in all cases;
thus, the commentary’s statement appears to be in contradiction with the words of the Parivāra.
Indeed, the Tathāgatas do not speak what is contradictory; therefore, in this matter, the method of the commentary is the recourse.
By this, all of it becomes of a single flavor. And in the *Parivāra-aṭṭhakathā* it is said:
"They should not be assigned means that from the time they have been determined, they should not be assigned.

The meaning is that from the time the three robes have been determined, the rain-cloak (*vassikasāṭikā*) and so forth should not be assigned against one's will within their respective spheres of determination.
The remainder of the text and its meaning have been stated here in the commentary; therefore, all of this is of one flavor. Here it is asked:
"If that is so, then it should be said, 'Nine robes are not to be determined.
For from the time they are assigned [to another], they are indeed not to be determined. To this it is replied: "The triple robe is to be determined, not assigned... [and so on]."

Regarding the statement, "One may determine [the robe] as a requisite cloth, but one must not assign it [to another]," it should be understood that nine robes are to be determined and must not be assigned. This is because, in all such cases, the prohibition of determination is shown, while no assignment is mentioned;
furthermore, the limit is shown by the phrase "beyond that" only in two instances. Another method: [The Buddha said,] "I allow..."
Monks, they are unwilling to determine their three robes. Why? Because for one who does not determine what has arisen during the proper season, an offense arises upon the lapse of that season;
and for one who does not determine what has arisen outside the proper season, an offense arises upon the lapse of ten days.
In this regard, that which has arisen during the proper season—even if it is insufficient—causes an offense when the ten-day period lapses; [this is the case] at the time of relinquishment.
“Venerable sir, this extra robe which has been worn by me is to be forfeited; I relinquish it to the Saṅgha,” and so forth—thus it should be forfeited.
The other [cases] are exactly as in the text. Therein, the first method is stated by way of the first formal rule: “Whosoever, monk, should wear an extra robe, it is to be forfeited”;
the second is stated by way of the subsequent supplementary rule.

And it should be understood that this case is to be treated in the same way: just as when the object to be relinquished is absent, one should confess only the offense without reciting the formal text (*yathāpāḷi*);
and just as in the relinquishment of a *vassikasāṭika* robe, one should relinquish it according to what is possible without reciting the formal text upon the mere thought of seeking it;
