so too should this be understood. As with an extra robe (*atirekacīvara*) that has exceeded the [one-year] period...

It is simply called "exceeded by ten days. Some say that the three robes separated for a year, those exceeded by a month, and those separated for six nights are called "separated for one night" and "separated for six nights" respectively;
likewise, this too is simply called "exceeded by ten days. Therefore, it is established that:
"I allow you, monks, to determine the three robes even when you do not wish to [be separated from them]."
Likewise, the meaning is that one should not designate [the robe] unwillingly. For when there is a desire, it is said, "I allow you to designate it," because the words state:
"Having relinquished it, an opportunity for designation is granted for the sake of the comfort of being apart from it, and there is no offense upon the lapse of ten days.
Similarly, one should not resolve upon a *vassikasāṭikā* (rainy-season robe) unwillingly, because an offense arises upon the lapse of ten days.
If it is asked, "For how long? [the answer is: for four months of the rainy season; however, when there is a need, one may assign it even beyond that. For it has been said:
"In all cases, it should be understood that assigning [an object] is not prohibited. And it has also been said:
"There is an offense in winter, but not in summer, nor in the rains. Therefore, it is stated in the Commentary: "Beyond that..."
“Having relinquished it, it should be assigned.
Herein, this is the investigation: when should it be relinquished? When should it be assigned? For it is said here, “after that [time]”;
and since during the winter, as soon as the bowl is received, that formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna) is lost, therefore it says, “having relinquished.”

It should not be said that [the formal act] is invalid because of the absence of a formal resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*); however, it should not be said that "it must be formally assigned within the four-month period," for it is stated:
"One may assign it after that. On this point, some say: "This must indeed be said.
Just as one who has completed his probation (*parivāsa*) and performed the penance (*mānatta*), even though the days of probation and penance have already concluded, so too [is it here].
Some say that even when the days for the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) have concluded, this [robe] remains formally determined (*sādhiṭṭhāna*).

However, this is the definitive conclusion of the masters of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathācariya*): "Having relinquished it on the full-moon day of Kattika, it should be formally assigned on the first day of the waxing moon (*pāṭipada*).
For this is stated in the *Parivāra-aṭṭhakathā*: "Having formally assigned it on the first day of the waxing moon following the full-moon day of Kattika..."
If one wears a rain-cloak (*vassikasāṭikā*) that has been set aside [for the rainy season], one incurs an offense in the winter. However, in the *Kurundi*, it is stated:
"If one does not formally relinquish it on the full-moon day of the month of Kattika and wears it in the winter, one incurs an offense"; this too is well-said. For it is said:
"One may resolve upon it for four months, and beyond that, one may assign it [to another]. In this regard, the method of the *Kurundi* is to be regarded as authoritative because it was stated later.
The latter [definition] is to be accepted, not the former. For one who wears [the robe] even during the summer inevitably incurs an offense within less than half a month.
Furthermore, the meaning of the *Kurundi* commentary is seen here as follows: "It is stated that an offense is incurred in winter, but not in summer.

[This refers to the case where] on the full moon day of Kattika, having failed to relinquish [the robe] and failing to assign it for use on that very day, one does so on the first day of the following month.

Some state the reason as follows: "One incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) because of not formally relinquishing (*apaccuddhāra*), but not because of not designating (*avikappana*), since it is possible for there to be a period of ten days [of non-designation].
If that were so, it would follow that during the winter, the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) is lost by merely holding the bowl;
and that is incorrect. For the formal determination is [lost] by these nine reasons: "by giving it to another... [and so on] ...by its being broken."

It is stated that [the formal act] is relinquished, and not "by crossing the boundary of the designated field. If it is argued that this was not stated because it is not common [to all robes], we say no;

for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to say "[it is relinquished] by way of being torn," whereas in all the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), the relinquishment of the formal act is stated specifically for the three robes (*ticīvara*) by way of their being torn. Therefore, on the first day of winter, due to the cause of not having formally relinquished [the robe],...
One incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense, not because of the failure to relinquish and transfer [the robe], but because of the failure to transfer it.
From the statement "one should transfer," it is understood that the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) does not lapse from that point.

For the intention is not that one incurs the offense in the winter by failing to transfer it on the first day of the month following the full moon of the Kattika festival; rather, it is because of the failure to relinquish it.
An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is incurred at the very moment of the first dawn of the winter season; therefore, it is said:
"without having formally relinquished [the robe] on the full-moon day of Kattika. However, once it has been relinquished, one receives the privilege of keeping it for ten days during the winter.
For it is said: "If the ten-day period is not sufficient, one must not let the robe-season pass," provided that [the robe] has arisen at the proper time.
Not at an improper time. And so it has been established: that which has not been relinquished does not become subject to forfeiture, provided it has not been worn;
therefore, it is proven that both the relinquishing and the formal assignment (vikappana) must be performed on the full-moon day of the month of Kattika.
And herein, just as one who assigns an extra robe must wear it for a maximum of ten days, so too [is it here].

It should be understood that within ten days it is "formally assigned" (*vikappita*); likewise, on the full moon of Kattika, by one who formally assigns it, it is both "determined" (*adhiṭṭhita*) for the four months of the rains, and thereafter, only within the sphere where there is no offense, does the formal assignment take place.
To this extent, it is illustrated that there is determination within the sphere of formal assignment, and formal assignment within the sphere of determination.

It exists. Otherwise, two pairs of dyads would have to be stated among the dyads [beginning with]: "There is an offense committed by means of formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna), there is an offense committed by means of non-determination; there is an offense committed by means of assignment (vikappanā), there is an offense committed by means of non-assignment.
In that regard, the first term of the first dyad is possible, for in the case of the rain-cloak (vassikasāṭikā) and so forth in the field of assignment...
By means of non-determination (*an-adhiṭṭhāna*), one incurs the offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for transgressing the discipline.

By this very [statement], the second phrase regarding the second wrong-doing has been stated. There is no such thing as "incurring [the offense] by means of determination" (*adhiṭṭhāna*), because there is no offense within ten days and because [the offense] can arise through formal assignment (*vikappanā*) and so forth.
Nor is there [an offense] incurred by means of assignment, since assignment is not prohibited in all cases; therefore, those [offenses]...

The pairs [of offenses] are not stated as "not obtainable. Here it is said: That offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) which was established on the authority of the statement, "One falls into an offense during the winter," is appropriate for one who intentionally fails to relinquish it; however, if it is due to forgetfulness, there is no offense for anyone.
For one who intentionally does not make a formal assignment (*avikappana*) of what was relinquished on the full moon day of the month of Kattika, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
On the following day, however, it becomes subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*); and for one who fails to assign it [to another], it remains subject to forfeiture here under the first rule.

As for what was stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*: "The rainy-season robe (*vassikasāṭikā*) loses its formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) even by the passing of the months of the rains, and the itch-covering cloth (*kaṇḍupaṭicchādi*) likewise loses it when the illness has subsided;
therefore, after that time, it must be assigned [to another]," by this [it is meant]:
It is contradictory; not only this, but it also contradicts the commentarial statement: “After that, having relinquished it, it should be assigned.

For “after that” refers to the winter season (*hemanta*); if there were a relinquishment during that time, then such statements as “the rain-cloak [is valid] even after the lapse of the rainy months” would be untenable, because there would be no relinquishment due to the absence of a formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*). And non-contradiction must be maintained; therefore, “relinquishment...”
If it is argued that the expression “merely a formal act” (*vattamatta*) is possible here as well, we say no, because it contradicts the statement in the *Kurundi*.

For in that [text], the relinquishment (*paccuddhāra*) is stated to take place on the full moon day of Kattika; therefore, since it is a day within the rainy season, the relinquishment is performed together with the formal resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*) at its conclusion.
Thus, the relinquishment is not merely a formal act. Consequently, the phrase “after that” must be intended to refer up until the full moon day. Just as...

Furthermore, this alternative view—that even "by the passing of the rainy-season month" or "by the subsiding of an illness" might have been stated here because [the robe] must necessarily be relinquished—is consistent with the fact that those points are not mentioned in the *Samantapāsādikā*.
Otherwise, they would have had to be mentioned here as well; therefore, the procedure exactly as previously stated is what is possible in this case.
Although it is possible [to assign it for a longer period], it was stated for the sake of making it easy to understand for people who are difficult to inform.

Since that [assignment] loses its fixed determination after the passing of the rains, and since an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is established on account of not having relinquished it by the first dawn of the winter season, therefore, one should relinquish and assign it specifically on the full-moon day of Kattika; for if it is not so assigned, [the offense remains].

“It should be stated: ‘It is indeed the occurrence of an offense involving forfeiture. Even at this point, one should not stop short, but rather seek a definitive explanation. And in this regard, there is [the following]:
‘Thus the Pāḷi of the Vinaya shows the non-existence [of the offense];
its meaning is consistent whether it is split or unsplit.’”
"One who desires to understand should seek out those who understand that meaning within the Vinaya.
When it is said, "Take it for yourself," it is well-given even without the words, "I take it for myself. The other...
If he accepts it, then it is well-grasped; if he does not accept it, then it is well-given by the giver. However, that object belongs to no one.

Likewise, if one says, "I take this for myself," and the owner consents, it is well-grasped even without the words "take it. If he does not consent, it remains the property of the owner alone, for it does not belong to him [the taker].
Regarding "an act of the Vinaya" (*vinayakamma*): if one takes it for the purpose of performing a formal act of the Vinaya, it is not permitted.
Nor is it permitted if, having taken it for one's own sake, one gives it back to that same person.

However, if one does so without expectation, having relinquished it to another, and then uses what was given back by that person—or uses it while placing trust in them—it is permitted. In that case as well, it is by way of a formal act of the Vinaya.
Some say it is not permissible. They themselves, regarding the phrase "he makes it large or small," state:
"In the case of the three robes, he cuts them so that they do not exceed one span in length, and he does the same for the others.

In such instances, having thoroughly understood the method of explanation of the ancient teachers through close attendance upon their lineage of teachers, and having reconciled [the matter] with that, [one should proceed].
One should speak mindfully and with clear comprehension, without confusing the minds of the listeners. This is our request.
The commentary on the first *kaṭhina* training rule is finished.
2. Commentary on the *udositaka* training rule.
471. They set out on tour through the countryside wearing only their inner robes (*santaruttara*). Why? Although it was stated first:
"Monks, one should not enter a village wearing only the inner robe; whoever should so enter, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," it was later stated:
"Monks, there are these five reasons for laying aside the outer cloak (*saṅghāṭī*), the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*), and the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*):"

Because it is stated [in the Vinaya]: “One is ill and needs to deposit [the robe], or there is a rain-season appointment, or one must go to the other side of a river, or the dwelling is secured by a bolt, or the kaṭhina has been spread”;
and because it is also stated in the Aṭṭhakathā regarding this: “Among these five cases, only being secured by a bolt is the criterion.
For it is permissible to go outside after depositing [the robe] in a dwelling that is indeed secured, but not in one that is not.”

It should be understood that even when the kaṭhina robe-season has not been formally established, [the Buddha] said, "Place those bhikkhus in dwellings protected by bolts," and having deposited the robes in the hands of those who were like-minded, he set out on a journey through the countryside with only his inner and outer robes, having obtained what was permissible for entering a village. 473.
*Avippavāsa-sammuti*: This means for the purpose of non-separation; it is for the purpose of the absence of that offense which arises from separation.
The meaning is: "to give consent. From that point on, it is permissible. For how long is it permissible?
It is permissible for one month, or more, as long as there is still the intention to go. Therefore it was said: "By one who lays down the burden, [the robe] must be relinquished.
There is no further need to perform the act of giving consent; if, after the lapse of twelve years—
There is another disease; it is permissible. Just like the formal act of ordination (*upasampadakamma*), a single authorization (*ekāsammuti*) is permissible for as long as one lives.
Furthermore, the phrase "or it has been made" and so forth should not be stated in this training rule (*sikkhāpada*). Why?
Because even when the obstacle of making [a robe] has been severed, an offense due to being separated from an un-designated robe is impossible; therefore, [the text says] "when the robe is finished."
If it is asked, "Should one say only this much: 'The robe of the bhikkhu has been determined'?"—the answer is no, because it depends on that.
For the determination depends upon the completion of the act of making; therefore, it is said, "'It has been made,' and so forth.
In that context, "made" is exactly as stated previously.

477–8. Regarding the purpose of defining the characteristic of non-separation (*avippavāsa*): here, the characteristic of non-separation is defined by such statements as, “Having deposited one’s robe within the village, one must dwell within the village. The characteristic of separation (*vippavāsa*) should be understood by way of its opposite.
Furthermore, in the passage beginning with “A village having a single common approach,” setting aside the caravan (*sattha*), the foot of a tree (*rukkhamūla*), and so forth...

In the remaining cases, whether it is under open space (*ajjhokāsa*), one should understand the state of being a single precinct (*ekūpacāra*) or different precincts (*nānūpacāra*) based on whether there is an enclosure (*parikkhepa*) or no enclosure.
Furthermore, since weapons are of two kinds—fixed (*niviṭṭha*) and unfixed (*aniviṭṭha*)—among these, the unfixed belong exclusively to a single family or various families and are always unenclosed;
whereas the fixed may be either enclosed or unenclosed. Therefore...
In that context, it is stated not by way of a perimeter and so forth, but by way of the interior; likewise for the open air. At the foot of a tree, it is by way of the shade.

Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the summary [of the rules] stating, "A caravan is of one common precinct or of different precincts," because such a distinction is not shown in the analysis (vibhaṅga).
Therefore, seven *abbhantara*s in front and behind the caravan, and one *abbhantara* on the side.
This is a single precinct; beyond that is a multiple precinct. Likewise, regarding the foot of a tree, the area where the shadow extends at midday is a single precinct;
the rest is a multiple precinct. Why? Because in that case, the enclosure is unlimited; the shadow alone is the measure.
The open space (*ajjhokāsa*) has already been explained in the text. [The measurement] of the alms-bowl and so forth is according to whether they belong to a single family.

It is written as "a single mode of access" (*ekūpacāratā*); therefore, it is abbreviated by considering that in the case of a dwelling (*nivesana*) and a warehouse (*udosita*), the previously stated delimitation applies, whereas in the case of watchtowers (*aṭṭa*) and so forth, it does not.

Beyond that, however, regarding fields, grain-stores, monasteries (*ārāma*), and monastic dwellings (*vihāra*), the terms "enclosed" and "unenclosed" are mentioned again because the subject matter has been concluded by the Teacher’s analysis (*satthavibhaṅga*). As for the statement beginning with "different rooms" (*nānāgabbhā*), etc.:
However, it was not mentioned regarding fields, grain, workshops, and monasteries because they are impossible [in that context].
Although it is possible in a monastery (*vihāra*), it was not mentioned there because it has been excluded. "Family" (*kula*) refers to the owner;
therefore, by the phrase "of one family or of many families," he illustrates the common or non-common status of the fourteen places for depositing robes, such as villages and so forth.
However, it was not mentioned because [the case] of an open space is impossible [there].

Furthermore, although there is no difference in the exemptions granted for enclosed villages and the like—whether they belong to a single family or various families—there is such a difference in the case of those that are enclosed;
therefore, it should be understood that the inclusion of "single or various families" and the inclusion of "single or various precincts" are purposeful. Even therein:

This is the distinction: in the case of the village (sattha) and the foot of a tree (rukkhamūla), the difference lies solely in the breach of the family (kulabheda), not in the breach of the precincts (upacārabheda). In the case of the open air (ajjhokāsa), however, there is a difference due to the breach of the precincts;

yet that [precinct] is not shown in the Canon (pāḷi). They say: "Because of the statement 'having exceeded that measure,' there is no fault even in the air (ākāsa) to the extent of two and a half ratanas."
“Sabhā” is the feminine gender; “sabhāyaṃ” is the neuter gender, which is why it was stated, “according to the method of changing genders.
It is said that “sabhāyaṃ” was specified in the nominative case for the purpose of showing the neuter gender; because that [nominative] is not being employed here, it is also [stated as] “dvāramūlaṃ.
Because it is not placed in its own designated location, the range of the hand (hatthapāsa) along the path does not provide protection.
"One must stay in the house where the robe has been deposited. For it is said: "One must stay either in the assembly hall or at the foot of the door;
one must not go beyond the reach of the hand. If it is argued that this cannot be known because of the restriction that "the dawn must be met while still within the reach of the hand," [we reply:
it cannot be known if one is inside the house; in such and such a manner...
Because it has been so stated, it is therefore said: "The logical connection is the authority.

This meaning is also clarified in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary) with reference to a small village that has a common gate for all: "If it has two gates, one should stay wherever one wishes—either in the middle, at the house, or in the assembly hall."
480-1. Those dwellings and so forth that do not count as a village are what is intended by "dwellings and so forth.
Even if a robe is not suspected [of being stolen] when left in the open air, it becomes subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) if it is placed within a distance of more than seven *abbhantara*s;
in this case, being within the boundary (*sīma*) does not protect it, but in the case of a caravan, it does protect it. "And the exception for a river is obtained," it is said.

It is established that, according to the statement, an exemption is obtained within the water-throw boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*). If the neighboring monastery is within the same boundary, the robe is not to be relinquished (*nissaggiya*).
Now—
“The dhutaṅga is severed when one is considered to be in danger with only an inner and outer robe;
there is no offense for one without a robe because of the success of the formal relinquishment and so forth.
This is an incidental discussion; herein follows the analysis preceded by an objection: some say, “The outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) has two layers.”
Regarding the verbal instruction: "Even a single-layered *saṅghāṭī* should not be formally resolved upon (*adhiṭṭhātabba*). If one resolves upon it, it does not take effect.
Having said this, when they confer full ordination (*upasampadā*) even upon those seeking it by giving them a double-layered *saṅghāṭī*, they should be corrected by this scriptural passage.
For the Blessed One said: "A cut-up *saṅghāṭī*, a cut-up upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*), a cut-up..."
“The inner robe” was first permitted. Then, regarding this matter—wherein it was said, “When a certain monk was having his three robes made, all [robes] cut [into pieces] were not sufficient;
two [robes] cut [into pieces] and one uncut were not sufficient;
two uncut [robes] and one cut were not sufficient”—[the Buddha said], “Monks, I allow even an extra [robe].”
Since it was permitted [by the Blessed One] that "one may add [a layer]," it is established that even a single-layered *saṅghāṭi* is allowable.
As for that which, when cut, is not sufficient [to be doubled], how could there be a doubling of it? This is also stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:

"One may add even an extra layer" means one may also give an incoming cloth (*āgantukapatta*). However, this [extra layer] is to be added only when [the robe] is insufficient; if it is sufficient, the incoming cloth...

"It is not permissible; it must indeed be cut. However, it is permissible for the kaṭhina-cloth to be already cut, because of its unique characteristic and because there is no statement saying, "The cut piece is not sufficient when doubled. This is how one should reach a conclusion here.

Regarding the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga): since those who are not fully ordained do not possess the ascetic practice of the three-robed one (tecīvarika), one is called a "three-robed one" only by virtue of possessing the three robes.

If it is argued that, because they lack such a formal resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*), the phrase "only by means of what has been resolved" (*adhiṭṭhiteneva*) should be stated [for them as well], we say no;

for that would entail a contradiction with the classification of the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*). Indeed, the breach of the ascetic practice occurs through the acceptance of a fourth robe, not through being separated from the three robes, nor through the acceptance of an extra robe, nor through the wearing of an extra robe. However, since this applies only to monks...
The Blessed One authorized nine robes by way of formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) and described them by way of their origin (*jāti*);

this is not the case for those who are not fully ordained. Therefore, because there is no fixed rule regarding robes for them, that ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*) was not authorized for householders as it was for others;
thus, one should reach the conclusion that it was not mentioned in the rules for undertaking that practice.
Regarding the phrase "regarded as suspicious": in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*, the individual factors for this training rule on suspicion (*sāsaṅka-sikkhāpada*) are not stated separately;
it is merely said, "The rest here should be understood according to the method stated in the second training rule of the *Cīvara-vagga*," yet that [method] was not actually stated there.
In that case, staying apart overnight is the fourth factor, whereas here it is staying apart for six nights; this is the distinction here.
Therefore, because of the similarity in factors and the similarity in conventional designation, they call this precisely a training rule involving apprehension.

This one is without limitation, while that one has a limitation because it is restricted to a maximum of one month. In that case, there is no offense for one who, having entered the village boundary even though outside the village, stays there and then departs;
here it is not so. Here, with each successive dawn, there is an offense of relinquishment (*nissaggiya*); in that case, however, it is not so.

This is the distinction between these two [offenses]: that this one is the seventh. As for the constituent factors (*aṅga*), however, they are not stated here because they are established by way of the opposite of the "factor of depositing the robe" (*cīvaranikkhepaṅgasampatti*) and by the method explained herein.

Although those [factors] are indeed not stated, nevertheless, the fourth factor ought to be specified, yet it has not been specified. For what reason? Because after having relinquished [the robe] according to the sequence of relinquishment stated here—

This is for the purpose of confessing the offense and demonstrating the release from the offense incurred therein. Even one who has been separated [from his robes] for a year is considered as one who has been separated for a single night, let alone one who has been separated for six days.
Nevertheless, if the requisite factors mentioned there are present, it must be relinquished according to the method stated therein.
Whether one relinquishes them in the winter or the summer, it is also according to the method stated here.
The teacher [Ācariya] says: "The fourth factor was not specified for the purpose of making it known that it is permissible to relinquish [the robe]; therefore, it is not a logical necessity.
Even a robe that has exceeded one month [of the *māsa-atikkanta* period] is indeed relinquished by calling it "exceeded ten days" (*dasāha-atikkanta*).

Some say that if it is less than a month by two [days], one may call it "exceeded ten days" and it is [then considered] "exceeded one month. Nevertheless, if it is a robe expected [to be received] again...
Having stated that it is an offense of expiation (*nissaggiya*) for [a robe] "exceeding ten days," one must then relinquish the original robe (*mūlacīvara*) by stating that it "exceeded one month.

As for the terms "inner and outer garment" (*santaruttara*), "outer cloak" (*saṅghāṭi*), or "robe" (*cīvara*): does this refer to the triple-robe (*ticīvara*) or something else? What is the point here?

If only the triple-robe were prohibited, there would be a contradiction with the rules concerning robes that have not been cut, cutting robes, washing robes, requesting robes, and so forth, because those cases would fall under the category of being included within the triple-robe.

Now, is there also a contradiction with other passages such as, "when the robe is finished," and so forth? It is said: this should not be understood as a fixed rule, because it must be taken according to what is possible.

For instance, in such passages as, "having laid aside the robes, they set out on a journey through the countryside wearing only the inner and upper garments," it refers specifically to the three robes (*tricīvara*). Likewise: "Monks, you should not enter a village wearing only the inner and upper garments."
In such passages as, "The robe should be prepared as at most one inner and one outer," and likewise in cases such as, "Sanghatis should be given;
a lower garment should be given; a Sanghati should be given; 'Come, friend, here is a Sanghati for you;
give me a cloth,'" it is said: "For all robes, in the sense of being stitched together, are called 'sanghati'."
...is said. Likewise, some say that here too [the phrase] “when the robe is finished” applies.

For while robes as much as needed were permitted during the [robe-making] period, when all of those are being made, when will they ever reach completion? Therefore, some say it refers only to the triple robe (*tricīvara*).

Regarding the statement, “There is no offense for one who has no robe, because of the accomplishment through relinquishment (*paccuddhāra*) and so forth,” what is meant? It refers to the *Udosita* training rule (*sikkhāpada*).

Some say that there is an offense for one who possesses only three robes when separated from them, because it would otherwise follow that the state of being without purpose [for the robe] would arise.

To this, it is said: there is no offense, because of the establishment of the act of relinquishing (*paccuddhāra*) and so forth. For it is stated: "There is no offense if one relinquishes or gives away [the robe] before dawn. Otherwise, for one who relinquishes it or gives it away before dawn, [the offense would persist] until—
If another does not take charge of it, one incurs an offense according to the method already stated.

Otherwise, regarding "separation for more than seven days," this refers to separation as the literal sense: when there is separation, it is due to separation; when there is no separation, it is due to non-separation.
The commentary on the Udosita training rule is finished.
3. Commentary on the Third Kathina Training Rule 497.
“It is not sufficient” means it does not reach the minimum limit; for that very reason, the minimum limit for the three robes (ticīvara) is stated as being five handfuls and so forth.
“Expectation regarding a robe” is *cīvarapaccāsā*. By this, he indicates: “May that robe be obtained later.”
"Whether [it happens] or not, until that expectation is cut off, I allow this root-cloth to be set aside.
In the phrase "cīvarapaccāsā," the ablative case is used in the sense of a limit (*maryādā*), or the nominative case is used in the sense of a locative. 499–500.
Regarding the passage beginning with "when the robe is finished... or the hope for a robe is cut off," it refers to any one of the three robes.

It is said: "The rest exist; he protects. When the obstacle regarding robes has been removed, and when the *kaṭhina* has been suspended—whether during the winter season or at another time—if an out-of-season robe (*akālacīvara*) should arise, it must be made up immediately.
If there is hope for its fulfillment, he does not protect [the robe]; if there is no hope, he does not protect it. "When the *kaṭhina* has not been spread..."

Based on the statement, "It arose during the eleventh month of the Kathina period," the time following the later Kattika month is indeed a [permissible] occasion, whether the Kathina has been spread or not.
Winter may be an occasion when it has been spread, and it may be a non-occasion when it has not been spread; beyond that, it is exclusively a non-occasion.
The phrase "given specifically" (ādissa dinnaṃ), although not applicable here, is mentioned for the sake of clarifying the meaning in the case of the nuns.
The remainder of the second *nissaggiya* offense is like [the rules regarding] out-of-season robes (*akālacīvara*).

For in that case, if one has received a gift specifically designated for the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs with the words, "Let those who have assembled divide it," and she then resolves it as "an out-of-season robe" while dividing it, there is an offense of expiation (*nissaggiya*).
This is because, just as in the case of "out-of-season robes"—that is, when the Kathina has not been spread during the eleventh month—...
The statement, "arisen [during the robe season], arisen during the seven months when the *kathina* has been spread," is spoken by way of a general summary (*atthuddhāra*);

this case is of the same nature. If one asks: "If that is so, for what purpose was it said, 'This is given to you, a single individual'?"—for surely that [gift] is not something to be distributed (*bhājanīya*)—it is stated because of its commonality with what is not to be distributed. Just as [the rule regarding] what is specifically assigned to the Saṅgha...
Because it is not to be shared by monks who have already performed the *kathina* ceremony, it is called "out-of-season robe-cloth" (*akālacīvara*);
the meaning is that this applies to private cloth as well as other types. Even so, someone might think: "Even if given specifically for an individual, it receives the same ten-day allowance.
For such a person, this [following] is to be expected: "When the robe has been finished and the *kathina* has been removed by the monk... (First *Kathina*).
Regarding the phrase "in the kaṭhina [period]," this is indeed purposeless. For even when the kaṭhina has been dismantled, it is understood that one may keep [the robe] for at most ten days;

therefore, if it is argued that this was said with reference specifically to what was given without specification, even so, even that which was given without specification receives an allowance of only ten days from the following Kattika month for those who have not spread the kaṭhina, as stated in the rule: "When the robe is finished..."

Because it is stated: "When the kaṭhina has been removed by a bhikkhu. If you say "Yes," [we reply] that this contradicts the statement: "Arising in the eleventh month when the kaṭhina has not been spread.
Therefore, one must reach a definitive conclusion here according to the method already explained.
It is said in the *Anugaṇṭhipada*: "In the first training rule, regarding all robes, by way of the 'robe as much as needed' (*yāvadatthacīvara*), within the period of the kaṭhina month..."
There is no offense even after the lapse of ten days because an exemption has been granted.

Just as an out-of-season robe (akālacīvara) given specifically within the period of the Kathina month receives the status of being exempted as a seasonable robe (kālacīvara), so too should it be understood that this applies in other months as well.
Therefore, [it is said]: "When the robe has been finished and the Kathina has been removed, if a robe should then come to a monk..."

Although this is established by the training rule beginning with “it might arise,” etc., it was stated as “it might arise as out-of-season robe-cloth” by the one permitting the last month of the Kattika season for those for whom the kaṭhina has not been spread.

For if this had not been stated, it would not be possible to say that what is called “out-of-season robe-cloth” is “that which arises during the eleventh month for those for whom the kaṭhina has not been spread. Indeed, from such a statement, [the distinction between] those for whom the kaṭhina has not been spread and those for whom it has been spread...
"Likewise, for all robes, there is no offense of forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) when ten days have passed in the month of Kattika.

Furthermore, it is said thus: "As for what was permitted by me—that 'an extra robe may be kept for a maximum of ten days during the first *kathina* period'—that too refers only to [an extra robe] that has arisen outside of the *kathina* month, not within it; such is the meaning."

It is illuminated. How? By prohibiting, through the supplementary rule "when the robe is finished and the kaṭhina has been removed," the offense that would otherwise be incurred after keeping an extra robe for more than ten days;
and by this training rule, prohibiting the offense that would be incurred upon the lapse of ten days for an out-of-season robe (*akālacīvara*) arising thereafter.

"...would arise," and so forth. By this, it is demonstrated that because of the statement, "Even if given at the proper time, if it is given specifically [for that purpose], this is called 'out-of-season robe-cloth' (akālacīvara)," one does not receive the ten-day grace period after the Kathina has been dismantled.

Furthermore, the possibility of receiving five days [of grace] after the Kathina has been dismantled, along with those [other allowances], is established by the passage: "When his robe is finished, the bhikkhu..."
Since it was stated—after defining the time for the arising of an out-of-season robe—that "when the kaṭhina has been removed, if an out-of-season robe should arise for a bhikkhu...

it must be made up quickly," this [delay] is thereby prohibited. By both of these [rules], it is established that a robe arising within the kaṭhina period does not receive the privilege [of being kept beyond the season] even for a single day after the removal of the kaṭhina.
Thus others say. Furthermore, it is stated: "But the teachers might say:

'When a robe has been finished by a bhikkhu and the kaṭhina has been suspended, if an out-of-season robe (akālacīvara) should arise for that bhikkhu... Herein, "when a robe has been finished by a bhikkhu..."
By saying, "When the kaṭhina has been removed," he makes it known that "in this interval, there is no occurrence of even one of the three types of out-of-season robes.
But why are they explained in detail in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*)? It is said:
This training rule was spoken with reference to its formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*); however, after first permitting the ten-day period, if that is not sufficient...
Since there is an expectation [of receiving it], by permitting [the monk] to keep it for a month after having increased that very expectation, this specific purpose is also illustrated:

namely, that even an out-of-season robe (akālacīvara) must be distributed in the presence [of the Sangha]. However, because that [rule] was stated by expanding upon the training rule (sikkhāpada), "It should be accepted by a monk who so desires," therefore all three [cases] are explained in detail in the word-commentary (padabhājana).

“‘It must be made up immediately’ means it must be made up within ten days”—this was stated in order to indicate that, given the capacity [to do so], it follows the definition of the previous training rule;
therefore, instead of saying “so quickly” or “so lightly,” it says “within ten days.

Let this be so for one who has performed the *kathina* ceremony; however, when it is asked how it is for one who has not performed the *kathina*, the answer is that it is a prohibition against not having performed it.
When it is said, "he shows [the robe]," he falls into distress because he does not see it.

At the rising of the sun on the thirty-first day, it becomes subject to relinquishment (*nissaggiya*); even if it has been joined with a large expected robe, it becomes subject to relinquishment by falling under that same category, provided there is the possibility of reaching the final measurement.
If such possibility does not exist, it is not so; if it is joined again, it becomes subject to relinquishment, but not if it was joined by another.
It becomes a different substance once cut. Some say that when a piece exceeding its original dimensions has been joined together, it acquires a new dimension;

this should be understood after careful investigation. However, in a certain *gaṇṭhipada*, regarding the statement, "This was given for the Saṅgha as an out-of-season robe (*akālacīvara*)," it is stated that there is no offense in the case of what was given to the Saṅgha.

If it is argued that this was stated by means of extracting the words—as in the case of "the seclusion of the ear" and so forth—and that it refers to the acquisition [of robes] from the Saṅgha, [we reply:

since this is already established by the phrase "or it may arise from the Saṅgha," it is indeed redundant. Furthermore, it has been stated that there is also a reading such as, "The Saṅgha or the group will receive the robes.
However, I have written all of this for the sake of proficiency regarding the *Gaṇṭhipada*.
One should speak only after having investigated thoroughly.
The commentary on the third *kaṭhina* training rule is finished.
4. Commentary on the training rule concerning old robes (*purāṇacīvara*).
503–505. *Bhattavissagga* means the determination regarding the meal (*bhattakiccādhiṭṭhāna*). "The division of the determination regarding the meal" is [the title] according to the ancients.
Regarding the phrase *tattha nāma tvam*: "In that case," meaning when the action performed by you is such that it ought not to have been done, you will indeed wash [it away].
Or else, the meaning is: "You, indeed, in that case. "Ordained in both Saṅghas" means in the presence of the monks.
It should be understood that this was stated because of the rejection of full ordination (*upasampadā*) and out of fear that such [faults] might follow from it.

Regarding the term "old robe" (*purāṇacīvara*), the phrase "even if worn once or even if wrapped once" was spoken solely for the purpose of illustrating its state of being old; therefore, it accords with the statement:
"A robe means any one of the six types of robes, the last of which is subject to formal assignment (*vikappanupaga*)."

Some say that the opportunity [for an offense] has not arisen. Others say it is not stated [as an offense] because the final [type of cloth] that does not come under the category of "allowable" is not intended here; rather, only that which comes under the category of "lower garment" and "upper robe" is intended.
For this very reason, a *dukkaṭa* is mentioned for a sitting mat or a rug. Therefore, [the offense] is not stated [here].

Because there is no mention of a specific size, anyone who has an old cloth washed incurs a *nissaggiya* [offense]; for this very reason, it says: "There is no offense, except in the case of a robe..."

"...he has another requisite washed," it is said. For even if he has a bag that is stained with impurity and has been used washed, it is indeed an offense of expiation (*nissaggiya*) because of its grossness and its unsuitability.
For this very reason, some say that the definition of a robe (*cīvara-pariccheda*) is not stated in this place in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*;
having investigated, one should accept what is more appropriate. "Having dyed it, [making] a fold..."
"Having made [it] allowable" means that it is permissible to wear or don only that which has been made allowable, and nothing else; thus it is stated.

By this, the position of the Elder Majjhima is supported, while the other is not. My own conjecture is that the passage beginning with "having dyed," etc., was spoken for the purpose of demonstrating the Vinaya procedure.
Just as there are three tetrads in the section on one who perceives a non-relative as a non-relative, so too are there [tetrads] in the sections on doubt regarding a relative and on a relative.
Thus there are nine tetrads. Here it may be asked: "If, after washing once, one sets aside the task of washing and then washes again thinking, 'It is not well-washed,' there ought to be no offense;
for in the second instance, it is as if one is washing without being told to do so.
It is replied: If the monk refuses, saying, "Enough, this much washing is sufficient," [then there is no offense].

Furthermore, it is appropriate to say that she who washes while not being told is "one who washes without being told. If this were not the case, it should be understood that she is indeed one who has been told.
Regarding the transformation of gender (*liṅgaparivattana*) for a bhikkhu, the offense is determined by way of one who is fully ordained on only one side, as in the case of the Sākiyānīs.

(506) "By means of a single instance" means by any of the first [three] cases. The reading is "by way of three sets of four. Because it is well known that one is fully ordained through the eightfold proclamation (*aṭṭhavācikā*) in the presence of bhikkhus, that is not mentioned; rather, only the Sākiyānīs are mentioned because they are not so well known.
The commentary on the training rule concerning old robes is finished.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Acceptance of Robes (Cīvarapaṭiggahaṇasikkhāpada) 508–510.

Regarding the phrase "when the training rule has not been laid down," it is recorded here that this refers to "the training rule concerning departing from the group. Some say that it refers to the training rule prohibiting forest-dwellers when it has not been laid down, but they state, "That is not good. "Due to being distressed" means due to fatigue.
512. "Vicinity" (*upacāra*) means twelve *hattha*s. Regarding the statement found in the *Mahāpaccarī* and the *Kurundi*:

if, during the night, many robes have been set aside by a large crowd through the act of giving with faith to a monk who is preaching the Dharma, there is no fault for one who takes them on the following day with a pure mind, thinking, "These are gifts given out of faith by the lay devotees."
There is an offense for one who takes [the robe] knowing, "These were given here by the bhikkhunīs.
"By way of being unintentional" means that although one knows they were given by the bhikkhunīs, one does not recognize it as such because there are many [robes] of hers.
"Having determined it to be a *paṃsukūla*" refers to one who takes it thinking, "I am taking a *paṃsukūla*," without intending, "This might have been given by the bhikkhunīs."

It is permissible. Even though this same meaning is stated in the *Kurundi* and other commentaries, others maintain that by the single expression “by way of being without consciousness,” the very possibility of taking [the object] “in whatever manner” has been prohibited as an improper path.
Thus, it is elaborated that the Elder Dhammasiri does not speak in this way, but speaks directly. This is his domain; this is his intention—just as...

It is stated: “Thinking, ‘I will take a rag-robe (paṃsukūla),’ it is permissible to take even that which belongs to a bhikkhunī if it has been set aside, provided one does not assign it [to her] but resolves upon it as a rag-robe.
Likewise, it is permissible for a monk who preaches the Dhamma to take what was given to a bhikkhunī if it is not recognized [as hers].
Therefore, this was stated in the Mahāpaccarī and the Kurundī because of the absence of intentionality.

"It does not come together. However, this negation is only appropriate when referring to the acceptance of an alternative option; otherwise, the preceding and following statements would be contradictory.
That is not correct, because it is not equal to a rag-robe (*paṃsukūla*). By virtue of being a rag-robe, it is placed by nuns on rubbish heaps and the like;
it does not remain as something belonging to her. For a rag-robe is ownerless and common to all.

Anyone else may also take it. Even though one already knows beforehand that "this is a robe for the bhikkhunīs," a *paṃsukūlika* (rag-robe wearer) is permitted to take it, because at that time it does not belong to her.
The phrase "having determined it as a rag-robe" is stated for the purpose of showing the practice of austerity (*sallekha*).
When the Tathāgata, while giving meat, ate even what was allowable out of austerity, he spoke of the robe as being subject to relinquishment (*nissaggiya*).
"How could one personally designate meat as 'cooked'?
If it is asked, "How then is it permissible to accept rag-robes (*paṃsukūla*)?", it is because she has not given them to him, and because the monk has not received them from that nun.
For even a rag-robe that is ownerless may be taken from the hand of another; it is not [permissible] otherwise.
It is permissible [to receive a robe] because the characteristics stated in the rule, “One may accept a robe from an unrelated bhikkhunī,” are fulfilled.
Some say it is permissible to take what belongs to an unrelated woman from the hand of a related woman.

Just as there is no offense for one who accepts [a robe] from the hands of a *sikkhamānā*, a *sāmaṇera*, and so forth, so too, according to the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*: “From the hand of an unrelated [woman]...”

"Taking" is stated as the factor [of the offense]. Likewise, some say there is no offense for one who takes from the hand of a nun who is not a relative what belongs to a female trainee (sikkhamānā), a novice nun (sāmaṇerī), a male lay follower (upāsaka), a female lay follower (upāsikā), a monk (bhikkhu), or a novice monk (sāmaṇera), because the aforementioned characteristic is absent;
for that very reason, [the text says]: "The robe of one ordained on only one side..."
Without saying "he receives," it is stated: "If he receives from the hand [of a woman], except in exchange, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Therefore, some say that even if the item belongs to an unrelated woman, for one who receives it from the hand of a person ordained on only one side, there is a dukkaṭa.
Both of these views should not be regarded as authoritative; the underlying reason must be investigated.
514. What need is there to mention cloth bags for bowls and so forth? This refers to many layers of cloth that are not subject to formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
For this very reason, it is said in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*: "In the case of requisites such as cloth bags for bowls that are not subject to formal determination.

Or, even if they are suitable for formal determination, because they are [merely] requisites for those [other items], there is no offense, just as in the case of the outer skin of a lotus root. Is a cloth water-strainer a requisite?
Is it not the case that [the robe] exists? It does exist; however, because it has the shape of a lower garment (*nivāsana*) and so forth, it is said that it is not permissible.

Therefore, in this context, "the final robe" refers to a robe that has been formally designated (*vikappanupaga*) by means of the lower garment and other such robes. The conclusion is that in the immediately preceding [text], it was only the suitability for being worn as a lower garment or an upper garment (*pārupana*) that was intended.
This being so, in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*, [the criteria are] the state of being the final robe suitable for designation and the absence of exchange.
If it is argued that, instead of stating only three factors—“taking from the hand of one who is not a relative”—the fourth factor, “not being a requisite,” should be stated;
this is not to be said. Why? Because in this training rule, requisites such as a bowl-bag and so forth are not counted among the robes (*acīvara*).

In the first *kathina* ceremony and others, the measure is what has undergone formal assignment (*vikappanupagata*), whereas here it is what has come to be used for the body (*kāyaparibhogupagata*). Thus, it is called “another requisite.”
Because it is stated, "having taken up whatever there may be, such as a bowl-bag," it is permissible to take even a bowl-bag that has not yet been formally assigned (*vikappanupaga*).

Furthermore, regarding the passage "a cloth and a water-strainer," since it says, "'robe' refers to the last [type of robe] that is fit for assignment," the cloth and water-strainer are indeed a robe (*cīvara*) itself, not a monastic requisite (*parikkhāra*).
The concluding statement, "But what need for further discussion? is also [to be understood in this way].
Some say it is "with intention" (*sādhaka*), but because one does not recognize the designation (*paṇṇatti*), it is without intention (*acittaka*) regarding the object (*vatthu*).
This is stated in the *Anugaṇṭhipada*: "Because one does not recognize that it belongs to an unrelated nun, and because one does not recognize it as a robe, it is without intention.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the acceptance of robes is finished.

6. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Solicitation from Strangers (Aññātakaviññatti-sikkhāpada) 515. Regarding the term *parikkhārānaṃ*: this is a genitive case used in the sense of the accusative. *Ekasāṭakaṃ* is a neuter singular noun.
By the statement, "O foolish man, he is a stranger," even one who has been invited [to give] may be unwilling to give; thus, a stranger stands in a place where there is no invitation.
It has been illuminated. Otherwise, it would contradict the statement: "There is no offense for those who have already been invited. 517.
"Neither should one request [cloth], nor should one break [the robe]" is said because there exist robes belonging to oneself that have not yet been cut, and because there is still hope for them.
How long does such hope last? Until one has entered another village.
Some say it extends for half a *yojana*. Some say it extends as far as the range of sight and hearing. Some say it extends as far as others do not see.
Some say it extends until the expectation [of fruit] is cut off. Some say it extends until the time of searching for branches and leaves, breaking them, and preparing them.
All of this is appropriate according to the circumstances. If one asks, "How is this known?"—[it is said]: "But if these..."
"Nothing at all is permitted of the household items and so forth described above, down to the covering of a castor-oil plant;
one must come having covered oneself with grass or leaves," according to the words of the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
"They are not to be given to the elders yet" means they are not to be given according to one's own wish; rather, when the elders say, "Give them, friends..."
"When they say [this], then [the robes] should be given. 'This being so, even young novices may stand in the place where the robe was cut;
it is permissible for them to break off branches and foliage, but not otherwise. For it is said: "It is cut by whomever [is present]"'—so it has been stated.
However, the Teacher says: 'They may give [the robes] even according to their own wish. For likewise, in the Aṭṭhakathā..."

Regarding the phrase "worn out through use," it is stated here that "it is appropriate to say that even a robe given by oneself after covering it with grass and leaves for teachers, preceptors, and others whose robes have been stolen, falls under this category.

Furthermore, if it should be argued that [the rule applies] only when the teacher and others have said, "Bring one, friend," and not otherwise, that is not so; for it is said, "or [a robe] stolen by some."
Because, according to the explanation given here, it would follow that there is no distinction between this second case and the previous one. Now, if it is asked:
for what purpose was it said, "They should not yet be given to the Elders"? [The answer is: As long as one is breaking off branches and foliage for the sake of the Elders, they should not be given;
rather, after one has personally worn those branches and foliage intended for the Elders, even without [further formalities]...

Things may be given either by the command of the elders or by one’s own preference; there is no offense of expiation (pācittiya) for destroying living plants, because it has been permitted even by the Teacher.

If it is argued that when it says, "with grass or with leaves," this refers only to what is allowable (kappiya), [we reply: No, because that would contradict the statement, "If he does not obtain that...
[etc. ...it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Here it is said: out of fear of an offense of wrong-doing...

If an object constituting a *pācittiya* offense must be transgressed against, and that is unavailable, may an object belonging to the Saṅgha constituting a *thullaccaya* offense be transgressed against?
And if that is unavailable, may even an object constituting a *pārājika* offense be transgressed against? No; because a *pārājika* offense is a "worldly transgression" (*lokavajja*).

Furthermore, not every instance of vegetation (*bhūtagāma*) constitutes a *pācittiya* offense; there are also objects for which it is a *dukkaṭa* offense and so forth, as well as objects for which there is no offense (*anāpatti*), such as those pertaining to time and the like.
Therefore, it should be understood that this is, at that time, a case where there is no offense. To what extent is a monk one whose robes have been taken away or whose robes have been lost?

Some say: "To this extent he is naked. Some say: "There is an offense for one who makes a request starting from the very last robe that has reached the stage of being formally assigned (*vikappanupaga*).
Some say: "By the absence of both the inner and outer robes. Some say: "By the absence of the three robes (*ticīvara*)."

Some [say]: "By way of having only an inner and outer robe. This is the correct view of some, because of the statement: "From that point on, one may accept a robe only as far as an inner and outer robe.
Therefore, when an inner and outer robe already exist, it is an offense of forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) upon receiving the last robe that has not yet been formally assigned (*vikappanupaga*).
If this is so, then [the rule] "having requested it, if one should receive it, it is an offense of forfeiture" [is established].
If it is argued that it must be understood as a training rule (*sikkhāpada*), that is not so; for the purpose [of the rule] is already established, and the verbal roots have different meanings.

What is meant? Just as when it is said, "He made known the act of sexual intercourse three times," the meaning is "he engaged in it," so too here, in the phrase "one should request a robe" (*cīvaraṃ viññāpeyyā*), the meaning is that one should engage in the act of requesting—that is, one should cause it to arise.
"Clad in that" means "clothed in that. It wears out for one who uses it alone because of the lack of others, not by mere touch.

"By oneself" is appropriate to mean "by one's own self"; therefore, for one who does not use it through improper use, but uses it by way of proper use, what has become worn out is called "worn out by use. When its counterparts have not been cut off, even giving it away is [considered] proper use.

The intended meaning is that it is thus included [in the summary]. It is stated: “Regarding these two *lesas*, Dhammasiri Thera said: ‘This is the opinion of the teachers who teach the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
(521) “He does not obtain [the opportunity] to sit or to lie down” means the intended meaning is that he does not obtain [to do so] at his pleasure.
In the phrase “for the sake of another,” the words “of relatives who have invited him” continue to apply here as well. For whose sake? For that very person’s sake.

The phrase “of relatives who have invited him” is stated for the purpose of showing that, just as there is a triple offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) in the case of non-relatives, so too it applies when one has not been invited.
Otherwise, since this would already be established by the rule “perceiving a relative as a relative,” [the specific mention would be redundant].
The remainder does not attain permanence. Furthermore, here, by the mention of "one who is unknown" (*aññātaka*), there is the mention of "one who has not been invited" (*appavārita*);

and by the mention of "one who has not been invited," there is the mention of "one who is unknown," for those who are unknown are indeed those who have not been invited. Likewise, by the mention of "one who is known" (*ñātaka*), there is the mention of "one who has been invited" (*pavārita*), though this is not the case everywhere.
By the mention of "one who has been invited," there is no mention of "one who is known"—this is the specific meaning of this [passage].
For the purpose of clarification, it is stated: "from relatives who have invited [one to accept].
For indeed, there is an offense for one who accepts a robe from a nun who is not a relative and has not invited him, except in exchange.
However, if he accepts out of trust from a relative who has invited him, there is no offense. Likewise, there is no offense regarding an old robe from a relative, or from one who has invited him.
However, it is only a triad-offense of expiation (pācittiya). It is permissible to give old robes to certain relatives, but not to those who have already been invited [to accept gifts].

Furthermore, the "cutting off of the triad" occurs by means of the very words of the matrix (mātikā), and not by anything else; even therein, it occurs by the first [word] alone and not by the second and so forth—this should be understood as the nature of the Dhamma in the Vinaya.
The commentary on the training rule concerning requesting from an unrelated person is finished.
7. Commentary on the training rule regarding more than that (Tatuttari). 522–4.
"A hall for holding" means a cloth-distribution hall. Having stood while grasping it with the hand, one should spread out the cloth within the hall.
“Stretching out” means an accusation. “By one who possesses only the three robes” means by one who possesses the three robes according to the Vinaya.

For such a person, even though there exist other requisites such as cloths set aside after being formally resolved upon (*adhiṭṭhita*), they are permitted to request and receive no more than an inner and outer robe (*santaruttara*) until their three robes are lost.
“Otherwise also” means: when one who uses a three-robed set of standard measure after having resolved it as a requisite cloth has lost it...
"One may receive even many [robes], but not more than the inner and outer robes" (Sv II 581).

Therefore, some explain this as a distribution [of robes] for one who possesses the three robes (*tricīvarika*), saying, "it is a distribution for one who has the three robes, not for one who has requisites-robes (*parikkhāracolika*). However, the Teacher says only this:
"'By another' means by one who has extra robes; 'in another way' means in a manner other than the limits of receiving [robes] as stated here."
"But otherwise" (*aññathā*) means: some say that if all three robes are lost, one may take as much as an inner and outer robe (*santaruttara-parama*);
if two or one are lost, it was stated [as "otherwise"] for the purpose of showing that by that [means]. There is no investigation at all in the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries;
therefore, it should be accepted after careful examination. One normally goes about with an inner and outer robe, but by virtue of the training rule concerning danger (*sāsaṅka-sikkhāpada*),...
Or by way of common consent, or because a third person has not been obtained.
(526) “Only a limited amount is permitted”—this was said for the purpose of demonstrating moderation.

If it is argued that an offense occurs when one takes more than that at the place of relatives and so forth, having misunderstood that [rule], that does not accord with the Canon, for it says: “There is no offense in the case of relatives or those who have invited one.”
This is the Pāli. And here, "one who has invited" (*pavāritā*) means one who has invited prior to the time of interruption, not at the time of interruption.
For it is said: "One should invite so that [food] may be brought. Therefore, it should be understood that if one invites for the sake of the time of interruption, both are indeed not invited.
For they are said to give only because of the reason of interruption, as if it were the reason of loss. Moreover—

Just as in the past, having given rise to the thought [of making one], it was an offense involving forfeiture under that training rule for one who had a rain-cloak made from a place where he had been invited by relatives,
so too here, even at a place where one has been invited by relatives, it is not permitted except for the reasons of being cut or lost; therefore,
the statement "only what is measured according to the commentaries is permitted" is indeed the authoritative standard.

The Elder Dhammasiri said that this is improper; why? Because this training rule was laid down for one who makes known [the meal] beyond that [limit], and in that regard, the text of the *mātikā* states, "an unrelated householder or housewife," while the text of the *vibhaṅga* states, "'unrelated' means not connected by mother...
[etc. ...not related," and in the section on non-offenses, it says, "for relatives" and "for those who have invited."
Therefore, [the claim] that it does not accord with the Pāḷi in all three versions is indeed improper; thus, others maintain that it was spoken solely with reference to *sallekha* (effacement).
Furthermore, in the commentaries on the subsequent *Kāṇamātā-sikkhāpada*, it is stated:
"Even for them, a measured amount is permissible, as it is prepared for the purpose of provisions and gifts," but it is not stated that "it does not accord with the Pāḷi."
In this regard, a distinction is perceived between that [previous rule] and this one; therefore, the Elder’s opinion appears to me as sound, and it should be investigated.
However, because this training rule was laid down specifically in the context of requesting for the sake of another, the phrase "for the sake of another" is not stated here.
"The rest is of obvious meaning"—this is the reading.
“It is for the sake of another” is not stated because it contradicts the introduction (*nidāna*). Nevertheless, the Teacher [holds] that it is obtained by the method stated immediately prior.

Although in such training rules connected with householders it is said, “a householder is anyone who dwells in a home,” nevertheless, setting aside the five who share the same Dhamma, the rest are those who have renounced the training.
And the heretics are to be understood.
The commentary on the training rule concerning what is superior to that is finished.
8. Commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning What Has Been Set Aside.
“Api hoti cittaṃ” means “there is also a thought. Regarding the reading “meyyā,” the meaning is “of me.
The reading is either “these are not easy [for him]” or “it is not easy for these [people]. It is written: “The meaning is that it is not easy for him to provide coverings for these [people].
Because of the statement “without having been previously invited,” even if one is invited at that very moment, one is as good as not invited.
The commentary on the first rule concerning what has been set aside is finished.
9. Commentary on the second rule concerning what has been set aside: 532.
What is the purpose of the second rule concerning what has been set aside? There is none; it was laid down solely by way of an occasion for its introduction.
It is like the training rule regarding sitting in private with a bhikkhunī.

This being the case, the *tanti* (the formal proclamation) would not need to be recited, because even without it the purpose would be accomplished, because [the Sangha] lacks authority [over the matter], and because it has been permitted that it need not be recited. For this was said:
"If the Sangha so desires, Ānanda... it may abolish [it]. All of this is without reason; for the Buddhas do not...
They do not utter speech without purpose, much less a training rule (*sikkhāpada*); therefore, it is said in the Commentary:
"For that is like a subsequent rule (*anupaññatti*)," and so forth. There is no subsequent rule that is without purpose;
since this is similar to that, it is shown to not be without purpose. This being the case, what then is the distinction here? To this he says: "In the first training rule..."
“Harm done to one [person] is [harm to] two when done to a second; this is the distinction here. By means of this specific meaning, what further additional meaning is shown?
First, it is stated in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*: “The additional meaning shown is that it is permissible to cause harm to both even within a single instance.
By this, he illustrates: “It is not merely by counting the robes already obtained...”
“By counting the offenses, and also by counting the bases [of the offense] for the person afflicted. And on this point there are these verses:
“By counting according to the basis, an offense may become manifold;”
Thus, for the purpose of demonstration, this second alternative is presented here:
"In the Vibhaṅga on the training rule concerning bodily contact, what is the meaning of 'this'?
Even with a single woman, there is multiplicity due to the number of applications of the offense."

Furthermore, this training rule should be understood as having the purpose of demonstrating the method for determining the application of all training rules belonging to that same class. And it has been said:
"Due to the plurality and mixture of unrelated women, there is likewise the plurality and mixture of offenses."
"In order to demonstrate the possibility of such methods as these, the Teacher spoke this second [method] which has been prepared.
This is its investigation preceded by a summary of the intended meaning: "A single monk [should use] an old robe..."
If she has two nuns, or many nuns, wash [the robe], the offense is counted according to the number of nuns. Likewise,
if she accepts a single robe shared by two or many [nuns], except in exchange, here too,
if she requests one [robe] shared by two or many, the offense is counted according to the number of persons requested.

The counting of offenses. In this same manner, the method should be applied to other such training rules as well. This, first of all, is the method regarding plurality. Regarding plurality in combination, however:
if one causes both a relative and a non-relative to wash [a robe], there is one *pācittiya* offense for the completion of the task from a single source.
Then, if the relative has already washed it slightly and stopped, and subsequently the non-relative washes it thoroughly; [there is still only one offense].

It is an offense involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*). Now, if a non-relative washes first and afterwards a relative makes it well-washed, because the effort was made by the non-relative, there is only an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the monk.

Whether one perceives her as a non-relative, is doubtful, or perceives her as a relative, when one causes a non-relative or a relative to wash, the enumeration of the various offenses—such as forfeiture and wrong-doing—should be understood according to the method already stated.

Likewise, for one who accepts a robe belonging to both a non-relative and a relative when it is given by both together as one, or when it is accepted from the hand of the non-relative alone, there is an offense of expiation (*nissaggiya*).

However, if it is from a relative, there is no offense. Furthermore, if one perceives both as non-relatives and so forth, the enumeration of the various offenses—such as *nissaggiya* and *dukkaṭa*—should be understood according to the method already stated.
Likewise, the method should be applied as far as possible even to the training rules concerning requests from unrelated persons (*aññātakaviññatti*).

This is the method regarding the mixed cases. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), however, it is meant that there are many [cases]: if one asks for [cloth] from several unrelated persons, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) according to the number of persons asked, whether they have been asked or not.

If one gives and another does not give, there is an offense of forfeiture (*nissaggiya*). If, however, one who was not asked gives, there is no offense of forfeiture. Furthermore, regarding those both asked and not asked...
If she gives what was requested for common use, it is indeed an offense of expiation (*nissaggiya*). If both give, it is indeed an offense of expiation.

If she gives what was not requested, there is no offense regarding the offense of expiation. If she gives what was not requested by virtue of the words of one who had requested, there is indeed no offense.
The same method should be applied, as appropriate, to cases such as "prepared for" (*upakkhaṭa*) and so forth.
The commentary on the second training rule concerning what has been set aside is finished.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Kings:
537. “Friends, we do not accept cloth-money... [as before] ...only at the proper time and what is allowable. Thus it is said.
This was stated because the training rule regarding the acceptance of silver had already been laid down previously.
Otherwise, if Venerable Upananda accepted even a single kahāpaṇa as the means of exchange for meat with his own hand, how would he not have accepted a robe-fund that was much larger than that?
Nevertheless, because it is connected with robes, they included it in the Cīvara-vagga.
538–9. Regarding the statement, “He breaks the reason for his coming,” some say that because of this, he is not permitted to reprove [the monk] again.

Some say it is because his coming has become purposeless, as he will not receive a robe since hospitality has already been rendered. Some say it was said because it lacks the defining characteristic of a formal reproach.
When one who has come saying, “I shall reprove you after standing [in my place],” he breaks that position; he acts [to invalidate it].
Some say that even if one performs all three, it is only a single offense because they constitute a single statement. Some say that one breaks three points. The Elder Upatissa says:

"One does not break the formal charge (*codanā*) and so forth; rather, desiring to charge him, one has done what should not be done, and thus there is an *dukkaṭa* for the breach of the rule of conduct.
However, the Elder Dhammasiri says: "If one sits on the seat, then by that single act of sitting, two [offenses are incurred]."
"He breaks two bases. If he accepts material gifts, by that single act of acceptance he breaks two bases.
If he speaks the Dhamma, by a single utterance within the limits prescribed for the teaching of the Dhamma, he breaks two bases;
it is with reference to this that it was said. When "where" is mentioned, it means one must go into his own presence.
It seems as though it has been said. Therefore it was stated: "But the phrasing does not coincide. "Commanded by the lay followers" means [commanded] by them.
"Without consenting to the root" means, since the root is unallowable (*akappiya*), not consenting to it; and that is by way of the mind, not by way of speech.
If, when this is said, one considers it to be showing what is unallowable, then even while desiring the unallowable with the mind...
If one indicates what is allowable by mouth, saying, "Give me a robe," it is not permitted. Upon receipt, there is an offense under the training rule concerning the acceptance of money (*rūpiya*).

Herein is the analysis: even if one consents in the mind, if one expresses it through a formal expression of what is allowable (*kappiya-vohāra*), saying, "Bring this and that allowable article worth a kahāpaṇa or worth a quarter [of a kahāpaṇa]," although one speaks with reference to money, [it is not an offense].

It is indeed permissible. Why? Because it is stated that regarding a certain plot of land suitable for cultivation, "if they say, 'We give [it] as a boundary,' it is permissible," and because it is stated that when one says, "We give [it] to the monastery," "it is not permissible to refuse.
However, in the *Anugaṇṭhipada*, it is said: "What is given with reference to the Saṅgha, saying 'We give [it] to the monastery,' is heavy property (*garubhaṇḍa*)."
It is not permissible for him to accept the water of dedication (*dakkhiṇodaka*), nor to say “Excellent!”, nor to offer a formal expression of thanks (*anumodana*).
Why? Because the Sangha lacks the designation “monastery” (*vihāra*), whereas the field itself possesses the designation “boundary” (*sīmā*).

That which is made an object by the mind is immeasurable; only the conventional expression of what is allowable (*kappiya-vohāra*) is a valid measure. Because only what is allowable has been declared, [the Blessed One said]: “But indeed, I do not...”
This is not contradicted even by the statement: "Monks, I say that gold and silver should not be accepted or sought after by any means whatsoever.

For it is with the intention that "by means of the mention of what is allowable (*kappiya*), the donor will himself know what is appropriate to do," that the donor, having understood this intention, places [the gold] into the hand of the steward (*kappiyakāraka*) for the monk.
“It becomes the property of those who are present. All of this is inappropriate; why? Because the statement regarding the monastery’s boundary is actually a statement regarding the donor.
And in this case, the word of the monk is the authority. For this very reason, it was said:
“Furthermore, when it is said, ‘I give my pond or lotus-pool to the Saṅgha,’ and [the donor] says, ‘Excellent, lay follower! The Saṅgha shall drink the water,’ and so forth...”

"It is indeed permissible to consume it. Otherwise, one would fall into the logical error that a monk’s statements regarding land connected to a field become valid by means of a statement concerning a boundary.
Furthermore, when a monk who does not reside in a monastery is shown silver and told, "I give this to the monastery," he must not refuse it, even though he knows it is being given for his own sake.

Likewise, there is no offense for one who speaks in such a manner with reference specifically to someone who knows that an object worth ten *kahāpaṇas* or more is an unallowable article, or who knows it is merely a *kahāpaṇa* or the like; thus [the rule] applies.

However, because it was stated without exception in the words, “But not in any way whatsoever, monks,” it is our opinion that one cannot apply a figurative interpretation (*lesa*); rather, it must be understood after careful consideration.
By the statement, “If he does not wish [it], it should not be spoken,” it is shown that there is no offense of *dukkaṭa* for failing to perform the aforementioned courtesy.

By the statement, “One should act as if toward those who are strangers and have not invited one,” it is shown that if one accomplishes [the task] without even performing the aforementioned courtesy, one is to be dealt with according to the training rule concerning requests made to strangers (*aññātaka-viññatti-sikkhāpada*).
