The preparers of what is allowable (*kappiyakāraka*) themselves...
If they give after being prompted, it is permissible. Some say, "The act of making [the gift] oneself is what is prohibited.

Regarding the phrase "The same method applies to alms-food and so forth," some say there is a *dukkaṭa* offense; however, that is not correct, because by the inclusion of the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "even when they are giving," it is precisely a *nissaggiya-pācittiya*.
Regarding gold and silver, [the text says]: "If requested for the Saṅgha, it is a *dukkaṭa*."
And they divert it. Since that [case] was not mentioned specifically as new, he shows that it is indeed a *pācittiya*.
They say, "It might even be a *nissaggiya* among the *yevāpanaka* training rules," but this must be examined. For, according to the statement, "For anyone else...
[as stated] in the Mahāpaccarī," for one who accepts [a gift] for the sake of non-ordained persons—even down to mother and father—[the offense is different].
This indicates that it is indeed a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing).
In all instances, "acceptance" (*sampaṭicchana*) is defined precisely by the characteristic stated thus: "one should take [it] oneself, or cause it to be taken, or consent to what has been set aside.
Even so, in some cases it must be refused, while in others it need not be refused.
In some cases, what is prohibited is permitted; likewise, there is something that is not prohibited and is permitted.
To demonstrate all of this, the detailed explanation beginning with “But if…” is commenced.

In that context, from the statement, “It is not permitted for a cetiya...,” it is established that it is permitted to accept what is given to a monastery (vihāra) as being unprohibited. Likewise, regarding the Elder’s [mother]...
Even when it is stated, "Demā" and so forth, the offense for accepting [the gift] is indeed a *pācittiya*. Regarding the phrase "he becomes one who has committed an offense" (*sāpattiko hoti*):
with reference to what offense does he become one who has committed an offense? Some say it is with the offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). It is not with just any offense;
rather, it is said "he becomes one who has committed an offense" because he merely censures [the donor] at an improper time. How so? "Monks, by five factors... [and so on].
Regarding the passage, "A co-resident who is possessed [of such faults] should be dismissed...

[omission] ...in dismissing him, there is no offense," it is not only said that an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) occurs for one who does not dismiss someone who is not conducting themselves properly. As it is said: "And you should not, monks, fail to dismiss one who is not conducting himself properly;
whoever does not dismiss him incurs an offense of wrong-doing. Therefore, even in the absence of excessive affection and so forth, for one who does not dismiss [such a person], [there is an offense].
It is seen that there is no offense (*anāpatti*). Furthermore, it is stated: "He is one who transgresses" (*sātisāro hoti*).
This should be understood in this same manner. If it is argued: "Is it not improper because the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) states, 'He is one who transgresses means he is at fault;

he incurs an offense'? No, for immediately after that, in order to prevent a false apprehension, it was stated: "One who conducts himself properly should not be expelled. Therefore, there is no offense.
Regarding the word *katā*: the teacher says that it constitutes an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*), though this must be investigated.
It has been stated: "Even a permissible commodity (*kappiyabhaṇḍa*) is indeed impermissible; thus, even milk obtained by exchanging it for grain produced from a pond is not allowed.
We shall explain the procedure regarding permissible transactions as follows: "by means of water," and so forth. [It is] difficult to dispose of.
The statement "it happens" is dissimilar to what follows later—namely, "That very thing is improper.
Why? Because grain has already been sorted"—therefore, it is well-stated. For this [case] refers to [grain] being mixed with what has arisen from the beginning through the agency of a bhikkhu.
What is called "new grain" is that which has not been prepared before. Regarding the phrase "or standing in the threshing floor, he guards it": "Do not take this much or that much."
If one guards [the goods] by means of such methods as saying, "This may be taken," or "Take this away, make a heap here," and so forth, that is improper (*akappiya*).

It is said: "If one guards them thinking, 'While I am present, they are protected,' or if one sees someone taking them and says, 'What are you doing?'—this is permissible. This is correct according to the training rule on the acceptance of money (*rūpiya-paṭiggahaṇa-sikkhāpada*).
“For one who lives guarding [the property] after closing the door,” so it is said. That is improper for him alone. Why? Because it has not been previously authorized.
However, it is not permitted to say, “Having cultivated the crop, bring it here.
The same principle applies to leaves as well. It is said, “Because it generates enthusiasm in those who would otherwise do it themselves. Why?
From the statement, "Because of the exchange of *kahāpaṇa* coins," it is established that this is even more so when they have been previously offered.

If the donors, or the people who purchased the village land, fields, monasteries, and so forth from the Saṅgha by means of a contract, say to the householders there, "These *kahāpaṇas* have been brought for the Saṅgha," one should simply say, "It is not allowable. If, however, it is the *kappiyakārakas* themselves...
They say: "It is not allowable for the Saṅgha to have coins (kahāpaṇa), but ghee and such things are permitted.

Therefore, having said, "Point out a person who makes what is allowable for the Saṅgha, or a secure place," and having had those [items] prepared by them—since they cannot be handled by anyone else—one directs [the attendant], saying, "Bring this ghee," and after it has been finished, [one assigns] the other allowable items to others.
It is like the fourth bowl among a set of four bowls. For it is said therein: "Having taken these kahāpaṇas, give this [bowl]";

having been given the kahāpaṇas and thus received, this bowl is not permitted for that very bhikkhu because of its improper acquisition, but it is permitted for others because the price was not accepted from them, and so forth. If this is so, then it would be unallowable for everyone.
Why? Because the kahāpaṇas have already been accounted for. If it is asked, "Is this poorly stated? No;

for this was said with reference to the place where the root [value] was accepted, just like the second and third bowls in the set of four bowls. Therefore, it is said in the section on "making oneself do it":
"It is not allowable"—only this much need be stated. Beyond that, it is called "accepting the root."
Because it involves training in a great domain, this is the "King's Training Rule";
like that of a king, it is difficult to understand even from the intention of the mind.
The commentary on the King’s Training Rule is finished.
The first chapter on robes is concluded. 2.
The Chapter on Silk.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule on Silk.
542. Regarding "made by a silkworm-rearer": those creatures who are commonly designated as "silkworm-rearers" because they produce cocoons are called *kosakārā*.
That which is produced from their cocoon (*kosa*) is called *kosiya*. If it was made by oneself, at the time of relinquishment, one should say: "I relinquish what was made by myself.
If it was made by both [oneself and others], it should be stated exactly according to the text. If it was half-finished by oneself and half-finished by others...
The fourfold set beginning with "he brings [the robe] to completion himself" has not been shown, even though it is possible; for this is the nature of the Vinaya:
that when one threefold or fourfold set has been shown, the other, even if possible, is not mentioned.
The commentary on the Kosiya training rule is finished.
2. Explanation of the Training Rule on Pure Black Wool (Suddhakāḷaka-sikkhāpada) 547. Regarding the phrase "pure black wool" (*suddhakāḷakānaṃ*):
here, whereas in the first rule it was stated, "even with a single thread of *kosiya* wool," there is no such statement here that "it must not be mixed even with a single other [fiber].
Therefore, even when it is mixed with others, provided that the appearance [of the black] is not discernible, [the rule applies].
It should be understood that this is called simply "purely black.
The commentary on the training rule on purely black [wool] is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule on Two Parts.

552. From the statement, “Having held up two scales, they should be taken,” it follows that, just as in the holding of scales one does not take more than the black [fibers], so too, by way of the upper limit, two portions of the black fibers should be taken. How is this known?
By the context of the prohibition against purely black [wool]. The lower limit is indicated by the phrases, “the third of white [wool]” and “the fourth of mottled [wool].”
In the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is stated: "If even a single black wool-fiber exceeds [the limit], it is an offense involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*).
Although this does not accord with the weighing on a scale, since the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) is unintentional, it is our opinion that the intended meaning is:
"Even if only a single fiber were to fall there among those previously weighed and set aside on the scale, it is an offense involving forfeiture."

Otherwise, two scales should not be used; rather, the lighter one should be used. For weighing is not performed by counting the hair. If it must indeed be done by counting, then what is the purpose of using the scale?

Some say this, and they claim: "In the case of *gocariya* and *odāta* [hairs], it is permissible to take them as a single unit and double it. This should be investigated, as it has not been examined in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).
The commentary on the training rule concerning two parts is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Six Years: 562.
“New” means with reference to its making; this indicates the counting of years starting from the very first act of making it.
The phrase "having made" indicates [the period] starting from the day of completion;
the phrase "should be kept" indicates [the period] starting from the time of use.

Since for one who has received formal authorization, even if many [robes] are made in each successive place he goes, provided they are within six years, therefore, what does "another new one" mean—is it another than what was made, or rather...

Is it different from what has been maintained? What is meant here? If it were different from what has been made, then it would be permissible to make another one of those two—either a *dukkaṭa* (offense) or one worn out through use; for that is not prohibited even without the old rug, because it is included among things not forbidden.
However, something other than what has been made is prohibited, and since this is "previously made," there is a contradiction with the immediately preceding training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
Now, if it were something other than what was held [in the previous year], it would follow that the conventional designation (*sammuti*) is meaningless.
If the first-made [robe] has not been used, does the intention mean that even with the existence of the conventional designation, another new one is not permitted?
In this regard, here is the demonstration of the definitive conclusion: the limit of six years each must be understood starting from the day of completion. In that context:
And when the seventh year has arrived, six years are fulfilled. This is, however, by way of the delimitation of months, not by way of the delimitation of years.
The seventh year is called both "fulfilled" and "incomplete.
Therefore, even if the six years are completed while the work is still unfinished, they receive another six years starting from the day of its final completion. And that...
Whether it has been used or not used, it is indeed called "worn.

Since it is said that "the term 'new' is spoken of with reference to its making," therefore, after six years, one should unravel that very same [robe]—whether on account of its having become difficult to maintain or due to the wear and tear of use—and make it anew; from the day of its completion, it may last for a maximum of six years.
It should be kept, or even more than that. If one completes it within [the prescribed period], then, with respect to the act of making it, that very same thing becomes "new";
therefore, it is an offense involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*). Otherwise, there would be no distinction from the phrase "with respect to the act of making it new.
This being the case, what follows? It is the *aṭṭuppatti* (the origin of the rule). For it says: "They dwell full of begging and full of requests."
In that context, it was stated, and that indicates the making of something else. If this is so, does it not follow that there is no distinction [between the two]?
It does not follow. This, however, is its distinction: because the meaning stated as "having obtained what was made by another, he uses it;

there is no offense" constitutes the distinction. What is meant? When it is said, "The term 'new' is spoken of with reference to making," [it implies that using what was made by another is distinct from making it oneself].
Just as the acquisition of an extra robe (*atirekacīvara*) constitutes its arising, so too does its acquisition constitute its "newness.
From the day it is obtained, it may be kept for a maximum of six years. If one should have it made [or cause it to be made] within less than six years...
[as stated], one incurs an offense of expiation (*nissaggiya*); therefore, what is called "new" is spoken of with reference to the very act of making, not to the acquisition.
Because it has not arisen for oneself within the past nine years, it is reckoned as "new.
If one should have it made when it has not been obtained, there is no rule such as "one may make it or have it made according to what is available. Why?
Because there is a specific distinction: having obtained something made by another, one uses it; thus, there is no offense.
The commentary on the six-year training rule is finished.
5. Commentary on the training rule concerning sitting-mats (nisīdana-santhata). 565.
Regarding the phrase “nāssudha koci,” here *assudha* is a particle used in the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). In that regard, although... [it is said] “thus”...
Although the plural form “bhanteti kho te bhikkhū” was spoken, nevertheless, the meaning should be understood as follows:
those bhikkhus having assented to the Blessed One, not one among those bhikkhus approached the Blessed One, except for one.
This is like [the usage] in such passages as “It is well grasped, venerable sir; we choose the Blessed One for one day,” and so forth. “I allow... etc.
"Let them approach me for a visit as they please" means: let them come for the purpose of seeing me.

"We [approach] the Venerable Upasena"—this is said because he is the leader of a group. All [the terms] are stated by way of being a forest-dweller (*āraññika*), an alms-food eater (*piṇḍapātika*), and a wearer of rag-robes (*paṃsukūlika*).
For this very reason, it is said in the Commentary: "Because it is designated as the fourth robe among those spread out. What?
If you say that none of them understand what a *cīvara* is, let it be as it may. What indeed is called a *cīvara*?
Any one of the six types that is subject to formal assignment (*vikappanupaga*) and is of the lowest quality. And what is meant by "woven" and "unwoven"?

It is only that which is woven. By what kind of thread? Surely he does not even see the thread; [it refers to] a pair of Benares cloths (*siveyyaka*) and the one made by supernormal power (*iddhimayika*) belonging to Devadatta.

"He makes it non-clothing. "If that is so, I say that even what has not been woven is [non-clothing]. This being the case, it is established that what is spread out (santhatam) is designated as "clothing" (cīvarasaññitā), because of its commonality with woolen cloth (kambala) by virtue of being made of wool (uṇṇāmaya). But did they resolve (adhiṭṭhahiṃsu) upon that which was spread out?

They resolved it poorly, because it was not clothing and because the spread-out rug had not reached the state of being subject to resolution. Or rather, if they did not resolve upon it, then previously in that regard—
Having established that "these [robes] are not perceived as robes," both [the robe and the perception] are untenable there because of the perception of them as robes.

But what does this mean by saying "it is not fit for formal assignment" (*adhiṭṭhānupaga*)? It follows from that very point; however, if it is not fit for distribution (*avikappanupaga*), it is not a robe.
Otherwise, it is established by the mere statement: "A robe is one of the six kinds of robes"—[which implies] "it is fit for distribution."
It should not be said that it is "the last. Thus, even if it does not come under the category of formal assignment (*vikappanupaga*), it is established as a robe;

and when not coming under formal determination (*anadhiṭṭhānupaga*) and not coming under formal assignment (*avikappanupaga*), it collectively receives the designation "robe. For this very reason, it was said:
"For one who possesses the three robes, a fourth robe, while being used, is permitted only as a shoulder-cloth (*aṃsakāsāva*)."
Furthermore, the designation "santhatam" (a rug) does not apply only to those [specific rugs]; it follows others as well, according to the statement:
"What is called an old *santhatam* is that which has been worn once as an inner robe (*nivāsa*) or once as an upper robe (*pāruta*).

However, the commentator of the *Aṭṭhakathā* explains this by clarifying the intended meaning regarding its non-clothing nature. [The phrase] "worn as an inner robe and as an upper robe" refers to these [rugs] when one is sitting or lying down.
The meaning [is as follows]. Moreover, even though this is so, the designation "robe" (cīvara) continues to apply to what has been spread out. For it is stated in the Khandhaka:

"One may determine (adhiṭṭhātuṃ) the sitting mat (nisīdana), but one must not assign it to another" (vikappetuṃ); in the Parivāra: "Nine robes are to be determined"; in the Nisīdana-sikkhāpada: "Ten spans (vidatthī) [long]" and here:
"'Sitting mat' is said to mean that which has a border (sadasaṃ)"; and in the Aṭṭhakathā regarding this.
“Having spread it out like a rug, one makes three fringes by cutting two places at one end in a space measuring one *vidatthi* according to the Sugata’s span;
with those fringes, it is called ‘with fringes’ (*sadasa*)”;
and, “The sitting mat must indeed be determined [as valid] according to the method already stated; moreover, it must be of the proper measure and only one, for two are not permitted.”
And it has been said: therefore, what is called a *nisīdana* (sitting mat) is a robe among the nine types of robes that must be formally determined (*adhiṭṭhātabba*);
and it is established that this is similar to a *santhata* (rug), being a specific kind of rug made of sheep’s wool.
Likewise, it is established that the *nisīdana* itself is the *nisīdana-santhata*. And in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*, it is stated: "It is one and the same. That being established—
The meaning is: "It is established as being designated as a robe when spread out. Why? Because of the commonality of the term "spread out" (*santhata*).
Here it is asked: How is it that only what is *with* a fringe (*sa-dasama*) does not fall under the category of a robe when spread out?

Since even many [patches], even those not formally resolved upon (*an-adhiṭṭhita*), and even large ones are permissible, yet only what is *with* a fringe falls under the category of a robe when spread out, therefore there must also be a formal resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
"It approaches" means: because it is included among those not yet spread out, even before six years have passed—and even without a formal authorization—one must first relinquish that old one;
for there is the statement: "And that too must be of the proper measure and only one; two are not permitted," provided it has not been relinquished.
Furthermore, it might be argued that a *santhata* (spread-out rug) is made solely for the purpose of lying down, whereas a *nisīdana* (sitting mat)...
"Only that which is not spread out. And this is not a fixed rule, because it is stated: "What is called 'old spread-out' means that which has been worn once and wrapped once.
Here it is said: one need not seek a reason for this, because the formulation of the Vinaya has no other scope.

However, this is the reasoning regarding the fact that a spread-out rug (*santhata*) is not a robe (*cīvara*): first, "But there are three kinds of spread-outs [which are] formal acts of the Vinaya... [and so on].
From the statement in the Aṭṭhakathā, “having made [them] and having obtained [them], it is not permissible to use them,” it is established that those [other materials] are unallowable;
and since six types beginning with linen were authorized by the Blessed One, it is established that silk (*koseyya*) is allowable.
This being so, even a robe made of pure silk has become allowable, let alone a robe that is a patchwork of silk mixed with other materials.

Likewise, since a blanket (*kambala*) is permitted, and that too is pure by virtue of being black in its natural state, let alone a rug made of a mixture of white wool and *gocari* grass, one incurs an offense. Furthermore, there is a mutual contradiction [between the two];
therefore, it is not called a "rug-cloth" (*santhata-cīvara*), but rather it is a "sitting mat" (*nisīdana*), because its measurement, shape, and delimitation are possible.
Regarding this, some teachers have said: "There are two kinds of sitting cloths (nisīdana): those that are spread out (santhata) and those that are not spread out.
Of these, the 'spread out' is indeed [the cloth] already spread. The 'not spread out' is of six kinds, such as linen (khoma) and so forth, or it may be something suitable for that;

this is the distinction between them. To this, it is asked: Why, then, was the training rule (sikkhāpada) "But a bhikkhu [should use] a spread-out [cloth]" not laid down here, instead of [simply saying] "a sitting-cloth" (nisīdanasanthata)?
"Designated"? It is said to be designated in that manner for the purpose of showing that those mats, though known as robes, have been discarded and thus lack the status of a robe.
Therefore, out of fear of breaking their ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), those monks discarded them and undertook all thirteen ascetic practices;
however, they are mentioned as only three by way of showing the head, and the Blessed One [acted] toward them...

The Blessed One permitted the *santhata* (spread). Then it occurred to them: "This *nisīdana-santhata* (seated-spread) is permitted by us as being of the same shape as a sitting-cloth (*nisīdana-cīvara*);
how much more so, then, would a spread already made [as a separate item] be so by virtue of being a fourth robe.
Therefore, lest they should lack the perception of it as a robe regarding that *santhata*, the Blessed One prescribed it as a "seated-spread" (*nisīdana-santhata*) for that purpose.

This is the underlying intention (*adhippāya*). If it is asked, "How is it known that the last two [cases] are permissible? It is because of the statement: "There is no offense if one obtains and uses what has been made by another.
The commentary on the training rule concerning sitting mats (*nisīdana-santhata-sikkhāpada*) is finished.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Eḷakaloma (6.
Eḷakalomasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā) 572–3. Regarding the phrase "for one traveling on a journey":

this indicates that even for one who has set out on an ordinary long journey, the [robes] that have arisen may be carried for a maximum of three *yojanas*, let alone for one who has not yet set out. For one traveling on a journey...

Or, the connection is with the term "nissaggiya" (to be forfeited). Precisely for that reason, since the intention to travel has ceased, there is no offense for one who is reckoned as "not having set out.
For according to this interpretation of the meaning: "If wool should arise for a bhikkhu... [etc.
...even in the absence of a carrier, for one who has set out on a journey along the road, it is a *nissaggiya pācittiya*."

The construction [of the sentence] should be understood as follows. The phrase “a monk who desires may accept them” indicates that an offense occurs when one carries items belonging to oneself beyond three *yojanas*.

By this, it is established that there is no offense for one who does not desire [to keep them] and who carries items belonging to others for more than three *yojanas*. This is the meaning of the words: “should arise for a monk.”
This is indeed explained by the phrase, “having obtained what was taken away. And in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*, it is stated:

“If one goes while having another monk carry [the goods], there is no offense for both. Therefore, it is established that if two monks go as far as three *yojanas* and then exchange their respective goods before carrying them off, there is no offense; for this very reason, in the section on non-offenses...
It is said, “he causes another to carry it. Who does he cause to carry it? One who knows or one who does not know. In this regard, if it refers to one who knows, one must not categorically state:
“If he sets it down thinking, ‘Another will carry it,’ then even when that other person carries it, there is still an offense.
For even one who knows may sometimes carry it himself; thus, [the former view] contradicts the Aṭṭhakathā. Now, if it refers to one who does not know, [it concerns] “in the vehicle of another...”
If one places it in a container and has someone carry it beyond three *yojanas* without their knowledge, it contradicts the Pāḷi which states, "[the goods] are subject to forfeiture.
Furthermore, if both [parties] together have a single article carried, that too would be subject to forfeiture.

This contradicts the logical principle (yutti) which states, "When there is no one else to carry them, they may be carried by hand for a maximum distance of three *yojanas*," without making any distinction.
And this is stated in the Pāḷi. Furthermore, the carrier is of two kinds: sentient and insentient.
The sentient carrier is also twofold, according to whether it knows or does not know its state as wool from sheep, or whether it knows "I am carrying this" or "This person is making me carry this.
Among these, an insentient carrier refers to a river current, a boat, or an ownerless vehicle. A sentient carrier is obvious.

Regarding this, the method of the *Anugaṇṭhipada* states that there is no offense if one causes another person—whether human or animal—to carry something, provided that person knows only as much as, "This person is making me carry this.
This is the interpretation consistent with both the Canon (*Pāḷi*) and the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).
Although it is stated here without distinction that "there being no one else to carry it," [it refers to cases such as] "in another's vehicle or goods..."
Furthermore, from the statement, "or [if he does it] unknowingly," it is understood that the one who actually takes it is intended there;

yet one who knows both that it is wool and "I am taking this" is not intended. Therefore it is said: "If he sets it aside thinking 'another will take it,' even though it is taken by him, there is still an offense," and so forth.
This is because of the absence of a causal agent (hetukattū) therein. For in the Pāḷi—
“Causes another to carry it” is stated from the perspective of the causal agent (*hetukattā*). The other two [cases] are possible here for one who knows.

By the phrase “having placed it in [the vehicle] without knowing,” the text indicates that if one places it in a vehicle or with goods and causes it to travel three *yojanas* while knowing either “this person is causing it to be carried” or “this person is making it pass this place,” they do not become subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*).

“Has it carried away” establishes this as a statement of the instrumental cause; therefore, in the commentary, the phrase “even while the owner is unaware” is said with reference to one who does not know, thinking, “He is having this carried away for me.
The phrase “reminds him, urges him, and makes him follow” is said with reference to one who knows, thinking, “He is making me pass through this place. Even one who is unaware...

It does not exceed the place where it was established by means of the reminders (*sāraṇā*) and so forth, nor does it follow after it. Now, if it exceeds that place by its own will without being restrained by the reminders and so forth, there is indeed an offense for the monk, because it is impossible for him to be the agent (*hetukattubhāva*).

We shall now explain this starting from the place as it was established: "Even when there is no one to take it away" (*asantepi hārake*)—this is said even with reference to the condition of not obtaining someone to take it away.
The first meaning is this: it is an offense of relinquishment (*nissaggiya*) precisely because of the act of taking itself, let alone when there is a person who takes it.
Taking the word *api* in the sense of emphasis, the second meaning is this: it is an offense of relinquishment only when there is no one to take it;

however, when there is someone to take it, there is no offense of relinquishment for one who causes it to be taken by that person. By the phrase "from the Saṅgha... or with one's own wealth," although—

This training rule (*sikkhāpada*) is one that does not require conscious intent (*acittaka*). However, it is explained that an offense occurs only when one has personally accepted wool from a sheep from the Saṅgha or others and travels more than three *yojanas* with it;
there is no offense for one who is unaware, or for one who has not accepted it, or for one who merely passes by something attached to a robe or other item.
In the *Anugaṇṭhipada*, however, it says: "For one who goes while lying down on top of a blanket..."
It is said: "If even a single hair is attached to the robe, there is indeed an offense because it has been disentangled from the blanket.
This is appropriate because, since the blanket was accepted, it was accepted according to one's own wish.
Since it is stated, "There is no offense regarding a finished article," therefore that [hair] counts as a finished article even if it is not many. For that—
By this, the skin is accepted, not the hair. Now, if even the hair is not accepted, it is a "made article" (*katabhaṇḍa*); the rule concerns an article made from hair that is difficult to separate.

This being so, one should show by way of principle that there is a *pācittiya* offense for three factors in the case of an unmade article, and a *dukkaṭa* offense for three factors in the case of a made article;

otherwise, because the triad has already been shown [in the previous case], it would be redundant. "With persistence" (*saussāhattā*) means because the departure has not been relinquished. Because it is unintentional (*acittakattā*).
The intention is that even without the intention to carry it, a monk incurs an offense because the hair exceeds three *yojanas* in length, corresponding to his own capacity;

however, this does not accord with the Pāḷi text regarding "no offense. This is because there is no offense when the distance is within three *yojanas* due to the internal application [of the effort].
By the phrase "carries for three *yojanas*," even one who wishes to lead it on foot for up to three *yojanas* is included within the limit of three *yojanas*.
It is stated that this shows one does not incur an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) at every step; this is appropriate because of the established meaning of the statement:
"having gone three *yojanas* with the intention of staying, he carries it further than that. Furthermore, it is said:
"'He causes another to carry it' means that while still having the effort [thinking] 'I will carry this,' he causes another to carry it. Otherwise, for one who is walking..."
"He placed [it there]; even if he was unaware of it, there may be no offense. Furthermore, it is said:

"But because it was stated according to the method beginning with 'if the vehicle does not come,' the Elder Upatissa declared that for elephants and so forth who have been incited by being carried away and the like, there is no offense only when the mental application (*ābhoga*) has arisen—such as 'we shall do this' or 'we shall carry it away'—and not when it has not arisen. Having reversed [the order]:
"Placed aside" means it has been set outside for both [the owner and the monk], according to the Elder Upatissa.
Some say there is no offense for one who takes a bundle placed outside the boundary and places it inside the boundary; however, this does not seem correct.

575. "Having obtained it, he carries it away" means he carries it beyond the first *yojana*, not from the second *yojana* onwards; the meaning is that there is no offense because there was no opportunity [to steal] once the goods had been prepared.
The commentary on the training rule regarding sheep’s wool is finished.
7. Commentary on the training rule regarding having sheep’s wool washed. 581.
Although in the training rule regarding the washing of old robes, it was stated—setting aside the robe—that one might have "another requisite washed,"...

It is stated in the section on non-offenses (*anāpattivāra*). However, some say that for this training rule (*sikkhāpada*), an offense occurs from the moment it arises through such acts as having wool washed.

Others say that the offense is [only] from the root-offense itself, and not from this [training rule]. Still others say that because wool is not a requisite (*aparikkhāra*), its loss is simply a non-grasping.
To clarify the meaning of this final method, there is this line of questioning:
Regarding the phrase “he causes to wash”: does this term denote the washing in its entirety by including the dyeing and the disentangling, or does it denote it partially by excluding those?
What follows from this? If it denotes the washing in its entirety, then this alone should be stated in all cases, and not the others.
If, however, it denotes it partially, then [the rules] such as “she washes what has not been mentioned” and “he causes to wash what has not been used” would apply here.

There is a contradiction: [the objection] that because it says, “If she dyes or disentangles [hair] without being told, it is an offense involving forfeiture (nissaggiya),” there would be the undesirable consequence [of an offense even for those not instructed]. [Response:
The Blessed One’s words are merely for the sake of elegance in teaching; in some places he uses three terms, in some places one term—they say these are indeed terms used without restriction.
If there is a contradiction here regarding the phrase “if she has the finished article washed,” then [it follows that] “she has the finished article disentangled,”...
If you argue that there is no offense because it would lead to an undesirable consequence—that is, "there is no offense" only in this specific case—is that not so?
No; for the disentangling of pure wool from unprocessed material must be given [as a penalty] from here.

If you argue that disentangling is permitted for those items that have been matted together by washing with water and so forth, then there ought to be no offense for disentangling an old rug (*purāṇasanthatassa*). And yet, that is not appropriate, as it has not been used.
Because of the statement, "he has it washed. By this, it is established that he has it washed, dyed, or disentangled after it has been used;

and thus it is proven that it is indeed an offense involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*). Furthermore, that which is called "used" refers specifically to a finished article. For it is not possible to use raw sheep’s wool;
otherwise, the statement "he has it washed after it has been used" would be meaningless. Indeed, not...
In this context, there is the statement, “He may have old sheep’s wool washed,” just as in the training rule (sikkhāpada) concerning old robes.
There, it was included by way of what is permissible once accepted; here, it is written [separately].

If it is argued that this is a fault of composition (lekhadosa), we say no, because there is no specific reason [to include it elsewhere], and in the training rule on old robes, “unworn manufactured goods” refers to items such as blankets, cloaks, rugs, and so forth.

And by way of the word. Although this meaning is established by this term [“dhovāpeti”], the expression “has [someone] wash” (*dhovāpeti*) may be either absolute (*nippadesa*) or relative (*sappadesa*).
It is absolute in such cases as “she washes what was not told [to her]. It is relative in “he has [someone] wash a finished article.
And in the case of “there is no offense if he has [someone] wash or dye an unfinished article,” or “if he has [someone] comb it out,” [it is likewise relative].
If it is argued that there is no offense because of the authoritative statement, "there is no offense," [we reply:

No, for it would follow that there is an offense precisely because of the authoritative statement. For if the statement, "he has it washed while it is not yet used," indicates that there is no offense for one who has the unfilled *saṇṭhata* (blanket) disentangled, then it is established that there is indeed an offense for one who has the used [blanket] disentangled.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the washing of sheep’s wool is finished.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Money (Rūpiya-sikkhāpada). 583–4.
“All” means all three kinds. As for the passage beginning, “pearls, gems, beryl, conch shells,” although this is mentioned in the training rule concerning kings, [it is included here as well].
"It was stated as a general observation that 'it is not permissible,' but it has also begun to be discussed in its own proper place by way of demonstrating the specific offense.
How is this so? The "own places" (sakaṭṭhāna) of pearls and so forth have been mentioned in the commentary on this [text], for they are not seen here in the Pāḷi;
they are likewise mentioned in the commentary on the Rājasikkhāpada. Not only...
Gold and silver, as well as other things such as fields and land, are prohibited in general terms as "unallowable and not to be accepted," rather than being specified individually.
In the Canon, however, they are mentioned only by their specific names:
"What is called 'cloth-money' (cīvaracetāpanna) is gold or silver, pearls or gems. Therefore, the Rāja-sikkhāpada alone is its proper place.

And here, by the mention of "pearls" and "gems," the inclusion of things belonging to those same categories is already established; therefore, this [category] was not mentioned first, because it was formulated at the very beginning.
If that is so, since it is not mentioned here, what is their own proper place? It is this very place, though not by its literal form, but by its meaning.

How so? For these are the objects for which there is forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) and the objects for which there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) under the Jewel Precept (*Ratana-sikkhāpada*), all taken together as "jewel."
[The items] have arrived; thus, the "article deemed a treasure" (*ratanasammata*) has been introduced as a permissible object (*kappiyavatthu*).

Among those ten treasures, it is established that the pair consisting of silver and gold is an object for which there is forfeiture (*nissaggiyavatthu*), while the remainder are objects for which there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭavatthu*). And because this is established here, in the section on non-offenses (*anāpattivāra*) for the Jewel Training Rule (*ratana-sikkhāpada*), it says:
"He takes [it] on trust as something deemed a treasure; he takes it for a limited time; he perceives it as a rag-robe (*paṃsukūla*)."

It was stated [as permissible], but not as a "jewel" (ratana). However, it is established that the seven kinds of grain, female and male slaves, fields, and so forth, are unallowable (akappiya) according to suttas such as the *Brahmajāla*;
therefore, it is established that these are here objects of wrong-doing (dukkaṭavatthu). For this very reason, in the *Anuyogavatta*, it is said:
"He knows the Dhamma, he knows what is in accordance with the Dhamma; he knows the Vinaya, he knows what is in accordance with the Vinaya. Likewise, even raw meat—

Does one incur an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)? No; because it is permitted here in the Vinaya by such statements as, “Monks, I allow raw meat in the case of a non-human affliction,” therefore even though raw meat is mentioned in the Sutta, it does not constitute an offense of wrong-doing.

Nevertheless, the Teacher says that there is indeed an offense of wrong-doing in accepting it for one’s own consumption; thus, this is not a mere conjecture. [As in the case where one says: “Place it here.”
They say: "When this has been said, there is only the acceptance of what has been set down.
If it is asked, "Is even the handling of what is unallowable not permitted?"—it is written here:

"'It stands depending on both the allowable and the unallowable' means that while it itself is unfit for use, it stands as an allowable article of equivalent value fit for use. [And] by way of being a rag-robe...
It is "based on what is allowable" because it stands upon what is allowable, since it is a standing place and since pointing out a protected spot is permissible.

It is "based on what is not allowable" because for one who says, "Take this," and so forth, it is not allowable. Thus, both "allowable" and "not allowable" refer to such statements as, "It is placed in this spot;
do you not see it? or "These very kahāpaṇas are more skillfully [arranged]," and so on.

Because it is allowable (*kappiya*), it stands supported by what is allowable. When one says, "Take this," because of the improper reflection (*dubbicārita*) on the part of the recipient—who is himself not allowable—it remains supported precisely by what is not allowable for him.
When one says, "Take this," and it has been taken by that person, it does not fall under the rule stated as "he may cause it to be taken";
rather, solely due to his improper reflection, that thing becomes not allowable for him alone.
"In the *Anugaṇṭhipada*, it is stated: 'Because the original receiving [of the gift] was pure, it is like the third bowl among the four bowls received later';
thus says the Elder Upatissa. What need for more? Because it is from a pure source, it is allowable (*kappiya*).

When there is a lapse of mindfulness, it becomes dependent on what is not allowable; therefore, this is not mere logic," says the Teacher. "In the same way, regarding the Saṅgha, a group, and so forth..."

It is said: "Even when [the gift] has been relinquished for the sake [of the Sangha], because it shares the same legal status [as the original object], one should exclude the specific offense. If it is said that "no allowable article was purchased," this indicates the absence of a means [to purchase]. "Having set aside a deposit" means:
if that lay follower says, "This gold is too much; this, Venerable Sir, must not be wasted this very day."
It is said: “Having spoken thus, he places it himself in the place of deposit, or has it placed there by another;
having deposited it as such, if the Saṅgha enjoys the profit obtained from that, it is called ‘enjoying the requisites.
585. This person, it is said, is endowed with these characteristics at the highest level. Thus, even one endowed with these factors may, at a later time, [act] through the influence of greed.
Or if, for any other reason, one causes it to fall after making a sign, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Regarding the dwelling as well, [the reflection] applies to every single use. For that indeed is permissible for one who dwells at the foot of a tree or even for one who dwells in the open air;
however, when there is the intention to dwell by way of standing, sitting, and so forth, it must be reflected upon with each and every use.
Some say that medicinal requisites may serve as a condition at all times. However, the Teacher says this is not a logical conclusion: for those not stored, they may be taken only after the meal;

for those stored, they may be taken even before the meal. For it is said: “If one accepts what is to be used within a watch of the night, what is to be used within seven days, or what is to be used for life, for the purpose of food...
[and so on]... there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). For every swallow, there is an offense of wrong-doing.”

For the *dukkaṭa* offense mentioned in the training rule on eating at the wrong time (*vikālabhojana*) is incurred by eating at the wrong time, not at the right time, because that is the time for food;

however, the offense mentioned in the training rule on storing up (*sannidhi*) is incurred even at the right time, because of the act of storing. For this very reason, only the two categories of "seven-day use" and "life-long use" are stated there [in the rule on storing].

If it is argued that this distinction cannot be obtained because of the phrase "when there is a requisite condition" (*sati paccaye*), we say no, because that would lead to an undesirable consequence (*aniṭṭha*).

And because of the lack of restriction in the wording. For in the Saṇṇidhi-sikkhāpada, it says: "There is no offense if one eats after storing up what is for the time-being (yāvakālika) for the duration of that time;

or if one eats after storing up what is for the watch of the night (yāmakālika) during that watch. Here, by the authority of the words, it refers to one who eats after storing up what is for the watch of the night specifically during the watch—neither before the meal, nor after the meal, nor during the day, nor during the night—but only during the watch itself.

"Non-offense" (anāpatti) refers to the absence of an undesirable consequence. Likewise, in that very same context, it is stated only: "If one stores a medicine for a watch of the night and consumes it after a watch has passed, or stores a medicine for seven days and consumes it after seven days have passed"; it is not stated, "if there is a requisite condition.
Therefore, because of the lack of a rule regarding the wording—since the mention of a "requisite condition" occurs in some instances and does not occur in others—[the rule applies].

There may also be no fixed rule regarding the offense. Even so, one still incurs the aforementioned *dukkaṭa*. If it is argued that this is not the case because *yāmakālika* (medicines for up to six hours) and the other types of medicine do not function as food, we say no;
for when mixed with ghee and such, they attain the status of "refined food" (*paṇītabhojana*).

Furthermore, among all things that may be taken at any time, that which is *yāvakālika* (to be taken until the end of the day) is coarse; therefore, there is no offense for one who receives it for the purpose of nutriment during the proper time.

How much more so, then, for non-gross items such as those permitted for the duration of a watch (yāmakālika) and so forth, since these are permitted solely for the purpose of food. If it is argued that there is no offense regarding items permitted for the duration of a day (yāvakālika) alone, this is not so;
for an offense can arise for one who takes them for a purpose other than food, just as it does for one who takes other things for the purpose of food.
Therefore, the conclusion stated above alone accords with both the canonical text (pāḷi) and logical reasoning (yutti).

Regarding "purification by confession" (*desanāsuddhi*): here, "confession" refers to a formal act of the Vinaya (*vinayakamma*); therefore, the emergence from an offense through that act is also called "confession.

Because it says "consumes" (*paṭisevati*) rather than "accepts" (*paṭiggaṇhāti*), there is no offense for one who, having failed to exercise mindfulness at the time of acceptance, exercises it at the time of consumption.
Those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) are like heirs who have already received their inheritance because they have fulfilled their task; therefore, for them...
They are for personal use. Otherwise, because they do not exceed the limit of what is to be consumed at the proper time (*yāvakālika*), it would contradict [the rules].

Borrowed use is not permitted: in the case of medicine, because it constitutes an offense; in other cases, because it is an improper use; and because it is like eating what has not been authorized, being like a debt. It is written:
"Indeed, from the very beginning there is no such thing as one who is shameless; therefore, no one should be suspected."
The co-residents and others are a burden. Regarding the phrase "because it was taken exactly as given," it is stated here:

"If one gives with one's own hand, it is not permitted"; however, "if, having taken an extra portion, one causes the portion set aside for one's own use on the following day to be given right there, it is permitted.
If one gives in exchange, provided it is righteous (*dhammiya*), it is permitted; if it is unrighteous (*adhammiya*), it is not.
“It is fitting to learn that by means of support through the Dhamma,” it is said. If one asks, “By what authority? It is by the authority of the statement in the Upasampadā-khandhaka:
“When harmony cannot be obtained, there is no offense in sharing [the requisites] or living together.
586. Regarding the phrase “given through forgetfulness”: here, “given through forgetfulness” means it has not been relinquished; therefore, while the recipient is still alive...
If, after receiving bound coins and so forth, the donors take them back again, the monk must confess only a *nissaggiya* offense.

If those donors, having purchased ghee and other items with that unallowable object, give them to the Saṅgha, it is permissible for that monk as well, because the property belongs to the donors themselves.
For the monk [acted] with the perception of "cloth" when thinking, "I am taking cloth."

It was taken in this way, not with the perception that it was money. And this training rule was spoken with reference to taking for one's own benefit; however, he did not take it for his own benefit or for the benefit of others.
Now, if those donors do not come and take it back, then having asked the donors, if it was relinquished for his own benefit, he should hand it over to the Saṅgha.
It has been stated, "The offense must be confessed; if it is not [an offense], then the offense itself must be confessed.

This is contradictory from beginning to end. For if there is a confession of an offense, it is established that silver was accepted; once that is established, the statement "what arises from that is allowable for him as well" is untenable.
If you argue, "It is indeed allowable"? No, because the object has not been relinquished.
"It is not logical that an offense should be confessed. If it is argued that it is logical because the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) is unintentional (*acittaka*), we say no;
for in all instances, there is the statement, "one accepts money" (*rūpiyaṃ paṭiggaṇhāti*). Indeed, it is stated, "one accepts money";
otherwise, the word "money" would be meaningless in every case, since its purpose would be established even without it. And by this [word], the cloth...

If it has been accepted and the donor has given only cloth, yet one takes with a thieving mind even the money contained within that cloth, one is to be dealt with according to the number of steps [taken].
And in the Commentary, regarding the statement "one perceives what is not money as money," it is said:
"One perceives gold and so forth as being coarse leaves and so forth," by way of the expression "he accepts money."
Furthermore, the passage beginning with “Moreover, those desiring merit” is stated for the purpose of showing another method;
for it is precisely because of this that it is said, “One should observe what has been obtained in this house. Otherwise, if one observes in a different manner, there would be doubt;
and when doubt exists, it is indeed a forfeiture (nissaggiya), according to the words, “being in doubt regarding money,” and so forth. Thus, this [other] method would be entirely useless.

One incurs an offense, yet it is not without purpose. Why? Because a kahāpaṇa coin or similar object tied to a hem of a robe was given through forgetfulness and accepted with the perception that it was a cloth;
therefore, it is neither money that was given nor money that was accepted. In this case, there is no requirement to confess an offense;
rather, that [money] must be returned to the donors themselves. Furthermore, whatever allowable goods are acquired from that [money] belongs to everyone.

The teacher [Vajirabuddhi] states that the phrase "Furthermore, those desiring merit" and so forth is not a logical inference (*takkā*), but is intended to show another rule for what is permissible (*kappati*).
The commentary on the training rule concerning money (*rūpiya-sikkhāpada*) is finished.
9. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Bartering with Money (*rūpiya-saṃvohāra-sikkhāpada*).

587. “The exchange of gold and silver” is stated as the upper limit; likewise is the scriptural passage beginning with, “Silver means a coin (kahāpaṇa) of the color of a teacher’s tooth,” and so forth.
From the triplet of rules beginning with, “If one perceives silver in what is not silver and exchanges it for silver,” and from the statement:
“But for one who exchanges an article subject to forfeiture (nissaggiya) for an article subject to an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)… [it is] an offense of forfeiture.”
Furthermore, from the statement in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “It is a *pācittiya* because it was purchased for something of greater value,” it is established that here a lower limit is also obtained.
The Teacher’s coin (*satthuvaṇṇa*) and the *kahāpaṇa*, as well as whatever others enter into common trade—thus should the conjunction (*samuccaya*) be understood here.
In this training rule, however, “of various kinds” (*nānappakāraka*) means even that which has been made...

Regarding the phrase “what has not been done, what has been done and left undone,” five triads (tikas) are stated here based on the threefold classification of money and the twofold classification of non-money;
since one triad is shown by the masters of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathācariya*) in accordance with that, there are six in total. Here it is said:
when one triad-breaker is shown in another training rule (*sikkhāpada*), even though others are possible, they are not [stated].

If it is asked, "Why is it shown right here when [other things] are also shown?"—the answer is: because it was stated in the *mātikā* as "of various kinds" (*nānappakāraka*), it is for the purpose of showing its state of being of various kinds right here.
If it is argued that this would lead to the same necessity of being discussed in the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) concerning buying and selling, the answer is no;
for the method of exposition has already been shown here. Furthermore, in the analysis (*vibhaṅga*) of money, at the end it says: "those which enter into commerce."
Because it has been stated thus, it is established that the teacher’s gold and so forth are indeed fit for use.
Consequently, one would fall into the error of thinking that one does not incur an offense of relinquishment (*nissaggiya*) through trade with gold and silver that are unfit for use;

therefore, in order to show that such an error would arise, the three sets of rules beginning with “exchanging what is made for what is made” have been stated. This being the case, [the phrase] “and those which enter into trade” in the *Rūpiyavibhaṅga*...

If it is argued: "It need not be stated [that they are included]; since even those things that do not constitute a direct exchange (*avaḷañjana*) are already included when that term is not explicitly mentioned, there will be no purpose for stating the three triads beginning with 'done' (*kata*) and so forth.

[Response: No, because there would follow the undesirable consequence (*pasaṅga*) that the exchange of allowable goods (*kappiya-bhaṇḍa*) for allowable goods would also constitute trading in money (*rūpiya-saṃvohāra*).
This is despite the statement, "Those which go into trade... [and the inclusion of] *kamuka* and *kathala*.

If it is argued that there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasanga*) of even the exchange of bronze vessels, cloth, and so forth, being considered "bartering with silver" (*rūpiya-saṃvohāra*), [the answer is] no.
This is because the inclusion of the word "made" (*kata*) and so forth indicates that only unallowable objects such as gold and silver are intended.

Therefore, by both [definitions], it refers to that ordinary silver which is divided into "made" and "unmade," as well as the collection of *kahāpaṇas* and *māsakas*, and that which falls under the designation of *kahāpaṇas* and so forth.

In both cases—here [in this rule] and in the preceding training rule—the intended meaning is established as "money" (rūpiya), and not rice and so forth, because the conventional designations such as "made" and so on are impossible in the case of the latter.
Up to this point, the purpose of the triad beginning with "made" has been stated.
Now, the remaining triads are discussed: for here, the object subject to forfeiture (nissaggiya-vatthu) is money, categorized according to the distinctions already mentioned.

Regarding the term *arūpiya* (non-monetary): since the remainder—whether it be an article subject to an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) or a permissible article—is not "monetary," it is considered *arūpiya*.

However, because one incurs an offense of wrong-doing in the case of an article subject to wrong-doing, the statement “there is no offense for the five who are in accordance with the Dhamma when [one] perceives what is non-monetary as non-monetary” cannot be taken as absolute.
Here, by the authority of the text, it refers to something other than the articles subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*).
Even pearls and the like are indeed called "non-material" (*arūpiya*). If it is argued that there is no offense for the five types of fellow practitioners (*sahadhammika*) in this regard, we say no;
because it contradicts the training rule regarding kings (*rājasikkhāpada*). For in that [rule], it is stated: "pearls or gems.

Therefore, it is established that pearls and the like are unallowable (*akappiya*) and are objects of an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*), since they are absent from the list of objects for relinquishment (*nissaggiya*). This being so, [regarding] "non-material..."

The statement, "There is no offense for one who perceives something as non-monetary when it is among five things that are allowable according to the Dhamma," was said with reference to purely allowable goods (*suddhakappiyabhaṇḍa*), not to all non-monetary items.

However, elsewhere—in the threefold set of offenses beginning with "perceiving what is non-monetary as monetary" and so forth, as well as in the threefold set shown in the Commentary—it should be understood that "all non-monetary items" is meant; therefore, [the following] is for the purpose of illustrating the nature of non-monetary items:
The second triad has been stated. For that very purpose, one triad is shown in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).

If it is asked, "Why was that not stated in the Canon (*pāḷi*)?"—it is because in that [triad], there is no need for the formal act (*kicca*) of granting permission to discard money (*rūpiya*) once it has already been exchanged for non-monetary goods (*arūpiya*).
For if that triad were stated, it would follow that permission to discard even allowable items (*kappiyavatthu*) as non-monetary goods would have to be granted; on account of that...

Is it not the case that the formal authorization (*sammuti*) for discarding money (*rūpiya*) should not even be mentioned? No; for otherwise, it would follow that there is no function for authorization even regarding money itself.

Therefore, if one perceives money as money and exchanges it for an allowable object (*kappiyavatthu*), just like the third bowl in the set of four bowls, that [money] must be surrendered to the Saṅgha or others.
Once surrendered, however, it becomes allowable for others, just like the third bowl.
Now, if it has been acquired by means of money that was accepted [as allowable], it is like a second bowl; even without a formal agreement (*sammuti*), it is permissible for any monk to discard it.
Beyond that, one should proceed according to the method stated in the passage beginning, "If a monastery attendant (*ārāmika*) comes there...
and so forth. In this context, the word "money" (*rūpiya*) or "non-money" (*arūpiya*) occurs everywhere in the locative case.
It should be understood that "one's own" refers to what belongs to oneself, while "what belongs to another" refers to what has come into the possession of another. Here it is said:
"The Elder Upatissa [held] that by the preceding training rule, the acceptance of money was prohibited;
by this [present] pure scriptural passage, however, commercial transaction with a 'maker of what is allowable' (kappiyakāraka) standing by means of allowable goods is prohibited."
589. Regarding "exchanging one article of forfeiture for another article of forfeiture" ... [and so on] ...

in the phrase "by means of this," it is stated that a single offense occurs simultaneously by way of two training rules (*sikkhāpada*) concerning one and the same object; however, that must be forfeited according to the latter rule.
Some say that by this, one also incurs an offense that was already incurred as an article of forfeiture. Of another...

"Exchanging by means of taking silver": since that [silver] does not exist when it has not been taken, there is an offense by this [act] alone, and not by the previous one, as was the case with slander.
For even when one speaks falsely by means of false speech, the offense is for the slander itself.

To show the reasoning for the statement "there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) by means of the object subject to relinquishment... the same method applies," he said, "For whoever... and so forth.
"Of one employing interest": here, if one says, "Having taken this, give me so much after a month or a year," there is trading in money.

If one says, "Let there be this much interest; take this much," without a *kappiyakāraka* (an agent for making things allowable), there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*), because it lacks the characteristics of buying and selling.
The phrase "to the owners of the principal in the principal," etc., is for the purpose of showing the means for making [the transaction] allowable.
It is stated that it is not only abandoned and unfit for use; however, if it is made [into a bowl] again in this way, it is permissible to use it.
If there is no means of making it allowable (*kappiyakaraṇa*) for its use, then what is allowable must be pointed out.
As for the means of making it allowable here according to the Canon, that same method applies to the third bowl as well: "And just as for one's own sake..."
It is stated: "When [the bowl] has been taken, such a means [is required]; likewise, even when it is taken for the sake of the Saṅgha, this same [means applies].
It is said that for these first and second bowls, as long as they are being used by a householder, there is no means of making them *kappiya* (permissible);

even for a period of many generations of men, they remain "indeed impermissible," as stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. However, in the *Anugaṇṭhipada*, it says: "Having sold the Saṅgha’s own *kappiya-bhaṇḍa* (permissible goods)..."
Even coins that have been brought must be accepted only after the formal act of acceptance (*paṭiggahaṇa*) has been relinquished;
therefore, if a *kappiyakāraka* says, "These are those coins," it is not permitted at all—it must be refused and not deliberated upon.

If one deliberates upon them, it is not allowable for anyone. If, however, one deliberates upon coins that have been accepted after the formal act of acceptance has been relinquished, [it is not an offense].
"It is not permissible for him alone"—this has been stated repeatedly.
The commentary on the training rule concerning trading with money is finished.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Buying and Selling.

593. Regarding "pieces of cloth" (*paṭapilotika*): it means by means of pieces of cloth. The phrase "he transgresses, there is an offense of wrong-doing" (*ajjhācarati, āpatti dukkaṭassa*) should be understood as applying to the preceding training rule as well.
The statement beginning with "his own goods," which is the reverse of the words "it has been bought and sold," was spoken for what reason?

Because it conforms to the expression "this [in exchange] for that. Furthermore, the misappropriation of what has been given in faith (*saddhādeyya*) here should be understood by way of the terms denoting impossibility (*aṭṭhānapada*).
The commentary on the training rule concerning buying and selling is finished.
The second chapter, the Chapter on Silk, is finished.
3. The Chapter on Alms Bowls.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule on Alms Bowls (Pattasikkhāpada) 598.

Regarding the phrase "accumulating many bowls" (*bahū patte sannicayaṃ*): here, *sannicayaṃ* is a neuter abstract noun. The meaning is that they will take many bowls and make an accumulation. It is written: "They are the ones who take [bowls] weighing thirteen and a half *pala*s.
Herein: "A *kuḍuva* consists of four *pala*s; four times a *kuḍuva* [is a *māsa*];"
"Fourfold for a meal, fourfold for a month"—thus they say it is "fourfold in sequence.
Having first shown this worldly convention, some elaborate further:
"Khādana means solid food such as soup and the like; 'the measure of a condiment' is said to be one-fourth part of the boiled rice."
Since it is stated in the *Brahmāyu-sutta-aṭṭhakathā*, one should understand that a condiment is appropriate as the fourth part of a morsel (*ālopasa*).
As for the statement, "Because the accumulation of bowls is prohibited for a bhikkhunī, the second [practice] is also prohibited for bhikkhus by way of conformity to that," this is not correct;
for in the Pāḷi it says, "Should he make an accumulation means: not formally determined (*anadhiṭṭhita*) and not assigned (*avikappita*)."
It has been stated. For in the Kathina-khandhaka, even a single item—just like accumulated storage—is called "accumulation" on the following day.
However, in the immediately preceding training rule (sikkhāpada), it is said that "the second is prohibited," thus the formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna) is fixed;
therefore, one is not permitted to determine two bowls. If one determines them as one, neither of the two is determined. Separately...
They say that one person resolves [the robe] while the second does not resolve it. However, many may also perform the act of assigning (*vikappana*).

Now, with reference to what is to be said, it is stated: "The distinction lies merely in the name. In this context, "name" refers to such designations as "middling," "middling-inferior," or "middling-superior," and so forth.

608. If it is argued that even a bowl that has been formally determined (*adhiṭṭhita*) loses its determination because it becomes white due to a harsh firing—on account of the statement, "For due to the deficiency of the firing, it does not attain the status of a bowl"—we say no.
This is because [the loss of determination] is not included among the nine ways in which determination is lost.
Therefore, it is only due to the deficiency of the first firing that it does not attain the status of a bowl; when such a case exists, one may request another bowl.
It is not permissible. For it is stated: “by one with less than five repairs. Indeed, when there is a hole or a crack, the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) is lost because of them;
thus, this prohibition does not apply once [the bowl] has been relinquished. Therefore, even after returning it and making a formal assignment (*vikappa*), one is not allowed to ask for another.
Thus, regarding the phrase “one who makes a bowl obtains the raw material,” it refers to starting from the day it was set aside after being cooked. One who wishes to give it...
"Having offered": here, the ten-day period should be understood as starting from the day it was given or the day it was heard of.
However, in the case of a change of sex, for a monk who is the owner of the bowl, it becomes *nissaggiya* after the lapse of ten days; for a nun, it becomes *nissaggiya* after the lapse of one night.
The commentary on the bowl training rule (*patta-sikkhāpada*) is finished.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Fewer than Five Bowls (Ūnapañcabandhana-sikkhāpada) 612–3.
"They request many bowls" means that while requesting one by one, many monks request many bowls;
or, the meaning is that many monks request bowls. "Monks, a bowl must not be requested; whoever..."

Regarding the statement, "If she should request it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," does this training rule (*sikkhāpada*) apply to one who has less than five repairs remaining, or not?
It does not apply; for some say that because it is stated, "If she requests it, there is wrong-doing in the act," it refers only to that [specific case].
Others say that even after obtaining it, having exhausted it, that wrong-doing was stated; therefore, by means of its acquisition, it is to be relinquished (*nissaggiya*).

By this [phrase], "it has been destroyed," it is shown that [the offense] has been eradicated. Otherwise, one would incur a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) along with a *nissaggiya* (relinquishment) offense, which would contradict the section on non-offenses (*anāpattivāra*).

Furthermore, any form of communication (*viññatti*) not performed at the time when it was permitted constitutes only a *dukkaṭa*. In the phrase "by means of breaking" (*bhinnehi*), the suffix indicates a characteristic mark of a state already attained (*itthambhūtalakkhaṇe*);
or else, the meaning is "by the act of breaking," where the instrumental case is used in the sense of a cause (*hetvatthe karaṇavacanaṃ*).
The commentary on the training rule concerning fewer than five ties is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Medicines (Bhesajja-sikkhāpada): 620.
Based on the statement, “She was adorned with a golden garland,” [it is understood that] except for those who share the same Dhamma, one may [use them] as one pleases for others.

It is permissible to give silver and to have it accepted; "it should be made to be taken away," says the Teacher. This must be investigated because of his mastery over psychic power (*iddhi*) and the range of that power.

By the statement, "The meat of which is allowable," it should be understood that although ghee and other such items belonging to those for whom meat is not allowable may themselves not be allowable, they are nevertheless not *nissaggiya* (relinquishable) objects. Likewise, they are not objects consisting of luxurious foods.
“Set aside after being received” means set aside for the purpose of consuming. For the other [type of food], it is permissible to consume it after having formally accepted it.
“Of both kinds” refers to those prepared from what was accepted after the meal and those accepted before the meal.
Having stated a pseudo-justification with the words “because meat is unallowable,” they ate at an improper time.

"It is said: 'The Elder’s intention is that one who wishes to eat only the butter must remove what is contained in the curd and buttermilk; for one who wishes to cook it, there is no need for his own cooking.
From the statement 'it will go to destruction,' it is established that ghee cooked by adding milk is permissible at an improper time (*vikāla*).
By 'medicines' (*bhesajjehi*) is meant the medicines to be used for as long as life lasts (*yāvajīvika*). [This refers to] prepared oil."
“Before the meal” means exactly that which has been prepared after having paid respect [to the donor]. Regarding “with warm water,” some say it indicates the state of being heated;
however, that is not correct. “From what has been extracted,” such as from oil-cakes and so forth. Because of the statement, “If received for the purpose of oil... [etc.

...it is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),” [this refers to] oil made from things received for purposes other than oil, even if seven days have elapsed; starting from the day it was made, [the rule applies].
"It is permissible for seven days" means that the shadow is still visible; some say *karamanda* is the heartwood of a tree.
(623) Because they cook oil by adding milk and other ingredients to the dregs (*kasaṭa*), therefore the dregs are not permitted;
only the oil is permitted. For this reason it was said: "He is apprehensive, as if [dealing with] the dregs of cooked oil. Together with the fat...
If it is argued that it is not permissible because it is cooked, then speak, venerable sirs, regarding the connection with "lumps of curd in butter" and so forth.
Regarding honey, the four time-periods (*kālika*) should be applied according to what is possible, as well as in the case of sugarcane. How so?

Honey containing bees and froth is "to be used until the end of the day" (*yāvakālika*). Honey free from bees but mixed with water is "to be used for a watch of the night" (*yāmakālika*); if unmixed, it is "to be used for seven days" (*sattāhakālika*).
Honey and molasses are pure and may be kept for life. Likewise, sugarcane or its juice with the fibers is "for the time of a day" (*yāvakālika*);

when the fibers are removed and mixed with water, it is "for the watch of the night" (*yāmakālika*); when not so mixed, it is "for seven days" (*sattāhakālika*); and dried fibers are to be understood as "for life. Why? Because of the distinction made by mixing with water.
What is meant? Among the four types of allowable times (kālika), each preceding one is heavy and each succeeding one is light.
And herein, this mixing with water makes the heavy light and the light heavy. For mangoes and the like are heavy because they are "allowable for as long as life lasts" (yāvakālika);
however, by being mixed with water, they are given the designation of "mango-drink" and so forth, and thus become light, being "allowable for a watch of the night" (yāmakālika).

It makes [it so]. From the statement in the Aṭṭhakathā, “What is called ‘molasses’ (phāṇita) arises from sugarcane, depending upon sugarcane juice,” it is established that sugarcane juice is for seven days.
In this regard, much has been said and applied, such as, “The mixing of water makes it ‘for a watch of the night’ (yāmakālika),” and so forth.
Furthermore, in this context, sugarcane juice—because it was authorized by the Buddha with the words, “Monks, I authorize sugarcane juice”—is like molasses-water.
Even if it is not mixed with water, sugarcane juice is permitted for one who is not ill because it shares the same nature as sugarcane juice;
for this very reason, the Commentary states: "Sugarcane juice that has been strained is permitted after the meal. The Teacher says that all of this is "not with buttermilk" (*no takka*).
However, some say: "Because of the statement, 'Phanita is produced from sugarcane,' and because of the Commentary's statement, 'taking sugarcane juice as the basis'..."
"And *ucchuraso* (sugarcane juice) is indeed *phāṇita* (molasses); therefore, one should proceed [with it] as with jaggery.

Some say: "Even though, according to the stated method, it is for a seven-day period, because it was separately authorized by the words, 'Bhikkhus, I authorize sugarcane juice,' it is permissible for one who is not ill even when it has not been mixed [with other substances].
Others say: "Precisely because it was separately authorized by the stated method, whether it is mixed or unmixed..."
Some say, "Or it may be for a watch of the night; however, molasses-water is strictly for seven days. Others say, "Like molasses-water, both of these are indeed for seven days only.
Regarding this, the following is the investigation according to the first teacher’s view:
since the permission for sugarcane juice is established by the very permission for treacle.

If one were to extract [the phrase] "sugarcane juice" separately and claim that the *anumati* (permission) is purposeless, then likewise the *Aṭṭhakathā* statement, "sugarcane juice that is free from sediment is permissible after the meal," would also be purposeless.

One might argue that it should have been stated as "it is permissible for seven days," yet it cannot be stated thus. If you say this is because the authority concerns what is permissible after the meal, we say no.

Because, in that context, there would be the undesirable consequence of it being impossible to say [it is permissible] for seven days. If you argue that it is stated because it has entered into the section on flavor (*rasa*) without regard for the distinction of time, [we reply:
one cannot say, "It is permissible for seven days when free from admixture.

If you argue that it is not to be so stated because the section on flavor concerns what is permissible after the meal, [we reply: No; for if it were stated thus, this [flavor] would be like any other flavor.

It is permissible only after the meal, and not beyond that; otherwise, one falls into an offense. If it is argued that it is said to be "permissible after the meal" because it cannot be consumed beyond that time, we say no, for that would entail the consequence [of it being] *yāvakālika* (suitable for the duration of the day).

That consequence does not apply even to sugarcane juice kept overnight, because by boiling it, there is the possibility of it turning into molasses and the like. This very point applies to the third and fourth teachers' views.
Investigation (*vicāraṇā*). In the second discourse, the investigation has been stated; however, the crushing (*vimadda*) will be clarified here in the *Bhesajjakkhandhaka*.
"Treacle" (*phāṇita*) means that which is produced from sugarcane; it is a specific term for treacle as a source-substance distinct from honey, palm-nut, coconut, and other sources.
By this, it is understood that [this refers to] treacle that constitutes a source-subject for forfeiture (*nissaggiya-vatthu*).
"Here, 'molasses' (phāṇita) means that which is produced from sugarcane itself, not that which is produced from honey-plant (madhuka) and so forth.
By this much, it is established that not everything produced from sugarcane is called "molasses" alone.
