For this very reason, in the Khandhaka, molasses was first permitted, and only afterwards was sugarcane juice permitted; likewise, in that same place, sugar (guḷa) and sugar-water (guḷodaka) were permitted.

However, regarding the phrase "starting from sugarcane juice" (*ucchurasaṃ upādāya*) and "uncooked" (*apakkā*), those who hold the view that "sugarcane juice is permissible for a watch of the night" explain the meaning as follows:
"Uncooked by others" means cooked by the bhikkhu himself; or "uncooked" means cooked without a [proper] vessel.
This is not correct, because it would follow that the statement "starting from sugarcane juice" would be rendered purposeless.
Because a bhikkhu has no authority over cooking. If it is argued that "cooking by oneself" (*sāmapāka*) is what is intended here, that is incorrect;
for even sugarcane juice that has not been cooked by oneself becomes molasses through their own intention, and because the subsequent method is shown in such passages as:
"molasses made from sugarcane juice received before midday and not strained. In that context, [the text says]: "made by oneself from unstrained sugarcane juice..."

The statement, "Only that which is non-material (nirāmisa) is permissible," indicates that whatever dregs or thick residue are produced there do not constitute a cooked meal (*sāmapāka*), but rather make it something accepted and prepared with a physical basis (*savatthuka*).
Therefore, the ancients say it is not permissible to accept [such things] at an improper time (*vikāla*).
Regarding crushed sugarcane and molasses, they say: "Because it is coarse and cooked with a physical basis—like a dye-liquid—it is permissible only before the meal (*purebhatta*)."

It has been stated. The teachers of the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* said: "In this way, the mention of 'molasses' (*phāṇita*) implies it is not sweet; therefore, it is not permitted after the meal. [The question is:
Is it because of its sweetness or its lack of sweetness?

It seems that the Elder Upatissa said that it was stated thus in the *Mahāpaccarī* in order to demonstrate the actual meaning. That is appropriate, for it was stated because it is produced from sugarcane.
For this very reason, he said: “But sugar-candy... is permissible. It is recorded that “they cook it by putting it into a pot of milk.
What is called *jallikā* is froth and so forth.
By speaking of it as being of the nature of medicine (*bhesajja*), the others are stated by way of their extraction of meaning. [The phrase] “capable of pervading for the purpose of food” means...
This was stated because it is said in the Khandhaka: "Whatever may be medicine, and whatever is considered medicine by the world, should serve the purpose of nutriment.
The investigation regarding this will be revealed in the Bhesajjakkhandhaka. 624.
"Door-panels and window-shutters" means the panels for the door and the windows. By the mere addition of astringent decoction (kasāva).
For those [substances] have abandoned their own intrinsic nature; therefore, it is said, "they are to be smeared.
They say that "kasāva" refers to *kanakalamba* and so forth. "He resolves" means he arouses the thought: "Now this shall not be for internal consumption, but shall be for external use.
In this context, the word "assigns" (*vikappeti*) does not exist. Resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*) also...
It was stated [in the *Mukhāruḷhi*] by way of a formal resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna*): “I resolve upon this butter,” because it cannot be said [otherwise].
As for the statement that “it is not permitted to consume it,” this was said with reference to the absence of mutual trust.
If there is mutual trust, it is permitted; for in the words “consume it yourself,” it has already been relinquished. Therefore, there is no offense for either of the two.

The connection [is as follows]: it is established that if it has not been relinquished, there is an offense. Therefore, a robe belonging to both [monks] must be formally determined (adhiṭṭhātabba) by whichever one of them is present. It is also logical [to conclude] that if he does not determine it, it becomes subject to forfeiture (nissaggiya).
If even a mere kākani measure of its value has been taken without being given, [it is said]: "It is not fit for determination... [etc. ...it does not attain its own status."
This is not the same as that, nor is it like what was given to the groups of Abhidhamma specialists. Why?

Because the Abhidhamma specialists may even be those who are not yet fully ordained (*anupasampanna*), and subsequently, when they have become Abhidhamma specialists, that [gift] becomes common property for them both.
In this case, however, both are indeed fully ordained; thus, there is for both of them the right to use it as they wish and a sense of ownership. It is not...
Thus, this is common to others as well; and as long as two or three bhikkhus do not make an agreement, saying, "We shall observe the rains retreat together," it remains protected.
This is similar to the point that "there is no offense because of non-division":

if one person gives to another what was received by a certain root [of ownership], or if he gives that to the other, since there is an act of receiving, there is an offense of relinquishment (nissaggiya) upon the lapse of seven days.
Therefore, that robe must be determined (adhiṭṭhātabba) by one of the two who are present together.
Although no formal procedure (payoga) is seen here because there is an absence of a determining procedure for the two who possess common requisites, nevertheless,

since an offense may arise for one of two who share all their belongings upon the lapse of time regarding oil and so forth that was accepted by him, [it must be determined] in the absence of such determination.

And it is said, "it must be determined," because it is a cause for a specific kind of scarcity. That is incorrect, because the bowl, the robe, and the seven-day medicine have dissimilar modes of procedure.
For in this case, regarding the bowl and the robe, an offense occurs upon the lapse of time for one who does not determine them once they have come under his own possession;
however, the seven-day medicine, even though it belongs to another and is held in common, [is subject to a different rule] for the recipient once it has been accepted.
If the time limit is exceeded, it constitutes an offense. In this case, the act of receiving is the determining factor, not the fact that the item belongs to oneself;

furthermore, it is a *nissaggiya* (to be relinquished) offense for keeping anything intended for a seven-day period beyond that time. It is not edible for anyone. There is no offense in using the bowl or robe belonging to another.
Moreover, even if this [seven-day medicine] has been kept past its time, it is permissible after one has relinquished it and subsequently obtained it again. However, as for the bowl and robe...
"Regarding the disciplinary act (*vinayakamma*) for him: it is allowable. Even for one who has not divided [the property], the giving of this [robe] is valid, but not that of the bowl and robe.
For it is said in the Commentary: "It belongs to two people... even if they give it to the resident pupil (*saddhivihārika*) and others without having divided it, it remains as if not given.
Since the very act of giving is not valid for him, how could there be a formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*)? One.
If one gives that bowl and robe to another on the tenth day, from that point onward he is permitted to keep them for ten days;

however, since this is not the same as the seven-day limit (*sattāhakālika*) when examined in every respect, they are not similar, and thus it should not be regarded as essential—this is the teacher’s reasoning. But "without relinquishing [them] by means of a formal disciplinary act" (*vinayakamma*)...
It is said: "Even if something has been relinquished to someone after being suddenly lost, it is not permissible to recover it and use it again.
If a robe has become subject to forfeiture because it was separated by a different country or separated by the ocean, that robe must be relinquished here by a monk standing in this place;
having made the relinquishment with a mind free from attachment, and without looking back at it, he should confess the offense.

It should be taken up again with his trust and formally determined; for it is said, "This same method applies to bowls and so forth," and "Even palm-sugar, coconut-syrup, or molasses is only seven-day medicine.
"If the property of two is received by one, it is a seven-day medicine;
if the seven days pass, he does not incur an offense, yet neither of the two is permitted to consume it."
Some say, "It is permissible," and others say, "The same rule applies even when [ghee or other items] belonging to another have been accepted and set aside.
However, no formal rule is found stating that ghee and so forth—which constitute an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)—must be relinquished and may then be used again.
The commentary on the training rule regarding medicines is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule on the Rain-Cloak (Vassikasāṭika) 627.

Regarding the phrase "having made it only one," the Elder Dhammasiri says that even when making a relative mindful by means of the characteristics of the rain-cloak, only one [rain-cloak] should be taken.
As for the "fourfold field," although it is threefold here—
It is seen; however, it should be understood in this way: that field which is permitted to be sought after is called the "field for seeking.
It is said, "In this way, the fields for making, wearing, and determining [the robe] are also [to be understood].

Here, the inclusion of the former by the latter is to be understood, not the inclusion of the latter by the former; "according to what is obtained" is the teacher's view. Its meaning is: by means of the field for determining...
The latter [robe] includes the three preceding ones; likewise, by way of the field of wearing (*nivāsana-khetta*), it includes the two preceding ones.
However, by way of the field of making (*karaṇa-khetta*), it includes only the one preceding one.

Herein, although there is no difference in time between the field of making and the field of wearing, there is a difference in action, because of the scriptural statement: "It should be worn having made it a bone [of contention]."
Therefore, it is stated in two ways because of the absence of one or the other, and because the purpose of that [other] is already accomplished.

If it is asked, "How is it known that there is no difference here?"—it is known from the Pāḷi, for the Pāḷi says: "When half a month of the summer remains, having made [the calculation], one should put on [the robe]," and likewise from the Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā.
Thus it was said: "The last half-month is also the field for making and wearing [the robes].
By this method, it is established that the field is indeed threefold. However, in some manuscripts of the *Samantapāsādikā*, it is stated:
"From the first day following the full moon of Jeṭṭha-Mūla until the Uposatha of the dark fortnight—this is one half-month, which is both the field for seeking [robes]..."

Regarding the phrase "and the field of application": for within this interval, it is permissible to seek out a rain-cloak (*vassikasāṭikā*) that has not yet been obtained, and to make one that has been obtained;

however, it is not permissible to wear it or to formally resolve (*adhiṭṭhātuṃ*) upon it. Such a reading is seen [in some texts], but it is not the correct reading, because it contradicts the commentary on the matrix (*mātikā*) of the aforementioned Canon.
Therefore, in that context, it should read: "It is permissible to seek out one that has not been obtained; it is not permissible to make one, nor to wear it, nor to resolve upon it."
The reading should be understood thus. In this way, first of all, the establishment of the prior period by means of the subsequent one is to be understood;

for it is not possible to establish the fields for making [the robe] and so forth by means of the prior one. Indeed, only this much is stated: “When one month of the hot season remains, the vassikasāṭika robe should be sought.
For it is not said in the Aṭṭhakathā: “This half-month is both the field for seeking and the field for making.”

If it is argued that this is because it has been so stated, we say no; for that is due to a scribal error, as it was established accordingly. However, there is an inclusion of the field of wearing by means of the field of making, because there is no difference in time;
for that very reason, the inclusion "as available" was made previously, and it was indeed established in that way.
There is no distinction, and the purpose has already been stated. By means of the field of wearing, there is the inclusion of the field of formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*).

It is not so; for the latter cannot be understood as being included within the former. If you argue that there is no contradiction with the Canon (Pāḷi), we say no, because its meaning has not been understood.
In the passage, "One month of the summer remains" or "Half a month of the summer remains," the word *iti* means "from this point onward.
Since the subsequent portion shows the field of offenses (*āpattikhett*), the other portion is thereby shown to be the field of non-offenses (*anāpattikhett*).

Even for one who procures [a robe] from a place where it was previously given or where relatives have invited [donations], there is an offense of expiation (*nissaggiya*) because it pertains to the "back-season.
Those naturally known as "givers of the rainy-season robes" are those who give annually to either the Saṅgha or an individual without having been specifically invited;
in such cases, merely bringing it to mind is permitted. For any other [cases], a transgression of duty (*dukkaṭa*) occurs if there is a breach of the rule.
From the statement, “If it has been performed... [omitted] ...it should be determined on the day of entering the rains residence...

[omitted] ...one receives the privilege for six months,” it is indicated that even during the rains residence, one receives the privilege until the final day of the rains season, provided the ceremony has not yet been performed.
If one asks why this was not specifically analyzed: because it is established by implication from the statement, “one receives the privilege for six months.”
It is already established that one obtains [the robe] by means of speech even if it has not been made;

yet, although this is established, the Teacher has undertaken this [section] in order to demonstrate it according to its own form (*sarūpa*), because its own form has not yet appeared, and in order to demonstrate it through logical proof (*upapatti*) since it is difficult to convince others.
"And as it is here, so too regarding a robe that arises within the *kathina* period, one should proceed exactly according to the method stated below."

What is stated in the *Anugaṇṭhipada* is poorly stated, precisely because it contradicts what precedes and follows it therein. Furthermore, that statement from the *Aṭṭhakathā* which was cited as a supporting authority does not actually establish that point.

As for the statement, "If it is not sufficient, one receives the exemption until the full moon of Kattika," this means that for one for whom it is insufficient, the exemption lasts until the full moon of Kattika; that is the field of exemption.

This indicates that beyond that point, not even a single day remains; therefore, it is established that one receives the exemption as long as the deficiency has not been remedied by the full moon of Kattika, but not thereafter.
Likewise, that same statement indicates that what has already been remedied does not receive the exemption;
therefore, the determination must be made on the full-moon day of Kattika itself. "If there is not enough [time], within ten days..."
It is written: "The end of the performance [of the Kathina] within the rains-retreat itself is the limit.
Here it is said: "One should not say 'by means of one, two, or more days,' and so forth. Why? Because the summer days are a time when there is no formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna);
therefore, for that very reason, one should not say in a general sense, 'it should be determined either within ten days or on that very day.'"
"Because of the possibility that the summer days would constitute the field for the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*). To this it is said:
No, because that meaning is not understood. When the commencement of the rains (*vassūpanāyikā*) is ten days away, the summer days are [still] ten days;

and even if the *vassikasāṭika* robe obtained on the first day is finished, it has not yet reached the field for formal determination on the day of the commencement of the rains, because it has exceeded ten days.
And it does not yet become an offense involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*); for this has been stated: "Even if ten days have passed before the commencement of the rains retreat, there is no offense.

Regarding the instruction that "it must be formally determined (*adhiṭṭhātabba*) within the ten days," this was said to clarify that it is not the case that one may determine it at any time during this interval, even on a day in the summer heat;
rather, if it arises on a summer day, and the field for determination is within ten days—
It must be determined within the field itself during the ten-day period; it is stated to show that one should not, having designated it as "not the field," allow the ten days to pass.
Why? Because even the summer days are included in the calculation; therefore, even on days that are not the [specific] field, they are counted, and thus it is said:
"It must be determined within the field itself during the ten-day period."
The commentary on the training rule concerning the rainy-season robe (*vassikasāṭika*) is finished.
5. Commentary on the training rule concerning the taking away of robes (*cīvaraacchindana*). 632.

The word "one's own" (*sāmaṃ*) is stated for the purpose of excluding the perception that it belongs to oneself. For it is only when there is the perception that it is one's own that there is the offense of causing another to take it away or of taking it away oneself.
It is an offense involving forfeiture; therefore, this is an indication of the root category of forfeiture.
Because it is stated as "a robe," it follows by implication that there is no offense involving forfeiture for one who takes what is not a robe.

Although the word-commentary (*padabhājana*)—“having given means having either given or caused to be given”—is appropriate, [it refers to] causing another person to give what belongs to someone else to a different monk. That...
"He should either take it himself or cause it to be taken by that very person"—this was not stated because of the fear of an undesirable consequence;

however, in terms of its actual meaning, it should be understood that if one causes someone else, such as a student (saddhivihārika), to give what belongs to oneself, or causes someone to give what belongs to another through that person's trust, and then takes it back or causes it to be taken back, it constitutes an offense of forfeiture (nissaggiya). And that...

He gave it away without regard for it. If that is so, what about this statement: "One who takes back what was given after having abandoned it should be dealt with according to the value of the goods"?
This was said with reference to one who takes it by means of some other theft, not by taking it while perceiving it as his own;
for that very reason it was said: "But because he took it with the perception that it was his own, there is no *pārājika* offense. Furthermore: "There is no offense..."
This is established by the statement: "He either gives it himself, or he takes it while placing trust in him.
To this extent, it is proven that there is no offense for one who does not take back what was given on a temporary basis.

The statement beginning with "He will receive the *upajjhāya* from us" illustrates the giving of [the status of] a novice (*sāmaṇera*), and that is not intended here. In the Canon, when [one is] fully ordained (*upasampanna*), there is a triad of *pācittiya* offenses.

If it is argued that a *tikadukkaṭa* offense also applies when [the robe] is given to one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*), we say no; for the intention behind that case is not understood here.

If, after giving [the robe] while the person was still unordained, one sees them ordained in the presence of another and takes it back out of anger—or if, after giving it to one who says, "I shall renounce the training and receive ordination in your presence," one later [takes it back]—then [it is an offense against one who is already ordained].
"If he seizes it, it is an offense entailing relinquishment (*nissaggiya*). This is the intended meaning here.
(633) "Even if he seizes much when once commanded, it is an offense entailing relinquishment"—because they form a single connected unit, there is one *pācittiya* offense;
with reference to this, it was said in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*: "When commanded, he takes many; there is one *pācittiya* offense."

However, as for the statement, "Offenses are counted by way of the objects," that was said with reference to the taking [of goods] by one who says, "Take them all," because there is a multiplicity of commands;
for that very reason it is stated there: "By a single utterance, there are numerous offenses.
This being so, the wording of the Canon and the two statements of the Commentary are mutually consistent, and even what belongs to another is subject to forfeiture (nissaggiya).
There is also the case of discarded rags (*paṃsukūla*); therefore it is said, "like gold tied within a cloth. This is stated for the purpose of defining the specific meaning of that term:
when one has covered [the object] as described, with a conscious intent not to take it away, it constitutes a verbal action (*vacīkamma*).

However, this should be understood to apply only to one who causes another to take it away by saying "Give it! while taking it by force; it is not appropriate [to say] that there is "no offense" simply because the other person gives it.

If you argue that this is because of the word [in the rule], or because of the statement in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā* which says, "Whether he gives while pleased or displeased, there is no offense," we say no.
This is because both statements refer to giving according to one's own preference, and because it would lead to the absurd conclusion that there is no offense when taking by force.
Furthermore, it is because of the canonical text (Pāḷi) stating, "Having given a robe to a bhikkhu himself," and because of the definition of the factors (*aṅga*) in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*.

The Teacher says that the claim—“Because it is stated as ‘the state of being ordained’ (*upasampannatā*), it indicates that the status of a monk (*bhikkhubhāva*) must be intended in both cases, namely, in giving and in taking”—is incorrect according to his reasoning. Why?

Because there would follow the undesirable consequence (*anāpatti-ppasaṅga*) that one who gives a robe to one who is not yet ordained and then takes it back at the time he becomes ordained would be without offense. [And regarding the statement: “A robe belonging to one who is not yet ordained...”

If it is argued that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in that case because of the statement, “...or having given another requisite... [etc.]... there is an offense of wrong-doing,” we say no, because that is unproven.

That the state of being fully ordained (*upasampanna*) at the very moment of giving is the determining factor is unproven—whether by commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), by the Canon (*pāḷi*), or by logical reasoning;
therefore, the meaning is that this is not tenable. Having given a robe to one who is not fully ordained...
For one who seizes a robe while the other is still unordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);

or for one who, having given it when the other was ordained, seizes it back while they are unordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing—this alternative interpretation of that statement is also possible;
therefore, because such an alternative interpretation is possible, [the former view] is not tenable, since [the offense occurs] at the time when they are unordained.

Since no separate offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) is prescribed for one who does not take back [the robe] at the time of full ordination after having given it, therefore—as in the training rules concerning the washing of old robes and so forth—the fact of being ordained later is the determining factor here as well.
Consequently, the meaning is that because "being ordained" is stated among the constituent factors (*aṅga*), that [objection] is not tenable.
In this context, "giving" is intended only when there is an expectation of something in return, not a gift given away with detachment (*nissaṭṭha-dāna*).
The Elder Dhammasiri says that this should be investigated.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the taking away of robes is finished. 6.
Commentary on the training rule concerning requesting cloth by means of a thread.

637. Although it is stated in the sixth [case] that "having personally requested thread," the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā* does not say "thread personally requested for the sake of a robe," but rather simply states among the factors, "thread requested for the sake of a robe.
Therefore, it should be understood that even thread requested by another for the sake of a robe is included.

In this context, there is no restriction for anyone regarding the neighbors. Although it is stated, “having requested it himself,” nevertheless, the connection should be understood as “he should have it woven himself” (*sāmaṃ vāyāpeyya*), meaning he should have it woven for his own sake; such is the meaning that should be known.
However, in the Canon, the construction is made with the proximate word; therefore, while the thread is requested by himself, what is requested by another is allowable.
One incurs [an offense]; however, even a robe woven by one who obtained the threads through manual labor or begging is allowable.
If the cloth has reached the maximum size suitable for dedication (*vikappanupaga*), one should dedicate it once while it is still being woven;

there is no need to perform the act of dedication again, because it attains unity with what has already been dedicated. But if, having shown the boundaries, one weaves it like a patchwork garment, with intervals...

It is said: "Once it has been determined, it must be determined again. They say that by the word "by way of acquisition," such things as "I shall have it woven" or "I shall have it set aside" are included within one [act].
The commentary on the training rule concerning the solicitation of thread is finished.
7. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning the Great Weaver (Mahāpesakāra-sikkhāpada) 642.

By his word, both the superior [robe] and the superior measurement made are permitted, but not the gift of food. In some manuscripts, after citing the word "robe" (*cīvara*), a detailed classification is stated; however, that does not accord with the text.
The commentary on the Training Rule concerning the Great Weaver is finished.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Urgent Robes (Accekacīvarasikkhāpada) 646.

As for what was said: “Monks, I allow you, having received an urgent robe, to set it aside until the Invitation ceremony has been performed,” those monks, however, misunderstood the meaning of that statement.
While setting aside their "urgent robe-cloth," they let the robe season pass by. Is this [robe] assigned, or unassigned?
It is assigned, or it belongs to a specific individual (*puggalika*). For that very reason, it is stated later: "Friends, these are our urgent robes.
However, if it is unassigned, because it belongs to the Saṅgha, it does not constitute an offense of relinquishment (*nissaggiya*) for anyone.

Furthermore, by the general statement, "Having accepted an urgent robe-cloth, it may be set aside," it is indeed permissible to set it aside from the day of entering the rains retreat or from the time of the *piṭṭhisamaya* (the period following the rains) until the *pavāraṇā* ceremony, because it belongs to the Saṅgha;

and even a personal robe-cloth is permissible, because it was given with the instruction, "Take it during the time of having completed the rains residence. For such a robe remains [permissible] as long as one has completed the rains residence.

As long as [the robe] has not yet come into the possession of that very donor, so too, even if [a robe] is given with the words, "Take it at the invitation ceremony," during the third or fourth year from now, it must be accepted only according to the manner in which it was given. This meaning is clear in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.

If it is argued that those [robes] do not become subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) once the time for the robe-season has passed, [the answer is]: No, because they were intended for [that specific purpose].

Because it has been given. Since this occasion (*samaya*) appears as "time" (*kāla*) in the phrase "given specifically at the proper time," whereas in the training rule regarding eating in a group (*gaṇabhojana-sikkhāpada*) and others it appears specifically as "occasion" (*samaya*), it should be understood that here they are stated together as "the robe-season occasion" (*cīvarakālasamaya*) for the purpose of showing their synonymy.
However, in the *Mātikā* (the summary table), such a robe has entered into the state of being one's own property.
This was said with reference to what belongs to an individual; for that very reason it says, "If a robe should arise for a bhikkhu who is in haste.
For a bhikkhu who has spent the rains residence in his own hut, if he is unable to give [the robe], he completes the duty of giving within the rains itself before departing;
the same applies to the Saṅgha. Therefore, this "robe for one in haste" exists from the time it arises.
There is that which, from the time it arises, enters the possession of either the Saṅgha or an individual;

there is that which is not given as *vassāvāsika* (the rainy-season gift), but rather enters the possession of either the Saṅgha or an individual only at the time of having completed the rains-residence, without entering [their possession] from the time it arose; and there is that which, having arisen as *vassāvāsika*, is given at the proper time.
Even when given on trust, if it does not pass into the possession of the individual, but instead remains the property of the Saṅgha or the property of the donor—
it is with reference to such a case that it is said, "it should be deposited after making a mark.
Because its status as one's own property has not been established, this may be kept for more than a year.
Therefore, it is established that the phrase “ten days yet to come” was spoken with reference to something other than this [robe].
Having obtained it earlier than ten days, one is not permitted to set it aside until the Pavāraṇā ceremony; therefore, it must be determined only when it has returned to its own state.
It is with reference to that very case that it is said, “ten days yet to come,” since it is stated: “If one determines or designates it within the period.”

This is stated in the section on non-offenses (*anāpattivāra*). However, that which is set aside after making a mark [of ownership] has not yet attained the status of one's own property because it must still be given away to another;
for with reference to such an object, it is impossible to say "one resolves upon it" (*adhiṭṭheti*) or "one assigns it" (*vikappeti*).

Furthermore, in this context, such an object does not become subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*), because it lacks the quality of being forfeitable to the Sangha. This same point is also made in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).
It is indeed very clear. If one asks, "Having made what mark should it be set aside?"—the point is that the robe belonging to another belongs to the Saṅgha;
therefore, by saying, "Having observed it, it will be easy to give back," the fact that it belongs to another is demonstrated.
“After that, there is no exemption even for a single day; because it has not exceeded ten days,” so it is written.
His intention appears to be that since it has not exceeded ten days from this point in time, one does not receive ten days beyond that time limit.
Regarding the phrase, “One certainly receives this exemption,” here [the reference is to] “the eleventh dawn.”
The reason was recorded as: "He rises [from his seat] during the robe-month. However, in the *Anugaṇṭhipada*, it is stated:

"By saying, 'One may set aside [the robe] on the eleventh day without having formally resolved upon it,' the Blessed One permits other types of robes as well, such as those not designated for urgent need;
others say this is by way of the example of the robe for urgent need. Which of these is well-spoken? Some say both are. How so? First, regarding the "robe for urgent need" (*accekacīvara*)—
This accords with the statement: "When the *kathina* has not been spread, it is one month plus ten days; when the *kathina* has been spread, it is five months plus ten days.
For according to the method of the *Anugaṇṭhipada*, here it would have to be stated as "eleven days plus," whereas the second [case] accords with the statement:
"'Not having arrived for ten days'... the meaning is 'not having reached [the limit] by ten days. Of this method...
Accordingly, the reading “the time for storing a robe that has arisen from the fifth day onwards is shown” is appropriate.

Likewise, according to the *Gaṇṭhipada*’s interpretation, it follows that one must say: “nine days before the full moon of the Kattika month of the three-month period. On the basis of that, [it is said]:
“Granted, this [robe] may indeed be kept as an extra robe for at most ten days; by this very [rule],”

The reading, “It is established; however, by way of the origin of the matter (*aṭṭhuppatti*), it was laid down as a training rule (*sikkhāpada*) after demonstrating a meaning as if it were unprecedented,” is appropriate.
What, then, is the essence here? That which was stated last is indeed the essence.

For this very reason, the Master of the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathācariya*) said, “starting from the fifth. This is because [this interpretation] accords with the ancient *gaṇṭhipadas* and the commentary.
Because it is consistent with the Pāḷi text, which states, “ten days yet to come,” the interpretation found in the *Gaṇṭhipada* (Commentary on Difficult Points) also accords with the Pāḷi.
How so? Because on the day of the Pavāraṇā ceremony, at the rising of the sun, the monk has completed his rains-residence;
therefore, counting from the sixth day together with this tenth day, the nine preceding days plus the tenth day constitute “ten days” (*dasāha*). By that “ten-day” period...

The instrumental case is used here in the sense of accompaniment (*sahayoga*). Because the full moon of the month of Kattika (Kārttika) has not yet reached the robe season (*cīvarasamaya*), it is called "not arrived" (*anāgatā*).
This is just as when, having relinquished the rainy-season garment (*vassikasāṭika*) on the full moon of the later Kattika and assigning it [to another], one says:
"One may determine it for four months, and beyond that, one may assign it. It is the same in this case. Here...
If it is asked why this is so stated, [the answer is] no, because it would follow that this [definition] would be purposeless.

If it is argued that the time for receiving an urgent robe (*accekacīvara*) has been fixed, [the answer is] no; for it is stated in the *Porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā-gaṇṭhipada* (the ancient commentary on difficult points):

"From the sixth day onwards, a robe that has arisen is not considered 'urgent' at all, because it is already established by the first *kathina* ceremony. Therefore, what is called an "urgent robe" refers to the period subsequent to that.

And there is a collection of offenses for one who accepts [the robe]. Yet that offense does not arise from the Canon (Pāḷi), nor from the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), nor is it possible through logical reasoning.
If you argue that it was stated merely by way of a narrative occasion (aṭṭhuppatti), we say no; for the narrative occasion for the "Ten Days" rule (Dasāhādhiccakārikā) is not seen in the Canon.
[The Canon says only]: "The monks, having accepted an urgent robe, let the robe-season period pass."
In this case, the origin of the rule (*aṭṭhuppatti*) is precisely this much.
For it should be understood that in the *Parivāra*, beginning with the words "On what matter?", only this much was stated.

If it is argued that this rule was laid down to show that an urgent robe (*accekacīvara*) must not exceed the robe-season, whereas the other may exceed it—that is not so, because it demonstrates the fault of the urgent robe itself.

Because there is no specific reason [to distinguish it], and because it would contradict such statements as, "Granted, this is established by the very rule that 'an extra robe may be kept for at most ten days,'" and because the aforementioned statement would be impossible. How so?
For if it were said that the full moon of Kattika is "not yet arrived" along with the ten-day period, then that full moon would be something other than the ten-day period.

[He] incurs [the offense]. If it were not "other" (*anaññā*), the word "together" (*saha*) would not be possible; for a conjunction of oneself with oneself is impossible, and the word "not yet arrived" (*anāgata*) would also be impossible.

For that full-moon day is indeed already arrived and attained. If it is argued: "Because it immediately follows the time of the robe-offering (*cīvarasamaya*), and because it has not reached the state of being one [with it], it is therefore 'not yet arrived' (*anāgatā*)"? No, because even so, the word "not yet arrived" remains possible.
For the term "future" (anāgata) is only possible when there is the possibility of arrival; indeed, neither *nibbāna* nor a conceptual designation (*paññatti*) is called "future.
Just as *nibbāna* [is not subject to time], that full-moon day (*puṇṇamā*)—which consists of three moments (*khaṇa*)—never reaches the state of being a temporal occasion (*samayabhāva*);
thus, [to claim otherwise] is simply illogical. Furthermore, the statement "one may conceive [it] after that" refers to taking the subsequent moment (*piṭṭhisamaya*).
It arises because of its stability. Furthermore, when the dawn has risen on the day of the *pavāraṇā*, that full-moon day falls short of the robe-season (*cīvarasamaya*) by exactly one day;
this is because it was previously joined with [the preceding day]. This being so, even though it has reached a state of unity, it is born as something that has not yet arrived at the robe-season.
Therefore, it should be understood that for the purpose of making the statement "it is always thus," someone has pointed this out based on a specific scriptural passage.
But for what purpose was it stated here that "a month plus ten days" and so forth? It is because of the possibility of completion.
For if dawn has already risen on the fifth day, the period of ten days plus a month is indeed completed for the robe already received;
having taken this into account, it was stated thus. Furthermore, even the daytime portion of that fifth day is reckoned as "yesterday" by the night that has arrived.
It is said, let alone before dawn; therefore it says, "Yesterday, friends, for us," and so forth.

This being the case, according to the first reading stated as "starting from the sixth day," even a set of three robes that has been set aside after relinquishing a non-extra robe certainly receives this allowance; and [the phrase] "a month plus ten days," and so forth.

And as for what has been written: it is not that those places were rewritten by this method because the meaning stated [in the commentary] is possible starting from the fifth word in the text; rather, they should be regarded exactly as they stand.
Thus, the Teacher says: "This is my opinion. The Elder Upatissa, however, maintains that this training rule is indeed *anissaggiya* (not involving forfeiture) on the full-moon day.

In the text where it says, “Starting from the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Pavāraṇā,” this method demonstrates the period for the storage of the robe-material that has arisen as described.
The text beginning with, “‘Urgent robe-material’ means a robe-material required for an urgent matter,” and so forth, applies.
Furthermore, the phrases “starting from the sixth day” and “Certainly, this [robe] may last at most ten days,” and so forth, [apply].
What has been written there is not the actual reading; therefore, having determined that one receives a dispensation for eleven days, it seems the teacher had it written as "starting from the fifth.

However, starting from the sixth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Pavāraṇā, even a non-urgent robe-cloth that has arisen, as well as a set-of-three robes that has been set aside after being relinquished, [are included] in this dispensation.
Regarding the readings "labhati yeva" and "for one with a robe in progress and the Kathina not spread, it is a month plus eleven days;
for one with the Kathina spread, it is five months plus eleven days," they engage in much elaboration here;
therefore, one should speak only after having reflected thoroughly, or else remain silent.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the early robe is finished.
9. Commentary on the training rule concerning danger:
"One of the three robes"—this procedure applies only to the triple-robe set; in the other case...

They say it was stated for the purpose of showing "as one pleases. Regarding the phrase "staying apart for more than four nights," this was said because staying in that very same lodging does not constitute being "apart. Why? Because of the knowledge of how robes are to be distributed.
Here, although it is stated even for more [than five hundred bow-lengths] based on the statement, "A forest lodging is defined as being at least five hundred bow-lengths from the last [village],"...

Furthermore, the lodging is exclusively forest-dwelling; he observes the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) because there is the possibility of an obstacle arising from the need to know how to manage his robes.
As for what was said—that one obtains [the robe] with a measurement exceeding four gāvutas—how is that understood?
It is known from the statement: "And there might be some reason for that bhikkhu to be separated from that robe."

If it is asked, "Could it be even for the measure of a *yojana*? No; because in the section on non-offenses, it is permitted that one may "enter a village boundary again, dwell there, and then depart.
If this is so, why is it said that "one does not obtain [the benefit] within the measure of a *yojana*"?

This was stated specifically with reference to a fixed residence (*nibaddhāvāsa*). In that case, is the ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*) broken? It is not broken; however, there is no discussion concerning the ascetic practices here.
Now, why is it said, "This should be understood as a thief of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga)"?

Because it is impossible. How is this known? From their absence among the factors. Since the dwelling appropriate for one who maintains the ascetic practices is indicated, his status as a maintainer of the ascetic practices is established.
If you say it is because of the authority of the word, no; even by the authority of the word, the Canon (Pāḷi) alone is the authority. "There is no offense... [and so forth].
For it is said: "Having entered the village boundary again and stayed there, he departs. If one asks: "After leaving the village boundary, having stayed for how long should he depart?
Some say: "On the very next day; therefore, the eighth dawn should be allowed to rise either at the fixed residence or at the place to which he is going.
Others say: "Within seven days," until the fixed residence [is reached].
Some say he "makes it allowable" (*kappeti*). Some say [the duration] lasts until the fatigue of the journey is dispelled.
If there is an obstacle, he may stay for seven days; there is no offense. If he makes a formal resolution to reside permanently (*nibaddhāvāsakappana*), there is an offense at the rising of the dawn.
Some say that if it is the seventh day, on that very day he must either take up his robe that was laid aside or relinquish it. If, meanwhile, a new path appears...
Or, by the relocation of the new village settlement, that lodging loses its qualification as a proper place. On that very day, the robe must either be taken up [with oneself] or relinquished.
If it is lost while one is staying apart for six nights, some say there is no offense because the permitted number of days has not been exceeded;
others say there is indeed an offense because the qualification is lacking. However, one should investigate which of these is more reasonable.

It should be taken up. If one is a bearer of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), having stayed within the village boundary, one should depart after staying in a place suitable for the maximum limit [of six nights].
If the village has already established a non-separation boundary (avippavāsa-sīma), there is no offense even if one stays within that boundary during another month.
According to the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*: "Even for one staying in the aforementioned lodging, it is only for six nights..."
"It has been said: 'If one intends to deposit the robe in a village, it is indeed an offense for another person to stay there even for less than six nights or for more.
The commentary on the training rule concerning danger is finished.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning What Has Been Designated.

657. Regarding the phrase "It is death for us, friends," does an intimation (viññatti) exist here or not? It exists. If that is so, what is the difference between this and the training rule concerning intimation from one who is unrelated (aññātakaviññatti)?

That [rule] applies only when one intimates to someone who is both unrelated and has not invited [one to give); this [rule] applies even when [the person] is related and has invited [one]. That [rule] applies only to one whose robe has not been lost;
this [rule] applies even to such a person. That [rule] applies only when one is intimating for a robe; this [rule] applies even when it is not for a robe.

This being so, this [rule] stands as an inclusion within that; therefore, when both sets of factors are fulfilled, by whom must it be [performed]? Some say: "It must be by this person, because for him there is no limitation. Others say: "It must be by both, because both have established the factors.
These are its factors: the robe being subject to selection, the absence of a specific occasion, and requesting from one who is not a relative.

And there are four [factors] regarding "acquisition" (*paṭilābha*) by her. Furthermore, for this [gift], there are three: its being dedicated to the Saṅgha, knowing [the recipient], and dedicating it to oneself; these constitute "acquisition.
Herein, the first position is untenable because, although an opportunity was provided, it was not investigated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* or the *Parivāra*. If it is argued:
"If that is so, then in those [texts] among the factors, 'not being dedicated to another' (*anaññapariṇatatā*) should be stated," [the answer is: No.
It should be stated, because it is established by its meaning. Since it is established by the two training rules concerning what has been dedicated (*pariṇata*), it is designated as "dedicated";
and because an offense can arise, one says, "Give some to me too. It is not explicitly indicated that "it is allowable," yet it is allowable because it was said, "We have some too.
In the passage, "What has been dedicated to the Saṅgha... [etc. ...there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," the word "to an individual" (*puggalassa*) is not mentioned.
Because it is presented here as a pure *pācittiya* offense, the phrase "another shrine" (*aññacetiyassa*) is not mentioned, since the Saṅgha is not a shrine;

for that very reason, even in the passage "what has been dedicated to a shrine... [etc.]... there is an offense of wrong-doing" (*dukkaṭa*), the phrases "another Saṅgha" or "another individual" (*aññapuggalassa*) are not mentioned.
Since it is likewise stated here: "what has been dedicated to an individual... [etc.]... there is an offense of wrong-doing."
And although the phrase "even for oneself" is not explicitly stated, they say that it is nevertheless implied.
However, some say it is not mentioned here because this training rule (sikkhāpada) concerns the dedication of one's own [merit].

Others say it is like the phrase "for the sake of another" in the subsequent training rule. That is not correct, because such a dedication to a person is not mentioned in this particular training rule. But the Elder Dhammasiri said:
“Whatever gain intended for oneself, or whatever was intended for another, one should divert it to the Saṅgha;
[otherwise] it is an offense of relinquishment, and there is also an offense of wrong-doing.

The meaning of this is: if one diverts to oneself what was intended for the Saṅgha, it is an offense of relinquishment. That same thing, if diverted to someone other [than the original recipient], [is likewise an offense].
[If one] diverts what was intended for another to oneself or to someone else, it is a *dukkaṭa*.

Therefore, because offenses mentioned in [the rules concerning] requesting from strangers and so forth can occur here as well, the word "oneself" (*attanō*) is not stated in these two cases of diverting.

For if that word were stated, there would be the possibility of it being merely a *dukkaṭa*; however, when it is not stated, one of the offenses mentioned in these [rules] occurs according to the respective tradition.
And here, since the two offenses—the unspoken accomplishment and the *dukkaṭa*—occur together, an opportunity has been provided for the Vinaya-holders to possess exhaustive knowledge.
Thus ends the "Thirtyfold Section," the Essence of the Essence of the Vinaya;
this is sufficient regarding the essence of the Vinaya.
Here, because it purifies the essence of all that has been completed by means of the Vinaya, it is called the "Essence of the Essence.
The commentary on the matured training rules is finished.
The third chapter on bowls is finished.
The commentary on the *nissaggiya* rules is finished.
The commentary on the *pācittiya* rules begins.
5. The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa) 1.
The Subsection on False Speech (Musāvādavagga) 1.
Commentary on the Training Rule on False Speech (Musāvādasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā)
1. Regarding the term *vādakkhitto*: here, it should be understood that the threefold path of discourse—consisting of *vāda*, *jalpa*, and *vitaṇḍā*—is spoken of collectively as simply "vāda.
Among these, because of the expression "with the sectarians" (*titthiyehi saddhiṃ*), they say that "the rest" [of the paths] are excluded, leaving only *vāda*.
Due to his skill in the points of defeat (*niggahaṭṭhāna*) and the futile rejoinders (*chalajāti*), he sometimes, having denied something in one instance, later admits it.
Likewise, having previously acknowledged some statement, he later denies it; or in this or another way, he evades with one thing while saying another.

Thus engaged, having promised to speak a deliberate lie, not desiring the truth, and deceiving by making a false agreement—being thus defeated in his argument, he wanders about fulfilling the basis for an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The intention should be understood in this way. Regarding "one's own doctrine": here, it refers to one's own doctrine as first undertaken, namely, "all phenomena are non-self.
It is not a tenet [of all schools] that "whatever is suffering is non-self," for when "all phenomena" is stated, even Nibbāna is included;
however, because it has been stated that "Nibbāna is supreme happiness," it is not suffering. There is no such possibility.

It exists. This opponent, having cited the sutta stating "that which is suffering is non-self," intends to attribute the fault already mentioned—that it is "contradictory" and "inconsistent"—by confusing the established doctrine.

Anticipating that he might perceive some fault in this first position, whether the fault has been attributed or not, [the author] disregards him, thinking "this is not my position," and states: "Nirvana alone is eternal."

Having seen the sutta beginning with “‘It is non-self,’ thus it was decided,” and having observed that his first position was faultless, he later admits that very same position, thinking, “This doctrine is mine alone.
Thus, perceiving the aforementioned benefit therein and admitting it, [he argues:
if all phenomena (*dhammā*) are non-self, they would not even be phenomena. For [the word] *dhammā* means those which bear their own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
For these are called "phenomena" (*dhammā*).

And since this word *atta* denotes intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), whether a fault has been imputed in this way or not, he perceives it as a fault and subsequently disregards that very first position, saying, "This is not my doctrine. Then that opponent [states] his own position:

The removal [of the opponent's position] by means of admitting [the point] during a refutation. Because of the statement, "He admits it against himself," it is said: "Admission (paṭiññā) is a different kind of refutation for you.

With the intention of refuting a meaning that exceeds its own nature—that is, referring to a self imagined merely by the foolish as something exceeding its own nature—I have declared the discourse of my admission: "All phenomena are non-self."

And since she remains in that very same state, there is for me no withdrawal of what was previously admitted; however, the disregard [expressed by] "this is not my doctrine" was made with the intention—
"I do not say 'all phenomena are non-self' with reference to a self consisting of intrinsic nature"—
and thus, for this other reason, it is not a withdrawal of what was previously admitted.

He conceals [the reason]. Because he previously made a formal admission based on the reason that "one should not say 'all phenomena are non-self' because the word *atta* (self) denotes an intrinsic nature," he has now withdrawn that admission.
The intention is that he conceals that other reason by means of another reason shown later.

Since he not only denies and asserts the meaning according to the method already shown, but also [denies and asserts] the words themselves, the Commentary first states the reason "because it is to be known" (*jānitabbato*).

Then, when the opponent says, "If it is impermanent because it is to be known, then for you, *nibbāna* would be impermanent," [the author replies]: "I do not say 'it is impermanent because it is to be known'..."
The reason has been stated: "I said 'because it is subject to birth' (jātidhammato)," and the intention [of the opponent] is that you, being deaf, perceive this as something else, and so forth.
It is further stated: "Having said 'because it must be known' (jānitabbato), he then says 'because it is subject to birth' (jātidhammato) and so on.
It is written: "When one denies [something] and then asserts it again, he conceals that denial by means of this [subsequent assertion]."
2. Regarding the phrase *jānitvā jānantassa ca*: it illustrates two meanings, namely "having known" (*jānitvā*) or "for one who knows" (*jānantassa*).
3. Furthermore, regarding the term *micchāvācāpariyāpannā*: this refers to being included within the fourfold wrong speech (*micchāvācā*).

Some say it refers to those categorized under names such as "Sīhala" and so forth; therefore, in the *mātikā*, both the speech of one who speaks thus and the volition (*cetanā*) that originates it are stated.
Because both are included. Since that statement in the *Vibhaṅga* does not exist without intimation (*viññatti*), therefore "verbal intimation" is also shown.

Having stated "the speech of one speaking thus" according to worldly convention, he says "or the volition that originates it" in order to show it from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*). "By the gross alone" refers to speech originated by volition.
It is subtle because it is produced by way of the object alone. 9.
"It has been seen" means it has been seen by him, or by him through the medium of access concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*);

it is not [meant] that he thinks, "I have not attended to it," or for one who says, "I did not see the cloth while it was being woven," and so forth—it is only with reference to ultimate emptiness (*paramattha-suññatā*).
For one who says, “I see neither woman nor man,” there is no falsehood.

Regarding the phrase “he certainly incurs an offense,” they say it is an offense of wrong speech (*dubbhāsita*). Why? Because it is stated that he is “engaging in play. This refers directly to “speech, voice... verbal intimations,” whereas the body is not direct [in this context].
The commentary on the training rule concerning false speech is finished.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule on False Speech (Omasavāda-sikkhāpada) 13.
"‘Again in another *ara*’ means having returned to that same place, one arrives again in another *ara*. This is what is written.
"The region where the *ara* is established" refers to the ground. "Again in that very *ara*" means arriving again at the ground in that same *ara*; such is the meaning.
Some [readers] think that this does not seem right. *Jāpito* means "defeated," or rather the reading is *parājito*. *Pāpesi* means "you overcome.
Regarding the Brahmin who was speaking pleasant words, it refers to a heavy burden. *Udabbahi* means "he dragged away"; or, the genitive case is used in the sense of disregard (*anādara*).
*Dhanañca naṃ alābhesi* means "he caused him to obtain wealth"—the intention is that he acted in such a way that he obtained wealth.
15. Regarding the previous account: *Avakaṇṇaka* means "one with cut ears. *Javakaṇṇaka* means "one with crooked ears. *Dhaniṭṭhaka* means "one who increases wealth";
it is also the name of one who increases prosperity (*sirivaḍḍhaka*) and one who increases the lineage (*kulavaḍḍhaka*). *Tacchakakamma* refers to those who perform the work of digging or hewing;
some say it refers to stone-workers. "Finger-calculation" (*muddā*) is counting by means of the fingers. "Calculation" (*gaṇanā*)...
"Great calculation," it is said in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*. "Diabetes (madhumeha) and lack of urine (omeha)" is how it is written.

Some say it refers to the accumulation of flesh in one with a large body. Regarding *yabha*, which means sexual intercourse: some say that even when one reviles by means of freedom from passion and so forth, one is indeed reviling by means of defilements;

likewise, when one reviles by saying "you are a stream-enterer," one is reviling by means of an offense. Because it is dependent on the gender-mark (*liṅga*), even being extremely white is itself considered a gender-mark.
16. "He speaks in all cases" is the summary (uddesa). "He utters" is the detailed explanation (vitthāra). Alternatively, by the word "speaks," he illustrates the making known of another.

26. However, in the sections concerning the designation of others, it is stated: "he speaks thus. Why? For the purpose of showing the sequence of the summary as previously demonstrated. Previously too, it was said:
"the low with the low, the low with the high, the high with the low, and the high with the high."
He establishes this by means of the word "thus" (*evaṃ*) as an illustration of the sequence of the enumeration, which is shown fourfold for each category beginning with birth (*jāti*).
For the intended meaning is that when it is said, "he speaks of the low as low," in that very place where it is stated, "he speaks thus," that specific mode is illustrated.
Otherwise, it would follow that such a mode could not occur through the mention of something else.

If it is argued that this is not possible, we say no; for there is no specific cause [for such a restriction], because it would entail the consequence of non-offense in those cases, and because the meaning of "non-restriction" is possible through the use of an indefinite description.

For the intention is that by means of an indefinite description—such as, "There are here some Caṇḍālas"—an indefinite meaning is possible for one who speaks referring either to a Caṇḍāla or a non-Caṇḍāla, such that an offense occurs [in the former case].

If it is argued that this much alone should be stated, since the sequence of the enumeration shown previously is thereby established— no, because if the word "thus" (*evaṃ*) were not construed with the word "speaks" (*vadeti*),
one would fail to understand that it demonstrates this specific manner [of speaking]. Alternatively, the purpose of the restriction is that even in the method of indirect indication,
there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) or an offense entailing expiation (*pācittiya*) only when one intends to inform another.

“*Vadeti*” (he speaks) should be understood as “he says. Alternatively, standing near oneself and commanding another bhikkhu, if one speaks or says something lowly about a lowly person, there is an offense of *pācittiya*. If one who is himself lowly speaks of a lowly person—a caṇḍāla...
pe ...a pukkusa—saying “pukkusa,” there is an offense of *pācittiya* for every single utterance. This same method applies to the sections concerning other designations as well.
The construction [of the sentence] should be understood. This meaning is to be sought among the "corrupt faults" (*duṭṭhadosa*).

Otherwise, either "speaks" (*vadeti*) or "says" (*bhaṇati*) would become purposeless in both the section on non-designation (*anaññāpadesavāra*) and the section on designation (*aññāpadesavāra*), or specifically in the sections on designation, since the smoothness of expression could occur even without it, as it is not stated in the Pāḷi from the perspective of the self (*attato*).
In this context, it should be understood that the term "sāṇattika" (with a formal admonition) is used. Regarding that, the connection between the words is: *vadati iti* = *vada iti*.

For one who speaks in the absence [of the accused], there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*), because it is stated in the Andhakaṭṭhakathā: "But for one who speaks in the presence [of the accused], there is an offense of wrong-doing even with all seven classes of offenses.
"Playfulness" (*davakamyatā*) means jesting; to demonstrate that, [the text says] "the state of having laughter as the primary intention."
It has been stated: "Even when speaking in the absence [of the person] out of a desire for sport, it is indeed a *dubbhāsita* (ill-spoken)," so say the teachers (*ācariyā*).

However, for one who speaks even while angry, provided it is for the purpose of censuring evil, there is a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing); yet there is no offense (*anāpatti*) when speaking in their absence.
The commentary on the training rule regarding abusive speech (*omasavāda-sikkhāpada*) is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule on Slander (Pesuññasikkhāpada) 36–7.

The reading is “Having heard from this one, [he tells] that one. “Having heard from these ones” is not good. “For the sake of division” means for the purpose of causing a split. Because all three lie down [to sleep] precisely because they possess the status of monks, the plural form “among monks” (*bhikkhūnaṃ*) is employed.
38–9. Having said, “The venerable one named so-and-so calls him a Caṇḍāla... [and so on]... a Pukkusa,” he brings about slander.
The construction [of the sentence] is as follows. Otherwise, it would follow that one must say, "He says, 'Pukkuso'.

Here, although the section concerning those who are not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*) is applicable, it has not been extracted because it follows the method already shown in the case of abusive speech (*omasavāda*), or because the intention was to show it briefly at the end.
For indeed, three *dukkaṭa* offenses are shown at the end. In demonstrating those, the Blessed One—since [the offense applies] to one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*)...
Having heard [it] from one who is ordained, he instigates slander against another who is ordained.

Desiring to show that these two phrases—stated either by way of a single perversion (*vipallāsa*) or by way of both perversions—are each an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*), and thus that both are stated together as one, he says at the very beginning:
“An ordained person, having heard it from one who is ordained, [instigates slander] against one who is ordained...”

“...he brings it forward, there is an offense of *pācittiya*,” he said. “Now, regarding these two cases, since even one who has committed a *pārājika* remains ordained, if one who is likewise ordained desires to revile another such person and insults them, or if, having heard [something] from such a person, one brings slander against another such person, there is an offense of *pācittiya*;
therefore, this initial term ‘one who is ordained’ applies everywhere.”
Some say that [the word "vuttaṃ"] was stated; however, that is not correct, because for one who has fallen into an offense without remainder, it is impossible to fall into that same offense again.

Therefore, it should be understood that this initial word was stated simply because the term "bhikkhu" is absent from the *mātikā*, and because the phrases "he speaks" and "he applies" would be impossible in the absence of a specification of the agent.
This is indeed not a formal injunction (*anāṇattika*) due to the absence of a textual recitation (*pāḷilesā*).
The genitive case in the phrase “of one who desires what is dear, not of one intending to cause a schism” is used with reference to the expectation of reconciliation;
because for one who has become silent there is no purpose in speaking, it is therefore said: “There is no offense for one speaking for the sake of censuring evil.
The commentary on the training rule against malicious talebearing is concluded.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Reciting the Dhamma Word by Word (Padasodhammasikkhāpada) 45–6.
Regarding the phrase “all this is called the Dhamma word by word,” the connection here is that “Dhamma” means what was spoken by the Buddha.
A “collection of syllables” refers to incomplete words. What was spoken by a Paccekabuddha is included within what was spoken by the Buddha. [This excludes] non-upāsakas and householders.

It should be understood that what is spoken [by the Buddha] falls under the category of "spoken by seers" (*isibhāsita*) and so forth. In some manuscripts, the phrase "spoken by deities" (*devatābhāsita*) does not appear;
where it does appear, that is the authentic text (*pāḷi*). This same principle applies even in verse composition:
even after uttering a single syllable, a place [for the next] is necessarily obtained. When reciting a sutta such as "Thus have I heard" (*evaṃ me sutaṃ*), one utters the vowel *e*.
If he stands [listening], there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for every syllable; if he stands after the sentence is incomplete, it is according to each word.
If even one of the first words among the phrases is contradicted, there is an offense of expiation for every subsequent word.

"Supported by the commentary" means standing by way of being supported by the commentary, referring to the commentary spoken previously in the vernacular language. "Supported by the text" (pāḷi) means...
It is found in the Pāḷi itself. There are also treatises such as the *Maggakathā*. 48.
"Vicinity" (*upacāra*) means twelve cubits (*dvādasahattha*). It is written: "'Opāpeti' means he speaks from one side; he comes together.
Although the taming of Apalāla and the instruction on virtue also arose during the time of the Blessed One, nevertheless, among those [teachings], whichever...

In the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, the phrase "they say" (*vadanti*) was used loosely to indicate that what was stated by quoting from the Buddha’s word (*buddhavacana*) constitutes precisely that same offense.

Because there is an abundance of such statements quoted from the Buddha’s word, the offense was declared in them according to the principle of majority (*tabbahulanaya*); therefore, its intended meaning (*adhippāya*) has been clarified in the *Mahāpaccarī*.
This is the meaning. It has been stated: “Others say it applies to all words alike.
If a teacher standing gives a recitation to those who are seated, some say he does not incur the offense mentioned in the rule, “I shall not teach the Dhamma while standing to one who is seated.

However, that is not correct, because giving a recitation is not something other than teaching the Dhamma; for [the offense would still apply] by virtue of giving a recitation to those such as one holding a sunshade.
From the fact that there would be no offense [in such a case], the existence of an offense is established. For this has been said:
"Both do not know the goal, both do not see the Dhamma:
he who recites the mantra, and he by whom it is studied contrary to the Dhamma."
The meaning here is "one studies in this"; therefore, even the giving of the text is indeed the teaching of the Dhamma. In the *Sekhiya-aṭṭhakathā*, it is said:

"But here, the classification of the Dhamma should be understood according to the method stated for the 'recitation of the words' (*padasodhamma*). Therefore, this very Dhamma is to be understood in all training rules connected with the Dhamma.
If that is so, then by way of the language of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra-bhāsā*) and so forth, the Dhamma of the mind—
If it were argued that there would be no offense for one descending [from a high seat] by way of a training rule (*sekhiya*), then there would be a contradiction with the *Chapaṅka-jātaka*.

If it is argued that this is because the *manta*s are external texts (*bāhiraga-gantha*), we say no; for their intended meaning (*adhippāya*) is not understood. For this is the intended meaning therein:
"Monks, it is unpleasant for me to have even a *manta*—let alone the Dhamma—recited while I am seated on a high seat."
“Even then, monks, it was displeasing to me to recite the *manta* while sitting on a low seat for one sitting on a high seat;
how much more so now... [pe] ...to teach the Dhamma? For this canonical passage (*pāḷi*) illuminates exactly the intended meaning as stated above, and nothing else.
For that very reason, there is a distinction in wording between “to recite the *manta*” and “to teach the Dhamma.”
[This is] done. Otherwise, it should have been stated as “teach the Dhamma” in both places.
However, regarding the phrase “Do not speak with me,” etc., it is stated thus in the *Anugaṇṭhipada*:
“If a bhikkhu wishes to speak with a sāmaṇera, and likewise a sāmaṇera wishes to speak with a bhikkhu, and they suddenly open [the conversation], [it is considered] ‘mostly’...”
In cases such as "he causes [the novice] to recite a well-mastered text," there is no offense; for to that extent, it does not constitute a bhikkhu’s formal instruction (*uddisati*) of a novice.
This is indeed appropriate because it is not mentioned in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*.
Furthermore, if there were an offense for having deliberated upon it there, one would incur both an action and a non-action; why? Because [it is determined] by the mind.
If one desires to speak privately, yet after being refused with the words, “Do not speak privately,” one nevertheless speaks privately, one incurs an offense.
However, there is no offense for one who does not wish to speak privately but speaks privately by accident or through a slip of the tongue; thus it is said:
“If he speaks when told, ‘Do not speak with me,’ there is no offense. Nevertheless, one who follows the opinion of the teachers regarding such matters [should act accordingly].
One should proceed in the various cases according to the method already stated. Why? Because it is not found in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*; precisely because it is not found there, there is no offense.
If the statement "there is no offense" were impossible in that case, it would be for this reason:

"Do not speak with me. If one speaks after being told this, there is no offense for the bhikkhu. Regarding this, the following investigation applies: "If one speaks after being told, 'Do not speak with me,' there is no offense for the bhikkhu."

This is appropriate because a bhikkhu lacks the desire to speak; and even if such a desire were present, there is no offense in the case of the three [activities] such as reciting the scriptures and so forth.
Now, if a bhikkhu—being incompetent—is told by a competent novice, "Do not speak with me," yet he speaks out of incompetence, there is indeed an offense because the desire to speak is fully present.
If, however, he speaks impulsively, there is no offense because that [desire] is absent.
If a monk, having said, "Do not speak with me," speaks with that person himself, there is indeed an offense.

For this training rule is not one where the act is contingent upon another act (a *kiriyākiriya* rule). If this training rule were a *kiriyākiriya* rule, it would be appropriate [to say] that there is no offense in that case;
such is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). In the *Mahāpaccarī*, with this very same intention, [it says]: "With me..."
It might be said, "Do not speak. For the action of a novice is not the authority here; however, when this intended meaning is stated, it is indeed highly appropriate—this is the sense.

This is the meaning of the syllables (*akkharattha*) and the meaning of the phonemes (*byañjanattha*). Although it has been said, "Whatever is the word, whatever is the subsequent word, whatever is the subsequent syllable, and whatever is the subsequent phoneme—all this is called 'mastery of words' (*padasodhammo*)," nevertheless...

“When he recites by the *pada*, there is an offense of *pācittiya* for every *pada*; when he recites by the syllable, there is an offense of *pācittiya* for every syllable”—only this pair has been applied here.
Why is that? Because by [mentioning] the *pada*, the *anupada* and the *anubyañjana* are included.
For it has been said: “The *anupada* is the second *pāda*. The *anubyañjana* is [the following] by means of the preceding *byañjana*...”
“...the subsequent syllable is similar,” therefore it is established that *anubyañjana* is merely a portion of the subsequent [syllable].

If it is argued that since it is stated, “A collection of letters and syllables is a word (*pada*),” one should speak of it as merely a word because of the inclusion of the triad beginning with *anupada*, we reply:
it should not be so stated, because of the specific wording. For when teaching by means of a word (*pada*), whether it be a word, a sub-word (*anupada*), or a sub-syllable (*anubyañjana*)—
...or he incurs an offense. It is not by means of a syllable. However, while teaching by means of a syllable, one incurs [an offense] regarding one of the words and so forth.
For instance, when teaching the first *va*-kāra in such passages as “varo varaññū varado varāharo,” one does not cause an elision (*opāteti*) at the second and subsequent *va*-kāras;
nor, when teaching the first *ro*-kāra, does one cause an elision at the second *ro*-kāra; nor, when teaching the first *ra*-kāra...
It is possible that there is an offense of *pācittiya* when one causes [the other] to stumble at the second syllable *ra*.
If it is argued that this is possible because it conforms to the secondary meaning (*anubyañjana*), we say no; for it contradicts the statement, "At every word there is an offense of *pācittiya*.

Indeed, this statement illustrates that there is one offense for each single word. This is because of the statement: "When it is said, 'Form is impermanent,' if one causes [the other] to stumble at the word 'form' (*rūpaṃ'), [there is an offense]."
If it is argued that for one reciting an entire *pāda*, an offense is established even when only the first syllable is uttered simultaneously, this is not so;
for it would contradict the rule: “For each syllable, there is an offense of *pācittiya*.

Therefore, since it is impossible to say that the *rū*-sound causes one to fall into [an offense], and because it is established that the *rū*-sound is included within the aforementioned category of phenomena (*dhamma*), one should not say that, but rather simply—
The phrase "when being taught that 'form is impermanent'" is stated for the purpose of showing the existence of syllables included within the aforementioned categories of Dhamma;
alternatively, it should be understood as a designation for the phonemes (anubyañjana) based on the smoothness of the expression, similar to the term "feeling" [being applied to the phonemes].
The commentary on the training rule regarding the memorization of words (padasodhamma-sikkhāpada) is concluded.
5. Commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning Sleeping Together (Paṭhamasahaseyyasikkhāpada) 50.
“One should not make a bed in common” is stated in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*).

In some versions, the reading is “a bed in common should not be made,” the intention being that it was prescribed that a bhikkhunī should not make [such a bed]. “Or a couch with a headrest” means precisely a couch provided with a headrest.

It is written: "it happens. Regarding the phrase "what is not allowable for these [novices], that is also [not allowable] for them," the ellipsis to be supplied is: "without going into the presence of the preceptor (upajjhāya) and others, one might share a sleeping place [with them]. 52.
Because it is stated, "one who is not fully ordained (anupasampanna) means anyone other than a bhikkhu," a woman is considered one who is not fully ordained.
It has been stated: "On the fourth night, a woman gives rise to two offenses of lying down together," and also: "Excluding a bhikkhu...
it is a male animal who constitutes the basis for a *pārājika* offense that is intended. Both of these points should be investigated.
Regarding the term "woman" (*mātugāma*) in the second training rule, it refers only to a human female, including a *yakkhinī* or a *petī*.
“Animals that have become the basis for a *pārājika* offense are not included among those [cases], because they constitute a *dukkaṭa* offense. Furthermore, it has been asked:
‘If there were a *dukkaṭa* offense even for oneself regarding one’s own training rule (*sikkhāpada*), then why is there a *pācittiya* in the first training rule?
And as for the statement in the Sinhalese Commentary, ‘There is no offense if [the act occurs] in front of an unenclosed area,’ the Andhaka Commentary provides the explanation of its meaning.”
It is said: "This was stated with reference to the foremost [monastery] in the world, excluding the earth. Again, "he dwells" means he dwells on the fourth day.
"When a bhikkhu has lain down" means when a bhikkhu has fallen asleep. "The pavilion where they have assembled" refers to the assembly hall in the Mahāvihāra.
