"Having stayed for three days in a place that is a field of wrongdoing (dukkata-khetta), on the fourth day, in a place sufficient for the offense of sharing a sleeping place..."
"‘If he lies down, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya),’ so some say; however, that is not correct.
The commentary on the first rule regarding sleeping together is finished.
6. Commentary on the second rule regarding sleeping together.
55. Regarding the phrases “Then those people” and “those travelers,” these are the readings. There is also the reading “for one night,” but that is not good.
Since a *dukkaṭa* offense is stated in the Canon for a paṇḍaka, they say, “with those possessing both sexual organs there is a root-offense,” as if it were stated regarding those with both organs;
and they say, “the *animitta* and others are women. Even though she is a dead woman...

It constitutes a matter of defeat (pārājika), yet because it stands on the side of what is not clung-to (anupādinnapakkha), one does not incur an offense here. Furthermore, the grounds for an offense of defeat need not be examined in this context.
The commentary on the second training rule regarding sleeping in the same bed is finished.
7. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Teaching the Dhamma.
66. Because of the statement, “one who is wise and capable,” there is no offense for one teaching even an unwise woman.

Here, female *yakkhas* and others, like human women, constitute grounds for a *dukkaṭa* offense because they are not gross [in their nature]. Some say that since the capability of a female being in the form of an animal or a human is mentioned, the other [types of females] also constitute grounds for a *dukkaṭa* offense alone.
[The term] “mātugāmāya” (to a woman) is used through a change of grammatical gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*).
It has been stated: "It is said that, setting aside the readings of the *Aṭṭhakathā* and other such works, one may speak according to one's own preference in Tamil and other languages.

Just as female spirits (*yakkhī*) and others became subject to an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*), why would a woman standing with a male spirit (*yakkha*) or the like—who has assumed a human form—be free from incurring an offense of wrong-doing when teaching the Dhamma?
If it is asked, "Does one incur a *pācittiya* offense?"—it is because there is not even the slightest association with a second person.

Even a human woman is not a "second" in this context, let alone a *yakkha* or other such beings. If it is argued that "he is not designated as having a second because he lacks a second," [we reply: No;

in that case, "having a second" refers to the presence of another for the purpose of indecent speech, whereas here it refers to the presence of another for the purpose of sitting. Furthermore, in this instance, it is not merely the act of sitting that is intended, but rather the act of teaching (*desanā*).
And because it involves lying down, it is gross; therefore, it is an illustration of incapacity.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the teaching of the Dhamma is finished.
8. Commentary on the training rule concerning the announcement of what has occurred.
67. It is said that “the case of the fourth *pārājika* offense and this [present case] are one and the same,” but this is not correct.

Why? Because in that [previous] instance, the term “foolish men” (*moghapurisa*) was used. My own conjecture is that since those [men] were not mixed with noble ones (*ariya*), the two cases are identical.
However, it has been written: “The noble ones also claimed [to possess such powers], because superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*) existed within them as well.”
“‘All [of this] is true, Blessed One’: because the superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) of both ordinary persons and noble ones were reported, it is called ‘true’;
it was not said with reference to one’s own superhuman state—so say others,” it is stated.
77. “By those not previously mentioned”: by those not mentioned in the fourth *pārājika*.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the false claim of having seen a ghost is finished.
9. Commentary on the training rule concerning the false claim of a grave offense (duṭṭhullārocanasikkhāpada), §§ 78–80:
“He made an effort with that very hand and discharged semen”—this reading is the correct sequence and is excellent.

It must be performed only after having obtained permission; this is stated in the Pāḷi itself. Although one should say "through fear" (*ottappena*), it is expressed as "through shame and fear" (*hirottappena*) in reference to others by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhī*).

It is not mentioned in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* because it is obvious; for it is established that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) simply by showing the impossibility of a formal act of expiation (*pācittiya*).
83. In this context, because it is included among the transgressions already mentioned, "action" (*kamma*) refers to the basis for that disciplinary penalty (*daṇḍakammavatthu*).
It has also been written previously: "one who has committed an offense involving action. In the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, the reading is "one who has committed an act of self-will" (*attakāmaṃ āpanno*);
they say, "this alone should be accepted," but this must be investigated.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the disclosure of what is grave is finished.
10. Commentary on the training rule concerning digging the earth. 86.
*Kaṭasakkharā* is a type of gravel that is soft like white clay. [The phrase] "in an unexcavated slope" is for the purpose of indicating a place where it is not customary to dig.
It is written: “It is said. It should be stated: “For the purpose of showing a place that is not subject to rain. “Mouse-dust” means dust thrown up by mice.
“Pure-minded” means that although they know, “If it continues in this way, the earth will split,” they do not desire the splitting of the earth;
thus they are called pure-minded. The two portions, beginning with dust, cause an offense.
Some say, "Since it is stated that there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) when [the ground] is half-covered and so forth, it is appropriate that it be an offense of wrong-doing.
In that case, it would be appropriate because such a substance is possible; however, here there are only two substances: earth that has been produced and earth that has not been produced.
Therefore, since one [offense] must correspond to two [substances], it is not appropriate. Here too, the mention of an offense of wrong-doing—
If you say it exists, that too is not logical, for it exists by way of perception (*saññā*), not by way of a physical basis (*vatthu*).
87. Regarding the statement "it is permissible to make fire": some say it is permissible because, at this stage, it takes up heat; therefore, it is allowed.
If that were so, when fire is made on the earth, the ground would remain warm even from afar, and one would have to disturb [the earth] to that extent; but that is not the case.

And since it is not permitted [to place fire on bare ground], some say that the fire burns whatever place it falls upon, and therefore it is permissible. However, even if it does not burn, because it has been stated,
"It is not permissible to place fire on ground that has not been burnt," one should understand that the fault lies simply in the act of throwing it oneself,
regardless of whether it catches fire once fallen.
The commentary on the training rule concerning digging the earth is finished.
The first chapter, the Chapter on False Speech, is completed according to the order of the commentary. 2.
The Chapter on Living Plants.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Plant Life (Bhūtagāma-sikkhāpada) 89.
By the phrase "being unable to restrain the axe," he makes known that [the action] has already been performed.
If one asks, "Why did he raise the axe?"—the answer to this is "of people," and so forth. From the words "he struck" and "he cut," [it follows that] there were tree-deities.
They say that hands are cut off, but they are not indestructible like those of the Cātumahārājika devas and others.
Regarding the words *bhavanti* and *ahuvuṃ*, the term *bhūta* has two temporal meanings. If the seed is shown by that which is produced from the seed, then that very thing is what belongs to it;
for this is precisely the resolution: "that very same cock is smeared with flesh. This is also stated in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).

For it is written: "perceiving seed in what is seed. Regarding that which is called "seed" and is termed a "class of living beings" (*bhūtagāma*), one should connect it as "seed of the class of living beings" within that seed.
It is said that because it lacks roots, it is not a complete class of living beings;

they state the reason that "only that which possesses roots and leaves is called a class of living beings. "Because it has no root from which a class of living beings arises, it is 'not having a root from which a class of living beings arises' (*abhūtagāmamūlattā*)."
“Because of the rootlessness of the group of beings,” or “for no other group of beings arises from that”—it is written in both ways.
The *piyaṅgu* is the *asanarukkha*; it has growing bark and edible fruit, and is also called the “yellow sal. It is included among the rootless groups of beings;
thus, this is merely a coconut. Because it is produced from the husk of a jar and because it conforms to the category of seed-plant life, it is a matter of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*).
It is not to be stored [with the thought], "Because it was poorly prepared," as it is written;

for it is stated that "from the statement 'of those trees whose branches grow,' it is established that there is no need to perform the ritual preparation (kappiyakaraṇa) for the branches of those from which they do not grow.
"Mudda-grass" is its name. "The reading is 'muñja-grass,'" so it is written.
“By means of the five ascetic conventions” (samaṇakappehi) means by means of the designations for ascetics; therefore, it must be said by the bhikkhu: “Make it allowable” (kappiyaṃ karohīti).
It is established that even when a novice (sāmaṇera) or another acts according to his instruction, he must say “It is allowable” before performing the preparation by fire and so forth.

Just like the preparation by fire and other such methods, seeds that have been extracted from their husks are also [included] under the phrase “by the five ascetic conventions” because they are allowable.
Those [terms] included here should be understood according to their availability as expressions for what is permissible for a recluse (*samaṇakappa*).

It is said: "If one wishes to say 'permissible' (*kappiya*), and says 'allowable' (*kappa*), they say 'it is allowed' (*vaṭṭati*). They state that the expression "permissible" may be used even in one's own respective language.
Because it is stated, "having said 'permissible' (*kappiya*)," the monk should say precisely "permissible."

"But by any other language," they say; this should be investigated. Because of the statement, "One pierces a wooden stake thinking, 'I will make the sugarcane allowable' (kappiya)," it is said that one fails with respect to what is intended to be made allowable.
However, the Teachers say: "'It is allowable' refers to having rice and so forth made allowable; it is permissible."

When explaining the reason for this, it should be understood that even if something is made by missing the mark due to its being in a state of being allowable (*vaṭṭanabhāvena*), it becomes allowable (*kappiya*).
If it were not allowable, then it would not be allowable when made from rice and so forth; thus, this must be investigated.

It is allowable to place a jar of moss that has grown on it in the sun, just as it is appropriate that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) when there is an intention to damage it. "It belongs to the same category as flower-strings and vessels..."

"Therefore, it is not permissible. However, they say that it is permissible even when a bunch of flowers is tied to a stalk, because the stalk has been made [into a receptacle] and the flower remains therein.
In the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*, it is stated: "The category of living beings (*bhūtagāma*) is shown by means of the category of seeds (*bījagāma*) for the purpose of exhaustive inclusion.
The commentary on the training rule regarding the destruction of living beings (*bhūtagāmasikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā*) is concluded.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule on Speaking Otherwise (Aññavādaka-sikkhāpada) 98–99.

*Aññaṃ vadati* means "speaking otherwise" (*aññavādaka*). It is written [in the text] as "he should make a statement. The reading is: "This refers to one who has become silent. *Ugghātetukāmo* means "desirous of confusing," or according to the ancients, "desirous of creating an obstacle.

100. Regarding such cases as "Venerable sir, it was clearly seen by me, yet this is not a kahāpaṇa coin," they say: "When the charge has not been brought, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for lying; when it has been brought, there are two offenses of expiation (*pācittiya*). This should be investigated.
102. Regarding the phrase "by means of what is not Dhamma, or by an incomplete assembly, or against one who does not deserve the legal act":

here it should be construed as, "When I have spoken, the Saṅgha will not perform a legal act that is not according to Dhamma, nor a legal act with an incomplete assembly, nor will it perform a legal act against me or against another who does not deserve such an act."
The commentary on the training rule concerning speaking otherwise is finished.
3. Commentary on the training rule concerning disparaging. 103. “Out of favoritism” (*chandāya*):

this is stated with a change of gender, as in the expression “syllable by syllable” (*akkharakkharāya*), or it means “for the sake of favor. The intended meaning is: for the sake of favor toward those whose lodgings he assigns.

106. In the phrases beginning with "one who is not fully ordained" (*anupasampanna*), the instrumental sense should be understood. "Another who is not fully ordained" means by another person who is not fully ordained.

"Of him" refers to one who is not fully ordained. It is stated: "At the time of formal authorization (*sammuti*), those lacking the five factors and so forth are called 'unauthorized,'" and "An authorization obtained by one who is fully ordained is destroyed by the renunciation of the training. "By the Sangha" means by the entire Sangha.
Having announced it through the formal ritual procedure (*kammavācā*), he has merely placed the burden upon himself, thinking, "This is your burden.
Here, the word "merely" (*kevala*) indicates only the state of having been announced by the ritual procedure. "By himself" means with the consent of the other monks.
If one asks, "How is there no offense for a first offender who disparages another with what is untrue? [The answer is: By this training rule (*sikkhāpada*) regarding false speech.
It appears as though two *pācittiya* offenses are stated for the preliminary action itself, such as in the cases of cutting trees and so forth; this requires investigation.
The commentary on the training rule concerning censuring is finished.
4. Commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning Lodgings.

110. From the statement, “In this way, this training rule was laid down by the Blessed One for the bhikkhus,” and from the statement in the *Parivāra*, “There is one original laying down (*paññatti*) and one supplementary laying down (*anupaññatti*),” it is established that there is a supplementary laying down here.
Even though this is established, the place of the original laying down is indicated by the passage beginning, “And furthermore, bhikkhus, you should recite this training rule as follows.”
It is not explicitly stated; rather, only this much was said: “I allow you, monks, for eight months... to store [it].
If one asks why that is so, it is because it need not be stated, as it is without distinction from the method already explained in the original formulation (paññatti).
If this is so, what is the subsequent formulation (anupaññatti) here? It is: “in the open air. This is the subsequent formulation, which applies even to the original formulation.
If it is asked, "Does it exist?"—it does exist. However, that [first phrase] indicates the mere location, while the second indicates the time consisting of four months of the rainy season.

It should be understood that the Blessed One said, "I allow you, monks... to set it down," demonstrating that he spoke of "in the open air" by combining both the time and the location into one. For this very reason, in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*...
It is said: "Wherever and whenever it is not permissible to spread [a rug], all that should be understood here as being included within the category of 'open air' (ajjhokāsa).
Since the winter season is a time when there is no offense, it is established that this training rule does not depend on its specific origin story;
for such is the distinction made by the force of the term "open air"—namely, during the rainy season, in a place where rain falls.
It is not permitted in the open air or under a pavilion and the like. During the winter season, it is not permitted in the natural open air;
however, in all such cases, it is permitted under a pavilion and the like even if it rains, provided that the snow and rain do not soak the lodging.
During the summer season, it is permitted even in the natural open air, provided that there is no appearance of unseasonable clouds. This is the distinction.
This is established both by the force of the two phrases, “eight months” and “in the convention of the rainy season.
Furthermore, it is precisely the distinction shown in the Commentary: that which is covered with leather and so forth, or newly woven, does not quickly perish.
“Following the body” means because it goes wherever the body goes. [In the case of] a bed belonging to the Saṅgha, etc.
The Elder Dhammasiri says it is not permissible to dwell having touched the body [with the bedding]. However, according to the statement in the Andhakaṭṭhakathā:

"But when donors give a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha, saying, 'Venerable sirs, enjoy this by using it in the open air as you please,' there is no offense in such a case," and because there is no prohibition here [in our text], it is permissible. "And other such cases..."
It is stated: "Others. It is written: "Facing the place where one sets foot means facing the spot where one places one's feet while sitting.
The teacher’s conjecture is: "Facing the place where one sets foot while sweeping. 111. It is written:
"With the lifting of the foot means because [the person] is standing outside the precincts. If they walk away, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the preacher of the Dhamma.
Why is it not an offense of expiation (pācittiya)? Because [the fan] must be taken after those who arrive later have caused the senior monks to rise.
However, because the preacher of the Dhamma is not to be made to rise, it is said: "Even though it was prescribed without a formal injunction, the responsibility for it rests upon him.

Regarding the phrase "only in the case of carrying": here, the Elder Dhammasiri says it means "carrying it about after having taken it up"; the Elder Upatissa says it means "making it one's own property. A *bījanī-pattaka* is a square-handled fan.
113. They say: “Because it is stated, ‘Whatever bhikkhu or sāmaṇera... [is] modest,’ it is not permissible for one who lacks modesty to go without having asked permission.
In the text, the phrase “it is obstructed by something,” and in the commentary, the word “obstructed,” refer specifically to the lodging;
therefore, it should be understood that such a case exists even there. The reading is “or without asking permission.”
The commentary on the first training rule concerning lodgings is finished.
5. Commentary on the second training rule concerning lodgings, §§116–117:
Only this much has been stated in the Aṭṭhakathās; nevertheless, the word-meanings (*padaṭṭhā*) and so forth are indeed obtainable there as well. (Source: *Anugaṇṭhipada*).
It is stated: "Other items such as rugs and the like are not mentioned because they are unallowable. And it is further stated:

"Although [the bed or chair] was already mentioned by the phrase 'a bed or a chair in a dwelling or in the vicinity of a dwelling,' the passage beginning with 'nevertheless' is commenced for the purpose of connecting [this case] with that.
Furthermore, this "at the foot of a tree" is merely a figurative expression (*upacāramatta*); there is nothing further to be said regarding it.
118. Regarding the rule that it is permissible to go even without having asked for permission: there is no offense even for one who goes out of forgetfulness;
however, asking for permission is a duty (*vatta*), and for one who intentionally does not ask, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) due to the breach of that duty.

It is as if it were appropriate to incur a *dukkaṭa* for one who departs after spreading out a communal bed (*saṅghika-seyyā*) in a private dwelling (*puggalika-senāsana*), or a private bed in a communal dwelling.
Why? Because it is stated: "Only the mere bed may be lost. Here, however, there are two kinds [of obstruction]: "obstructed" and "one who is obstructed.
The commentary on the second training rule concerning lodgings is concluded.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Intrusion.

121. Some say that "the elder monks" refers specifically to the group of six (Chabbaggiyas). Regarding the passage beginning with "having washed his feet," the construction should be understood as follows:
for one entering [the dwelling], from the stone for washing feet up to the bed or chair; or for one leaving for the sake of urination, from the bed or chair up to the place of urination.
This being the case, it should not have been said, "for one leaving for the sake of urination," but rather, "from the place of urination..."
Or it should be stated: "for one who is departing. In some manuscripts, the term *passāvaṭṭhānaṃ* (urinal) appears. For indeed, in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*, it is said:
"The precinct (*upacāra*) extends from the stone for washing the feet for one entering, as far as the bed and chair; and for one departing, from the bed and chair as far as the urinal.
Therefore, [it refers to] for one entering after having washed his feet, or for the sake of urination...
In some manuscripts, the reading is: "And for one departing, from the stone used for washing the feet placed at the door, from the place for urination, and from the bed and chair.
That is not the correct reading. Why? Because the vicinity of the bed and chair has already been stated.
For one entering, it extends as far as the vicinity of the bed and chair; for one departing, it begins from there and extends as far as the place for urination, the latrine, and the walking path.
The Teacher says that the reading is of such a kind as it accords with this meaning. 122.
"Leaving aside the vicinity" means leaving aside the vicinity mentioned here. It is written: "Even when spreading [the bedding] within the vicinity for seeing or hearing.
The commentary on the training rule concerning encroaching is finished.
7. Commentary on the Training Rule on Expelling (Nikkaḍḍhanasikkhāpada) 126–7.

Regarding the phrase "six or seven gate-houses," it is the gate-house of the entrance that is intended here. Even if one hears the command "Come out," there is no offense if one leaves of one's own accord; in this context, the vicinity refers specifically to the fire-hall and so forth.
The commentary on the training rule on expelling is finished.

It is written that "even a balance given at the height of a man's neck [when measuring] is indeed an aerial hut," yet it is stated that "that is not what is intended here.

9. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Large Dwellings (Mahallakavihārasikkhāpada) 135.
"As far as the door-frame" means as far as the vicinity of the door; that is to say, as far as the wall—that is well stated. "The measure of the width of the door-panel":

since the space of one cubit [on each side] is intended, this includes the precinct extending around the width of the door-panel; therefore, even if the precinct is not fully completed, [it is still considered a large dwelling].
It exists. Because it "makes light" (ālokaṃ karoti), it is called "light"; because it "shuts off" (sandheti) or "covers" (pidheti), it is a "joint" (sandhi); thus they are named "light-joints.
There is no need for plastering work on the window shutters or for the removal of weeds.
136. "Bricks" (iṭṭhakā) refers to roof-tiles, slabs of stone, and so forth. Regarding "over the covering" (chadanūpari): first, in this case, once—
Having covered it without remainder and having tied it again with the binding-rod, it should be covered in the same manner a second time.
It is said, "When the third and fourth times arrive, one should determine two paths, command the third path, and depart";
this is consistent with the statement, "he has it covered again and again."
The Ancients, however, say: "It is permissible to resolve upon three courses of action at the very first instance;
from the fourth [instance] onwards, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya); from the fourth application [of plaster], there is an offense.

In this regard, the rule for roofing corresponds to the source-text (nidāna), while the rule for plastering corresponds to the cutting of the hair mentioned in the commentary. Nevertheless, that [explanation] is not appropriate. Both in the source-text and in the commentary...

The Teacher says that it is not consistent [with the rules] for one to resolve upon the third round of roofing when the roof has already been completed— whether entirely covered or even partially uncovered—

on many occasions. Regarding the phrases "two roofs" and "two coverings," the Elder Upatissa says that one should depart after having commanded, "From the third time onwards, have it roofed in this manner."
The commentary on the training rule concerning large dwellings is finished.

144. "By following the discourse" means by following the discussion as to what kind of virtue, what kind of conduct, and from which family a candidate for the office of instructor of bhikkhunīs has gone forth, and so on.

145–147. "Outside the monastery" means from one area where the boundary has been fixed (*baddhasīma*) to another where no boundary has been fixed; the meaning is "from the village boundary.

Regarding the phrase "even by way of a dream," it is stated here according to the method of general prevalence (*bāhullanaya*), as not all [cases] apply. For some of the group of six monks were twenty years old and some were even more than twenty years old;
by this, it is understood that this rule was laid down during the period of the Middle Enlightenment.

Having stated, “He is virtuous,” in order to show specifically the kind of virtue intended here—since virtue is fourfold—the words beginning with “restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha” are spoken.
In the *Gaṇṭhānugaṇṭhi* sections it is said: “The restraints of mindfulness and so forth are not intended here; therefore, the Master of the Commentary shows the reading from the *Vibhaṅga*.

“From the point of view of the meaning” (*atthato*) means from the meaning of the canonical text (*pāḷiatthato*). “From the point of view of the reason” (*kāraṇato*) means from the logical justification for the reason.
The intended meaning is "from the commentary" (*aṭṭhakathāto*). Alternatively, "by way of cause" (*kāraṇato*) means by way of the phenomenon (*dhammato*);

thus, it is said to mean "by way of the phenomenon. Alternatively, "by way of meaning" (*atthato*) means by way of the fruit (*phalato*). "By way of cause" (*kāraṇato*) means by way of the reason (*hetuto*).

It is written: "Even the *Dhammapada* [is included] together with the *Jātaka*. Regarding the phrase "to speak the question": in the expression "he speaks when asked the question," [it refers to] one who has been asked by a bhikkhunī.
"It is not possible to say, 'I do not know. The reading is "na kho pana taṃ bhagavantaṃ.
Some write "na kho panetaṃ," but that is not correct. Because of the expression "wearing garments of saffron color," it is not permissible even for one who has committed a *pārājika* offense.
For a nun, only physical contact is mentioned. Indeed, by means of sexual intercourse, one becomes a defiler of a nun.
148–9. Those who have received full ordination (*upasampadā*) in the presence of monks are those who have changed their gender, such as the five hundred Sākiyan women.

From the statement, "But for the sake of [avoiding] the offense of preaching the Dhamma," it is established that by the inclusion of the term "women" (*mātugāma*), the category of *bhikkhunīs* is included everywhere.
However, by the inclusion of the term "*bhikkhunī*," women are included in the training rule concerning crossing over horizontally (swimming).
Not elsewhere. The canonical text (pāḷi) reads “osāretabbā,” meaning “the text should be recited. The commentary (aṭṭhakathā) reads “osāretabbaṃ.
If it is argued that because there is no fault in paying homage in one place, it is permissible for many to pay homage through a single person, [we reply:
there is nothing to be done by the monks; it must be done by the nun herself, therefore it is not permissible. “Sitting anywhere... [is the phrase].
They say: "for one sitting within twelve *hattha*s [of the boundary].

"Not desiring to go having been invited" means that monks who desire to go having been invited are not intended here; rather, those desiring to enter the rains residence (*vassa*) are intended—this is the meaning.
"From where" means from the nuns' dwelling (*bhikkhunī-vihāra*). "There" means in the nuns' dwelling. Although it says "monks who give exhortation,"...
A residence is considered "with monks" by virtue of those who give the exhortation (*ovāda*), not because all [monks] are present;

nevertheless, since one must certainly go for the sake of requesting the exhortation and for the sake of communal living when there is no monk to give the exhortation, it should be understood that it is "with monks" even if there are only other [monks] present. "It must be protected" means that there is an offense for interrupting the rains retreat (*vassaccheda*).
[The nuns] must be protected. Why? Because of the phrase beginning with “in times of distress,” and so forth. It was stated that one should ask, “Is this Uposatha on the fourteenth day?
However, even then, it was actually on the thirteenth; nowadays, nuns go [to the monastery] precisely on the fourteenth and ask, “Venerable sir, when is the Uposatha?
This was apparently said with the intention of referring to [those who are like] wives or mistresses. “She should go...”

The reading is: “...this is an offense. “Two or three” means by two or by three. The intention is that the plural form “by them” (*tāhi*) is stated with reference to those who have come together from one [place].

The detailed explanation of the statement, “Whether it be a single bhikkhunī or many bhikkhunīs sent from many bhikkhunī dwellings for the purpose of exhortation,” begins with: “The community of bhikkhunīs and the noble ladies, bhikkhunīs,” and so forth.
It is stated: “‘The community of bhikkhunīs and the noble bhikkhunīs,’ etc., is the speech sent by [the messenger] from various residences”; and it is written:
“Approaching five times is stated according to the instructions for an incomplete Saṅgha, an individual, or one staying in different dwellings with a companion.
Even in a residence where the recitation of the Pātimokkha does not take place, there too [the messenger must perform] the formal request.
Having accepted [the invitation], on the following day, he should say to the one by whom it was received, "There is no monk appointed as an instructor of the nuns," and so forth.
If there is one appointed, he must be pointed out. It is said: "If he himself is appointed, he should say, 'I am [he]'";
if he is appointed, or if the receiver of the instruction recites the Pātimokkha, it must be done by another.
Some say that one must have it announced; others say, "It is also permissible for one to announce it oneself. In certain manuscripts, it is written, "I invite the noble ones" (*ayyānaṃ pavāreti*);
if that were the case, one should say, "I invite the noble sir" (*ayyassa pavāremi*), but this is not found in the manuscript.
The commentary on the training rule regarding exhortation is finished.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Setting Sun (Atthaṅgatasikkhāpada) 153.
*Munātīti* means "he knows. *Antaradhāyatīpi* means "it also disappears. Herein, if there is anything superior to that, I see it; whatever is variegated, for that purpose.
*Taggha* is a particle of reason. *Saha uppādamanantarā kiriyā*: action immediately following the arising [of the mind]. And those which are... (*yamā ca te*)... [are]... [the sense-spheres].

"Do not lead [the mind] elsewhere by means of the mind. Just as at dawn one might see the sun risen from the water and standing there, so too behold the Buddha Aṅgīrasa shining brightly; the connection is that he is not only shining like a lotus, but is also blazing like the sun in the sky.
Alternatively, behold the Buddha Aṅgīrasa shining like a lotus and blazing like the sun.
To the Buddha. Just as you might see at dawn a full-blown *kokanuda* lotus, known as the white water-lily, whose fragrance has not yet faded, so too behold the radiant Aṅgīrasa, the Buddha.
Since the splendor of the Blessed One is illuminated by both [the simile and the description], one should honor the Buddha who is beautiful with qualities thus illuminated;
having honored him, one should worship that splendor. And because he is worthy of worship, one should spend one's time [in his service].
*Lakkhaye*. The canonical text (*pāḷi*) reads: “For one who has received full ordination on one side.
The commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) reading is: “For those who have received full ordination on one side.

From the statement beginning with “You are incapable,” it appears that there is no offense for one who, out of compassion, causes a student (*saddhivihārika*) or others to be expelled from monasteries belonging to the Saṅgha. [He is] incapable.
Some say that since the Elder did this intentionally, a logical justification must be sought here. My own conjecture is that it was done by the Elder prior to the promulgation of the training rule.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the setting of the sun is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Nuns’ Quarters (Bhikkhunupassaya-sikkhāpada) 162.
Some say that because of the statement, “even if staying for a single night,” it is permissible to go and exhort [the nuns] where they do not stay overnight.
If this were so, it would follow as a logical conclusion that it is permissible to go to a pre-arranged meeting place to exhort them. From that...
One should not say, "A residence with monks is to be desired only within half a yojana.
If a monk who instructs nuns intends to go half a yojana to give instruction, and the community of nuns intends to go half a yojana to listen, it should be said that "it is permissible";
however, this was not stated [in the rule], therefore it is not permissible. This is according to the lower limit.
However, it is said: "even for a single night. From that point on, it becomes a residence (*upassaya*);
the meaning is not that it becomes one merely by being designated as such. Wherever the nuns have gone to dwell, that place acquires the designation of a residence;

one should not go there to give the exhortation (*ovāda*). Some say it is permissible during the day in a single dwelling (*ekāvāsa*), but after careful consideration, the more appropriate view should be adopted.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the nuns’ quarters is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Material Goods (Āmisa-sikkhāpada): 164.
From the scriptural statement, “One who has been fully ordained but not authorized by the Saṅgha,” it follows that [the offense applies] whether one is authorized by [an individual] or by the Saṅgha.
And because of the commentarial statement, "It was established by making it a burden," [the instruction] is for one endowed with eight factors—
whether appointed or desiring to live apart— to request, "Let this be your burden until I return," and having so requested,
it is established; or, in the absence of such a person, it is established by the Saṅgha itself as a burden, in order to exhort her regarding the eight Garudhammas.
It is established that one obtains [the result] even by means of another factor, let alone by another method. Furthermore, regarding the rule:

“If a bhikkhu, not being authorized, should exhort bhikkhunīs, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya),” it should be understood that this was stated with reference to what has been set aside after first making it a burden.
This is precisely the opinion of the residents of the Abhayagiri monastery; however, in the *Anugaṇṭhipada*, having rejected this approach, it states: “There is none...”

Having stated, "Regarding the passage beginning with 'Koci,' one who at present is an unappointed instructor is called a 'bhikkhunovādaka' (an instructor of bhikkhunīs)," he further addressed the point raised in the *Andhakaṭṭhakathā*: "'[The text says:

"One who is fully ordained but has not been appointed by the formal act (*kammavācā*)—let the Bhikkhu Saṅgha nevertheless provide assistance to the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha; instruct the bhikkhunīs, and ensure the comfortable dwelling of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha.'"'"
"Having been requested in this manner and appointed, he then requests permission from the Saṅgha of monks; thereafter, that elder exhorts the bhikkhunīs.
Such [an act] is not authorized by the Saṅgha of monks—herein, the meaning should be understood in the same manner as stated previously.
However, in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*, it says: "Not being authorized, having heard the words of the bhikkhunīs who had come to the village for the purpose of exhortation..."
It is stated that "giving a reply [constitutes] the consent of the Saṅgha, not [the formal act] consisting of a motion followed by a fourth proclamation";
this accords with the opinion of the *Anugaṇṭhipada*. The statement found in the *Andhakaṭṭhakathā* also accords with that, as does the canonical text itself;
for neither the receiver of the exhortation nor the reciter of the Pātimokkha becomes a "teacher of the nuns" merely by the words "May he conduct himself in a pleasing manner."
[The opponent says: "He is [qualified]. If he is, then even one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*) should be called 'a teacher of the nuns' by that same statement.
[The respondent asks: "If he is, then what is the purpose of the learning (*bāhusacca*) mentioned in the *Gaṇṭhānugaṇṭhi* passages, which state:

'One who is unappointed (*asammata*) is one who, by virtue of being unappointed, has been placed by the Saṅgha with the burden: "You are very learned; teach!"'"? In this case, what is the use of great learning?

In the *Anugaṇṭhipada* itself it is stated: "Having heard that 'one who dwells at Abhayagiri says [this],' the Elder Dhammasiri later grants permission, thinking, 'He may exhort [the nuns] either by being formally appointed or by being commanded.
What is the point of saying more? By merely saying, "Let him act with inspiring confidence (*pāsādika*)," one becomes an exhorter of nuns (*bhikkhunovādaka*).
In the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), what is the purpose of the phrase "having taken up the burden"?

No one else is permitted to speak even that much; otherwise, this canonical text would be contradicted: "I allow you, monks, for all except the foolish, the sick, and those about to travel, to receive the exhortation. How so?
For him, because of the statement, "Monks, the exhortation must not be declined," there is no distinction between being appointed or unappointed.
Regarding the word *koci*, one might say, "Let him accomplish it with inspiring confidence," and one who speaks thus would be subject to an offense here according to the first rule.

Let that be so, because he is not appointed and because the burden has not been assigned. Furthermore, if he were to act as the instructor of the nuns, there would be an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) due to his disparagement; all of this is undesirable. Therefore, in the Commentary, it says: "In this regard..."

The Master [the commentator] says: because it was not stated, "one who is called an exhorter of bhikkhunīs," one who has been established as such by being assigned that responsibility is indeed permitted to exhort them, and no one else.
The commentary on the training rule concerning material gifts is finished.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Giving of Robes.
169. The question: "Will you accept it?
The commentary on the training rule regarding the giving of robes is concluded.
6. Commentary on the training rule regarding the sewing of robes.
176. "Having deceived" means: instead of saying, "It is for your relative," he said only, "For a certain bhikkhunī.
For when they heard the words "for a certain [person]," they sewed it, perceiving it as belonging to one who was not a relative.
In this training rule, the canonical text (pāḷi) states only this much: "A robe means any one of the six kinds of robes. Therefore, it is so stated.

“‘Robe’ means that which is used for wearing as an undergarment or as an upper garment,” and so forth. Furthermore, the phrase “the last [robe] is subject to assignment” has been written; this is a scribal error.

7. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Arrangements (Saṃvidhāna).
181. Regarding "they corrupted those bhikkhunīs," the word *dūsayiṃsu* should be understood as a derivative form (*vipariṇāma*).

182–4. "Going together" (*sampadanti*) means they go on foot. "In the manner already stated" refers to the definition beginning with, "It is called a 'confluence' (*sampāta*) because they come together there," and so forth.

No conventional designation (*upacāra*) applies to what is already included within the term "foot-path" (*padagata*), for because of their extreme proximity, it would be as if they were mixed together. [The area] is delimited by the crowing of a cock.
In the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, it is written: “That too is by way of conventional designation. And: “It was stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* because for the most part the arrangement is such;
therefore, it is not a careless scribal error. And: “It was stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* as the upper limit;
one should understand that beyond that, it is what is characterized as reaching one hundred and fifty leagues (*addhayojana-lakkhaṇa*).”
And it is said: “It is indeed a kappiya-bhūmi (an area where things are allowable)... [etc.]... they do not say so. The reason for this is difficult to see.
Which, then, is the rule (tantra)? It is said: “If one makes an appointment, saying ‘Let us go,’ there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
In that context, the present-tense form “let us go” cannot possibly apply to a non-path, such as a nunnery or similar location.
Because it is a place where people enter from within their houses and so forth, and because it is a location where high beds and such arise;

nor is it the same as the dwellings of non-Buddhist sectarians (*titthiya*), since it is a residence for those who have gone forth (*pabbajita*). The word "at" (*dvāre*) is used in the locative case in the sense of proximity;

therefore, to demonstrate this, he further says, "on the street" (*rathikāya*). In the remaining commentaries, it is stated: "Even if an arrangement has been made within this interval, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the bhikkhu."

Because it has been reached, it does not coincide [with the previous definition]. From the statement “within the village boundary,” the offense occurs precisely upon entering the precincts (*upacāra*) of another village.
From the statement “at half a *yojana*,” it is appropriate that the offense occurs only upon crossing [that distance].
185. Regarding “the breaking up of the kingdom,” this refers to its destruction. In the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*, it says: “The three types of appointments (*saṅketa*) are by way of time, day, and path.”
"In that case, there is an offense only by the latter [alternative]," it is said. The meaning is: if, having replied, "By this path," they go by another way, there is indeed an offense.
The commentary on the training rule concerning prior arrangement (saṃvidhāna-sikkhāpada) is finished.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Boarding a Boat (Nāvābhirūhana-sikkhāpada) 189.
If it is asked, "From where does one go to another village by river?", he says: "Of whichever river," and so forth.
"By the counting of other villages" means that, excluding the village landing place where one boarded, it is the counting of any other village. "A woman is also included here."

This was the teacher’s reasoning; for that very reason, it was not stated that "there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who has been ordained together with both [the male and female Sanghas], but there is no offense for a trainee nun (sikkhamānā) or a novice nun (sāmaṇerī).
This same principle applies to other similar cases as well.
191. Because it is stated, "having made an arrangement out of a desire for play, based on worldly enjoyment and intimacy with friends," it refers to an unwholesome state of mind (akusalacitta).
Should it be said that these are "worldly offenses"? It should not be so said; the phrase "with play as their primary aim" is stated by way of general tendency.
And in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*, it is stated: "There are three types of consciousness and three types of feeling.

Alternatively, at the time of making an appointment, a monk who has play as his primary aim makes the appointment; there is an offense for the monk in entering another village or in traveling beyond half a *yojana*. [This occurs when] he is with a wholesome mind.
Or when one is reflecting, or seeing such things as a cetiya, or when one falls asleep due to fatigue with an indeterminate (abyākata) state of mind—
thus it should be understood that three types of consciousness are included.
The commentary on the training rule concerning boarding a boat is finished.
9. Commentary on the Training Rule on Ripening (Paripācita-sikkhāpada) 192.

"A servant" (*ceṭaka*) means a child. "A young calf" (*taruṇapotaka*): the ancient teachers [say this]. It is recorded: "This was laid down for the purpose of cutting off the faction of wicked bhikkhus; therefore, an offense is stated only in regard to the five kinds of cooked food. 194–197. "Prepared" (*nipphādita*):
this does not apply to what has been specifically requested (*viññatti*), but rather to what has been prepared through indirect talk (*parikathā*) and so forth. Therefore, by this training rule...
There is no offense; it is with reference to this that it was said, “In all cases there is no offense.

The reading is: "And for Upananda, by means of the fourth training rule.

1. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Alms-food from a Public Rest House (Āvasathapiṇḍasikkhāpada).
203–4. *Pūgassā* means "by a group. *Kukkuccāyanto* refers to making a definitive conclusion by thinking, "There must be an escape from this [transgression], yet we do not know it";
thus one is called "feeling remorse" (*kukkuccāyanto*).
Just as the Venerable Upāli, grasping the underlying principle, said, "Friend, there is no offense even in a dream," so too did the Elder say, "There is no offense for one who is ill."
Why does he not define it? Because the formulation of the Vinaya rules concerns what is not-self (*anattā*);
because it has been rejected on the grounds that "this is not one's own domain"; and because the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) is incomplete.
For it was only after the first *pārājika* training rule had been formulated in its complete form that the Elder said, "There is no offense even in a dream," adding, "excepting a dream."

"According to the sequence of the words stated": because there is no affliction for the donors when it is specifically for a limited amount rather than as much as they wish, therefore it is said, "not specifically for a limited amount. 208.
"'On one day on the way'—this was said with reference to only one [day]," and "'The same method applies'—it refers to the very method already stated."
It has been written: "Having gone to show [the way], he says 'hi' and so forth upon his return";
"Having become pure in mind, one is permitted to eat while walking in one's natural gait"; and "For one who is not ill but perceives himself as ill, it originates from bodily action.
The commentary on the training rule regarding alms-food from a public rest-house is finished.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Group Meals (Gaṇabhojana-sikkhāpada) 209–218.
"Secretly concealed" means not being publicly visible. "One person with one [other]" means that one person's meal is not called "I have been invited by another.
Because it is stated, "If they take [food] together, it constitutes a group meal," four [monks]...
Some say that if lay followers invite four monks separately and give [the food] while they are standing within arm’s reach of one another, it constitutes *gaṇabhojana* (eating in a group);
however, this does not seem correct. It is written: "From the act of requesting, when there is an announcement and the group takes [the food] together, there is an offense under this training rule;
when they take it separately, there is an offense for requesting fine foods, soups, and rice. From the act of requesting...

It is stated [in some sources] that "passing urine was permitted in the Commentary by way of a specific occasion (aṭṭhuppatti), and there is no offense in that case regarding soup, boiled rice, and so forth";
however, that is not correct. Why? Because only two modes [of offense] are mentioned in the *Parivāra*; therefore, it is wrongly said in the Commentary that it was "permitted.
It is evident from the very occasion itself [that this is so], and thus [it is not included] in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*).

It should be said: "It is so stated. Regarding "taking together": even if those who have already taken their food remain standing until others finish taking theirs, they are indeed said to be "taking together. They say: "If she goes away, there is no offense.
Here it is asked: "It was stated that 'in this case, the act of receiving itself is the measure'; then why is it called 'eating in a group' (*gaṇabhojana*) in the Pāḷi?"
Is it said that “where four [monks]... eat, this is called *gaṇabhojana* (eating in a group)”? It is replied:
“Where” (*yattha*) is a locative case used in the sense of the accusative. “Four” (*cattāro*) indicates the minimum limit for a group.

“Of five kinds of food” (*pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ*) indicates the food sufficient to constitute an offense. “Invited by one or another kind of food” (*aññatarena bhojanena nimantitā*)— [The rest of the passage continues with the definition of the types of food and the conditions under which the offense is incurred.]

This is an illustration of an improper invitation (*akappiya-nimantana*). However, because eating in a group (*gaṇabhojana*) has already been mentioned by way of an invitation itself, it is said: "They eat having been invited.

It is not stated, "They eat after requesting some kind of food," because that is already evident from the very origin story (*aṭṭhuppatti*). The connection should be understood as: "whatever they eat. In this regard:
“They eat” is a statement regarding the rule for the recipient; for monks do not eat what has not been formally received.
This is what is meant: “Because of eating food received from a group, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Having sewn the visiting monk’s cloth-strip with a false thread, they place it there so that, when the wind blows, it becomes as if it were a single layer, [holding it] with their hands.
“He strikes” means he turns [the cloth] over. “Rolling back” means he performs a turning of the thread for those who are taking up the weaving, so that the thread may be easily grasped;
and he performs a turning of the warp for those who are sewing the strips, so that the sewing may be easy.
The one intended here is the maker of new robes, not the other. “Having asked permission from Bimbisāra, while the requisites were still being prepared...”
They say, "The time had passed, and later, when the training rule on group meals was laid down, he approached the Blessed One and asked," because otherwise it would contradict the commentary.
[Regarding the phrase] "two or three as one": by the statement beginning with "even those who accepted an improper invitation," [it refers to] the condition of an improper invitation.

Thus he demonstrates that there is no offense [in this case], whereas from an explicit request (*viññatti*), there is indeed an offense. "With one who is not invited as the fourth" means one for whom the fourth person is not invited;

this same method applies everywhere. "Having caused to enter" means having caused to sit down. "The fourfold group obtained at the time of giving robes," "the fourfold group obtained at the time of making robes," and so forth—these are what are meant by "those.
"Those" refers to those foods with which there is no disagreement. "Great Elder" refers to one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*).
"Standing" means that the sign was indicated by one who was standing. "Having gone here and there" means having gone near the monks on carriage-roads and so forth.

However, in some manuscripts of this training rule, the following reading is seen: "I allow you, monks, to eat a meal in a group at the time of giving robes. Thus indeed [it was said] by the Blessed One to the monks. In some [other manuscripts],...
“Having said, ‘Let him eat,’ [the Buddha said], ‘And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule’—this reading is excellent.
The commentary on the training rule concerning eating in a group is finished.
3. Commentary on the training rule concerning eating in succession.

221. *Adhiṭṭhitā* means constantly occurring. *Badarasāḷava* is a preparation made by mixing jujube powder, sugar, and so forth. *Kirakammakārena* means by the agent of the action (*kamma*) of "making" (*kira*). 226.
Regarding the phrase, “Having made an assignment (*vikappetvā*), take it,” the ancient elders said:

“Without making an assignment in the presence of the Blessed One, he went out from his house and made the assignment in the vicinity of a certain monk on the street. By the one making the assignment...”
However, one should say, "I give this expected meal of mine to so-and-so," and the other should say, "Use what belongs to him, or do with it as you see fit.

Regarding "among five fellow-practitioners": if one wishes to assign [an item] to a fellow-practitioner standing face-to-face, but does not see that fellow-practitioner, [one may assign it] to a householder.
Some say that one may eat after saying, either in the presence [of the person] or by oneself, "I assign this to such-and-such among the five fellow-practitioners";
however, if that were so, the inference would arise that the Elder, while sitting right there, utters those words and then accepts the food.
But in the *Mahāpaccarī* and other texts, only assigning in the absence [of the person] is mentioned.
This accords with the statement, "Therefore, Ānanda, having made a formal assignment (*vikappetvā*), take it"; nevertheless, in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā* it says:

"Therefore, if a bhikkhu [says] to one among five fellow practitioners (sahadhammika), either in their presence, 'I give my expected meal to you' or 'I assign it to you,' or [says], 'I give it to so-and-so' or 'I assign it to him'..."

From the statement, "either [in person] or thus in the absence of others," it is seen that this should be said only in the presence of one who is in accordance with the Dhamma, and not by oneself alone.
Since this latter method also accords with the words of the ancient *gaṇṭhi* (commentary on difficult points), the meaning here should be understood according to the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*.
Here, although there is the statement, "Those people... gave food," which refers to an improper invitation (*akappiya-nimantanā*), [the following applies]:
Although it is thus perceived, nevertheless, because it was the cause for the arising of remorse in the Elder, it should be understood that he was invited by means of that meal.
Otherwise, it would contradict the subsequent statement, "He eats two or three invitations together," as well as the section on non-offenses (anāpatti). 229.
Herein, this is the investigation: following the statement, "If another person takes the bowl, it should not be given," subsequently...
There is no purpose served by an improper invitation; rather, the purpose of an improper invitation lies precisely in its preliminary stage.

Regarding the statement, "Venerable sir, may you come tomorrow as well," which of these constitutes an improper invitation? Therefore, in this case, the underlying intention (*adhippāya*) is the authoritative criterion.
This is not so, because of the statement: "If one eats food obtained after having gone on alms-round, there is an offense. In that regard—

Just as in the phrase “even though, Bhante,” the meaning is understood not by taking the mere words at face value, but by following the sequence of what is improper regarding an invitation, so too in the phrase “having wandered for alms,” the meaning should be understood as referring to food obtained through an improper invitation in the interim.
For it is said that upon seeing him wandering for alms, [someone says]: “Venerable sir, here is food.”
Even if it is given with the words "Take [this]," it is called "obtained by an improper invitation. However, in common parlance, it is said to be "food obtained by wandering for alms";
this case should be understood in the same way. Otherwise, in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*, it says:
"In the case of one invited to eat from five kinds of food... [etc. ...in the food of another and another," according to the method already stated regarding eating in a group (*gaṇabhojana*).

There is a contradiction with what has been stated. For this statement—by explaining the meaning as "he who, having first been invited, goes taking that first invitation, eats the meal of each successive person who gave the invitation"—indicates that an offense occurs only when eating the meal obtained from an invitation.
This is also evident from the statement: "Two or three invitations [may be accepted] together."

It is for the sake of consistency; otherwise, it would have been sufficient to say, "from the food of another than the one by whom he was invited," or in the Canon, it would have been sufficient to say, "he eats together with an invitation.

The phrase beginning with "by whichever [person]" was stated in order to prevent the contingency of an offense at the first meal of a second invitation. This is according to the sequence of invitations.
If it is argued that the Pāḷi says "he eats," [we reply] no, because it contradicts such Pāḷi passages as, "there is no offense in the case of regular meals," and so forth.
Furthermore, in the *Gaṇṭhipada* it is asked: "Why is it not permitted to eat almsfood obtained by wandering for alms?
[The answer is: "'Eating in succession' means being invited with one of the five kinds of staple foods; setting that aside, of the five..."
It is written: “Because it is stated that ‘one eats any one of the various kinds of food; this is what is called eating in succession (paramparabhojana).
If this were so, would it follow that even a regular meal (niccabhatta) and the like are not permitted? If you say that a regular meal and the like are designated (odissaka), that is not correct;
for [the prohibition applies] to that which is produced by one’s own wealth other than those [specific items], or to rice-gruel cooked in the morning obtained from the Saṅgha.

If it were a solid mass, then for one living dependent on a village consisting of a single hut, there would be the undesirable consequence that even the regular meal obtained through alms-round would become unallowable.
If you argue that what is obtained there by means of alms-round is not allowable because it causes a lack of confidence in those who invite [the monks], we say no;
for [the rule] applies everywhere except in the case of the five kinds of cooked food.

Because it contradicts the statement, “there is no offense. For even one who has eaten hard food (khādanīya) belonging to another, by not eating the meal offered by invitation (nimantanabhojana), certainly causes a loss of confidence (appasāda).

Therefore, that which brings about a loss of confidence is immeasurable; consequently, specific meals such as regular daily meals (niccabhatta) and so forth cannot be considered [offenses] under this category.
Furthermore, having reconciled the method explained here with the method stated previously:
"Whatever is acceptable, that should be accepted"—this is the determination of some teachers.
However, the teacher’s own determination will be made clear at the end. It is stated: "The intended meaning is that even when drinking milk or juice, it is unmixed.
In the *Gaṇṭhipada*, it is written: "Having been mixed with rice below, it remains on top."

“Mahā-upāsaka” refers to the head of the household. In the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, the statement “it is an offense (*āpatti*)” appears to contradict the statement in the *Kuruṇḍī* that “it is permissible (*vaṭṭati*).
It is written: “The intention of both [texts] has been examined in the *Mahāpaccarī*. Regarding “on account of conduct,” it is said:
“because of what must be stated later, namely, ‘without having asked a monk who is present. This refers to verbal action (*vacī-kamma*).
Non-designation (*avikappana*). Here, because of the statement in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “A great lay follower invites monks... [omission] ...there is an offense for one who eats food received later.
There is an offense for one who eats food obtained by wandering for alms,” and because of the *Pāḷi* text:
“We ate after having wandered for alms early in the morning,” and in the *Khandhaka*: “And you should not, O monks, [eat] except... [omission].
And because of the statement: "At an invitation, one may consume the boiled rice and gruel of another;

whoever should consume it otherwise, he is to be dealt with according to the rule," whether [the food] was announced after being invited or not, for a monk who has accepted the first invitation, any other food belonging to another—other than the food of that first invitation—is an offense of eating in succession (*paramparabhojana*).
He prepares it. It is permissible [to eat] what belongs to oneself, or what has been received from the Saṅgha or a group, or what belongs to one who is not a householder;

however, because it was first fixed by invitation, even food belonging to another—such as regular meals (*niccabhatta*) and so forth—is permissible. The statement in the *Khandhaka*: “And you, monks...
[as far as] ...should be dealt with according to the rule,” is a regulation regarding the practice of eating food belonging to another.
"Therefore, 'hand' alone is our logic," says the Teacher.
The commentary on the training rule regarding eating in succession is finished.
4. Commentary on the training rule regarding Kāṇamātā.
31–3. *Paṭiyālōkaṃ* means the western region. *Pūvagaṇanāya* means by way of counting leftover cakes; this is the meaning.

If one takes it with the perception that "it has been prepared for the purpose of provisions for a journey (*apātheyya*) and so forth," there is no offense because the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) lacks the requisite intention (*acittaka*).

However, if one takes what has already been stored away, one is certainly not released from the offense. But in the case of not sharing [the food], there is no offense because it is unallowable (*akappiya*).

Some say that the state of being without consciousness (*acittakatā*) is due solely to the absence of knowing the formal rule (*paññatti*), and not due to the absence of knowing the physical object (*vatthu*). This is not so;

for it is not stated among the factors in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā* that there must be "knowledge of the fact that [food] has been prepared for the purpose of provisions and so forth. However, in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*, it is stated thus:
"When one or several [alms-bowls] have been taken, filling two or three bowls, either by failing to inform them or by oneself..."

Or, having understood [the situation], whoever takes more incurs a *dukkaṭa*. When three or four have entered together, if one has taken two bowlfuls and the second takes two as well, if the first does not prevent him, there is a *pācittiya* for the first.
If he prevents him, there is no offense; there is only a *dukkaṭa* for the second. If he intentionally does not speak, according to the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*:
According to the stated method, it is a *pācittiya*; according to the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*, it is a *dukkaṭa*.

Regarding the phrase "accepting what is in excess," the fifth factor is stated therein; therefore, because it was not accepted, it is not a *pācittiya*, but because of the failure to do what ought to be done, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
Otherwise, this would result in a case of both doing and not doing, or else non-restraint or non-reporting would constitute the sixth factor.
It may be said: regarding the phrase "of those belonging to the same Nikāya," it is stated here:

"If the monks residing nearby, or those who have come to the nearby assembly hall, do not accept what has been brought by those of a different faction, and if one knows that they will cause it to be given only to the monastery attendants (*ārāmika*) and so forth, then it is permissible to give it wherever it reaches for consumption. This is because of the statement, "two or three bowlfuls."
Some who consider themselves experts in the Vinaya say, "There is no offense for one who takes even more than that from a basket or similar container," but let that view remain theirs alone;
the teachers, however, say, "Even from a basket or similar container, one should take no more than two or three bowlfuls according to the measure of a large bowl.
For this is the discourse concerning the upper limit."
The commentary on the training rule concerning Kāṇamātā is finished.
5. Commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning Invitation (Pavāraṇā). 236.

Although those who have been invited by an invitation for as much as they require are indeed intended here by the term “invited,” it is nevertheless the latter [type of invitation] that is intended in this context, because of the specific origin story (*aṭṭhuppatti*).

237. Because it is said, “Enough of all this,” it is called *atiritta* (leftover). The meaning, it is said, is: “This too is an excess for you, a monk; you shall receive nothing other than this. 238–9.
Since the term “eaten” (*bhuttāvī*) is already established by the phrase “food is seen,” there is no separate establishment of meaning [for the former].
If there were, it would result in a sixfold set of factors. Furthermore, the passage beginning with “And it is said” refers to the factors of the invitation (*pavāraṇa*).

The observation of the five factors. "A 'scrap' (varaka) is any kind of scrap. Regarding the statement, "But it certainly produces an invitation (pavāraṇā)," they separately make a scrap or water [into the mouth];
this does not produce an invitation. Or, while drinking gruel, if one drinks water first, it is permissible.
It is written: "A scrap remaining below does not produce an invitation. The Elder Upatissa says, "It certainly produces [an invitation]."
The teachers do not accept that [explanation]. "Roasted flour" (*bhajjitapiṭṭha*) refers simply to rice powder.
A "flour-cake" (*sattumodaka*) is a sweetmeat made by kneading together roasted *sattu* grains.
Because it is stated, "He rejects two [mouthfuls] the size of a grain of boiled rice... he does not invite [the other monks to eat]," this excludes those such as the *paracaṅkamaka*.
It is said that the Elder Dhammasiri maintains that if one drinks boiled gruel after having put it aside, and then refuses another portion of the same kind, there is no *pavāraṇā*.
If one refuses another [portion] while still eating, one does not perform the *pavāraṇā*. Why?

Because there is no such thing as "unfinished eating," which is defined as food remaining on the plate. This applies even if one is eating in a dining hall, regarding a portion that has not yet reached oneself.
He refuses what is brought to him, but does not invite [the donor to offer more]. Although he may refuse, if a monastery attendant pours [food] into his bowl, it is not permissible to eat from that;
for this falls under the category of what has arisen specifically as a rejection by the Buddha.
Just as when an immoral person gives a portion of alms-food set aside from the Saṅgha, he refuses it and does not invite [the donor to offer more].
This is the meaning: “If one who is modest gives what is unsuitable [for the recipient], he rejects it because of his lack of desire for that enjoyment;
others say he ‘invites’ (pavāreti) [the donor to reconsider]. Regarding “at the distribution of food” (parivesanāya): this refers to the dining hall. As for “meat-soup” (maṃsarasa):

since the term *maṃsarasa* is formed by reaching the compound *maṃsañ ca rasañ ca*, it occurs as a rejection when the word “meat-soup” is spoken; [alternatively,] it means the juice of meat (*maṃsassa rasaṃ*).
"Conflict is not intended here," it is said. Regarding "meat-and-curd mixture" (maṃsakarambaka): ... [omission] ... it is permissible; thus it is simply pure gruel (suddhayāgu).
It is indeed a mixture of curd that has not been offered as an invitation (appavāraṇa); therefore, one does not invite [the guest to eat it]. For this reason, it is stated later:
"And this should not be equated with a curd-mixture," and so forth. Therefore, regarding one who says, "Bring that and take some sour gruel (kañjiya)":
It has been stated: "If one refuses it, there is no *pavāraṇā*," and "Because it was not said, 'Take the mixed rice-gruel,' and because it was said,

'He gives it after separating the mixture,'" [it follows that] since in these two phrases— namely, "mixed with rice-gruel" and "rice-gruel mixed"— there is no mention by name of one who is eligible for the *pavāraṇā*, therefore,
if in that case the rice-gruel is either more abundant or equal in amount [to the other food], one does not perform the *pavāraṇā*.

Why? Because in that case, both the one who brings forward the food and the one who refuses it have the perception that it is *yāgu* (rice gruel). If the *yāgu* is thin and the solid food (*bhatta*) is more abundant, he invites [the guest] to eat. Why?
The Teacher’s reasoning is that in that situation, both of them have a different perception [of what is being offered].

Since there exists a name for one who is entitled to an invitation when the food is mixed with solid food, he always indeed invites [the guest]. However, in the case of mixed food, according to the method already stated...
The reason must be stated. "He gives separately" means that he presses it firmly with his hand and strains it so that the rice does not fall out.

Regarding the phrase "made unallowable": here, it refers to food that has been made leftover together with unallowable items such as plantain fruits by those who have not performed the *kappiya* rite.
Even after having them made allowable, it is permissible to set aside the plantains, fruits, and so forth, and eat the remainder.

Furthermore, because they were mixed together, it is permissible for one to have them made allowable again, place them in another vessel, have them declared as leftover (*atiritta*), and then eat them. Why?
Because, they say, no formal act of the Vinaya (*vinayakamma*) had previously been performed regarding them. And by one who has already eaten...

From the statement, "It is done by one who has been invited and has risen from his seat," it is established that this must be performed by one who has finished eating but has not yet been invited to leave,
and who has risen from his seat; therefore, in the case of two people traveling on a journey in the early morning,

if one has been invited but does not rise and remains seated there, while the other, having wandered for alms, does not eat the alms-food he received himself [but gives it to the first], saying, "This is enough..."

It is stated that one may indeed perform [the act] by saying "all"; however, in the bright fortnight (sukkapakkha), this is already established by the phrase "it has been performed by one who has finished eating.
In that case, one's own seven factors are not fulfilled; it should be understood that in the dark fortnight (kaṇhapakkha), seven are stated by way of their opposites.
[The act is performed] by one who has finished eating, by one who has not been invited to continue, and by one who has risen from his seat—or by one who has not risen.

Or if it has been done, it is permissible. Furthermore, to illustrate this alternative meaning—namely, "by one who has invited [others] but has not yet risen from his seat"—it is also permissible to say, "the seven factors have been stated.

However, he is not allowed to do it again, because there is the logical consequence that what was already done would have to be done by him once more. For it is said: "That which has not been done is what must be done."
Then, if that first person wishes to do it again, he is permitted to do what was not previously done in another vessel.

The second person is also permitted to do it in the first vessel. For it is said: "That by which [the act] was not done, by that it must be done. It is with reference to this very point that it is said: "He may not do again that same thing which was previously made allowable by the other."

"It is written: 'One obtains [the benefit]; it must be performed by another. In this context, *taṃ* means 'that which was first done. Regarding the phrase 'having sent [a messenger], it should be caused to be performed':
if one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*) has gone there, then one monk staying there should receive [the offering] and have it performed by another;
thus, in that case, a single person alone is not permitted to do it in this manner. 'Whatever illness...'"

They say: "Because of the words beginning with ‘having set aside for [the Sangha],’ even a portion that falls to a sick person in a monastery or similar place is called ‘leftover from the sick’ (gilānātiritta);
therefore, it is permissible. Regarding "for the sake of food," some say it refers only to the wrong time (vikāla).
It should be understood that bodily action consists in swallowing, while verbal action consists in not causing [others] to speak with the words, "Venerable sirs, make it leftover."
The commentary on the first *pavāraṇā* training rule is finished.
6. Commentary on the second *pavāraṇā* training rule: 243.
"Common to all" refers to that which is common to all *pavāraṇās*: namely, the phrase "as much as you wish."
The commentary on the second *pavāraṇā* training rule is finished.
7. Commentary on the training rule regarding eating at improper times (247–249).
"Dances of actors" (*naṭanāṭakāni*) refers to dramatic performances such as the *Sītāharaṇa* and others. "Roots and edible [foods]" (*mūlañ ca khādanīyañ ca*) means...
Roots that are edible. This method applies everywhere. "Flour" means powder.
"Salt-root" means the root of *yūpa*. "Caccu-root" is the root of *neḷiya*. "Tambaka" is *vaca*. "Taṇḍuleyyaka" is *cūḷakuhu*. "Vatthuleyyaka" is *mahākuhu*.

*Kaseruka* and *kaṭibalava* are its names. *Ambāṭaka*, *amūlaka*, *piḍhala*, and *kakkula* [are synonyms].
*Masālu*, *kinaḷa*, *āluva*, *kaḷi*, *taḍḍhiaḷi*, *alasa*, and *kaṭissala* are the names for *mera*.
