*Daṇḍokira*, *udakajoti*, and *kaṇḍaka*. It is written that it is also called *siṅghatakoti*.
*Phaggava* is *hakiḷi*. *Nattamāla* is *karañji*.
*Sellu* is *loholiyaṃ*. *Kāsamaddaka* is *kuduvavali* or *anasikina*. *Ummādiya* is *melelidiya*. *Cīnamugga*.
*Venamutti*, *huramugga*, *rājamāsa*, *māhavili*, *aggimanta*, *muñci*, *sunipaṇṇaka*, *tipilava*, *nināḷikā*, *tilaka*.

Regarding the phrase "the salt-pan born on the ground" (*bhūmiyaṃ jātaloṇī*), it is stated with the qualification "on the ground" because the name "salt-pan" (*loṇī*) is common [to other things as well].
Why was [the statement] "the Brahmī-palm, we give it to you, O Panasa," made lax by saying "the island-dwellers say"?
If it is asked why [it is] so stated: it is said, "Because it does not share the same characteristic as that which 'suffices for the purpose of solid food' (khādanīya).
*Padeliviniteki*. *Sulasipaṇṇa* is the leaf of the *tasāpalika* tree.

*Agandhikapuppha* is the flower of the *cekavādi* tree, which has a stain like *celepati*. *Jīvantīpuppha* is the flower of the *jīvitandiga* tree. *Bakula* is *muthuvala*. *Kuyyaka* is *punapunnāma*, *puṇṇarā*, or *jātisumana*. *Navamālikā* is *cehemala*.
The *tintiṇika* is the *kacinī*. The *vileyi* is the *mātuluṅga*. The *lavano* is the *pussaphala*. The *supuli* is the *timbarūsaka*.
The *tigibberehi* is the *susatudhuta*. The *tipusavātiṅgaṇa* is prepared with the three pungent spices (*dhutatika*). The *coca* is the *variyyeli*. The *moca* is the *atireli*.
Some say that the *goṭṭhaphala* is the *pūvaphala*. It is said that the *koṭṭhasa* is the *acchiva*.
Some say *asamussi* is *bimba*. *Kāsmarī* is *sepaṇṇi*. *Atitemā* is *kariyametī*. *Jātiphala* is *kataṃmā*. *Kaṭukaphala* is *tiriraka*.
Young fruit is *kiriupulu*. The lotus seed is *kiñcakkhaṭṭhi*. White mustard is *siddhatthaka*. Black mustard (*rājika*) is red.
*Hiṅgu* and *hiṅgujatu* refer to all varieties of asafoetida; here, *hiṅgujatu* refers to the leaves and stalks that have been cooked.
It should be made. A *sipāṭikā* is made by boiling branches. Some say it is made by mixing [the branches] with other materials.
*Taka-kaṭṭhaja* refers to a toy for playing with fire. *Nikitissa-kālesaya*. *Timera*; a *takapatti* (oil-vessel) should be made by boiling *pasākhā* leaves.
It is written: "A *takapaṇṇi* (oil-leaf vessel) should be made exactly like that."
The commentary on the training rule regarding eating at the improper time is finished.
8. Commentary on the training rule regarding storing up food (Sannidhikāraka-sikkhāpada). 253.
"It is called 'storing up' on the following day" means that it exists on the next day. "Received today" does not refer merely to what was received [on that very day].
Now, regarding what has been learned, it is stated in that very *Aṭṭhakathā*: “‘He receives; there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)’:

thus, for one who, desiring to swallow anything stored away—whether it be *yāvakālika* or *yāmakālika*—takes it at the very moment of receiving it, there is an offense of wrong-doing. If it was received at that first [moment], [then...]
"One should not say, 'In the case of receiving [the medicine],' therefore it should be understood that what was taken at its own time is called 'received today. Here it is said:
just as the five medicines, though already stored, are not intended [for immediate use], there is no offense in exceeding the seven-day limit.
Is it not the case that, because it is not something to be swallowed, here too what has been "taken up" (uggahitaka) is not intended? To this it is said:

It is appropriate that "what has been taken up" is not intended in the Bhesajja-sikkhāpada, because there is the possibility of an offense arising merely by one's own transgression of the [stipulated] time.
Here, however, it is not appropriate, because there is no possibility of an offense arising merely by one's own transgression of the time; [an offense occurs] only through swallowing.

For the intended meaning here is that there is an offense; therefore, according to the opinion of the *Anugaṇṭhipada*, one who learns [the food] today and eats it on the following day incurs two offenses.
Regarding this, the analysis is as follows: if, desiring to eat for oneself, one learns [the food] today and eats it on the following day, there are two offenses.
He incurs [an offense]. One who, having received food intended solely for novices and others, accepts it again on the following day and eats it, should not be charged with an offense.
Regarding the rule "he accepts, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," this is the intended meaning:
if, like Belaṭṭhasīsa, one accepts today for the sake of the second, third, or subsequent days, for the purpose of storing it for novices and others...
If he gives it, then on the following day, there is the possibility of an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for accepting it for the purpose of consuming it.

If he himself keeps it aside after receiving it, and on the following day, seeing that refuse has fallen [there], he accepts it either out of doubt or for the sake of acceptance itself, then there is the possibility of an offense of wrong-doing precisely from that act of acceptance. If he does not accept it, [there is no offense].
There is no *dukkaṭa* offense for that. For it has been said: "In this case, it is just as [the rule] beginning with, 'If one steps across with one foot, there is an offense of *thullaccaya*'.
However, for one who steps across both feet simultaneously, there is no *thullaccaya* offense for him;
it should be understood that the present case is similar. Here, [the offense occurs] only when the state of having been accepted is not yet abandoned, [and] storage (*sannidhi*)...
The Elder Dhammasiri says, “One who causes it to be produced [commits an offense],” but this contradicts the Canon, which states: “If he accepts it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
However, oil that has been drunk from a bowl is not subject to the formal designation [of a medicinal substance]. Even though it drips out when being warmed over a heat, it is nevertheless stated:
“Just as in the training rule on medicine. Otherwise, even ghee and other substances drunk from a bowl would, upon the lapse of seven days, [be considered medicine].

"Should they incur an offense": "Having received it oneself"—here too, the procedure is exactly as previously stated. This is consistent with the discussion regarding bowls that are difficult to wash.
"For the purpose of food" may be understood even when [the food] is obtained at the proper time. "Ordinary food" (*pakati-āmisa*) refers to allowable food (*kappiya-āmisa*).

Regarding the two offenses for one who swallows with a mouth containing food: "Yesterday, non-timely food (*yāmakālika*) was received; today, before the meal, [if one swallows it] with a mouth containing food..."
It is written: "For one who swallows with the mouth, there are two *pācittiya* offenses.
For even that which was received today as *yāvakālika* (to be consumed during the day) becomes stored (*sannidhi*) if it is mixed with a drink that has passed the watch of the night.
Regarding unallowable meats, there is a *thullaccaya* for human flesh, and a *dukkaṭa* is increased for other meats.

255. Regarding the statement, "The seven-day [medicines] and the lifetime [medicines] are for the purpose of food," some say that even if taken at the proper time, it is indeed a *dukkaṭa* offense because one has not avoided storage (*sannidhi*).
If it is argued that what is received on that very day is permissible before the midday meal, we say no;

for there is no distinction made in either the Canon (*pāḷi*) or the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*). In the Medicines Training Rule (*Bhesajja-sikkhāpada*), it is stated that one may consume [the medicines] as desired before the midday meal.

Why? Upatissa says: "Ghee and so forth are included under the category of food (*āhāra*); therefore, it is stated from the perspective of their belonging to that category, not from the perspective of being medicinal substances.
The commentary on the training rule regarding the storage of food is finished.
9. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Luxurious Foods.
259. *Akappiyasappinā*: with the ghee of those whose meat is not allowable. It is written: "Apart from vasā-tela (fat-oil), there is no such thing as 'unallowable ghee'.
*Visaṅketaṃ*: regarding this, it is said, "There is also no requesting of soup or boiled rice.
*Kāyikāni*: those to be committed by means of the body.
261. "He is to be dealt with according to the Mahānāma training rule" means:

if, when the Saṅgha has invited [for a meal], one requests the fivefold [medicines] such as ghee for the purpose of medicine, it is included here under the phrase "medicine that is to be used as medicine.
Therefore, it is said, "therein, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya). In the *Pāḷimuttaka* [commentary], it is written: "For a bhikkhunī also, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)."
The commentary on the training rule concerning fine food is finished.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Tooth-sticks (Dantapona).
264–5. “The mouth-door” means the throat-pipe. “Merely for the purpose of utterance” means just enough to be lifted up. “Having discarded the dregs” means...
It is stated that it is permissible even if not discarded, by way of its customary practice. "Beyond arm's reach" refers to the donor.
"Gives to a monk" means to another monk. "Gruel" refers to any liquid substance. "The bowl must be received" is because there is no formal offering when it is placed on the ground.
"Just as there is no fault if it falls first [into the bowl], so too..."
It is written: "For those who pour it out and then remove it, there is no fault even if it falls [on the ground], because it was brought [to that place].
*Carukena* means with a small morsel. Regarding *jāgarantassapi*, it is written: "By the word *api*, it is meant 'even for one who is sleeping. *Kecī* refers to the residents of Abhayagiri.

By them, it is shown that in the case of bodily contact, an offense of a grave nature (*thullaccaya*) applies whether by means of something connected to the body or by means of something connected to that [body].
This is the meaning. The expression “by means of something connected with what is connected to the body” is merely a verbal formula.
It is written as “by means of a knife or by means of something received,” but that is poorly written, because even if there is dirt, there is no further need for it to be received.

“For the sake of some” means for the sake of those who are not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*). It is written: “That [gift] was relinquished the very moment it touched the hand of a novice monk (*sāmaṇera*).”
"A load that can be carried by a person of medium size" means it is what should be lifted by a man of average build.

Regarding the statement "only the original acceptance is permitted," those who say, "Because it is stated 'for the purpose of warding off flies,' it is permitted even for food accepted and taken for the purpose of not eating," should be told:
"If one accepts oil for rubbing on the head and [thinks], 'This is for rubbing on the head'..."
"If one were to pass seven days as if without volitional effort (*anābhoga*), would it become an offense involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*)? and so forth.

However, the intended meaning of the Sutta should be understood as follows: "It was stated that [the food] may be accepted beforehand with the perception: 'If the seeds fall into the bowl while he is threshing for the purpose of warding off flies, it will be possible to consume it comfortably. This is from the discussion on the exchange (*parivattana*).

It is said: "If the thought arises in the minds of the bhikkhus, 'When our own rice is exhausted, we can still provide for ourselves by means of this [rice] which is in their hands and belongs to the novices,' then, according to the Elder Upatissa, such an exchange is 'for a purpose' (sātthaka).
If this is so, it follows that for those with pure minds, it would indeed be useless; likewise, [the text says], 'This novice is wise...'"

The Teacher says: "If one has the thought, 'He will give it after exchanging it for a bowl,' and 'We ourselves shall eat this either through his trust or by asking for it,' it is not permitted to eat;
even if an exchange has been made, an offense has been committed. What need is there to say more?
It must be accepted only by those who are indifferent, not by those who have expectations"—this is what was stated for the purpose of showing this very meaning. Furthermore, if...
It is established by the statement: "If one is able to purify the thought [of ownership], then it is permissible to eat what has been received.
When the bowl is placed on a stand, it is free from attachment regarding its state of having been formally accepted. As for seawater, it is not subject to formal acceptance.
The milk of a female deer is permissible precisely because it is milk. Furthermore, there is no offense for one who drinks their own milk directly from the mouth.
It was stated [in the commentary] that this was said "to show" [this point]. Furthermore, it was written: "For here, the great elements (mahābhūta) residing in the body are intended.
Both of these statements contradict the method [of the Vinaya] beginning with the words, "Whether it be permissible meat or milk," and so forth.
Moreover, [the text says]: "He places his own alms-food into a vessel not formally received, which belongs to another bhikkhu, thinking: 'This..."
If one says "only a little" or speaks for some other reason, that is not allowable for anyone. Why? Because it constitutes an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) under the Vinaya.
The intention is that it is a *dukkaṭa* because one has accepted it oneself and placed it [in the bowl] without following the Vinaya procedure.
For what purpose, then, does one not eat such food? Because it is stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) that "it has been formally received. For it is thus...

Regarding this, it is stated in the *Anugaṇṭhipada*: “If one touches anything—be it fruit on the ground or in a vessel, or any kind of food—even if it is sufficient for a lifetime—if one does so without having received it and without knowing [the rules], it is not permitted; it becomes ‘received’ (*uggahitaka*).
Therefore, according to this opinion, if a monk places alms-food in another monk’s bowl while the latter’s bowl has not yet been formally received, [it is a violation].

Thus it is established that this is "unallowable" (*akappiya*) because it has been accepted. This very meaning should be explained by correlating it with the statement: "If [one obtains] in a vessel for cooking rice-gruel for oneself or for the monks...
having made it non-material (*nirāmisa*), it may be consumed. The phrase "or allowable meat or milk" is stated by way of a relevant connection (*pasaṅga*).
Some say that if curd is obtained, that too is intended here.
The commentary on the training rule concerning tooth-sticks is finished.
The fourth chapter, the Chapter on Food, is completed according to the sequence of the commentary. 5.
The Chapter on Naked Ascetics (Acelaka-vagga).
1. Commentary on the Training Rule on the Naked Ascetics (Acelaka-sikkhāpada) 269.

Between the distribution of scraps of food, a certain female wanderer entered and stood there because she had received some *pūva* (fried cakes). "Causes to be given" means by one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*).
The commentary on the training rule on the naked ascetics is finished.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule on Sending Away (Uyyojana-sikkhāpada) 276.

"Of one who abandons": this is a genitive case used in the sense of disregard. The meaning is also: "for the sender, while he is abandoning [the person], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Here, "one not fully ordained" refers to a novice (sāmaṇera).
The commentary on the training rule on sending away is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Eating with [a Family] (Sabhojana-sikkhāpada) 280.

Regarding the term *sabhojana* (“with food”): here, the first alternative corresponds to the third phrase, “a woman and a man”; the second alternative corresponds to the first two [phrases]. *Kule* means in a household. Entering and sitting down with a conscious intention constitutes the offense with mental volition (*sacittaka*).
The commentary on the training rule regarding eating with a family is concluded.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Concealment in Secret (Rahopaṭicchanna-sikkhāpada). 284.

Here, this is the fifth [rule] for Upananda, whereas it was the fourth [for others]. Therefore, in the commentary on the tenth [rule] of the Bhikkhunī-vagga, the reading "by the third training rule" regarding Upananda above should be understood as "by the fourth.
The commentary on the training rule concerning concealment in secret is finished.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule on Sitting in Secret (Rahonisajja-sikkhāpada) 289. The training rule on sitting in secret is indeed of plain meaning. 6.
Commentary on the Training Rule on Wandering (Cāritta-sikkhāpada)
294. "With his own retinue" means "with those invited," according to the ancients.
If one goes for alms before the meal and then eats, there might be an offense of successive transgression (*paramparāpatti*);
that [offense] would not exist after the meal.
If one who is about to depart after a meal goes to his former home,
some say it is indeed an offense, while others say there is no offense. For they consider it an offense when entering another family.
"Expectation of equal food," so say others here.
"Considered equal to the food of a courtesan, they meet him at the invitation.
"Equal distribution," say some; "presence before one's eyes," say others.
"By those seeking certainty, through the analysis of what is to be investigated,
and by the wise [understanding] 'conduct'— thus the learned know this training rule.
The commentary on the training rule concerning conduct is finished.
7. Commentary on the Mahānāma Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 310.
"At the proper time" means this. Since this procedure applies only to the invitation (pavāraṇā) of the Saṅgha, it is therefore stated: "of relatives who have invited [one another].
For [the relatives] say according to the facts: "By this [gift] you have invited us; we have need of this and that."

One who is ill is permitted to request [food] after having first announced it. As for what was stated regarding the training rule on "dainty foods" (*paṇītabhojana*), namely that "one should act according to the Mahānāma training rule," this refers to when one has been invited by the Saṅgha;

if one requests the fivefold set of medicines, such as ghee and so forth, for the purpose of medicine, it is written that it is a *pācittiya* offense because of the statement: "one does not request medicine when there is a need for medicine."
The commentary on the Mahānāma training rule is finished.
8. Commentary on the training rule concerning an army on march (Uyyuttasenasikkhāpada) 311–5.
“By me having seen” means by what was seen by me, or by my own sight. “Even a single man with a spear in his hand” refers to one who is included among the ranks [of the army].
The commentary on the training rule concerning being stationed with an army is finished.
9. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Dwelling with an Army: 319.
In the ninth [rule], the area must be delimited either by the perimeter of the army, or by a place suitable for a perimeter, or by the boundary of the space for walking about.
The commentary on the training rule concerning military camps is finished.
10. Commentary on the training rule concerning military exercises: 324.
In the tenth [rule], if one goes to see each [display] individually, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Wherever one stands and sees [it], [there is an offense].
"An offense of expiation (pācittiya)," and so forth. However, in the eighth [offense], if one goes to see each [unit] individually, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

"Wherever one stands and sees, there is an offense of wrong-doing"—this is the canonical text (pāḷi). Why? Because even though the measure of the constituent factors (aṅga) is the same, it is distinguished by the specific type of military formation.
In the tenth [offense], however, there may be an offense of wrong-doing due to seeing the eighth constituent factor.
The commentary on the training rule concerning wrestling is finished.
By way of the sequence of commentaries, the fifth chapter, the Acelaka-vagga, is completed. 6.
The Surāpāna-vagga (Chapter on Drinking Liquor).
1. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding the Drinking of Liquor:
Concerning the Venerable Muni Sāgata, by way of the illustration of his great supernormal power;
In order to show the fault of that drink,
he had already set out for Bhaddavatikā.
Therefore, having seen [the danger], he crushed the elephant.
It should be understood that he went to Kosambī for the purpose of prohibiting the drinking of liquor,
having already departed [from Sāvatthī] by means of his psychic power.
326–8. *Pasupālaka* means goat-herders. [The unwholesome state arises] starting from the seed of that which one becomes intoxicated by.
Some say: "Because it is stated that in the case of those with consciousness, the mind is exclusively unwholesome, it is unwholesome for one who drinks after having recognized the substance.

If this were so, when it is said, "It should not be said that it must be drunk only through an unwholesome state," [the reply is]: "This refers specifically to the position of those with consciousness."

They say this. This being so, when it is stated that "it should be called a wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate consciousness," they also say that this too was "stated according to the method of the majority.
In the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī* as well, without making a distinction, it is simply called "unwholesome consciousness"; therefore, they say, "It flows only by means of the unwholesome."
The commentary on the training rule concerning the drinking of fermented liquor is finished.
2. Commentary on the training rule concerning poking with the finger. 330.
The training rule concerning poking with the finger has a meaning that is quite obvious.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Envy (Hasadhamma-sikkhāpada) 336.

Regarding the third [offense], how is there a threefold experience of feeling? For one who, with the sole intention of envy, throws water [at another] thinking, "I shall cause suffering to another," there is the feeling of pain. The rest is plain.
If this [offense] is released by perception (saññāvimokkha), how can it be a triad of *pācittiya* offenses?
"It is not play, it is as if play"—this might be due to a wrong grasp.
To the extent that one asks, "How is this play?", this is indeed play;
yet here, perceiving it as non-play, one should undertake it for the sake of the Vinaya.
Because he is exclusively unskilled and his mind delights in play,
therefore only an unwholesome state of mind is found here.
The commentary on the training rule concerning laughing is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule on Disrespect (Anādariyasikkhāpada) 344.
It is written: "It is not permissible for one who, having transgressed what is forbidden by the world, says, 'This is our teacher’s instruction.
That which one commits with a defiled mind, or that which a noble person (ariyapuggala) commits before a training rule has been laid down—[these are the cases].
“Transgresses” refers to the schools of teachers such as the Sabbatthivādins, who maintain that this is a worldly offense (*lokavajja*).
Among those, the second and third alternatives are not intended here, because the training rules (*sekhiya*) are worldly offenses.
Regarding the phrase “the teacher’s instruction is censurable,” it is said: “Since sugarcane juice is for seven days, its dregs are for life.”
“Furthermore, the sugarcane stalk is merely a combination of two things; therefore, it is permissible to eat a sugarcane stalk at an improper time, just like sugar or a cucumber.
Such a recently arisen, censurable traditional doctrine must not be accepted. However, regarding what is prohibited by the formal rule (*paṇṇatti*), it is permissible—referring to the rule:
“One should not push open a door with one’s hand while holding a bowl”—[the question arises] as to which hand holds the bowl...

"Having grasped [the flower] with that hand, one should not offer it; it should be offered with the other. Having understood this meaning and acting accordingly, one should not be charged with an offense. And:
"It is permissible to take a flower from the Buddha’s Bodhi tree or from a shrine (cetiya) in that manner. Thus acts the Abhayagirivāsika. If the Mahāvihāravāsins speak thus:
“You must not speak thus,” he should be corrected. Therefore it was said: “Only for those who have mastered the Sutta and that which is in conformity with the Sutta,” and so forth.
And it was stated: “The Elder Upatissa said all this. It is also written: “That which is in conformity with the Sutta is the Aṭṭhakathā.
The commentary on the training rule concerning disrespect is finished.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Terrifying Others (Bhiṃsāpanasikkhāpada) 345. The training rule concerning terrifying others is of plain meaning. 6.
Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Fire (Jotisikkhāpada)
354. Because of the statement, “one who has need for drying,” there is no offense for one who has no such need.
The commentary on the training rule concerning fire is finished.
7. Commentary on the training rule concerning bathing.
364. The training rule on bathing has a meaning that is already clear.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule on Making [Robes] Discolored:

368. *Alabhi* means "gain" (*labha*). Just as it is said, "one who cooks is a 'cook' (*paca*)," and "a path is so called because one travels upon it" (*pathati*), so too, "one gains is a 'gainer' (*labhi*)."
Why is it not stated as "gain"? Because here, only gain that has been finalized is intended. "Maggati" means to sew along the seam.
One sews what is unallowable together with what is allowable. As long as one does not abandon the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*), for that duration it remains previously allowable.
If one does not abandon the allowance, the teacher’s opinion is that it must be made allowable again.
The commentary on the training rule concerning making [the robe] discolored is finished.
9. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Reassignment (Vikappaṇa-sikkhāpada). 374.
In this context, "use" refers to bodily action; "not relinquishing" refers to verbal action.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the assignment [of robes] is finished.
10. Commentary on the Tenth Training Rule Concerning the Storing of Robes: 379.
Since, in the tenth [rule], both the sitting mat (*nisīdana-santhata*) and the robe-sitting mat (*cīvara-nisīdana*) are exactly the same, therefore...
Having combined both of these together, he said: "A 'seat-cloth' (nisīdana) is called that which has a border.

Even there, since the mention of "robe" includes the robe-seat-cloth (cīvaranisīdana), the meaning is that only the spread-out seat-cloth (santhatanisīdana) is intended. If this is so, should it not be stated as:
"A 'spread-out seat-cloth' (nisīdanasanthata) is called that which has a border"? No; because otherwise, the other would result in being neither a seat nor having a border.

In this context, because the sitting mat (*nisīdana-saṇṭhata*) constitutes an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*), it should be understood that the other [items] also constitute offenses of expiation, as they are of the same nature.
Regarding needle-cases with owners, the ancient teachers state that there is an offense according to the number of needles.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the storing away of robes is finished.
The sixth chapter, the Chapter on Drinking Liquor, is completed according to the sequence of the commentary. 7.
The Chapter on Living Beings.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Intentionally Killing a Living Being.
382. The training rule regarding intentionally killing living beings has already been explained.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Water Containing Living Beings:
387. Even if one knows that there are living beings, if one drinks without considering whether they will die, there is no offense.
"A flower that is thrown into water, and this act of entering the water—
thus should the difference between these two always be understood by one possessing wisdom.
The commentary on the training rule concerning living beings is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule on Reopening (Ukkoṭana-sikkhāpada) 392.

Regarding the third [training rule], twelve reopenings (ukkoṭa) are to be understood. Among these, "the legal act has not been performed," "the legal act was poorly performed," and "the legal act must be performed again" apply to a legal issue concerning an accusation (anuvādādhikaraṇa). "Not removed," "poorly removed," and "not to be removed again" [apply to a legal issue concerning an offense]...

They are found in a legal issue concerning disputes (*vivādādhikaraṇa*) when it is undecided, wrongly decided, or must be decided again; they are found in a legal issue concerning offenses (*āpattādhikaraṇa*).
They are found in a legal issue concerning duties (*kiccādhikaraṇa*) when it is not settled, wrongly settled, or must be settled again—this is the method of the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*);
however, in the Canon (*Pāḷi*), only a mere outline is shown here.
The commentary on the training rule concerning reopening [a legal case] is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Grave Matters (Duṭṭhulla-sikkhāpada):
If it is asked, "How is it known that 'the Pārājikas' are shown here by way of a summary of their meaning? It is known from the text of the Parivāra.

For it is said therein: “On account of a legal issue arising from an offense (āpattādhikaraṇa), how many offenses does one incur? On account of a legal issue arising from an offense, one incurs four offenses.
If a bhikkhunī knowingly conceals a pārājika offense, she incurs a pārājika offense.
If she conceals it while being in doubt, she incurs a thullaccaya offense. [If] a bhikkhu [conceals] a saṅghādisesa...”
“He conceals it, there is an offense of *pācittiya*. He conceals a failure in conduct (*ācāra-vipatti*), there is an offense of *dukkaṭa*.
If it is argued that a monk who conceals a *pārājika* does not incur an offense because it was not so stated, [the answer is] no;
for without concealment by a defiled mind, an offense is impossible. This must also be stated in the section on *dukkaṭa*.

It should be understood that the *pārājika* offenses are not mentioned again because they were already stated first together with the *saṅghādisesa* offenses by way of their formal definition (*atthuddhāra*).
Regarding the phrase "as long as the limit is not broken," this refers to anyone who, even for the sake of concealment, might report [the offense] to another.
Or rather, he has fallen into an offense with a mind of concealment itself.
For him, the limit is not broken merely by not reporting it again for the sake of concealing another [offense]; how much less so by the act of turning back and speaking?
It is not broken by the failure to report the final [offense], but is broken precisely by the lack of concealment; therefore, for the purpose of non-concealment—
It must be reported for what has not been previously reported; from that point on, the limit is cut off. In the absence of that [prior report], one must report again in order to avoid concealment;
even in this way, the limit is cut off—this is how it appears to us, says the Teacher.

Regarding the phrase "by the third for the second," since those who say "the second is called the first" have been refuted by the statement that "the person (puggala) is not to be mentioned as the subject matter (vatthu)," [the second is indeed the second].
It is not proper. Even if one informs another person, it is still not proper. Why? Because one has already heard it previously but did not inform that other person.
They say, "Having heard it, one ought to inform another.
The commentary on the training rule concerning grave offenses (duṭṭhulla-sikkhāpada) is finished.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule for Those Under Twenty Years of Age 404.
"In many ways" means because it arises again and again. Regarding "decrease and increase":
if there is a deficiency of twelve months while in the mother’s womb, a decrease must be made; once born, an increase must be made. If there is an increase while in the mother’s womb...
It is said: "A reduction [of days] must be made for one who has already given birth. The so-called "Full Moon Day of Departure" (nikkhamanīyapuṇṇamāsī) is the full moon day of the month of Sāvaṇa.
It is written: "On the first day" (pāṭipadadivase) means on the second day that has arrived.
For he becomes twenty years old from the day of his birth; although there are indeed extra days for the remaining two years, therefore—
Having become free from doubt, they grant full ordination. "With reference to that" means:
not counting the year of gestation nor the year obtained by the *pavāraṇā* ceremony, but counting from the day of birth, one is nineteen years old.
Regarding the statement "nineteen years old," it is written [elsewhere] as "having abandoned the year of gestation alone"; that is a poorly written version.
406. “He ordains another” means that he ordains while acting as either a preceptor (upajjhāya) or a teacher (ācariya). Some teachers say:
“Since one who is born spontaneously (opapātika) is sixteen years old [at birth], one must wait for four more years before his full ordination (upasampadā) can be performed.
The commentary on the training rule (sikkhāpada) concerning those under twenty years of age is concluded.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding a Caravan Traveling by Theft (Theyyasattha-sikkhāpada) 409.
If it is a pure group of women traveling as a caravan by theft, there are two offenses. If, however, they are nuns, the time [of travel] is protected.
Some say: "Because one has established the state of being a caravan traveling by theft, and because it must be protected, one indeed protects those who share the same Dhamma."
Some say that if there is no intent to steal, there is no accordance with the Dhamma, and therefore it does not protect [from the offense].
If it is argued that when there is no intent to steal, there is accordance with the Dhamma, then in the other case [of intending to steal], one falls into a rule that has not been relinquished.

If a bhikkhu is traveling with a caravan intending to steal, it is according to the specific basis [of the offense]. "With a caravan intending to steal, perceiving it as such, having made an appointment together..."
Furthermore, the word "together" (*saddhiṃ*) is absent in some [manuscripts], which is inappropriate; likewise for the second [offense].
The commentary on the training rule concerning a caravan of thieves is concluded.
7. Commentary on the training rule concerning making arrangements (*saṃvidhāna*).
412. Furthermore, there is a reading that says, “At that time, a certain woman...,” though this is absent in some [manuscripts].

Some maintain that its absence is preferable because of the governing context of the phrase “at that time. Here, these three—those fully ordained on one side, probationary nuns (*sikkhamānā*), and novice nuns (*sāmaṇerī*)—are also included.
However, their time [of ordination] is protected; this is their [distinction].
And there is a distinction regarding the woman.

Furthermore, some say that because of the words "one who is wise and capable," those who are incapable do not constitute an offense; however, that is not correct, because it constitutes an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
[In the case where] "the bhikkhu makes an appointment, but the woman does not make an appointment, there is an offense..."
For it is said: “...a *dukkaṭa* offense. Thus it should be examined.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the arrangement [of a meal] is finished.
8. Commentary on the Ariṭṭha Training Rule.
417. Even for a householder, the act of violating a bhikkhunī is an obstacle to liberation; therefore, his admission into the order (pabbajjā) is also prohibited.

[The offenses] that obstruct the ripening of kamma are so called because they lack a root-cause (ahetuka). Those previously committed intentionally but now forgotten, when perceived as pure, are indeed obstacles.
"The rest" refers to those arising from birth (jātika). "By way of essence" means by way of intrinsic nature (bhāva). In the sense of being a basis for litigation, it is *adhikaraṇa*.

The ancient masters have said: [They are] like a wall in the sense of being pounded down, and in the sense of being cut; they are like a sword and a meat-slicer in the sense of cutting off wholesome states;

they are like a spear and a stake in the sense of piercing the mind. In the text on non-offenses (*anāpatti-pāḷi*), the phrase "for a beginner" (*ādikammikassa*) was written as a conventional addition.
The commentary on the training rule concerning Ariṭṭha is finished.
9. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Associating with One Who Has Been Suspended (Ukkhittasambhogasikkhāpada) 425.
Regarding the phrase “by one who has not relinquished that view,” it is stated: “This indicates the state of being of a different communion due to a difference in tenets.
As for the expression “with a mind of three [types],” the meaning here should be understood as: “one might assume co-residence with a mind that is indeterminate as fruition (vipākābyākata).”
Otherwise, because the training rule possesses consciousness, it would not be appropriate [to classify it] with reference to the indeterminate (abyākata) action.
The commentary on the training rule concerning social intercourse with one who has been suspended is finished.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Thorns.
428. "Where you do not see them"—the word "them" (*te*) refers to those [beings]. Alternatively, it means: "We do not see your form and so forth.

This novice monk becomes one who has committed a defeat (*pārājika*). Regarding the statement in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*: "If he relinquishes that view, having informed the Saṅgha, he should be ordained with the Saṅgha’s consent," that is not correct;
for what is intended here is expulsion through disciplinary action (*daṇḍakamma-nāsanā*).

If he were one who has committed a *pārājika* offense, there would be what is called "the removal of the insignia" (*liṅganāsanā*). Furthermore, the view that "for one who indulges in those [prohibited acts], they are not sufficient to constitute an obstacle" is not the same as the view held toward the Teacher—that He is not a Teacher and so forth.
If the person in whom such a view arises were to become a *pārājika*, then in his case too one must proceed in exactly the same way:
since he does not abide in restraint, he should be destroyed by the very removal of his insignia; such is the teacher’s reasoning.
The commentary on the Kaṇṭaka training rule is finished.
The seventh chapter, the Sappāṇaka-vagga, is completed according to the sequence of the commentary.
8. The Sahadhammika-vagga.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Fellow Practitioners (Sahadhammika-sikkhāpada): 434. The training rule concerning fellow practitioners is of plain meaning.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Scrutiny (Vilekhana-sikkhāpada).
438. Regarding the phrase "and an offense through forgetfulness," the word *ca* (and) here indicates that one does not do what ought to be done;
it is implied that it is not merely the four [offenses]. A "country" (*janapada*) is a portion of a kingdom. During the time of the Buddha, the Ariṭṭhakas were enemies of the Teaching.
By the statement, "They are not capable of causing an obstacle," they were indicating that the Blessed One was not omniscient. After the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna...
The Vajjiputtakas are those who illustrate the ten points; for they are adversaries of the Vinaya teaching.
However, the proponents of "importing from outside" (*parūpahāra*) and so forth are adversaries of the Suttanta and Abhidhamma. Who then are they?

To show that it is not all Mahāsāṅghikas and others, but only some, he uses the qualifying expression: "the proponents of importing from outside... and so forth. Among them, those who are deceivers and of evil intent, having uttered what is untrue...
Having eaten the excellent food they had obtained, they fell asleep with muddled mindfulness and committed an emission of semen.
When others saw this and said, "The Arahant has committed an emission of semen," they deceived the people by saying, "It was Māra’s hosts who brought it about.
And even those who were practicing rightly and were free from deceit, upon hearing that report, some—being of that same view—[fell into doubt].

And they are possessed of overweening pride (*adhimāna*). Even when they have seen their own emission of semen (*sukkavissaṭṭhi*), they do not resolve upon it; rather, they perceive what has not been attained as already attained.

Likewise, there is for an *arahant* the "crossing beyond" ignorance and doubt regarding names, clans, and so forth, just as there is the "crossing beyond" truths by others, meaning that names are designated by others; this should be applied according to the circumstances as appropriate.
In this context, the Vinaya-dhara [intends] that by showing such Sutta passages as, "Monks, it is impossible, it is out of the question, that an Arahant should emit semen...
[they are] those who have seen the Dhamma... independent of others in the Teacher’s Dispensation," he refutes those who oppose the Dispensation;
this is his intention. The others, however, maintain that "the scriptural texts (pariyatti) are the root. Regarding the Pātimokkha—

"This was stated by way of the introductory narrative (*nidāna*): 'While it was being pointed out. The analytical sections (*vibhaṅga-pada*) of the Tathāgata are established. Even though they are established, what are its constituent parts? They are:
the desire to censure, [the act] in the presence of one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*), and the disparagement of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*).
The commentary on the training rule regarding remorse (*vilekhana-sikkhāpada*) is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule on Deceiving (Mohana-sikkhāpada).
444. The training rule on deceiving has an obvious meaning. 4. Commentary on the Training Rule on Striking (Pahāra-sikkhāpada).

"Rattacitto" means with lust for physical contact. However, having seen someone wishing to cause harm, one thinks, "If I kill this person, there will be no escape for me," and being angry, gives a blow while prioritizing the perception of that being as a living creature; for him, it remains exactly as the basis [of the offense].
The commentary on the training rule regarding striking is finished.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule on the Seven-Leaf Foe (Talasattikasikkhāpada) 456.
Because of the statement, "The body or what is connected to the body," that which one raises against the body and so forth is called a *tala* (blade).
A *tala* itself is a *talasattika*. Some say it is called a *sattika* (foe) in the sense of being capable of striking. Regarding this, [the text says]: "Even a lotus leaf..."

This [rule] restricts [the application]. For in this way, when one is angry, if by the force of anger one rejects whatever comes to hand—without considering whether it is capable of striking—and even if that object is pleasant to the touch, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) alone.

Since, according to the preceding rule, an offense of expiation occurs when one strikes with the desire to strike, whereas by this [present rule], an offense of expiation occurs merely upon the act of spitting out with the sole desire to utter [the word].
However, this blow was struck after having missed [the target]; therefore, it is not an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) because it was given with the intention of striking.
Is this *dukkaṭa* due to the cause of the blow, or rather due to the cause of vomiting? It is indeed a *dukkaṭa* due to the cause of the blow.
As for the previous case, since it is a *pācittiya* due to the cause of vomiting, it is appropriate that it be a *pācittiya* together with a *dukkaṭa*. For the former instance involved vomiting.
"The subsequent blow: the Master [Ācariya] says that our reasoning is that the prior vomiting cannot be rendered free from the basis for an offense merely by depending on the subsequent blow.
'Whatever part of the hand or other limb is broken by that blow, it is only a dukkaṭa'—by this too, there is a dukkaṭa due to the blow;
it is established that the vomiting remains exactly as it was with respect to its original basis."
It should be thoroughly investigated. Some say that even for one who utters [a curse] out of anger upon seeing animals and others performing impure acts, the intention is solely for liberation.
The commentary on the *Talasattika-sikkhāpada* is finished.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule on Groundless Accusations (Amūlakasikkhāpada) 462.

"Against one who is fully ordained, perceiving him as not fully ordained, with a groundless *saṅghādisesa* offense" should be understood as referring to the basis for an offense of *saṅghādisesa*, such as the emission of semen or physical contact. For there is no such thing as an offense of *saṅghādisesa* for one who is not fully ordained.
The commentary on the training rule regarding groundlessness is finished.
7. Commentary on the training rule regarding intentional lying (Sañcicca-sikkhāpada). 468.
Regarding the phrase "he thinks [the person] is under twenty years of age": here, even if one does not personally think so oneself, [one speaks] for the purpose of causing remorse.
If one says, “I think,” should one be charged with lying? It need not be so, provided the other factors are complete;
however, the mere word “I think” does not necessarily constitute the completion of those factors. This is established in the ultimate sense (paramattha) in certain instances.
As in the case of “I think the water is burning,” whether it causes another to feel remorse or not, that [intention] is not the deciding factor; this is stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*.
The phrase “arousing remorse” is stated according to his intention.
The commentary on the training rule concerning intentional action is finished.
8. Commentary on the training rule concerning eavesdropping.
473. Regarding the phrase "having heard these," the word "speech" (*vacana*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the text.
"Of one section" (*ekaparicchedāni*) means they are of one section according to this method: "it may be an act of commission, it may be an act of omission.

Here, although the offense conditioned by speaking otherwise is an act of commission and the offense conditioned by causing vexation is an act of omission, nevertheless, taking both together as a single training rule (*sikkhāpada*), that which is designated as "speaking otherwise" [is treated as such].

The training rule (sikkhāpada) may be considered an act (kiriyā) with respect to the first [offense], and it may be considered a non-act (akiriyā) with respect to the second; such is the meaning to be understood.
The commentary on the training rule concerning eavesdropping (upassuti-sikkhāpada) is finished.
9. Commentary on the training rule concerning the obstructing of legal acts (kamma-paṭibāhana-sikkhāpada).
474. Because of the statement, "Of legal acts," some monks give their consent (*chanda*) saying, "I give my consent for legal acts.
That is merely their intention (*matimatta*), not actual practice. Is there no offense when one reviles based on what is illegal (*adhamma*), or when one reopens a settled matter (*ukkoṭeti*)?
No; because at the time of giving consent it was not done [legally], and subsequently, due to causes such as reviling an illegal act, there is no offense.

If it is argued that this statement is made without distinction because it is stated in the section on non-offenses (*anāpattivāra*), since one is released from the offense by means of performing the act for one who does not deserve it—whether by an illegal procedure (*adhamma*) or an incomplete assembly (*vagga*)—we say no.
This is because at the time of giving consent (*chandadāna*), there is no intention to perform an illegal act, and because the fault would apply only to the performer.

If it is argued that it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the community (*gaṇa*), [we reply] that it applies only to those who give their consent through a declaration of purity (*pārisuddhi*).

They do not constitute a formal group (*gaṇa*) because they have not attained the status of a quorum for the ritual act (*akammappatta*). Even in the context of the retinue (*parivāra*), those who give their consent for the ritual act are mentioned separately within the groups eligible for the ritual.
Nevertheless, consent for an illegal ritual (*adhammakamma*) must not be given; for if one gives it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) due to giving what is improper.
Regarding this, the Master [Buddhaghosa] says: "For in that case, they are not freed from the offense of wrong-doing arising from the journey; therefore, it is not my opinion."
The commentary on the training rule concerning the obstruction of kamma is finished.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Not Going After Consent Has Not Been Given (481):

"If one does not come to the assembly and does not give consent, there is no offense," say some. "It is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," say others, because of the intention to create an obstacle for the legitimate legal act (*dhammakamma*).

Some say that one may give *chanda* (consent) in the midst of the Saṅgha. If it is argued that once *chanda* has been given, even if one enters the midst of the Saṅgha and then departs again, the *chanda* would not be nullified—the answer is that it is indeed nullified.
Why? Because it contradicts such statements as, "One who is outside the reach of the hand is entitled to [receive] *chanda*.
However, some maintain that what is stated in the Pāḷi refers specifically to one who is stepping beyond the reach of the hand out of a desire to give.
The commentary on the training rule concerning going after having given one’s consent is finished.
11. Commentary on the Training Rule on the Weak: 484–5.
“She gave” means she gave after having obtained permission. “The monks”: here, those of the group of six (Chabbaggiya) excluded themselves.
Instead of saying "the Saṅgha," they said "the bhikkhus. "They divert" means they lead away.

Therein, the extraction of the word "gain" (lābha) is for the purpose of indicating gain in general—by way of extracting the meaning of whatever [term] might be intended here—even though it is not specifically intended in this context.
For only the robe-cloth is intended here; therefore, it is stated: "If another requisite is given, it is forfeited; there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)."
It has been stated. The terms *dinnaṃ* (given) and *parikkhāraṃ* (requisite) are used in the accusative case with the sense of the locative.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the weak is finished.
12. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Diversion [of Requisites].

491. If one causes another person who wishes to give to a relative to give instead to someone else, there is likewise an offense. In all cases, one may allow a person who wishes to give after having consulted [the intended recipient] to dispose of it as they please.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the redirection of gifts is finished.
The eighth chapter, the Section on Fellow Practitioners, is completed according to the order of the commentary.
9. The Chapter on Jewels (Ratanavagga) 1.
Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Inner Palace (Antepurasikkhāpada) 494–7.
In the manner in which he attends upon the Blessed One, it is not fitting that this man should be wicked.
"Is not a sin" (na hoti pāpa) is the meaning; or it has the sense of a reason. "That" (taṃ) is merely a particle, or its meaning is "whatever" (yataḥ).
"Crushing by an elephant" (hatthisammadda) means a crushing by a crowd; the meaning is trampling and pulverizing. 498.
"Jewel" (ratana) refers to the chief queen; nevertheless, here even other women of noble lineage are not protected, according to the section on non-offenses.
Because there is no statement saying, “she does not become a chief queen. If he is indeed a khattiya, he has not been consecrated;
or if he is indeed consecrated, he is not a khattiya who protects [the realm]—so says the teacher.

Since it is stated as a constituent factor in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā* under the section on non-offenses (*anāpatti*), the state of being consecrated alone is the criterion. Some say that the rest is the superior limit (*ukkaṭṭhaparicchedo*).

500–501. “Not perceiving it as a sleeping chamber while it is a sleeping chamber”: here, the breach of the triad is also applicable. A “sleeping chamber” refers to an unenclosed area such as the foot of a tree, and so forth.
The commentary on the rule regarding the royal harem is finished.
2. Commentary on the Jewel Rule (Ratana-sikkhāpada)
504. There are the phrases: “May the householders accept the meal,” and “The householders [give it] to me.
506. According to the *Kurundi* commentary, it is stated that even in a house, if monks have suspicions, they should stand there and announce [the offering].
“Appropriate” means either taking refuse-rags from what is considered a treasure, or going without concern toward actual treasures.
Thus it is written. They say that even on a temporary basis, one is not permitted to accept what is untouchable (*anāmāsa*).
"Having incited" means having requested, according to the method stated: "The Noble Ones stand for the sake of [what is offered]; this is the solicitation of the Noble Ones.
The commentary on the Jewel Training Rule (*Ratana-sikkhāpada*) is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule on Entering a Village at an Improper Time (Vikālagāmappavisaṇasikkhāpada) 511–2. Regarding the incident of being bitten by a snake:

that bhikkhu went without having asked a bhikkhu who was present, and remorse arose in him. "In the manner explained under the taking of what is not given" refers to this statement: "a village and the vicinity of a village.
The commentary on the training rule on entering a village at an improper time is concluded.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule on the Needle Case (Sūcighara-sikkhāpada) 517.

“That” refers to the instrument for splitting. “Its” [refers] to the first instance of a *pācittiya* offense, because it must be confessed after having committed the act of splitting. This same method applies to the others as well.
520. “In a sheath” means in a sheath-handle.
The commentary on the training rule regarding the needle-case is finished.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding the Bed (Mañcasikkhāpada) 521–2.

Regarding the phrases “on a high bed” (*ucce mañce*) and “on a tall bed” (*uccā mañce*), these occur in some versions. “Long” (*āyata*) means broad. “With legs eight finger-breadths [in height]” (*aṭṭhaṅgulapādaka*) is a neuter abstract noun, or it refers to legs measuring eight finger-breadths.
The commentary on the training rule concerning couches is finished.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Coverings of Cotton Down (Tūlonaddha).
528. "Cotton down" (*poṭakitūla*) refers to any kind of grass-cotton. Having torn it out upon obtaining it, one must confess a *pācittiya* offense.
In this case, although it appears as if it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) merely by way of acquisition, the offense should be understood to occur only upon consumption;
the statement, "Having acquired what was made by another, if he consumes it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," is the proof here.
The commentary on the training rule concerning stuffing with cotton is finished.
7. Commentary on the Training Rule on the Sitting Mat (Nisīdana-sikkhāpada) 531.

Although the specific origin of the sitting mat is not seen here, nevertheless, because it was permitted in the Cīvara-kkhandhaka and because it is included under the statement, "The nine kinds of robes are to be determined [as one's own]," its origin is indeed the same as that of the robe.

It should be understood thus: “Having spread it like a rug (santhatasadisaṃ) means ‘with a border’ (sadasaṃ). This is a comparison made because of the previously mentioned sitting-rug (nisīdana-santhatatta).

Some say that if one obtains it with a border, it is permissible, but if not, even one without a border is allowed; however, that is not correct, because its specific shape is restricted by the statement:
“A sitting-rug is said to be one with a border.”
The commentary on the training rule concerning sitting cloths is finished.
8. Commentary on the training rule concerning itch-cloths (kaṇḍupaṭicchādi): 539.
If "itch-cloth" means that which covers rashes, boils, and so forth arising below the navel and above the kneecaps;
It is intended that, according to the Sugata’s own span (sugatavidatthi), it is four spans in length and two spans across;
yet even this is seen to be an excessively large measurement. For every man is seven spans tall by his own span, and one span of the Sugata is equal to three spans of an average-sized man; therefore—
"The itch-covering cloth attains the standard measurement for an ordinary man across [the width], but it attains double that lengthwise.

Let it be so; this would be the Blessed One’s intention: that if one so desires, its maximum limit will cover even the entire body, and one who wishes to wear it by folding it many times, like a saṅghāṭi robe covering the whole body, may do so.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the kaṇḍupaṭicchādi (itch-covering cloth) is finished.
9. Commentary on the training rule concerning the vassikasāṭika (rainy-season robe): 542.
The vassikasāṭika was also permitted by way of a maximum limit. During the rainy season, some [monks] used it as a substitute for the outer robe (saṅghāṭi).
"This is what the Blessed One intended by 'they shall use [it]'. Nevertheless, although it was permitted on this basis,

those monks wore them in a manner other than the prescribed limit— exceeding the proper measure— because this rule was laid down in reference to the specific case where they were "wearing itch-cloths of unlimited size" and "wearing rain-cloaks."
It should be understood that having made this the maximum limit for them, it was permitted. This same method applies to the tenth [offense] as well.
The commentary on the *Vassikasāṭika-sikkhāpada* is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Nanda-thera-sikkhāpada*.
551. Regarding the phrase "there he makes a mattress or a pillow," it is appropriate to understand that he makes them for the purpose of being shared by many monks in length.
The commentary on the training rule (sikkhāpada) of the Elder Nanda is finished.
By way of the sequence of the commentaries, the ninth chapter, the Jewel Chapter (Ratanavagga), is completed.
The commentary on the Section on Offenses Entailing Confession (Pācittiyakaṇḍa) is finished.
6. The Section on Offenses Requiring Admission (Pāṭidesanīyakaṇḍa). 1. Commentary on the First Training Rule on Offenses Requiring Admission.

553–5. Since it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary) that this is "a demonstration of the manner in which the offense is to be confessed," the offense must be confessed exactly according to what has come down in the *Pāḷi* (Canon), and not otherwise.

This is according to the method beginning with "perceiving it as being inside a house when it is inside a house," and "perceiving what is not solid food or soft food as solid food or soft food," and "perceiving a nun as not a nun," and so forth.
The other three triplets of permutations should also be applied and demonstrated.
The commentary on the first *pāṭidesanīya* training rule is concluded.
2. Commentary on the second *pāṭidesanīya* training rule.

559. Although it is stated that “they eat having been invited” means “they eat having been invited by any one of the five kinds of food,” nevertheless, in this context, being invited by an improper invitation is not a constituent factor.

This is because there is no mention of such a case in either the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā* or here in the section on non-offenses (*anāpattivāra*). Therefore, the meaning of the word “invited” is according to what was previously established.
It has been stated. It should be understood that three other triads (tikacchedā) should also be shown by applying them, as they are mentioned in the word-commentary (padabhājana).
For whether [the food] is being eaten in such a manner, for those who do not prevent such a bhikkhunī, it is indeed a *pāṭidesanīya* offense.
There are two readings: “this one directs” (*vosāsati*) and “directing” (*vosāsantī*). By the expression “with every swallow” (*ajjhohāre ajjhohāre*), again...
The singular form in the phrase “a blameworthy matter, friend” (*gārayhaṃ āvuso dhammaṃ*) is contradictory. It was stated with reference to having committed [the offense] at the very first swallow;
likewise, it appears elsewhere from the statement “we have fallen into [it]. Some say that it is permissible for one person to represent many, but that is not correct.
My own conjecture is that this is because it is stated in the text as “by those monks,” and so forth.
One may say, "I have committed [an offense]," together with another, because it must be confessed by one, two, or three;

thus, it is appropriate for all to speak in this way. They say, "We have committed [the offense] together. If one has not been restrained, one may also say, "Friend, I have committed a blameworthy thing."
The commentary on the second training rule concerning confession is finished.
562–570. The third and fourth training rules are of obvious meaning.
The commentary on the section on offenses requiring confession is finished.
7. The Section on Training (Sekhiyakaṇḍa) 1. Explanation of the Chapter on Being Evenly Rounded (Parimaṇḍalavagga) 576.
It is said: “By one who has trained in the training” means by means of the four paths. Because [one must] lower [the robe] by the measure of eight finger-breadths...
When one is seated with the robe already wrapped around the body, it remains at a distance of only four finger-breadths; therefore, both these commentarial explanations are of a single scope.
The phrase "two and a half cubits" refers to a fine cloth, or it is said in reference to a single-layered robe (*ekapaṭṭa*), for that indeed remains in its proper place.
The Elder Upatissa says that the phrase "even measuring two cubits" is said in reference to a double-layered robe (*dupaṭṭa*). [The other] refers to a single-layered robe.
It should be understood that a "two-patta" [robe] is said to be "measured at two cubits" by way of its lower limit.
For it is stated in the *Nissaggiya-aṭṭhakathā*: "Even two cubits across is permissible," and this is because it was said:
"In the event of non-availability, even a measurement of two cubits across is permissible. All of this refers to what is suitable for formal determination (*adhiṭṭhānupaga*).
It has been stated. Upon seeing something contrary [to the rule], one should prepare [the remedy]. If one does not prepare it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

This is because it is stated that the offense is "due to disrespect" with reference to the intentional mind that recognizes the formal rule (paṇṇatti), and not with reference to the mind that recognizes the physical object;

for even if one knows "this was done in such a way," there is no offense [in that regard]. The opinion of the Elder Phussadeva is also tenable from one perspective. Likewise is the opinion of the Elder Upatissa.

That which is naturally blameworthy, whether a training rule has been laid down or not, is "blameworthy by nature" (*lokavajja*). This, however, is blameworthy only when a rule has been laid down, not when one has not;
therefore, because it is unlike other things blameworthy by nature, it is not "blameworthy by nature.

Because it is blameworthy starting from the moment of the formal proclamation (*paṇṇatti*), it is "blameworthy by formal rule" (*paṇṇattivajja*). Because it must be committed with a mind of disrespect, it is "with mind" (*sacittaka*).
Because that state of mind possesses three types of feeling, it is "threefold-feeling" (*tivedana*).

Since what is called a "mind of disrespect" is exclusively unwholesome and is by its very nature a fault, it is therefore a "worldly fault" (*lokavajja*). Intentional transgression occurs only for one who is experiencing mental pain;

thus, it is "painful feeling" (*dukkhavedana*). However, in the *Gaṇṭhipada*, it is said: "Like the taking of life and so forth, the fault of wearing [robes] improperly and the like is censured by the world."
"It is not [an offense], for it is excluded by the formal rule (paṇṇatti-vajja)," so says the Elder Phussadeva;

thus it is written. 577. "Even in a monastery" refers to times such as when attending upon the Buddha; therefore, it is said "it should be worn" with reference to the function of the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga). In the first and second training rules, it is permitted due to causes such as feverishness, but not in connection with entering inside a house.
582. Regarding the phrase "standing in one place," even while walking, one is indeed permitted to look about for the absence of danger.

Likewise, it is written that "they honor [the bowl] in the village"; however, since it was stated [elsewhere] that "standing in one place," it should be understood that this was said with reference to such an obstacle.
The commentary on the Parimaṇḍala-vagga is finished.
2. Commentary on the Chapter on Excessive Laughter (Ujjagghikavagga) 586.
Regarding the phrase *hasanīyasmiṃ*: the locative case is used here in the sense of a cause (*hetvatthe bhummam*); thus, the meaning is "on account of a cause for laughter.

It is said that there is no offense for one who offers an expression of thanks (*anumodanā*) and so forth with a loud voice within a house. For instance, even the Elder Mahinda [did this] in the elephant stables and other such places.
He told it to the great multitude.
591. Some monks say, "One has entered upon residence merely by the depositing of requisites"; that is merely their own opinion.
If nuns have entered upon residence, the nuns' quarters themselves constitute the *kappiya-bhūmi* (the place where things are allowable). "Where..."

Because of the statement, "Even if bhikkhunīs stay for only a single night, this is a bhikkhunī-upassaya," it is permissible for one who goes thinking, "I am going to their vicinity" or "I am going to the dwelling-house occupied by them," to go as he pleases.
For that house does not thereby become reckoned as an *antaraghara* (a house within the village); such is the opinion of the Teacher.
The commentary on the Ujjagghikavagga is finished.
3. Commentary on the Khambhakatavagga. 604.
Regarding the description of the size of the bowl, it is as stated [in the previous section]. *Oloṇī* is called *kudhita*; the meaning is that it is full and heaped up with cow’s milk products.
605. Regarding the phrase "he descends below": here they say that if there is sufficient space for descending, even if it is piled up in one spot, there is no offense.
They also say that "it is permissible for one who places [the bowl] after covering its bottom and top with lotus leaves and the like;
this is what is meant by 'obtained'. Herein, because it is said, "almsfood should be received so as to be level to the brim,"...

The statement indicates that almsfood should be received when it is level with [the rim of] the bowl; therefore, it indicates that even if the almsfood being given into the bowl held in one’s own hand is heaped up, it is permissible.
For the statement, “If one receives almsfood that has been heaped up, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),” refers first to the almsfood that has been heaped up and then...

It indicates that there is an offense for one who receives [food] with [the hand]. Even if it is received with a bowl, it is permissible provided it is not heaped up, because it has been received without being heaped up;
however, there is no formal act (payoga) except in the case of the previous location.
Furthermore, some say "samatittika" is a neuter abstract noun (bhāvanapuṃsaka); therefore, this should be accepted after careful consideration.
The commentary on the Khambhakatavagga is finished.
4. Commentary on the Sakkaccavagga. 609.

Regarding the training rule on requesting curry and boiled rice: it is not stated that "curry means two kinds of curry," because by the inclusion of the term "curry," [all] superior foods are already covered.

This is for the purpose of including all remaining types of food. In the section on non-offenses (*anāpattivāra*), the phrase “for relatives, for those who have invited one, for the sake of another, or with one’s own wealth” is additional.

In some manuscripts, only this much is stated: “There is no offense if it was unintentional, if there was forgetfulness, if one did not know, if one was ill, or in cases of distress”; however, that is not correct, [as it omits] “with equal curry... [and so forth].
In this section on non-offenses regarding the thought, "I shall eat almsfood," the phrase "for the sake of another" is written in some places;

however, that was written through negligence. Even in the case of one who, having placed [the food] in the mouth, later feels regret and wishes to swallow it, if it enters suddenly, this is called "unintentionally. Whether requested or unrequested, in a single instance...
It is written: "One who takes and eats what is placed in its proper place without first reflecting upon it is said to act 'without mindfulness.
Furthermore, in certain manuscripts within the section on non-offenses (*anāpatti*), it is written "rasarase," and it is stated that this [reading] should be accepted.
The commentary on the *Sakkacca-vagga* is concluded.
5. Commentary on the Chapter on Lumps (Kabaḷavagga) 618.

Regarding the statement, “All [the food] with the hand,” some say that there is no offense for one who puts a portion into the mouth. Others say, “Because of the word ‘all,’ even a single portion is not permitted. The latter view is correct, because no distinction is made in the section on non-offenses.
624. Regarding the one who drops rice grains, the readings are both “while throwing away refuse, rice grains are dropped” and “while throwing away refuse.”
The commentary on the Kabaḷavagga is finished.
6. Commentary on the Surusuruvagga 627.
The readings are both "surusuru" and "surosuro. "Sītīkata" means "made cool. It is recorded that "Silakabuddho" is merely a humorous expression used by the Noble Ones (ariya).
631. Regarding the phrase "by way of the repulsive": if it were rejected by way of the repulsive, then one could not say, "just as in the case of those who enjoy sensual pleasures.
If it is argued that this is because they do not perceive it as repulsive, we say no; for it is possible to grasp it by way of its characteristic of being a matter of mastery.
For they are indeed indifferent to it. "Washing of the bowl" refers to the water used for washing the bowl, which is associated with the act of eating.
634. The readings are both “*chattapādukāya*” and “*chattapāde*. 637. A “bow” (*cāpa*) is a weapon for striking with seven [arrows].
It is also written: “All other varieties of the bow have entered into the *kodaṇḍa*. “Fastened” (*paṭimukka*) means inserted; the sense is that it is attached.
The commentary on the *surusuru*-group is finished.
7. Commentary on the Chapter on Sandals (Pādukavagga) 640.

Just as one who has himself mounted a vehicle is not fit to speak to another who is likewise mounted on a vehicle, so too one holding an umbrella is not fit to speak to one who likewise holds an umbrella.

As it is here, so it is elsewhere. 647. In the case of the *Chapaka* story, the reading "If I do not obtain [it]" exists, as does "If I do not obtain ten," and the phrase "in the case of one who is not ill" also occurs;
that is not good, for it is within the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) itself.

"Beautiful. The connection is: "I too know that it has been praised. That livelihood, consisting of the acquisition of wealth and grain, occurs through ruin—that is, it proceeds as a cause for ruin in the future, in the states of misery (*apāya*).
Alternatively, "through ruin" (*vinipātena*) is used in the instrumental case to express the sense of a cause;
the intended meaning is that it proceeds for the sake of ruin. "By unrighteous conduct" means for the sake of unrighteous conduct.
And they also recite: “Asmā kumbhimiva.
The commentary on the Pāduka-vagga is finished.
The commentary on the miscellaneous section (Pakiṇṇaka).

Because they arise from body, speech, and mind, they are called "originating from formal admonition" (*samanubhāsana-samutthāna*). Formal admonition is an action; these [offenses] are actions. Regarding the statement "originating from teaching the Dhamma, from speech and mind":

if it is argued that they should be described as "from body, speech, and mind" because they possess the nature of bodily and vocal intimation (*viññatti*), just as in the cases of loud laughter, high-pitched sounds, and so forth—this should not be said. They should not be so described.

It is appropriate in that case because of the existence of bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti) such as sitting down, walking, and putting food into the mouth; it is not so in the teaching of the Dhamma, because such [intimation] is absent there.
The commentary on the miscellaneous matters is finished.
The commentary on the Section on the Training Rules (Sekhiyakaṇḍa) is finished.
