1. Commentary on the Section on Defeat (Pārājikakaṇḍa):
Commentary on the Commencement of the Text.
Just as in the Vibhaṅga, this has been composed in detail for the sake of the bhikkhus.
Without having [already] explained even for the nuns, I shall now set forth the method for the knots and the words.
The meaning is that the sequence for the commentary on that which is the *Vibhaṅga* for the nuns has been reached.
The explanation of the commencement of the book is finished.
1. Commentary on the First Pārājika Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 656–7.

In those various instances, *vīmaṃsā* refers to situational wisdom (*ṭhānuppattikapaññā*). “Precisely according to the sequence of the words” means precisely according to the sequence of the words in the matrix (*mātikā*). It is written: “‘It is said’ means that the analysis of the intentions of the compilers of the Council has been stated.
658. “‘Come, bhikkhunī’—she is a bhikkhunī; she is a bhikkhunī who is fully ordained through the three goings for refuge. This...
However, some say it was spoken by way of the elegance of the teaching (*desanāvilāsa*). Others say it exists during the time of other Buddhas;

that, however, does not seem correct, because it would follow that it could also occur during our own Buddha’s time, and because we see the prohibition against the "Come, Bhikkhunī" formula (*ehibhikkhunī*) serving as its shadow.
As it is said in the *Dhammapada* regarding the story of Visākhā: "As the result of that gift of robes, this great adornment of creepers..."
[She] obtained [it]. For the gift of robes by women reaches its peak through great garlands and ornaments, whereas for men it is through supernaturally produced bowls and robes.

However, the occurrence of a nun who has received full ordination (*upasampadā*) through the threefold going for refuge might occasionally happen at the time of another Buddha, but it certainly does not exist at our own Buddha’s time.
Nevertheless, due to the elegance of the teaching, she was mentioned according to the sequence of the monks’ instruction.

The description of the bhikkhunīs has been stated; for that very reason, although bhikkhunīs—who are ordained on one side—are actually existing, they were not mentioned there by way of the community of bhikkhus.
Their existence is to be understood from this commentary of the Parivāra:
"Those ordained together on both sides..."
"One might accept a robe from the hands of both [persons];
there may be various offenses.
This question has been conceived by those skilled in wisdom."
Alternatively, some say that even one who was already fully ordained at the time of being a worldling through the "Come,
monk" formula and the going for refuge, yet remains in the state of a bhikkhunī due to the manifestation of female gender,

is reckoned as an "ehibhikkhunī" in relation to the full ordination of a male, and is also reckoned as a "bhikkhunī ordained by the three goings for refuge. Otherwise, they argue, that statement would be contradicted.
It should be accepted after due consideration. The phrase "a wise person capable" is said because it succeeds in ensuring that the two [nuns] do not fall under the control of others.
In this regard, when receiving any kind of material gift, their hands may sometimes come into contact with the hands of men;
or when paying respects, their heads may sometimes touch the feet of men.
Or, at the time of shaving the hair, the head of men may be mixed with their hands; for this mind is indeed excessively quick to seek [its object] and difficult to guard.

Therefore, out of compassion, thinking, "May there not be an offense entailing defeat (pārājika) for the bhikkhunīs too quickly," the Blessed Buddhas established the delimitation of the field for an offense entailing defeat and the delimitation of the field for a grave offense (thullaccaya).
It should be understood that they teach [the rules] individually.

Regarding the statement, "That was spoken by way of the majority (tabbahulanaya)," the sequence of the sub-commentary (*anugaṇṭhipada*) is as follows: because it is for the most part originated by action, it is called "originated by action" (*kiriyasamuṭṭhāna*).
Furthermore, instead of saying "one should engage in physical contact," it says "one should consent."
Because it has been stated thus, it should be understood that [the offense] also originates from non-action (*akiriya*).

And just as here, so too below, after stating the origination from action (*kiriyasamuṭṭhāna*) by way of the method beginning with, "For one who practices the sexual act with a human woman on the three paths, there is an offense of defeat (*pārājika*)," immediately following that, [it says]:
"If a monk’s adversaries... if he consents to the insertion, there is an offense of defeat," and so forth.

Since it is stated according to the method [of the Vibhaṅga] that there is also non-action origination (*akiriyasamuṭṭhānatā*), the first *pārājika* offense should also be understood as having action origination (*kiriyasamuṭṭhānatā*) by way of the predominant method.
For action origination is not seen in the mere admission [of the organ], the consenting, and so forth. And here, the movement of the sexual organ (*aṅgajāta*) should not be regarded as essential;
for it is said: "If he does not consent to the insertion, does not consent to what has been inserted, does not consent to what remains..."

In the passage, “He does not consent; he consents to the extraction [of the semen]; there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika),” the state of “not consenting” is established because it possesses its own natural, complete movement.

For here, a movement resulting from sexual intercourse is not seen at all due to the condition of non-consent; therefore, the origination by action should be understood according to the principle of the majority of cases.
Why, then, is the principle of the majority of cases not explicitly stated in the various commentaries?
Why? Because in the summary (mātikā), the rule “Whatever monk should engage in sexual intercourse” is stated explicitly as originating from action (kiriyasamuṭṭhāna);
therefore, without examining the method of the analysis (vibhaṅga) in accordance with that, it is simply stated as “originating from action.

And just as in these cases, the state of originating from action is stated according to the principle of what is predominant, so too in the case of liquor and the like, it is [predominantly] unwholesome (akusala).
It must be understood in this way, and not otherwise. For only when it is stated, "That which one commits through unwholesome [volition] alone is a natural offense (*lokavajja*);

the rest are offenses by rule (*paṇṇattivajja*)," is the defining characteristic for the restriction between natural and rule-based offenses established. It is not so when it is stated without saying that, but rather:
"That for which, on the side of being with consciousness, the mind is exclusively unwholesome, is a natural offense; the rest are offenses by rule."

The word "worldly reproach" (*lokavajja*) would be meaningless even in the case of not knowing the substance, because [the offense] must still be incurred through an unwholesome state of mind (*akusala*).
Since there is no arising of an unwholesome consciousness (*akusalacittuppāda*) regarding the transgression of drinking liquor in that instance, therefore the Khandhaka Commentary states:
"But in the case of drinking intoxicants, for a bhikkhu who drinks an intoxicant starting from the seed even without knowing it, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*)."
It is stated that "a novice monk incurs a breach of the precepts if he drinks while knowing [it is alcohol], but not if he does so unknowingly";

it is *not* stated that "even when there is an arising of unwholesome consciousness capable of accomplishing acts such as the destruction of life on the side of not knowing the object, the novice monk does not incur a breach of the precepts.
This is because the statement of insistence [on the former view] treats the drinking of liquor by novice monks as being of the same nature as the destruction of life and other such offenses.

“However, for one who transgresses by way of what is to be drunk and so forth, having understood the basis [of the offense] as ‘these are surā and the rest,’ there is no possibility of it being unwholesome (akusala).
Therefore it was said: ‘In the case of one who possesses consciousness,’ and so forth.

Furthermore, here, by means of this logical statement, since [unwholesome states] do not enter into Arahants, there is a restriction of the unwholesome in both the cases of those with consciousness and those without consciousness.”
Why? Because, by way of natural law (*dhammatā*), even those in training (*sekkha*) do not enter [into unwholesome states].

To show the absence of an unwholesome certainty (*akusala-niyama*) in the case of one without consciousness, examples such as drops of liquor and so forth should be cited, like a drop of water placed in the mouth of one who is sleeping.

For when the meaning is grasped according to the method of predominance (*tabbahulanaya*), it accords with the earlier and later parts of the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*). "Together with the Text (*Pāḷi*), its meaning is without distinction hereafter... [so it is said].
"It will become manifest," so it is said by others. This is what must be investigated here:

If, according to the position that it is the knowledge of the object [that constitutes an offense], drinking intoxicants could occur without unwholesome consciousness (*akusala*), why is it that the Noble Ones (*ariya*) do not drink even the juice of the *nāḷi* plant when they perceive it as a beverage and the like?
For the transgression of a basis for the breaking of virtue does not occur among the Noble Ones even without a conscious intention, but rather solely by way of their inherent nature (*dhammatā*).
Furthermore, why is it that even for a bhikkhunī, drinking liquor—as in the case of a sāmaṇera—is not considered intentional (sacittaka)?
If you say it is because it is improper (appatirūpa), then it is equally improper for sāmaṇeras as well;

for they too are indeed fellow practitioners of the Dhamma (sahadhammika). If you say it is because of its great blameworthiness (mahāsāvajja), then it is exactly the same for sāmaṇeras. [Regarding] sāmaṇeras...

If you argue that only an offense with conscious intent (*sacittaka*) constitutes a *pārājika*, while other cases are merely grounds for disciplinary action (*daṇḍakamma-vatthu*), then there would be no *pārājika* for monks regarding the drinking of intoxicants either.

In this case, there should not be a threefold *pācittiya* offense. Furthermore, for one who perceives what is not an intoxicant as an intoxicant, an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) should be prescribed.
A matter that is a *pācittiya* for a monk becomes a *pārājika* for novices (*sāmaṇera*), including those who are animal-novice novices.

If it is argued that [the offense] occurs even when one is without consciousness (*acittaka*), then a *pārājika* offense for novices (*sāmaṇera*) regarding the drinking of intoxicants and the like would have to be established even in the absence of consciousness.
If it is argued that a *pārājika* cannot occur without consciousness, we say no; for a *pārājika* can also occur as a transgression of the formal rule (*paṇṇattivajja*).

This same fault applies to the position of other schools (*nikāyantara*). For us, however, the drinking of intoxicants is indeed a transgression by nature (*lokavajja*). Why, then, is only the drinking of fermented liquor (*surāpāna*) mentioned here as being by way of natural law (*dhammatā*)?
"Do the Noble Ones not do these things? It is not only the drinking of fermented liquor that the Noble Ones refrain from doing by virtue of their nature;

they also do not, out of anger, commit acts such as decapitation against living beings because they perceive them as living beings; they do not transgress against another's wife because they perceive her as their own wife;
they do not speak false speech that destroys welfare because they perceive it as destroying welfare; and [they refrain from wrong views] because of their perception of right view.
It should be understood that they do not adopt wrong view. Even the teachers state that there is no fixed unwholesomeness (*akusalaniyama*) regarding the drinking of intoxicants;

therefore, in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā-ṭīkā* (Gaṇṭhipada), in the section concerning what is forbidden by the world and what is forbidden by the rule (*paṇṇattivajja*), it is written: "In the context of 'with mind' (*sacittaka*), it is unwholesome [only] for the purpose of including the drinking of intoxicants and so forth;
otherwise, one would have to say 'for whom it is exclusively unwholesome. [This concerns] the state of being originated by action (*kriyā-samutthānatā*).

In this case, it is according to the majority [of the rule], not according to the first *pārājika*. How so? The training rule on physical contact (*kāyasaṃsagga*) originates from the first *pārājika*.
Here, when there is physical contact between a monk and a nun, the nun incurs the offense even if she merely consents with her mind while the monk is touching her body;
the monk does not incur it in this way. Rather, the monk incurs the offense only by actually making the contact himself.
In the same way, regarding the first *pārājika* offense as well, one incurs it only when there is physical contact (*copana*), not when there is none.

Regarding the phrase "consents to the insertion," here "consenting to the insertion" means the arising of the intention for sexual intercourse; even though this is so, it is stated that "it must be taken after investigation.
The commentary on the first *pārājika* training rule is finished.
2. Commentary on the Second Pārājika Training Rule:
From the statement, "But why, noble lady, did you knowingly commit an offense involving defeat?
and from the statement, "I have committed one of the eight offenses involving defeat," at the end [it says], "Noble ladies, these have been recited."

Because of such statements as "the eight rules involving defeat," and because of the statement in the *Parivāra* that "the common formulation is a formulation for both [orders]," when the Blessed One reached the *Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga*, he established the common training rules precisely on account of the same incidents that had arisen for the monks,
beginning with: "Whatever bhikkhunī should intentionally engage in sexual intercourse, even so much as..."

Having laid down the matrix (mātikā) both with and without specific distinctions by way of such passages as, “Even with one who has gone among the animals, it is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika), one who is not in communion,” and so forth,
[the Blessed One] then expanded upon it in detail by sequentially explaining the word-commentary (padabhājana), the classification of offenses (āpattibheda), the analysis of the triads (tikaccheda),

and the section on non-offenses (anāpattivāra) in their entirety. However, it should be understood that only those rules of promulgation that are not common [to other Vinayas] were expanded upon here by the compilers of the Council (saṅgītikāraka).

666. In this context, the phrase "of the eight *pārājikas*" is a statement formulated by the compilers of the Council (*saṅgītikāraka*) solely according to their own method, because prior to this [point], the sixth, seventh, and eighth *pārājikas* had not yet been promulgated.
However, if one were to take even the very first training rule (*sikkhāpada*) as it was promulgated by the Blessed One, it could have been said, "of the six *pārājikas*.
Furthermore, if one were to take into account those promulgated after this point, it would be "of the eight."
Some teachers maintain that the statement "of the pārājikas" was formulated at a later stage. However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā* it is said:
"And this pārājika was laid down later; therefore, it is stated as 'of eight' in the Vibhaṅga," and so forth.
Consequently, according to the opinion of the *Aṭṭhakathā* teachers, it is established that these were chanted exactly in the order they were laid down.
The reading is “aññāsiṃ. It should not be taken as “aññāsī.

Because of the statement, “in the very same manner as stated in the *duṭṭhulla-sikkhāpada*,” it is established that whoever conceals a concealable offense (*vajja*) is indeed one who conceals a concealable offense.
Although the concealment of an offense occurs through affection, nevertheless, the mind that transgresses the training rule is exclusively one of displeasure (*domanassa*).
Having established that it "is," it is called "painful feeling.
The commentary on the second Pārājika training rule is finished.
3. Commentary on the third Pārājika training rule.
669. This [phrase] "having exhorted and reminded" refers merely to this underlying intention (*adhippāyamatta*). Herein is the analysis:
A bhikkhu who holds the same view as one whose legal act of suspension (*ukkhepana*) has been carried out, yet belongs to a different community due to a difference in doctrine, is not to be saluted;
like one suspended for an improper legal act, he does not complete the quorum for a formal act, nor does he receive a shared sleeping place. It is not so, however, with a bhikkhunī. For she...
As long as [the formal act] has not been carried out, one remains a member completing the quorum and obtains communal residence.

Even one who follows those who follow a different tenet or a different communion, or one who follows a suspended monk, is likewise [considered] one who follows a suspended monk. If the suspended monk dies, the monk who followed him remains one belonging to a different communion due to that tenet.
The same applies if he has gone away, or if he has gone over to another sect, or if he has renounced the training and returned to the status of a novice.

"Even when [the offense] has been settled," say some. According to their opinion, even if the one who was subject to the *ukkhepanīyakamma* (act of suspension) has become such [i.e., settled], a nun who follows her must still be formally admonished;
thus they fall into this [error]. The act of formal admonition depends upon the Saṅgha; it appears as though it would be improper for the Saṅgha to intentionally remove a previous offense.
Furthermore, the *ukkhepanīyakamma* applies merely to the non-seeing of an offense, or merely to the non-remedy of one.
If it is argued that this applies merely to the relinquishing of wrong views,
and that it is not logical to say they should be expelled from the Teaching merely by following such a person after having been formally admonished— this must certainly not be said.
For this would apply even to cases that do not constitute a *pārājika* offense by extension, since the Vinaya has no other scope.
The commentary on the third *pārājika* training rule is finished.
4. Commentary on the fourth *pārājika* training rule:
675. "By means of the affection for physical contact, [the Buddha] showed that [offense] by way of intimacy with friends, which is reckoned as worldly pleasure."
"Vuttaṃ" (it is said) is written [in the text]. "Tissitthiyo" means among three women, or three women. "Taṃ na seveyya" means he does not consort with them.
"Anariyā" refers to those who possess both sexual organs (*ubhatobyañjanā*). "Byañjane" means in one's own sexual organ. "Na seveyya" means he does not consort with it.
"Na cācareyya" means he does not practice [such conduct]. "Vaṇṇāvaṇṇo" refers to the emission of semen in two ways. "Gamanuppādanaṃ" refers to acting as a go-between (*sañcarittaṃ*).
"676. 'Whether it be wrapped around or thrown over'—here the meaning is that one consents to the taking of a cloth that has been wrapped around or thrown over.
The commentary on the fourth *pārājika* training rule is finished.
The commentary on the section on *pārājika* offenses is finished."
2. Commentary on the Saṅghādisesa Section 1.
Commentary on the First Saṅghādisesa Training Rule 681.

“Brought” (āhata) means introduced; the intended meaning is “brought in. An “improper price” (akappiya-aḍḍa) refers to [money] belonging either to the Saṅgha or to an individual monastery attendant (ārāmika).
Or, for the sake of a property, or by virtue of being the Saṅgha’s steward, one goes to the site of a legal dispute and addresses it oneself, saying, “This is our slave, or slave-girl;

this is our pond, field, monastery, monastery-site, ox, cow, buffalo, goat, or cock,” and so forth—it is unallowable. “This is our monastery-attendant, or monastery-attendant-woman; this is the pond... [and so on].
When asked—or even unasked—it is permissible to say: "This has been given by [Name] into the hands of the Saṅgha for milking;
whatever four requisites arise from this field or this grove, and whatever milk arises from the cows, buffaloes, and goats from here, has been given by [Name] to the Saṅgha.
It is said that by using the expression "she is milking" rather than saying "it is done," what was not yet completed is [rendered as being in progress].
He is called one who speaks with reference [to that]. "The neck" means it is merely the neck itself; it is not a *pārājika* offense.
Regarding the phrase "having had it made, it should be given back": if it is a weapon, its edge must not be sharpened, but it should be made known [as such] in another way.
Because it is said, "three minds, three feelings," [it refers to] "by way of human intent and by way of angry intent."
It should be understood that this is stated by way of general rule.
The commentary on the first Saṅghādisesa training rule is finished.
2. Commentary on the second Saṅghādisesa training rule.
683. "Bhaṭiputtaka-gaṇā" refers to groups of young men who were formerly soldiers. "Kappanti" means they are allowable. "Kappagatika" means having the nature of what is allowable.

"Even when others have departed" means when, setting aside one's own group, the other [groups] have departed. Or, it may be said that even noble ones (ariya), being unaware of the formal rule (paṇṇatti), perform the act of restoration;
this is because at the moment of the offense—at the conclusion of the formal proclamation (kammavācā)—they possess a state of moral indeterminacy (vipākābyākata).
Or it should be understood that it is stated as “three minds. “There is no offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the act of sending away,” so it is said in the ancient *gaṇṭhipada*.
The commentary on the second Saṅghādisesa training rule is finished.
3. Commentary on the third Saṅghādisesa training rule.
687. It is said that Bhaddākāpilānī was the former wife of Mahākassapa. Regarding the phrase "the village where the family of her relatives [resides]":
the meaning is that she went to that village which was situated near the family of her relatives.

Alternatively, it is also appropriate to treat it as having two objects—like the expression "he leads this goat to the village"—and thus understand: "she went to the village" and "she went to the family of her relatives."
692. By the statement, “For one who crosses the precincts of an unenclosed village,” it should be understood in this way:
regarding entry into a village at an improper time, the precincts are to be delimited by exactly two throws of a clod;
otherwise, just as here [in the case of an enclosed village], having treated the places suitable for enclosure as if they were actually enclosed, it is said, “for one who crosses.”
Thus, in that case as well, one might say, "of one who is crossing beyond the precincts of an unenclosed village.

However, since in that instance what is intended by "precinct" is a single stone's throw beyond the place suitable for an enclosure, it was therefore stated—"of one who is entering the precincts of an unenclosed village"—in order to clarify that meaning. That which...
However, in the Andhaka-ṭīkā, having identified "upacāra" as referring only to the space eligible for a boundary,

and without noticing the specific distinction in the Pāḷi text, it was stated— "when entering the precincts"— for the purpose of showing that there is no difference between the boundary and the space eligible for a boundary;
[otherwise], for one crossing the precincts of an unenclosed village, the precincts here would have to be considered a boundary.
Regarding the statement, "For one who crosses the first boundary of that precinct, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);

for one who crosses the second boundary, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya)," that must certainly not be accepted because of the presence of specific distinctions in the Canon (pāḷi). It has been said:
"In some [recensions], it is seen as 'for one entering the precinct of an unenclosed village,' but others say that this is not to be accepted."
In this regard, it is said that "without having clearly observed the specific wording of the text" is poorly stated; why?
Because even in the training rule concerning entering a village at an improper time, the reading "of one who crosses the precincts" (upacāraṃ atikkamantassa) is seen in some places;

the Master [Buddhaghosa] maintains that this was taken from the reading of the Andhaka Aṭṭhakathā. However, for an unenclosed area, the reading "crossing the precincts" (upacārokkamana) alone is appropriate, not "crossing over" (atikkamana).
Why? Because it contradicts the Pāḷi and the Commentaries in many places, and it even contradicts this very training rule (sikkhāpada).
How? For one who lags behind from a group, an offense occurs in the forest, not in the village.

Furthermore, as an illustration, the verse beginning "The training rules were laid down by the Best of Buddhas" is shown; therefore, for one who crosses a river that falls within the vicinity [of the monastery], [there is an offense].

Furthermore, it has been stated: "One must reach the conclusion that, based on the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) on the *Parivāra* verses beginning with 'For one walking there are four offenses, and for one standing there are likewise that many,' the reading is indeed the transgression of the vicinity (*upacārokkamana*).
Having reflected well upon this, one should explain it.
"In this context, walking on foot alone is intended; for that reason, it says 'she crosses over with the first foot,' and so forth.

This indicates that since such [walking] is absent in the training rules concerning entering a village at the wrong time and others, there is no offense for one who enters by means of a vehicle or by psychic power (*iddhi*), or for one who travels a long distance. Regarding this, some say that because it is improper, there is no release from the offense.

It should be understood after careful consideration. The grounds of a bhikkhunī’s dwelling are not called "between villages" (*gāmantara*), because they are included within the area of a village due to being a *kappiya-bhūmi* (an allowable site).

Furthermore, from the subsequent statement, "If one [bhikkhunī] stands outside while the others are entering the Great Bodhi courtyard, she incurs an offense," it is established that a bhikkhu’s dwelling is not a *kappiya-bhūmi*. Therefore...
"Like the Khaṇḍhadhamma Monastery in Kañcīnagara and like the Sārīdhamma Monastery in Kāvīrapaṭṭana, there is yet another such monastery;

therefore, for the sake of the ease of defining boundaries, even when one enters or exits a continuous stretch [of land] between two villages for the purpose of formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna), others say that an offense regarding the interval between villages occurs. Regarding the phrase "because it is common to four villages": here—
It should be understood that when establishing the boundary (sīmā) for such a monastery, those four villages must also be cleared.
For a nun who enters that monastery after having made an agreement with a woman or with a caravan of thieves, there are four offenses simultaneously.
Some say this is because it is stated: "In each successive village, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya)."

Regarding the phrase "the second lifting of the foot is a *saṅghādisesa* offense": here, if the second lifting of the foot occurs within a *kappiya-bhūmi* (an area where what is allowable is permitted), it is not a *saṅghādisesa*;
it is only a *saṅghādisesa* when it occurs outside of a *kappiya-bhūmi*. It has been written: "They move about on both banks;
this is permissible, because the range of sight is possible here"—this is correct. For here, the range of hearing extends across the riverbank.
“Or within a village boundary, it is immeasurable. However, in the *Andhaka-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated:

“If one descends to a river on the opposite bank and fetches firewood or leaves from within the range of sight, there is no offense. If one dries the three robes on the opposite bank, there is no offense.
This was said because [the action] was undertaken with the intention of crossing over; “if one returns to this very side, there is an offense.”
It is said: “For those who have entered for the purpose of bathing and other such duties, where is it permissible for a dwelling to arise?

Regarding the measurement between villages, the Commentary states that after descending into a river from the opposite bank, it is not permissible—even by way of crossing a small distance from one’s own village—to go out and enter [another village] while within the range of sight of the timber or leaves.
"In a forest where there is no village" means in a forest characterized by the absence of a village. By this, the field of offense (*āpattikhetta*) is shown.

Because this is the field of offense, therefore, when a nun passes beyond the boundary pillar (*indakhīla*) of a village from the nunnery, she incurs an offense for leaving the group in the absence of a village;
this is all the more so in the absence of the range of sight or sound (*dassana-savana-upacāra*).

One commits the offense at the very moment of crossing the boundary pillar (*indakhīla*). If there is a single bhikkhunī there, one commits the offense at the moment of crossing the range of sight or hearing of that bhikkhunī.

One should not assume that this rule applies only during the time of traveling on a forest path. However, for the purpose of showing that one commits the offense from this point onward when departing from a village, it is stated as "a forest without a village. For this has been said: "Those who have attained... (*ārādhikā*)... [and so forth].

“They are inclusive and modest; having provoked them, one must not go elsewhere. If one goes, one is not released from the offenses of leaving the group, crossing a river between villages, and staying apart at night.
Regarding this, it is said: “The offense of leaving the group is incurred only once.
The others, however, should be understood as occurring village by village, bank by bank, and dawn by dawn. In that regard, the words “For it has been said” and so forth [follow].
They are non-producers because they must be taken according to their possibility. It is written:
“The phrase ‘in the courtyard of the Great Bodhi,’ etc., is stated to show that one incurs this offense even when standing in a place near a village.
The commentary on the third Saṅghādisesa training rule is finished.
4. Commentary on the Fourth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule 694.
*Paṭivattā* means they give a reply. *Kammadosaṃ* (defect in the formal act) is written as: "without knowing the consent of the community," and so forth.
*Kattabbaṭṭhānadosaṃ* (defect in the place where it ought to be done) is the opinion of the ancients. *Kārakagaṇassa* means of the performing Saṅgha. [The text continues: "the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha..."
If it is argued that because it is stated "having assembled [them]," the performing Saṅgha is also this very same group—[the answer is:
the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada* states, "Without first addressing the performing Saṅgha, this Thullanandā forcibly reinstated that bhikkhunī.
Therefore, even in the presence of the performing bhikkhus, that formal act (*kamma*) is not valid if their consent is not first obtained.
"It should be settled" is established; the intention is that once it has been settled, it must not be done by force.
And it is stated therein: "A bhikkhunī also is permitted to make a confession of her view. 698.
Regarding the statement, "If one reinstates [a person] when the Saṅgha of those who perform the formal act is absent, there is no offense": to what extent is it said that they are "absent"?
This has not been examined in all respects. Some say it is due to the death of the makers [of the robe]. Some say it is due to the absence of even one [maker]. Some say it is when there is one dyer.
Some say it is in one province. Some say it is in one village.

Some say it is in one residence. Some say it is wherever it is possible to obtain leave. Some say it is within half a yojana. In that case, when the community of makers is not present in that residence—
The teachers praise this [rule], saying that there is no offense if one restores [the robe] or if it is possible to seek permission; this is the proper conduct (*sāmīci*).
The commentary on the fourth *saṅghādisesa* training rule is finished.
5. Commentary on the fifth *saṅghādisesa* training rule.
701. “The statement ‘this was not said’ means that the fact of the nun’s lustful state (*avassuta*) is not to be regarded as a restrictive rule;
this non-statement accords with the Canon (*pāḷi*). Which Canon? This one: ‘If she accepts [the gift] knowing him to be lustful.
For if the lustful state of the person were not a criterion, what would be the purpose of this Canon? [It is for the sake of the following: ‘There is no offense...’”
Only this much would need to be said: "Both are lustful, and she who is lustful accepts [the gift]. For one's own state of being free from lust alone is the criterion.
However, the meaning of this section on non-offenses (*anāpattivāra*) is as follows:
if both are free from lust, there is no offense in any respect. But if a nun, while being free from lust herself, [perceives] one who is lustful as "lust-free," [there is no offense].
If she accepts it from his hand with the perception [that he is not lustful], there is likewise no offense.

Now, even if she herself is not lustful, if she perceives another who is either not lustful or lustful as being "lustful," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). For this was said in the immediately preceding training rule:
"Why, noble lady, do you not accept it? 'He is lustful, noble lady'... 'I am not lustful.'"
The commentary on the fifth Saṅghādisesa training rule is finished.
6. Commentary on the sixth Saṅghādisesa training rule: 705.
*Tenā* means "therefore. Because the instigator neither gives nor receives, therefore no receiving exists.
The meaning is as follows: [it is] for the purpose of her enjoyment. "An unwholesome mind" is stated by way of generality.
They say: "Even for one who speaks with the perception that 'it is permissible,' there is an offense.
The commentary on the sixth Saṅghādisesa training rule is finished.
7. Commentary on the Seventh Saṅghādisesa Training Rule 712–4.

Offenses committed prior to the formal act (kammavācā) are not suspended. According to the ancients, the offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) and grave offense (thullaccaya) are suspended when the motion (ñatti) for a Saṅghādisesa has been reached. This accords with the canonical text: "by her who commits [it]."
Regarding the phrase “having heard, they do not speak”: if they do not speak because of fear that it would create an obstacle to their holy life (*brahmacariya*), there is no offense.

Because it is stated, “In the case of an illegal formal act, if one perceives it as an illegal formal act, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*),” the statement “there is no offense for one who does not admonish” refers specifically to the *saṅghādisesa* offense.
The commentary on the seventh Saṅghādisesa training rule is finished.
8. Commentary on the eighth Saṅghādisesa training rule: 715.
*Paccākatā* means defeated. The only difference between this [rule] and the training rule concerning the corrupter of families (*kuladūsaka*) is merely the introductory narrative (*nidāna*).
For it is said there: "He is to be addressed solely for the sake of relinquishing that speech, not for the purpose of preventing the corruption of a family.

This being so, since both these offenses share a common ground with one another, does this [latter offense] become like a subsequent rule (*anupaññatti*) to that [former], and therefore this becomes entirely purposeless?
It should not be viewed in this way, because of the difference in the underlying matter (*vatthu*).
And the distinction between the two is due to the difference in the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*).
The commentary on the eighth *saṅghādisesa* training rule is concluded.
9. Commentary on the ninth *saṅghādisesa* training rule.
723. “By bodily or verbal contact”—this is the remainder of the text.
The commentary on the ninth Saṅghādisesa training rule is finished.
The commentary on the section on Saṅghādisesa offenses is finished.
3. Commentary on the Section on Forfeiture (Nissaggiyakanda) 1.
Commentary on the First Offense of Expiation involving Forfeiture (Paṭhamanissaggiyapācittiya-sikkhāpada) 733.
The first offense of expiation involving forfeiture is indeed straightforward.
2. Commentary on the Second Nissaggiya-Pācittiya Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 740.
They gave the out-of-season robe-cloth either because the object [of the rule] was fulfilled, or because they did not wish to incur an offense, or because there was no formal instruction [to do so].
It should be brought forward exactly as it was received; the intention is that it must not be divided, as it belongs to an individual (puggalika). For in substance, the other case is also [the same].

It must be brought forward exactly as it was received. In the *Gaṇṭhipada*, however, it says: "Received as given" means received from one who has relinquished it [saying], "I give this to you, Venerable Lady.
"As given" means according to the manner of relinquishment by the donors. "Must be brought forward" means it should be distributed because it is not out-of-season robe-cloth;
this is the intended meaning. Here, only the robe-cloth obtained by the distributor herself becomes subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*); that—
It is written: "Even after performing a formal act of discipline (*vinayakamma*), one does not obtain [the object] oneself.

If this were said with reference to what is obtained through relinquishment (*nissaṭṭha*), then because it is stated—"One should give it to the Saṅgha, or to a group (*gaṇa*), or to an individual (*puggala*);
they should give it; 'I give it to the Noble Lady' (*ayyāya*)"—all three of these phrases ought to have been mentioned. Therefore, it is not merely...

Only that which was received from what was relinquished should be brought forward according to the original gift; even a portion received by other bhikkhunīs should likewise be brought forward according to the original gift.

(741) Furthermore, regarding the statement, "There is no offense for one who perceives it as out-of-season robe-cloth when it is actually in-season robe-cloth," this refers to an offense that must be incurred by way of the condition of the vessel.
It indicates only this much: that one does not commit an offense; it does not indicate the sense that [the object] has been acquired, or that it need not be returned as given.
However, if one takes it by stealth, she should be dealt with according to the value of the goods.
The commentary on the second Nissaggiya Pācittiya training rule is finished.
3. Commentary on the Third Nissaggiya Pācittiya Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 744.
Because it was taken with the perception that it was one's own, a Pācittiya offense and a Dukkaṭa offense are stated. Otherwise, one should be dealt with according to the value of the goods.
The commentary on the third Nissaggiya Pācittiya training rule is finished.
4. Commentary on the Fourth Nissaggiya-Pācittiya Training Rule 752.
There are three factors: the desire to obtain [it] by means of a stain (lesa), the requesting of another person who understands, and the acquisition [of the object].
Therefore, even if one does not obtain what was first requested but obtains something else that is smaller than that, it is still a *nissaggiya* offense because the necessary factors are fulfilled.
This same method applies elsewhere as well.
The commentary on the fourth Nissaggiya Pācittiya training rule is finished.
5. Commentary on the fifth Nissaggiya Pācittiya training rule.
753. “Having protected the oil, [I have taken] even the ghee from my own family home,” so indeed is the reading.
The commentary on the fifth Nissaggiya Pācittiya training rule is finished.
6. Commentary on the sixth Nissaggiya Pācittiya training rule.
758–762. *Pāvārikassa* means of a cloth merchant. For her by whom it was purchased, there is an offense of relinquishment (*nissaggiya*), as well as the recovery of what was forfeited.
However, they say that for the others—even those who, having learned of it, consented to their own allotted share according to the year of seniority—there is no offense of relinquishment;
rather, they too must simply bring it back in accordance with how it was received. Even after recovering what was forfeited, [it must be returned] in accordance with how it was received.
Because it is stated, "it must be brought back," they say that what was taken by the others was well-taken. In this case, there is no exemption even for one who is ill.
The commentary on the sixth Nissaggiya Pācittiya training rule is finished.
7. Commentary on the seventh Nissaggiya Pācittiya training rule.
764. Regarding the seventh [offense], although it is stated without qualification as “having requested it herself,” the meaning should nevertheless be understood as:
by means of something intended for another, designated for oneself, and obtained through a formal request.
This meaning is consistent with the sense of this canonical passage: “The bhikkhunīs, having themselves requested that requisite and having had medicine purchased with it, consumed it.”

This is how it should be understood. Its meaning is as follows: by using that requisite to purchase medicine—and by the word "and" (ca), indicating that he also purchased medicine by means of his own begging—he said, "having himself begged and purchased medicine.
Otherwise, [the text would have read] "having used that requisite to purchase medicine, they themselves also begged and consumed it."
The text (*pāḷi*) should be recited in this sequence.
However, in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), the mere intended meaning of that very term—“by means of what has been personally requested” (*saṃyācikenā ti sayaṃ yācitvā*)—is stated.
For such is the nature of the word-commentary. [This applies] to the commentary on the phrases beginning with “a gift dedicated to the Saṅgha” (*saṅghikaṃ lābhaṃ pariṇataṃ*).
However, that [previous rule] is already evident. Otherwise, what other additional meaning could be included by the word *saṃyācita* (requested), since none is seen?
Thus, that very term would be purposeless, and this training rule (*sikkhāpada*) would be no different from the preceding one.
For one’s own property may be used as one wishes. And here, by way of requesting for the Saṅgha, [it is] from one side...
It should be understood that what is obtained through begging after having made an offering is "obtained by means of a formal request" (*saṃyācika*).
Otherwise, if this term *saṃyācika* were used in the same sense hereafter, it would become indistinguishable from the previous usage;

consequently, this training rule (*sikkhāpada*)—namely, "by means of a formal request for one's own sake"—would not need to be stated separately, because the offense incurred therein would already have been included here. Furthermore, it is not [indistinguishable] because there is a difference between the two types of offenses involved.
If it is argued that there is only one offense because they were acquired by having them bought together, this is not so;

for it would follow that the term "by means of begging" (saṃyācika) would be rendered purposeless, and likewise, it would follow that there would be only one offense when items belonging to the Saṅgha, the community, or an individual are mixed together and then acquired.
The commentary on the seventh Nissaggiya Pācittiya training rule is concluded.
8. Commentary on the Eighth Nissaggiya Pācittiya Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 769.
"Of a group" means of a group such as those specializing in the Abhidhamma, or of a group consisting of fewer than four members.
The commentary on the eighth Nissaggiya Pācittiya training rule is finished.
9. Commentary on the Ninth Nissaggiya Pācittiya Training Rule. 774.
“By means of hinting” means by what was obtained through solicitation, and not by any other means.
The commentary on the ninth Nissaggiya Pācittiya training rule is concluded.
10. Commentary on the Tenth Nissaggiya Pācittiya Training Rule 779. Regarding the tenth, it should be formulated as follows:

“Whatever nun should exchange an individual requisite intended for one purpose and designated for that specific purpose for something else, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya). [It should be] “by means of an individual [requisite].”
By this eleventh [rule], "by way of invitation," it should be understood according to the sequence of their occurrence.
Although this was not explicitly stated because there was no specific incident (aṭṭhuppatti) regarding it, it must nevertheless be understood by its meaning.

In this context, however, the shadow of non-offense is seen in the case of the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual when they have invited [one] to a place; and in the case of an individual, when [the donor] is a relative. All of this is for us...
One should not regard this as authoritative simply because it was stated according to the influence of mere reasoning (*takkānusāra*).

Rather, having investigated and seen what constitutes a stable reason, one should accept exactly that which those skilled in the formal procedures of the Vinaya (*vinayakkamakovida*) authorize. However, in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*, it is said:
"Even in times of distress, only another valuable article (*garubhaṇḍa*) may be bartered for; anything else is not permitted for a bhikkhu."
"But it is permissible," it is said.
The commentary on the tenth Nissaggiya Pācittiya training rule is finished.
11. Commentary on the eleventh Nissaggiya Pācittiya training rule.
784. Instead of saying “in the first section of the second chapter,” it is stated here as “in the eleventh.
Why? Because in the Bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga, after reaching the section of thirty rules (Tiṃsaka-khaṇḍa), the sequence of sections is not explicitly mentioned.

Since a formal request (viññatti) is not prohibited in a place where one has been invited (pavārita), the Blessed One might speak by way of an invitation regarding the Dhamma in a place where one is invited by a person who is not a relative (aññātaka-appavārita).
It should be understood that by the phrase "for whatever purpose," the limit expressed in the rule "only up to four kaṃsa-measures may be requested" is being shown.

Otherwise, it would lead to undesirable conclusions, such as: "the training rule does not accord with the introduction (nidāna)," "the section on non-offenses does not accord with the training rule," and "one may request up to four kaṃsa-measures even when no formal request has been made.
Therefore, in the Commentary on the Matrix (Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā):

"Should cause to be given": except for those who share the same Dhamma, relatives, and those who have been invited [to give], if someone else, out of some quality or other, being satisfied, should say, "Whatever you need," then the meaning is to be understood according to the method stated for "requesting," as it was said: "it should be requested.
However, in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*, it is said: "This was stated with reference to a limited invitation. There is no offense..."
Regarding the phrase “when invited by relatives,” this is said with reference to a constant invitation (*niccapavāraṇā*) that occurs in every way.
A “constant invitation” is one that proceeds thus: “Whenever you have need of anything, you may say so.

However, it is stated that even if they give more than four sets [of robes], saying, “Here, take this cloak for the cold,” it is permissible to accept them. This same principle applies to the tenth [offense] as well.
The commentary on the eleventh offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya) is finished.
The commentary on the thirty rules in the Bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga is finished.
The commentary on the Section on Relinquishment (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa) is finished.
4. Commentary on the Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa) 1.
The Chapter on Garlic (Lasuṇavagga) 1.
Commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning Garlic (Paṭhamalasuṇasikkhāpada)

793–7. Regarding the phrase "with garlic," the words "I invite [criticism]" (*pavāremi*) are to be supplied as the remainder of the text. It is said that *badara-sāḷava* is a prepared food made from dried *badara* fruits that have been ground into powder.
The commentary on the first training rule concerning garlic is finished.
2. Commentary on the second training rule.
800. "Should have it removed" (saṃharāpeyya) should be understood according to the word-commentary as "either removes it himself or has it removed.

Although the classification of offenses is not explicitly shown here, nevertheless, for preliminary acts such as searching for razors, tweezers, knives, and so forth, or heating them, a dukkaṭa offense is appropriate;
and just as it is here, so too is there a classification of offenses for acts such as slapping with the palm of the hand.
It is not mentioned in the Pāḷi. However, depending on the circumstances, an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) may arise during the preliminary actions.

Thus, in this case, there is an offense of wrong-doing for the monk both regarding the act itself and regarding the garlic. This is called "action-and-non-action" (kiriya-akiriya), according to the ancients. In that context, it is not stated as "non-action" (akiriya).
The commentary on the second training rule is finished.
802–6. The third and fourth training rules are of obvious meaning.
5. Commentary on the Fifth Training Rule: 812.
Regarding the fifth rule, even if one experiences physical contact, there is no offense provided it is for the purpose of cleansing with water and remains within the aforementioned limits.
Regarding the phrase "of two joints" (*dvinnam pabbānam*): it should be understood that when two fingers are inserted together, each finger constitutes one joint, making two joints;
however, when only one finger is inserted, it is not permissible to have more than two joints.
This same method is also shown in the *Mahāpaccarī*. Thus it is written.
The commentary on the fifth training rule is finished.
815. The sixth training rule is of obvious meaning.
7. Commentary on the seventh training rule.
820–822. “Carrying it to the city” (*nagaraṃ atiharantī*) is the reading. In some places, it says “carrying it to the city gate” (*nagaradvāre atiharantī*);
in that case, the meaning is “by way of the gate. Or else, this very reading [is correct]. That [former reading] is contradictory to what precedes and follows;

this was stated with reference to the argument [found later] where it says “it was stated again,” and not with reference to the argument stated there previously. Herein, “even having requested his mother” means:
It is written that “it contradicts the word,” but that is poorly written; for this was not said with reference to a contradiction by that [statement].
If there is a *pācittiya* offense in the act of doing, then there must also be a *pācittiya* offense in having it done.

If, on the other hand, there is a *dukkaṭa* offense in having it done, then there must also be a *dukkaṭa* offense in the act of doing itself. For there is no distinction between the act of doing and having it done.
The intended meaning is: "when there is the act of undertaking.
(823) "It is permissible to accept" means that it is permissible to say "Very well" without refusing;
for it is not permissible to actually receive [the food], because of the prohibition against touching [raw grain]. "But raw grain, even at a place where one is invited by a relative..."

"It is not permissible," it was said. However, in the *Anugaṇṭhipada*, it is stated: "For one who eats grain obtained through what is allowable (*kappiya*) after having had it roasted, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

The same principle applies to other types of food as well. Furthermore, because of the statement, "There is no offense when it is due to illness," it is established that even the seven kinds of grain are not to be touched;
for this very reason, in the *Aṭṭhakathā* cited below regarding the basis for an offense of wrong-doing, even the seven kinds of grain...

And it is said: "Those that are taken up are not to be touched. If edible things were allowable items (*kappiyavatthu*), then just as it was stated without distinction regarding relatives who have invited one—"she requests other food"—so too would it have been stated:

"There is no offense if she requests for the sake of others when invited by relatives; there is no offense for one who is insane or for a first-offender. But since this was not stated, [it follows that] they are not allowable.
Because it is both a matter of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*) and because it is an improper thing (*anāmāsa*), it is not permissible to ask even one’s mother for the seven kinds of grain;
therefore, in order to clarify that point with reference to the seven kinds of grain, it is said: "There is no offense if it is on account of illness.
Just as it is permissible for a bhikkhunī on account of illness, so too is it for a bhikkhu. Or, just as...
However, it is not permitted for a bhikkhunī to have [grain] roasted and so forth, nor is it permitted for a bhikkhu in the same way.
This is also stated in the Andhakaṭṭhakathā: "A certain foolish bhikkhu, not knowing what is allowable (kappiya), said this:
'It is not permitted for bhikkhus to accept raw grain. Having had this grain roasted, pounded, and cooked, one may [use] rice-gruel and solid food...'"
"If you say, 'Give the meal,' there is an offense for the monk who gives the order, but for all others there is no offense.
Therefore, it is not permissible to tell the monastery attendants, "Pound the grain for the Sangha stewards.
However, it is permissible to say such things as, "Take a daily allowance and prepare the rice," or "You take this much, you take that much."

As for what was said, “But it is permissible to accept what is obtained without a formal intimation for the purpose of building work,” that too is well-said, because it was stated with reference to the principle explained below:
when it is said, “We give this pond, field, or site for the monastery,” it is said, “It is permissible to accept.
[Likewise,] when it is said, “We give grain for the purpose of building work...”

When this is said, one should say, "Very well. Furthermore, what was stated above—"In that regard, it is not permissible to accept an article involving forfeiture for oneself, or for the sake of the Saṅgha, a group, an individual, or a shrine...

[and so on] ...as for an article involving an offense of wrong-doing, one incurs only an offense of wrong-doing even when accepting it for the sake of anyone"—that too is well-said. Why? Because: "I wish to give grain for the sake of the shrine..."
When it was said, "Venerable sir, please accept this for that purpose," [the Buddha] did not accept it because it was improper to do so. And it was further stated, "But this is not of such a kind.
This, it is said, is the opinion of the Elder Upatissa regarding every possible means. However, the Elder Dhammasiri spoke thus:
"In the past, acceptance for the sake of new construction was not prohibited; even that which was accepted for the sake of the Saṅgha..."
"It is indeed unallowable for the recipient.
The commentary on the seventh training rule is finished.
8. Commentary on the eighth training rule.

824. The Ancients read: "one who has received his royal wages. Its meaning is: one whose food and wages have been provided is a "royal wage-receiver. They explain the meaning as: "that very thing is the path of wages; that very thing is the food and wages. *Ummuka* means a firebrand. 826.
Here, discarding is an action (*kiriyā*); not looking is a non-action (*akiriyā*).
The commentary on the eighth training rule is finished.
9. Commentary on the Ninth Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 832.
Regarding the phrase “having informed the owner, he discards [it],” it does not appear in some manuscripts, while it does appear in others.

Indeed, its presence is preferable because of the nature of this training rule as being both an action and a non-action. In this context, the field-keepers and the guardians of the monastery and so forth are indeed the owners.

"It has been said: 'If there is no agreement that "no refuse is to be discarded in the Saṅgha’s field or monastery," it is permissible for a bhikkhu to discard it because it belongs to the Saṅgha, but not for bhikkhunīs.
For them as well, it is permissible in the same manner when it belongs to the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha, but not for a bhikkhu there. Even so, it must be done only in a fitting manner.'"
The commentary on the ninth training rule is finished.
10. Commentary on the tenth training rule: 833.
Regarding the phrase "well-performed song," even ordinary singing is not permitted to be heard. [It is] "accompanied by song..."
However, it is stated in the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*: "It is permissible to listen to the Dhamma.
But in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*, after stating that "even singing the Dhamma is not permissible," it says: "If it is said, 'Let us sing and recite for the Buddha,' it is not permissible to accept;
there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). It further states: "'We shall perform an offering,' or 'We shall teach a Jātaka or a Vatthu'..."
And it is said: "When this has been spoken, it is proper to accept it by saying, 'Very well.
836. A single occasion means looking [at them] on a single day. "Of those very people" means those whose dancing one watches.
"A bhikkhunī herself is not permitted to dance, sing, or play music," and so forth—this is not found in this training rule (sikkhāpada).
Why? Because it originates from the *eḷakaloma* (sheep’s wool) rule. If this is so, why was it stated [in the *Mahāpadesa*]?

Because it is obtained through the method of the Great Authorities (*mahāpadesa*) in accordance with the Suttas. If one is not permitted to see or hear dancing and such things, let alone to perform them oneself, then it is stated [there] because it is obtainable by way of that principle.
Otherwise, the Great Authorities would be purposeless. This same method should be applied elsewhere as well. “The origin (*samuṭṭhāna*) also...”
It has been written: "Without taking what was stated here [in the previous section], it should be understood by way of the six origins (samuṭṭhāna).

If that was written with reference to verbal action such as saying, "Dance, sing, or recite something else," then it is well-written, because there is no speech in the case of the origin consisting of wool (eḷakaloma-samuṭṭhāna).
If, however, it was written with reference to bodily action such as "dancing oneself," etc., [then it is not].
"Written" means poorly written. For that which originates from sheep's wool is exclusively bodily action;

therefore, without taking up what was extracted [in the previous context], it should be understood here as being included by the word "etc. (ādi). Regarding the phrase "because this originates from sheep's wool," the term used here expresses a reason;
however, in the phrase "the Great Authorities in accordance with the Sutta," what was extracted [from the previous context] should be taken. Thus...
It should be understood that this was written according to what was available. The Elder Upatissa stated:
"This is said to have its origin in wool (*eḷakaloma*) by way of a training rule (*sikkhāpada*) spoken extemporaneously. It was further stated:

"If this training rule had its origin in wool, the one who gave the order would be released, yet he is not released. When asked "Why?", the commentator (*aṭṭhakathācariya*) replied: "Because it is so stated in all the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*)."
The Elder Dhammasiri says:
"Standing in the monastery" means not only while standing there, but one also gains [the benefit] by going from there [to another place], even through all postures (*iriyāpatha*).
It has been written: "But 'standing in the monastery' means being included within the monastery; otherwise, even if sitting, one would not gain [the benefit]. That is indeed well-written.
The commentary on the tenth training rule is finished.
The commentary on the Garlic Chapter is finished.
2. Commentary on the Darkness Chapter.
1. Commentary on the First Training Rule (Sikkhāpada).
839. The Ancients say: "Even during the day there is darkness; for the purpose of excluding that [daytime], the phrase 'in the darkness of night' is stated.
Regarding the term *santiṭṭheyya* (should stand): by this reference to standing, all four modes of deportment (*iriyāpatha*) are included. Therefore...
If she performs walking meditation or other activities together with a man while within his reach of hand, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for her.

As for the phrase “or converses,” this was stated merely by way of the introductory context (*nidāna*), because there is no distinction [in the offense]. For it has been said: “‘Or converses’: standing within a man’s reach of hand, she converses; there is an offense of expiation. However, some say that this is not correct. Why? Because...
For that man, while standing within arm’s reach, one *pācittiya* offense is incurred;
and by conversing with him, another is incurred—thus it is not the case that no offense is committed. How is this known? By way of the constituent factors (*aṅga*).
For these four factors apply here: the darkness of night, standing within arm’s reach of the man, the absence of a companion, and the expectation of privacy.
The factors have been stated. In that regard, if there were a single offense based on the condition of standing, it would have four factors;
if there were a single offense based on the condition of conversing, it would likewise have five factors.
Therefore, in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*, it ought to have said "four or five factors," yet it was not so stated; thus, [the offense] is not [based] on the condition of conversing.
"There is no separate [offense]" means that it certainly exists; some say that the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā* statement also has that same meaning.

How so? Because of the simultaneous arising of two offenses. What is meant? When there is conversation, two *pācittiya* offenses arise together at once: one four-factored offense to be incurred by reason of the place, and one four-factored offense to be incurred by reason of the conversation.

This is improper because it contradicts the Canon (Pāḷi). For in the Canon it is said: "‘Or she converses’ means: if she converses while standing within arm’s reach of a man, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for her.
If there were two [women], it would not be possible to say, "there is an offense of two expiations.
This same principle should be understood as applicable, as appropriate, to the second woman and those following her as well. Here, by the second [woman] also...
If there is a secluded intention with a nun, and that man is alone (without a second), then according to the count of men, there are offenses.

If, however, there is a second nun, and she also has a secluded intention with that man, yet that second nun does not constitute a sufficient companion, then some say that both incur the offense; but having investigated further—

It should be accepted. However, in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*, it is stated: “If she stands within arm’s reach, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); this contradicts the Canon (*pāḷi*). For the Canon says:
“If he stands within arm’s reach of a man, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*); for what more need be said?

This is because in the commentary on the summary of the fourth training rule (*mātikāṭṭhakathā*), it is stated: “In the cases of standing together and so forth, there are three offenses of expiation,” and so on.
The offense is to be understood by counting the bases (*vatthu*). As for the statement, "In this case, there are four or five factors," this is the definitive conclusion (*sanniṭṭhāna*).
The commentary on the first training rule is finished.
2–3–4. Commentary on the second, third, and fourth training rules.

The second, third, and fourth [rules] are clear. In all instances, it is stated in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada* (Ancient Commentary on Knots): “‘Converses’ means he speaks any kind of frivolous talk (*tiracchānakathā*).

Regarding the fourth [rule], however, this is the distinction: since it was stated first as “one with one,” if one were to think that a *pācittiya* offense does not arise when one sends away a second nun, is that so?
It does arise. Why? Because it depends merely upon the three factors of standing together and so forth.
This has been established because, even if that specific speech or other private deliberation is impossible, the two [terms] can still have a single meaning;
for it is stated only thus: "He stands or converses having left the reach of the hand.
Why is it not stated: "Or he whispers into the ear"? Because such whispering is impossible once the reach of the hand has been exceeded.
Because the third phrase has been excluded, even though it is possible, the expression “or sends away a companion” was not stated;
therefore, the meaning is that if one stands apart or converses after having left the reach of hand-contact, or if one sends away a companion, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
This same method applies to the cases beginning with “by a *yakkha*,” and so forth. In that regard:

If it is argued that "within arm's reach" (*hatthapāse*) or "having left arm's reach" (*hatthapāsaṃ vijahitvā*) was not stated because there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in both cases, and that in the section on non-offenses (*anāpattivāra*) "whispers into the ear" (*nikaṇṇikaṃ vā jappeti*) was also not stated because it is impossible—[we reply:
It is possible; for when there is a task to be done, one may whisper into the ear, and thus it is possible.
If it is asked why it was not stated in this way, [the answer is: because in a discourse concerning what is blameless (*anavajjakathā*), whispering into the ear...
Because there is no purpose [in doing so], and because even a discourse on the Dhamma concerning Udāyin has been prohibited.
The commentary on the second, third, and fourth training rules is finished.
5. Commentary on the Fifth Training Rule.

856. Regarding the statement, “A ‘family’ (kula) consists of four types of families”: some say that it is permissible [to eat] in a monastery of non-Buddhist sects because the designation of a “family” does not apply there;
others say it is not permissible because non-Buddhists are included among the [four classes of] kṣatriyas and so forth.

If it is argued that this is improper because such a place is a “permissible ground” (kappiya-bhūmi), we say no, for the aforementioned kṣatriyas and so forth can indeed exist there. Nevertheless, what is intended here is the “family as alms-resort” (gocara-kula).
“The precinct extends twelve cubits”—thus it is written.
The commentary on the fifth training rule is finished.
6. Commentary on the sixth training rule.
860. It should not be said, "One for one who is sitting, one for one who is lying down," instead of saying "one for one who goes after having sat down," and so forth. [Objection:
Is it not the case that this offense does not arise on account of going? [Reply: No, because it is stated with the intention of referring to the final act.
By the statement, "two for one who lies down after having sat down," it is shown that going is not intended here.
Likewise, it should also be stated: "For one who lies down after having sat, there are two.
If this is so, why is it not stated that "when he lies down upon it, there is an offense of two pācittiyas"?

Because lying down is possible even without having first sat down. Some say that for one who sits down for the purpose of lying down and then lies down, there is only one offense because it constitutes a single act of lying down.
The commentary on the sixth training rule is finished.
7. Commentary on the seventh training rule: 867.
In the section on non-offenses, it is not stated as "in a place permanently assigned," but rather as "having spread it out oneself, or having had it spread out."
Because it has been so stated. Here, in the sixth [case], according to the method stated, if one sits down or lies down on what is naturally prepared, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) alone.

Elsewhere, it is permanently prepared. Here, according to the method stated, if one sits down or lies down after having had it spread out or having caused it to be spread out, it is an offense of expiation alone. In both cases, according to the method stated in the fifth [case]—

If one departs without having asked for permission, it is indeed a *pācittiya*. The Master [Buddhaghosa] maintains that this is not a matter for mere conjecture, because the time other than that specified in the *mātikā* under the section on non-offenses (*anāpattivāra*) has not been touched upon here.

Furthermore, according to the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) regarding the fifth, sixth, and seventh training rules (*sikkhāpada*) in this context—namely, "one incurs an offense at the time of the purpose (*atthāpatti*), not at another time," and "one incurs an offense by night, not by day"—[the same principle applies].
Because the offenses included herein have not been transgressed, it is indeed appropriate— following the method of the Great Authorities (Mahāpadesa)—
to demonstrate these three types [of offenses] by applying them according to their possibility across the three times.
The commentary on the seventh training rule is concluded.
8. Commentary on the Eighth Training Rule. 869.
In the eighth [rule], an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) may occur for a bhikkhu.
The commentary on the eighth training rule is finished.
9. Commentary on the Ninth Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 875–7.
It should be understood that an offense occurs when one makes an oath in the manner already described, whether by way of a false grasp or a correct grasp.
Since it is stated in the Mātikā, "oneself or another," therefore [the offense applies] regarding oneself alone.
She might make an oath; for that, there is one [offense]. Taking it as the ultimate [goal], for that there is one. Taking both as the goal, two offenses are possible for her.
However, the "cutting of the triad" here occurs with reference to making an oath taking it as the ultimate [goal].
The commentary on the ninth training rule is concluded.
10. Commentary on the Tenth Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 882.

Regarding the tenth [rule], the section on non-offenses concerns crying alone, not killing. Therefore, even one who is afflicted by the loss of relatives and so forth might kill themselves rather than cry; in such a case, there is still an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
The commentary on the tenth training rule is finished.
The commentary on the Andhakāravagga is finished.
3. Commentary on the Naggavagga: 1–2.
Commentary on the First and Second Training Rules.
883. The first and second [rules] of the *Naggavagga* (Chapter on Nakedness) are clear. In the first, this is the distinction:
for a bhikkhu bathing in such a manner, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*), except in a sauna or when using a water-covering [garment].

The Ancients say: "The Blessed One did not rebuke [the bhikkhus] there because he himself had not yet authorized the *udakasāṭika* (bathing robe). [The rule states: "Having dressed in only one [robe], and having put it on, one should bathe."
"It is not allowable," so it is stated in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*.
The commentary on the first and second training rules is finished.
3. Commentary on the Third Training Rule.
894. In the third [offense], even for one who lays down the burden after four or five days have passed, there is indeed an offense.
For one who lays down the burden when there has been a change of gender, it is a dukkaṭa because of the threefold dukkaṭa.
Regarding the phrase "together with several bhikkhunīs," it is stated in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada* that "even four are 'several'."
The commentary on the third training rule is finished.
4. Commentary on the fourth training rule: 898.

Regarding the phrase "going with the outer robe" (*saṅghāṭicāra*) in the fourth [rule], this procedure applies specifically to those [robes] that have been formally determined (*adhiṭṭhita*) as the outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) and so forth.
It is said that it does not apply to other [robes]. In this regard, there is an offense of expiation (nissaggiya) due to being separated from the three robes themselves.

Even during the period for making robes, there is indeed an offense for one who exceeds the five-day limit for the distribution of the outer robe (saṅghāṭi). It is stated in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*: "It is not permissible to confer full ordination (upasampadā) without these robes."
The commentary on the fourth training rule is finished.
5. Commentary on the fifth training rule: 906.
Regarding the fifth section on non-offenses, the phrase "or by not being separated from her" is obtained according to the sense.
The commentary on the fifth training rule is finished.
907–911. The sixth and seventh [rules] are self-evident. 8.
Commentary on the eighth training rule.
916. It is said that *sokajjhāyikā* refers to illusionists (*māyākārā*). The ancient teachers also called them *vilumpakā* (plunderers) and *bhaṇḍakā* (tricksters).
The commentary on the eighth training rule is finished.
9. Commentary on the Ninth Training Rule.
920. Because it was said, "How indeed could she let [the time] pass?", it is established that Thullanandā caused [the robe season] to be exceeded by waiting for the time when robes are due.
The commentary on the ninth training rule is finished.
10. Commentary on the tenth training rule.
927. Regarding the phrase "In the tenth, they said this to the family": here, "family" (*kula*) refers to the people therein; therefore, the plural form is used.
The commentary on the tenth training rule is finished.
The commentary on the section on nakedness is finished.
4. Commentary on the Tuvatta-vagga 1.
Commentary on the First Training Rule 934–5.
"If another lies down while one is already lying down, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for both"—this refers to the one who lay down first.
Having said, "non-causing-to-stand-up," some say that this is both an action and a non-action; however, that contradicts the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
For it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that it is "action. Now, for whom is there an offense? It is for both, depending on the act of lying down.
In this section on non-offenses, there is no mention of "having shown the delimitation"; therefore, one may lie down after having established the delimitation.
Some say it is not allowable; others say it is allowable if it is more spacious. "It is allowable to lie down after placing a barrier between" is written in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*.
The commentary on the first training rule is finished.
2. Commentary on the Second Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 940.
Regarding the phrase "having shown the demarcation": here, some say that it is permissible to let the upper robe fall between the two [shoulders] after making a fold in the middle;
however, the demarcation must be such that it does not remain fixed in place, but rather passes beyond it.
“For one who twists [the hair], it is indeed an offense. And in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*, it is stated as “action-and-non-action.
The commentary on the second training rule is finished.
3. Commentary on the third training rule.
941. If a senior nun arrives at one’s own place of recitation, or at the time of paying respects, there is no requirement to seek permission.

One should seek permission in a single room. Regarding this, it is stated in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*: “If a senior elder nun resides in that room while the other is present face-to-face, permission must be sought from her, because she is in the vicinity.”

956. It should be understood that the term "householder" (gahapati) refers to anyone other than those who share the same Dhamma; therefore, it is indeed possible that even one who is associated with improper association by a bhikkhu or a sāmaṇera need not be formally admonished.

9. Commentary on the Ninth Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 969.
"Single-facultied" (*ekindriya*) means single-facultied by way of the body-faculty (*kāyindriya*) alone; this is the opinion of the Nigaṇṭhas, the naked ascetics.
However, the followers of Kapila (*Kāpila*), thinking there are "five faculties," speak thus: "Because they possess the eye-faculty, gourds, creepers, and so forth [are sentient]... where...
They go toward their respective objects. Because they possess ears, plantains conceive fruit upon hearing the thundering of clouds.
Because they possess noses, jackfruit trees and others bear fruit through the scent of a corpse. Because they possess tongues, they drink water;
for these reasons, all are called "foot-stalks" (trees). Because they possess the sensitivity of their own bodies, Aśoka trees blossom through contact with women.
"Saṅghāta" means destruction. 970.

Here, by interrupting the rains residence, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). It should be understood that having first resided [in the rains retreat] and subsequently setting out on a journey, one incurs an offense of expiation (pācittiya) on account of wandering. Alternatively, if one wanders without having completed the rains residence, it is on account of departing before the [proper] time.
One incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense. However, in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*, it is stated: "For one who goes on a journey within seven days or within the rainy season, there is a *pācittiya* offense.
But it is permissible [to go] for a purpose lasting seven days; for a monk, however, there is a *dukkaṭa* offense. 972.
Regarding the phrase "oppressed by someone," the Teacher says: "The reason for breaking the rains-retreat is not mere conjecture. To what extent does this constitute a "journey"?

Does it happen? This has not been examined in every respect. Since it was stated in the immediately preceding training rule, “even as far as five or six yojanas,” that [distance] is likely the lower limit.
The commentary on the ninth training rule is finished.
