978. That which is called the "pleasure grove" (*kīḷanaupavana*) should be regarded as being like a city park belonging to a certain city.
That which is called the "garden" (*uyyāna*) should be regarded as being like the Nandana garden located right there. Regarding the reading:

"But for her who, standing right there, looks toward various directions and sees [them], there are separate offenses," when this has been said, the phrase previously mentioned—"not lifting up"—[is to be understood].
Some maintain that this [distance] is established as being in one and the same direction; furthermore, there is the "approach" (upacāra) and the "two throws of a clod" (dve leḍḍupātā).

984. Regarding the phrase “by means of immovable wild beasts” (*asaṃhārimena vāḷehi*) and “by means of movable wild beasts” (*saṃhārimena vāḷehi*), there are two readings.

It has been written [in some versions] as: “having made it separately, and afterwards together with those wild beasts. In any case, a seat constructed by having wild-beast forms raised up is called a “couch” (*pallaṅka*);
for in the section concerning non-offenses, there is no statement such as “he uses what is made by immovable wild beasts,” which would otherwise imply an offense.

1001. In the sixth *Bhikkhu-vibhaṅga*, there is a single common exclusion with the training rule concerning naked ascetics (*acelaka*). Here, however, there is the distinction of the householder; therefore, they say it is "not shared.

Commentary on the second training rule.

1030. If a bhikkhunī reviles a bhikkhu, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) by this training rule. If she reviles a bhikkhunī, she incurs an offense under the rule concerning abusive speech (omasavāda). In the case of abusive speech, [the offense] takes effect only when face-to-face;

here, however, it applies even when out of sight. Regarding this, the analysis is as follows: since in the bhikkhu-vibhaṅga, under the training rule on abusive speech, the bhikkhunī stands in the place of one who is not fully ordained (anupasampanna), so too in the bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga, under the training rule on abusive speech, the bhikkhu stands in the place of one who is not fully ordained for the bhikkhunī.

"It remains" is established. In this context, an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is stated for reviling one who is not fully ordained, whereas an offense entailing confession (pācittiya) is stated for reviling a fully ordained monk.
Therefore, these two training rules, when compared with respect to a monk, do not harmonize with one another.
It must be understood how they do harmonize. Regarding this, in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*:
According to the method already stated, in the training rule regarding abusive speech (*omasavāda*) for bhikkhunīs, the term "one who is not fully ordained" (*anupasampanna*) should not be included;
this is what is appropriate here. Regarding the phrase "should revile": this refers to cases other than the grounds for verbal abuse (*akkosa-vatthu*).

For some say that if any one of those grounds exists, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for abusive speech; however, that is not correct. Since there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in a verbal abuse outside the canonical grounds for abuse, this [rule] applies to such cases of wrong-doing.

A pācittiya offense has been specified by them; therefore, the censure here should be understood as being based solely on the words that have come down in the Pāḷi text, namely, “These women are fools.
The commentary on the second training rule is finished.
1033. The third training rule is of plain meaning. 4. Commentary on the Fourth Training Rule: 1038.
Regarding the phrase "whether invited or having been offered food," it is stated thus in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*: "Even one who has been offered food..."
She receives rice-gruel to drink, but she does not receive solid food. In this context, however, the gruel does not fall under the category of "hard food" (*khādanīya*) or "soft food" (*bhojanīya*).
A nun who has been invited to a meal may, after wandering for alms, eat as she wishes once she has informed her host.
For nuns, there is no offense regarding eating in succession. [The nun] who was invited [should eat] that meal...
"Whether one has already eaten or not, once one has been invited to stop eating (*pavāritā*), one is not permitted to eat after having [the food] made allowable (*kappiyaṃ kārāpetvā*);
and when being invited by an invitation that is not allowable (*akappiya-nimantana*), one is not permitted to accept two invitations.

In this regard, it is stated in the *Pāḷi* that "even one who has been invited to stop eating is permitted to drink rice-gruel," because this is authorized both in the *Pāḷi* and in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. "One who is invited but not yet invited to stop eating..."
"For she drinks gruel"—thus it is stated in the Pāḷi. Herein, this is the conclusion preceded by the commentary on the training rule:

"Whether invited or having been dismissed"—here, by the word "or," if one who has been invited with an improper invitation and has not been dismissed should eat or consume any other kind of solid or soft food, excluding gruel, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Except for seeking permission from the owners. What benefit has arisen for the bhikkhunīs by the absence of eating in succession?
There is no attainment of a specific merit for them; it has merely become more evident. Even the bhikkhus are permitted to eat only after having assigned portions and mixed them together.
They obtain [food] at the proper time as they please. What is the purpose of this seeking of permission? Whether they have been invited or not invited...
Or, having had nothing allowable prepared, they do not even receive what is left over from the sick;
and when invited and then dismissed [from the meal], they do not receive even rice-gruel; nor do they receive it even after seeking permission.
The commentary on the fourth training rule is finished.
The commentary on the Ārāmavagga is finished.
7. Commentary on the Gabbhinivagga: 1.
Commentary on the First and Subsequent Training Rules.

1067. “A pregnant woman” (*gabbhinī*) is stated because of the presence of a fetus even through [acts such as] seeing and so forth. Furthermore, the state of having been invited (*pavārita*) is not seen in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*).
1074. Regarding the phrase “or a nurse” (*dhāti vā*): some say that one who has been brought there after the child was given to her masters rears him; likewise for a mother. 1080.

It is said that the inhabitants of Dīpa prefer the reading “a trainee nun” (*sikkhamānā*), because of its being both an action and a non-action (*kiriyākiriyattā*), whereas the inhabitants of Jambudīpa [prefer another].

“Sikkhamānā”: its meaning is “one training” because she measures herself by the rules of training (*sikkhādhamma*). Here, it is not the actual action that is intended, but rather the designation (*saññā*).
One who has not trained in these [rules] must not be ordained, because it would constitute an offense for the preceptor (*upajjhāyinī*) and others.
They say, “Her ordination indeed takes place.”
1082. *Dhammakamma* refers here to the formal act of full ordination (*upasampadākamma*). 1112. *Vuṭṭhāpitā*:

that elder nun by whom a candidate for full ordination was raised from the stage of a female novice is called "the one who has raised her" (*vuṭṭhāpitā*); for the sake of further specification, she is therefore called "the presiding nun" (*pavattinī*).
The commentary on the first and subsequent training rules is concluded.
The commentary on the Chapter on Pregnant Women is finished.
8. Commentary on the Chapter on Maidens: 2.
Commentary on the Second and Subsequent Training Rules.
1124. Although it is stated here, as in the passage: “I allow, monks, for a maiden of eighteen years...
to grant the formal authorization for training,” it is not stated: “I allow, monks, for a married woman of ten years... to grant the formal authorization for training.
Therefore, the formal authorization for training must be granted only to a married woman who has reached the full twelve years [of marriage].
It has been stated: "Some say that permission for training (*sikkhā-sammuti*) should be granted to one who has gone forth as a householder;

thus, it is permissible even for one who is ten years old. Why? Because it is stated in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*: "There is no offense if she ordains one who is full twelve years [of age] while perceiving her as such;
and there is no offense if she ordains a householder... [etc. ...who has completed her training, perceiving her as such."
What is the point of this objection? For it has been stated: “The formal authorization for training (sikkhā-sammuti) should be granted to one who has gone to live as a householder for ten years.
And it is written: “If they say, ‘It is not even permissible to call her one who has gone to live as a householder,’ then the legal act (kamma) is invalid.

1146. “Surely I alone am foolish... [etc. ... I am shameless, she who is the Saṅgha. Here, the meaning is: “She who is I alone am indeed foolish. There is also the reading “yaṃ saṅgho”; in that case, the meaning is: “Since the Saṅgha grants it, therefore I alone am indeed foolish.”
1159. One who associates with men, associates with boys, is fierce, and dwells in grief is called a *sikkhamānā*.
Why, then, is it said in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) that this *sikkhamānā* is "one who has trained in the six rules"?
It should be understood that she is so called because she previously took up the training and because her previous training was complete.
1166–7. Regarding the phrase "having seen an abundance of solid and soft food": it is said that the relatives of a *sikkhamānā* had prepared [the meal].

Having seen this, she dismissed the elder monks. After dismissing them, she obtained their consent (*chanda*), and having previously formed a group with those who had given their consent, she made the rest give their consent as well, and then had the formal act (*kamma*) performed.
It is stated in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*. Regarding the phrase "having relinquished the consent" (*chandaṃ vissajjetvā*), it is stated in the *Anugaṇṭhipada* as follows:
"This task should not be performed today. By saying 'as you please,' it is relinquished.
Therefore, even if anyone who is talkative or foolish says 'as you please,' because [the matter] depends on the Elder, it is only when the Elder's permission is present [that the consent is valid]."
It has been relinquished; it does not exist in the absence of mindfulness. Nevertheless, they perform the formal act (*kamma*) only after taking up the consent (*chanda*) once more;
this is the application (*payoga*). However, there is no purpose in taking it up [again]. If the senior monk of the Sangha relinquishes it, it must be performed only after taking up the consent.
Regarding the phrase "having relinquished the consent and having physically withdrawn," here there is a restriction: "in such-and-such a place..."
"If they go even after leaving the reach of hand-contact [thinking], 'We will do it at the proper place,' there is no fault.

Even though there is no fault, they nevertheless go without leaving the reach of hand-contact; this is the formal application. "In the case of a *rattipārivāsiya* (a postponement for the sake of the night), only the *uposatha* and *pavāraṇā* are not permitted;
however, other business is permitted. Even the *uposatha* and *pavāraṇā* are not permitted on a day that is not an *uposatha* or *pavāraṇā* day."
It is not permitted; however, the other [type] is permitted at all times.

In the case of *parisapārivāsiya*, if one does not leave the reach of hand (*hatthapāsa*) while performing the fourfold assembly for matters requiring a quorum of four during the four movements [of walking, standing, sitting, or lying down], or if one goes separately here and there during the other five, ten, or twenty movements, it is permitted to perform the act after returning again to the place of assembly. In the case of *ajjhāsayapārivāsiya*, [one must remain within] the reach of hand...

"If they remain sitting exactly as they were sitting without having left the reach of hand (hatthapāsa), it is permissible to perform [the act] again because they have not left the reach of hand," so it is stated in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*.

According to the opinion of those ancients, it is shown that only the "transference of consent" (*chandapārivāsiya*) is not permissible; some say that here too, that [offense] is not mentioned separately because it is impossible. Regarding the giver of consent...
The Teacher says: "When [the assembly] has reached the gathering and departed, the giving of one's consent beforehand is called *chandapārivāsi* (consent left behind), not *takkā* (a formal motion).

Herein is the definitive conclusion: regarding *parisapārivāsi* (leaving the assembly behind), the Commentary states: "They rise up without having relinquished their consent, thinking 'We shall go elsewhere'...
[it is said] it is permissible to perform the formal act (*kamma*). In this context, there is the abandonment of the range of hand-contact (*hatthapāsa*).

It is not evident. However, in this context, it is stated in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada* that one must simply ensure that those who have reached the stage for the formal act (*kamma*) do not depart from the range of hand-contact (*hatthapāsa*). If it is argued: "Even though it is not evident, it is permissible because it has not been prohibited," [the answer is]:
No, because it has indeed been prohibited. How so? Regarding "consent" (*chanda*), when monks who have reached the stage for the formal act have assembled within a single boundary (*sīmā*)...

[The formal act] succeeds when [the monks] have arrived, not when they have not assembled. For here it is stated: "without relinquishing the consent" (*chanda*) and "because the consent was not relinquished";
however, it is not stated: "without relinquishing the intention" (*ajjhāsaya*) or "because the intention was not relinquished.

Therefore, it is established that the non-relinquishment of consent occurs only through not letting go of the hand's reach (*hatthapāsa*) of those who have reached the stage of performing the formal act (*kammappatta*), and not through letting go.
And there is this [verse]:
“Since the arrival of that which prevents its own absence,
Therefore, among the assembled monks, it is due to the breaking of that.”

Just as a resolution (chanda) that has lapsed overnight is permissible by way of conformity with it—whether it be a resolution for the morrow, a purity (pārisuddhi), or an invitation (pavāraṇā)—it is permissible to perform an act (kamma) by means of that.
However, the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā are not permissible on a day other than the Uposatha day; the others are permissible. [If] the fifteenth-day Uposatha is performed on the fourteenth day...

It is appropriate to perform it on the fourteenth day because that is the proper occasion (*khettatta*). Some teachers maintain that it is not appropriate to perform the fourteenth-day *uposatha* on the fifteenth day, because the fifteenth is not the proper occasion, being instead the non-*uposatha* day and the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pāṭipada*);

therefore, according to their opinion, it is not appropriate to perform the fourteenth-day *uposatha* as the third or seventh [day] on the fifteenth. However, regarding what is stated here in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "If..."
"If they have sat down thinking, 'We shall perform the Uposatha on the fourteenth day,' it is permissible for them to perform it on the fifteenth. Then, [others] avoid this by saying:

"If they have sat down on the fifteenth itself thinking, 'We shall perform the Uposatha on the fourteenth,' it is permissible for them to perform that Uposatha of their own on the following day as the 'fifteenth'";
such is their opinion when such circumstances exist.
This does not agree with the statement in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*: "It is also permissible to perform the Uposatha on another fourteenth.
For it is not stated there that "it is also permissible to perform the fourteenth-day [Uposatha] on another fifteenth.
Nevertheless, because it is included within the permitted days—namely, "once a fortnight, either on the fourteenth or the fifteenth"—[the practice is justified].
It is established that when the fourteenth-day observance day is concealed, the subsequent fifteenth day does not become the Uposatha day.
Even though this is established, it should be understood that the statement, "The resident monks [observe] the fifteenth day, while the visiting monks [observe] the fourteenth;
the residents must follow the visitors if they are equal in number or fewer," would be rendered purposeless in this case.
The commentary on the second and subsequent training rules is concluded.
The commentary on the section on unmarried girls is concluded.

11. Commentary on the Eleventh and Subsequent Training Rules 1214.
It is stated with reference to the precinct (*upacāra*): "The precinct is twelve cubits," so it is written. 1221.

Regarding the passage, "Having made space for the Sutta, he asks about the Vinaya or the Abhidhamma": here, since the three Piṭakas are mentioned by their respective names, it is thereby demonstrated that the Abhidhamma was spoken by the Buddha.

1224–5. *Thana* (breasts) and *udara* (belly) constitute *thanudara*. Regarding this, it is stated in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*: "The measurement across for the bodice (*saṃkaccikā*) is one and a half cubits.

In many manuscripts, the reading is "entering the precinct (*upacāra*) of an unenclosed village," whereas in few it is "transgressing the precinct," as found in the *Saṅghādisesa-khaṇḍa*; the latter alone [is correct].

Regarding the reading: In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, the statement—"For one who crosses over the enclosure, there is a *dukkaṭa* offense when she has crossed with one foot, and a *pācittiya* offense with the second;
the same rule applies even to the precinct"—also indicates that the reading is "for one who crosses over the precinct.

The commentary on the Chapter on Umbrellas and Footwear is finished. The commentary on the Conclusion is finished.
Because gatherings at crossroads and the like are stated to be “unconscious offenses against worldly convention” (*acittaka lokavajja*),
they are “unconscious” (*acittaka*) because one commits them through merely seeing or smearing, even without knowing it as “dancing” or “scent.
They are “offenses against worldly convention” (*lokavajja*) because they are unwholesome (*akusala*) for one who sees or smears while knowing it as “dancing” or “scent.”

Acts such as causing a thief to rise up are *sacittaka* (involving consciousness), because an offense exists only when the act is performed after having identified the object through such terms as "thief.
Since acts such as conferring full ordination (*upasampadā*) must never be done with an unwholesome mind, they are *paṇṇattivajja* (offenses by rule). It is written:

"In this context, the distinction between *sacittaka* and *acittaka* should not be understood in terms of knowing or not knowing the rule (*paṇṇatti*), but rather in terms of knowing or not knowing the object (*vatthu*)."

In the *Anugaṇṭhipada*, however, it is stated: "Since things such as mountain-top festivals (*giraggasamajja*) are said to be ‘worldly offenses without conscious intent’ (*acittaka-lokavajja*), [the offense applies] when one sees the illusions of a magician—such as his skull-bones and so forth—without recognizing them by name as ‘dancing,’ ‘a girdle (*saṅghāṇī’),’ or ‘perfume’;
or when one ties a girdle around one’s waist for the purpose of wearing a rosary and the like; or [when one smells] the scent of sweat..."
Because there is an offense for one who, with the thought "I will remove it and perform an offering to the Buddha," applies perfume and then bathes;
and because they are called "without intention" (acittaka) when, through a mind that does not recognize the object either by name or by its characteristics,
one takes a waist-band in the dark under the perception "this is a waist-band" and wears it at the waist.
Because there is an offense at the time of smearing after having perceived the scent as clay, these [actions] must be called "without intention" (*acittakāni*).
At that time there is no offense; for that very reason, even in the section on the perception of a hip-belt as not being a hip-belt, the text does not state, "there is an offense of *pācittiya*.
Just as from the statement, "he wears a waist-thread because of a field ailment," [it follows that it is without intention] even without...

It is established that it is possible to wear a girdle and so forth even without unwholesome (akusala) states; likewise, it is established that it is not possible to drink liquor even without unwholesome states when it is for the sake of curing an illness.
This is because there is no passage in the Canon stating, "There is no offense if one drinks intoxicants for the sake of curing an illness.
[Otherwise,] there would be an offense for drinking liquor at the time of swallowing liquor placed in a fist full of honey, even in the absence of unwholesome states.
And it is established that one "commits [an offense]" because it is stated: "If one drinks liquor while perceiving it as not being liquor, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

What need for further elaboration? Since they are known to be "a girdle" and "perfume" along with the perception of them as objects of sensual enjoyment, those who wear them—even in the absence of a cause for non-offense—are called "worldly offenses" (lokavajja) because they are exclusively unwholesome.
By this same method, the principle applies to the remaining cases as well.
“It should be brought [to this conclusion]. Herein, regarding the section on drinking fermented liquor, there is the statement:
‘This is the doctrine of the Elder Upatissa. And in the *Asaṃkaccika-sikkhāpada*: “The reading is ‘when they enter the vicinity of an unenclosed village’”;

and “the requesting of fine food; the training rule concerning naked ascetics (*acelaka*); engaging in walking tours when invited; concealing a grave offense; and ordaining one who is less than twenty years of age.”
“Traveling along a road in company with a woman; entering a royal palace;
entering a village at an improper time without informing a monk who is present; sitting down; and the rain-cloak—this is the reading. Thus it is said.
The commentary on the conclusion is finished.
The commentary on the Section on Pacittiya Offenses is finished.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Two Vibhaṅgas is finished.

Commentary on the Mahāvagga 1.
Commentary on the Mahākhandhaka: Commentary on the Discourse on Enlightenment (Bodhikathā)
Now is the time to explain the divisions of the *Khandhaka*, such as the "Līna-pada" and so forth.
Therefore, for the sake of easy comprehension in brief, I shall speak only on the previously unexplained meaning of the Vinaya.

In this regard, in what sense is this called the *Khandhaka*? It is because it is a collection (*samūha*) of sections (*khandha*), just like the *Vibhaṅga*. But how are they [the sections] categorized?

Because it makes manifest and illuminates the aggregates (*khandha*). Here, by "aggregates" (*khandha*), what is intended are the designations (*paññatti*) comprised of the disciplinary acts (*vinayakamma*) such as admission (*pabbajjā*) and so forth, as well as those comprised of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) regarding conduct and prohibitions.
For these things, such as admission, are called "designations" because they were designated by the Blessed One.
Furthermore, the word "aggregate" (*khandha*) is seen in the context of designations in such expressions as "a log of wood," "a mass of fire," and "a mass of water."

Just as [the term "chapter" applies], because these twenty sections beginning with the Pabbajjā-khandhaka explain and describe those aggregates (khandhas) designated as conventional designations (paññatti), they are called "Khandhakas.
The final two [sections] are so named because they resemble them; this is like the expression "time of virtue" (sīlassa vela), where it resembles time (velā).
Furthermore, the etymological analysis of "portion" (bhāga) and "heap" (rāsi) is also applicable here, since those designations consist of both portions and heaps.
And because they are divided [into sections]. But what is the reason for the sequential order of these Khandhakas?
This question is not possible, because even if they were stated otherwise, one would not exceed the sequence of their respective contexts.

Or rather, since the entry into the Dispensation is preceded by going forth and full ordination, the Mahākhandhaka, which compiles those matters, was stated first. If one asks "By whom?", it was by the Elders who compiled the Dhamma.
The Blessed One, however, spoke those [passages] here and there according to the specific circumstances as they arose, not according to this sequential order.
The Elders, for their part, having grouped together similar types of passages for various purposes, recited them in this sequential order.
The purpose for the remaining [passages] will be made clear in their respective places.

"Skilled in the aggregates" (*khandhakovidā*) means they are skilled in the meaning of the aggregates in the sense of their classification, division, and grouping; the meaning is that they have reached the perfection of the analytical knowledge of language (*nirutti-paṭisambhidā*).
This is a commentary on those words whose meanings are not [otherwise] explicit. Why, then, are they specified in this way?

Because the remaining portions are connected [to them]. Here, the inclusion of the "arising of the matrix" (*mātikā-ṭhuppatti*) should also be understood by the very inclusion of the word-commentary (*padabhājaniya*).
Regarding those meanings which have been explained in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) by means of specific words, we shall state those specific words here once again.

It was asked: "When will there be the conclusion of the commentary (*vaṇṇanā*) for each of those meanings? That [question] is appropriate to be answered by providing an exposition (*niddesa*) of them.
Furthermore, as for the text (*pāḷi*) that is already plain and clear, what need is there to provide a commentary for it? For the meanings are not obscure.

[Objection: "Is that statement not possible even through such expressions as 'by way of intention' (*adhippāya*) and 'by way of connection' (*anusandhi*)? [Reply: No; for here, by the inclusion of the term "meaning" (*attha*), specific words are already included.

For those [words] should be understood as "meaning" either in the sense of being inseparable from meaning, or in the sense of denotation, or through the metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of the term "meaning.

As for the phrase "the method of commentary" (*saṃvaṇṇanā-naya*): "commentary" (*saṃvaṇṇanā*) is called "method" (*naya*) because it demonstrates the procedure of inquiry and exclusion (*uhāpoha*) regarding what has not yet been stated.
1. *Uruvelā* is the name of a village obtained by way of the aforementioned heap of sand; therefore, this locative case is used in the sense of proximity.
To demonstrate that state [of being near], it is said, "on the bank of the river Nerañjarā," and so forth.

Otherwise, one would fall into the logical error of [the Buddha] dwelling within that very heap of sand, which would contradict such statements as, "he entered Uruvelā for alms," and "to the village of Uruvelasena," and so on.
However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, only the primary cause (*mūlakāraṇa*) is shown. Regarding that, the statement beginning with “…pe…” and ending with “…should be understood” is the concluding remark.
If one asks, “For what purpose? it is for the purpose of showing the occurrence of the aforementioned word-meanings with reference to the village.
Furthermore, the statement, “That village receives such a name by way of its precincts (*tadupacāra*),” is treated as established even without being explicitly stated.
It should be understood that this was not stated; or rather, "Uruvelā" is also the name of the village situated near the aforementioned heap of sand.

In that context, the Venerable Elder Upāli did not say "dwelling at Uruvelā" with reference to the village here, because there was no purpose for it to be his alms-resort village. For the Blessed One did not make that village his alms-resort.

It should be understood that the Master of the Commentary said this with the intention of showing that he dwelt there at that time; therefore, referring to his dwelling at the foot of the Bodhi tree near the heap of sand,
he established the determination of the second place of arising by means of three phrases, illustrating the Perfect Enlightenment in the forest further away from the Blessed One’s village.
It should be understood as "thero" (the Elder); otherwise, there would be no purpose for the expression of these three words.

In that context, it is called a "nadī" (river) because it goes while roaring (*nadantā gacchati*). Regarding the phrase "nelaṅgalāya," although one should have said "nelañjalāya," the letter *la* was changed to *ra*, thus it is stated as "nerañjarāya";
the meaning is "of the one with faultless water" (*niddosajalā*) because it is free from mud and moss, or this may simply be its name, "Nīlajalā" (Blue Water).

Regarding the phrase "at the foot of the Bodhi tree," here *bodhi* refers to full enlightenment (*abhisambodha*). In its essential meaning, this is the knowledge of the fourth path of the Blessed One, according to the statement in the *Paṭisambhidā*:

"This name is derived from liberation" (*vimokkhantika*). Although it is possible to say that the knowledge of the fourth fruit—which serves as the designation for it—is also *bodhi*, nevertheless, because it performs the function of what is to be done, it is specifically the knowledge of the fourth path.

In this context, it should be understood as "enlightenment" (*bodhi*). For that very reason, it is shown as such in the Canon with the words, "for the sake of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints through the third true knowledge.
However, in the Commentary, it is referred to as "factors of enlightenment" (*bojjhaṅga*) and "states conducive to enlightenment" (*bodhipakkhiyā dhammā*).
Therein, since the knowledge in the four paths is called "enlightenment," [the term is used] with the intention of wishing to speak of it in its general sense.
“Bodhi is called the knowledge in the four paths”—this is stated because the knowledge intended here is included within that [definition].

Alternatively, since there is no passage in the Pāḷi where the Blessed One is said to have attained the first three paths, one might raise the objection of a different school's view (*samayantara*) that only the knowledge of the fourth path arose for the Blessed One, and that he did not become a Buddha after having already attained the state of a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) and so forth. To prevent such an objection:

The phrase “in four ways” is stated because the Bodhi-tree is established as a synonym for enlightenment through its existence as the fourth decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the threefold [enlightenment].

According to the statement, “both the person and the lodging are conditions by way of the decisive support condition,” it should be understood that the “Bodhi-tree” is like a “fruit-tree”—that is, a tree which has enlightenment as its cause and which produces enlightenment—as a tree whose cause is enlightenment. Herein, since... [kevalaṃ]
"Bodhi" is also the name for a tree; therefore it is said later, "it is called 'bodhi' [because it is a tree].
However, the qualifying term [“nigrodha,” etc. is used to exclude the possibility of it being any other kind of bodhi-tree.

For the knowledge of the Path (maggañāṇa), being a root of the wholesome (kusalamūla), might otherwise receive the designation of both "bodhi" and "root. The connection is: "He sat down as one newly awakened to enlightenment (paṭhamābhisambuddho)."
By this, he shows that for eight days together with the day of his full enlightenment, he remained seated in a single cross-legged posture (*ekapallaṅka*).

Here, the word "single" (*eka*) indicates that the cross-legged posture—counted as one because it is appropriate for the application of the life of renunciation—was uninterrupted by any other posture and was unshaken. Regarding the term "the bliss of liberation" (*vimuttisukha*): here...
Nor is it possible for there to be "happiness in liberation" [in the sense of a separate state].

Because the Blessed One possesses the fifth jhāna, liberation—consisting of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti)—itself is called the "nibbāna-happiness" in the sense of being its follower; thus, it is the "happiness of liberation.

He sat experiencing and feeling that by entering into it. He sat awaiting it because he did not wish to let the time for those to be trained pass, and not out of attachment to the happiness of liberation.
"Atha kho" (then) is a pair of particles used to introduce a new section.
By this, it is shown that while experiencing the bliss of liberation, he did not attend to dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*); rather, it indicates that he emerged from that state.

Because of its profundity and because it generates a sense of satisfaction, he repeatedly attended to dependent origination—which had already been well-attended to by way of penetration (*paṭivedha*).

It is not because of the intention to see something previously unknown. Because the Blessed One has directly realized all phenomena and is free from delusion, or because he attends to what has already been penetrated, such attention produces a joy unprecedented for him, like a king reviewing a territory already conquered.
For it is said: "There is a superhuman delight for one who clearly sees the Dhamma. Regarding the night...
"During the first watch" is the accusative case used in the sense of absolute connection; by this, he shows its various alternative forms.

Although it was stated all at once that "he brought it to mind in direct and reverse order," nevertheless, the phrase "with ignorance as condition," and so forth, is used for the purpose of showing it according to this sequence.
And therein, although the intended meaning is the mere contemplation of the process of occurrence, [the specific details are provided].

How is this made known? By means of the first [forward order], whereas the attention given in reverse order is for the purpose of establishing the actual state of the conditions and the conditionally arisen phenomena in the forward order.

Since the cessation of volitional formations occurs only through the cessation of ignorance and not otherwise, it is therefore shown that ignorance is the condition for volitional formations, and volitional formations are the fruit of that [ignorance].

Likewise, the application of attention in conformity (*anuloma-manasikāra*) through the reviewing of Nibbāna is for the purpose of establishing the cessation of the fruit by means of the cessation of its causes.
And here, Nibbāna is shown by way of its efficacy; for it is not merely the cessation of ignorance and the other [defilements].
In this regard, it is established that "conformity" is not intended by the statement, "When he understood the destruction of conditions. This refers to the reviewing of the Path.
Nothing further needs to be said; for in both cases, the path is shown there by way of its function, its object, and its domain. Regarding this, it is said:
"He attended to dependent origination in reverse order"—this is not incorrect, for it is not by way of a mere formal designation in reverse order that [the path is shown].
Is it not stated that Nibbāna ought to be dependent origination? It is replied: No, because its meaning is understood differently.

For "anuloma-paṭiloma" is a neuter noun in the locative case (*bhāvanapuṃsaka*). The meaning there is that he attended to that dependent origination both in forward order (*anulomato*) and in reverse order (*paṭilomato*).
Otherwise, one would fall into the undesirable consequence of [the term] applying to cessation (*nirodha*) in reverse order.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the fixed sequence in this reverse order is established by the very fact of the fixed sequence in the forward order.
This being so, it is established that what is called the "reverse" of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) is non-dependent origination (apaṭiccasamuppāda).
Therefore, it was said in the Commentary: “‘Cessation occurs’ means non-arising occurs,” and so forth. Such being the case, there is no contradiction between what precedes and what follows.

How so? For by the phrase "dependent" (*paṭicca*), through the discernment of the conditions for the fruit and the demonstration that its emergence is contingent upon those conditions, a non-emergence is impossible;

therefore, some say that its "inverse nature" (*paṭilomatā*) should be understood through the negation of both [non-dependence and non-origination] as "not dependent origination" (*apaṭiccasamuppāda*).
That is incorrect, because its state as a direct sequence (*anuloma*) is thus determined.
Because there is no presence of any further excellence, it should be understood that non-dependent origination is its reverse.
For this very reason, the Blessed One stated in the Pāḷi the cessation of conditions and of what has arisen through conditions.

Therein, by way of the total fading away and cessation of the condition—namely, ignorance—it shows the cessation of the condition; and by way of the absence of the condition’s grasping of the fruit, [it shows the cessation of what has arisen].

It also illuminates the cessation of both conditions and the things produced by those conditions. Since there are two kinds of cessation mentioned in the Canon, and because they are identical in meaning to non-arising (*anuppāda*), it is stated in the Commentary: "Cessation occurs means non-arising occurs.
If this were so, would it not follow that Nibbāna is merely the cessation of conditions and the things produced by them? No, for the intention is to illustrate its sovereign power.
"Viditavelāyaṃ" means "at the time of mental attention"; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of [the factors] being unknown prior to that.

Regarding the phrase "jhāyanto," although the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhammā*) manifest or the phenomena of the Four Noble Truths are revealed through the contemplation of characteristics (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*), nevertheless, this is stated for the purpose of showing the distinction between the vehicles of serenity (*samatha*) and so forth during the preliminary stage.
The inclusion of "contemplation of the object" (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*) refers to the grasping of the phenomena of the Four Noble Truths.

While this might seem to contradict the section on the vision of conformity and dependent origination (*anuloma-paṭiccasamuppāda*), it should nevertheless be understood as being stated from the perspective of the attainment: "He who fully understands suffering abandons its origin.

2. The phrase "of the destruction of conditions" (*paccayakkhayassa*) is stated by way of a synonym for the function [of Nibbāna]. By this, both the Nibbāna that is the destruction of conditions and the Nibbāna that is the support for that [destruction] are indicated.
Thus, two kinds of Nibbāna are shown. Granted, it does not merely effect the destruction of conditions, but also effects the destruction of that which arises from conditions.

Since the cessation of both is thus demonstrated, nevertheless, because the cessation of the fruit follows from the cessation of the cause, it is stated as "the destruction of conditions. These are the phenomena of the kind already mentioned.
In this context, it should be understood that the inclusion of the Four Noble Truths is made by way of an inversion of the method stated in the first verse.
Regarding the phrase "the meaning consisting of origin and cessation": here, "origin" is by way of its function (*kicca*), and "cessation" is by way of its objective activity (*ārammaṇakiriyā*).
By this, two kinds of cessation are shown; the meaning is that they are presented by virtue of their respective powers. This is because the place where he sat cross-legged...
“Pallaṅka” is said; therefore, the place for attaining the fruit [of the path] is called “pallaṅka.
Commentary on the Discourse to the Cowherd (Ajapāla):
4. “He exchanged greetings”: out of a desire for their welfare, the Blessed One exchanged greetings with that brahmin. “Vedehi antaṃ” means...
In this context, "the end" refers to Nibbāna. Regarding the phrase "having reached the end of the Vedas," this refers here to Arahantship. The construction should be made as follows:

because he is a "reacher of the end of the Vedas" in the first sense, therefore he is one who has "lived the holy life"; because he is a "reacher of the end of the Vedas" in the second sense, therefore he is one who has "lived the holy life.
Although the meaning associated with the Four Noble Truths is expressed for the Brahmin, it is [also] stated in the Udāna verse.
The resolution is that it is called the "Setting in Motion of the Wheel of Dhamma" with reference to the absence of a verbal proclamation of what has been realized.
The commentary on the Discourse to the Cowherd is finished.
The commentary on the Discourse at Mucalinda begins.

5. In the account of Mucalinda, the phrase "this is the matter" is said with reference to the matter that is now to be explained. "That seclusion" refers to seclusion from the substrata of existence (*upadhiviveka*).

By the words "harmless happiness in the world," he shows the first path, because through it there is the accomplishment of abandoning ill-will (*vyāpāda*) that arises by way of the intent to kill beings. By the words "restraint toward living beings," he shows the second path.
It shows this: for a person on the path is restrained toward living beings by virtue of having abandoned the remaining instances of ill will, due to the absence of any intention to harm.
In this way, the four paths are indeed included in their proper sequence.
The commentary on the Mucalinda story is concluded.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Rājāyatana Tree: 6.
The Rājāyatana is a *pāṭali* tree. The phrase "having come from the four directions" is an ellipsis [to be supplied]. It is said that there are four demarcations of lines given upon its trunk;
out of reverence for the deity and because of seeing the Blessed One’s physical body, those merchants...

Out of faith, they took refuge. It should be understood that upon hearing the deity’s words, "The Blessed One has attained full enlightenment at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree," they knew both the existence of a community of disciples and the presence of the Dhamma he had fully awakened to.
The connection is that those who know are called "Buddhas."
The commentary on the Discourse to Rājāyatana is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on Brahmā’s Entreaty: 7.

Regarding the passage beginning “I have attained the Dhamma,” the term *dhamma* refers to the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths; because it is profound, it is difficult to see. Because it is difficult to see...
"Difficult to awaken to": it is peaceful; it is extinguished (*nibbuto*); it is sublime (*paṇīto*), meaning it is unsurpassed.

This pair is stated specifically with reference to the supramundane (*lokuttara*). "Beyond the sphere of reasoning" (*atakkāvacaro*): it cannot be fathomed by means of reasoning or formal investigation;

the meaning is that it must be traversed by wisdom alone. "To be experienced by the wise" (*paṇḍitavedanīyo*): it is to be experienced by the wise who have entered upon the right practice. "The stilling of all formations" (*sabbasaṅkhārasamatho*), and so forth.
Everything is indeed Nibbāna; for although it is one and the same, it is spoken of in various ways by way of metaphorical designation (*phalūpacāra*).
"Rāma" refers to people. "Anacchariyā" means not wonderful (*an-acchariyā*) in each and every respect.

This is said of those who have previously heard of the Blessed One’s practice during the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga-paṭipadā*), or who have previously realized the profundity of the Dhamma. Although all four paths of the Blessed One are easy to practice (*sukha-paṭipadā*),...

Nevertheless, with reference to the practice of the Bodhisattva, it was said: "With difficulty by me. Regarding the phrase "made manifest" (*pakāsitaṃ*), there are readings in both ways as "to be made manifest" (*pakāsituṃ*).
By those who are perverted, that is, by those joined with [wrong] views; "those stained by passion" (*rāgarattā*) means those stained by the passion of sensual desire and the passion of views.
Those who grasp at a self, impermanence, and so forth, will not see, they will not perceive.
8. It is said that Sahampati uttered this cry, "Alas, the world is perishing! in such a way that the Brahmās of the ten-thousandfold world-system, upon hearing it, assembled together.

Those whose nature is such that the dust of passion and so forth is slight and limited within the eye of wisdom—due to its being continuous and latent—are called "of a nature with little dust. "Assavanatā" means by reason of not hearing [the Dhamma].
"By teachers who are pure. "Open this" means reveal this. "The door to the Deathless" refers to the Noble Path or the Dhamma of the Four Truths;

it has been repeatedly awakened to and penetrated by means of the threefold clear knowledge (*vijjā*) and the fourfold path-knowledge. "On the rock" means on one made of stone. Because it is free from dust, it is suitable for easy viewing;
thus, a man with sight, having come here and there, remains as he is, [beholding] the people all around.
May you pass [through]. You too, O Sumedha of beautiful wisdom, O All-Seeing One, for the sake of attaining the knowledge of omniscience;

a conqueror of battle because of having conquered all battles against the defilements; a caravan leader because of your capacity to lead the people to be trained across the wilderness of birth and so forth;
debtless because of the absence of the deer-like craving for sensual pleasures.

9. By means of the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakkhu*), which consists of the knowledge of the degrees of the faculties of others (*indriyaparopariyattañāṇa*) and the knowledge of underlying tendencies and dispositions (*āsayānusayañāṇa*).
For these two types of knowledge are given the name "Buddha-eye. "In a place of blue lotuses" means in a grove of blue lotuses. The same applies to the remaining cases.

"Those that grow submerged within" refers to those that are nourished while remaining submerged; among them, those that rise above the water and remain there come into contact with the rays of the sun.
Those that are standing waiting to bloom today will flower today. Those that stand level with the water will flower tomorrow.
Those that have risen above the water will flower on the third day. Furthermore, there are others, such as the *saroga* lotus and so forth, which do not rise above the water;
these will not flower at all, but will instead become food for fish and turtles.

These [passages] have been included in the Canon (Pāḷi), but they should be cited and explained. By means of these, the four types of persons—the one who gains knowledge through a condensed statement (ugghaṭitaññū), the one who gains knowledge through detailed exposition (vipañcitaññū), the one who is led to understanding (neyya), and the one for whom the words are the limit (padaparama)—should be correlated. "He replied" (paccabhāsi) means he spoke back.

"Opened up" (apārutā) means disclosed. This is the meaning of the final two phrases: "Indeed, although this sublime and supreme Dhamma was familiar to me and flowed smoothly, I did not speak it because I perceived weariness of body and speech."
The commentary on the Discourse on the Request by Brahmā is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the Discourse to the Group of Five.
10. Furthermore, [the Buddha thought]: "Now I shall cause all people to bring forth the vessel of faith; I will fulfill their aspirations. Thus he said, "of a nature with little dust in one's eyes."

Because his defilements have been suppressed by meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), he is one whose nature is free from defilement (*nikkilesajātiko*). If it is argued that "he will understand," the compilers of the Dhamma did not establish this as a definitive conclusion;

they were conversant with the procedures of the Vinaya. The intention was, "I shall teach so that he might penetrate [the truth]," and this is likely a hypothetical assumption (*abhūtaparikappa*), similar to the expression, "his head would even split apart. For it is for the purpose of illustrating his state of resolute conviction (*adhimuttabhāva*) in the world that...
This statement is for the purpose of showing that [the Blessed One] was unaware of his [Sāriputta’s] passing away through his own instruction.
Furthermore, the purposes here include showing that he had no disciples remaining, and so forth. "The knowledge of the Blessed One, too" refers to the knowledge of omniscience;
it arose with his death as its object. Because of that, prior to that [death], when there was the teaching of the Dhamma, it had as its object the state of knowing quickly.
He illuminates [this]. He also demonstrates the direct realization of death through personal experience, rather than through the instruction of others.

This is well said, for even among Buddhas there is no simultaneous convergence of multiple knowledges. For the occurrence of consciousness is preceded by consciousness; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the simultaneous manifestation of nine beings.
Furthermore, if all phenomena were grasped at once, there would be the undesirable consequence of knowing contradictory times simultaneously. Therefore, regarding a single knowledge...

There is the fault of falling into a state of falsity; therefore, the Blessed One should be understood as "Omniscient" (*sabbaññū*) because his knowledge is unimpeded regarding all things that can be known, and not because he knows everything simultaneously at all times.

If it is argued [that he is not omniscient] because he did not know the deaths of Āḷāra and others, we say no, for by knowing those things, even an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) would fall into the undesirable consequence of being omniscient. For when there is the absence of one thing, there is the absence of another.

If it is argued: "The consequence that his [the Buddha’s] non-existence follows from their [the disciples'] non-existence is established in the world. Since it is stated, 'Knowledge arose even for the Blessed One,' his knowing of their death is established;
thus, by the very fact that he knew they were dead, it is established that the Blessed One is omniscient, and not because he was previously unaware until he informed the deities?
[Response: No, because he understood them in between after having discerned the specific distinction.
And because of the fault that [the Buddha] would have attained omniscience through a deity. For he did not know by means of anyone else’s word.
Furthermore, if it is asked: "What is this so-called 'knowing' in that context? Is it the arising of knowledge having that as its object?

No, for that would entail the absolute non-existence of an omniscient one in the world. For it is said: "Indeed, by me alone, in a single moment of knowledge, all knowledge [is known], and likewise for others..."

Then there would be no arising of knowledge regarding that [object]. Furthermore, if it is argued that the establishment of the manifestation of knowledge regarding the domain of all phenomena for the Omniscient One means that this knowledge itself is not its own object, we say no;

because there would be no demonstration of the cause. Moreover, in the passage, "Knowledge arose even for the Blessed One," there is a specific statement by which, immediately after the time of announcing [the matter] to the deities, [it refers to] the Blessed One’s...
“Knowledge arose” means it is made known. For the sequence of meaning does not depend merely on the sequence of the words;

therefore, this [interpretation] is incorrect. “He died within the night” means he died during the first watch. Some also say “during the middle watch. In both cases, he was one who had lost great wealth.
[This refers to] that which is to be attained in the form of the paths and fruits within seven days, or within a single day.
Because they had fallen away [from their respective attainments], there was great loss; thus they were "great losers" (*mahājāni*).
Among those two, Āḷāra was reborn in the existence of the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana-bhava*), and Udaka in the peak of existence (*bhavagga*);

therefore, it should be understood that the Blessed One thought thus with reference to their being reborn at an inopportune time for the teaching of the Dhamma, and not with reference to their having passed away from this human world. And [he considered] their state of being unredeemable by one who is not a Buddha.
"The Master [Buddhaghosa] says: 'Our reasoning is based on an underlying intention (*sandhāya*); otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence [of contradiction].
At the time of the Bodhisatta’s birth, there were eight brahmins who received his dreams and examined his physical marks (*lakkhaṇa*).
Among them, three made two-fold predictions: 'Endowed with these marks, if he dwells at home, he will be a king...'"
“He becomes a wheel-turning monarch, or, going forth, he becomes a Buddha. Thus, the five brahmins gave categorical answers, saying, “He does not remain in the household;
he will surely become a Buddha. Of them, the first three reached the further shore of the mantras as they had been taught.
But these [last two], while crossing to the further shore of the mantras, renounced the great mass of merit they had acquired for the sake of the Bodhisatta.
They went forth even earlier. It is with reference to them that it was said, "the group-of-five.
Some also say, "their sons," but that is rejected in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*). Why, then, did the Blessed One think here, "They have been very helpful to me"?
Does he teach the Dhamma only to those who have been helpful, and not to others? No, he does not fail to teach it.

The method of the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary) is that it was stated merely by way of recollecting his benefactor. [It was said] for the purpose of manifesting one's own state of gratitude and thankfulness;
for the purpose of praising gratitude and so forth; for the purpose of enjoining others to the state of being grateful and so on;

and for the purpose of preventing the contingency of [others] understanding [the meaning] too quickly. 11. "Between Gayā and Bodhi" means in the middle between Gayā and Bodhi, at a distance of three *gāvutas*.
In this context: Gayā is three *gāvutas* from the Seat of Enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). The city of Bārāṇasī is eighteen *yojanas*.
However, Upaka saw the Blessed One between the Seat of Enlightenment and Gayā.
Because it is joined with the word *antara*, the accusative case has been employed. And in such instances, grammarians employ only a single form of the word *antara*.
The same should be applied to the second line as well; for if it were not applied, the accusative case would not be reached. Here, however, it is stated having indeed been applied.
"All-conqueror" (*sabbābhibhū*) means he stands having overcome all phenomena of the three planes.

"In the destruction of craving" (*taṇhakkhaye*) means in Nibbāna. "Liberated" (*vimutto*) means liberated from the object. "There is no rival for me" (*natthi me paṭipuggalo*) means there is no one who is my equal.
The meaning is "without equal"; the sense is that there is no person who can be my adversary, because none is capable of remaining in the world after exposing faults in my omniscience.
"And I shall beat the drum of the Deathless" means: "I go forth with the intention of striking the drum of the Deathless for the sake of attaining the eye of Dhamma."
"You ought to become an infinite Conqueror (Anantajina); you are worthy"—this is the meaning. This too is the name of his own Teacher.
"Hupeyyāsī" means, "Friend, may it indeed be so. "Pakkāmī" means he went to the country named Vaṅkahāra.
The Blessed One, having become weary of Cāpā, the daughter of that deer-hunter there, returned once more; this one is a Non-returner (Anāgāmī).
Seeing that he possessed the necessary supporting conditions (*upanissaya-sampatti*), [the Elder] spoke with him.
He likewise came, went forth, and becoming a non-returner (*anāgāmī*), eventually passed away; having been reborn in the Aviha heaven, he attained *arahantship*.
12. "They settled" means they made an agreement. "Fallen from exertion" means fallen away from or deprived of his striving.
The intention is that he did not make any such distinction in speech as, "Do you recognize this that was spoken? or, "It is indeed speech that was spoken.
"They desired to hear the Blessed One" means they became desirous of hearing the Blessed One's words.
"Aññā" means having known; the sense is "to know."

13. Now, for what purpose did he address them? It was for the sake of making an even more thorough admission [of the truth], for the purpose of illustrating the weightiness and rarity of the Dhamma, and for the purpose of preventing any confusion regarding the words.

In this context, "these two" is a term for the two extremes, because other factors are also included within them. Furthermore, according to the method of connection: craving and ignorance are the two defilements that constitute the head of the process of saṃsāra. And these...
Because they are the opposites of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), they are called "extremes.

Among them, the fool who, by way of craving, devotes himself to the pursuit of sensual pleasure abandons serenity; likewise, one who, by way of ignorance, devotes himself to the pursuit of self-mortification abandons insight.
Thus it is said: "It is not possible to attain the Deathless without abandoning both these two extremes."
Moreover, this is a demonstration of the abandoning of dullness and agitation.

For one who is dull has abandoned the exertion of energy and indulges in sensual pleasure, while the other, with over-exerted energy, indulges in self-mortification. Both of these are called "extremes" because they are opposed to the evenness of energy.
Furthermore, three modes of practice are taught in the Dispensation: the excessive, the emaciated, and the middle. Among these, the excessive...
“‘One who destroys living beings thinks: "There is no fault in sensual pleasures. Such [teachings] are the extreme. ‘One who is naked, one who lives in the open air’—such [teachings] are the austere.
‘This very Noble Eightfold Path’—such [teachings] are the middle.

Therein, devotion to the pursuit of sensual pleasure is called the extreme way of practice because it is the root of all unwholesome states. Devotion to self-mortification is called the austere way because it involves the burning of oneself.”
Both of these are called "extremes" because they are opposed to the middle way; it is with reference to these alone that [the Buddha] says, "these two.
For what purpose does the Blessed One apply this specifically to those who have gone forth, saying, "These should not be cultivated by one who has gone forth," rather than to householders?
Because those who have gone forth are intent upon that [middle way], because they are capable of easily avoiding [the extremes], and because [the teaching] is directed primarily toward them.
And those who have gone forth are emphasized here, not householders. If this is so, for what purpose does he speak of devotion to the pursuit of sensual pleasure?
Is it not the case that they have already renounced sensual pleasures by nature and have gone forth for the sake of escaping them? No;
because they rely on two extremes. For they seek purification through sensual pleasure in this world, being devoted to the pursuit of self-mortification.

It should be understood that, by the fruit of that very asceticism, they aspire to divine sensual pleasures after death and are thus devoted to an even more intense pursuit of the indulgence in sensual pleasures.
Furthermore, the meaning of "extreme" (*anta*) here should be understood in the sense of what is contemptible (*kucchita*), as in such passages as:
"Bhikkhus, this is the lowest of livelihoods, namely, living as a beggar."

Regarding the phrase "the devotion to the pleasure of sensual desires (*kāmasukhallikānuyoga*) among sensual desires": here, "sensual desires" refers to both the object-sensual-desire (*vatthukāma*) and, secondly, the defilement-sensual-desire (*kilesakāma*).

The pleasure associated with that [defilement] is what is called "sensual pleasure" (*kāmasukha*) here. By this, he illustrates that the pleasure of karmic fruition (*vipākasukha*) is blameless (*niravajja*).
"Attachment" (*allīyana*) means delighting in that [pleasure]. "Devotion" (*anuyoga*) means the aspiration for such devotion in future lives.

It is "inferior" (*hīna*) in the sense of being base, because it leads to decline in the side of the wholesome, because it is cultivated by inferior persons, and because it originates from inferior elements.
It is "village-born" (*gammo*) because it is a quality belonging to beings living in villages. It is "of the worldlings" (*pothujjaniko*) because it is common to ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*).

It is "un-noble" (*anariya*) because it is not intended for the noble ones (*ariya*), because it is opposed to the Dhamma of the noble ones, because it produces what is un-noble, and because it is itself an un-noble state.

It should be understood [as such] because it is practiced by the ignoble. It is "conducive to harm" because it brings about the fear of the saṃsāra designated as harm, and because it produces harmful results.
"Self-mortification" (attakilamatha) is simply the exhaustion of oneself. That proceeds based on specific practices such as asceticism, penance, and self-inflicted hardships preceded by wrong views;
the pursuit of that through the influence of such views is called the "pursuit of self-mortification. It consists in the distress resulting from the separation from the self and the loss of wealth.
Because it proceeds without skillful means, even when successful, it causes one to fall into the wombs of deer, goats, dogs, and pigs;
and when it ripens, it leads to hell—thus it is "conducive to harm. *Ete tu* means "but these.

By saying "by the Tathāgata," he reveals that he has come without falsehood (*avitathāgama*); by this he shows: "These were not merely thought out by me as a thinker, but rather [they were taught] by me as a Tathāgata."
"He has fully awakened by means of the knowledge of full awakening. Furthermore, with the words "the maker of vision" and so forth, he praises that very path.
By the phrase "the maker of vision," the purification of the eye of knowledge is stated, just as medicine is for a sick man.
By the phrase "the maker of knowledge," the dispelling of darkness is stated. "For the sake of peace" means for the subsiding of the fever of the defilements.
"Spoken. "For direct knowledge" refers to the penetration of the truths. "For full enlightenment" refers to the penetration of the truths.
"For Nibbāna"—this should be explained by applying it as appropriate: either to the element of Nibbāna with residue remaining or to the element of Nibbāna without residue remaining.

14. Why, then, did the Blessed One here—not as elsewhere—fail to deliver a gradual discourse (*anupubbikathā*) and instead, at the very outset, speak of the two extremes that are not to be cultivated before teaching the Middle Way?
It was for the purpose of warding off false conceits regarding a self and so forth, and for the purpose of warding off practice upon a wrong path;

having spoken of the avoidance of the two extremes, it was for the purpose of demonstrating his own state of being free from excessive indulgence (*abāhullika*) and so on, by way of illustrating his own specific attainments.
And after that, in order to apply them to that [Middle Way] by illuminating it as the Middle Practice (majjhimapaṭipadā), he taught the Right Practice (sammāpaṭipadā).
Then, desiring to teach the Dhamma of the Four Truths both briefly and in detail for the purpose of showing the objective sphere of that Noble Path—which is reckoned as the Middle Practice—he said:
"But this, monks, is suffering," and so forth. This is the meaning here.
The connection (*anusandhi*). This sequence should be understood for the purpose of clarifying the connection of the Sutta, beginning with: “‘This is the noble truth of suffering,’ monks.
It is said that after hearing the aforementioned practice, Koṇḍañña remarked: “How could there be the arising of the practice spoken of by the Blessed One?
For this practice is possible only when there is the non-arising of the defilements.”

Not otherwise. If the arising of the defilements were from greed alone, like that of hunger and thirst, then their non-arising would occur through the cultivation of its opposite, or they would arise only when one is in that same state.
Their non-arising would likewise occur through the cultivation of bodily exertion that is the opposite of that state.
Both of these have been called "extremes" by the Blessed One; therefore, how could there be right practice for this?
“...how could its arising be possible? The Blessed One said: “Because of the non-cultivation of the means. If one asks how:
“Knowledge [arises] from the root of saṃsāra, and that knowledge is abandoned through knowledge;
while life exists, that [knowledge] occurs, and that [life] depends on the means for sustaining life.”
“Therefore, for the sake of knowledge, the wise person should protect his own life,
and he should preserve the virtue that serves as the means to attain knowledge.
Just as life does not exist in this world once the body has perished,”
In the same way, for one whose virtue is broken, there is no possibility for the arising of wisdom.
Therefore, being mindful and desiring wisdom, one should protect both life and virtue;
one should neither indulge in sensual pleasures nor engage in the destruction of the body.
“Having fallen into craving for sensual pleasures— the base and the vulgar—
the deluded one, being unpurified, goes to exhaustion;
but he who enters upon the supreme middle way, [attains the goal].”
Thus he quickly attains supreme liberation.
Having heard these words of the Sugata,
that sage, having obtained wisdom born of hearing, [attains it].
Entering into knowledge born of reflection,
he cut through this question and asked:
"Having abandoned the terrible state that is the basis for penetration..."
"How indeed do you practice austerity?
Speak of that very thing, O bhikkhu, as you go your way;
thus one approaches the fading away of the truth of suffering."
"By seeing alone, there is the experience of suffering;
therein lies the condition for aversion.
Having heard the Sage’s words, Koṇḍañña—
Rising up suddenly and joyful, he said:
"O Blessed One, explain this to me:
how a bhikkhu perceives the truth of suffering."
"It should be understood that the perfection of wisdom consisting in cultivation (bhāvanāmayi-paññā) is preceded by the fulfillment of wisdom consisting in reflection (cintāmayi-paññā);

for this reason, it is said that the Blessed One spoke this Sutta. Why did the Blessed One not expand upon the teaching of the Truths to Koṇḍañña immediately after [his realization], but instead stated the sequence of his own attainment?
[It was because he thought: "I do not teach a tradition derived from another; rather, I have attained it in this very way myself."
For the purpose of seeing. Therein, by the phrase “dhammas not heard before,” he demonstrates these two points:
namely, that this Dhamma was not heard by me from Āḷāra or Uddaka, but rather knowledge arose in me regarding things never heard before;
thus he proclaims the power of the Middle Way. Furthermore, because one who has practiced in this way—even without...
"One sees the Noble Truths through the instruction of another; therefore, why do you not see them through my instruction?

(15) The five terms beginning with "the eye" (*cakkhu*) are indeed synonyms for knowledge (*ñāṇa*). For knowledge is so called because it illuminates the truths and because it knows the meaning that has become like an eye.

It is wisdom (*paññā*) because it knows by way of various modes. It is clear vision (*vijjā*) because it tears asunder the defilements and because it pierces through [them]. It is so called because it destroys the darkness that obscures the truths.
It should be understood as "light" because it reveals the ultimate destination of those [truths].

In this regard, by the first section, he shows the wisdom that establishes the truths without confusing one with another; by the second, the wisdom that delimits the manner in which they are to be practiced;
and by the third, he shows the final determination of the function of knowledge regarding the truths.
16. By the two words *yāvakīvañca*, it is simply said "as long as," just as in the passage beginning with "thus the mind and the intellect" (*iti cittamanoti*).
Unshakable liberation (*akuppā vimutti*) is so called because of its unshakeability by lust and the other defilements. An exposition (*veyyākaraṇa*) is a teaching on the Dhamma;
for it is called an "exposition" because it explains and reveals the phenomena (*dhammā*). Regarding the phrase "dustless and stainless" (*virajaṃ vītamalaṃ*), here "dustless" (*virajaṃ*)...
It is "free from stain" because it is free from the doctrine of discordant causes. It is "dustless" because of the abandonment of the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*).

It is "free from stain" because of the abandonment of the annihilationist view (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*). It is "dustless" because of the abandonment of the obsessions (*pariyuṭṭhāna*). It is "free from stain" because of the abandonment of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*).
"The eye of Dhamma" (*dhammacakkhu*) is the vision of mere phenomena (*dhammamatta*); therein there is no being (*satta*), no soul (*jīva*), no agent (*kāraka*), and no experiencer (*vedaka*).
It blows; for this very reason it was said: “Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease.
This was stated in order to show the manner in which that Dhamma-eye arises. For it arises by making cessation its object, penetrating the conditioned state precisely through its functional aspect.

17. Regarding the phrase "the Wheel of Dhamma" (*dhammacakka*), here the knowledge of teaching (*desanāñāṇa*) is intended, though the knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedhañāṇa*) is also certainly obtained.
Why did the deities raise a cry of acclaim here? Because light was gained through the dispelling of the darkness of various speculative views;
because relief was attained through the transcending of the fear of the states of woe (*apāya*); and because they were moved by joy and gladness upon seeing the celestial hosts and their mansions.
They cite such reasons as these. Some say that the manifestation of the earthquake and the great sound occurred solely by way of natural law (*dhammatā*).
Others say the earthquake was due to the deities' desire to play, the gathering of a vast assembly of gods, and the radiating of the network of light from the Blessed One’s body.

18. The meaning is: the distinction between going-forth (*pabbajjā*) and full ordination (*upasampadā*). In this context, the word *iti* indicates the conclusion of the statement regarding the cause for his attainment of full ordination through the "Come, monk" (*ehibhikkhu*) formula.
For his status as a monk ends with that [formula]. The passage beginning with "well-expounded" (*svākkhāta*) is a statement showing the purpose of the address "Come.
The syntactical connection of the words is: the Blessed One said, "Come, monk," and he also said, "The Dhamma is well-expounded; live... [etc. ...for the sake of doing [it]."
"Practice the holy life there" means: attain the remaining holy life of the three paths. For what purpose? The meaning is: for the sake of making a complete end to suffering.
Because it was accomplished by this word of the Blessed One, "Come, monk," it is called the "ordination by the 'Come, monk' formula" through a metaphorical designation of its cause.
That itself constitutes the lifelong ordination of that venerable one.

The meaning is "it has been. By this, the Commentary demonstrates two points: that there is no interruption of her full ordination (*upasampadā*) through such acts as renouncing the training, nor is there any need for another form of full ordination;

and that this applies to all eight types of full ordination—namely, those by the "Come, monk! formula, by exhortation, by acceptance of the questions and answers, and by acceptance of the *garudhammas*.
For one who has received ordination through any one of the four [methods], there is no interruption in between, nor is there any need for another ordination;

however, for the other [method], there is. But those of other schools say: "The ordination of Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas consists of what is termed 'entry into the fixed course' (niyāmokkanti), while the ordination by formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatutthakamma*) is twofold, according to whether it is to be performed by a group of ten or a group of five."
“Having broken [the obstacles], there is the tenfold full ordination. What, then, is meant here by “full ordination” (upasampadā) in terms of its meaning?

It is the internal continuity consisting of the five aggregates, which has been permeated by the volition that accepts them, and which is produced through the performance of the action attained therein—namely, the state of one beyond training (asekha). But what is meant here by “permeation” (paribhāvanā)?
It is the state of being opposed to the practice of those qualities that are contrary to it; for the sake of attaining that [state].
By virtue of that cultivation, one is in some instances said to be "endowed with" (*samannāgata*). As it is said:
"Endowed with greed, monks, one is incapable of developing the four foundations of mindfulness," and so forth. Here, those belonging to other schools say:

"There exists a phenomenon included within the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*), dissociated from consciousness, which consists of the acquisition (*patti*) of the aforementioned full admission (*upasampadā*)."
"As long as there is no interruption in the continuity of that [ordination] as it arises in successive order from before to after, for that long one is ordained;
otherwise, at the moment of the arising of another state, the consequence would follow that the one who was ordained becomes unordained.
They should be told, "Bring a sutta. If they should say, "That which belongs to those ten Asekkhas..."
“There are no such suttas as: ‘The noble acquisition and possession of phenomena by depending [on them] is abandoned,’ and so forth.
If this were the case, the fault of possessing non-existent phenomena and other beings would accrue to these [suttas].
Why? Because of the existence of such suttas. As it is said: “Monks, a wheel-turning monarch possesses seven treasures...”
“He is possessed [of them],” and so on in detail. In that context, the word “possessed” (*samannāgata*) expresses mastery (*vasibhāva*). If it is asked:

“Does he have mastery—that is, the power of free disposal—over those treasures mentioned there?”—in this case, mastery is expressed by the word “possessed,” whereas elsewhere it is understood as acquisition;
thus, it is a different state of affairs. What is the distinguishing reason here? There is none; therefore...
Full ordination (*upasampadā*) possesses the very characteristics already described. This same method should be applied to the going forth (*pabbajjā*) and other stages as well.

Although the Dhammacakkhu arose separately for each on different days—such as for the Elder Vappa on the first day of the fortnight, and so forth, up to the Elder Assaji on the fourth day—nevertheless, by virtue of the commonality of their instruction, [the account applies] to Vappa and Bhaddiya.
It should be understood that Mahānāma and Assaji are mentioned here together.
20. For what purpose does [the Buddha] illuminate the characteristic of non-self right at the beginning, saying, "Form, bhikkhus, is non-self"?
Because even during their time as worldlings (puthujjana), the other two characteristics were evident to them. For by seeing the impermanence of pleasant sensual pleasures, they...
"Agitated, they went forth"—first, the characteristic of impermanence became partially manifest to them;
and for those who had gone forth, physical suffering resulting from the pursuit of self-mortification and mental suffering, which has that [physical suffering] as its condition, also became manifest.
Therefore, setting aside both of these, he began to illuminate the characteristic of non-self alone. And while illuminating that:
In order to illustrate [the nature of the aggregates] by means of the characteristic of suffering (*dukkhalakkhaṇa*) alone, he said: "If, monks, this form were the self," and so forth.
For what purpose? Because, even more than the characteristic of impermanence (*aniccalakkhaṇa*), the characteristic of suffering is more clearly manifest to them.

Indeed, because they are devoted to the practice of self-mortification and because that is their ultimate resort, the characteristic of suffering is very well-known to them; therefore, by means of that which is so well-known, [he first explains it].
Having illustrated the characteristic of non-self, he will speak again to illustrate that very same point by means of both [the aggregates and the self]:
"What do you think, monks, is form permanent or impermanent? "Is it fitting (kallaṃ nu)" means "is it appropriate? "This is mine" is the grasping of craving (*taṇhāggāha*).

"I am this" is the grasping of conceit (*mānaggāha*). "This is my self" is the grasping of views (*diṭṭhiggāha*). And here, the grasping of craving is by way of the eight hundred modes of the movement of craving (*taṇhāvicarita*).
The grasping at conceit should be understood by way of the ninefold conceit; the grasping at views by way of the sixty-two views.
The commentary on the Discourse to the Group of Five is finished.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Going-forth begins.
25. At the time when the Blessed One, having established the group of five monks in Arhatship on the fifth day,
and having explained the Nāḷaka practice to the Elder Nāḷaka on the seventh day,
dwelt at Bārāṇasī awaiting Yaśas— knowing on the full moon of the month of Bhaddapada that his faculties had reached maturity— at that time there was one named Yaśas.
