The connection [is as follows]: it is said that from the time of his birth, the fame of that family—consisting either of its reputation or its retinue—increased preeminently; therefore, his parents gave him this name.
For what purpose did the Venerable Thera Upāli say, "He was delicate," and so forth? It was for the sake of generating an exhortation toward renunciation in people of later generations.

Thus, even for those endowed with the most excellent enjoyments, having been made to abandon those supreme enjoyments by even a slight sign of the foul (asubhanimitta), and disregarding whether it was the right or wrong time, they departed from their homes, casting aside a vast mass of wealth like a blade of grass out of delight in seclusion;
the intention [of the author] is: "For whom else would this not have happened? "Of one who was possessed" means being in a state of oneness with them.

"Of one who has approached, not secluded"—this is the meaning. "Fell asleep" means that having restrained the mind's engagement even with pleasant objects, it overcame and surpassed them, bringing the mind under its own control; this is the meaning.
"Throughout the entire night" refers to all three watches. By this, he shows the reason for the attendants' observation of his change of state. Furthermore, the word "night" here—
It should be understood that [the offense] occurs at the time of sunrise and during the watch of the night.
Here, it should be understood as occurring during the watch, as well as when one is separated from the three robes. "At the waist" means on the side of the waist.

"At the throat" means below the throat. For the meaning is: while she was sleeping with her throat placed over the *mudiṅga* drum, he saw the *mudiṅga* at her throat. "Āḷambara" refers to a small drum (*paṇava*). Of that which has openings on both sides...
"Slender and long": this is a designation for a body that is broad and level. "They prattle on":
they prattle on with incoherent chatter by way of seeing dreams and so forth. "He thought it was a cemetery": the connection is that he saw his own retinue as if it were a cemetery.
"Disadvantage": the state of being unattractive (*aśubha*). "The mind becomes established in disenchantment": [this refers to] the desire for liberation (*vimuñcitukāmatā*).
The meaning is that his mind inclines toward longing (*ukkaṇṭhā*). "He uttered an *udāna*" means he let out a joyful utterance, thinking: "From this time forth, I shall no longer be with these women.
It is said that two factors became evident to him upon seeing the negligence of his attendants:
the powerful nature of the defilements and the extreme coarseness of the aspect of the foul (*asubha*). This being so, [he spoke] regarding that which was even more coarse...
And by way of the aspect of foulness (*asubhākāra*), this entire world is oppressed and infatuated here due to the defilements (*kilesa*).
As he repeatedly saw that "alas, the defilements are more powerful," those two aspects became manifest to him;
it was because of this that he spoke thus. By the phrase "having put on golden sandals," his unrestrained and unhindered movement is indicated. For he—

Because his heart was pierced by a powerful sense of urgency, even though his attendants were awake, he went forth unrestrained, suspecting himself [of being a non-human], unable to bear their power to prevent his departure. "Non-humans" (*amanussa*) refers to deities (*devatā*).

For they are called "non-humans" because of their commonality with humans regarding qualities such as the penetration of the path to a happy rebirth and the maintenance of a physical form; for those of a different species are not so called.

Animals and the like are called "non-Brahmins" (*abrāhmaṇa*) or "outcasts" (*vasala*), but outcasts and others are called "non-Brahmins" solely on account of their commonality of birth (*jātisabhāgatā*).
Likewise, deities are called "non-humans" (*amanussa*) because of their commonality with humans in some respect;
otherwise, since they would not be humans, even animals would have to be called "non-humans."
26. Having seen the dense forest, he uttered this inspired exclamation not far from the Blessed One out of joy, thinking, "I am well-freed from the city.
"This, indeed, O Yasa," the Blessed One said, referring to Nibbāna. For that [Nibbāna] is unafflicted by the defilements such as craving and is untouched by them;
moreover, it generates satisfaction even by the mere sight of it. "I shall teach the Dhamma"—[thinking thus], while merely sitting here, [he spoke].
The intention is: "You shall realize [this]. The particle *kira* is used in the senses of incredibility, incapacity, or derision;

here it signifies incapacity. Regarding the phrase "having removed his golden sandals," this means "having descended from the golden sandals. For this nominative case ending is used in the sense of the ablative (*nissakka*).
Immediately upon his sitting down, without engaging in any other conversation of welcome—
Without taking leave of him, he delivered a gradual discourse. This was because the householder’s faculties were fully matured;
because, in order not to miss the moment of penetration, his mind was inclined toward hearing the teaching on the evil states that are unafflicted and untroubled;
and because the Blessed One saw that the householder Seṭṭhi had not yet arrived. For what purpose did the Blessed One [speak] to him whose heart was so deeply stirred?

Why did he first speak of the benefits of the means for various states of existence (bhava) for one who desires liberation? It was for the purpose of showing the disadvantage of all states of existence.
For he saw only the state of being afflicted and beset by calamities in the human world, and not so in the heavens; thus, one might at times imagine the heavenly world to be happiness.
Fearing that one might direct the mind toward Nirvana with a perception of happiness regarding those [heavens], [the Buddha spoke of the disadvantages of all existences].
Desiring to show the danger [of sensual pleasures], he began with a graduated discourse.

In this context, by speaking of giving, the benefits of giving, and the benefits of virtue, he is said to deliver a discourse on giving and virtue. By speaking of the praise of heaven, he is said to deliver a discourse on heaven.
Therein, by speaking of the impermanence, the unreliability, and the great danger of both objective sensual desires and the defilement of sensual desire, [he speaks of] sensual pleasures...
It reveals the danger (*ādīnava*), the degradation (*okāra*), and the defilement (*saṃkilesa*).

And by speaking of the benefit (*ānisaṃsa*) as being the opposite of those—due to their absence and due to its being the escape from them in the case of renunciation (*nekkhamma*)—it is said that it "reveals the benefit in renunciation.
In this context, "degradation" (*okāra*) means a state of inferiority or baseness. "Defilement" (*saṃkilesa*) means being corrupted, or the sense of affliction and torment.
The mind becomes pliant through the power of the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*), because the yoke of views and the yoke of doubt have been destroyed by the faculty of wisdom.

Through association with the faculty of mindfulness (*satindriya*), the mind becomes malleable; by warding off the entry of defilements such as cruelty and aggression, it causes the co-nascent mind to become malleable by introducing wholesome states such as mental malleability. [This pertains to] the faculty of concentration (*samādhindriya*).
By its power, the mind is free from hindrances; for that [faculty] is specifically the antidote to the hindrances.

By the power of the faculty of energy, the mind is uplifted; for that is the antidote to the state of sluggishness characterized by sloth and torpor. By the power of the faculty of faith, the mind is serene, because its characteristic is serenity.
Regarding the term "exalted" (*sāmukkaṃsikā*), the Elder Upāli [explains it] as being by way of its object.

He proclaims them. For the Truths are the objects of the teaching that points out the supreme goal. Otherwise, one would fall into the error of claiming that the "teaching of the Dhamma pointing out the supreme goal" refers to suffering and so forth;
for those [Truths] are what are demonstrated when that [teaching] is explained.
27. "In the four directions" means in the four quarters. "He performed volitional formations" means he formed them. If it is asked, "For what purpose?"—[it was] for both.

It is for the purpose of preventing obstacles to the specific attainment that ought to be reached. If he were to see his son, the son’s acquisition of the Dhamma-eye and the arising of Arahantship would not occur, nor would the merchant’s acquisition of the Dhamma-eye.
Furthermore, even one who has seen the Truth, when saying, "Give back your mother's life," what else could he not do? And Yaśas, having heard those words, although he was already an Arahant...
Having not himself rejected [the matter], what else could he rely upon while looking up to the Blessed One?
Because both had attained the pinnacle of the specific excellence to be reached, the Blessed One again quelled that [dispute].
"Previously, while still a householder" refers to the time when he was a stream-enterer; for a stream-enterer is worthy of dwelling in the midst of a household.
"One who has become a householder" means one who has not gone forth. Although he has just now gone forth, because he is incapable of dwelling in a household, he is not called a "householder";
therefore, it was said thus. The connection is with the words "by whom [it] was seen," meaning "by whom it was seen.
By the statement, "Just as previously when he was a householder," the method [of comparison] is obtained; therefore, subsequently...
The householder spoke thus with reference to the fame associated with the wearing of the white garments of a layman: "With the young man Yasa as his attendant monk.

In that context, "lead the holy life" means: first of all, lead and fulfill the holy life consisting of virtuous conduct (*ābhisamācārika-sīla*), until the complete making of an end to suffering, until the moment of the final passing-away consciousness (*cuti-citta*). This is said with reference to the holy life of outward marks (*liṅga-brahmacariya*).

The ancients say this, and it is logical. For it was with reference merely to the outward signs [of the monastic life] that the Venerable One said, "Venerable Sir, may I receive the going-forth and the full ordination.
Why did the Blessed One teach the Dhamma to Yasa’s mother and Pajāpatī even without their having first performed the meal-offering?
It was because, being overwhelmed by the arrow of grief at Yasa’s going-forth, they would not have given alms with a joyful mind.

Fearing that they might fall into dejection toward the Teacher and thus fail to attain penetration of the Path, the Blessed One first made their hearts free from the dart of sorrow, and then performed his meal duties.
Regarding the phrase "of the chief and sub-chiefs," the ancients explain it as "of those who are chiefs in successive order. "Of the chiefs and the sub-chiefs" refers to those...
"Families" refers to those families that are pre-eminent and most pre-eminent; [it means] "of those pre-eminent and most pre-eminent families. Thus it is written.
"Dhamma-Vinaya" refers to the holy life (*brahmacariya*) of the Dispensation and the Word of the Buddha (*pāvacana*); in this context, they are one in meaning.

Alternatively, it is "Dhamma-Vinaya" because it is discipline through the Dhamma, not by means of the science of punishment; or it is "discipline for the sake of the Dhamma," meaning it has a non-harming purpose, or it is [so called] because of the Dhamma.
The Vinaya is not non-Dhamma; or, the Dhamma-Vinaya is the Dhamma that is the Vinaya, not non-Dhamma;
or, it is the discipline (*vinaya*) of the teachings (*dhammānaṃ*), not of others, because they constitute the body of the Dhamma or because the Blessed One is the Lord of the Dhamma;

thus it is the discipline of that Dhamma, not that of the logicians—this is the "Dhamma-Vinaya. Alternatively, by way of grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), "Dhamma-Vinaya" is like a blue lotus: it is both the Dhamma and...

Regarding the term *vinaya*: the gender of this word is established by its designation as masculine (*pulliṅga*), even though the "Dhamma and Vinaya" (*dhammavinaya*)—like a fruit and its seed—is neuter, like the word *napuṃsaka*.
Alternatively, that which possesses the Dhamma and the Vinaya is "the Dhamma-Vinaya," just as a man might be called "one with a white cloth.
Or, the Vinaya associated with the Dhamma is "the Dhamma-Vinaya," like a horse-chariot; such applications should be understood according to these methods.
34. “Having led him to a separate boundary (khaṇḍasīma)” is stated for the purpose of announcing the shaving of the hair and warding off [objections].
By this it is meant that it is not permissible to say, “In a monastery where there are other monks, let someone else shave his hair as well.

“Having given the going-forth (pabbājetvā)” is stated for the purpose of clarifying the intention behind saying, “Come, having clothed yourself in the saffron robes. If the preceptor, without performing the shaving of the hair and beard and so forth, [proceeds] for the sake of the going-forth...
If one gives the refuges, the going forth does not take effect. If one confers full ordination after having announced the *kammavācā*, the full ordination takes effect.

Some say this is indeed logical because it shows that full ordination is accomplished even for those who have not yet obtained the robes, and because there is no failure of the formal act (*kamma*). And on this point there is this verse:
"Going forth belongs to one with the proper marks; the other [full ordination] belongs even to one without the marks."
"Others say that for one who has previously discarded his former dress, those two [conditions] apply.
For it is their intention that only a robe-cloth (kāsāva) given by a monk either with his own hand or by command is permissible, while what is not given is not permissible;
this is so only when robes already exist, because it is impossible otherwise when they do not exist. And furthermore, monks:
"One should be granted the going-forth; one should be ordained. [The sequence] "First...

and so on, up to "...I allow, monks, the going-forth and the ordination by these three goings for refuge"—here the intention is shown as: "I allow the going-forth and the ordination by means of these three goings for refuge given in this specific sequence, and not by mere [isolated] ones."
“For one who previously had the marks [of a monk], there may be two [offenses] even for one who is naked;
not for another—this is our position—because it conforms to all the readings,” says the Teacher (Ācariya).
Regarding the statement by the Teacher that “it is not permitted to take what has not been given,” it is written here: “They say that going forth does not succeed.”
In the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada* it is likewise written: "The places [of articulation] are the chest and so forth; the means [of articulation] are the lips and so forth.

Having made the final sound nasalized and having formed a single connection, one should speak without pausing in the middle at the time of giving [the word]. Even when breaking [the word] for the sake of recitation, the break must occur only at the aforementioned place;
it is not permitted elsewhere. Thus it is written regarding the end of a nasal sound (*anunāsika*).

The Elder Upatissa says that when [the formula] is being given, even if it becomes mixed with the sound "ma" as one stumbles while saying "I go for refuge to the Buddha," it is still valid because it has entered the field [of the precepts].
The Elder Dhammasiri says that while it is permissible to speak by mixing [the sounds], at the time of speaking, one must not make a pause at the place of the nasalization (anunāsika).
It is stated: "In this way, it is also [valid] for the formal act (kammavācā). This is due to purity on both sides.
Regarding the phrase "it is permissible": here, the Mahāthera speaks having made [the candidate] non-quadrangular (acaturassa) due to reasons such as having fallen-out teeth;
a learned novice standing nearby causes the learned candidate who seeks ordination to speak. It is not permissible for one to cause another to speak what has not been spoken by the Mahāthera.
However, if the other bhikkhu speaks during the formal ritual (kammavācā), it is permissible, for it is the Saṅgha that performs the ritual.
"Not a person" (na puggalo): This is because it must be rejected according to the general method of formal acts (*kammavācā*) performed within different boundaries (*sīmā*).
Now, if the candidate for ordination is unable to recite the fourfold formula spoken by the Elder, the novice himself speaks it and causes him to recite it;

in this case, there is indeed "purity on both sides" (*ubhatosuddhi*), because what was spoken by the Elder has effectively been spoken. When going for refuge to the Buddha, regarding that which is not shared...

When going for refuge to the Dhamma while [taking] the qualities of the Buddha, one goes for refuge to Nibbāna; when going for refuge to the Saṅgha, one goes for refuge to the qualities of those in training (sekha-dhamma) and the qualities of those beyond training (asekha-dhamma).
Thus, the construction should be made by way of including what was not previously mentioned. Otherwise, there would be the fault of confusing the three refuges.
"All that is allowable and unallowable for him" refers to matters other than the ten training precepts, such as grasping and non-grasping, and so forth.

“Because of the statement ‘He is to be trained in the matters of proper conduct (ābhisamācārika),’ he must fulfill the morality of proper conduct, such as the training rules (sekhiya) and the duties toward the preceptor (upajjhāya-vatta).
In this regard, it is shown that one becomes liable to disciplinary action if one fails to do what is prescribed or does what is prohibited.
The commentary on the Discussion of Going-forth (Pabbajjā-kathā-vaṇṇanā) is finished.
Commentary on the Second Discourse on Māra (Dutiyamārakathāvaṇṇanā) 35.

Because of the expression “for that reason,” it should be understood that in the text the ablative case (*nissakkavacana*) in “from wise attention and right striving” (*yonisomanasikārāsammappadhānā*) is used in the sense of a cause (*hetvattha*).
The commentary on the Second Discourse on Māra is finished.
Commentary on the Story of the Miracle at Uruvelā (37–8):
“Let us dwell together”—this was said, it is said, as a kind word for the purpose of winning him over, meaning “you and I shall dwell together.
“Fire by fire” means power by power; or, the fire-element by the fire-element. Of both...
The genitive case in the phrase *sajotibhūtānaṃ* (of those who have become aflame) is used in the sense of disregard (*anādara*), or else in the sense of the locative absolute (*bhāvasattamī*).
The fire-hall itself was ablaze, but no being dwelling there was consumed; for the domain of psychic power (*iddhivisaya*) is inconceivable.

But why did the Blessed One not resolve that even the fire-hall itself should not be ablaze? Because it would have led to an excessive lack of wonder regarding his own freedom from the arising of suffering.

For what purpose does he destroy that which belongs to another and was produced with great effort? It is because of his intention, through the power of his supernormal success (*iddhi*), to restore it to its former state.
"Exhausted" (*pariyādinna*) means brought to destruction. "By brilliance, brilliance" (*tejasā tejaṃ*) means by power, power.
Because the fire-chamber is small, the other meaning is not possible. This is the meaning of the phrase: "unable to endure the smear."

This fits very well. For in that context, "smeared" (*makkha*) refers to the defilement of supernatural power (*iddhānubhāva*). Regarding the phrase "by one who has obtained," the ancients say it means "by a lotus leaf.
Their opinion is that the Blessed One was standing there in a cluster of lotuses.
39. "Given" (*dinna*) means "consented to. "Fearless" (*abhīta*) means "without dread. Why? Because he had transcended fear by means of the Path.
“*Sumanamanaso* means the mind (*mano*) known as a beautiful heart (*sundara-citta*); or it is simply *sumano* (well-minded),” so it is written. *Tejovā* means like fire.
*Dhātukusalo* means skilled in the fire element (*tejodhātu*). Because of the characteristics of grammar (*saddalakkhaṇa*), there is also a prefix (*upasagga*) [implied].
The meaning is simply: "skilled in the attainments of the fire element. *Udicchare* means they looked up. "*Saṃparivāresun*" means they surrounded.
And it is written thus; the meaning is that they speak in this way. "Hatā" means "equal," and the intention here is that they become as if black.
They remain in a state corresponding to their tranquility, without performing even the slightest mental disturbance (*vyāpāra*).
And in order to show those rays which are of many colors, he said, "blue and then red," and so forth.
40. *Catuddisā* means in the four directions.
44. *Paṃsukūlaṃ uppannaṃ* means it has arisen by way of being obtained for one who is searching for it.
And that search is for the purpose of displaying various wonderful miracles. This is "that"; these are "those. Taking two together, he says: "I am coming."
“Āyamahaṃ”: this refers to him. “Yathā mayaṃ”: because we [are]. 50–51. *Udakavāha* means a flood of water;
the ancients call it a stream of water. “*Yāya tvaṃ*”: this was said with reference to the preliminary stage of the path of insight (*pubbabhāga-vipassanā-paṭipadā*).
“*Cirapaṭikā*”: from long ago; it has been a long time since the subduing of the Nāgas. It is also called “*cirapaṭisaṅkhā*” (long-considered).

They say: because they were placed separately and individually, intermingled with hair (*kesamissa*), in the passage beginning with "Kesamissa," the ancients [hold that] the hair and so forth are what is meant by "intermingled with hair" (*kesamissa*). Regarding "mixed with a khārikāja": here, *khārī* refers to the requisites of an ascetic.
"He sent forth two or three ascetics"—he sent forth two or three *tāpasa*s. It is said: "More than sixteen thousand miracles."
54. Because he was well-versed in the fire sacrifice, the Blessed One spoke to them on the discourse concerning what is aflame (*ādittapariyāya*).

In that context, some things are "aflame" by way of their object, such as the eye and so forth, [being aflame] with the fire of lust; some are aflame by way of association, namely through the feeling and so forth conditioned by eye-contact;
some are aflame in the sense of being overcome, namely the eye and so forth themselves by birth and so forth; and some are aflame in the sense of being a condition.
In this context, the state of being "on fire" (ādittatā) should be understood according to what is applicable, such as through sorrow and so forth.

Although here only the characteristic of suffering (*dukkha-lakkhaṇa*) is manifest, it should be understood that by means of that, the other two characteristics are also seen by them, because the mode of suffering illuminates the other modes.
However, because these [beings] are obsessed by craving for peaceful happiness, the characteristic of suffering comes first for them.
It should be understood that the teaching has been given.
The commentary on the account of the miracles at Uruvelā is finished.
The commentary on the account of the meeting with Bimbisāra.
55–7. Women who have become objects of sensual desire are "desirable women" (*kāmitthiyo*). The second and subsequent [types] are those who provide consolation.
Because even before the Blessed One had appeared, the "uproar regarding a Buddha" (*buddhakolāhala*) first arose in the world for a thousand years.
And the *Brahmās*, having manifested in the form of Brahmins, inserted into the Vedas a body of scripture (*pariyatti*) consisting of about three thousand [stanzas] related to the Buddha.
They recite that the discourse on the Buddha, beginning from the Blessed One’s birth, was produced by brahmins skilled in the marks (*lakkhaṇa*) and spread throughout the world;

therefore, [the verses] are appropriate and not otherwise. By the verses beginning with “Bimbisāra, standing in his palace, saw him,” it is established that Bimbisāra had already been consecrated even during the time of the Bodhisatta.

58. Here, friends, a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed has abandoned five factors, possesses six factors, has a single guard, has four supports, has shaken off individual dogmatic views, has utterly relinquished seeking, has undisturbed intention, has tranquilized bodily formations, and is well-liberated in mind and well-liberated in wisdom.
These are called the ten abodes of the noble ones. [The eight attainments of form and formlessness, and the attainment of cessation.]

The ancients also say: "It is the attainment of great compassion. In this regard, there are five factors consisting of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). Equanimity with six factors (*chaḷaṅgupekkhā*) has six factors. With mindfulness as its protection, it has one protection.
"Having reflected, one resorts to one thing; one endures one thing; one avoids one thing;
having reflected, one dispels one thing"—this is the fourfold consolation (*caturāpassena*). There are the various individual truths of the many recluses and brahmins, which are four.
Thus, his individual truths have been dispelled. The search for sensual pleasures and the search for existence have been abandoned;
the search for the holy life has been stilled. Thus, he has completely relinquished all searches. Thoughts of sensuality, ill will, and cruelty have been abandoned;
thus, his thoughts are undisturbed. With the abandoning of pleasure... [and so on] ...he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
Thus he is one whose mind is well-liberated. He understands: "Lust has been abandoned, its root cut off...
it is of a nature not to arise again"; he understands: "Hatred... Delusion is of a nature not to arise again. Thus he is one whose wisdom is well-liberated.
"Knowledge of what is possible and impossible, and of the ripening of kamma, and knowledge that leads everywhere..."
“The Sage knows the manifold elements of the world, the inclinations of living beings, and the relative degrees of the faculties; likewise,
his knowledge of the defilements and so forth regarding the jhānas and other states constitutes the threefold clear vision.”

These are the ten powers. The factors of one beyond training (*asekha*) are: right view of one beyond training... [and so on] ...right liberation of one beyond training, and the knowledge and vision of the liberation of one beyond training. Therein, the tenth is that of one beyond training. "And by means of these ten perfections," say the ancients.
The commentary on the account of the meeting with Bimbisāra is finished.
The commentary on the account of the going forth of Sāriputta and Moggallāna.
60. *Kiṃ kāhasi* means "what will he do? It signifies that many phonemes have been uttered, such as "kiṃ karoti" (what does he do?
or "kiṃ karosi" (what are you doing?). *Paṭipādento* means concluding. They also read it as "paccabyathā, paccabyatha. Regarding the phrase *kappanahutehi*:
here, ten times one hundred is one thousand (*sahassa*); one hundred times one thousand is one hundred thousand (*satasahassa*); one hundred times one hundred thousand is... [ten million].

One should understand that ten million is a *koṭi*; one hundred thousand times ten million is a *pakoṭi*; one hundred thousand times ten million *pakoṭis* is a *koṭipakoṭi*; and one hundred thousand times ten million *koṭipakoṭis* is a *nahuta*.
Regarding the phrase "by hundreds of thousands of *kappa*-nahutas," the reading of the Khuddakabhāṇakas is that this refers to what has passed according to such a sequence.

63. The reading is “kulacchedāya,” which means “for the destruction of the family. The connection is to be made with the elliptical remainder of the text: people will no longer accuse them, thinking, “Indeed, the recluses, sons of the Sakyans, lead [the community] by the Dhamma, not by what is contrary to the Dhamma.”
It should be understood that the Elder has thus concluded the introduction.
And there are these verses here: “By demonstrating the process of establishing the root of this work, the General of the Dhamma—”
The compilers of the Dhamma, who were experts in the procedures of the Vinaya,
established the conclusion of the Nidānas:
"The meaning and words are indeed contained within the Nidāna."
Having understood this as the conclusion of the introduction,
from here on, one should know that there is only the investigation of the words connected with the meaning of the Vinaya.
The commentary on the account of the going-forth of Sāriputta and Moggallāna is finished.
Commentary on the Account of the Duties Toward a Preceptor (Upajjhāyavatta): 64.

For those whose preceptor is the Buddha, as distinct from others who are "Come, monk" (ehibhikkhu) [ordinands], there is no separate [requirement] regarding the wearing of the lower robe and the upper robe.
Because they were dissimilar to one another, they were described as "ill-clad, ill-dressed, and lacking in proper decorum.

Not only did they wander for alms in such a state, but they also stood over people while they were eating, and so forth. People complained because of their inability to endure thirst, whereas others [complained] out of faith in the excellence of their deportment.
65. By whom and who should the preceptor (upajjhāya) be chosen? Regarding this, some have written: "At that time, he [should choose] the one in whose presence he was ordained;
at present, it is the one in whose presence he seeks full ordination (upasampadā). And this refers to the acceptance by the preceptor, saying 'It is well' (*sādhu*).
They understand it thus: when the preceptor has accepted by saying "It is well," etc., for the sake of the co-resident student (*saddhivihārika*).
The phrase “I accept it well and properly” is merely a custom established by the bhikkhus; it is not found anywhere [in the texts].
Therefore, even without that phrase, the preceptor is indeed accepted. In this context, *sāhu* means “well” (*sādhu*).
*Lahu* means “light”; it means, “You are not a burden to me. *Opāyika* means connected with skillful means (*upāya*).
The meaning is: "By this means, from now on, you have become a burden to me. "Patirūpaṃ" means: "It is suitable;
it is appropriate for you to take a preceptor," such is the meaning. 66.
"In exactly that same manner, water for washing the face [should be used] when the season is uniform. "From now on" refers to [the rule]: "Not [using water] for the preceptor..."

"Starting from the manner described here in the phrase 'while speaking'": some explain that this indicates there is no offense according to the manner described in the passage, "One should not go too far, nor should one go too near. Is this offense intentional (*sacittaka*) or unintentional (*acittaka*)?
It is intentional because it is conditioned by disrespect (*anādariya*). How is its being conditioned by disrespect made known?

Why? Because it is comprised by the conditions of disrespect (*anādariya*). For, in the recitation of the *Pātimokkha*, the failure to set a limit on the number of people for the training rules (*sekhiya*) is for the purpose of including them within the offenses contained in the *Khandhaka*.

However, this characteristic should be understood as applying only to conduct (*cāritta*), not to avoidance (*vāritta*), because offenses such as eating unwholesome meat and so forth are unintentional (*acittaka*). [The offenses] belonging to the *Khandhaka* and the *Vāritta* are [included] by those...
The Master says: "Inclusion [occurs] only within the training rules (*sekhiya*) and prohibitions (*vārita*), by means of unintentional requests for soup, boiled rice, requisites, and so forth.
Wherever a prohibition is made by means of the negative particle (*na*), does a downfall of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) occur in all such cases? Yes.
In all cases where the method of the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) has not been shown. For later in the Commentary it says: "But if [the hair] has been blackened..."
The method is shown by such passages as: "Or it may be plastered with lime, or it may be dust-free clay; it is permissible to place [the bowl] on such ground," and so forth.
Here it is asked: since in the Pāḷi itself it says, "If dissatisfaction has arisen in the preceptor, or a wrong view..."
In order to show that the method stated in the Commentary is logical by virtue of the Blessed One’s own words, [the author asks]:
"What is the wording of the Blessed One’s statement regarding the phrase 'neither too far nor too near'? It is replied:
"They say 'having arrived earlier, the seat should be prepared,' and so forth," because this specifies the location. It is only with the preceptor’s permission...
If it is argued that this refers to the "first going," no; because [that] is unestablished, and even if it were established, it would be established by the method already stated.
For permission granted to one who has been forbidden does not constitute a non-offense; nevertheless, it should be accepted after due consideration. "Koṭṭhaka" means a gatehouse.
It should neither be relinquished nor hidden away.
The commentary on the section concerning the duties toward the preceptor is finished.
Commentary on the section concerning improper conduct, etc.: 68.
Regarding the phrase "there is no excessive affection based on the household," here "affection based on the household" should be understood as exclusively unwholesome (*akusala*).
Since this characteristic is common even to those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), [one might ask]: "Is it not because those whose taints are destroyed lack improper conduct? No;
for there is no need to bow down to them, since their possession of that [characteristic] is already established.

Therefore, it should be understood that "love" (pema) in this context refers to the sense of ownership, thinking "this is my burden," just as in the passage: "If one person is accomplished in the observance of duties... [etc.]... there is no offense for them. If—
A single bhikkhu who is perfect in his duties says, "Venerable sirs, you remain free from anxiety;
I shall attend to your co-resident or pupil when they are ill, I shall exhort them when they need exhortation, and I shall take responsibility for their various duties.
Then those co-residents and others say, "Venerable sir, you alone..."
"They say, 'Be free from anxiety,' or they do not accept the duties; from that point on, there is no offense for the teachers and preceptors.
The commentary on the discussion regarding improper conduct is finished.

73. Having stated, "‘Putimutta’ means urine like a putrid body," it is nevertheless written that "medicine released and discarded due to its state of putrefaction is ‘putimutta-bhesajja’ (putrid-urine medicine). In all instances, the word *itthannāmo* contains only a single negative particle (*na*).

The commentary on the narrative concerning the teacher’s duties (*ācariyavatta*).
76. Regarding the statement, “I shall dwell depending on the venerable one,” it should be understood by supplying the words, “I dwell depending on the venerable one’s instruction.

Alternatively, *nissāya* may be taken as *nissayā*, meaning “by means of dependence”; thus, it is said to be “by means of dependence. Or, in the phrase *āyasmato*, the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative.

Commentary on the Discussion of the Cessation of Dependence (Nissayapaṭippassaddhikathāvaṇṇanā) 83.
"Gone to another region" means having gone beyond the village after having left his residence there.
Regarding the rule "one must go to where dependence can be obtained," here too, in the case of going with the thought "I will go in a few days," the method is exactly as stated for the preceptor.
This effort protects [him]. "Do not retreat here" means "do not go here. Those who are "of the same class" (sabhāgā) are the disciples of the preceptor (upajjhāya).
Having received dependence (nissaya) there—if one asks, "What is the distinction in that case?"—it is said:
"Perhaps he might forgive [the offense]. It is permissible to dwell [there] because it has been relinquished by the preceptor; thus, it is the same as being under the preceptor's authority.
The meaning is "useless. If the preceptor is slow to provide assistance, then from that point on, the preceptor himself is the formal support (*nissaya*).
If the preceptor is shameless, the student, after having restrained him many times, may abandon the preceptor who does not desist;
even without being dismissed from *nissaya*, he may live by taking *nissaya* from another.
If the preceptor’s gender changes, [the dependence] is not maintained for even a single day.

If he is a pakkhapaṇḍaka (a paṇḍaka during certain phases of the moon), and if he is one who has received formal dependence, it is permissible if the preceptor says, "Wait for my favorable period," or if he waits of his own accord.
If the preceptor has been subjected to an act of suspension, [the dependence is not maintained] because of being situated on a ground of different communion.
It subsides. However, having seen him conducting himself correctly, he may wait for the subsiding of the legal procedure.

If he is one who is practicing the *mānatta* penance, he must wait for his rehabilitation (*abbhāna*). If he has been undergoing a long period of probation (*parivāsa*), he must receive formal dependence (*nissaya*) from another;
the presence of his preceptor (*upajjhāya*) is not a sufficient condition. For one who is undergoing probation or the *mānatta* penance, formal dependence [from the preceptor] is not required.

It should be given. As for what was stated in the *Pārivāsikakkhandhaka-ṭīkā*: “Even for one who consents on behalf of his co-residents, it is merely a *dukkaṭa* offense,” and so forth—that indeed establishes the meaning as previously explained. However, as for what was stated:
“If sons of good family who have gone forth out of faith say, ‘Venerable sir, you perform only the formal act of the Vinaya,’ yet they themselves still carry out the duties (*vatta*)...”
"She merely asks for permission to enter the village; from the time she is forbidden, there is no offense.

This should be understood as being stated either for the purpose of indicating the mere absence of a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) due to her compliance with the formal duty (*vatta*), or with reference to the fact that the co-residents are dependent [upon her].
Therefore, if they act exactly according to what was forbidden by the preceptor, their formal dependence (*nissaya*) [remains intact].
"It has subsided" means it is accomplished.
"He returns after having passed two clods' throws" means that up to this point he is said to have gone away from his district;
therefore, even if the resident pupil has not relinquished his duties, the formal dependence (*nissaya*) is suspended. [The teacher and preceptor] do not pass beyond two clods' throws.
It is written: "It is permissible to dwell within the distance of two stone-throw lengths, even if it is across a monastery enclosure, whether that enclosure is fenced or unfenced.
The Teacher [Buddhaghosa] states that "only in an unfenced [monastery]" is not his own opinion;

rather, the intended meaning here is that they dwell in another monastery that is unfenced and free from the area suitable for an enclosure. And regarding the word "monastery" (*vihāra*) here, [it refers to] such a monastery as...
"The single hut standing in front is intended," says the Elder Upatissa. In this regard, the statement of the Elder Dhammasiri accords with the commentary’s general statement:
"If both the teacher and the pupil [are within range] by anyone... the formal support (nissaya) is not suspended.
"In an unenclosed area" means within two stone-throw distances of an enclosure.

It may be either enclosed or unenclosed. Because it is stated that "outside the boundary" (*bahisīma*), and because it is established that one may reside even after crossing two *leḍḍupāta* throws within the monastery boundary (*antovihārasīmā*), the doctrine of the Elder Upatissa is not consistent [with the Vinaya].
For in a single residence—whether enclosed or unenclosed—the formal support (*nissaya*) does not cease, even for one residing as far as three *yojana*s away.

And that [monastery] is delimited by the precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*); and that precinct boundary is delimited, in the case of an enclosed monastery, by the enclosure itself, and in the case of an unenclosed one, by the place suitable for an enclosure. It is a single residence (*ekāvāsa*).

If it is argued that this is because a boundary was authorized in the *Uposathakkhandhaka* regarding the doubt concerning a single residence, [the answer is] no, according to the commentary on the *Cīvarakkhandhaka*.
Because it has been deliberated upon. As it is said: "Let the Saṅgha residing within the boundary divide and take [the property]. Within which boundary should it be divided?
The Elder Mahāsiva reportedly said, "Within the non-separation boundary (avippavāsa-sīmā). Then they said to him: "The so-called non-separation boundary can extend even three *yojanas*;
if that were the case, those staying within three *yojanas* would receive the gains, and while staying within three *yojanas*, they would perform the duties for newcomers..."
Having filled [the bowl], he will enter the monastery; being about to depart, he will ask for leave regarding his lodging after traveling three yojanas;
for one undergoing formal dependence (*nissaya*), the dependence shall cease upon exceeding three yojanas;
one on probation (*pārivāsika*) must cause the dawn to rise after having traveled three yojanas; and for a nun, it concerns entering the monastery while standing at a distance of three yojanas.
"She will have to take leave"—all this is permissible by way of defining the precinct boundary (*upacāra-sīmā*).
Therefore, it is established that even for one staying beyond two *leḍḍupāta*s within the precinct boundary, the dependence (*nissaya*) does not cease upon exceeding three *yojana*s.
And here, although the precinct boundary may be three *yojana*s in extent, [the following applies].

Or else, there would be the consequence of the aforementioned faults for an excess [of buildings]. For it has been stated that [the term "dwelling"] increases when the residences increase and decreases when they decrease;
therefore, here what is intended by "monastery" (*vihāra*) is a single hut situated at the edge of such a monastery.
Since that too is merely a small hut (*kuṭikā*) of that very monastery, it constitutes a "residence" (*āvāsa*). If, however, only a separate residence were intended, [then the following would apply].

“It should not be said that ‘the hut stands before [it]. However, within two *leḍḍu*-throws (the distance of a stone’s throw) in an unenclosed area, in a separate residence (*nānāvāsa*), the formal support (*nissaya*) does not cease.

That which was stated as ‘not a mere thought’ refers to such a separate residence according to the principle of the non-cessation of the taking of lodgings (*senāsanaggāha*). For the taking of lodgings is [defined] by the act of taking.”
"Because the *ālaya* (attachment) is stilled," it is stilled in the other case due to its characteristic nature. Here is the canonical text regarding this:
"Now at that time, the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan son spent the rains retreat alone in two residences...
'Give, monks, a single portion to this foolish man. And in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), it is said of this: "And this..."

It is said that [the formal act] occurs within a single boundary (*ekasīmā*) through various gains and various modes of access; however, the taking of lodgings (*senāsanaggāha*) ceases when there are separate boundaries.
Unenclosed dwellings that have different residences fall under the category of having a single mode of access (*ekūpacāra*).
Furthermore, an enclosed area that has a single mode of access falls under the category of being unenclosed. Within this extent—within two throws of a clod (*leḍḍupāta*)—in an unenclosed space...
However, for one living in another monastery, the formal dependence (*nissaya*) does not cease; rather, it ceases only when [the boundary] is enclosed—this is the meaning established here.
To this, it is said: even if one has gone beyond two *leḍḍupāta* (the distance of a stone’s throw), the dependence does not cease even if [the boundary] exists.
For it is stated in the *Nissaggiya-aṭṭhakathā*: "If, while they are still going and have not yet arrived..."
"When the dawn breaks while [the robe] is with the young novices, the robe becomes subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*), yet the formal dependence (*nissaya*) is not dissolved.
It is said in reply: That was stated by the preceptor (*upajjhāya*) with the intention that they might meet again; here, however, it refers to a permanent residence (*dhuvavāsa*).
Therefore, they do not obstruct one another. Some, however, say: "Having passed beyond two *leḍḍupāta*s" refers to the daily [distance].
They say that this was stated by way of residing after having announced [the date], but it is my conjecture that this is merely their own opinion.

For neither in the Canon nor in the Commentary is it seen that one must reside after announcing it every day; rather, it should be understood that this is a practice adopted by those who do not understand the tradition.
The commentary on the Discussion of the Cessation of Dependence is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Five Things to be Ordained (84):
Regarding the passage beginning with "Not by the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training," etc., it is in accordance with the saying: "First, one should establish oneself in what is suitable."

This was stated by way of the factors of an offense, not by way of the factor of the offense itself. It is stated as "blue" because of its association with blue, just as it is said: "by means of the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation of one beyond training.
One who has failed in virtue regarding higher morality is one who, having committed an offense, has not emerged from it.
The commentary on the discussion of the five qualities for one to be ordained is finished.
Commentary on the Account of the Former Member of Another Sect (Aññatitthiyapubbavatthukathāvaṇṇanā): 86.
Regarding the phrase "one who was formerly a member of another sect," there are two possible interpretations.

One interpretation is that, with reference to his becoming a monk while still a follower of another sect, he was "formerly a member of another sect"; thus, that monk returned to that very same sectarian fold—this is one meaning.
Thus, one who has gone over to another sect and returned again in the guise of a householder is a "former member of another sect";

he, having come back, is not to be ordained—this is one meaning. Excluding that person who has gone over to another sect, in the passage "whosoever, monks, was formerly a member of another sect," it is not only one wearing the dress of a householder who is referred to by the word "former" (*pubba*);
rather, in that case, it refers to one who, while in his own adopted sectarian dress...

Even while staying [in the world]. Because he has become a non-Buddhist by way of his views, he is one who was formerly a member of another sect (*atitthiyapubbo*); however, when he comes back after having gone away, there is no requirement for him to undergo the *parivāsa* probation.

Is the state of a novice’s going-forth produced for this former member of another sect by means of taking the robes of a monk and going for refuge, or is it not produced? What is the point here? If it is produced, then: "O monks, whoever... [and so forth].

Furthermore, the statement, "If anyone who was formerly a member of another sect desires the going-forth (pabbajjā) and desires the full admission (upasampadā) in this Dhamma and Vinaya, a probationary period (parivāsa) of four months must be granted to him," would be contradicted [if he were not already ordained].

On the other hand, if he were not [already] born [into the Saṅgha], the non-attachment to the going-forth during the formal act of probation (parivāsakammavācā) would be contradicted. Regarding this, the Mahāvihāravāsins [hold that it applies] even while he is still a novice (sāmaṇera).

They say, "Parivāsa (probation) should be granted. Others do not say so. For they [hold that] the scriptural passage, "Monks, when one who was formerly a member of another sect has come as a seeker of success, he should be ordained," must be maintained;

and if it is argued that because of the common usage of the term "formerly a member of another sect" both before and after [the novice stage], he does not become a *sāmaṇera* [merely by that designation], then if that were so, one would have to refuse ordination altogether.
"He should be ordained" [is the rule], yet this contradicts the Sutta stated at the very beginning.
Furthermore, the reading "one who has gone over to another sect" (*titthāyatanaṃ saṅkanto*) is not elegant.

If he violates any one of the offenses such as the destruction of life (*pāṇātipāta*), it appears that even if four months have elapsed, he must complete them again. It was also stated that his restraint is for the purpose of making him a monk.
Some say that because [the refuges] have been formally authorized, there is nothing further to be said regarding the precepts; this must be investigated and then accepted.
If the refuges are broken, it is the novice monk alone who is affected.
The commentary on the discussion concerning those formerly belonging to other sects is concluded.

Commentary on the Discussion of the Five Bases for Non-Obstruction (Pañcābādhavatthukathāvaṇṇanā) 88. "The back of the nail" refers to the back of the nail of the little finger. Some say: "In a concealed place, even a large [area] is permitted from the back of the nail;
the same applies to the others. This seems not to accord with the Aṭṭhakathā. There is also the "lotus-seed-calyx" (padumakaṇṇikā).
[He] ascended [the throne] variegated with the color of red lotuses.
The commentary on the discourse concerning the five bases of affliction is finished.
The commentary on the discourse concerning the base of the thief.

91–2. "Dhammasāmī" means that because he himself is the Lord of the Dhamma, he ordained even the thief Aṅgulimāla—who should not have been ordained by the bhikkhus—and spoke thus for the sake of the future;
this is the meaning. In the palm-leaf manuscripts, it is also written as "kharabhedako.
"Sannisinnāsu" means when they had become tranquil.
The commentary on the account of the cloak-robe (coravatthu) is finished.
Commentary on the account of the debtor-slave (iṇāyikadāsavatthu): 96.
“See my mere bowl and robe; I shall give this [to you]”—this is proper conduct (sāmīci), and therefore there is no offense. “Half by half” means little by little.
97. *Desacāritta* (local custom) refers to various local practices such as the presentation of a formal charge (*sāvanapaṇṇāropanādi*).
It is written: “It is permissible for the son of Devadāsī. It is stated: “If one wishes to ordain a monastery attendant (*ārāmika*), he should be ordained after giving another [person] in his place.
This is the intended meaning here according to the *Mahāpaccarivāda*: because they were given with the words, “We give these to the Saṅgha of monks,” they are not their slaves.
It is written: “An *ārāmika* (monastery attendant) is not to be called a slave, nor is he to be called a freeman; therefore, he is not a slave.
The practice of pouring oil on the head (*takkāsiñcana*) is customary in the island of Sri Lanka. Furthermore, they are to be ordained because they serve as monastery attendants for the Saṅgha.
One is permitted to make a masterless slave a freeman by one’s own authority. [Regarding the case of] a slave who, having been ordained, flees upon seeing his own master: there is an offense.
And it is written: "They say, 'There is none. The meaning is that he would be a slave to himself, [that is,] a monk.
Some say: "The king is the master of a slave who has no master; therefore, having asked permission from the king or the people in that village, he may be ordained.
It is written: "Having made him a free man (*bhujissa*). They state the resolution for this: "In such a way that he becomes a free man..."
"It should be done in such a way. Having spoken thus with this intention, some have written that "there is no purpose [in it].
It is permissible only for the sake of making [the slave] a free man; therefore it was said, "If they see [him], they will pursue him. There is no offense.
They say that the statement, "I am indeed impure," was also spoken specifically with reference to that.
The commentary on the account of the debtor and the slave is finished.
Commentary on the account of the smith’s tools, etc.: 98.
Regarding the term “smith’s tools,” here the boy comes along having set aside only his small head-dress; therefore, [the rule] regarding asking for permission...

He receives it. If he, or someone else, takes it away, there is no offense. They say: "If one grants the refuges and ordains someone without having shaved their hair and beard due to forgetfulness, [the hair] will indeed grow.
101–3. Herein, regarding the family: "Both his... [and] the minor marks"—this is the analysis of all methods; the details are in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*.
It is written: "He is known," and even though the reading "he knows the offense" has not yet occurred [in the text], it is stated:
"If he knows that by doing this, one incurs such-and-such an offense, it is permissible. Furthermore, it is said: "But that must be understood as having been mastered from before;
the same rule applies to teachers and preceptors as well."
The commentary on the story of the blacksmith’s tools, clothing, and so forth is finished.
Commentary on the story of Rāhula: 105.
With about sixty verses beginning with “Now the trees are leafless, O Blessed One,” he thus commanded me.
The word *iti* should be supplied here. "Lotus-rain" refers to water having the color of a lotus leaf;
while that [water] is raining, those who wish to get wet indeed get wet. "Starting from the crown" means starting from the head.
"With glossy, dark-blue, soft, and curled hair..."
With a forehead like the stainless surface of the sun,
with well-proportioned, lofty, and beautiful eyes and nose,
the lion among men is spread with a network of rays.
By means of the opening verses. Or else:
"With beautiful feet marked by the wheel, with long heels adorned with the [thirty-two] characteristics;"
With feet adorned by yak-tail whisks and parasols—
this indeed is your father, a lion among men.
"The excellent Sakyan prince, so delicate..."
With a body full of the auspicious marks,
that hero among men has gone for the welfare of the world;
for he is your father, a lion among men.
“The color of his face resembles the full moon;
beloved even by gods and men, he is a bull among men;
his gait possesses the grace of a lordly elephant in rut.”
For this is your father, a lion among men.
Born of the foremost kṣatriya lineage,
his feet are worshipped by gods and humans.
With a mind established in virtue and concentration—
this indeed is your father, the lion among men.
With a long, well-proportioned, and well-shaped nose...
With a face like a cowherd’s and deep blue eyes,
with arms as dark blue as Indra’s bow—
this indeed is your father, the lion among men.
With a neck well-proportioned like a rounded pillar,
with jaws like those of a lion, and a body like that of the king of beasts;
with the excellent complexion of fine gold—
For this is your father, a lion among men:
with a pure, deep, and sweet voice, and a beautiful tongue as red as vermilion.
With twenty white, well-tamed tusks—
this indeed is your father, the lion among men.
With hair as beautiful and deep blue as the color of collyrium...
With a forehead as pure as a gold plate,
and a face as bright and clean as the white medicinal herb—
this indeed is your father, the lion among men.
Like the moon traveling on a dark path,
its form encircled by a host of stars,
the Lord of Ascetics stands amidst his disciples.
"For he was your father, a lion among men"—thus [it is said]. "Uddiṭṭhe" means:

"In this way one should conduct oneself"; this is the reading of the *Dhammapada* verse beginning with "uttiṭṭhe. "Dhamma" refers to the practice of wandering for alms from house to house. Having abandoned improper livelihood, one should practice good conduct.

"Cutting the hair" means avoiding the five-crested style and adopting the single-crested style. "Tying the cloth" refers here to the "cloth" (*paṭṭa*), which is a particular ornament customary in that family.

"House-blessing" means a house festival. "Umbrella-blessing" refers to the ceremonial investiture of the crown prince’s parasol. "Following the cycle" means following the cycle of defilements (*kilesa*).
It is "accompanied by affliction" because it is a condition for distress. The Elder [addressed] the brahmin Rādha.

If it is asked: "Why did he say, 'Venerable sir, how shall I ordain Rāhula,' after having already gone forth previously?"—in this context, the prohibition of full admission (*upasampadā*) is intended.
Therefore, knowing that "the Blessed One had prohibited only full admission, whereas now the Blessed One intends to remove doubts regarding the future," he spoke thus.
By way of matter originated by mind (*cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa*), [he said]: "the marrow of the bones..."
It is said that "having struck [the ground]. The diversity among Buddhas and Wheel-turning Monarchs (cakkavattis) should be understood by way of their proficiency (*byatta*) and other qualities;
otherwise, even Nanda and others who had gone forth would have become Buddhas, because of the statement: "If one goes forth, he becomes a Buddha.
It is appropriate to send someone to show [the way], and it is appropriate to grant the going-forth with the thought, "I shall ask for permission," because [the candidate] has reached a foreign land.
One who is released from the authority of his mother and father even by worldly convention is called a "wanderer at will" (*serivihārī*);
therefore, because they appear to stand on the side of what is non-existent for him, it is entirely incorrect to say, "They do not harbor ill-will toward his teacher of the going-forth.

The common worldly expression is that those who have gone forth share the same destination. For this very reason, in this context, the departure to another country [is mentioned] by way of the attainment of suffering and so forth.

It has been made to have a consistent meaning. Regarding the phrase "having gone abroad": here, "abroad" (videsā) means a place other than where one's mother and father reside, not a place other than where one was born.
If the literal sense alone were the authority, it would lead to the absurd conclusion that even a son whose parents are deceased should not be ordained;
therefore, a son must not be ordained unless he has received permission from his parents who are still present in the place where they ought to be.

The intended meaning here should be understood in this way; otherwise, it would contradict the Pāḷi, and the relaxation of the grounds for an offense (*āpattiṭṭhāna*) as described in the Aṭṭhakathā would not be tenable.
Let this much stand for now. If one asks, "How is the method beginning with 'I shall burn down the monastery' not contradictory?
[the answer is: because she went forth out of necessity due to the fear of impending calamity upon herself or her relatives, and for the sake of protecting her son.
And because of his having gone forth. For this being so, he has gone forth by himself, not having been persuaded to go forth by anyone.
Thus, it does not contradict the sequence of the introduction [in the Sutta], which states: “He is dear for the sake of protecting his son, or out of love for his son.
The commentary on the story of Rāhula is finished.

Commentary on the Account of the Matter Concerning Punishment for Violating the Training Rules (Sikkhāpada-daṇḍakamma-vatthu-kathā-vaṇṇanā) 107. "One’s own cell" refers to what belongs to an individual. "To be taken through the mouth-door" means it must be consumed by way of the mouth-door.
They impose a restriction or prohibition regarding what is to be assigned therein. Alternatively: "I allow you, monks—"
Regarding the phrase "to create an obstruction," the intention is that they create the very obstruction which has been permitted by means of food that enters through the mouth-door.
The commentary on the section concerning the basis for the disciplinary action of the training rule is concluded.
Now begins the commentary on the section concerning the basis for creating an obstruction without asking permission, and so forth.
108. "Of another, even of a bhikkhu who is immoral"—this is the meaning. Some write "dussīlabhikkhūpi," but that is not good.
The Ancients, however, say: "If he does not desist even when told up to three times, he should be expelled after obtaining the permission of the Saṅgha;
even if he asks for re-ordination, he should be ordained only after obtaining permission. [This applies] to bhikkhus.
It is similar to the formal act of full ordination (*upasampadā-kammavācā*).

In this regard, just as one who has been fully ordained, having renounced the training, remains in his original state of dress and robes and later performs such acts as salutation toward a fellow monk of equal seniority who was previously junior to him;
even so, a novice who has again taken refuge [in the Triple Gem] likewise [performs these acts].
He performs salutations and other formalities toward the novice again. It is said that in this case, the mark [of seniority] does not establish one’s status as being more senior.
Some say that eating at the improper time is a transgression for novices.
One should be made to confess the transgression in the manner beginning with: “Venerable sir, a transgression has overcome me. By not relinquishing a wrong view, you—
It is said: "Sāmaṇera, as soon as he says 'Go,' he becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense. They say:
"Because it is stated 'up to the third time,' it follows that the refuges are not broken merely by speaking in dispraise of the Buddha and so forth, nor merely by adopting a wrong view.
This being the case, it is my opinion that even for one committing the destruction of life and so forth, that [refuge] still remains. "For one who is without virtue..."

Some say, "Furthermore, expulsion (*nāsanā*) was mentioned," and that seems appropriate. For it should be considered that the Blessed One does not authorize the removal of the marks (*liṅganāsana*) for one who is virtuous;
rather, according to the ancients, he includes both those capable and incapable under the heading of "one who has violated a nun.
Just as this matter is shown here by the phrase "he does not even receive the going-forth (*pabbajjā*)," so too [is it shown] by the case of "the paṇḍaka."

“Monks, one who has not received full ordination must not be fully ordained; one who has received full ordination must be expelled”—by such methods as these, it is shown that there is no going forth (pabbajjā) for them.
For, apart from this specific case, there is no other ground upon which their going forth is prohibited.
“Monks, a violator of a bhikkhunī, if he has not received full ordination, must not be fully ordained... [and so on].
Others say: "Even though it was stated, 'Once he has been ordained, he is to be expelled,' since his going forth was prohibited, their going forth was likewise prohibited;
this is shown by the fact that he is again designated as a 'defiler of nuns. What is the point of this?
Is it not stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "And regarding him whose going forth is prohibited herein, with reference to him this [was said]..."?
It was said: “One who has not received full ordination must not be ordained; one who has already received full ordination must be expelled.
The commentary on the section concerning the prohibition against ordaining without asking for permission is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the section concerning eunuchs.

109. Because one who is a *paṇḍaka* by means of artificial means (*opakkamika*) lacks a [proper] organ, ordination (*pabbajjā*) is forbidden for one who has not yet gone forth, and full admission (*upasampadā*) must not be conferred upon one who has already gone forth.
If there is an act of approaching [the opposite sex] after having been previously fully admitted, the teacher says that it is our opinion that expulsion (*nāsanā*) should not be carried out.
One whose organ has been severed is not a *paṇḍaka*. Among the five types of eunuchs (*napuṃsaka*), only the *paṇḍaka* is one who lacks [sexual function].
The other four should be understood as being of a natural disposition (*sabhāvaka*). However, their disposition is that of a *paṇḍaka*.

Some say that even these four are indeed men; others say that there is also a female *paṇḍaka* who belongs to this class. Since the state of being a *paṇḍaka* necessarily arises once the [sexual] act has been performed, he does not receive the going-forth (*pabbajjā*).
"But if it does not arise for anyone, then the going-forth [is permitted]."
It is said: "She speaks a legal decision regarding one who has been forbidden [from ordination].
It is written: "The intention is that she should be ordained on the side of those who are not *paṇḍakas*, but once ordained, she should be expelled on the side of the *paṇḍakas*.
However, in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*, seven types of *paṇḍakas* are mentioned, including the monthly *paṇḍaka* and the *lekhapaṇḍaka*.
In this context, it is said that the *lekhapaṇḍaka* is one whose seed has been destroyed by means of incantations (*manta*). Regarding this, it is stated:
"Those who have gone forth as *opakkamikalekhapaṇḍakas* should not be expelled. He who ordains them commits an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
The commentary on the discussion concerning the *paṇḍaka* is concluded.

Commentary on the Discussion of the Matter of One Living in Communion through Theft (Theyyasaṃvāsaka-vatthu-kathāvaṇṇanā) 110. Regarding the term "one living in communion through theft" (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*):

although, from the perspective of both the literal expression and its meaning, it is understood that one who lives in communion solely for the purpose of [participating in] communal acts is a "one living in communion through theft," nevertheless, there are three kinds of those who live in communion through theft. Furthermore, in this context, "communion" (*saṃvāsa*) does not refer to communion consisting of communal acts and so forth.
However, in this context, "co-residence" (saṃvāsa) refers to the classification of formal acts such as the counting of a bhikkhu’s years since ordination.

For the intention of the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) is that it is possible to commit theft regarding this [classification], but not regarding the other. There is an offense for one who, having gone abroad and being asked by those who have gone forth, says "I am ten years [ordained]," and so on.
Some say there is no offense in speaking thus to laypeople. Regarding those who have assumed the outward signs out of fear of kings and the like:

Even though there was a deceptive intention in thinking, "Let the householder know me as a recluse," no fault arose because the monks lacked both the desire to deceive and the desire to live together with him. Furthermore, it is written:
"Regarding 'the meals of all sectarians'—for one who comes to a monastery and takes what belongs to the Saṅgha, it is difficult to maintain the status of a resident; therefore, this was said."
Because it is stated, “one who is fully ordained,” if they ordain even a householder, he becomes one who has attained full ordination.

By the phrase, “at the very time he is not yet ordained,” it is shown that if he hears [the proclamation] at the time of his ordination, he is indeed one who has attained full ordination even if it is not announced.
In the *Andhaka-aṭṭhakathā* and in the ancient *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries, a monk of immoral conduct is called a “thief-associate.”
It should be understood that this was said by way of the expression: "Monks, you have eaten the alms of the kingdom through theft.
For this very reason, it says: "That must not be taken. By the phrase "in large baskets, etc.," what belongs to a householder is indicated.

One who, being himself a novice, takes [alms] by counting false years [of seniority] becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense; however, he is one who lives in communion through theft (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*).

Just as [the case of] a non-existent [debt], so too is the monk; however, he must be dealt with according to the value of the goods—this is the intended meaning behind the statement, "or even a novice himself," and so forth.
Furthermore, since this one called a "thievish companion" (theyyasaṃvāsaka) is indeed one who has gone forth and not one who has not gone forth, it was said:
"Monks, a thievish companion who has not gone forth should not be given the going-forth; one who has gone forth should be expelled."

Considering that it is impossible for such a person to speak [properly], the Pāḷi was established starting from the *paṇḍaka* (eunuch) with the words, "One who is not ordained should not be ordained," and so forth;

this is because they are incapable of the mere act of ordination itself, which would otherwise imply that all eleven of them were eligible for going-forth (*pabbajjā*). Furthermore, the Pāḷi was established in that very manner to avoid the undesirable consequence (*aniṭṭha-dosa*) [of granting full ordination].
This is because [the other categories] involve leaving the order to join another sect (*titthiya-pakkamana*) and causing a schism in the Saṅgha (*saṅgha-bhedana*).
It applies only to one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*), not to one who is not; and both types of such persons are indeed those who have gone forth (*pabbajita*), not those who have not.

Therefore, since there is the scriptural passage stating, "Monks, one who has gone over to another sect (*titthiyapakkantaka*), being one who has not gone forth, is not to be admitted into the going-forth," it would follow as an undesirable consequence (*aniṭṭhappasaṅga*) that both of them must not be admitted into the going-forth.
However, among the three types of those living in communion through theft (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*)...

One who makes a novice his residence is one who shares a residence by way of the outward mark; one who makes a fully ordained monk his residence is one who shares a residence by way of communal living;

and there is also one who shares a residence by way of both. For here, "communal living" (saṃvāsa) does not refer to the mere association with a novice; for that very reason, some say that in the commentary it is stated:

"In this context, 'communal living' refers to every variety of activity, beginning with the counting of a monk’s years of seniority. [This applies to] the acts of paying respects according to seniority, receiving [offerings], and being excluded from seats.
The Teacher says "neither" because of the commonality of dwelling with the status of a novice (sāmaṇera).
The commentary on the discussion of the subject of one who dwells as a thief (theyyasaṃvāsaka) is finished.
The commentary on the discussion of one who has gone over to another sect (titthiyapakkantaka).

“Bhikkhus, one who has gone over to the faction of the titthiyas,” and so forth—although this should have been stated in the very context of the Pasūra incident which serves as its own nidāna, it was not mentioned there because no formal authorization (adhikāra) had been prohibited.
It is stated here precisely because it can occur here even without being a *theyyasaṃvāsaka* (one living in communion by theft).
In that regard, the statement “then indeed he should not be ordained” occurs right here [in this rule] concerning the full ordination (*upasampadā*) of Pasūra.

It should be understood that this is because of the fear of the fault of granting permission for the going-forth (pabbajjā)— due to the Blessed One’s prohibition against granting full ordination (upasampadā) merely on the grounds of seeing a desire to beg,
saying, “He has come; he must not be ordained”— and because of the adherence held even when the mere outward mark (liṅga) has been taken,

whether it is accepted as such or not, regarding the state of being a renegade from the sects (titthiyapakkantaka), and the notion that the naked mark itself is the most excellent among those who are not to be saluted.

Or if he approaches [the woman], he is not released; regarding this, they say: "There is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) at every step, because, thinking 'I shall become a forest-dweller (*ājīvaka*),' he has gone with a distracted mind, and thus he does not go naked. It is my opinion that it is appropriate according to both [criteria].

For so long as his conviction (*laddhi*) protects him, there is no offense because he has not formally accepted [the act]. As for the phrase "spoken by an ordained monk (*upasampanna-bhikkhu*)," how is it?
Is it discernible? Some say: "By the authority of the words of the *Aṭṭhakathā*. Some say: "By way of the introduction (*nidāna*). Some say:
"Because Pasūra was ordained, [the rule] refers specifically to those who have been ordained and then gone over to the faction of the heretics. As the Teacher said:
"The preceptor has gone away, or has disrobed, or has died, or has gone over to another faction (*pakkhasaṅkanta*). Regarding "gone over to another faction":

Some say it is because of the non-existence [of these qualities] in the cases of the novice’s training rules and the grounds for censure. Others say it is because, when one who was formerly a member of another sect has received full ordination, there is the imposition of a probationary period (*parivāsa*) for the sake of his ordination—due to the fear that he might defect to their side—which did not exist during the time he was not yet ordained.

If it is asked, "Does this apply to the purpose of going forth (*pabbajjā*) as well? The answer is no, because this has already been investigated previously, and because one who has not gone forth lacks the higher virtue (*adhisīla*). For the *pātimokkha* morality is indeed the higher virtue.
...and that does not exist for one who has not gone forth. Furthermore, regarding the duties of probation (*parivāsa-vatta*), higher virtue (*adhisīla*) is prescribed. As it is said:
"Furthermore, monks, a former member of another sect should have a keen desire for the recitation (*uddesa*), for interrogation (*paripucchā*), and for higher virtue.
Moreover: "Monks, if a Sakyan by birth who was formerly a member of another sect comes [to the Order]..."
"One who has come [back] should be ordained"—this is stated here because it indicates the mere act of ordination (*upasampadā*).

Indeed, this indicates the mere act of ordination because the granting of the probationary period (*parivāsa*) is established for that very person. This textual passage is intended to demonstrate the necessity of granting the probationary period.
The commentary on the discussion regarding those who have gone over to other sects is concluded.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Animal Realm (Tiracchānagatavatthukathāvaṇṇanā) 111.

“From the nāga womb” means from the nāga womb; the intention is: because of one’s own nāga birth. For what reason? Because all [nāgas] constantly engage in sexual intercourse with their own kind and cast off sleep.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Animal Realm is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Basis for Killing One’s Mother, etc., §§112–115. "Apavāhana" means washing away; the meaning is "desiring to put on the saffron-colored robe.

"With a corrupt mind": what kind of mind? The intention is "with a murderous mind. Some say that "corrupt mind" refers to the state of having produced blood [from a wound]; however, that is not correct.
The commentary on the discussion of the cases concerning the matricide and so forth is finished.
Commentary on the discussion of the cases concerning those with both sexual organs (ubhatobyañjanaka): 116.
It is written: "If the intention is that they receive this name by means of the sex-sign arisen at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi)."
The commentary on the discussion of the case of the hermaphrodite (*ubhatobyañjanaka*) is finished.

Regarding the commentary on the discussion of the cases of those without a preceptor (*anupajjhāyaka*), etc., [it says]: "Some say 'it is subject to transgression' (*kuppati*); that should not be accepted"—as for what was stated there, if it is a matter to be performed by a group of five (*pañcavaggakaraṇīya*),...

Because it has been stated in such a manner as, "Monks, if a monk with a nun as the fifth member were to perform an act, it is no act and is not to be performed," and so forth, it is well said that an act is only invalidated when eunuchs and others serve as the quorum-filler (*gaṇapūraṇa*), but not in all cases;
otherwise, there would be [the following objection]: "If one were to perform an act with a eunuch as preceptor (*upajjhāya*), it is no act and is not to be performed," and so forth.
It may be that it should be according to the Pāḷi.

Just as at the time of conferring full ordination upon one whose bowl and robes are incomplete, even though the statement in the *kammavācā* says, "His bowl and robes are complete," and thus the ordination is performed by praising a non-existent fact, the ordination is nevertheless valid despite that non-existence;
so too [in the case of]: "This Buddharakkhita [is the pupil] of the Venerable Dhammarakkhita..."

Regarding the phrase "one desiring full ordination": even if one has performed the formal act (kamma) by nominating a non-existent or unsuitable person—such as a eunuch—as preceptor (*upajjhāya*) and so forth, the full ordination is indeed valid, provided that those who complete the quorum are present. This is because there is no such statement as:
"Monks, one should not be ordained with a eunuch as preceptor; whoever should ordain him, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*), and that person is unordained," and so forth.
This meaning is established. For the Buddhas do not fail to speak what is appropriate to be said; therefore it was stated:
“But whichever bhikkhu, knowing [the person] to be under twenty years of age... that person is unordained,” and so forth.

Likewise, from the statement, “An experienced and competent bhikkhu should inform the Saṅgha,” [it follows that] by teachers such as those who live in communion through theft (theyyasaṃvāsaka), etc.,...
Furthermore, the statement, "When the proclamation has been made, the full ordination does not succeed because they are not monks," should not be accepted.
