Moreover, when the success and failure of formal acts (*kamma*) are being explained according to the method beginning with, "These four formal acts fail in five ways," it is said:
"Formal acts fail in seven ways: by way of the subject matter (*vatthu*), or by way of the motion (*ñatti*)," and so forth.

It should not be accepted [as a separate ground for invalidation] because it was not mentioned [in the definition], namely: "whether from the proclamation, or from the boundary, or from the assembly, or from the preceptor, or from the teacher.
If it is argued that by the phrase "or from the assembly" the teachers and preceptors are included, this is not so;
for in the analysis of the passage, "In twelve ways the formal acts fail due to the assembly," they are not designated by that same name.

Regarding this point, it has been said: "Since this matter can be understood by means of the textual passages (pāḷi) stated in their own form here and there, therefore, having shown the method (nayamukha), it is 'concise'—this is its investigation of the reasoning. Herein, this should be examined:

when those monks conferred full ordination (upasampadā) upon one who had no preceptor (anupajjhāyaka), did they praise that non-existent basis according to the aforementioned method, or was it out of fear of false speech (musāvāda)?

They do not announce those very steps. What is the point here? If they did not announce them because of the absence of a preceptor (*upajjhāya*), there would be the contingency of a failure (*vipatti*) mentioned as "he does not designate a person.
But if they did announce them, they would be guilty of false speech (*musāvāda*).
It is said in reply: They indeed announced them out of fear of the aforementioned contingency of failure; however, "the formal act (*kamma*) is not invalidated."
This is because it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, not because lying is impossible, nor because [the act] cannot be accomplished through lying;

for it is indeed possible to bring about the failure or success of a ritual act (*kamma*) by means of lying. Therefore, the meaning of the statement, "They confer full ordination without a preceptor," must be sought in a way that is free from both faults.

The reasoning here is this: "Just as previously, even though preceptors for the going-forth and full ordination existed, it was stated—'At that time, monks were without a preceptor' (*anupajjhāyaka*) and so forth—because [the candidate] had not been formally accepted according to the procedure for accepting a preceptor;
so too here, although a preceptor did exist, it was stated—'they confer full ordination on one without a preceptor'—because [the candidate] had not been formally accepted."

However, having designated the person who has been accepted by the *kammavācā*-teacher as the preceptor (*upajjhāya*)—under the understanding that he is indeed the preceptor—one should announce the *kammavācā*.
Or, one may announce the *kammavācā* after having obtained the consent (*chanda*) of a preceptor who, for some reason, does not provide physical presence;
or when a preceptor, having given his sponsorship (*upajjha*) to one seeking ordination, [is absent] after the person has already been ordained.

In such a case, whether being questioned or not being questioned, if the novice admits before the giving of the preceptor that he has renounced the training or that he has committed an ultimate offense;
or if the preceptor is in another boundary like the bringer of consent (*chandahāraka*) and others; [in these instances], the formal act (*kammavācā*) is valid.

In the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada* it is stated: “Because it was said, ‘Monks, I allow full ordination in border regions by a group of five, with a Vinaya-master as the fifth,’ some say that the preceptor must be present as the fifth member who is a Vinaya-master.
If that reading is authoritative, then [the rule applies] in the Middle Countries.
Because of the absence of the formal act (kamma-vācā). If it is argued that the formal act is valid even when the preceptor is not present, and thus [the ordination] is attained—no;
why? Because in the case of the success of a formal act, the very text stating "he points to a person" is our authority.
For in that context, a person designated as a "preceptor" who is not present is not fit to be pointed to; therefore, just as in that case there is a pointing to the Saṅgha, [so too here].

The grasping of a person (puggalaparāmasana) is to be understood. When they confer full ordination by means of a Saṅgha, a group, or a preceptor, it is because, in effect, those [preceptors] are persons.

According to the ancients, when they confer full ordination with a paṇḍaka or similar person as preceptor, it is because such was not known at the time of the ordination. This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the subject matter concerning those who have not attained [the status of a preceptor].
118. "One who confers full ordination [saying] 'the bowl and robes are complete'":

this refers to the preceptor of the formal act (kammavācācariya) who, with the perception that "the bowl and robes are complete," proclaims the formal act saying "the bowl and robes are complete" by means of peaceful phrasing, regardless of whether the actual requirements are fulfilled.

This is just as nowadays, even one whose mother and father have passed away or are living abroad is asked, "Have you been permitted by your mother and father? when he has not actually received their permission.
When questioned, he says, "Yes, venerable sir. What more need be said? However, the essential point here is this:

because the characteristic [of a valid ordination] has not yet been defined by the statement, "At that time, four types of actions fail in five ways," they ordain those who lack a preceptor and so forth;
and because the persons to be avoided have not been mentioned, they ordain those with foolish preceptors and so forth. This concerns the inquiry regarding the thirteen obstacles.

Because they were not seen, they conferred full ordination on one who lacked a bowl and robes. [The Buddha said: "Monks, I allow you to confer full ordination by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha-kamma*).

Thus, it should be understood that in this case, the failure to say "he is complete as regards bowl and robes" during the very first permitted formal proclamation (*kammavācā*) is the proof; for that statement was permitted only in due course.
Commentary on the Discussion of Subjects such as Those with Severed Hands (119).
Let this matter rest for now; however, how could it be possible from the very beginning for the statements, “They ordain a mute,” and “They ordain a deaf person,” to arise?
[For the Buddha] first said: “Monks, I authorize these three goings for refuge...”
Is it because [going forth] was authorized by the words beginning with "Pabbajjā" and so on? It is said in reply: "And furthermore, monks, he should be given the going forth.
He should be told: 'Speak thus'... up to ... 'For the third time, I go to the Saṅgha for refuge.
Here, having grasped the meaning of this statement—"He should be told: 'Speak thus'"—incorrectly, they gave the going forth to a mute. [The instruction was: "'Speak thus'..."
Having instructed that candidate for the going-forth, the preceptor himself should say, "I go for refuge to the Sangha for the third time.
Whether that candidate for the going-forth, being thus instructed, repeats the words of the preceptor after them or not, in each such instance the Blessed One has declared:
"He makes his declaration by body, he makes his declaration by speech, or he makes his declaration by both body and speech."
He says: "The preceptor has been accepted; the consent has been given; the purity has been given; the invitation has been given.
Or, by inference from that, the going for refuge is requested by the body by that one desiring the going-forth.
Even in the world, one who indicates by means of the body is said to "speak thus"; taking this figurative sense, [it applies] even to a mute person.
It should be understood that they "admit [him] into the order. In the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*, having raised the question, "How do they admit a mute?", it is stated:
"Because of the existence of bodily confidence, they gave him a blow with the body and, making their meaning known by means of hand gestures, they admitted him into the order.
What need for much? This, however, is the essential point here: just as previously, while the section on admission was being discussed, there was the expression "admission" (*pabbajjā*).

Having interrupted [the discussion], the expression was made specifically in terms of full ordination (*upasampadā*) by way of the passage beginning, "Monks, one who is a paṇḍaka, if not yet ordained, should not be ordained.
Although such an expression was not used in the case of the *theyyasaṃvāsaka* (one who lives by theft) because it is impossible there, only the going-forth (*pabbajjā*) was performed;
nevertheless, throughout all cases, what is intended by the expression is full ordination, due to its inherent influence.

This is because, when going forth (*pabbajjā*) has been prohibited, it is understood that full ordination (*upasampadā*) has also been prohibited. Likewise, here, while the section on full ordination is being discussed, one should understand that the term "going forth" is employed with reference to full ordination itself, having set aside the specific expression for full ordination.
Granted, that [term] should not have been used, since it is impossible in the case of the "mute words" (*mūgapada*); nevertheless, by virtue of that [usage], from the very beginning—
It appears as though the expression for full ordination (*upasampadā*) ought to be used;
nevertheless, following that very word "mute" (*mūga*), the expression for going forth (*pabbajjā*) was employed from the beginning in order to prevent a wrong understanding. How so?
Because of the statement: "Monks, a mute person has not attained admission; if the Saṅgha admits him, he is admitted," it follows that a mute person becomes fully ordained (*upasampanna*).
It is established. He holds the false view: "One is merely ordained (*upasampanna*), but not one who has gone forth (*pabbajita*), because going forth is impossible for him.

Having caused him to abandon that [view], it should be understood that the Blessed One produces this correct understanding: "Whoever is ordained is indeed one who has gone forth; however, among those who have gone forth, some are ordained and some are not ordained."

Furthermore, the term "going forth" (pabbajjā) is used here both to demonstrate that those who have gone forth with severed hands and so on are indeed well-gone-forth, and to prevent the suspicion that they lack the status of having gone forth.

How so? Because there is a prohibition such as, "Monks, one with a severed hand should not be given the going forth," and because there is no place where it is stated that "those who have gone forth are well-gone-forth," there arises the suspicion regarding their lack of the status of having gone forth.
It would be so. Just as one would place mud where there is no mud, so too, with reference to full ordination (*upasampadā*), the Blessed One prohibited it by way of such statements as:
"Monks, one whose hand has been severed has not reached the state of being admitted; if the Saṅgha admits him, he is not admitted," and so forth.
However, by that very same principle, all those who have gone forth are indeed well-gone-forth (*supabbajita*).

[Otherwise] it would illuminate [the following undesirable consequence]: all of these would indeed be fully ordained (upasampanna), but not gone forth (pabbajita). How so? Because of such statements as:
"Monks, one with severed hands should not be given the going-forth; if he has already gone forth, he should be expelled," or "Monks, one with severed hands should not be given the going-forth;
whoever should give him the going-forth, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)."
The intention is that when the phrase "and he has not gone forth" is established as a textual rule (tanti) in the Campeyyakkhandhaka— where it is stated that "he is one who has been reintegrated"—
then either the undesirable position arises that "these people, such as those with severed hands and so forth, are only fully ordained (upasampanna), but not gone forth (pabbajita)," or else,
even if they are both fully ordained and gone forth, they must be expelled. This is the intended meaning.

But here this must be investigated: since there is no statement saying "and he has not gone forth," does it not follow that the going forth of a mute is established, and thus the undesirable position—that even the going forth is a purification on one side only—would arise?
It does not so arise because of the correct understanding that here "going forth" by expression actually intends "full ordination" (upasampadā).
Otherwise, if the meaning were taken according to the literal phrasing, [that undesirable conclusion would follow].
Furthermore, another undesirable category is reached, namely the absence of the offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) as it has been prescribed. How so?

Regarding the statement, “Monks, one who is mute should not be ordained; whoever should ordain him, there is an offense of wrong-doing,” the offense of wrong-doing mentioned occurs at the conclusion of the ordination, not because of its being incomplete.
For he incurs only the offense of wrong-doing pertaining to the preliminary effort first; therefore, in the case of a mute person...
Because there would be no completion of the going-forth (*pabbajjā*) itself, the occasion for this *dukkaṭa* offense would not be possible at any time.

However, when the meaning is understood by way of full ordination (*upasampadā*), it becomes possible because of the accomplishment of the formal act (*kamma*). For this very reason, in the Canon it says:
"Monks, a paṇḍaka should not be ordained; whoever should ordain one, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa*. Thus, the *dukkaṭa* [is established].
It is not prescribed. Because it is not prescribed, only the *dukkaṭa* offense for the preliminary effort (*pubbapayoga*) is possible here, and not the other;
by this much, it is established that "in that context, it is the full ordination (*upasampadā*) expressed by the term 'going forth' (*pabbajjā*) that is intended, not the mere going forth.

Here it is asked: "How is it known that the going forth of a novice (*sāmaṇera-pabbajjā*) does not arise from bodily action? It is said: because of the teaching in the *tikā* beginning with "he makes known by means of the body. And there is this [verse]:
“Even a hare might find a foothold in the great ocean, but one who has grasped poorly cannot find a footing in the ocean of the Vinaya, which is deep in four ways. Regarding the term *brahmujugatta*:
here, taking the word *brahma* in the sense of “faultless” and in the sense of “supreme,” [it refers to] that which is faultless...
"Having offered [this], he whose limbs are straight is 'one with limbs straight as Brahmā' (brahmujugatto)"—thus it is written.

Alternatively, without taking the lords of the gods and others as examples because they enjoy sensual pleasures, one who has limbs straight like Brahmā is "one with limbs straight as Brahmā. A jar with a large belly is a "large-bellied jar" (mahākucchighaṭo).
One who is similar to that is called "like a large-bellied jar. As for the term "galagaṇḍī," how is it that this is merely a designation?
Is it evident? It is evident from the statement: “Monks, one who is afflicted by the five diseases should not be admitted into the order.

Here, “laziness” is also intended; thus, it is not only that alone, but also those afflicted by the five diseases, those beginning with the king’s servants mentioned in the Canon down to the slaves, and those whose parents have not given their permission as mentioned in the Rāhula narrative—these ten as well.

"Persons" here refers to those intended [in this context]. For the purpose of illustrating that very meaning, the Elder Upāli—though he had previously stated the characteristics of being struck by a written galewood staff—brought that forward and spoke here in the *Hatthacchinna-pāḷi*. For that very reason, in the *Campeyyakkhandhaka*, it says:
"Bhikkhus, there is a person who has not yet reached restoration; if the Saṅgha restores him, one part is restored and one part is not."

In the analysis (*vibhaṅga*) of this term "one who has been suspended" (*dosārita*), seven types of persons—those afflicted by the five diseases, royal servants, thieves, traitors, eunuchs, slaves, and those whose parents have not given permission—are not included, nor are they eligible [for reintegration]. Otherwise, these too would have had to be mentioned in that analysis.
If you argue that they are not mentioned there because they are incapable [of being reintegrated], then if that were the case, [the text would have to say]: "The Saṅgha reinstates him... [and so on].
Just as the *paṇḍakas* and others ought to have been mentioned in the analysis (*vibhaṅga*) of the phrase "one who has been ejected for hatred," yet they were not;

and since they are not mentioned in either case, these [others] cannot be considered "neither" (i.e., neither *paṇḍakas* nor those ejected for hatred), therefore, in order to include the ten aforementioned types that were not explicitly stated, the "likewise written" (*likhitaka*) and so forth are mentioned again.
Now, for what purpose are they mentioned here out of their regular order?

Even though debtors and slaves have been released from their obligations, they are still to be given back to their masters; this is for the purpose of showing that they remain under the latter's authority.
For this very reason, it is stated there: "Even one who has run away must be brought back and given," and so forth.

Furthermore, it should be understood that if a thief who has committed a crime goes forth into homelessness, or if a king’s servant has committed an offense, they are already included by the mention of "debtors. Alternatively, [this refers to] one possessing the characteristics as previously described.
Since even all debtors and slaves are not subject to being called "one who has been reintegrated" (*sosārito*), the teaching proceeds from above rather than from below in order to avoid them;
this is because it is explained that a written slave (*likhitaka*) must be sent to another region since he is described as "one who has been reintegrated.
It should be understood that the same applies to those who cause schisms in the community and so forth.

To this extent, it should be understood that by means of his own skill in teaching— through the grasping of what was previously grasped— the Blessed One has illustrated both the accomplishment of the formal acts of going-forth and full ordination for the ten aforementioned individuals, as well as the diversity of persons through the use of inverted order, for those who are proficient in teaching. And there is a verse on this point:

“Having spoken what is appropriate to be said with words, and having shown through the method of teaching what is desired though it was not explicitly stated, the discourse of the Sugata illuminates and makes even the mind variegated. Regarding this, it is asked:
In the Campeyya Khandhaka, since one who is less than twenty years of age is not mentioned in either case, could such a person be considered neither [of the two]?
It cannot be [the "neither"] simply because it was not mentioned. For if there were to be a third category, it would necessarily have been mentioned by the Blessed One;
yet it was not mentioned. Therefore, that is not the "neither. Then, which side does it belong to?
It belongs to the side of those who have committed an offense. But why was it not mentioned? Because it is prohibited by the training rule (*sikkhāpada*). [The text continues: "Enmity..."

“Having bound,” meaning having bound again. It is written: “This is a designation for the procedure to be performed after binding the foot with various kinds of medicinal herbs and inserting it into a pit.
Or, like an elephant with its head covered by a cloth (*kappasīsa*). A “cow-food tube” (*gobhattanāḷikā*) is a tube made for the purpose of providing food and drink to cows.
One who has an “upward-turned face” (*upakkamukha*) is said to have a face turned away from anger; he is a wind-purifier (*vātaṇḍika*).
One named *Aṇḍaka* is one afflicted with a growth on the testicles. One named *Vikaṭa* is one who moves horizontally on his hands and feet.
Regarding the reading "Guṇi kuṇī," it is said there are two versions. And as for those whose going forth (*pabbajjā*) is prohibited, their full ordination (*upasampadā*) is also prohibited;
this is because those such as the hand-chopped and others were mentioned specifically by way of full ordination. Therefore, it is they alone [who are meant].
This was said with reference to those whose hands have been cut off and so forth.
The commentary on the discussion of the subject matter concerning those whose hands have been cut off and so forth is finished.
The commentary on the discussion of the subject matter concerning dependence on shameless persons.
120. “Monks, dependence (nissaya) must not be given to those who are shameless.
By this, both the enjoyment of the Dhamma and the enjoyment of material goods with shameless monks or novices are prohibited, because they lack the state of being dependent.
As it is said: “Monks, a pupil should be supported and assisted by a teacher through recitation and interrogation...”

Because it is possible for even a preceptor (upajjhāya) to give formal instruction and guidance—as seen in such passages as “by exhortation and instruction”—he too must be understood as a source of dependence (nissaya) for his co-resident disciple (saddhivihārika).
Therefore, it is established that if a preceptor is shameless (alajjī), one should not live in dependence upon him.
A monk who shares equally in the right practice of monks is a "fellow" (sabhāga). His state of being so is...
“Bhikkhu-sabhāgatā”: that state of being in common with the bhikkhus. It is permissible to stay there with the intention, "I shall remain until I know [where the boundary is].

"In common with the bhikkhus" means: what is that? It is the state of possessing a sense of shame (*lajjibhāva*). Regarding the phrase, "It should be taken for seven days...": here, one who thinks, "I will stay for only seven days;

what is the use of knowing the state of being in common with the bhikkhus?"—such a person does not obtain permission to stay after having laid down the burden of the task upon learning [the boundary].
It is written: "The meaning [is as follows]. However, one who knows that he will be in the company of monks may think, "I shall go tomorrow;

what need have I for reporting my dependence (nissaya)? In such a case, he does not incur an offense by letting dawn break. If he lies down with the intention, "I shall depart before dawn breaks," and dawn rises while he is still there, it is permissible.
121. Regarding the commentary on the discussion of the grounds for dependence (nissaya-vatthu) such as traveling on a journey:

it was stated, “A bhikkhu who has set out on a long journey, being unable to obtain dependence, may live without dependence,” because living without dependence during the rainy season is explicitly prohibited in the Canon itself for one traveling on a journey during that time. This [statement]...

The period of seven days is immeasurable because it is possible to travel on a journey due to the interruption of rain and so forth, and because it is possible for one who is traveling to pass away during that time.
Regarding the phrase “on the way... there is no offense,” this refers specifically to the absence of a person to provide formal dependence (*nissaya*).
It is stated in accordance with the reading “relying upon him” (*tassa nissāya*); the meaning is “relying upon that. By the statement, “When a suitable person to provide dependence arrives,”...
It is established that this rule applies only at the time when it is absolutely necessary. It has been stated: "But during the rains retreat, because there is no arrival of anyone [else].

If he, while living on either a watery shore or a dry land shore, hears—when the commencement of the rains is near—that "a certain great elder will arrive," and if he waits for him, it is permissible. If he continues to wait...
"It is the day for entering the rains residence; let it be so, one must go there where one can obtain a preceptor.
If it is permissible to go even due to the absence of a reciter of the Pātimokkha, how much more so due to the absence of a preceptor.
Some say that if, while going, he perceives a danger to life or a danger to the holy life, he should remain right there.
122. “I am not able to take the name of the elder,” [thinking this, one] says by way of a characteristic, “So-and-so, the venerable one of such-and-such [a clan].
From the statement, “Also by clan,” it is established that it is permissible to use whatever designation they are commonly known by;
therefore, even when asked, “What is the name of your preceptor? one may speak by treating the clan as the name.
"It is established; therefore, the proclamation (anussāvana) must be performed using whichever name among the four types of names [is appropriate]," they say.
A single person may have many names; in that case, it is not permissible to use one name for the motion (ñatti) and another for the proclamation.
The proclamations must be identical both in meaning and in phrasing. In some instances...

Having stated, "Of the venerable elder Buddharakkhita," if in some places one announces simply "Buddharakkhita," some say that this is not called "omitting the announcement" because the name has not been omitted. If, after stating "Of the venerable Buddharakkhita" in some places,
one announces "Of Buddharakkhita, the venerable" in others, it is because it conforms to the wording [of the source].
Some say that one may even descend into the field itself. Some say that because of the risk of confusing the phrasing, it is not permitted during the formal proclamation (*anussāvana*).
However, if one speaks in that same manner in all places, it is permitted, as it conforms to the characteristics granted by the Blessed One.
If it is argued that it is not permitted otherwise because it contradicts those characteristics, we say no; for it conforms to the practical application (*payoga*). In that case [it is] thus; here—
If it is argued that the application [of the rule] is otherwise, we say no, because of the contradiction with the characteristics of failure. It is not in every respect;

for only the formal announcements (*sāvana*) and the causing of them to be announced (*āhāpanā*) are included in the Canon (*pāḷi*) for the purpose of clarifying its meaning. Thus, no exemption is possible regarding other types of announcements, as this would contradict the established practice (*āciṇṇakappa*).
If it is asked, "What is the measure of that [practice]?"—the measure is the teacher’s grasp [of the tradition], since that is the standard.
123. Regarding the phrase "two [kinds of] single-announcement" (*dve ekānussāvanā*), it is written in the *Gaṇṭhipada* as follows:
"'Single-announcement occurring from one side'—this refers to the act of announcement performed with one preceptor and one teacher.
The meaning is that I authorize that act of announcement by one preceptor together with various teachers; however, it is not [authorized] by various preceptors with one teacher."
The meaning of "I authorize" is as follows. Having stated it in the same way in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*, it is said:
"Beyond three [monks], it is not permissible for them to act together in any manner whatsoever. The Teacher [Dhammapāla] says: "That is correct, for the Saṅgha does not perform an act upon itself.
However, this point must be considered here. How so? When four or more persons seeking full ordination (upasampadā) are designated by the conventional term "Saṅgha"...

They do not obtain the status of a bhikkhu because they have not reached [the required age]. The Master [Buddhaghosa] states that it is not his own reasoning (*takka*) that nothing beyond that [age] is permitted, but rather that it was stated by the Blessed One after having delimited [the categories] as "three.

This same meaning, having been investigated in many ways, is also stated in the *Anugaṇṭhipada*. Likewise, it is found in the *Andhaka-aṭṭhakathā* as well. There is no difference of opinion regarding this interpretation of the meaning in all instances.
There is. However, as for this discussion in the Parivāra concerning those two who are both full twenty years of age,
yet have one preceptor, one teacher, and one formal act (*kammavācā*), such that one is fully ordained and the other is not— having shown that,
some say it is permissible if one teacher proclaims a single formal act for two or three seeking full ordination, using a single preceptor.

That is improper; for it is not possible at that moment to display the formal act (*kammavācā*) endowed with the characteristics of syllables such as laxity or hardness, because of falling into faults such as release from the vow (*vimuttadosa*).
This was said with reference to making [the components] separate; to illustrate this, [it says]:
"Three [monks] who are full twenty years of age, one preceptor for the three, one teacher, one formal act, two who are ordained."

It was not stated, "one who is not fully ordained. For if it had been stated thus, it would have been possible to exclude the three types of persons dwelling in the air and show a formal act (*kammavācā*) suitable for two persons dwelling within the boundary;
in order to prevent that undesirable consequence, the word "both" was used.

In that context, by the expression "twenty years of age," the perfection of the subject matter (*vatthusampatti*) is indicated; and because the assembly is the primary factor, by the mention of the preceptor and teacher...
The perfection of the assembly and the perfection of the proclamation during the formal act (*kammavācā*) have been shown; however, the perfection of the boundary (*sīma*) alone has not been shown.
From that, failure arises because the formal acts occur at different moments. If they were simultaneous, there would be either the perfection of both or the failure of both;
it is not possible for one to have perfection while the other has failure, because this would entail the fault of the characteristics being disjoined and so forth.
That which was stated—that both of these [monks] must indeed be within the boundary—is established because it demonstrates the successful performance of the ritual (*kamma*) for both together;
thus, it is proven that a single proclamation for two [monks] is permissible when they have one preceptor (*upajjhāya*) and one teacher (*ācariya*).

Furthermore, the simultaneous formal questioning (*samanubhāsana*) for two or three [monks] together is shown in the Canon itself (*pāḷi*), and this [explanation] accords with that. This is the view of the teachers of the Commentaries (*aṭṭhakathācariya*).
"It is neither permitted nor prohibited; it should be adopted after consideration," says the teacher; however, this contradicts the nature of things (*dhammatā*).
For this is the nature of the Buddhas: namely, that in whatever instances there is a diversity of statements, they speak what is appropriate to be said regarding those weighty matters.
In this regard, the ordination by messenger (*dūtena upasampadā*) and so forth serve as examples.
And because there is no difference here from the previously authorized *kammavācā* (formal ritual procedure), it was said, "I allow you, monks,
to perform two or three *ekānussāvana*s (single proclamations)," but it was not stated, "And furthermore, monks, it should be performed thus.
Even though there is a difference [in other cases], it should be understood according to the *kammavācā* as stated for two or many [monks] in those respective instances.
If it is asked, "Why was it not stated?"—the Teacher says: "It is not the nature of things (*dhammatā*) that one should speak regarding light matters and remain silent regarding grave ones.
However, in a certain *gaṇṭhipada* (commentary on difficult points), this is elaborated thus: "'Two [recitations] with a single proclamation' means two [acts] performed together as one proclamation.
The reading is 'by one,' meaning by one teacher. 'In the same manner as before' refers to [the phrase] 'by one or by two teachers.'"
It is exactly according to the method already stated; therefore, two or three [monks] may be announced by a single teacher (*ācariya*).

As for the reading “by two or by three,” if it is argued that this is not permissible because it was stated in the case of “different teachers and different preceptors” (*nānācariyā nānupajjhāyā*) that “this must be done by one preceptor, and certainly not by one who has no preceptor,” we reply:
it is permissible. How so? Because when there is an announcement by one person, it is called a “single announcement” (*ekānussāvana*).
Because the compound (*viggaha*) is well-known, the compound itself was stated as "at the proclamation by one" (*ekato anussāvane*) in order to show precisely what is meant by "lapsed" (*līna*).

Therefore, with reference to straightforwardness alone, the meaning is: "I allow [ordination] by a single proclamation (*ekānussāvana*), that is, by a single preceptor (*upajjhāya*); but certainly not by one who does not have a preceptor. It is with reference to this that the compound is analyzed in two ways; therefore—
Others say otherwise: "It is already established that it is not permissible for there to be various teachers or various preceptors.
This means that one may perform the formal announcement (*anussāvana*) with one preceptor for another preceptor, but I do not authorize [it] with different preceptors.
What is meant? "One teacher, or two or three persons seeking full ordination..."
It is said that it was stated: "Of two or three preceptors—I certainly do not permit this. However, in another commentary (*gaṇṭhipada*), it is explained:
"Because the analysis of the compound *ekenānussāvanena* (by one proclamation) is evident, it was stated as 'by one' in order to make that clear.
When this is said, the wise will certainly understand. If they understand it because it is already evident, what is the purpose of the word 'by one'?"
"Why is this? Although they know [the answer], because they have not attained mastery, there arises a dispute; yet it cannot be known [by them].
Furthermore, when it is said 'by one [person],' it is stated that all of that [knowledge] does not belong to him. Thus, many teachers and logicians here proliferate [their views] in various ways.
Having thoroughly examined all of this and having attended upon a family of elders (garukula),...
The meaning must be understood according to the tradition (vaṃsa). It has already been stated that "there is no difference of opinion regarding this interpretation of the meaning in all instances.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Procedure for Full Ordination (Upasampadā-vidhi-kathā-vaṇṇanā): 125.
Regarding the phrase "a leper, one with a tumor," etc., by the inclusion of "leper" and so forth, those such as those with severed hands are also included.
The ancients [say] that, therefore, by means of the phrases “you are a human” and “you are a man,” he performs the avoidance of individuals who are either capable or incapable [of progress].

By the phrases “you are free” and “you are not in debt,” he supports the second alternative among the various interpretations of meaning stated previously in the section concerning those with severed hands.
In that context, rather than stating “you are not in debt” and “you are free” in their regular order, they are stated in reverse order.
By his own word he is a free man, and not a hired servant of the king by way of food and wages. However, because he is dependent on the king, he belongs to the class of the king’s servants;
thus, in order to ask whether he belongs to the opposite class, it is said, "Are you not a king’s servant?
Otherwise, since all [others] would already be included by the mention of those afflicted by the five diseases, the others need not have been mentioned.
Alternatively, all [of them] could be so addressed.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Four Supports, etc. (128–129):

The passage beginning with “The shadow must be measured at that very moment” is stated for the purpose of knowing who are elders and who are non-elders, following the instruction to have the bhikkhus pay homage at the feet [of the senior]. It is said that the ancient reading was “cirena āgamāsī,” which means “he took a long time. Alternatively, it means “he delayed for a long time.”
130. There is no offense in sharing material goods or living together with one who has been suspended (ukkhitaka).

This means that although an offense of expiation (pācittiya) was prescribed on account of sharing and living together, there is no offense in this particular case. How is this known? From the inclusion of the term "living together" (saṃvāsa).
However, one certainly incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) on account of sharing [material goods] with one who is shameless (alajjī), but not on account of living together; for indeed...
Living together with one who is shameless is prohibited. Here, "living together" (saṃvāsa) means residing together in a dwelling sufficient for a shared bed;

it does not refer to the "communion" (saṃvāsa) mentioned in the passage, "He is one who has committed a pārājika offense and is no longer in communion. This kind of living together is not permitted with one who has been suspended (ukkhitaka).
However, certain forms of living together with one who is shameless are permitted. The other [kind of communion] is indeed excluded from the enjoyment of the Teaching (dhamma-sambhoga). This...
However, the sutta beginning with “one who has been suspended disrobes” is stated here because it shares the common characteristic of illustrating who may or may not be ordained.
Furthermore, purity from an offense comes only through the sequence of practice, not by disrobing;
therefore, even if an ordained bhikkhu commits an offense as slight as a minor transgression (dubbhāsita), he might later disrobe and then return.

"He attains [the status of one who has been ordained]"; he is purified only by confessing that offense and not otherwise—this is for the purpose of showing the purification of one who has been ordained.

In the case of one who has been suspended for the non-confession of an offense unique to him (asādhāraṇāpatti), if his sex changes and he emerges from the offense, and his original sex subsequently arises again, there is only the state of being of a different communion (nānāsaṃvāsakatā);
the same applies even in the case of one who returns after having left the Order (vibbhama). This is according to the method already stated.
If it is argued that [the act] has not been completed because he did not emerge from the ordination, [we reply: no, because his gender has changed.

It is not because the legal act (*kamma*) was rendered impure by his renunciation (*vibbhama*). For if the act were rendered impure, there would follow the consequence of a failure in the legal procedure for re-ordination. Yet, there is neither a failure of the procedure nor a cessation of the procedure. Furthermore, one who is not ordained due to renunciation does not invalidate the legal act through the state of belonging to a different community (*nānāsaṃvāsaka*).
This is because it was spoken by the Teacher (Dhammissara) with direct impact. For that very reason, the future tense was used in the phrase "you will see.

However, it should be understood that this was said for the purpose of demonstrating all these various interpretations of the meaning: that such a householder—like one who has laid down the training or one undergoing probation—remains in the state of an unordained person through acts such as renunciation (vibbhama), even while standing on the ground of a regular monk (pakatatta).
However, one who was previously suspended for a specific offense, having changed his gender and then returned to his original gender, should be questioned again with "Do you see [the offense]?
If he says, "Yes, I see it," he should be reinstated.
He should not be told "Confess [the offense]," because he has already been cleared by the change of gender. One who was suspended for that same offense should be questioned: "What is your remedy?"
If he says, "It has been done," and [the other] says, "Yes, it has been done," he should be reinstated.
Some say that if he says, "There is no remedial action to be performed by me," he should not be reinstated. This procedure applies to an offense that is not shared, not to one that is shared.
Regarding this, some say that for one who has been suspended, the legal act is nullified simply by the change of sex. Having investigated this, one should adopt what is most appropriate.
The Teacher [states this]. However, in the *Anugaṇṭhipada*, it is said:

"The use by one who is shameless (*alajjin*) is to be delimited by way of giving with one's own hand and so forth; the claim of those who say, 'It is permissible to give with one's own hand to a shameless person after pointing out that he fulfills the qualities conducive to harmony (*sāraṇīya-dhamma*) and so on,' must be refuted.
How? According to the legal decision (*vinicchaya*) that it is not permissible to give with one's own hand to one who has been suspended (*ukkhitaka*)."

"However, it is indeed permissible to cause [it] to be given. Although there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) due to the consumption by one who is shameless, nevertheless, this person is not shameless;
therefore, with reference to the state of being entirely free from offense, it is said: "There is no offense in sharing food or living together.
How is this understood? It should be understood through the meaning, because of the fact that sugarcane juice and molasses are for a seven-day period and for life respectively.
Having formed the perception that "it is permissible to eat sugarcane at an improper time," and having eaten it, one does not see the *pācittiya* offense arising from that cause;
this is due to the perception that "it is permissible. Or again, one who, having admitted to having committed an offense, persists in the resolve, "I will not make amends"—these two:
‘One who intentionally commits an offense, conceals an offense, and goes upon a wrong path—such a person is called one devoid of shame.
Since they do not fall away from the characteristics thus stated, they are not devoid of shame; therefore, [the text says]: “He who does not perform the confession and remediation of offenses...”

By this specific statement—“there is no offense in engaging in transactions such as consumption with him”—the principle is established that even with another person, although there is no trading in money, there is nonetheless an offense through buying and selling;
and the principle is also given that with the [other] five, there is no offense whatsoever. Thus, having distinguished [the cases] regarding those points where an offense occurs—
And because it is not stated here in that way according to the word [of the text], there is no sharing of food with one who is shameless (*alajjī*).

However, others say: "Even when being associated with, one associates with the faction of the shameless"—by this means as well, the meaning should be sought by correlating each respective point everywhere.
But the Teachers do not speak thus. It is said: "If I do not see..."
Because it is stated, “He speaks [thus], he should not be ordained,” it is established that even for one who has disrobed, the offenses previously committed do not cease.
For this very reason, teachers cause the renunciation of training to be performed only after having had the offense confessed.

Furthermore, regarding the statement, “There is no offense in sharing or living together,” it should be suspected that this refers to one who does not perceive an existing offense previously committed.

Some say it was stated for the purpose of making known that [the offense] has been pacified. "You will see" was said with reference to the future because, being a householder, it was not permitted to teach [the Dhamma].

"Having ordained you, you will see" was said with reference to the future rather than saying simply "you will see," because there remains the business to be done by means of probation (parivāsa) and so forth;
"having reinstated you" refers to the process of rehabilitation (abbhāna). In this regard:
Because there is nothing further to be done, it is said, "Do you see [it]? All of this is stated with reference to a formal admission (*paṭijānana*) in every respect.
Even in a single instance, if one does not admit again, one should not live in communion (*saṃvāsa*) with that person in accordance with the offense;

what is meant is that this is due to their state of shamelessness (*alajjibhāva*). Regarding the phrase "by views" (*diṭṭhiyā*) and so forth, "reinstatement" (*osāraṇa*) refers to performing the same ritual acts (*samānakamma*) and so on.
The meaning is "the act of performing. Regarding "there is no offense in communal association": there is no offense in communal association with one who has been suspended. Why?
Because the formal act of suspension has been rendered inoperative due to the suspended person’s status as a layperson; for that very reason, it is said, "when harmony cannot be obtained.
Now, some say this refers to what must be done regarding his status as a monk. In both cases, the procedure for the inoperativeness of the formal act is the same.
They know this; therefore, in all instances, one should speak after having carefully observed what is appropriate and what is inappropriate.
This Khandhaka, named "Going-forth," contains various methods and constitutes the very root of the Teaching.
"Having known, he makes it known correctly to another;
therefore, his authority lies within the teaching of the Sage.
The commentary on the Mahākhandhaka is finished.
2. Commentary on the Uposatha Khandhaka: Explanation of the Discourse on the Permission for Assembling, etc. 132–3.
“At that time”: having laid down the burden of reciting the Pātimokkha as his own exhortation, [the Blessed One] addressed the bhikkhus alone...
Having authorized the performance of the Uposatha separately, it was established by way of a formal agreement (*samaya*). Who, then, is "he"?

It is the time when the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) sufficient for the recitation of the Pātimokkha at the medium-length *Bodhi* [recitation] have been completed. For this very reason he said, "He should authorize them to recite the Pātimokkha.

And with the words, "And thus, monks, it should be recited," [the Buddha spoke] both out of a desire to establish the recitation of the Nidāna and for the purpose of indicating the limit of the recitation of the training rules.

It has been stated. Otherwise, since the sequence for reciting all the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) was already shown by the words, "And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule thus," the statement now, "And furthermore, monks, it should be recited thus," would become redundant;
moreover, this was said with reference to the Uposatha ceremony for the entire Saṅgha.
134. “What if the venerable ones... [as before] ...should assemble? This is the application of the office for many.

Therein, although the monk is addressed as “sir” (*sāmi*) by virtue of the Vinaya, he says “Venerable sir, may it please you to hear me” in order to show that he is not merely the senior of the Saṅgha, and to demonstrate his fitness for speech worthy of respect from the Saṅgha.
In that context, if he himself is the elder, he should address the monk as “friend” (*āvuso*).
It is appropriate. How is this understood? At the time of the Buddha, it was rare indeed to find a senior monk of the Saṅgha who was incompetent.
And since the Blessed One himself demonstrated this in the application of all formal acts (*kammavācā*) by saying, "Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs," is that so?
Yes, it is so, because he showed it thus. With reference to the Saṅgha, even the senior monk of the Saṅgha must say, "Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs."

This is because the application of the formal procedure (*kammavācā*) for Mahākassapa is seen in the phrase "Friend" (*āvuso*) used with reference to a bhikkhu, and because the application of the purification fast-day (*pārisuddhi-uposatha*) is seen in the elder bhikkhu’s statement, "I am pure, friends.
The phrase "If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha" is said with reference to obstacles to performing the fast-day ceremony that may arise subsequently. Regarding the fast-day...
Because it possesses many varieties in its form, he said, "One should recite the Pātimokkha. At this point, he concluded the motion (*ñatti*).

For the Uposatha ceremony consists precisely of a formal act with a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*). If it is argued that this is not so because a third proclamation is impossible here, we say no;
for it is unlike other formal acts consisting of a motion followed by four proclamations (*ñatticatutthakamma*), since in this case the phrase "Let the Sangha hear me" is not initiated four times.

If it is argued that because it is dissimilar to other *ñattidutiyakamma* (formal acts consisting of a motion and one proclamation), even this *ñattidutiyakamma* should not be performed [as such], we say no;

for a *ñattidutiyakamma* may also be carried out in another way. To explain: while certain *ñattidutiyakamma* may appropriately be performed by means of a mere *apalokana* (informal announcement), others may not appropriately be performed otherwise. How is this known? This very *uposatha* formal act serves as the indicator.
Regarding the question, “What is the preliminary duty for the Saṅgha?”—this should not be stated after the motion (*ñatti*) has been concluded, for it is performed prior to the motion itself.
Therefore, should one say: “Let the venerable Saṅgha hear me; what is the preliminary duty for the Saṅgha, if there is one for the Saṅgha”?
Even so, it should not be said, because that [duty] is not included within the motion.
If it is argued that, for lack of purpose, this should not be stated in all cases, we say no;

for it must be stated precisely where it has been handed down, as it depends upon the subsequent words—this is what is meant. If the Saṅgha or an individual performs the Uposatha without performing these preliminary duties, they incur an offense upon exceeding the field of suspension (*ṭhapanakkhetta*).
For when that field has been exceeded, the sweeping, the preparation of seats, water, and lamps [are no longer required].

There is the release from the offense. Because that offense arises from the failure to perform the duties that ought to be performed prior to the Uposatha ceremony, it does not depend upon the conclusion of the formal act (*kamma*), unlike the offense of intentional lying regarding what has occurred here [in the assembly].
Therefore, the monk reciting the Pātimokkha, wishing to say, "Venerable sirs, announce your purity," first [examines] the condition of whether they are pure or impure.
He causes [the monks] to remember the preliminary duties (*pubbakicca*). For when these have been performed, the conditions are pure; when they have not been performed, the conditions are impure.
Therefore, with the intention of considering both cases, he does not say "done" or "not done," but rather asks, "What is the Saṅgha’s preliminary duty?
In that regard, first, for the sake of showing the sequence for declaring purity (*pārisuddhi*) in the case where it has not been done, [he says] later: "For whom..."
“If there should be an offense, one should disclose it,” he says; and on the side of those who have committed one, he will say, “If there is no offense, one should remain silent.
Venerable sirs, announce your purity. For what reason? Because I shall recite the Pātimokkha.
And here, by not referring to the present tense in the phrase “I am reciting,” but rather by referring to the future tense in the phrase “I shall recite,” [the time for confession is indicated].

Some say that the phrase "I shall recite the Pātimokkha" was spoken with reference to the recitation of the Pātimokkha mentioned here [in the Vinaya] in the passage, "Now he should authorize the recitation of the Pātimokkha for them.

However, because it is stated, "Bhikkhus, there are these five recitations of the Pātimokkha," it refers to that which is called the recitation of the Nidāna occurring at the conclusion of the currently recited Pātimokkha: "Is there [anyone...]"?

The statement "I shall recite the Pātimokkha" is spoken here with reference specifically to the field of offenses (*āpattikhettam*), because it includes the threefold proclamation beginning with "Are you pure?
and so forth; for the term for the whole can be applied to its parts, and since that very proclamation constitutes the field of offenses.
For when this is said, the field of offenses will subsequently follow; therefore, all of you who fear offenses should [attend] from the very beginning.
The meaning "announce your purity" (*pārisuddhiṃ ārocetha*) is possible.
However, when spoken in the present tense as "Venerable sirs, announce your purity," that very statement is not possible, because the announcement must first be desired;

all the more so is the statement "I shall recite the Pātimokkha" impossible, since there is no prior performance of that announcement. This method applies to the *santi* [the presence of the assembly].
It is appropriate to announce an offense, but not to remain silent; for silence is reached at the conclusion of the formal act (*kamma*).

Even so, it is indeed appropriate in this case. For the reciter of the *Pātimokkha*, having seen the monks remaining silent without having disclosed their mutual offenses, becomes one whose purity has been announced by that very silence, and [he says]: "Let the Sangha listen..."
“May it be so for me, Bhante,” he said, and began the recitation of the Pātimokkha.
Here it may be asked: since it was previously stated, “The Saṅgha should perform the Uposatha;
it should recite the Pātimokkha,” shouldn’t it likewise be said here, “The Saṅgha will perform the Uposatha; it will recite the Pātimokkha”? Why, then, [is it stated] in terms of the individual...

Regarding the phrase "the recitation" (*uddesa*), because it is a defining characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), it should be stated exactly according to its literal meaning. Nevertheless, should one say, "I will perform the Uposatha; I will recite the Pātimokkha"?
It should not be so stated, because it would contradict the defining characteristic and lead to an undesirable consequence.
For only by means of the recitation for an individual is the Uposatha performed for the Saṅgha; it is not [performed] merely by an individual performing the Uposatha.

And since he himself will perform that [recitation] and not the Saṅgha, the undesirable consequence (aniṭṭha) arises once again. When it was said, “Listen,” because of the fear of the consequence of a lack of mental concord, they said, “We listen.
If it is argued that one should have said, “We shall listen,” because it was said, “I shall recite”? It should not be so said;
rather, because there is no intention to regard it as a ground for an offense, one should simply say, “We listen. By means of a single word alone—
His intention was that it had been exceeded. If this is so, for what purpose was it undertaken by all?

It is for the purpose of preventing the contingency of there being no mental concord (acittasāmaggī) on the part of one who has committed [an offense] by means of the non-common expression "I shall recite.
By the phrase "by one who remembers," he shows that the conscious lying (sampajānamusāvāda) possesses a mind. [It is] an obstructive factor (antarāyiko dhammo).
“Spoken by the Blessed One”: thus he demonstrates the great danger of this lie, which—though originating from non-action and being so minor—is nevertheless [grave].

Why must it be confessed by one who desires purity—that is, by one desiring the purity characterized by the state of a householder (which includes both the state of non-offense regarding a remaining offense and the state of a householder itself)? Because it would otherwise not avoid becoming an obstacle.

Because it is a condition for living in comfort. Here, the phrase "today is the Uposatha of the fifteenth" is not stated because, with the intention of specifying the day later on, it was not mentioned [at that time]. Thus, those monks recited it on every day. 135.
By the words "this is the beginning," only the *sīla-pātimokkha* (the Pātimokkha of virtue) is meant, even though the *gantha-pātimokkha* (the Pātimokkha as a text) is intended.
“Of five or” is stated according to those mentioned in the *mātikā*. “One who has not committed [an offense]” is a teaching expressed by way of reference to the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*).
However, in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*, it says: “‘Let him perform the *uposatha*’—up to this point is the motion (*ñatti*).

The threefold proclamation, namely the triad of statements beginning with ‘Whosoever may have an offense...’, and finally ‘A second time, a third time I ask you... is called the formal announcement (*anussāvanā*).”
This is twofold: therein, the first is for one who has remembered the offense while sitting [in confession], and the second is for one who has not remembered it, for the purpose of reminding.
It is stated as "by way of speech" (*vacīdvāra*) in its manifest sense;

although it is also performed by bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*), because there is no bodily action (*kāyakamma*), it must be made manifest solely by verbal intimation (*vacīviññatti*). "In the midst of the Saṅgha," and so forth.
This is indeed a statement of definition. If one is seated in the midst of the Saṅgha for the purpose of performing the Saṅgha’s Uposatha, it should be declared in that midst of the Saṅgha.
If one is seated in the midst of a group (gaṇa) for the purpose of performing the group’s Uposatha, it should be declared in that midst of the group.
If one wishes to perform the Uposatha of pure confession (pārisuddhi-uposatha) in the presence of only a single person, it should be declared openly to that one individual. By this, it is not only...
This false speech occurs specifically in the midst of the Saṅgha;

however, even in the case of a *gaṇa-uposatha*—where, despite the absence of the prescribed procedure such as "Venerable sirs, announce your purity"—if one who has committed an offense intends to perform the *uposatha* but does so while remaining silent without having announced it, he incurs an offense of intentional lying (*sampajāna-musāvāda*). This is the meaning of this [passage].
"Logicians say that this is a statement of characteristics (lakkhaṇavacana) by way of manifestation," they claim;
their intention being that otherwise it would not have been stated as "in the midst of the Saṅgha. "It was stated with the purpose of announcing [the offense]," says the Teacher;
for one who announces, intending "I announce to the Saṅgha," while manifesting it, is said to manifest it in the midst of the Saṅgha. Of oneself...
“Proclaiming in the midst of a group while sitting on both sides [is prohibited].

When one proclaims with the intention, “I shall proclaim it to one who is like me,” this is called “proclaiming to a single person. It should be understood that the further analysis of a term already analyzed previously is for the purpose of illustrating a specific nuance of meaning.
Having stated, “Monks, you must not [do so] daily... [otherwise there is] an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),” he then said, “Monks, I authorize [it] on the Uposatha day...”
The phrase "to recite the Pātimokkha" indicates that the offense of *dukkaṭa* occurs only on a day that is not an Uposatha; however, on an Uposatha day, it is permissible even if it is done daily.
Therefore, those monks, having recited it on the fourteenth day, recited it again on the fifteenth day;
thus he said, "once a fortnight. In this context, by the former [statement], he indicates that the day of concord is indeed the Uposatha day.
By rejecting both [cases] on the eighth day, he prevents the over-extension of the rejection to every single day.

What is meant? If the Saṅgha has been split but becomes united on the first day of the fortnight (pāṭipada), one who performs the Uposatha of unity on that day incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for both [acts]; thus it is said that by being united, one is prevented from both.

If the *sāmaggī-uposatha* (unification uposatha) is not performed daily, it must be performed day and night. And if, within that fortnight, the regular (*pakati*) uposatha is not performed daily, it must be performed day and night.
Furthermore, if within that fortnight the regular uposatha has not been formally assigned (*anuddiṭṭha*), it follows that the *sāmaggī-uposatha* must be performed.
If you argue that this should not be understood as an exceptional rule (*apavāda-naya*), we say no.

Because it would lead to an undesirable consequence. What is meant? Having performed the concordance *uposatha* on the day of concordance, when the regular *uposatha* day arrives again within that same fortnight, the regular *uposatha* should not be performed [again].
This is an exception (*apavāda*). An exception prevents the application of a general rule (*ussagga*) in cases other than those for which it is specifically intended.
"To what extent, then, is there concord (*sāmaggī*)?"—this is the intended meaning here: "What is this so-called concord? It is the assembly of those who are like-minded (*sabhāga*).
And who are those called 'like-minded'? Are they all those who share the same Dhamma, or do they become 'like-minded' merely by sharing the same monastery?
In that regard, if concord among those who share the same Dhamma is what is called concord, then [it applies] to all of them, even when they have been separately divided.
Harmony is to be desired. By way of the residence, it is meant "those who share a single dwelling. Otherwise, it would follow that harmony exists only within a single dwelling.
"May you not come" means "may you not fail to come.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Authorization of the Boundary (*Sīmānujānanakathāvaṇṇanā*).

138. Having rejected the unity [of the Saṅgha] on the basis of those who have gone to a single residence (*ekāvāsa*), the Blessed One, wishing to authorize it on the basis of those who have gone to a single boundary (*ekasīma*), said: "I authorize you, monks, to establish a boundary. Now, he might wish to state the delimitation of the residence.
To this extent, a single residence is as far as a single boundary. Thus: "I authorize you, monks, to establish a boundary."

One might say so. Therefore, it should be understood that here the delimitation of a single residence (*ekāvāsa*) does not occur by way of a boundary fixed by formal authorization (*anuññātabaddhasīmā*), but rather occurs only by way of a precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*). If one asks how this is to be known, it is from the Canon itself, as it says:

"Now at that time, the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan son spent the rains retreat alone in two residences... [omitted] ...because of a single intention" (*ekādhippāya*). Otherwise, [the text would not have stated this].

The interruption of the rains-residence (*vassaccheda*) would entail an undesirable consequence; how so? If unity were established solely by means of residing in a single dwelling, it would not be possible in cases of many dwellings or non-dwellings.
Consequently, one going to that [other] dwelling would perform the Uposatha outside [the original boundary]. This would contradict the Canon, which states:
"Monks, on the day of the Uposatha, one should not go to a non-dwelling where there are monks," and so forth—even when the Saṅgha is present in a non-dwelling.

Because the Uposatha is not to be performed [in such cases]. Even if concord (*sāmaggī*) is obtained in what is not a single residence (*anāvāsa*), one cannot say, "Concord exists to the extent that there is a single residence.
Therefore, since the former method is entirely rejected by the latter, it should be understood that concord exists even on the basis of being in different residences.
This applies in cases such as: "Having said, 'Let us perform that formal act (*kamma*'), they did not do so," and so forth.
They say that because one looks toward the future as well, it is not permissible when it is said, "Let us do [it]. It is written:
"It is permissible to proclaim the boundary markers even without first purifying the boundary. At the minimum limit, it is eight-and-a-half *ratana*s in height, the size of an elephant.
Regarding the statement, "If only one is bound, it should not be done," here [it refers to] "below the four mountain peaks in the four directions..."

Because they rest upon a stone that is like a flat slab, even though they are in a state of being joined together, if there is no connection with them above the ground, it is permissible to designate them as "not included" (abbohārika) based merely on their connection with the ground below.
For this very reason, it is said: "Even a back-slab, though very large, is reckoned simply as a stone. [This applies] below the ground level.

Regarding its great size, it is stated in the *Anugaṇṭhipada*: "When its magnitude is considered, it is indeed a mountain. Regarding the phrase "a heap of sand made by piling it up," the Elder Dhammasiri says:
"If grass, shrubs, and trees grow upon it, it becomes a mountain; [if they do not], it is not so," says the Elder Upatissa.

Regarding "stone," they say that even stone made of plaster (*sudhā*) is permissible; this should be investigated, as it is excluded from the category of bricks. "The measure of thirty-two *palas* of a lump of clay" refers to its weight, not to a numerical count of measures. "That too" refers to a stone that has risen up like a stump.
Regarding the phrase "even the mere sign of four or five trees," the word *nimitta* (sign) does not appear in some versions.

Here, if there are three heartwood trees and two sapless trees, a plurality of heartwood trees should be desired. It is said: "A cemetery also comes under the designation of 'a forest' here because it is naturally grown.
However, some say: "If two out of the four have heartwood within them, it is sufficient."
If the inner lining is thick or even, it is permissible. Therefore, they say that even if there are many [layers], it is permissible provided two have an inner lining.

Regarding the phrase "in the latter part": here they say, "It is permissible because it has gone from the place bound by these [folds]; likewise, even on a long journey, it is permissible because the place reached is different from the place where it was taken.
Regarding "every half-month" (*anvaddhamāsa*): here it is written as "a half-month followed by," or "the following of a half-month. [The term] *antaravāsaka*...
Because it is stated, "it becomes cool," some say that it is permissible to perform [the rite] only in water of such a measure.
By the word "becomes cool," the defining characteristic of a river is stated according to its lower limit.
In such a river, at whatever place the water flows for four months—whether covering little or much—one may perform [the rite] even while standing in shallow water.

Some say it is permissible. They say that because it is stated that "the river-mark is at the place where the water flows," if the water flows for that same distance beyond the bridge, it is indeed a river.
Water standing in natural ponds and the like may be made a mark even if it is not immediately adjacent, by using the term "natural pond" and so forth.
It is like a marker at the boundary on the far bank of a river.
If that area later reaches the status of a village field, it is permissible to establish another boundary there. "To be removed" means that which is to be taken away after being lifted up.
"Having set aside the precinct of the boundary for monasteries with unbonded boundaries" means "having set aside the space to be established in the future."
It is written. Regarding the phrase "but by those who have reached the boundary marker," they say:

"Because there is no purpose for all [monks] to come when one person intends to perform the act within the boundary for half [the assembly], it is stated 'by those who have reached the boundary marker'; and that is according to the proper custom.
It is also written: "Non-arrival is permissible because, since the boundary has not been formally bound, there is no such thing as a 'deficient assembly' (vagga)."

It is stated: "When one is standing in another village precinct at the time of designating the signs (*nimitta*), and when the boundary for common affiliation (*samānasaṃvāsaka-sīmā*) is being formally established, there is no purpose for coming.
Regarding the phrase "the signal of a drum," it is written: "having said, 'We shall bring the formal establishment to its conclusion.
By this, it is established that it is permissible at such a time. What is the purpose of this? It is for the sake of creating ease (*sukhakaraṇattha*).

Some say that the word "first" was spoken for the purpose of showing that if an obstacle arises at the time of binding the great boundary, a comfortable dwelling can still be achieved even with that much [of the assembly], rather than causing the fatigue of a large gathering of people for the sake of making it easy for fewer.
How is it known that it is not permissible beyond that point? Because a formal act of the Saṅgha (saṅghakamma) has twenty members as its maximum requirement.
If one includes twenty-one bhikkhus together with the smith, it is permissible. This should be understood as the extent required for sitting comfortably.
Some say that if others are also designated using that same boundary marker and they tie [the ropes], it is permissible.

However, regarding the passage beginning "But when they are tied thus... the boundary line divides the village field," the delimitation of the unity of the community is not based on the dwelling place.
However, it is stated for the purpose of showing [the boundary] by way of its limits. The phrase "having placed [it] on a stone that has reached the sign" is stated subsequent to that mobile sign.
From this point on, there is a sequence of difficult points (*gaṇṭhipada*): they will not be able [to remove it];
that is, failing to observe non-separation, those who strive with the thought, "We shall abolish [the status of] one who is of the same communion," will not be able to abolish it.
“‘The measure of one ratana’ is stated because it is easy to understand as an interval; even a mere finger’s breadth is permissible.
Tying [the rope] starting from the boundary of the plot (khaṇḍasīma) is the established practice. By following the established practice, confusion is removed.
‘In a hut or house’ means in a hut-dwelling or an underground dwelling. ‘Like a mortar’ means like a small pit for a ground-mortar. ‘In front’ means—”
Some say it was said with reference to the ground-floor cell.

"It does not descend below" means that because signs have been established and marked out beyond the wall, it does not descend into the space below; the meaning is that it is a multi-storied mansion (pāsāda) built above. "Attached to the wall" means those things depending on the wall.
It is said that even these things attached to the wall are not called "a single continuous unit. "The entire mansion stands within the boundary" means it is a single continuous unit.
Let it be so, or let it not be. The mountain called *tālamūlaka* (palm-root) becomes gradually thinner. "Sky-cleft" (*ākāsapabbhāra*) refers to a cleft that is unenclosed.
A "hollow rock" (*susirapāsāṇa*) is a cave. "Inside the mountain" (*antopabbata*) means inside a cave within the mountain.
However, with reference to the door, it is said later "from this side" (*orato*); the intention is that in every respect one enters from outside the boundary of the cave.

"Having cleared the great boundary (*mahāsīma*)" means that even if it is situated far away, as long as it is within the boundary, reaches the boundary, or is connected to the boundary, one must stand without touching it;
this is the intended meaning. If this is so, then it should be said: "It is permissible to perform the formal act (*kamma*) after removing those who depend upon it.
In the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* as well, it says only this much: "It should be done after clearing the boundary."

It has been stated. Some say that even the Great Elders (mahātherā) said, “It must be cleared. There is also a reading: “The formal act (kamma) should be performed after clearing the great boundary (mahāsīma).
Furthermore, since he will later say, “In the manner already stated,” some maintain that the common reading alone is superior.
Regarding the phrase “in the former manner”: the meaning is that even when [the monks] have risen from within the broken boundary (khaṇḍasīmā) and descended into the great boundary.
It is not permissible to perform [the ritual] after having caused [a tree] to be uprooted. Why? Because it remains within [the territory].

According to others, the root that has gone into the earth beneath the tree constitutes a fragmentary boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*), or it is "not to be reckoned" (*abbhohārika*). However, when [the tree] is cut in the middle, a root situated in the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) belongs to the great boundary itself;
a root situated in a fragmentary boundary belongs to that very fragmentary boundary, because of its dependence on the soil, moisture, and so forth belonging to that [boundary].

It is said: “Because it has been supported. Having stated, “It is permissible to perform the formal act (kamma) while sitting on a tree that has grown up after the boundary was established, just as in the case of a house built within the subsequent boundary,” they give the reason:

“It is not permissible to perform it while sitting on a tree that stood at the time of the original demarcation, because [the tree] did not come into existence within the upper boundary. This being the case, there would be a re-ascension at the time of the binding.
It follows that [the tree] does not exist [as such] before, but arises only at the time of being bound.

However, a tree that has already grown later is nonetheless reckoned as a boundary because it is connected to that [original site]; the same should be understood for a tree that grew there previously.
Because of the expression “whatever [there may be],” even grass and so forth are included. Even the Great Elders (Mahātherā) perform the rite only after clearing away the grass.
140. Because there is a corner in the middle, it is therefore said, “from corner to corner. They say, “And one incurs an offense because of its being unintentional.
“It carries across” means it covers over. Which [carries across]? The boundary.
Some say this was stated considering that a boat smaller than the one described by the words “by the very smallest... [it] carries across” does not count as a boat; however, that is not correct.
Because that [measure] is also intended in the section concerning boat-merchandise in the second *pārājika*. Some say it was stated according to the weight-carrying capacity of a middle-sized man.

The Teacher’s conjecture is that it was for the purpose of avoiding the fault mentioned—namely, "or she might go alone to the other side of a river"—since the possibility of crossing a river exists even for bhikkhunīs.
In both cases, the word *dhura* (burden/weight) is taken; by that...
The Uposatha day is specifically prescribed for the purpose of avoiding obstacles to the Uposatha.
And here, "boat" refers to a standard-sized boat intended for general use—a fixed boat—and not a raft; such is the Teacher’s opinion.
The meaning is: "constructed by cutting down a tree. If it is within one village precinct, standing inside all the boundary markers...
The monks should be appointed after they have come within arm’s reach. If it is a field consisting of separate villages, even not coming [to the assembly] is permissible.
An island is not included merely by the marking of boundaries on both banks; therefore, the boundaries must indeed be marked on the island itself.
They say: "A monk sitting downstream on the river subverts the formal act; for the river flows only upstream."
The commentary on the discussion regarding the authorization of the boundary (*sīmānujānanakathāvaṇṇanā*) is finished.
Commentary on the discussion regarding the Uposatha hall and so forth (141):
Because of the statement, “Whatever dwelling or... cave the Saṅgha desires,” it is not only upon the earth that [the boundary is established].
It is established that a boundary is permitted even above monasteries (*vihāra*) and the like, because the observance-day ritual (*uposathakamma*) is the primary concern.
If it is asked, "How is it known that the boundary has that as its primary purpose? It is because it was permitted specifically for that purpose;

and because, although the status of being "in common affiliation" (*samānasaṃvāsā*) is already established by the formal agreement (*sammuti*), there is the separate statement "under one observance-day ritual" (*ekūposathā*). [The text continues: "Setting aside the observance-day ritual, the remaining rituals..."
It is written: "They are of common residence. The reading of the Pāḷi is: "Having removed one [from the group]. 142. "Of how many years?
This is said with reference to those who are in concord within a single boundary (*sīmā*). Otherwise, for those situated in different boundaries, the hearing [of the proclamation] is the criterion;
even within a single boundary, for those standing beyond arm's reach, the hearing alone is the criterion.
One incurs what is undesirable. In that context, "whether authorized or unauthorized" refers to authorization for the Uposatha hall, not to authorization for the boundary (*sīmā*).
How is this known? By the context, by the subsequent prescription regarding the giving of consent (*chandadāna*), and by the subsequent prescription regarding the giving of purity (*pārisuddhi*).
Herein, it should be understood that the first [reason] precludes the first undesirable consequence, and the latter [reasons] preclude the latter.
“Face of the Uposatha” means the place for the Uposatha. It is written: “Of the face of the Uposatha means of the place of the Uposatha hall.
How is it known that it is permissible to designate any signs whatsoever?
Because only this much has been stated: “First, the signs must be designated; having designated the signs... Since they were stated first, they are not [here] being mentioned.
Why? That, however, is not the reason; for there is no indolence in the teaching of the Buddhas.
