Some say that at the time of abolishing the boundary (*sīmā*), the abolition of the boundary is accomplished only after first abolishing the Uposatha hall.

The Teacher says: "That is incorrect, because the authorization of the Uposatha hall is established even when the boundary is unbonded; therefore, that is not a valid argument. *Uposathamukha* refers to the Uposatha hall.
The teachers say: "The declaration of the sign for the commencement of the Uposatha should be performed according to the method prescribed for the boundary (sīmā).

Some maintain that it is permissible for even a single person to declare it. They say: 'Whether it be a palace or one of the other structures such as a pavilion, the formal proclamation (kammavācā) must simply state, "the commencement of the Uposatha.
It is recorded that 'an ancient dwelling' refers to the original dwelling."
The characteristic is that one says, "There is the measure of a jar.
Commentary on the Discussion on the Allowance for the Non-separation Boundary (Avippavāsa-sīmānujānanakathāvaṇṇanā), §§143–144:
Alternatively, there is the reading "manamhi vūḷho. In this context, "manamhi vūḷho" means "I have been carried away by the mind" (*manaṃ vūḷho amhi*).
"Excluding the village and the vicinity of the village" means excluding what is reckoned as the village—that is, the interior of the house—and the vicinity of the village.
Some say that "village" refers to an enclosed village, while "vicinity of the village" refers to an unenclosed one;
however, this contradicts the Aṭṭhakathā. Therefore, "village" here refers to dwellings, streets, and so forth.
The term "vicinity of a village" (*gāmūpacāra*) is stated with reference to places that qualify as a boundary (*parikkhepa*). However, there are many different ways this is recited here.
What does that matter? One should accept it in such a way that the canonical text (*pāḷi*) and the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) harmonize, after having thoroughly examined both.

[In this regard,] the previous formal act (*kammavācā*) for monks is not permissible if [the area] is included within the village and its vicinity, or within a common residence boundary (*samānasaṃvāsaka-sīmā*).

It is appropriate [to include] the "non-separation boundary" (*avippavāsa-sīmā*) upon a formally agreed-upon [boundary]. But where only the forest itself has been agreed upon, why is it not permissible there?
If it is argued that in such a case the statement, "except for the village and the vicinity of the village," is purposeless—this is replied:
it is indeed so; however, that statement [is necessary] because of the risk of omitting the formal proclamation (*anussāvana*).
By this very intention, it might have been said that "the previous *kammavācā* is not valid. Or rather, it was stated because there is an absence of two *kammavācās* for a single purpose.

If it is argued: "Since it was stated that 'they do not serve as complements to one another's *kamma*,' would this same procedure apply even to two separate Saṅghas belonging to different fraternities (*nānāsaṃvāsaka*)?"
One does not incur an offense because receiving and storing [food] have been permitted; because [the offenses of] disparaging and so forth apply without distinction;

and because it depends merely upon the cessation of the formal act (*kamma*). "Of that" means of the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs. "They do not make the proclamation of the formal act incomplete" means they do not invalidate the formal act.
"In this case" refers to the phrase "except for the village. "If the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsa-sīmā*) of the bhikkhus includes both the village and the vicinity of the village..."
If it does not enter [the category of being "bound"], then why is non-separation (*avippavāsa*) authorized at the time of establishing a boundary (*sīmābandhana*) within a village? It was written:
"By way of established custom (*āciṇṇakappa*), and not with regard to any other purpose. For it is said: "In terms of its actual meaning (*atthato*), it remains unbound even outside [the village].
Since a common-residence boundary (*samānasamvāsasīmā*) established within a village does not count as part of the village itself, [it is not subject to the same restrictions].
Therefore, some [say this]. That too is reckoned as a boundary; the meaning is that it is reckoned as a non-separation boundary (*avippavāsa-sīmā*).

However, this must be investigated here: when a boundary has been tied off enclosing a village, should the formal act of non-separation (*kammavācā*) be performed while standing in a forest area for the sake of the further authorization of non-separation, or rather while standing in the village? [The answer is: while standing in the village.
"Even when a *kappiya-bhūmi* (a place where food may be prepared) has been established, [the offense] still applies.

The Teacher says: "Because it conforms to the fault of being established outside the boundary, it should not be done while standing on an *akappiya-bhūmi* (an improper place); this same principle applies to the act of abolishing [the boundary] as well.
It is said that within a *khaṇḍa-sīmā* (a partial or broken boundary), the *mahā-sīmā* (great boundary) is referred to as the "boundary of non-separation" (*avippavāsa-sīmā*) and so forth.
146. “Whichever venerable one approves of the abolition of this boundary—which is for a common residence and a single Uposatha—let him be silent.
This is the reading found in some Andhaka manuscripts and some Sinhalese manuscripts.
In some, they write first, “the abolition of this boundary,” while in others, “the abolition of this boundary [which is] for a common residence and a single Uposatha.”
Commentary on the Discussion of the Village Boundary, etc. (147).
“And that” means both the village boundary that was given after being demarcated and the other [natural] one. If it is asked, “Which is that? he says, “Natural villages,” and so forth.

The intention is that they are just like boundaries that have been formally fixed; thus, both that [demarcated] one and the other [natural] one exist. For that very reason, [it provides] the exemption from the offense of being separated from the three robes...

Some say that the singular form "labhati" (he receives) is used, which is not appropriate because [the boundary] belongs to both villages; they also employ the plural form "honti, na labhanti" (they are, they do not receive).
Regarding the statement "that one and the other," they say that the village boundary given by dividing it in the middle refers to the original villages and so forth as being undivided.
The reading is "bhikkhuvasati" (a monk dwells), though it is also written as "vasanti" (they dwell).

Because it is stated, “Then, from his standing place,” the singular number alone is appropriate. Regarding the statement, “Bhikkhus, all rivers are non-boundaries (asīmā),” what kind of boundary does this exclude?
The teachers say it excludes a fixed boundary (*baddhasīmā*), because it would involve falling under one or another of the eleven types of faulty boundaries (*vipattisīmā*).
If the river and so forth were to exist after the boundary has already been fixed, then the contingency of its exclusion arises.
Therefore, he rejects [the idea] that there is no boundary at all. Just as an entire village constitutes a village boundary (*gāmasīmā*), so too an entire river is not a boundary.

However, the teacher says: "It is not a mere conjecture [to say] that this demonstrates the diversity of boundaries, namely that for each individual monk there is a 'water-splashing boundary' (*udakukkhepasīmā*).
But as for the phrase "a water-splash all around a man of medium height," it refers to [the area] of a single river sufficient for a quorum of four or more [monks].

This was stated for the purpose of showing the delimitation of the boundary at the time of performing formal acts (*kamma*) requiring a quorum of four or more monks, such as those performed separately from the rest of the Saṅgha.

The teachers (*ācariyas*) maintain that this is also for the purpose of showing the delimitation regarding being separated or not separated from the three robes; it is like the demonstration of the delimitation of the "seven-fathom boundary" (*sattabbhantara-sīmā*).
Therefore, it is established that even in the absence of a delimitation by the throwing of water, it is permissible to perform formal acts within a river.

But this is the distinction: in that case, if he has gone by boat, it is according to the method stated regarding a boat; if he has gone by caravan, it is according to the method stated regarding a caravan.
If he has stayed for more than four months, the non-separation from the three robes should be understood according to the method stated regarding a village.
Even there, this is the distinction: if the caravan is within the range of a water-splash, the measure is the boundary of the water-splash.

Some [say this]. The teachers say that the Teacher alone is the authority. However, in the passage beginning "If there are many bhikkhus here," it was stated as "bhikkhus" rather than saying "many Saṅghas" because some wished to speak of the *adhiṭṭhāna-uposatha*, some the *gaṇa-uposatha*, and some the *saṅgha-uposatha*.

Regarding the statement "But a deficient [number] is not permitted," the Elder Upatissa says it is because of the possibility of the boundaries (*sīmā*) being broken. While they are establishing [the boundary],...
Indeed, nothing deficient should be left out. It is stated: "It is even permissible to leave it out. Regarding the phrase "but for one who is going," it is written here:
"It is permissible to perform [the act] while turning back without exceeding the limit of the water-sprinkling (udakukkhepa).

Is the statement beginning with "a motion (ñatti) in another boundary" said out of fear of a failure of the ritual (kamma) regarding the boundary, or rather out of fear regarding the assembly (parisā)? [This concerns] a single ritual act.

"Because it is impossible for there to be multiple boundaries [within a single boundary]" means: because it is impossible for a single formal act (*ekakamma*) to be performed by a Saṅgha residing within multiple boundaries;

some say it is also "because of the assembly. However, our own view is that this is not the case, as it would entail the fault already mentioned—namely, that "one fails to hear [the proclamation]. For the Master [Buddhaghosa] explains: one "fails" (*hāpeti*) when one does not bring a single formal act to completion within a single boundary.
Regarding "a branch of a tree growing on the riverbank that has entered into the river," and regarding "having hewn a stump on the riverbank," and regarding "if,
however, the bridge or the bridge-piers are established on the outer bank," and regarding "the clearing of the boundary" (sīmāsodhana),
which means bringing the handspan (hatthapāsa) within the village boundary— having separated [the area] from a tree growing within a broken boundary (khaṇḍasīmā).
It is proper to do so. Why? Because for a boat tied to a tree on the bank, the village is the support. It is also written:
"A bridge standing touching the village boundary on both sides is to be compared to a tree standing touching both the minor boundary (khaṇḍasīmā) and the great boundary (mahāsīmā).
In that regard, first of all, this must be considered in the former method: what kind of action is performed in such a place?
Does it count as having been performed within a river, or within a village boundary, or in both places?
What follows from this? If it counts as having been performed within a river, only the water-throw boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*) needs to be cleared, not the other.
If it counts as having been performed within a village boundary, the water-throw boundary need not be cleared. If it counts as having been performed in both places...
It follows as an undesirable consequence that it would be permissible to perform a single formal act (*ekakamma*) across two boundaries.
Furthermore, from that, it follows as an undesirable consequence that there would be a motion (*ñatti*) for one boundary and a proclamation (*anussāvanā*) for another;

and it also follows as an undesirable consequence that it would be permissible to perform a formal act through bodily consensus (*kāyasāmaggi*) at the site of both a fragmented boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*) and a great boundary (*mahāsīma*). To this, it is said: regarding the aforementioned formal act...
It becomes counted in both places, and one does not incur the aforementioned undesirable consequence. Why?

They say it is "because the motion (ñatti) and the proclamations (anussāvana) take place within each respective boundary, or because the officiating bhikkhus are stationed within each respective boundary.
However, this is not the reason, because it is possible to be present in both places. Rather, it is because [the act] was performed in a location where the boundaries have attained unity (ekībhāva).
This is the immovable cause. For it is appropriate to perform a formal act (*kamma*) when two river-village boundaries have become one.
If there is a river, the ocean, or a natural lake within a seven-league boundary, a monk standing therein does not count as being within that seven-league boundary.
This applies provided he has not reached the defining characteristics of the river and so forth.
Whether it be a lamp, a stone, or a tree, it is reckoned as being within seven *abbhantara*s.
If that place is one frequented by people, it is reckoned as belonging to the village field (*gāmakhettasaṅkhya*). As for what constitutes a village field:
the teachers say that from where people travel—if all [the inhabitants] travel there—it is reckoned as a separate village field.
In the later tradition, if a bridge stands without touching the location that defines the river’s boundary, it is reckoned as part of the village boundary.
If there is only one village there, one should clear that [area] and perform the ritual; if there are two villages on the two banks, one must clear both villages and then perform the ritual.
For when it is done in this way, it is considered performed for both sides. By this same method, [the procedure applies] to two rivers or to mountain lakes (*jātassara*).
And the accomplishment of a single act [of boundary-making] should be understood. This method, moreover, applies even to partial boundaries (*khaṇḍasīmā*) and great boundaries (*mahāsīmā*).
If a bridge stands touching the location characterized by a river, the water-throw boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*) must also be cleared away.
Furthermore, there is only one [valid] boundary for those situated in the air, excluding those who have gone [by vehicle] without [the ritual].
Having understood this, he points out that for a single legal act (*ekakamma*), there must be a common boundary (*sīma*).
Whether it be a single boundary, two boundaries, three boundaries,
or four boundaries— for such a case, there may be a single legal act, yet there may be a disturbance of the assembly (*parisā*).
However, there is this distinction here: for those establishing it by a river, the connection with trees and so forth outside the splash of water is not a valid limit.
For those establishing it in a village, a monk standing outside the splash of water from a tree connected to the river is not a valid limit;
within that distance, he is a valid limit. In the case of a fixed boundary (*baddhasīmā*), a monk standing within the fixed boundary is a valid limit for a tree connected to that fixed boundary.
It should be understood; for this very reason it was said: "Having cleared the boundary, the formal act (kamma) should be performed.

Furthermore, the statement, "If a bridge or the pillars of a bridge are established on the outer bank, it is not permissible to perform the act," establishes that—just as in the case of shoots and so forth—the entire boundary must be cleared.
This should be investigated. Regarding the phrase, "But at a time of excessive rain... [the following applies].
"Excessive rain" should be understood as that which occurs during the four-month [rains] period;
therefore, if there is excessive rain for all four months, the entire area submerged by the flood is indeed a river.

Alternatively, if the flood from even a single instance of excessive rain remains or flows for four months, then the entire area submerged by the flood established on the outer bank is also indeed a river. A river...

"Having overflowed from the place where it flows": this means that after the river itself, or another river, or an unprecedented area has reached the characteristics of a river according to its own course, it is permissible starting from the point where it begins to flow.
"Having overflowed the boundary of a village or town" is said with reference to a period of four months. "On a path not used for travel" refers to that very day.
It is written: "Because it is impossible to perform the act of going and returning. However, that which is stated in the *Andhakaṭṭhakathā* should not be accepted.
Why? Because that same fault would apply even in the case of a river. Regarding the phrase "tipusa, etc.," the word "etc.
includes lotuses (*kamala*), water lilies (*uppala*), and so forth. Even a pond where no [lotuses] have grown is merely reckoned as a village boundary.
The meaning is that it "goes" to what is reckoned as the village boundary of those by whom it was made;

or, if it was made by villages standing on all sides, it goes to what is reckoned as the boundary of all those villages; or, if it is a place not connected with other village fields, it goes to what is reckoned as the separate village boundary.

148. By the phrase *saṃsaṭṭhaviṭapā* ("with intermingling branches"), it indicates proximity; by that, it indicates that here "intermixture" (*sambheda*) refers to the physical overlapping of locations.

However, as it expands, it causes a confusion of boundaries (*sīmāsaṅkara*). Because it must be called a "partially bound boundary" (*ekadesabaddhasīmā*) due to its entry into the site of a previously established boundary, there is the fault of confusion.
Regarding the rule, "Monks, a boundary must not be intermixed with a boundary," [the commentary states] "first... [and so on].
"Some explain the intention [of the rule] as follows: 'Once a boundary has been bound, a boundary that one intends to bind oneself later must not overlap it.
Because there is no overlapping within a boundary already authorized, this intended meaning is consistent with the act of encompassing;
therefore, a boundary bound first must not overlap a boundary to be bound later, whether in its entirety or in part."
It is called "mixing" because one performs the formal act of appointment without demarcating the boundary-interval within the first established boundary by including its boundary-marks.
It is called "overlapping" when one completely or partially covers another person's established boundary by including its boundary-marks.
For this very reason, it says: "By one appointing a boundary, having set aside the boundary-interval," and so forth. This is the meaning.
—First, having set up the boundary markers for the boundary to be bound later, one should establish the boundary within the space between the previously bound boundary and those markers.
These two failures do not occur mutually between the boundaries of monks and nuns.
However, regarding the statement "that [boundary], when expanding, creates a confusion of boundaries," here there is only a confusion of boundaries.

He performs [the rite]. Regarding this, some say that actions performed therein do not become invalid; however, that is incorrect because the cutting of branches and shoots and the purification of the boundary have been prescribed.
Having thoroughly investigated all of this and having attended upon teachers of noble lineage, one should accept what is appropriate to be accepted and discard the rest.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Breach of the Uposatha, etc., 149:
“Monks, there are these two Uposathas. This was said because, at that time, the concordant Uposatha had not yet been authorized.
Regarding the preliminary duties for the concordant Uposatha, one should say, “Today is the Uposatha of concord,” but not during the formal ritual recitation (*kammavācā*).
The Blessed One has shown the formal application (*payoga*), and the method for reciting it according to the sequence of the Pāḷi has been shown by the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathā.
Likewise, it should be understood that the sequence for reciting the five types of Pātimokkha is established.
Regarding the statement, "If three or two recite the Pātimokkha, it is called 'united by non-Dhamma' (*adhammena samagga*)," here, while it is true that there is unity (*sāmaggī*) of the Saṅgha...
It is called "factional" (*vagga*) because, despite the establishment of concord (*sāmaggī*) according to the respective action, it exists as the opposite of concord;
thus, it is designated "concordant" (*samagga*) by way of being the opposite of factional, and "factional" by way of being the opposite of concordant.

Alternatively, it should be understood that it is so stated because of the possibility of formal acts for a group (*gaṇakamma*) and the like occurring uniquely, and because of the possibility of that [act] being either concordant or factional. Regarding the phrase "factional by way of Dhamma": here—

The performance of the *pārisuddhi* (declaration of purity) is legitimate; however, because the consent (*chanda*) belongs only to the Saṅgha and not to a group (*gaṇa*), it is considered a "deficient assembly" (*vagga*).
They say: "What has been done once is well-done, yet one incurs an offense; they are not permitted to do it again. [Others say:
"It is permissible for four [monks] to recite the Pātimokkha after bringing the consent of one among five."
They say that this is appropriate; for when it has reached the monks who are the conveyors of the consent (*chandahāraka*), the Saṅgha is thereby complete.
Therefore, it is stated with the understanding that the consent has reached the Saṅgha.
[End of] the commentary on the discussion regarding the reciter of the Pātimokkha.
150. Because it is stated in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*: “Having said, ‘Let the Saṅgha, venerable sirs, hear me... [etc. ...for when it has been revealed, there is comfort;
therefore I ask the venerable ones... [etc. ...therefore you are silent.
Thus do I understand this,’ one has recited the remainder by means of the Sutta according to the method beginning with, ‘Venerable sirs, the Nidāna has been recited.’”

Regarding the phrase, “I bear this in mind; it has indeed been heard by the venerable ones,” one should understand that after saying “I bear this in mind,” the statement “The introduction has been recited, venerable ones” is abbreviated; for that very reason, it is written in the manner of the minor *peyyāla* (elliptical formula).
Likewise, in the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*, it says: “For when it has been made manifest, there is ease; therein, venerable ones...”
Regarding this, some hold that the statement, "Venerable sirs, the introduction has been recited," should be understood as being abbreviated.
Others say, "When it is stated, 'It should be trained in by those who do not dispute,' the recitation of the introduction is considered finished;
therefore, one incurs an offense by failing to make it explicit. That is not correct. Why? Because of the concluding statement, "Having recited the introduction..."
For the completion of the introduction has been stated, and at the conclusion of the introduction, the offense is stated.
"Recitation" (*sarabhañña*) is defined as speaking with a melodic tone; this is what is written. "Having resolved upon recitation" means having generated the thought, "I am performing recitation.
They say that it is permissible to speak merely by saying "I ask permission. However, in the case of silence...
It is logical. "Furthermore, even if one who is overcome by gain and so forth prevents [the act], that is not a valid authority," they say.
Explaining that "this is the same method," it means that if he interrupts, he must again ask for permission.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion regarding the protest against an illegal legal act (*adhamma-kamma*).
154. “For the sake of their being free from distress”: the Saṅgha does not perform its formal act for the Saṅgha itself; furthermore, there is distress for many others as well, therefore it was said.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Requesting of the Reciter of the Pātimokkha, etc.: 155.
Although it was stated previously that “the Pātimokkha is headed by the Elders,” it was later stated without distinction: “Whoever therein is competent and capable...”
Because it is stated, "it is to be entrusted to him," it is established that the word "Venerable Sir" (*bhante*) is used even by the Elder.
From the statement, "Go, friend, either briefly or in detail," it is established that even in the absence of obstacles, one's own strength is the measure [of what should be taught].
*Commentary on the Discussion of the Basis for Traveling to Other Directions, etc.*

163. The reading is: “If he has fellow-monks who are attendants. It is written that “in the season and the year” refers to the winter and summer seasons. 164. Commentary on the explanation of the giving of purity (*pārisuddhi*):
Regarding the phrase “I give purity,” [the question arises]:
“Does one who is guilty of an offense give it to the elders? For in the case of a conscious lie, a *dukkaṭa* offense would occur.”

It was written by the Teacher. What, then, is the reason? It is because the offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) arising from intentional lying is said to be originated by non-action solely because it was so stated by the Blessed One. However, in the phrase “I give my purity,” action is evident;
therefore, it appears as if there were an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for intentional lying. This must be thoroughly investigated.
For those are indeed called "great teachers. In that context, "I give" is said as a sign of having performed one's own Uposatha ritual.
And "take it" and "announce it" are said for the purpose of releasing one from the *dukkaṭa* offense incurred by a carrier failing to announce [the consent].
This same principle applies to the giving of consent (*chandadāna*) as well. Therein, "I give" is a statement indicating the harmony of one's own mind.

The rest is exactly as previously stated; thus the Elder Upatissa describes it. Alternatively, the first [clause] refers to the state of being in harmony, the second to the state that must subsequently be established, and the third is stated for the purpose of releasing the *dukkaṭa* offense of one who conveys the consent.
In both cases, because of the statement, "When the Saṅgha has been reached, he departs," etc., the giving of consent and purification occurs only when the Saṅgha is in harmony.

It grows; it is established that it does not fail when incomplete. From such statements as, "When one who has been suspended acknowledges having reached the Saṅgha, the formal act of purification (pārisuddhi) is brought forth," it is established that even for those who have been suspended and the like, the giving of consent and purification is valid.
Furthermore, this is understood to be so only through the perception of them as regular members (pakatatta), and not otherwise—this is the inference.
If [the consent] is given to a novice (sāmaṇera) after knowing [his status], it does not proceed and there is an offense; if it is given without knowing [his status], it does proceed.
And it goes [to the assembly]; "there is no offense," say some. Regarding the term *biḷālasaṅkhalikā* (cat’s-chain) as a form of purity (*pārisuddhi*):
here, the word *saṅkhalikā* is connected with what follows immediately; and by another [term], *saṅkhalikā*, there is simply what is called *saṅkhalikā-pārisuddhi*.
Thus says the Elder Upatissa. If that were so, the qualification would be purposeless. It is precisely because it is bound like a cat’s chain [that it is so called].
It exists only within the household because it is bound to it. The intended meaning, it is said, is that just as she does not go anywhere, so too this [craving] does not go anywhere.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Giving of Desire and So Forth.

165–7. “Having given their consent (*chanda*), a monk who has gone to a broken boundary (*khaṇḍasīma*), or to the interval between boundaries (*sīmantarika*), or outside the boundary (*bahissīma*), and then returned, does not invalidate the formal act (*kamma*).

Therefore, having taken the consent of the monks who were departing and bound a broken boundary, they do not take their consent again when binding the monastery boundary (*vihārasīma*) once more,” so they say. This is because of the statement beginning with, “Stay for a moment to one side.”
It is established that any formal act (*bhikkhu-kamma*) is not permitted when laypeople and others are within arm’s reach. "Outside the boundary" (*nissīma*) means beyond the boundary.
Since there is no requirement for a formal resolution (*sammuti-dāna*) for that [act], the meaning is that it is permissible even when such people are present.
"Water together with a seat" is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "even fifteen," the word "even" (*api*) includes the fourteenth day; therefore, it is stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*:
“If it is not so for us. Regarding the resolution, “Today is my Uposatha on the fifteenth day,” some say that this is always the case and never otherwise.
Commentary on the discussion of the method for remedying offenses (169–170).
“I confess”: whether spoken in any language whatsoever, there is indeed both the confession and the acceptance [of the offense], provided it is done by means of a manifestation of what has been seen.

Some say it is because [the offense] has been declared as a purification. One who is in doubt should say: "Venerable sir, I am in doubt regarding one grave offense (thullaccaya); when I become free from doubt, I shall then make amends for that offense.
When this has been done, as long as he is not free from doubt, he is not permitted to accept a similar offense, nor is he permitted to perform other formal acts (kamma).
He is called "pure. Furthermore, having become free from doubt, he should confess. "Not" means that this is found neither in the Canon nor in the Commentary;

however, once confessed, there is no fault. Likewise, regarding the thought, "Having emerged from this, I shall make amends for that offense," this applies when the entire Saṅgha has fallen into a similar offense and is in a state of doubt. And likewise...

It is written: "If it is said, 'The entire Saṅgha, having fallen into a common offense, will perform the confession of that offense in his presence when they see themselves as pure,' then one is permitted to perform the Uposatha.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion beginning with the "Fifteenfold Non-offense" (Anāpattipannarasaka).

172–3. Regarding the reading “atthaññe” in the first section and “athaññe” in the subsequent section: they see [the monks] either having already entered the boundary or in the process of entering it. However, those who perceive them as [legitimate] Dhamma-monks do so through ignorance. The reading “The group of fifteen on doubt is likewise clear” is the text.
178. Commentary on the Summary Discussion on Entering the Boundary:
From the statement “It should not be given against one’s will,” it is established that it should be given when there is consent.
Commentary on the Discourse on Seeing the Mark, etc. (180).
"They do not agree" means, it is said, that they belong to different sects due to their differing tenets (*laddhi*).

For in the case of one who belongs to a different sect due to a formal act (*kamma*), once he has been made to relinquish his view, the act of reinstatement (*osāraṇakamma*) must be performed for him. When this has been done, [one may perform] the Uposatha together with him.
It is proper to perform [the formal act]. It is stated that by the other [method], it may be performed merely by relinquishing one's own view.

For one who knows that another has been suspended for not acknowledging an offense, for not making amends for an offense, or for not relinquishing a wrong view, and who performs [the formal act] together with him, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Therefore, some say these should be understood as "those who follow the suspended."
Commentary on the Section on Whether One Should Go or Not (Nagantabbagantabbavārakathāvaṇṇanā) 181.
With reference to what is it said, "One should not go"? Because of the statement, "Except by means of the Saṅgha," this refers to a monastery where a hundred bhikkhus reside;
if they all, for some business, go out in groups of ten each to separate places such as various water-throwing boundaries (*udakukkhepasīmā*), etc.

Having stood [there], they are permitted to perform the Uposatha. One should not go to various boundaries—such as a new construction hall or others—for the purpose of designating the Uposatha boundary, whether it be a *sīmā* or a river.
Because a light recitation of the *Pātimokkha* cannot be performed after having abandoned a heavy one, the phrase "except by the Saṅgha" is established [as a restriction].
In that context: "In whatever residence those who perform the Uposatha... [omission] ...having not performed..."
From the statement, "One should not go," it is established that it is permissible to leave a residence even when the Uposatha has been relinquished. It is said:

"Therefore, it is permissible for those who have relinquished the Uposatha to go for the purpose of performing the Pārisuddhi Uposatha, or to enter a partial boundary (khaṇḍasīma)," according to others.
By this, it is shown that there is no obstacle to the Uposatha; thus, it was written as "an obstacle to one's own Uposatha."
Commentary on the Discussion Showing Persons Who Should Be Avoided (183):

It is permissible to sit down after having resolved, "I will not perform [the formal act] out of fear of quarrels and the like within the assembly where one who has committed the final offense is seated. In other matters, there is no offense for that person's seated assembly.

Some [teachers] say: "Because of the statement, ‘And monks, the Uposatha should not be performed on a non-Uposatha day except for the sake of concord in the Saṅgha,’ it appears as if it were stated by way of its meaning that a day of concord is a non-Uposatha day.
The teachers [hold] that this was said by way of the statement, “Monks, there are these two Uposathas”; otherwise, it would contradict the Parivāra-Paritta.
If the Saṅgha is united on either the fourteenth or the fifteenth day,

it should be understood that this instruction was given to show that the Uposatha should be performed in the ordinary manner, without saying, "Today is the Uposatha of unity. Otherwise, if there is unity during the two aforementioned occasions,
one should not perform the Uposatha then, but rather the Uposatha of unity should be performed on the next non-Uposatha day.
[He] commits [an offense]. Since it was previously prohibited in another way, there is no need for a prohibition here.
For it was stated previously: "Monks, the Pātimokkha should not be recited daily. Alternatively, because it was stated previously:
"Monks, I allow you to recite the Pātimokkha on the Uposatha day," [it refers to] once a fortnight, either on the fourteenth or the fifteenth.
Furthermore, because the statements "or" and "Monks, there are these two Uposatha days" are spoken later on, it would follow by implication that the Uposatha should not be performed on any other day;

this unintended consequence must be avoided. Therefore, it should be understood that this teaching was given in order to show that when there is concord within the Saṅgha, even a day that is not normally an Uposatha day becomes what is called an "Uposatha day" by way of its natural occurrence.
The commentary on the Uposatha Khandhaka is finished.
3. Commentary on the Vassūpanāyika Khandhaka:
The Explanation of the Discourse on the Permission for Entering the Rains Retreat.

In the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* as well, the reading is "saṅkāsayissantī" (they will cause to be stored), whereas it is said that those dwelling on the Island read "saṅkāpayissantī" (they will cause to be sent).
Regarding the reflection, "How many indeed are the entries into the rains?
and when it was asked, "For what reason?", the entry into the rains that was stated—namely, "I allow you, monks, to enter the rains"—refers to this three-month rains residence.
Having said, "I approach," one should enter [the rains residence]. There are four months of the rainy season. In that regard, there are two types of three-month periods:
the first three months and the last three months. Therefore, this thought arose among those bhikkhus.
[This concludes] the commentary on the discussion regarding the prohibition against wandering during the rains, and so forth.
185. "An offense is to be understood as occurring either by departing without regard [for the invitation] or by causing dawn to rise elsewhere.
Regarding this, first of all, he departs with some business while the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) is yet seven days away.
"Monks, whether that monk should return to that residence or not return, for that monk, monks..."
It should be understood that this was stated with reference to the earlier period, because of the statement: "The earlier period is recognized, and there is no offense for failing to inform.

For it is said: "If he departs on that very day without having business to attend to, or departs while having business to attend to, then, monks, that monk’s earlier period is not recognized, and there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for failing to inform."
Commentary on the Discussion of the Allowance for a Seven-Day Task (Sattāhakaraṇīyānujānanakathāvaṇṇanā) 187–8.

Regarding the second [case], because of the statement: “If he spends those seven days outside [the monastery], monks, that monk’s previous residence is not recognized, and there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the promise,” it is [forbidden] beyond the seven days.
This should be understood. For it has been said: "If he makes a retreat within those seven days, monks, that monk’s previous period is recognized, and there is no offense regarding the promise.
Even though two reasons [for breaking the rains residence] exist, an offense should be understood to occur when the reason for breaking the rains residence is absent;
therefore, these three statements should be applied according to their respective applicability.
The formal procedures (*viggaha*) are thus applied. "Three are omitted" means because of their absence.
199. Commentary on the Discourse Granting Permission for One Who Has Been Sent:
"Monks, I allow you to go on business for the Saṅgha; a seven-day period of return must be observed."
According to the word [of the Buddha], it is permissible to go during the rains retreat with the intention of returning.
In that regard, even if they have come by way of a desire for the Dhamma, the source of income for the Saṅgha is destroyed. Therefore, it is said: "having prepared lodgings. *Āgata* means "coming";

here the suffix *-ttha* is used in the sense of the agent (*tapaccaya*). Regarding the phrase "to go on account of business for the Saṅgha," here [it refers] specifically to those matters connected with lodgings.
Regarding matters concerning the Saṅgha, and not others—so says the Elder Dhammasiri.
In the Commentary as well, having cited that same passage, only the lodging is shown by the words, "whatever lodgings such as the Uposatha hall," and so forth;
therefore, this must be investigated.

If one has been invited to go [to a meal], it is not permissible to go; for him there is a breach of the rains-residence (*vassa*) and an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*), which they call a "breach of the rains.
Regarding the phrase "one who is indeed invited": even if lay followers have made an agreement, saying, "On such-and-such a day we shall perform acts of giving and so forth;
let everyone assemble," it is permissible to go. From the ninth [day] of the invitation (*pavāraṇā*).

From that time on, it is appropriate for everyone to go to seek rag-robe (paṃsukūla) clothings, just as was done at Kāvīrapaṭṭana, because they are prepared and set aside by lay followers (upāsaka) every year according to a fixed rule. This is also stated in the Andhakaṭṭhakathā:
"Either a formal agreement (katikā) has been made by the Saṅgha of monks saying, 'Let the monks from all around come,' or an announcement has been made."

The teachers [state]: "In that case, since there is no interruption of the night for one going there, it is also permissible even if they have been invited once with the request, 'May you come every year.

And: "Others say that the manner of performing [the offering] is seen as having been proclaimed at Kāvīrapaṭṭana by making a commitment starting from the robe-season and preparing [offerings] for those who have arrived from all directions."
However, they do not speak thus.
[This concludes] the commentary on the discussion regarding the interruption of the rains residence due to obstacles and non-offenses. 201.
Because of the statement, "If he has gone far away, the dawn must be made to rise by means of the seven-day interval," in whatever...

It is said: "Others explain that when an obstacle exists, it is permissible to interrupt the rains-retreat; and even while that obstacle persists, it is permissible to spend the time on a seven-day mission without having interrupted the retreat. However, the Vinaya-holders do not accept this;

therefore, it should be understood that the statement "the dawn must be made to rise by means of the seven-day interval" was spoken as a provision for specific circumstances such as those arising there.
With reference to this, it was said: "But the teachers do not speak thus. "A cow" (gāvuṃ) means a bull (balibaddha).
"Standing outside the boundary" (bahisīmāya ṭhitānaṃ)—the Elder Upatissa says this refers even to those standing within a broken boundary (khaṇḍasīmā).

"In the case of a break in the rains-residence" (vassacchede assa) means in the event of that break in the rains-residence. For those who are making him leave the monastery for elsewhere, they should assemble right there and say: "By this and by this..."
And having made an announcement, "For this reason, let us lead [the candidate] to this named place and have him ordained in this monastery," it should be performed.
Regarding the commentary on the discussion of entering the rains-retreat with a *vajja* (a companion):
"There is no offense for one who has gone with a *vajja* if there is a break in the rains-retreat"—the intended meaning, it is said, is that there is no interruption of the rains-retreat.
Because it is not a monastery (*avihāra*), one should not say, "In this monastery," but rather only, "I enter the rains retreat here. It has been written:
"However, since it is not permissible to enter the rains retreat in a caravan (*sattha*), neither 'In this monastery for these three months' nor 'I enter the rains retreat here' is permitted;
the intention is that it is permissible merely by making a formal declaration of attachment (*ālaya*)."
However, that contradicts the *Aṭṭhakathā*. For it is stated there: "One must say three times, 'I enter the rains residence here.
If it is argued that even the words of the *Aṭṭhakathā* contradict themselves from beginning to end, we say no; this is due to a failure to understand the intended meaning.
The Teacher’s path is twofold: stationary and mobile. Regarding these, when stationary, one should dwell in a hut after saying, "I enter the rains residence here."
It is with reference to this that it was said: “I allow you, monks, to enter upon the rains residence in a caravan.
However, in the case of a wandering caravan, because there is no hut, it is not permitted to enter upon the rains residence. It is permitted if there is a palanquin or a cart-hut;
likewise, it is permitted on a journey as well. In these three instances, there is no offense for a monk in breaking the rains residence.
Regarding the phrase "and he is entitled to perform the *pavāraṇā*," here is the investigation:

When it was said, "Monks, I allow you to go where there is a caravan," was this stated for the purpose of protecting the rains-retreat (*vassa*), or rather for the purpose of avoiding the offense of interrupting the rains-retreat?
For if it were for the purpose of protecting the rains-retreat, [it would contradict] the rule: "Monks, one should not enter the rains-retreat without a dwelling place."

This is contradictory. If it is established that [the statement] "he is not permitted to perform the *pavāraṇā*" was said for the purpose of avoiding the offense of interrupting the rains-retreat, what is the reasoning here?
For it is only these three types who are permitted to perform the *pavāraṇā*, and no others.

Indeed, one who is harassed by wild animals and the like is permitted [to perform it] as long as he does not abandon the place he has reached; he is not permitted [to do so] once he abandons it—this is the reasoning here.

The Teacher says: "Even one who has gone to a village may perform the *pavāraṇā* there; thus, [the rule applies] to 'one'. For he who previously did not enter the rains residence with the thought, "I enter the rains here," but entered with the thought, "In this monastery," is excluded.
Otherwise, it would be permissible for one to enter simply intending a village, thinking, "I enter the rains here," even without a monastery. If it is argued, "Let him do so"?

This is because there is no statement such as, "I allow you, monks, to enter the rains residence in a caravan, on a journey, or on a boat," whereas there is no such statement regarding entering the rains residence in a village. Since the statement,
"In three places there is no offense for a monk in breaking the rains residence," indicates that entering the rains residence exists in those cases—
because if it did not exist, there would be no possibility of breaking it— it follows [that the same applies] to a caravan...
It is established that this was said with reference to a time when there is no hut available.
Regarding the three cases where a bhikkhu incurs no offense for breaking the rains-retreat, it is written: "There is no offense for one who goes together with them;
however, there is an offense for going after having separated from them, and he is not permitted to perform the *pavāraṇā* ceremony. Therefore, as for what was stated:
In the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), it says: "Then the caravan, having reached the place desired by the bhikkhu, passes right through the village boundary...
or it stops in a certain village along the way, or it disperses," and so forth.

This [passage] should be understood as being for the purpose of showing that even for those who have traveled while in violation [of the rules], there is no traveling in violation; therefore, they must perform the *pavāraṇā*.

If it is argued: "In that context, since it is stated, 'Having made a hut with a roof of leaves, one should enter the rains residence,' it is established that it is permissible to climb a tree for the sake of a lodging;
this does not contradict the Canon," we say no. This is because [the climbing] is already established by the very prohibition of that [practice], and because it is prohibited here once again:
"Monks, one who has no lodging should not enter the rains residence."

If it is argued that this prohibition is redundant—since the prohibition “Monks, one should not enter the rains residence in the open air” would already be established by this [present rule]—we say no.
This is because it would follow that the open air is not considered a *senāsana* (lodging), whereas it is established as a *senāsana* by the statement, “In the open air, on a heap of straw.
Even one dwelling in the open air of a four-sided hall is [considered to be] in the four-sided hall.
It is said, "He dwells there," and therefore it follows that it is permissible there;

consequently, one who is "without a fixed dwelling" (asenāsanika) here should be understood as one who has not had a dwelling assigned to him for the purpose of his permanent residence, either by himself or by another.
Otherwise, since there would be an excess of one of the two prohibitions, it would follow that it is permissible to enter the rains retreat even at the foot of a tree or in the open air.

And if it is argued that even for one who has not assigned a lodging it is permissible to dwell in a womb-like enclosure, and if it is asked how it is known that only a lodging with a door-secure fastening is intended here, [the answer is]: from the introductory narrative (*nidāna*).

For this offense regarding entering the rains residence without a lodging is stated thus: "Now at that time, monks entered the rains residence without lodgings; [they were] afflicted by cold and heat..."
Since it was prescribed in this context [of the rule] "being weary," it is established that here "lodging" (senāsana) is intended precisely as the exclusion of cold and so forth.
If it is argued that, this being the case, the indication of the prima facie position (pubbapakkha) is established, we say no;

for it serves to indicate the occurrence of a subsequent meaning. As it is said in the description of the second jhāna: "With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, without applied thought..."

The words "without investigation" (*avicāra*) serve as the illustration. If it is argued that—by virtue of the prohibition against being in the open air—the prohibition applies only to being outside in the open air, and not to being in the open air within a four-sided hall or similar structure, and therefore the introductory narrative (*nidāna*) is not authoritative—this is not so, because of the rule of necessity.
For it has already been established that some training rules (*sikkhāpada*) depend upon an introductory narrative; this one is such a dependent rule.

How is it understood that this [rule] is "without regard" (*anapekkha*)? For here, unlike in the *Ubhatovibhaṅga*, there is neither a word-by-word commentary (*padabhājana*) on the training rules nor a section on non-offenses (*anāpattivāra*). Even here, it is understood from the manner of the teaching itself.
For by these two introductory statements—"When it rains, they run even to the foot of a tree or to the edge of a well"—whether outside or inside, [it is shown].
Or, "all that is a place sheltered from rain" is what is meant here by "open air.

It is established that even a place not sheltered from rain must be free from a pit (anibbakoṣa) in this context. By the phrase "one should not approach it," there is a prohibition against making it one's abode, as well as a prohibition against saying, "I am spending the rains retreat here. Regarding the cremation of a corpse, [the rule applies] to the ashes and the bones...
“The hut is built for the sake of [the monk] himself,” says the Andhaka Aṭṭhakathā. It is recorded that “a ṭaṅkitamañca is a stone house with a grass roof.
It is stated: “If one lives in a dwelling that is not bolted shut, but in a place provided by oneself that is bolted shut and shares common access, it is permissible.
There is also a practical application: “One who does not possess a lodging should not enter the rains residence,” according to the Pāḷi.
And there is the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*); therefore, it must be investigated.
Regarding the explanation of the discussion on illegal agreements and so forth:
"It is stated in the *Mahāvibhaṅga*"—here, this is the statement of the Andhaka commentary concerning one who is less than fifteen years [of seniority].
A novice should not dwell here in this monastery; he should not wander for rag-robes; he should not accept scraps of cloth as alms;
he should not eat in another monastery; he should not eat anything belonging to another monk or nun;
we should neither address one another nor converse with one another; there should be no recitation of the scriptures; and an earthen bowl is permitted.
“There is no staying for one whose requisites are incomplete.

(206) Regarding “false speech”: deception is intended here. Some say, “It is stated that [the offense occurs] because of having promised through deception,” and others say, “Householders understand it as false speech because it conforms to the words spoken by the king.
(207) “The first rains-residence is not recognized. Why? Because when the thought ‘I shall stay during the second [rains-residence]’ has arisen, the taking of the first lodging [is invalidated].”
It subsides. Again, when the thought arises, "I shall dwell in the very first [monastery]," the second [thought] subsides.
It is written: "There is no rule for dwelling in both. However, in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*, it says:
"If one does not remain in the place first taken, but takes a lodging in another monastery and dwells there for two or three days, then the original taking of the first [lodging] subsides."
"The first period is not recognized; the taking of the later period does not cease. For this is called 'cessation by way of the day.
Then, if one dwells elsewhere during the latter three months and the first period is not recognized, this is called 'cessation by way of the taking of lodgings. Thus it is said. Both of these...

The eight alternatives (atthavikappa) are not intended here. Wherever this [formal] agreement has been made, there the earlier period (*purimikā*) is not recognized, and for making such an agreement, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). But where is the earlier period recognized?

On the road between two residences, wherever the later period (*pacchimaggāha*) is taken on that very day, there—at the place where it was first taken—one may stay for seven days for a necessary purpose.

Regarding the phrase "there is no interruption of the rains for one who is traveling," it was stated in the section beginning with "he departs on that very day because there is something to be done" that "something to be done" means "a seven-day business.
In the *Pāḷimuttakaratthacchedavinicchaya*, it is stated as "listening to the Dhamma and so forth. This applies to the four cases at the beginning.

Because the departure with no expectation [of returning] is what is intended here, the phrase "on account of a seven-day business" was not stated; for when that [expectation] exists, there is no departure without expectation.
In this regard, the first two instances were stated with reference to one who has not entered the rains residence;

therefore, it is established that for one who has entered the rains residence, there is no breaking of the rains residence if he goes on account of a seven-day business on that very day and returns within the seven days. As for the last...
The two instances mentioned regarding one who has arrived [for the invitation ceremony] refer to departing without concern [for the ceremony].

The statement, "If one departs for a necessary business when the invitation is seven days away," is spoken for the purpose of showing that for one who spends more than seven days beyond that limit, there is a breach of the rains-residence (*vassa*).
In that context, because there is no mention of the phrase "one departs for what is not a necessary business," one may depart without a cause that would interrupt the nights [of the residence].
It is established that it is not permissible [to go]. However, it is permissible to go after having performed the *pavāraṇā*, because the *pavāraṇā* is dependent upon that very day.
Regarding the phrase "or he may not come," this refers to being hindered by obstacles. The Teacher, however, says:

"The phrase 'one who has no business' (*akaraṇīyo*) was not stated in order to show that even one who is indifferent—thinking, 'I shall not return here again'—is permitted to go only if he still has business to attend to. [This is said] regarding the Island of Ceylon.
It is said: "There is indeed what is called the 'Short Invitation' (*cūḷapavāraṇā*); having performed that invitation, they go about their business as they please and provide their services.
And it is further stated: "In that regard, there are six sunrises during the rains retreat and one outside;
therefore, he has resided for three months," and "The Teacher does not speak thus. In all these cases...
"Enters a dwelling" means, according to the ancients, that one enters a cell obtained by one's own seniority (*vassaga*).
"But through negligence one does not enter for the rains" refers here to the failure to state, "I shall stay in this dwelling for these three months. It is written in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:

"Even for one who goes with the thought, 'I will go and stay in another dwelling,' there is a breach of the rains-residence (*vassaccheda*), except for the reason of interrupting the night as stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*."

208. "He has agreed to the later [rains-residence]" (*paṭissuto hoti pacchimikāya*) means that he has agreed either by a monk who has gone forth in the interim or by one whose rains-residence has been interrupted.
However, another [opinion] holds that one should not make an agreement for the later [rains-residence] without having first entered the earlier one.

Having established the conclusion that "in all cases, a break in the nights constitutes a break in the rains-residence," they say this. Yet some do not accept it. To prove that [position], [the text] proceeds in many ways.
They proliferate. What is the use of that?
The commentary on the Vassūpanāyikakkhandhaka is finished.
4. Commentary on the Pavāraṇākkhandhaka.
Commentary on the Discussion of Dwelling Uncomfortably (Aphāsukavihārakathāvaṇṇanā) 210.
Because it is said, "Friends, I invite the Saṅgha," it appears as though one should later say, "May the Saṅgha speak to me.
However, the intended meaning here is this: since I am inviting the Saṅgha, therefore, in that regard—
"Whether they be elders, those of middle standing, or newcomers—let all the venerable ones speak to me without distinction.
(Commentary on the Division of the Invitation) 212.
"Monks, there are these two kinds of invitation (*pavāraṇā*). In this regard, when such a matter arises, one may invite [the Saṅgha] anywhere.
It is permissible. For that very reason, even now, the monks at the Mahāvihāra perform the *pavāraṇā* on the fourteenth day and grant formal unity (*kāyasāmaggi*) on the fifteenth day.
They also go to Cetiyagiri on the eighth day for the great festival; this too is for those who wish to perform the *pavāraṇā* on the fourteenth day.
[The rule states: "If one departs for some business seven days before the *pavāraṇā*, there is no offense."

This was written because it has been practiced according to the word [of the Buddha]. "If he does not resolve [upon it], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)"—this refers to the dukkaṭa mentioned for one individual;
that same preliminary duty (pubbakicca) stated for him must also be applied to the Saṅgha and the Gaṇa.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion regarding the authorization for granting the invitation (pavāraṇā).
213. "And by that bhikkhunī" refers to the one who gives the invitation (pavāraṇādāyaka). Regarding the commentary on the section beginning with the "Fifteen Cases of No Offense":

they say, "Since it is stated that 'when that invitation has been announced and the Saṅgha has invited, for all there is a well-invited [invitation],' the one who gives the invitation is also considered to have invited, solely by means of the invitation."
"222. When the assembly has not yet risen": this refers to when they have already performed the *pavāraṇā* and are subsequently conversing with one another. "When some have risen":
this means when some remain seated as they were, while others have gone to their respective places. "The *pavāraṇā* must be performed again": it must be performed once more by all gathering together.
"They arrive in equal numbers; the *pavāraṇā* should be performed in their presence."

It is written: "The invitation (pavāraṇā) should be performed in the very presence of those who have arrived and are seated, even though they have not been brought [to the assembly]; this same method applies in the Uposatha-kkhandhaka.
When the entire assembly has risen and they arrive together in equal numbers, the invitation should be performed in their presence. [This means]:
"If all have risen and departed, and it is impossible to convene them [again], one may perform the invitation after having convened some of them."

"It is permissible," they say. Why? Because it is said that since there is no formal act (*saṅghakamma*) to be performed after a motion (*ñatti*) has been established, it does not constitute a quorum-deficient assembly (*vagga*).
In this case, however, whether some have departed or all have departed, one should invite for the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) only after having assembled everyone and established the motion.
It is not permissible to invite after having assembled only some; [one should address them as]: "Venerable sirs, the Saṅgha..."
This is because of the statement, "I invite [criticism]. For all those who have assembled are subsequently speakers of what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
Even though they know that some have not yet arrived, it is as if the invitation were being made in the presence of only certain individuals.
Having brought together the four assemblies in person, there is the relinquishing of robes and other items for which one has incurred an offense of relinquishment (*nissaggiya*).

The invitation (*pavāraṇā*) does not take place as if [the community were] separate, because it is entirely dependent [on one another]. The statement, "The invitation for those who are in concord has been prescribed," is the proof here. The Elder Upatissa says:
"It is not permissible in any other way than this, because it has not been authorized in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
It is stated: "The invitation should be performed in the presence of those who are fewer in number, or without having put forward a formal motion (*ñatti*). Those called "incoming" (*āgantuka*)...
They are either those who have come from nine *yojanas* away, or those who have completed their rains-residence on ships or carts. 237. It is written:
"There is wrong view with ten bases, such as 'the Tathāgata does not exist' and so forth. It is stated: "'There is no giving,' and so forth.
239. It is written: "'Having investigated, we shall know'; therefore, one should perform the *pavāraṇā* ceremony together with him."
The commentary on the Pavāraṇā-khandhaka is finished.
5. Commentary on the Camma-khandhaka:
Explanation of the Story concerning Soṇa Koḷivisa.
242. Regarding the phrase “having caused eighty thousand village headmen to assemble,” this is the explanatory statement for the word “kāreti.

In that context, although one should say “among eighty thousand villages,” it is stated as “among eighty thousand village headmen (*gāmikasahassāni*). The village headmen are those who lead the villages; there were thousands of them.
The expression “decorated with craftsmanship” is used figuratively (*upacārena*). [This refers to] those things arisen from karma-conditioned temperature (*kamma-paccaya-utu-samuṭṭhāna*).

For that is their appearance, like the color of collyrium. Where it should have been said, "for some particular purpose" (*kenacideva karaṇīyena*), it is stated as "for some [purpose]" (*kenacideva*).
Here, the word *evaṃ* functions in the sense of a simile. It occurs in the senses of comparison, instruction, questioning, restriction, admission, and simile.
In the phrase "of those looking ahead," the genitive case is used in the sense of disregard. Then, from the fragrant chamber (*gandhakuṭī*) of the Blessed One...
Seeing that the door was securely fastened, he went by means of psychic power (*iddhi*)—which is skillful in assuming desired forms—and having entered the hut, he announced [his arrival].
"In the shadow of the monastery" (*vihārapacchāyāyaṃ*) means in the increasing shade of the monastery. "Aho nūna" is written as "Aho, how great!
The Blessed One’s wandering about together with many [monks] is for the purpose of demonstrating the exertion of energy (*vīriyārambha*) of the Venerable Soṇa.
It was for the purpose of encouraging those who had not yet initiated energy, and also to show that sandals were permitted for the protection of the feet of those who are delicate.
Regarding the commentary on the story of Soṇa’s going forth (243):
"And there, take the sign" means: observe the characteristic form of those faculties.

244. "He is resolute" means he stands having penetrated and made [the truth] directly manifest. By the terms "resolute toward renunciation" (*nekkhammādhimutta*) and so forth, both Nibbāna and Arahantship are expressed.
For that [Nibbāna] is called "renunciation" (*nekkhamma*) because it has emerged from all defilements;

"seclusion" (*paviveka*) because it is secluded from the household life; and "non-affliction" (*abyāpajja*) because of the absence of affliction. [Arahantship is so called] with reference to clinging...

It is said: "Because it arises at the time of the destruction of clinging, it is called 'the destruction of clinging'; because it arises at the time of the destruction of craving, it is called 'the destruction of craving';
and because of the absence of delusion, it is called 'non-delusion. Some say that all these terms refer to Arahantship. "It might be so" means: it might perhaps be so;
or it might occur to that venerable one thus. "Returning" means knowing.
“*Karaṇīyamattānan*” means one’s own. Or rather, that very reading [is correct]. “*Nekkhammādhimutto*” (intent upon renunciation) refers here specifically to *arahantship*.
Regarding the remaining [terms], some say it is *nibbāna*. “*Asammohādhimutto*” (intent upon non-delusion) refers here specifically to *nibbāna*.

Regarding the remaining [terms], some say it is *arahantship*. Others say, “In all of these, both are present. And for one who is intent upon mental seclusion (*paviveka*) and the destruction of clinging (*upādānakkhaya*).
The genitive case is used here in the sense of an instrument (upayoga). Having seen the arising and passing away of the sense bases (*āyatana*).
Commentary on the Discussion Refuting All [Colors] such as Blue, etc. (246):

The reading is “having wiped with a colored cloth. Since it is stated, “having removed the patches and so forth,” the claim of those who say, “it is permissible to use it after making two or three holes,” should not be accepted.
Commentary on the Discussion Regarding the Prohibition of Vehicles, etc.

(254) Because it is stated, “exceeding four finger-breadths,” some say that [a foot-washing stand] is permissible if it is less than four finger-breadths. Regarding the phrase “red-soled foot-washing stands on both sides,” it is written here: “However, a *kāṣāya* [robe] is permissible, but one dyed with safflower and the like is not.
Commentary on the Discussion Regarding the Prohibition of All Leather, etc.
255. "Whose is this? they ask; "Whose is this for you? 256.
"Householder’s bedding" means that which is made for the sake of householders. It is written: "The meaning is that I allow [it] to sit upon anywhere.
Although it is stated in the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā* that "with the exception of the stuffed mattress (*tūlikā*), all [other items] such as the woolen rug (*gonaka*)..."

It was said, "Those sewn with jewels are permitted," yet when one arrives at the method of the Vinaya, since one must stand by what is weighty, the meaning here should be understood according to the manner stated in this [Vinaya] context.

Furthermore, because the teaching in the Suttanta was spoken with reference to householders and others as well, it was stated—omitting [the specific items] for the sake of including them—"a mattress... is permitted."
"It appears," say others; thus it is stated. 259.
*Migamātuka* is its name; *vātamiga* is also its name. "The black lion, the black-faced monkey"—so it is written.
"The hide is not permitted": by whatever method the hide will be permitted, that shall be made clear further on.
It is stated: "The exemption on account of one's own personal [need] is prohibited.

Although this was already established by the rule, "Monks, no hide whatsoever should be worn," the specific mention of "not a cow-hide" is for the sake of avoiding the implication of permission in the subsequent passage: "Monks, I allow hides as coverings in all border regions."
It should be understood that it has been stated thus.
The commentary on the Chapter on Leather (Cammakkhandhaka) is finished.
6. Commentary on the Chapter on Medicines (Bhesajjakkhandhaka).
Commentary on the Discussion of the Five Medicines, etc.

(260): It should be understood that the statement, “Whatever medicine there may be,” was spoken according to what is available, independent of the formal cause (*nidāna*), because a contradiction is shown later with the words, “Why would they be even more so for both of those? and so forth. [This applies] according to the specific cause.

If it is asked why this was not stated, it is because the intention was to refer to something else. For even at the time of all Buddhas, the Blessed One’s intention was expressed by that statement with the view toward the seven-day duration of ghee and other such items;
for that very reason it was said: "It should serve as food, yet no coarse food should be discerned.
Thus, in the phrase "having received it at the proper time, one should consume it at the proper time," [the meaning is established].
And no limitation of time was made. But how could it be otherwise? For the Blessed One’s intention was to look toward something else;
having accepted those root-medicines and so forth, the limitation of time is "for as long as life lasts.
As for the statement, "Monks, I allow you to accept those five medicines at the proper time and consume them at the proper time," that [refers to] "storing up" (sannidhi).
It should be understood that this was spoken with the intention: "I allow [it] to be consumed at the proper time on successive days.
Otherwise, because there would be no sense of exceeding the limit, the arising of the thought, "Whatever medicinal food there may be," and so forth, would not be possible.
Since the permission for refined foods is already established, these [allowances] were stated with regard to what is suitable and appropriate for a specific illness.
Why is that? Because it shows the attainment of a state of even greater emaciation and so forth.

If it is argued that, just as it is said "treacle is derived from sugarcane juice," so too one should say "ghee is derived from butter," and thus butter should not be mentioned separately—[we reply] no, because the intention is to show a distinction.
Just as, although [the substance] is established by the mention of treacle, subsequently...
Sugar-cane juice is permitted separately because it is included under the general category of "sugar-cane" due to its intended use in place of molasses-water.
Likewise, it should be understood that fresh butter is permitted separately because of the specific rule shown for it.
That specific rule, however, is to be understood by way of the commentary on the *Bhesajja-sikkhāpada* (the Medicinal Rules). For it is said therein: "Having boiled ghee..."
"If one wishes to consume [the food] after having prepared it, it is permissible to cook it even if it has not been washed. In this context, clarified butter (*sappi*) must be cooked;
it is not uncooked. Likewise with molasses (*phāṇita*). Fresh butter (*navanīta*), however, is indeed uncooked. Here it may be asked:
"Should sugarcane juice also be mentioned in the text as being for a seven-day period, just like fresh butter? It should not be so mentioned.

Why? Because when it is stated in the *Sattāhakālika-pāḷi*, just as molasses (*phāṇita*) is prohibited for one who is not ill by way of the mention of sugar (*guḷa*), so too would sugarcane juice (*ucchuraso*) be [prohibited];
however, since it is not mentioned there, like sugar, it does not fall under the category of molasses.
By not being mentioned here and being mentioned later, it is established in the very place of "sugar-water. For that very purpose...

If it is argued that [the juice] is called *yāmakālika* (allowable for a watch of the night) because it is mentioned in the section on fermented cane-juice (*vaṭṭanaka-pānaka*) after the meal, [we reply]: No, because that contradicts the *Aṭṭhakathā*. If it is argued that the sense of "derived from" (*upādāya*) is not the sense of "supported by" (*nissaya*), what is meant [by the statement]? Regarding this passage from the *Nissaggiya-aṭṭhakathā*:

"Derived from sugarcane juice (*ucchurasa*), it should be understood as a sugarcane product, namely, molasses (*phāṇita*)," in that context, the word "derived from" (*upādāya*)— [The rest of the sentence continues: ...is used in the sense of "supported by. Therefore, even though the juice is a product of sugarcane, it is not permissible to consume it after the meal; thus, it is indeed *yāmakālika*. Furthermore, the term *yāmakālika* refers to the time limit, meaning it is allowable until the end of the first watch of the night. It is not the case that it is *yāmakālika* simply because it is mentioned in the section on fermented cane-juice after the meal. If one were to claim otherwise, it would contradict the *Aṭṭhakathā*. If it is argued that the sense of "derived from" is not the sense of "supported by," then what is the meaning of the *Aṭṭhakathā* statement: "Derived from sugarcane juice, it should be understood as a sugarcane product, namely, molasses"? In that regard, the word "derived from" (*upādāya*)...
The meaning is "having depended upon" or "having made a condition. No, because no further action (*aparakiriyā*) is seen [in this case].

Just as in such passages as "dependent on the eye and forms," where following the intensive term "dependent on" (*paṭicca*), a further action—"arises"—is seen, it is not so here that a further action is seen after "having taken up sugarcane juice" (*ucchurasaṃ upādāya*). This is incorrect.

In that case, [one might ask]: "Is it not possible here as well, since [the meaning] is established even in the absence of those [additional words]? Just as in the passage, 'The four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements,' where the statement of excellence (*ussukkavacana*) is established even in the absence of further action, so too might it be here? No, because in that case there is a dependence on a supplementary reading (*pāṭhasesa*).

For example, it was stated [in the previous context] with reference to the four great elements as the basis (*upādāya*), [and thus the term for what they produce is required]. As for the "active" (*pavattaka*):
The phrase "or it is form" (*vā rūpaṃ*) refers to that canonical text as a textual supplement (*pāṭhasesa*);
however, this statement from the *Aṭṭhakathā* does not depend on any such textual supplement. For the masters of the *Aṭṭhakathās* are proponents of completeness.

Or rather, it is merely a designation for that form. Just as in passages such as "there is form derived from clinging" (*atthi rūpaṃ upādāya*), it is a mere designation, so too should it be understood here.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "starting with sugarcane juice" (*ucchurasaṃ upādāya*), the meaning is "beginning from sugarcane juice, starting from that point. Therefore, some say that it is incorrect to state:
"A monk who, not being ill, requests and eats rice mixed with sugarcane juice should be dealt with according to the training rule on exquisite food (*paṇītabhojana-sikkhāpada*);
a nun [who does so] should be dealt with according to the offense to be confessed (*pāṭidesanīya*). They [cite] a specific reason for this:
Having shown the non-existence [of such a thing],

they should be explained. Up to this point, having wrongly grasped the meaning of phrases such as "taking sugarcane juice as the basis" (*ucchurasaṃ upādāya*)— meaning "starting with sugarcane juice"—
if one were to think that by the statement "taking sugarcane juice as the basis," sugarcane juice would be molasses (*phāṇita*), or [if one were to think it is] "uncooked,"...
The statement [“or cooked”] is redundant because sugarcane juice has already been included by the term “uncooked.

Then, since it is established that sugarcane juice is molasses by the statement “or cooked,” the subsequent reply—that the statement “having taken sugarcane juice” is redundant—is proven to be no answer at all.
If, by these [terms], “or uncooked” refers to what is uncooked by the bhikkhu himself...
"Or, 'cooked without a base' (avatthukapakkā vā) means that it was cooked by the bhikkhu himself without a [proper] base.
Therefore, the meaning shown by stating otherwise—that it should be said as 'cooked with a base' (savatthukapakkā vā)—is poorly shown. Why?
Because in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* it is stated: 'Either boiled sugarcane juice or crushed sugarcane juice is permitted only before the meal.'"
And because the statement "or cooked with its base" contradicts the established position (*laddhi*), and because it was not [explicitly] stated [as an exception], and because it was said:

"In the *Mahāpaccarī*, however, having asked 'Is this cooked with its base allowable or not allowable?', it was replied: 'Regarding sugarcane jaggery, there is nothing that is called "not allowable" after the meal';
therefore, that [interpretation] is correct," thus [it follows that] "or cooked with its base."
The meaning has indeed already been stated; therefore, it is established that [the purpose] is not clearly shown. "For the purpose of food" (āhāratthaṃ) means the function of food.
And its meaning is the maintenance of the function of food.
262. "By the use of oil" means by use for a period of seven days.
263. Regarding the phrase "with mindfulness as the condition" (*sati-paccayā*), the nature of mindfulness as a condition should be understood in two ways:

by way of one who is ill and one who is not ill. For in the section on non-offenses (*anāpatti-vāra*) concerning the training rule against eating at improper times, the nature of mindfulness as a condition is stated without distinction for all three types of medicines, such as those to be kept for a watch of the night (*yāma-kālika*).
In this Khandhaka, it says: "I allow you, monks, sugar for one who is ill; I allow you, monks, sugar-water for one who is not ill."

"It is said: ‘For one who is ill, salted sour gruel; for one who is not ill, water mixed with it. Therefore, it is established that the condition of non-existence (asati-paccayatā) is twofold, according to whether one is ill or not ill.
Otherwise, if the condition were absent, one would incur an offense regarding sugar-water and the like; from that, there would be a contradiction with the Canon (Pāḷi).
‘With flour’ means with ground sesame oil. ‘Kōṭṭhaphala’ is the fruit of the kōṭṭha tree; or it means ‘madanaphala’ (the fruit of the madana tree).”
