And it is written [as follows]: That which is called *hiṅgujatu* is produced from the boiling of the stalks, shoots, and sprouts of the *hiṅgu* tree.
That which is called *hiṅgusipāṭikā* is produced from the boiling of its roots and branches. That which is called *taka* is the water used for boiling the bark of that tree.
*Takapattī* is the water used for boiling its leaves. *Takapaṇṇī* is the water used for boiling its fruit. Alternatively, *taka* means lac (*lākhā*).
“*Takapattī* means *kittimaloma* (the rust on copper). *Takapaṇṇī* means *pakkalākhā* (the lacquer tree)” is what is written. *Ubbhida* means made of saline soil or dust. 264. *Chakaṇa* is cow dung.
*Pākatika-cuṇṇa* (ordinary powder) means uncooked alkaline powder; regarding this, they say, “Except for fragrant powders, everything is permitted.
*Cālitehi* means strained. 265. “Made with various ingredients” means with various medicinal herbs.
Commentary on the Discussion on the Allowance of Molasses, etc. (274):

The phrase “cooked by oneself and cooked evenly” indicates two types [of cooking]. Therefore, in the case of milk and so forth, cooking consists merely of heating. By that means, they become equal to well-cooked rice and the like. (276–278):

Regarding the places where the expression “headed by the Buddha” (*buddhappamukha*) occurs, they say that instead of saying “the community of monks” (*bhikkhusaṅgha*), it is called simply “the Saṅgha” (*saṅgha*) in order to include the Blessed One as well. *Nāga* means an elephant.
279. It is permissible for a monk or a nun to insert [a finger] into the anus or the urinary passage respectively, provided it is done in the natural direction (*anuloma*).
Burning is permitted because there is no prohibition against it. If it is argued that it is not permitted because it conforms to the procedure for using a lancet (*satthavattikamma*), we say no;

this is because it is a prohibition of what was already prohibited, and it serves to indicate that the prohibition applies only to that specific instance. What is meant is this: even though the use of a lancet was previously prohibited...
Having summarized [the preceding], he subsequently prohibited surgical treatment twice, saying: "Monks, ... pe ... there is a grave offense (thullaccaya).
By this, it is meant that two finger-breadths around the private parts must be avoided.
This indicates that there is nothing beyond the application of the knife. Furthermore, previously, surgical treatment was already prohibited specifically regarding the private parts.
Afterwards, even two finger-breadths around the constriction is forbidden; therefore, it is established that this is a prohibition of that [specific act] alone, and not of anything else.
Here, as in the cases of "a weapon means one should seek a weapon-bearer for it," etc., everything by which one cuts is included.
Thus it is said, "or with a thorn," and so forth. Furthermore, regarding the administration of caustic here, [it is explained] in the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga.

It should be understood that [the rule] was authorized by means of a plastered opening on the side. However, some, having altered the reading to "or surgical operation" (*satthakamma*), perform a vaginal procedure (*vatthikamma*).
It is said that "vaginal" (*vatthi*) refers to the *agghikā* (the labia). They explain the meaning as follows: "Surgical operation" (*vatthikamma*) is the cutting with that [instrument].
Regarding them, the word-analysis (*padabhājanīya*) for the phrase "or he should seek one who carries a knife" is as follows: [text continues].
Having shown [the example], it should be rejected. "Testicular enlargement" (*aṇḍavuḍḍhi*) refers to hydrocele (*vātaṇḍaka*). "Adānavatti" refers to varicocele (*ānahavatti*).
Commentary on the Discussion Regarding the Prohibition of Human Flesh (280):
Because it was stated, "Monks, human flesh... [omitted] ...is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*)," [it follows that] "And monks,... [omitted].
Because it is stated, "for not investigating... [and so on]... for an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," one incurs two offenses:
the wrong-doing of not investigating and the grave offense (thullaccaya). Therefore, even in the case of allowable meat, there is only the wrong-doing due to the failure to investigate.

Some say: "One incurs [the offense] only when knowing it to be meat. In the case of cakes and such, what investigation could there be for one who does not know [it to be meat]? Even one who does not know [it to be meat]...
"Some say it is incurred because it is stated in general terms.
[Commentary on the Discussion Prohibiting Elephant Meat, etc. 281. Regarding the statement, "For these...
all is not permitted," this is a word intended merely to illustrate the unallowable nature of all ten types of human flesh and so forth.

This is not a statement intended to show a classification of offenses. The claim that "for one who eats, whether knowing [the nature of the meat] or not, there is indeed an offense" is likewise an indefinite statement, because it does not specify "this particular offense.

The intention of both these points can be understood through the principles established below, where it was stated that for human flesh and so forth, there are offenses of *thullaccaya* (grave) and *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing).
Thus it was said. Herein, this is the intended meaning:

because the flesh and so forth of these beings, such as humans, are unallowable, therefore there is an offense of *thullaccaya* regarding the flesh and so forth of humans. For all others, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa* in every case.
Indeed, in the text itself, having included blood and so forth within the category of flesh, it says: "Monks, human flesh... [etc. ...is an offense of *thullaccaya*."

It has been stated. In that very context, an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) was prescribed even for the flesh and so forth of hands and other parts. Therefore, it is said in the *Sīhaḷaṭṭhakathā*:
“In the case of human flesh, hair, nails, bone, or blood, there is indeed a grave offense (*thullaccaya*).
By this very [statement]: “Bone, blood, skin, hair, and flesh are not permitted.”
The meaning and the intended purpose of the verse from the *Khuddasikkhā* are easy to understand.
Regarding the phrase "in receiving," a dukkaṭa offense due to disrespect is stated here. Some say, "Even [receiving] water, human beings, and so forth, is not permitted.
Although the dangers mentioned by the Nāga king exist, it is stated as "due to repulsiveness" (*paṭikūlatāya*) by taking only the context of the censure.
283. Regarding the commentary on the story of the rice-gruel, honey, and molasses:
“He should be dealt with according to the rule”—this is the statement of the compilers of the Council.

For some say that the Blessed One did not lay down that very same training rule twice, thinking, “In such cases as these. However, it was said with reference specifically to the first laying down of the rule.
Nevertheless, those monks did not become guilty of an offense. How so? Because of the origin story (*aṭṭhuppatti*) regarding the training rule on eating in succession.
It is said: "Furthermore, we ate after having gone for alms at the proper time. And in the *Mātikāvibhaṅga*: "'Eating in succession' means:
having been invited by one of the five kinds of soft food, setting that aside, [to eat] another of the five..."
It is said: "One eats any one of the various kinds of food; this is what is called 'successive eating' (*paramparabhojana*).
Therefore, it is established that "other food" refers to anything whatsoever obtained from an invitation.

Since it was not food obtained from an invitation for a meal-offering (*bhojjayāga*), those monks ate it, [thinking] "there is no offense in this case. Herein, "according to the rule" (*yathādhammo*)...
However, because it was stated, "he should be made to do so," it is permitted that there is an offense only for one who eats food obtained through an invitation from another, and not otherwise.

From that point on, in the section concerning his non-offense, it is said: "at a regular meal, at a ticket-meal, at a fortnightly meal, at an Uposatha meal, or on the first day of the lunar half-month.
Previously, when this was laid down at Vesālī, there was no [offense]; if there were, [it would have been mentioned].

There is no contradiction with the analysis of the introduction to the matrix (*aṭṭhuppattimātikāvibhaṅga*), because it is stated in the introduction: “Moreover, we ate after having wandered for alms at the proper time,” and because it is also stated without qualification in the word-analysis (*padabhājana*): “he eats one or another of the five kinds of cooked food.
Therefore, setting aside food that was invited [to eat] either before or after [the meal],...
For one who eats even when not invited, there is an offense, and not otherwise; for although it has been stated, "Monks,
one should not partake of another's meal-soup except when invited," nevertheless,
there is an offense for one who eats a meal obtained later that is distinct from the first meal for which one was invited, as well as for one who eats regular meals and so forth.

By stating "as if one were committing [an offense] when it has already been committed," the Blessed One both prevents the contingency of a subsequent supplementary rule (*anupaññatti*) and prevents the contingency of an offense in the case of eating without being invited;
and by applying the first promulgated training rule (*sikkhāpada*) to this specific meaning, the Blessed One said, "He is to be dealt with according to the rule.
Therefore, from that point onward, it applies only to one who eats an invitation meal after having previously [refused it].
It is an offense. Among those [cases], it is not included among the "regular meal" (niccabhatta) and so forth;

therefore, the Venerable Elder Upāli, in the section on non-offenses for that [rule], recited it by inserting the five phrases beginning with "in the case of a regular meal. For those Great Nāgas were knowers of the underlying intent (adhippāya);
thus, they first [recorded] exactly what was stated by the Blessed One: "Excepting the five kinds of cooked food, there is no offense in all cases."
The Teacher says: "Even later, while protecting that [rule], it was stated that one should eat only the gruel to be consumed, without touching the honey-ball.
Here it is asked: Just as the Elder, having obtained the privilege later on, made an insertion regarding the permanent meal and so forth, so too in the Kathina-khandhaka...
Why is it not stated: "Monks, for you who have laid out the kaṭhina, these six things shall be allowable," after including "eating in succession"?
It is said: for the purpose of demonstrating the aforementioned occasion [of the offense].
Otherwise, this training rule would have been prescribed by half-measures in both places—namely, at Vesālī and at Andhakavinda. If that were not so, one would be guilty of an offense.

There might be monks who are not guilty of an offense, yet because they perceive scruples even when [the gift] has not been refused, it was said: “In that case, Brahmin, give it to the monks. For the monks, being scrupulous, did not accept it.
Indeed, even though they had consumed it by the Blessed One’s command, “Enjoy it,” they wondered: “Is this specifically designated for us?”
"To dispel the doubt of those who had fallen into uncertainty, it was said: 'Monks, I allow gruel and honey-balls.
In this way, having set aside the training rule concerning "successive eating" (*paramparabhojana*) which was laid down here, [the Buddha considered] how they would eat successive meals.
Regarding this, some teachers say that by means of the very training rule on successive eating, [the allowance for] another...

Although they knew that "eating [solid food] is not permitted," because it was separately authorized with the words, "Monks, I allow rice-gruel (yāgu)," they ate it under the impression that it was permissible—
just like the great offering of fire-brands and other such things. Therefore, when it was said, "Furthermore,
we are accustomed to rice-gruel for breakfast," and so forth, that is incorrect, as it contradicts the introduction and the analysis of the matrix (mātikā) in that context.
Because it would lead to the impossibility of regular meals and the like in the section on non-offenses; because it would not transcend the state of the monks being guilty of an offense;

and because it would lead to the Blessed One appearing to authorize what was wrongly grasped—since those monks [might think] that the Blessed One, in certain instances according to the Vinaya, rejects even what is permissible, saying, "Song-accompanied food is unfit for me to eat."
Therefore, with respect to the Blessed One’s underlying intention (*adhippāya*), it was said: “Being scrupulous, they did not accept [it]”;
yet with respect to the training rule (*sikkhāpada*), the Blessed One himself said, “Monks, I allow rice-gruel,” for the sole purpose of making his own intention clear.
For the Blessed One’s intention is indeed difficult to grasp. Thus, even the milk-rice of Bhāradvāja was considered unfit as food.
He rejected [the former] because it involved a request for what had not been prepared.

However, regarding the triple-sugar gruel prepared after being requested by the Elder Ānanda, he did not say, "Ānanda, whatever has been requested is also improper," but rather said, "Ānanda, whatever has been stored within [the monastery], etc.
By this, he demonstrated the underlying intention that if it were not stored within, it would be allowable; thus, the training rules concerning the requesting of fine foods, soups, and rice.
"It is permitted even for the Blessed One, let alone for us," they thought. 284.
"Sugar was permitted by the Blessed One only for one who is ill" refers to what was stated by way of the words, "Now, those things which are restorative tonics for sick bhikkhus.
For that very reason, they felt scruples regarding the acceptance of these here.

However, here, although it should have been stated, "Monks, I allow molasses-water for one who is ill," because the context concerns molasses, [the text] first mentions what was previously allowed and then allows molasses-water even for one who is not ill.

This demonstrates the distinction that, for one who is ill, molasses may be consumed when there is a valid reason, whereas molasses-water is permissible even when there is no such reason. In this regard:

Regarding the statement, "Sugar-water [mixed with] seven-day medicines becomes a seven-day medicine; because it was specifically permitted by the Blessed One, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) upon exceeding seven days," that is not correct.
Because it has been mixed with water, it loses its status as a seven-day medicine.

Just as mangoes and the like, when mixed with water, become "time-limited for a watch" (*yāmakālika*), so too, having lost their status as seven-day medicines, they become "for life" (*yāvajīvika*) immediately thereafter.
They say it is "stuck," which is appropriate; and because the Blessed One has specifically permitted it, there is no fault in the absence of formal reflection (*paccavekkhaṇā*).

They say that because it is called "sugar-water," it "follows the nature of water. If a mixture with water follows the nature of water, then honey might also be so, since it has been permitted in that same way.
Let it not be so; it should be consumed without having been formally received (*appaṭiggahetvā*).

It might be argued that [the term "empty place"] refers to the course of water, but that is not the case; rather, it is stated in a certain *gaṇṭhipada* (commentary on difficult points) that "it must be understood after investigating all instances.
285. "An empty place" (*suññāgāra*) refers to the fourth jhāna.
[End of] the commentary on the discussion regarding the authorization of the kitchen grounds (*kappiyabhūmi*).

they say it is stated that there may be [the offense] even with the speech of one among many. Because it says “having touched,” it is not permitted if he has not touched.

Commentary on the Discourse on the Authorization of the Kathina: 306. It is written: “*Kathina* means ‘firm’ because it is capable of encompassing the five benefits.

Likewise, the practice of wandering without having formally undertaken [the observance] applies to one who has not resolved upon the three robes.
There is no [possibility] for one who does not possess extra robes (*atecīvarika*), because it is impossible for him to receive a fourth robe or subsequent robes beyond what is required.

For the other [type of practitioner], however, it is obtained by way of non-determination (*anadhiṭṭhāna*). The arising of robes (*cīvaruppāda*) belongs only to one who is not a wearer of rag-robes (*apaṃsukūlika*).

The phrase "within the boundary where the kaṭhina has been spread" is said with reference to the precinct boundary (*upacārasīma*); for one standing within the precinct boundary, there is participation in the distribution of robes from the deceased and so forth, whereas within a formally bound boundary (*baddhasīmā*), [the distribution] is otherwise.
Because there is no arising [of the robe] therein, this should be understood as intended here as the *upacāra-sīmā* (the precinct boundary).
Who obtains the spreading of the *kathina*? This means: who accomplishes it? Five persons accomplish it.
For there are, at the very least, four donors of the *kathina-cloth* and one recipient. "In that case, monks, if this community of monks consists of a quorum of four..."

Because it is stated in the Campeyyakkhandhaka that "except for the three formal acts—ordination, the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*), and rehabilitation"—it should be understood that [the distribution of the *kaṭhina* cloth] is not to be performed by a group of five.

Some say, "To whomsoever the Saṅgha gives the *kaṭhina* cloth, it is permissible to give it even if he is outside the boundary and not within arm's reach (*hatthapāsa*)," but that [is incorrect]; it must indeed be done while he is within arm's reach.
It must be given. Why? Because it is stated: “Because he has reached the point for the formal act (*kamma*). It is further stated:
“When robes are purchased with rice and such items produced locally, those robes accrue only to those who have performed the *kaṭhina* ceremony;
however, when rice and such items are purchased with robes, they accrue to everyone. Those who have been invited at the first invitation receive [the benefit].

This was stated according to the highest limit. If it is asked: "How is it known that the Kathina should be spread by making others who have completed the rains-residence—though not invited due to obstacles—the fillers of the quorum?
It is because the *Parivāra* uses the singular number when stating: "The Kathina is considered spread for two persons: for the one who spreads it and for the one who gives thanks."
And because of the statement right there: "The kaṭhina has been spread for the Saṅgha; the kaṭhina has been spread for a group or for an individual.

As for the point that even those who have spent the rains in another monastery do not receive [the robe], does this apply within a single boundary (*ekasīma*) or within different boundaries (*nānāsīma*)?
What is the case here? First, if it is within a single boundary, then as stated further on: "But if there are many monasteries within a single boundary..."
This contradicts the statement in the Aṭṭhakathā: “Having assembled all the bhikkhus together, the kaṭhina should be spread in one place; it is not permitted to spread it separately.
For this statement demonstrates that there is only a single spreading of the kaṭhina for everyone.
Furthermore, if [the kaṭhina were spread] in different boundaries, it would contradict the allowance for Upananda’s gift made with a single intention.
For this has been said: "Give, monks, a single [robe] to that foolish man.
This statement demonstrates that the success of the *kaṭhina*-distribution for him occurs even in two separate residences. Since there is no prohibition, only non-contradiction is required;
therefore, whether within a single boundary or different boundaries, even those who have completed the rains retreat in another monastery within a different precinct [may participate].

The intended meaning should be understood as: "They obtain [the benefits]. It is said: "One who has received full ordination during the later period (pacchimikā) is permitted to perform the invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā) at the first invitation;

he becomes one who has entered the rains-residence (vassiko) and obtains the benefit. Thus, the entry into the rains-residence for novices (sāmaṇera) was authorized, and novices obtain the benefits of the robe-making season (kathina)."

The phrase "sufficient for any one of the three robes" appears to contradict the canonical text: "The kaṭhina is not considered spread unless provided with the outer robe (saṅghāṭi), the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga), and the inner robe (antaravāsaka).

If it is argued that this canonical passage demonstrates that the kaṭhina is not considered spread even if one of the three robes is missing, we say no; for the meaning of that [latter] passage is understood differently.
The Blessed One spoke that passage with the intention of demonstrating that the *kathina* is not considered "spread" if one is separated from any one of the three robes.

If it is argued that, in that case, the phrase "except for the outer robe (*saṅghāṭī*), the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*), and the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*)" should not have been stated, the answer is no;
for this is due solely to understanding the underlying intention. For one who intends to spread the *kathina* using the outer robe, [the rule applies] "except for the outer robe."
It is not spread. This same method applies to the other cases as well; this is the intended meaning here.
For that very reason, in the bright fortnight, only a single robe is mentioned by way of the formula beginning with "the outer cloak (saṅghāṭī) is spread. This being so, [it is said]:
"In twenty-four ways the kaṭhina is not spread; in seventeen ways the kaṭhina is spread," according to what is appropriate.
It should be understood that this is stated according to the highest limit; therefore, even if all twenty-four modes—such as the black side being scraped away...

up to... the absence of rejoicing in the place outside the boundary—are entirely non-existent, and even if some of those that cannot occur, such as the making of a sign, are present, the *kaṭhina* is not considered "laid. This is the intended meaning. It is the same regarding the white side.

The intention should be understood as follows: the *kaṭhina* robe is considered properly spread (*atthatam*) by way of being any one of the seventeen modes—beginning with "unbeaten and beaten" (*ahatāhatakappa*)—and so forth, up to "boundary-based" (*sīmaṭṭha*) and "rejoicing" (*anumodana*), provided that these are possible, even if all the others are entirely absent.
Otherwise, there would be mutual contradiction; therefore, it should be understood by applying them according to what is possible.

In this regard, here is a brief illustration: regarding the dark fortnight, based on the authoritative statement, "When the kaṭhina has been spread with an upper robe, it is not considered 'spread' if there is neither a double-layered outer robe nor an inner robe," that kaṭhina would be unspread.
And regarding the bright fortnight, [it is said]: "It is considered 'spread' when [the robe] is not marked."

Regarding the measure of the word: even if the formal proclamation (*parikathā*) has been made when the *kaṭhina* robe has been spread without a specific sign, the *kaṭhina* is nonetheless considered to have been spread.
Thus, there is this twofold contradiction. It should be understood that a resolution occurs when the underlying intention (*adhippāya*) is grasped according to the method already stated.
By the phrase "which bestows great benefit," he illustrates, as it were, an attachment to requisites; nevertheless, by the Blessed One—
Having established that the door [of the rule] was opened by way of the prescription for seeking robes as much as needed, it serves for the benefit of the Saṅgha.
It is written: "‘It is not to be done’—there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who does not do it out of disrespect.

Regarding the phrase "We express our appreciation" (anumodāma), this is stated in a comprehensive sense. "I express my appreciation" (anumodāmi) should be said by a single person; otherwise, [it would be improper].
"It is not permissible," it is said, according to the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*.
Once one has determined the *kathina* robe-cloth, as soon as the words "I spread the *kathina* with this outer robe (*saṅghāṭī*)" are uttered, the *kathina* is considered spread for that individual.

However, only a single formal act (*kammavācā*) is permitted; thus, there is a formal act only for the cloth intended for the *kathina*, whereas for the giving of the remaining robes, there is only a formal motion (*apalokana*).

The word "attho" (the meaning) has been written. Regarding the phrase "within one boundary" (*ekasīmāya*), the meaning "within one precinct-boundary" (*eka-upacāra-sīmā*) is appropriate. However, some maintain that "bound boundary" (*baddha-sīmā*) is intended;
for when [the robe] is spread within one place within a single boundary, it is considered spread everywhere because it is said, "all the bhikkhus having assembled.
Even by those who offer the expression of thanks (*anumodana*), it is indeed considered spread, provided it is within the limits of the precinct.

In each respective case, what is obtainable by those [respective individuals] is indeed obtained. Even for those who have entered [the assembly], it must be obtained by all because it has been spread out;
this is the distinction. They say that it is stated exactly like this in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, but this should be investigated.
308. It is a "great-ground" (mahābhūmika) dharma because it possesses twenty-four modes. "Long-sewn" (*dīghasibbita*) means sewn later on.
"Having turned it over, [one performs] the sewing," so it is written. "Kaṇḍusa" means a preliminary binding.

"The first layer has been joined and set aside" means that, seeing the *kathina* cloth to be weak, those desiring to sew it by making it double-layered—having joined it with their own strong, natural cloth because the natural cloth was larger than the *kathina* cloth—[set it aside].
The intention is that first, having adjusted it to the appropriate size for heating, it is made by binding it with cords upon a binding-board.
Because the cloth for the *kaṭhina* robe has not yet arrived, the cloth already bound becomes the "stomach-patch" (*kucchicimilika*).
This is shown by the citation of the words spoken in the *Mahāpaccarī* and the *Kuruṇḍī*; there is only a difference in the phrasing, but none in the meaning.

"It should be understood as 'how' (*kata*). If it is asked, 'What does this illustrate?'—someone might think that a robe made in such a way, even if it is a *dupaṭṭa* (two-layered) robe, would fall under the category of a regular robe (*pakaticīvara*) because of its large size, and not under the category of a *kathina* robe;
but it should not be viewed in that way. Even a *kathina* robe, though it remains in a state of being a patched-together rag, [is still a *kathina* robe] even if it is large."
"That natural robe is indeed his own *kathina* robe.

Because a minimum of five [measures] is required, one who wishes to sew by cutting the *kathina* cloth into many pieces takes a strip from the *kathina* robe and applies that strip to another robe that is not a *kathina* robe—so it is written. Or else, there are many *kathina* cloths.
Rags that have been given are small and insignificant for the purpose of a single robe, while large ones are given for the purpose of making up a deficiency.
Regarding "from a kaṭhina robe": a monk takes a strip from one part of a kaṭhina robe and joins it to another.
Here it is asked: should rags that are the smallest allowable size for a kaṭhina cloth be given after they have been formally assigned, or rather...
"Are they even minor items? In this case, because they do not count as robes (*acīvara-saṅkhyattā*), it is not permitted to give them [as part of the Kathina].

Some say that the formal act (*kammavācā*) does not take effect there. Because of the method given in the Canon—namely, "it is covered with rag-robes"—this refers to cloth for the Kathina that exists in the state of a worn-out rag;
since it has not entered into formal determination (*anadhiṭṭhānupagga*) by its own nature, it is indeed of the category of old robes (*purāṇacīvara*).

Because the *aṭṭhakathā* explains that even small items may be given by way of consent for them to become part of the *kathina* robe—even for one who is not eligible for the formal resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*)—it is permissible to give even minor articles.
For some say that this is allowable on the grounds that the one performing the *kathina* spreading will assemble them and make them into a *kathina* robe;
however, one should adopt the more reasonable interpretation.
“Stored up for a long time” means it has been kept for many days. “Dependent on the Saṅgha” means because it was made by the Saṅgha.
It is called “an offense entailing relinquishment” (*nissaggiya*) because it must be relinquished once the night has passed. “Five pieces” means that which has five patches as its measure;

the meaning is “by that [measure] or by what is in excess. “Cut on that very day” means given by the Saṅgha immediately after the formal act (*kammavācā*) for the spreading of the Kathina has been recited.
On that very day, it must be formally cut off and made circular.
For it is said in the *Parivāra* that "the preliminary action (*pubbakaraṇa*) is comprised of seven factors" when it has already been given; this does not refer to what is being given by the donor.

Therefore, if the donor gives it to the Saṅgha once the preliminary action is completed, it should be accepted and then granted through the formal act (*kammavācā*). And by that [act], on that very...

Having established the boundary and spread out the robe-cloth, the Saṅgha should be asked for its formal approval (anumodana), because there is nothing further to be done once the preliminary procedure (pubbakaraṇa) has been performed.
Indeed, the statement beginning with "not merely by scratching" was said with reference specifically to what is in the hand of the one spreading the cloth.
Even that which has already completed the preliminary procedure must be washed and dried again; this is the authority of the word.
Why? Because what has been cut cannot be cut again. If it is argued that it must be cut in another place, we say no;

for according to the authority of the statement in the section on ordination, "having caused the hair and beard to be shaved off," there would follow the absurd consequence that even for one who is already shaven, one would have to search for hair, place it on the head, have it shaved off again, and then ordain him.
This is not the case here, as indicated by the negative particle *na*.

If it is argued that this is because it is prohibited, we say no; for since it is prohibited by the negative particle in the phrase "not apart from the outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*)," it would follow as an undesirable consequence that when the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) is spread out, it is not considered "spread out. Therefore, one should not hold such a misconception.
Furthermore, because it is stated that "one standing outside the boundary of the precincts," the very same determination explained previously must be accepted.

309. Regarding the statement, "The *kathina* is spread by means of what has not been stored up": here, is both kinds of storage intended only for the month of the *kathina*-spreading, or even prior to that?
Or rather, when should it be given by the donor—only during the month of the *kathina*-spreading, or even prior to that?
And even during the month of the *kathina*-spreading, on which specific day should it be given for the purpose of spreading the *kathina*?

It must be investigated whether it is permissible or not permissible to give [the robe]. During the month of the *kathina* ceremony itself, both types of storage (*sannidhi*) are likewise impermissible.
Even by the donor, it is not permissible to give [the cloth] specifically intended for the *kathina* robe, just as with the *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season) robe.

Why? Because it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary) in the manner beginning with: "There is a duty for the giver of the *kathina*. If one objects, "This is merely the highest limit," we say: No.
Because it is said, “The *kathina* is called ‘excessively strict’ (*atiukkaṭṭha*) and is not permitted,” [one might ask]: “Is this not said with reference to its arrival? No;
this too is said with reference to its arrival itself, meaning that what was given previously is not permitted.
310. “Of the *kathina*” means of the *kathina*-spreading. “For the sake of its suspension” (*ubbhārāya*) means for the sake of its cessation, that is to say, for the sake of its non-occurrence.

If it is asked, "What is the purpose of showing the lifting [of the robe-restriction]? It is for the sake of generating restraint regarding those [five days] by showing the limit of the time when there is no offense.

Otherwise, because it is stated in the Vibhaṅga: "The robe-season is called the last month of the rainy season when the Kathina has not been spread, and five months when the Kathina has been spread," [it would follow that] even in the absence of the lifting [of the restriction] due to departing in the interim and so forth, [the offense would apply] for five [days].
It might be a misconception to think that there is no offense for five months.
Therefore, it should be understood that by perceiving what is a field of offense as a non-field of offense, one incurs various offenses and creates an obstacle to the gains of other monks.
[End of] the commentary on the discussion of the sevenfold set on taking up.

311. Regarding the statement that "for both types of *sanniṭṭhānantika* (those involving a formal decision), the obstacles are severed at once," this is stated here as well as in the *Parivāra-aṭṭhakathā*.
This accords with the *Khandhaka-pāḷi*, because in both cases the burden has been laid down simultaneously. [Objection:
"This was stated specifically regarding the *sanniṭṭhānantika* occurring outside the boundary (*bahisīmā*), as stated in the *Parivāra*. [Response: That which is stated in the *Parivāra*...
“There are four ways of terminating the *kathina*: it may be terminated within the boundary (*sīma*), it may be terminated outside the boundary;

[the four are] that which ends with completion, that which ends with determination, that which ends with loss, and that which ends with the cutting off of expectation. In this context, the method shown here is precisely how that which ends with determination is terminated outside the boundary.
How is that which ends with determination terminated within the boundary? Taking up robe-cloth that has not yet been made...
"He went [thinking], 'I will not return. Not finding a comfortable stay at each place he went, he returned to that very same monastery;
thus his attachment to the robe remained. But as soon as the thought arises, 'I will not have this robe made,' it is severed.
Therefore, it is relinquished within the boundary (sīmā). Thus, there are two kinds of 'conclusion by determination' (sanniṭṭhānantika)," according to the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*.

That which is written is appropriate; otherwise, within the boundary (*sīmā*), the declaration made with the thought, "I shall not have this robe made," would not coincide with the other [conditions], and thus it would be superfluous.
"One who has crossed the boundary" means one who has crossed the boundary of the robe-making period (*cīvarakāla*).
When there is a formal declaration (*ubbhāra*), the obstacle regarding the robe (*cīvarapalibodha*) appears as if it were first severed; nevertheless, because of the lingering expectation...

Regarding the phrase "he is enthusiastic about making robes," this refers to his underlying intention (*lesa*); it is said that "the two obstacles are severed simultaneously" by virtue of his retinue.
Because it is stated [elsewhere] that "the robe has been made," this [simultaneous severance] is not possible here. 316.
One who departs without leaving behind any of one's requisites is said to "depart having taken them with him."

“There is no distinction regarding the suspension of the *kaṭhina*. The ‘instances of undertaking’ (*samādāya-vāra*) are stated solely for the purpose of showing the sequence, based on the distinction of the individual’s intention (*puggalādhippāya*);
so it is written in all the *gaṇṭhi* commentaries. However, here the purpose of the individual’s intention must be examined.

Because there is no [rule] ending with departure (*pakkamanantika*), the phrase ‘as far as possible’ (*yathāsambhava*) is used. Even in the case of an incomplete act, by way of relinquishing the responsibility (*dhuranikkhepa*)...”

If it is argued that "the category of departure (*pakkamanantika*) is possible, therefore the category of departure must also be stated," [we reply]: No, because it would entail the characteristic of being determined by the act of informing (*sanniṭṭhānantika*).
Furthermore, for one whose robe has not yet been made, there is no category of hearing (*savanantika*).
Herein, this is the analysis of the categories starting from the beginning: there are seven categories of "taking up" (*ādāya*), and likewise two categories of "undertaking" (*samādāya*).
There are seven groups of six. Then, excluding the case of departing, there are two groups of six: those concerning taking up an unfinished robe and those concerning undertaking [the robe].
Following that, three groups of three are shown by way of the cases of completion, determination, and loss;
therein, the first group of three refers to not employing the procedure of thinking "I will not return" within the boundary.

This [offense] occurs outside the boundary with the thought, "I will not return"; therefore, the factors of departing from the boundary (*pakkamanantika*) and crossing the boundary (*sīmātikkantikasaubbhāra*) are not applicable there.
Even though the offense of "frustrating expectations" (*āsāvacchedika*) is possible, it is not mentioned because of the aforementioned reason.
The second triad occurs within the boundary with the thought, "I will not return"; although the factor of departing from the boundary is possible here, nevertheless—
"In the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada* it is said: 'Because only those for whom the obstacle of robes (*cīvarapalibodha*) is severed are intended [by this rule], it is not mentioned.
Furthermore, the reasoning is that in all fifteen cases, only the robe that has been left unfinished is intended. The ancients say:

'When there is both a determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) and an unfinished robe, it is not subject to the end of the completion (*niṭṭhānantika*); when there is a remainder after completion, it is not subject to the end of destruction (*nāsanantika*')."
The third triad proceeds by qualifying [the previous] with the term *anadhiṭṭhita* (not determined); in meaning, it corresponds to the first triad.
It is said that its purpose is to demonstrate the meaning of that [first triad].

Since these three alternative meanings can be shown by means of these very three methods for the suspension of the Kathina, they alone have been joined together by way of a single connection; otherwise, the first triad...
There would be a set of six (chaṭṭaka), just as there is a set of six at the end of this set of fifteen.
Following the third triad, the fourth triad—which could have occurred—occurs instead through the specific wording: "within the boundary, 'I shall return'.
And when joined in that way, it follows a sequence that is not in conflict with the others, such as the *savanantika* and so forth; therefore, rather than being a fourth triad, it is a set of six.
It should be understood as "already made. Thus, the first group of fifteen [rules]—consisting of three triads and one hexad—is to be understood.
Now, this same group of fifteen is designated as the second, the "Fifteen on Taking Up," by means of a specific prefix (*upasagga*).
Again, "taking up a robe that has been left unfinished" is the third group of fifteen; "having taken up" is the fourth group of fifteen.
This has been shown. Thus, four sets of fifteen [cases] are to be understood.
Therein, in the first and second sets of fifteen, "unmade robe-cloth" is intended in every respect; in the other two, it should be construed as "unfinished.
"It may be accepted at a place previously designated with the expectation of robe-cloth; it is not permitted elsewhere. If the expectation of robe-cloth is cut off..."
"Once a robe has arisen, it does not constitute a 'robe-obstacle' (cīvarapalibodha)," so it is said in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*.
Regarding the third Kathina rule among the *Nissaggiya* offenses, the expectation of a robe that has arrived is here termed "expectation of a robe" (*cīvarāsa*).

Considering that wherever there is an expectation of a robe, that location is called "expectation of a robe" by way of metaphorical designation (*adhikaraṇūpacāra*), [the text says] "he attends upon that expectation of a robe," and so forth.
It has been said; therefore, the meaning should be understood as "he obtains it without expectation," that is, "he obtains it in a place where there is no expectation," and so forth.

Here, one section consists of the fourfold treatment by way of *niṭṭhāna* (conclusion), *sanniṭṭhāna* (decision), *nāsana* (removal), and *āsāvacchedika* (cutting off expectation); thus this constitutes one tetrad.

Consequently, the three triads mentioned previously, when augmented by the [section on] cutting off expectation, become three tetrads; thus, there is one "twelvefold set of non-expectation" (*anāsā-dvādasaka*).
It should be understood. Although the sequence of the first set of twelve [cases] is obtained in the immediately following set of twelve [cases],
nevertheless, in order to show the distinction by making that one set of twelve self-evident, it is stated from the beginning,
"I shall return within the boundary," in contrast to the statement in the second tetrad, "He hears it while he has gone outside the boundary," and so forth.
In the third tetrad, it should be understood that [the phrase] "for the purpose of making room for those beginning with 'one who has heard'" is intended.

Furthermore, although this group of twelve can be obtained by way of non-expectation (*anāsā*), it should be understood that it is not shown here because it is established by implication from what has already been stated.
Thus, two groups of twelve have been extracted here. In the "twelve to be done" (*karaṇīya-dvādasaka*) as well, there is the group of twelve by way of non-expectation as it has been shown.

Two sets of twelve factors—the "unspoken-established" (avuttasiddha) and the "twelve [factors] regarding expectation" (āsāyadvādasaka)—are to be extracted. Now, there is the ninefold set concerning departure for a specific direction (disaṃgamika).
In that context, because the phrase "one who departs for a specific direction" itself establishes by implication that "he will not return," that point was not explicitly stated.
By this much, the absence of the obstacle of the residence (āvāsapalibodha) has been shown.
321. By the phrase “not neglecting his share of robe-cloth,” he shows that he possesses the obstacle of robe-cloth (*cīvara-palibodha*).

“Share” (*paṭivīsa*) means the portion of robe-cloth one is entitled to receive for oneself. “Not neglecting” (*apavilāyamāna*) means desiring it. When there is an acquisition of robe-cloth for him, there is one triad based on the following:

[the robe being obtained] at the residence where he has spent the rains retreat, by way of formal determination (*niṭṭhāna*), by way of formal authorization (*sanniṭṭhāna*), and by way of the end of the [robe-]season (*nāsanantika*); and of those very same [conditions],...
By way of one [robe] on the way and one at the destination, a single set of nine should be understood through three triads.
Following that, the "fivefold comfortable dwelling" (*phāsuvihāra-pañcaka*) is stated by way of the *niṭṭhāna-sanniṭṭhāna-nāsana*, the *kasī-mātikkantika*, and the *saubbhāra*.
In both cases, the impossibility of the remaining robe-removal (*kathinuddhāra*) is self-evident. However, this is the distinction regarding the fivefold [set] here:
The section on undertaking [the robe] is not possible because of the intention to return, thinking, "I shall return.
(325) "Monks, these two are obstacles to the kaṭhina": they are the conditions for the non-continuation of the spreading of the kaṭhina.
The commentary on the Kaṭhina-khandhaka is finished.
8. Commentary on the Chapter on Robes:
Explanation of the Discourse on the Matter of Jīvaka.
326. *Rājagahako* means a resident of Rājagaha.
328. Because he was of a nature free from delusion, he attained full consciousness before long. "I am your father; in what sense? Because you were nourished by me. 329.
The reading is "Sakke vissaṭṭhamatte" (as soon as [the child] was entrusted to Sakka); it refers to the very moment of being entrusted in the eighth training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
Commentary on the Story of King Pajjota.

334. Regarding the phrase "sitting down to eat": here they say, "In the *Dhammapada* it is stated, 'Having seen [him] outside the city'; therefore, what was given on two days was taken by him one from each, and thus it is consistent with what is stated in the two commentaries.
336. Regarding the commentary on the account of the thirty-fold purgative:
as for the phrase "mouthful by mouthful," although sugar and other substances were placed therein, the Blessed One himself consumed them; therefore, there is no fault.
Commentary on the Discourse Requesting Permission for Marriage (Varayācanakathāvaṇṇanā) 337.
It is said that what is called a *mahāpiṭṭhiyaka-ajava* is a flower measuring more than four finger-breadths.
Commentary on the Discourse Beginning with the Allowance of Blankets (Kambalānujānanādikathāvaṇṇanā).
340. "In the vicinity" (*upacāre*) means in the vicinity of the charnel ground (*susāna*). Some say it is also permissible outside [the boundary].

Having shown the making of an agreement (*katikā*), saying, "Let what belongs to me be yours and mine," and having been told so by the other, it is permissible; thus they state the procedure for shared requisites. 342.
Since it is stated that "it is also permissible to designate even a broken boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*)," the remaining formal acts (*kamma*) may also be performed while sitting there.

Commentary on the Minor Section (Cūḷavagga) 1. Commentary on the Chapter on Formal Acts (Kammakkhandhaka)
Commentary on the Discussion of the Twelvefold Set of Unlawful Acts (Adhammakammadvādasaka):
The three sets beginning with "it is done in the absence of the accused" (*asammukhā kataṃ*) are merely for the sake of the teaching.

For an unlawful act is not necessarily constituted by the convergence of all three factors; it is indeed constituted even by a single one. This meaning is established by the textual passage beginning with, "Monks, in the case of three... (*tiṇṇaṃ, bhikkhave*).
It is to be established. The statement, "It is done without prior consent," is said with reference to one who is conscientious (*lajjin*).
Regarding the dark side, it says, "It is done for an offense that does not lead to confession"; regarding the bright side, it says, "It is done for an offense that leads to confession.
These two points are followed later by: "Monks, when a monk possesses three factors, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may perform an act of censure (*tajjanīyakamma*) against him..."

[If one were to] act [thus], it would contradict the statement: “He has failed in virtue regarding higher morality. For one who has committed an offense that does not require confession is indeed said to have “failed in virtue regarding higher morality.
This is logical; however, the intention of the agent must be considered here.
Regarding this, the Elder Upatissa said: “For specifically, being a maker of strife is a constituent factor of the act of censure (tajjanīya-kamma).”
It is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that this is consistent with the introduction (*nidāna*) as it appears in the *Pāḷi*;

therefore, even in the case of all three categories [of offenses], having brought about a dispute, this formal act (*kamma*) should be performed by way of the offense committed on account of that dispute.

Consequently, regarding the phrase "one who has failed in virtue with respect to higher virtue," here too—whether at an earlier or later stage, or at the time of the formal charge and reminder—it is on account of a dispute that...
"It must be dealt with solely by way of the offense committed, and not merely on account of a *saṅghādisesa* offense. It is written:
"Regarding 'an offense that does not lead to confession' (*adesanāgāminiyā āpattiyā*), one should state only 'an offense involving defeat' (*pārājikāpattiyā*);

the subsequent phrase 'transgression regarding higher virtue in matters of defeat or *saṅghādisesa*' is stated in the ancient *Gaṇṭhipada*. "'One who has failed in virtue regarding higher virtue' refers to a *saṅghādisesa* offense."
“Intending [this],” it is written in the *Gaṇṭhipada*. This accords with the earlier statement in the ancient *Gaṇṭhipada*;
therefore, in that context, the latter *pārājika* rule may have been stated by way of a summary of the meaning (*atthuddhāra*). And in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is said:
“‘Not leading to confession’ means either a *pārājika* offense or a *saṅghādisesa* offense. In that case, the *pārājika* offense is mentioned by way of a summary of the meaning.

It may have been so stated. Since in the *Gaṇṭhipada* only this much was written—“‘One who has failed in virtue regarding higher morality’ refers to the *saṅghādisesa*” —therefore, throughout the *Gaṇṭhipada*, according to the entire method, a *tajjanīya-kamma* (act of censure) should not be performed on account of a quarrel arising from an offense involving a *pārājika* transgression, because there is no purpose [for it];
rather, it should be performed on account of a *saṅghādisesa* transgression. This is the meaning.
It is established. If it is argued that this is not so because of the statement, "it has been done regarding an offense subject to confession during the bright fortnight," we say no;
for it is possible to apply the designation "subject to confession" to a *saṅghādisesa* offense by way of a particular method.
That formal act (*kamma*) by which censure is carried out is called a *tajjanīya-kamma* (act of censure). That formal act by which [one is] dependent...
They must be clothed; it is that which is depended upon, shared, and assigned—this is called the *niyassakamma* (act of subordination).
That by which one who has corrupted families is expelled from that residence and from the village is called the *pabbājanīyakamma* (act of banishment).

This should be understood as the miscellaneous analysis regarding the censure transaction and others. What is the censure transaction? What is the root of the censure transaction?
What is its basis? What is its conclusion? Why is it called a "censure transaction"? What...
A *tajjanīya-kamma* (act of censure) is the successful performance [of the act] when the basis exists. What is the root of a *tajjanīya-kamma*? The Saṅgha is the root.
What is the basis of a *tajjanīya-kamma*? The basis for an offense arising from quarreling. What is its conclusion?
The conclusion is through cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Why is it called a *tajjanīya-kamma*? Because the Saṅgha [censures] the person who causes quarrels, regarding both the quarrel and the schism.
By showing fear, it generates patience and generates tranquility; therefore, it is called a "censure transaction" (*tajjanīyakamma*).
How is a censure transaction performed? How is it not performed? In what way is a censure transaction performed?
In what way is it not performed? By whom is a censeure transaction performed? By whom is it not performed? Where...

Where has the act of censure been performed, and where has it not been performed? At what time has the act of censure been performed, and at what time has it not been performed? How is the act of censure performed?

It is performed by a unanimous Saṅgha through a formal procedure consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha-kamma*). How is it not performed? It is not performed when done by a factional Saṅgha through a formal procedure consisting of one motion and three proclamations.

And how is it done? By the perfection of the performance. And how is it not done? By the failure of the performance. And by whom is it done? By the Saṅgha. And by whom is it not done? By a group or by an individual. And where is it done?
In the presence of that person against whom the Saṅgha performs the act of censure.
And where is it not performed? It is when the Saṅgha performs the act of censure against a person who is not present before them.
At what time is it performed? When an offense arising from a quarrel exists. At what time is it not performed?
When no offense arising from a quarrel exists. In how many ways is the act of censure [performed]?
It is appropriate; in how many ways is it inappropriate? It is appropriate for a censure transaction (*tajjanīya-kamma*) in seven ways, and inappropriate in seven ways.
What are the seven ways in which it is appropriate, and what are the seven ways in which it is inappropriate?
[It is inappropriate] when no offense arising from quarreling exists, or when that person is not present.
Either the Saṅgha is incomplete, or there is a person not in communion present in that assembly;
or he has not been accused, or has not been formally charged, or the offense has not been attributed to him. By these seven ways, a procedure of censure is not fit to be carried out;
by the other seven ways, it is fit. This applies to the remaining formal acts as well.
The commentary on the Kammakkhandhaka is finished.

No; because in the classification of performing the formal act with a quorum of four or more, the person eligible for consent is mentioned without distinction.

That has been stated in general terms. And this is a specific characteristic; therefore, even though there is a disclosure of views (*diṭṭhāvikamma*), this [offense] does not become "done by way of rejection" (*paṭikuṭṭhakata*)?

Even for those who, when the second motion (*ñatti*) has been established by way of commonality, depart after giving their consent at that moment—while the second-motion formal proclamation (*kammavācā*) has not yet begun or is not yet finished—their [act] does not indeed cease. Those...
Regarding the phrase "they do not exist there," the meaning should be understood as: "those who, by the method already described, do not exist there.

"but those who, having committed an offense together with them, did not go there, or having come..."
Or, having given their consent, they sat in the surrounding cells and so forth; thus the preceding and the following are connected.
It is said: "In that regard, the irrevocability of the legal act (*kamma*) is to be understood by the manifestation of what has been seen in the text.
Commentary on the Discussion of Legal Issues (*Adhikaraṇakathāvaṇṇanā*).
220. A conflict of thought (*cittuppāda*) is a dispute (*vivāda*). By way of metaphorical attribution (*kāraṇūpacāra*), even the word "dispute" comes to be reckoned as wholesome and so forth.
With reference to this, it is said: "It is a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) because of its state of being a legal issue through the means of settling.
