455. *Appeva nāma* means "it would indeed be well. *Mūlā dāyakā pesalakā* means "the donors are excellent. It is written as *kullakavihārena*, meaning "by means of a small monastery.
It is called a *kullakavihāra* because it is an introduction to the forms [of the Dhamma]. But how is this known?

By which [rule] is that which has been stored up for life (*yāvajīvika*) mixed with what is for the time being (*yāvakālika*), received on that very day, and thus becomes a mixture of flavors, yet remains reckoned as having been received on that very day?
Does it follow that [food] having been brought and stored goes by the very number of *tadāhupatiggahita* (received on that day)? It is said:
Because of the statement, “Monks, whatever is for life (*yāvajīvika*) is, on that very day, received as for the time-being (*yāvakālika*)”;

therefore, it is established that if food received for life that was previously received is mixed with food received on that day, it goes by the number of what was previously received. Otherwise, [the rule regarding] food for seven days...

Just as it was stated in the passage, "Monks, what has been received for life-long use is allowable for seven days," so too here one might say, "Monks, what has been received for life-long use is allowable at the proper time [along with] what is for the time-being"; however, that was not said.

Therefore, it should be understood that what was received previously, when mixed with foodstuffs, belongs to the category of foodstuffs alone. In the *Gaṇṭhipada*, however, regarding "that which is stored... [the text continues].
It has been said, "either solid food (khādanīya) or soft food (bhojanīya). One must not take the mere words [literally].

457. "Here" means in this text. The meaning is that by the mere statement, "It is allowable at the proper time, it is not allowable at the improper time," one incurs the offense of eating at the improper time (vikālabhojana-pācittiya) [if one thinks], "It is allowable at the improper time"; and by [the statement], "It is not allowable," one incurs the offense of eating what has been stored (sannidhibhojana-pācittiya).
It is written: "The meaning is 'it brings [the duration]'; if it has a mixed flavor, even if received today, it lasts for as long as life—this is the meaning. Regarding "in the Suttavibhaṅga":
the meaning is both in the Sutta known as the Mātikā and in its Vibhaṅga known as the word-by-word commentary (padabhājanīya).
This is indeed found there. Which one? "For one who lets [the time] pass, it is an offense involving cutting off (chedanaka). This is it.
If I saw that sitting mat as being three spans in measure, how could it be a sitting mat?
For its characteristic is that it must have a border.
If it is three spans in measure, and the border there is one span;
Because it is called "sitting mat" (nisīdana), there may be cutting [of the cloth] for that purpose.
If one asks, "How could there be cutting if it is not called 'sitting mat'?"— it should not be said so, because [the rule applies to any cloth] measuring a span (vidatthi) in size.
"It is allowable for a sitting-cloth (nisīdana) to be of the size of a 'six-measure'—this is the reason [given].
How could this not be appropriate as the name for a sitting-cloth?
Because it is called a 'sitting-cloth,' yet it exceeds the prescribed measure."
Because it is caused by his consent, there would be a "cutting-off" offense in that case.
Regarding gold and silver:
in the Canon, gold and silver are prohibited for the individual alone.
"Of the Saṅgha" means for the Saṅgha, and if that is entirely permissible.
Yet, eating at the improper time is prohibited for an individual alone;
how can it be consistent to say "not for the Saṅgha" while [eating at the improper time] is permissible for the Saṅgha?
The commentary on the Sattasatika-kkhandhaka is finished.
The commentary on the Cūḷavagga is finished.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Commentary on the Parivāra:
Commentary on the Sixteen Major Sections;
Commentary on the Section on Formal Rules (Paññattivāra).

1–2. The meaning is: "In the Dispensation (sāsana) of the body of the Dhamma-aggregate (dhammakkhandha), which consists of virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
"Parivāra" refers to the supplement (parivāra) of that [text] which has been included in the collection (saṅgaha).

"The formulation that constitutes the Vinaya" is *vinayapaññatti*. Having stated [the phrase] "by one who knows the time for formulation" according to the method of pairs (*dukanaya*), it is then stated again according to the method of the Suttas (*suttantanaya*).

Furthermore, it is said: “Moreover, by means of the recollection of past lives, etc. In this context, “seeing” (passana) refers to the vision of penetrative knowledge (paṭivedhañāṇa) associated with the divine eye because it is a mode of seeing.

“He sees by means of the wisdom of teaching” refers to [the knowledge of] dispositions (āsaya), underlying tendencies (anusaya), and so forth. “By means of questioning” (pucchāya) is the locative case.

“Again, here” (punapi ettha) refers to the answering of the question. “Wrong view” (micchādiṭṭhi) refers to the view of nihilism (natthikadiṭṭhi) and the view of grasping at extremes (antaggāhikadiṭṭhi).

Because of the statement, “These are prescribed for the sake of livelihood,” it should be understood that, with the exception of these six training rules, the remainder are called failures of conduct (*ācāravipatti*).

Regarding the phrase, “one incurs an offense by means of the body”: here, having made the mind of pursuit the constituent factor in the preliminary stage, and having generated the intimation (*viññatti*) known as the door of the body, one incurs the offense known as the arising of the mental state that has proceeded [thereafter].

"Although the intimation (viññatti) is originated by the mind, nevertheless, because the meaning intended by the mind is accomplished through that intimation, it is said to be 'committed via the door of the body'.
This was stated with reference to this specific meaning, and not to the settling of the three types of disputes such as quarreling.
"Until the end of life" means making one's life the limit. "By the ancient Mahātheras" refers to the Mahātheras of the island of Sri Lanka.
The meaning is that it was established at the time of being committed to writing. It is said: "The recitation recorded in books (*potthakāruḷhasaṅgīti*) was like the Fourth Council.

The commentary on the section concerning the formulation of rules (*paññattivāra*) in the *Mahāvibhaṅga* is finished. Now follows the commentary on the section concerning the occurrence of offenses (*katāpattivāra*).

166. In the section on offenses committed (*katāpattivāra*), the phrase "a bed belonging to the Saṅgha" and so forth is stated by way of exceeding the range of a clod-throw (*leḍḍupāta*), because an offense is incurred even within the monastery due to its being an open space.

In the second [offense], regarding "having spread out a bed," it is stated that "one crosses the enclosure" because an offense is incurred upon going outside the monastery—even if one returns that same day—due to the fact that the bed was spread inside.
171. Regarding the statement, "One who intentionally deprives a living being of life incurs four offenses":

although in that training rule (*sikkhāpada*) only an animal (*tiracchānagata-pāṇa*) is intended, nevertheless, because the term "living being" (*pāṇa*) is used as a common designation, it is stated as "four" by way of extracting the underlying meaning.
This same method applies to other similar instances as well.

173. Regarding "entering a village at the wrong time," because it is stated, "If he steps over the first foot across the enclosure, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," they say that one does not incur the offense within the precinct (upacāra); rather, it is established that one incurs the offense only after stepping across the enclosure. 193.
In the section on conditions (paccaya-vāra), there is indeed a distinction from the previous section. When it was asked, "How many offenses does one incur while engaging in sexual intercourse?
the scope for the "jatu-maṭṭhaka" (the case of the one smeared with lac) had not yet arisen; however, here, regarding "sexual intercourse... [the discussion continues].
When it is stated, "by way of the condition of consumption," because there is no specific description of the person, the *jatumaṭṭhaka* (the "wax-seventeen") is included;
thus there is this distinction. It is the same in such instances.
The commentary on the sixteen great sections in the Mahāvibhaṅga and the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga is concluded.

Commentary on the Headings of the Origins (Samuṭṭhāna-sīsavaṇṇanā) 257. "Selfless" (*anattā*) means devoid of a self (*attavirahitā*), as in the expression "food without salt" (*alavaṇabhojana*) and so forth. He is like the moon because of his coolness through compassion (*karuṇā*).
He is like the sun because he dispels the darkness of the defilements (*kilesa-timira*). Because they teach these [teachings], he is also called Aṅgīrasa. He taught the three Piṭakas.

The meaning is: "of one among them. If the Vinaya remains, it is in this way that the true Dhamma of practice and so forth is led forth—that is, it proceeds; such is the meaning. But how does this [Vinaya] remain?
He says: "And from both," and so forth. The meaning is: they remain bound together by the Parivāra.
Within that very Parivāra, in the Sutta, the fixed origin (samuṭṭhāna) has been made—that is, it has been stated.
This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). "Unmixed origins" means origins that are not confused, origins that are distinct from others, and origins that are unlike anything else.

Since the Vinaya endures when the Parivāra exists, and the True Dhamma endures when the Vinaya exists, and since these origins are seen in the Sutta, therefore the meaning is "training" (*sikkhā*). [As it says] in the Parivāra: "One who loves the Dhamma is truly dear."
This was stated for the purpose of generating reverence. Regarding the phrase "therein" (*tattha*), it means "therein [in the sense] that 'they are seen'.
It is stated: "It originates from a single origin; the first *pārājika* originates from a single origin. For in the Canon (*pāḷi*), the origin as specified is indeed seen.
The meaning of the previous method is: "In the commentary (*parivāra*) to that very [text], the origin has been definitively established."
"Yathāñāyanti" means "according to reality" (yathābhūtam). The reading is "sañcarittābhāsanañca," though there is also the variant "sañcarittānubhāsanañca.
The meaning is "by those that are not faults of the method (nayavajja), but are faults of the discipline (vinayavajja).
This concludes the commentary on the origin of the first *pārājika* offense.
258. Regarding the rule concerning the non-following of a mentor: this refers to the training rule stated thus, "Whichever nun, however, does not follow a mentor who has ordained her for two years.
This reading is not found in some manuscripts. It originates from the first Pārājika offense, number seventy-six.
Commentary on the Origin of the Second Pārājika: 259.

Regarding the reading, “Having given robes while causing remorse, and having given robes while censuring those for whom a legitimate legal act (*dhammika-kamma*) has been performed with their consent (*chanda*), and having censured them”:
the word “having given” is stated out of sequence; therefore—
They say that the reading "having given a legitimate *kukkucca* (remorse)" is superior; this should be accepted after due consideration.
269. "Unmade" means new. [End of] the intermediate section.
Commentary on the Section of Questions (Katipucchāvāra) 271. *Paṭiniddesa* means explaining again and again. The meaning is: "the restraints trained by means of the classes of offenses.
Because these [terms] are stated with the sense of exclusion (*nivatti*) in the phrase "far from" (*ārakā*), that [exclusion] is now stated again in its own form.

Wishing to speak further, he said, “or intensely. Just as in the expressions “the house is filled with smoke” or “it is smoldering,” it crushes—that is, destroys—the enmity of lust and the other defilements.
“By this” refers to the abstinence (*virati*). The root *vel* means to move. A bridge (*setu*) is so called because it binds (*sinoti*) or ties together the path leading to liberation (*niyyāna*).
“The destruction of the bridge” (*setughāta*) refers to the abstinence that serves as the antidote to transgression; it is the arising of a state of consciousness that brings about that purpose.
Thus it was said. "The assembly for hearing the Dhamma" is written as "the multitude of those listening to the Dhamma.
If he does not go, or if he sits distracted, that is physical immodesty, which is a bodily misconduct.
Having stated "in negligence," "in the loss of mindfulness" is said to demonstrate its meaning.
272–3. "In one's own continuum" means either in one's own continuum or in another's continuum. "But disputing thus" means disputing on account of the grounds for schism (*bhedakaravatthu*).
"By both" refers to the elders and the novices. "It" refers to the bodily action of loving-kindness (*mettā-kāyakamma*).

For those persons to whom one shows affection, there is the Dhamma consisting of that bodily action of loving-kindness. "To this extent" is a demonstration of the distribution of material gifts (*āmisa*).
*Asukassa ca* (“and to such-and-such a person”) is a demonstration of the classification of individuals.
Because it was stated that “it is even permissible not to give to one who is immoral,” the consumption [of offerings] by those lacking a sense of shame is thereby prohibited.

Some say that the statement “it must indeed be given to all” indicates, through a definitive conclusion, that it should be given without making a distinction by one who does not know [the recipient’s character]. It is stated in the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā) that “it must indeed be given to all.”

Regarding this, it is said: "Others say that for those who are shameless (*alajjī*) or have been expelled (*ukkhitaka*), one should not give with one's own hand under the heading of 'use' (*paribhoga*), but rather cause [them] to be given.
"Giving after investigating" (*vicinitvā dānaṃ*) means "giving having discriminated" (*viceyya dānaṃ*). Since this distinction must indeed be made, the connection is:

"Because he makes this [distinction], the classification of persons (*puggalavibhāga*) has not been made. "By natural appearance" (*pakativaṇṇena*) means by an appearance that is dissimilar [to the natural one]. "This very thing... [and so on].

"Attained" means they are not clung to because they cannot be clung to by others. Having made Nibbāna the object by means of the conformable [states] which have conditioned phenomena as their objects, one goes forth.
This concludes the commentary on the section on the six origins of offenses and so forth.
276. “One may incur a *dubbhāsita* (wrong speech) through the first origin of offenses (*āpatti-samuṭṭhāna*)?”—it should be said, “No,” because it is incurred solely by means of speech and mind.

277. Regarding the phrase “he builds a hut”: this is stated here for the purpose of showing the sequential arising of the *dukkaṭa*, *thullaccaya*, and *saṅghādisesa* offenses within a single subject matter, without mentioning the offense of matchmaking (*sañcaritta*). For one does not incur [the *saṅghādisesa*] in matchmaking alone.
It has been said: "By this method, however, the reason for not taking [the offenses] in their regular sequence everywhere should be understood.
(283) "One who sees seclusion" means one who sees the fivefold seclusion, beginning with seclusion by way of substitution (*tadaṅga-viveka*).
(284) "One's own grave offense" refers to a *saṅghādisesa* offense.
288. *Vivādādhikaraṇapaccayā* means: the condition of having previously committed [an offense] oneself or with others. *Omasati* means:
while disputing, "This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya," one insults [the opponent] by saying, "What do you know?
and so forth. By means of the three methods of settlement: *sammukhāvinaya*, *paṭiññātakaraṇa*, and *tiṇavatthāraka*. And herein, *sammukhāvinaya*...
"Because it is desired in all cases, it has been applied by means of both [methods], such as 'by means of resolution face-to-face and by means of acting according to what is admitted,' and so forth.
This same method applies everywhere," it is said.

Regarding the phrase "excluding seven offenses," it is said: "Although there are no others remaining, nevertheless, the question was asked for the purpose of generating proficiency through systematic order."
The Intermediate Section is finished.
Explanation of the Classification of the Methods of Settlement; Explanation of the Section on the Synonyms for Legal Issues (*adhikaraṇa*).

293–4. Because greed is the cause of dispute, it is said that "greed is the precursor. The same applies to the remaining [defilements]. Terms such as "grounds" (*ṭhāna*) and so forth are synonyms for "cause.
For a cause is called a "ground" (*ṭhāna*) because things stand (*tiṭṭhanti*) upon it; it is called a "basis" (*vatthu*) because things dwell (*vasanti*) upon it;

and it is called a "plane" (*bhūmi*) because things come into being (*bhavanti*) upon it. What are those things that stand, dwell, and come into being? They are the legal issues arising from disputes (*vivādādhikaraṇa*), and so forth.
Because one disputes while being possessed of wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate states of mind, it is said: "nine roots.
The twelve roots consist of such factors as "he is angry" and "he is resentful. Because one who reviles follows up with one of the four failures, it is said: "the four failures are the grounds.
The fourteen roots consist of the twelve mentioned in the context of legal issues arising from disputes (*vivādādhikaraṇa*), plus body and speech.
295–6. Regarding the phrase "the seven classes of offenses are the grounds," it is stated here:
"For one who conceals an offense after having committed it, the offense previously committed becomes the ground for that [concealed] offense.

Because of the statement, "There is no wholesome [state] in a legal issue concerning an offense (āpattādhikaraṇa)," there is no wholesome cause for a legal issue concerning an offense; however, a wholesome consciousness is a constituent factor (aṅga).
It is written: "There are four legal acts (*kamma*) and four grounds. Regarding this, it is said: "A legal act is that which is established in the Canon as 'it should be done in this way.

For those who perform it according to the established Canon, the performance is called a 'legal issue arising from business' (*kiccādhikaraṇa*). And: "Alternatively, a legal act is characterized by that which ought to be performed in accordance with the Canon; performing it in that very manner is the 'legal issue arising from business.
[These refer to] the legal acts consisting of a motion (*ñatti*), a motion followed by a second resolution (*ñattidutiya*), and a motion followed by a fourth resolution (*ñatticatuttha*).
They arise from a formal motion (*ñatti*); a formal act by way of notification (*apalokanakamma*) arises from notification.

It is written that "the legal issue arising from a dispute (*kiccādhikaraṇa*) is settled and resolved by means of one method of settlement"—this is the meaning. "Could be" (*siyuṃ*) means they exist. And how could they be? How do they come to be? Regarding the legal issue arising from a dispute, there are two;
apart from those two, it is not settled by others.
297. "Common" (*sādhāraṇa*) means they are to be brought together with that. 298. "Belonging to that side" (*tabbhāgiya*) means belonging to that category. 299.

Asking whether all methods of settling (*samatha*) are capable of being brought together when acting in harmony, he said: "The methods of settling are common to the method of settling. The methods of settling may be common to a method of settling, or they may not be common.
300. Regarding the section on "settling by means of settling" (*samatha-samatha*), the same method applies as in the section on "belonging to that" (*tabbhāgiya*).
301. The meaning is: these are "settlings by means of settling," not "settlement in the presence" (*sammukhāvinaya*).

302. It is also said: "Settlements are the discipline" (*samathā vinayo*). Therefore, the section on discipline (*vinayavāra*) may be cited as "the discipline is settlement in the presence. "Not settlement in the presence" refers to the remaining methods of settling, such as settlement through recollection (*sativinaya*), excluding settlement in the presence itself.
303. Regarding the statement, "When it is confessed in the presence of the Saṅgha, that confession is what is called 'presence' (sammukhatā) for the Saṅgha," they say:
"This was said with reference to the intention to confess, such as 'one who is skilled in *saṃmukhāvinaya*,' and so forth.
There is no *saṃmukhāvinaya* that is unskillful; for *saṃmukhāvinaya* consists of three factors: the presence of the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the person.
Without these, it does not exist. In that regard, when performed by wholesome minds, it is wholesome; when performed by Arahants, it is indeterminate.
Because these are the opposites of the unwholesome, there is no possibility of the unwholesome arising therein; therefore, it is written: "There is no unwholesome *sammukhāvinaya*. [And]:
"When a majority decision (*yebhuyyasikā*) is used to settle a dispute by those who speak contrary to the Dhamma, regarding the person who distributes the voting sticks..."
When one who speaks according to the Dhamma is skilled, it is unskillful when even those who speak according to the Dhamma take voting tickets for one who speaks contrary to the Dhamma;
in all such cases, there is indeterminate status by way of the Arahant alone. For one who is not an Arahant, the settlement by recollection (*sativinaya*) is unskillful if given intentionally;

the settlement on account of past insanity (*amūḷhavinaya*) is unskillful if given to one who is not insane; and the act of making one confess (*paṭiññātakaraṇa*) is unskillful if done to one who is insane because of his lack of awareness.

It is written: "The *tassapāpiyasikā* [procedure] is unwholesome when applied to one who is pure; the *tiṇavatthāraka* [covering over as with grass] is unwholesome in the case of a great quarrel; and [the same applies] when acting intentionally.
This concludes the commentary on the section concerning the questions and the sections.
304. "It is obtained" is the question.
305. "At whatever time by means of *sammukhā-vinaya*," etc., is the answer to that. At whatever time by means of *sammukhā-vinaya*... [and so forth].

And when a legal issue is settled by a majority decision (*yebhuyyasikā*), at that time, wherever a majority decision is applicable, there a resolution in the presence of the parties (*sammukhāvinaya*) is also applicable;

such is the connection in all cases. Wherever a settlement based on admission (*paṭiññātakaraṇa*) is applicable, there a resolution in the presence of the parties is also applicable; in this regard, there may be one, two, or many offenses.
If a monk who has committed an offense, when asked, "Have you committed such-and-such an offense? confesses the offense by saying "Yes," both [requirements] are obtained.

In that regard, regarding the *sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence) as described—namely, being in the presence of the Saṅgha, the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the person—if the confession is made in the presence of the Saṅgha, it is "being in the presence of the Saṅgha. If it is confessed in that very same place, it is also "being in the presence of the Dhamma and Vinaya."
If they do not dispute with one another but each confesses [the offense], it is "in the presence of the person" (*puggalasammukhatā*).

If it is confessed in the very presence of that same person, it is also obtained as "in the presence of the Dhamma and Vinaya" (*dhammavinayasammukhatā*). Or, at the time when one person confesses an offense in the presence of another, and the other says, "Do you see it?
and he replies, "I see it," there is what is designated as "face-to-face settlement" (*sammukhāvinaya*), consisting of the presence of the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the person.
And the act of acting according to what has been admitted is obtained.

306. The settling of legal issues is called "conciliation" (samatha); that does not exist without a legal issue. Therefore, it is not possible to separate them and establish a distinction between them.

309–310. Regarding the phrase “disputes are settled by means of settling methods,” here “are settled” (*sammanti*) means they are resolved (*sampajjanti*). Alternatively, the meaning is that disputes are settled or calmed (*vūpasammanti*);

therefore, [the rule] “a majority decision is settled by means of resolution in the presence of the accused” (*yebhuyyasikā sammukhāvinayena sammati*) is compatible with resolution in the presence (*sammukhāvinaya*), but not with confession of memory (*sativinaya*) and the others, because those are of no assistance to it.

The meaning is as follows: regarding the statement "the methods of settling (*samatha*) are settled by means of the legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*)," the meaning here is that the methods of settling reach their cessation.
311. The reading is: "The resolution face-to-face (*sammukhāvinaya*) is not settled by means of a legal issue involving a dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*).

Furthermore, because it shares the same status as the majority decision (*yebhuyyasikā*), and because it is stated at the conclusion that "the resolution face-to-face is not settled by anything," the resolution face-to-face itself—

It is said that it cannot be settled by means of *samatha* (calming) or by means of a legal question (*adhikaraṇa*). A verdict based on mindfulness (*sativinaya*) is settled by means of a legal question concerning business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*).

A verdict based on past insanity (*amūḷhavinaya*), a formal act of further penalty (*tassapāpiyasika*), and the covering over as with grass (*tiṇavatthāraka*) are also settled by means of a legal question concerning business. 313.
A legal question arising from a dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*) is settled by means of a legal question concerning business, [as follows]: "Let the venerable ones hear me... [etc. ...first..."

“I cast the voting ticket”—in this way, a legal issue arising from a dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*) is settled by a legal issue concerning business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*). Legal issues arising from accusations (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*) and legal issues arising from offenses (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) are also settled by a legal issue concerning business.

It has been written: “One should understand that the reading is such that ‘An act not performed is a wrongly performed act’—in this way, even a legal issue concerning business is settled by a legal issue concerning business. However, in a certain commentary (*gaṇṭhipada*), it says:

Regarding the statement, “‘The methods of settling (samatha) are settled by legal issues (adhikaraṇa)’—since all methods of settling are settled by the legal issue of business (kiccādhikaraṇa), therefore the reading ‘the methods of settling are settled by the legal issue of business’ should be accepted,” it has been said. 314.
As for the question, “Which legal issue does the legal issue of dispute (vivādādhikaraṇa) originate?”—it does not originate any legal issue merely by the words, “This is not the Dhamma.”
318–9. The reading is: “What is included within the legal question (*adhikaraṇapariyāpanna*)?
A legal question of dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*) belongs to a legal question of dispute means that a dispute arising later belongs to a dispute that arose earlier.

A legal question of dispute belongs to two methods of settlement (*samatha*) means that it belongs [to them] as if they were saying, “You are capable of settling this,” [and the dispute thinks], “We shall settle it.”
It is as if it were being spoken by two [methods]; thus it is comprised within the two methods of tranquility (*samatha*).
The commentary on the classification of *samatha* is finished.
Now begins the commentary on the section of questions regarding the *Khandhaka*.
Commentary on the Answers to the Questions (Pucchāvissajjanāvaṇṇanā) 320.
The "Introduction" (Nidāna) consists of the time, the city, the location, and the Blessed One.

It is the exposition of the setting, the individuals, and so forth. Regarding those [rules] in the *Upasampadakkhandhaka* such as, "Monks, a person less than twenty years of age is not to be ordained," and so on...
The connection is: "the supreme words have been spoken by way of method. Regarding the phrase "that and that offense of each respective word is so called":
the intention is that whatever offense was prescribed by the rule, "Monks, a person less than twenty years of age is not to be ordained," that is the offense of that specific word.
"In the *Cammasaṃyutta*" means in the *Cammakkhandhaka*.
Commentary on the Numerical Method (Ekuttarikanaya): Commentary on the Section on Single Items (Ekakavāra) 321.
Regarding the statement, "In the numerical method, offenses (āpatti) should be known," one might ask: what is the ultimate nature of an offense? Or rather—

Are they not of an indefinable nature? They are indeed of an indefinable nature. For it is said in the *Parivāra*: “The basis (*vatthu*) must be known; the clan (*gotta*) must be known; the name (*nāma*) must be known;
the offense (*āpatti*) must be known. In the analysis (*vibhaṅga*) of these terms, it says:

“‘Sexual intercourse’ (*methunadhamma*) refers to both the basis and the clan; ‘an offense entailing defeat’ (*pārājika*) refers to both the name and the offense. Thus, name and clan together constitute “name-and-clan” (*nāmagotta*).
Because of the statement, "it does not decay," it is a mere conventional designation (sammutimatta). Therefore, it is said:

"Certain conventional designations, being excluded from the triad of the wholesome (kusalattika), are phenomena that cannot be described [as wholesome or unwholesome]. As for what was stated in the Samathakkhandhaka—that "a legal issue arising from an offense (āpattādhikaraṇa) may be unwholesome or may be indeterminate"—that refers to how "a legal issue arising from a dispute (vivādādhikaraṇa) may be wholesome or may be unwholesome."

It is stated here figuratively (pariyāyato), just as in the passage, "it might be indeterminate" (*siyā abyākataṃ*). For in terms of meaning, what is called a "dispute" (*vivāda*) is a particular kind of conventional designation (*sammuti-viśeṣa*).

One who possesses a mind is designated by the conventional expression, "that [mind] might be wholesome by way of its mental concomitants" (*taṃ cittapariyāyena pana siyā kusalaṃ*), and likewise for a legal issue arising from an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*);
this is how it should be understood. Therefore, it is said in the Commentary: "One who is committing an offense..."

"For one enters [into an offense] with either an unwholesome mind, or a wholesome or indeterminate mind. Otherwise, the state of being settled through the methods of reconciliation (*samatha*) would not be possible.

For the methods of reconciliation do not function by taking as their object what is unwholesome and so forth, nor does what is wholesome and so forth become pacified by means of the methods of reconciliation.
Furthermore, there is no such thing as a dispute or a reproach that is wholesome, which ought to be pacified by the methods of reconciliation for what is wholesome and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "he incurs [an offense]," for such individuals, even the mere occurrence of a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) would not be possible;

therefore, the state of being wholesome (*kusala*) and so forth regarding legal issues and the methods of settling them (*samatha*) is obtained through figurative teaching (*pariyāyadesanā*), and not otherwise. For this very reason, as in the case of the *sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence of), the triad is not fulfilled in the case of a legal issue concerning an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*).
This is because the volition (*sañcetanā*) of one who intentionally incurs an offense is exclusively unwholesome.
It exists. For the other [type of action], whether accompanied by consciousness or devoid of consciousness, it is called "indeterminate" (abyākata) by way of its mere appearance at that time.
For instance, in such passages as, "If, being urged three times, one should procure that robe, this is wholesome (kusala)," the word *kusala* does not mean a pleasant result;
whereas in such passages as, "for the sake of warding off unwholesome states pertaining to future lives," [it does].

Nor is it unwholesome (*akusala*). Because it is merely the appearance of that [unwholesome state] in another person—whether they possess consciousness (*sacittaka*) or are without consciousness (*acittaka*)—it is called "indeterminate" (*abyākata*).

For just as one who demands twice might still bring about the production of that robe, so too, by way of what was stated here—that "the legal issue arising from an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) is unwholesome"—it is designated as unwholesome on account of that.

The grounds for training (*vinītavatthu*) should be understood; from among them, there are those that do not constitute a robe (*acīvaraka*) and those that are offenses during the interim (*antarāpattika*).

It should also be understood that they are called "definite" (*niyata*) by virtue of having reached the characteristic of being immediate (*anantarika*). In the exposition of conventional designations (*sammuti*), there is also an exposition of the heavy and the light. Otherwise, it would have been stated:

"Those that are non-obstructive are both rule-transgressions (*paṇṇattivajja*) and blameless rule-designations (*anavajjapaṇṇatti*). [This refers to] the offense of building a hut (*kuṭikāra*) and the offense of a large dwelling (*mahallaka*).
[They are] obstructive because they are declared to be worldly transgressions and blameworthy.
[The claim that] intentional lying, abusive speech, and so forth would not be grave offenses, or that this [offense] would therefore be light—this entire view is the opinion of certain teachers;
they say, "All of it is incorrect. Why? Because, by the statement, "What is called a *pārājika* is both a name and an offense," if it were an offense...

It should not be said that the phenomenon (*dhamma*) itself is the "inexpressible" (*na vattabbadhammo*), nor that the basis (*vatthu*) is the "inexpressible," because they are spoken of as being in a state of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇabhāva*) with the "clan" (*gotta*).
Therefore, the term "sexual intercourse" (*methunadhammo*) indicates both the phenomenon and the basis known as misconduct (*ajjhācāra*).
And because it receives its name from the act of misconduct and possesses a unique name, it is also called "clan" (*gotta*); such is the meaning therein.

Regarding the question, "What is the precursor to a legal issue arising from an offense? it is stated: "Greed is the precursor; hatred, delusion, non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion are precursors.
And regarding the question, "How many roots are there? it is stated: "There are six roots: three unwholesome roots and three indeterminate roots.
Because of these statements, it is said that, in an absolute sense, a legal issue arising from an offense may be unwholesome or it may be indeterminate.
In the *Samathakkhandhaka*, however, it is stated in that very same way by way of intentional speech (*sandhāyabhāsita*).

Therefore, the legal issue of offenses (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) consists, in its essential nature and without figurative interpretation, of the four unwholesome aggregates (*akusala-khandha*) and the indeterminate material form (*rūpa-abyākata*).

Because it is stated that "there is no wholesome legal issue of offenses," only the wholesome is excluded; [however,] for those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), there is the indeterminate of functional activity (*kiriya-abyākata*).
When the wholesome is excluded, the functional-indeterminate (*kiriyābyākata*) is also necessarily excluded.
When that is excluded, the result-indeterminate (*vipākābyākata*), which is in every respect unobstructed (*avāvaṭa*), is also necessarily excluded.

Some say that there is nothing at all to be said regarding the indeterminate nibbāna; however, that is incorrect because it has been stated that "there are six causes. Although it was stated in general terms, nevertheless...

In this context, only the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) is intended, not the functional cause (*kiriya-hetu*); for those [latter] possess a wholesome nature (*kusala-sabhāva*), and therefore they are matter (*rūpa*) and are indeterminate as ripening (*vipāka-abyākata*).
Regarding that, the bases for training (*vinīta-vatthu*) are derived from the unwholesome offense.

For the other [the wholesome], it is stated that there was a concealment at the outset by means of a wholesome mind. Furthermore, its status as a formal rule concerning obstacles and fixed offenses (*antarāyika-niyata-sāvajja-paññatti*) is established through its synonyms.
It should be understood [in terms of] what is prohibited by rule (*paṇṇattivajja*) and what is committed intentionally (*sañcicca*). Therefore,

just as the statement "the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) may have an object (*sārammaṇa*) or may be without an object (*anārammaṇa*)," one should combine together the offenses prohibited by worldly convention (*lokavajja*), which are either exclusively unwholesome (*ekantākusala*) or not exclusively unwholesome (*anekantākusala*),

with the offenses prohibited by rule (*paṇṇattivajja*), which are either exclusively indeterminate (*ekantābyākata*) or not exclusively indeterminate (*anekantābyākata*), and thus [define] the "legal issue arising from an offense" (*āpattādhikaraṇa*).

It has been stated: "It may be unwholesome (akusala), or it may be indeterminate (abyākata). However, in the *Samathakkhandhaka*, that was said with reference specifically to offenses against the rules of training (*paṇṇattivajja*).
For this is said in the Commentary and in the *Gaṇṭhipada*: "Regarding the statement, 'The legal issue of offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) may be unwholesome, or it may be indeterminate;
there is no legal issue of offense that is wholesome,' the meaning is to be understood as being spoken with reference to that."

It should be understood as follows: for in regard to an offense such as digging the earth, when one is ignorant of the rule (*apakataññu*), a wholesome mind (*kusalacitta*) is a factor at the time of clearing away weeds and so forth; the intention is that the material indeterminate (*rūpābyākata*) process consisting of the act of digging and so on gives rise to the offense.
This is with reference to what was said: "There is an offense that one commits with a wholesome mind, [and] with a wholesome mind..."
"...emerges," and so forth. For if that [unwholesome state] were present, it would be impossible to say, "There is no unwholesome legal issue arising from an offense.

Since this was not said with reference to the consciousness that actually originates the offense, it was therefore not said with reference to a consciousness capable of serving as a constituent factor [for the offense].
If it had been said with reference to that, one ought to have said, "It may be wholesome."
And it was not stated [there]. Therefore, this was said with reference to the following:

as for that legal issue of offenses (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) which is a transgression against worldly convention (*lokavajja*), that is exclusively unwholesome; in that case, there is no alternative possibility such as "it might be unwholesome.
However, as for that which is a transgression against the formal rule (*paṇṇattivajja*), it is unwholesome only for one who intentionally transgresses it, thinking, "I am violating this offense."

However, for one who commits an offense through sleeping in the same bed and so forth while unintentionally and unknowingly doing so, the material result (*rūpa-vipāka*) is indeterminate (*abyākata*) because it does not arise from a volitional effort.
Therefore, with reference to this distinction—that is, regarding the offense against the formal rule (*paññatti-vajja*) based on whether it was intentional or unintentional—it was said:
"A legal issue arising from an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) may be unwholesome (*akusala*), or it may be indeterminate; there is no legal issue arising from an offense that is wholesome (*kusala*)."

If, however, someone ignorant of the Vinaya were to say, "Whatever one commits with a wholesome mind is called a 'legal issue arising from an offense' (āpattādhikaraṇa) that is wholesome," then for such a speaker, one who possesses a wholesome mind would have to commit those offenses—such as the wool-wool offense (*eḷakaloma-samudācāra*) and others—which arise even when one is without mind (*acittaka*).
Yet one does not commit them. What is the reason? Because even though they exist there [in the Vinaya], [they are not committed by a wholesome mind].
A wholesome state of mind (*kusalacitta*) is a factor (*aṅga*) for the offense. What is meant by "one's own being" (*attabhāva*), "intrinsic nature" (*sabhāva*), or "natural disposition" (*pakati*)?
Which, then, at that time, constitutes the intrinsic nature as a factor for that offense? It is said:

it is one or the other of these two—body and speech—which have moved or proceeded by way of bodily and vocal intimation (*kāyavacīviññatti*). That is to say, either the body that has moved or the speech that has proceeded.
The nature of the factors [of body and speech] is indeterminate (*avyākata*) because they are included within the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*). What is meant by this?
It means that at that time, both body and speech constitute an *adhikaraṇa* (legal issue) arising from an offense.

However, as for the indeterminate state of body and speech at the moment of an unwholesome offense, these are not subject to conventional designation (*abbohārika*), just like mental action (*manokamma*) at the time of bodily and vocal action. For at that time, body and speech—
They stand at the point of causing an offense. It is with reference to this that it was said: "The factors that cause an offense must be known.
How many roots are there? There are six origins of offenses as the roots," and so forth.

But when body and speech are merely the instruments (*aṅga*) for an offense, then—as in the expression "mind is the sovereign of mind"—they [the bodily and vocal actions] are subordinate to the subsequent application, just as the prior applications are to the final application.
Because they function as conditions, they do not forfeit their designation as "causes of offenses" and so forth.
Just as it is stated that even when they exist [as such], "How many bases are there for an offense-dispute? Seven classes of offenses are the bases. How many grounds are there?
Seven classes of offenses are the grounds," likewise, even when they exist [as such], those things which cause offenses are simply called "origins of offenses."

They should be understood as follows: at this point, what is called an "offense" (*āpatti*) consists, without distinction, of all four unwholesome aggregates (*akusalakkhandha*) at the time of intentional transgression, with the exception of the reporting of what has occurred;

specifically, however, all [offenses] are exclusively unwholesome (*akusala*), whereas those that are not exclusively unwholesome include various types such as attending a festival on a mountain top, visiting a brothel, attending a gathering of women, adorning oneself, and using perfumes, cosmetics, and ointments.
The ten types [of bodily contact], distinguished by their own names as beginning with massaging (*ummaddana*) and rubbing (*parimaddana*) for bhikkhunīs and others,

are unwholesome (*akusala*) only at the time when there is a conscious mind (*sacittaka-kāla*) and the object is known. Because that [conscious state] is absent at the time of being unconscious (*acittaka-kāla*),

for one who transgresses those respective objects through a wholesome mind (*kusalacitta*)— such as under the heading of meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*) and so forth— without an offense or a formal legal procedure (*anāpattādhikaraṇa*), the offense is merely neutral form (*rūpa-abyākata*).

However, some here explain that even for one who wears a hip-string in a secluded place with the perception that it is a hip-string, or who applies scents, pigments, and so forth with the perception that they are clay, there is an offense;
therefore, [these cases] are indeed unintentional. They should be refuted by pointing out the absence of such a reading as:
"If she wears a hip-string with the perception that it is not a hip-string, there is an offense of *pācittiya*. Regarding the offense of drinking fermented liquor:

However, even those [liquids] that do not produce consciousness are exclusively unwholesome (*akusala*). For this very reason it is said: "If one drinks what is not intoxicant while perceiving it as intoxicant, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).

Since, in this case, it is impossible to drink fermented liquor (*surā*) even for the sake of curing an illness without it being unwholesome, therefore—unlike the cases mentioned above where [liquids] are not invariably unwholesome among the world-transgressions (*lokavajja*)—here it is stated: "There is no offense in drinking fermented liquor for the sake of curing an illness."

It was not stated [as an offense]. However, things such as well-prepared soups are indeed non-intoxicants (*amajja*). In that regard, for the purpose of dispelling remorse, it is stated that "there is no offense," just as in the case of water used for cleaning the teeth.

The offense of revealing what has actually occurred (*bhūtārocanā*) is exclusively the non-defined by way of form (*rūpa-abyākata*). Likewise, sleeping together during a state of mindlessness (*acittaka*) is exclusively the non-defined by way of the result of form (*rūpa-vipāka-abyākata*).
In that context, even though unwholesome states exist up until the end of a dream, they do not constitute an offense because they lack the necessary factors (*anaṅga*).
There is no discussion of the wholesome at all, because there is no offense (*anāpatti*) due to the very nature of the wholesome.

Likewise, by this method [of the term] "functional" (*kiriya*), it is shown that in all cases, as far as applicable, [the unwholesome] is divided into three ways: as unwholesome, as pure matter (*suddharūpa*), or as having fruition (*savipāka*).
This is the meaning demonstrated.

In this regard, with the exception of drinking fermented liquor and certain offenses of formal precept (*paṇṇattivajja*), those that are exclusively unwholesome (*ekantākusala*) are necessarily accompanied by consciousness (*sacittaka*).
The telling of what has actually occurred (*bhūtārocana*) is exclusively without consciousness (*acittaka*). The remainder—including drinking fermented liquor—is not exclusively unwholesome;

it is both a worldly offense (*lokavajja*) and, for the most part, indeterminate (*anekantābyākata*) as a formal precept offense (*paṇṇattivajja*), and it is generally both with and without consciousness. Thus, every training rule (*sikkhāpada*) is of three types.
As for that which is "with mind" (sacittaka) here, it is "with mind" solely by means of the mind that knows the object of sexual intercourse and so forth;
all training rules (sekhiya) are "with mind" solely by means of the mind that knows the formal designation (paṇṇatti), because of the statement, "on account of disrespect.
Thus, "with mind" is twofold. It is exclusively "without mind" (acittaka) due to the absence of the mind that knows the formal designation, not due to the absence of the mind that knows the object.
Due to the absence of that [mind], drinking liquor is exclusively unwholesome; engaging in sexual misconduct is exclusively indeterminate.
It is "without mind" (acittaka) because of the absence of both—the mind that knows the physical object or the mind that knows the designation—and because of the state of being without mind.
However, drinking liquor is "with mind" (sacittaka), occurring precisely through the mind that knows the physical object. This applies to noble persons, to others, or to both.
By the state of one [factor] being other than that, the remainder—whether mental or non-mental—is determined.

Specifically, it is non-mental by virtue of the absence of the mind that knows the physical basis (*vatthu*), or by virtue of the absence of the mind that knows the designation (*paññatti*) for one who has not yet understood, which constitutes its non-mental state.
In this context, that which is exclusively non-mental as well as that which is mental is both termed "non-mental. This, then, is the analysis regarding the phrase "the offense must be known."

“An intermediate offense for one undergoing purification from the root” (*mūlavisuddhiyā antarāpatti*) refers to an offense committed by one who, having committed an intermediate offense, has been sent back to the beginning (*mūlāyapaṭikassana*) and remains there. “This is an intermediate offense for one undergoing purification according to the value [of the offense]” (*agghavisuddhiyā antarāpatti*) refers to an offense committed by one who, having committed several offenses, dwells after determining the value of them all based on the longest period of concealment among those offenses. “Furthermore... “I shall incur it”—this refers to a mind accompanied by resolve. “This applies only to a bhikkhunī,” so it is written.

“It is indeed a *pārājika* offense”—this is stated to show that it occurs on account of what is actual. “But others say that when [the offense] has been confessed in this way, no offense whatsoever is cleared;
however, that should not be accepted,” so it is said. This is because it was stated: “In the case of not fulfilling a legitimate promise.”
There is no offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in a formal declaration that is contrary to the Dhamma.
It is said: "If one who previously had a pure mind says, 'May you disrobe,' and having agreed by saying 'Very well,' he does not actually disrobe, there is no offense;

this applies in all such cases. There is also a textual reading: "The one who makes it known must be understood. This refers to the fifteen qualities beginning with, "I shall speak at the proper time, not at an improper time."
“Capable of committing an offense” means capable of falling into an offense.
Commentary on the Section of Twos, 322:
Regarding concealment and exposure: “If a bhikkhu should be separated from his three robes for even one night... at most six nights.”

Even if one who has committed an offense as described by the words “by him,” etc., becomes a completer of the quorum for a formal act (*kamma*), he still subverts that act because of being of a different affiliation (*nānāsaṃvāsaka*).
Regarding the phrase “either by means of a formal act or by the drawing of voting tickets (*salākaggāha*): here, the recitation (*uddesa*) and the formal act (*kamma*) are one and the same;

that is, the recitation of the *Pātimokkha* and the formal act are identical in meaning. The sense is that if either of these is performed, it results in a schism in the Saṅgha. “The preliminary stages” (*pubbabhāga*)...
Prior to the schism of the Saṅgha. It is stated that the schism occurs through either one of these two [factors] called "measure," and not by the others.

"Established in the Vinaya" means those established in the Vinaya; "Romaka" refers to what was produced in the Romaka country; because salt was permitted, they are mentioned in the pairs (duka). This is the commentary on the section on the triads (tika).
323. You must not behave [in this way]. "Having performed a bodily action associated with speech" means having performed an act of homage with the body;
that is the meaning. "To destroy" means to ruin. "Having suppressed" means having overcome. "Of one who speaks" means of one who is speaking.
The phrase "support should be given to a fool" occurs in the Duka [section], but here it is stated that "it should not be given," because of the abundance of offenses.

The meaning is that one should not take [the instruction] literally; when it is said, "Do not go out from this monastery, or come into the presence of those who hold the Vinaya to receive a formal decision," one should not accept his word. Regarding "group-meal" (*gaṇabhojana*):
if three people eat together, there is no offense for a group-meal; it is with reference to this that the term "triple" (*tika*) is used. "Asleep" (*pasutta*).
This is stated by way of general usage. Alternatively, the meaning is "having laid it down. It is recorded that when one says, "I am going after setting this aside;
please give me a temporary one, Venerable Sir," it is not permitted to give [the robe] except for the purpose of new construction and so forth.

The meaning is that one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) if one wears a rain-cloak (vassikasāṭikā) that was set aside after being formally assigned on the first day of the last month of the rainy season.
“Without having relinquished” means without having performed the act of relinquishment (*paccuddharaṇa*).

It should be understood that the statement “one may assign it” (*vikappetuṃ*) was spoken for the purpose of showing that one incurs an offense during the winter due to the failure to assign it, whereas the assignment itself must be performed on the full-moon day of the month of Kattika.
This method refers to the failure to assign; the former [offense] arises from the condition of using what has been assigned.
*Sandhāya*. Regarding the phrase “the covering cloth is allowable everywhere”: the meaning is that the covering cloth is permitted in all instances.
Some, failing to perceive this point, write: “The covering cloth is allowable everywhere; by means of it, [the body] is covered.
However, because the grammatical analysis (*viggaha*) is “that which covers the cloth itself is the ‘cloth-covering’,” the expression “by means of it” (*tāya*) is not tenable.
“*Tenā*” means “it must be so”; all of this has been written in a certain *gaṇṭhipada* (commentary), and it should be accepted after due consideration.

Regarding the commentary on the section on the fourfold [offenses]: “One incurs an offense in four ways... [omission] ...one incurs it through the formal act (*kammavācā*). Herein, as for the offense—
One commits an offense through the formal act (*kammavācā*), yet it is not there that the body and so forth [are found] as having committed it;

therefore, one commits it by means of seven factors that constitute an offense together with the formal act. If this were the case, there would be a contradiction with the statement, "There are six origins of offenses" (*cha āpattisamuṭṭhānāni*), for those very factors that constitute an offense are what is meant [by the origins].
Now, even in that case, the body and so forth are obtained either collectively or individually.

The statement "it is not tenable [to say] 'in four ways'" implies that it should rather be said, "'one incurs an offense in six ways,'" and thus these scriptural passages appear to be in contradiction.
How are they not in contradiction? Because of the distinction between those offenses involving intimation (*saviññatti*) and those not involving intimation (*aviññatti*).
Regarding the offense that consists of the action of the body and so forth, some one incurs through the body with intimation, and some through [the body] with intimation...
One incurs [an offense] by means of speech; one incurs certain [offenses] by means of informative bodily and vocal actions;

however, that offense which consists of non-action, one incurs it by means of the formal act (*kammavācā*), and that indeed occurs only through the remaining non-informative bodily and vocal actions, not without them—as in:
"If he does not relinquish [it] by body or speech, at the conclusion of the formal act, there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*."
Regarding the verbal [offense], or generally speaking, one commits a certain offense by body, a certain one by speech, and a certain one by both body and speech.

Furthermore, it should be understood that among these, what is committed by both body and speech is committed in some cases solely by body and speech, while in other cases it is committed through the formal act (*kammavācā*).
In this way, there is no contradiction.
In this regard, the analysis of the meaning is as follows in brief:

"One commits by means of the body" means that one commits a certain offense by performing with the body what should not be performed through intimation (*viññatti*), or by failing to perform what should be performed without intimation; both of these are called bodily action (*kāyakamma*).
For even that which is not actually done is spoken of in the world as "done," as in the expressions: "I have committed a misdeed (*dukkaṭa*)" or "I have not performed merit."

In such passages as these, and in the Dispensation (Sāsana) in such statements as, "Friend Ānanda, this was an offense for you, in that you did not ask the Blessed One," and so forth—likewise here, according to the method of the Vinaya, even non-doing by means of the body is called "bodily action" (*kāyakamma*).

This same principle applies to such phrases as "one commits [an offense] by speech" (*vācāya āpajjati*), and so on. He goes before (*puratīti*) is a "man" (*puriso*); [the root] *pura* is used in the sense of going at the head. He goes before (*puratīti*) is [thus] *purato*.
He goes; he becomes the leader in all matters. Regarding "by way of what first arose":

among those belonging to the first eon (*paṭhamakappiya*), the male characteristic (*purisaliṅga*) first arises; the meaning is that the male characteristic, having attained the designation "the former," is born.

As for "thirty-six": here, even though the *pārājikas* are not common [to all], they are indeed included within the category of those who have committed a *pārājika*. Those who have fallen into a *pārājika* offense...
Because of the incapacity for the state of a bhikkhu. They say, "However, they are extracted by means of the commonality [of the term] through the expression of non-commonality.
And they say, "The reading is 'one hundred and thirty training rules'.
Regarding the four *pārājika* offenses common to both the bhikkhu and the bhikkhunī: there is a difference in the underlying matter (*vatthu*), but not a difference in the offense (*āpatti*).
The first question is here called the second. Regarding the statement, "There is a commonality of offense but not a commonality of basis," there is no distinction [to be made] by this.
"Speech with wisdom" means speech arising from intelligence (*mati*). "Worthy of salutation" means that they salute her by raising their heads while remaining exactly as they were seated.
Because it is not to be performed starting from a newly ordained nun (*navamabhikkhunī*), they do not rise from their seats. "Without distinction" means...
The meaning is: anyone who is senior, having approached either the preceptor or another person who has not finished eating.
For even one who has not finished eating must rise and offer a seat.
"Even when saying 'it is not allowable here'" means that if one stands in a border region and says, "It is not allowable here," one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense for transgressing the Vinaya.
For one who says that what is allowable (*kappiya*) is "not allowable" is indeed abolishing what has been established.

Likewise, standing here on the grounds of such expressions as "they are allowable," the meaning is that when one says "they are allowable here," the monk who has come under the Discipline (*vinaya*) must be questioned regarding the Discipline.
Commentary on the Fivefold Section (*pañcakavāra*).

325. A person does not incur an offense. Because of the statement, “Having been invited and having partaken of a meal, [if he goes] without informing a bhikkhu who is present,” for one who lives on alms-food (piṇḍapātika), wandering without prior invitation is permissible.

Eating after having made a mental application (ābhoga) such as “It is the time for the sick,” and having resolved upon the food, is what is meant by eating. “My expectation of a meal is from such-and-such a person...”
“I give”—thus there is no formal assignment (*avikappanā*). Speaking of faults in the absence of another is *ayaso* (infamy); censuring them in their presence is *garahā*.
Because the ruin of virtue and view are included within the Vinaya, the other two are mentioned along with them to complete the group of five.

Because it is stated, “by a group having a holder of the Vinaya as the fifth,” the group of five is established. The meaning is: “there was a certain elder in a certain monastery. “From the realm of the Yonakas.”
"From China," it is written. "He recollected eight eons" means he produced the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsañāṇa*).

"Standing in the next place" is the meaning. "Having reached the stage of the formal act (*kamma*) by means of the motion (*ñatti*)" means that at the time the motion is established, one reaches the stage of the formal act;
the success of the formal act occurs again through the proclamation (*kammavācā*). "The field of the motion" is the place where [the act] must be performed by means of the motion alone. Of that...

The field (*khetta*): in a formal act consisting of a motion followed by a second proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*), the first announcement is called its "occasion" (*okāsa*). Regarding the forest-dweller (*āraññaka*):
the meaning is that such and such benefits exist; thus, it means "this exists.
Explanation of the Sixfold Cycle (*chakkavāra*).
326. This was stated because it is recited in the Vibhaṅga thus: "It may be kept for a maximum of six years.
There are nine sets of six, with fourteen as the maximum. How so? The first is one set of six; then, among the remaining eight, there is one [set] together with each [of the others].
Thus, three sets of six are stated in the intermediate peyyāla. How so? "By the fourth origin of offenses..."
By way of the fifth [section], beginning with “one incurs six offenses,” and by the sixth, there are three sets of six.
There are six roots of dispute, such as greed and so forth; likewise for formal accusation. For the rain-cloak, there are six spans in length; for the Sugata’s robe, there are six spans across.
When departing after taking an unfinished robe, it is subject to completion; when departing after making a formal determination, it is subject to relinquishment.

In the group of seven, there are seven including the *pakkamananti*ka. This is the commentary on the section of seven.

327. Those [offenses] stated under the group of six (chaḷaka) should be applied according to the group of seven (sattaka). Thus, the fourteen [cases] stated under the group of six should be applied according to the group of seven.

Regarding the seventh, "at the rising of the dawn it is an offense entailing relinquishment" refers to the offense entailing relinquishment stated thus: "That bhikkhu may be separated from that robe for a maximum of six nights; if he should remain separated from it longer than that..."
In the Campeyya Khandhaka, following the section on the Sugata-cīvara, there are seven cases stated in the manner beginning:
"But here, monks, a monk has no offense to be seen, yet the Saṅgha, or several [monks], or a single person accuses him.

328. Performing the Uposatha and other duties together with him is the benefit; not performing them is the disadvantage. Therefore, the meaning is:
"by one who perceives these eight benefits. It is said: "Disrepute and abuse. Even before, he thinks: "I shall speak falsely."
While speaking, one thinks, "I am speaking a lie," and after having spoken, one thinks, "A lie has been spoken by me.
Having set aside one's view, preference, inclination, disposition, and perception—thus it is "made unallowable" and "made unaccepted," and so forth;

these are the eight cases of what is not left over (*anatiritta*). Ghee and the other [eight substances] become subject to relinquishment (*nissaggiya*) at the rising of the sun on the eighth day. There are eight verbal [formulas] for the bhikkhunīs.

Full ordination (*upasampadā*) consists of the motion and three proclamations (*ñatti-catuttha*) before both assemblies. There are eight privileges, beginning with the granting of the rainy-season robe (*vassikasāṭika*).
Commentary on the Chapter on the Novice (329):
The Saṅgha is split by nine monks. There is a detailed exposition regarding the nine types of meat, excluding human flesh. It is beautiful.

"Not beautiful" refers to the nine robes, beginning with the outer cloak (*saṅghāṭī*). From the time they have been formally determined (*adhiṭṭhita*), those very robes must not be assigned to another;

the intention is that from the time they have been determined, they must not be assigned without first being relinquished (*apaccuddharitvā*). Nine spans (*vidatthi*) constitute the measure of a Sugata’s robe.
Regarding the phrase "he exhorts a faction of the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha while perceiving it as a faction," and so forth, this refers to an illegal act (*adhammakamma*).
Two groups of nine are stated by way of the *pācittiya* [offenses].
Regarding the commentary on the section of ten:
"There is a legal issue that is trivial and not yet finalized," and so forth; these are the ten illegal methods of taking voting tickets (*salākaggāha*).
“Those who act contrary [to the rule] are unrighteous. The connection is that one must possess the qualities described in the *Samathakkhandhaka*.
Regarding the statement, “having put on a bodice or a hem,” this is because these things are allowable (*kappiya*). There are ten types of women, beginning with those protected by their mother.
There are ten types of wives, beginning with those purchased for money. Having granted her permission to train, when she is twelve years old—[the teacher] herself being twelve years old—...
The formal authorization for ordination (*vuṭṭhāpanasammuti*) should be granted [thinking], "He will become [one who knows].

Regarding the one who is a holder of the Vinaya (*vinayadhara*), five factors are stated starting from "he does not know what is an offense and what is not an offense" up to "both his words and their literal expressions...
Furthermore, again starting from "he does not know what is an offense and what is not an offense," five [factors] are stated up to "he is not skilled in deciding legal disputes (*adhikaraṇa*)."
“They, having made five and five in such a manner, become ten,” so it is written.
Although the statement “support (nissaya) must be given to a nun who is ten years [of standing]” does not appear in some manuscripts, nevertheless, that is indeed the reading.
The commentary on the section of eleven.
331. They do not purify, nor do they illuminate. [They refer to] disease itself, the affliction of disease, or the obstacle of disease.
The commentary on the method of single enumerations is finished.
Commentary on the answers to questions concerning the Uposatha and other matters.
332. “I invite the Saṅgha, venerable sir,” and so forth—this is called the discourse on the invitation (pavāraṇā), similar to the verses in the Vinīta section.
334. Regarding the phrase “in dependence upon ten reasons”:
here, it is because [the text] demonstrates the specific virtues involved in the promulgation of each respective training rule (sikkhāpada).

And because one sees the danger in not making a formal announcement, there is well-being for the Saṅgha. In this regard, when it is possible, the virtue of making an announcement regarding what is a worldly offense (*lokavajja*) that does not otherwise come under formal rule (*apaṇṇatti*) is the purity of application (*payoga*).
However, when it is possible to make an announcement regarding a training rule (*sekhiya*) that is a worldly offense, the virtue is the purity of practice (*paṭipatti*);
whereas for an offense against the formal rule (*paṇṇattivajja*), the virtue is the purity of intention (*āsaya*).

Because it brings about qualities such as fewness of desires, for that very reason it says: "Having spoken in praise of fewness of desires for one who has few desires, for the sake of being easy to support and easy to satisfy.
It should be understood that the purification of the ascetic’s conduct is its quality.

Alternatively, when a world-transgression is pointed out, there is well-being for the Saṅgha because the danger is made manifest; when a formal rule-transgression is pointed out, there is comfort for the Saṅgha.
It is evident because of its manifest benefits. Likewise, by the first [training], there is the restraint of the unruly; by the second, the comfortable dwelling of the well-behaved.

By the first, there is the warding off of taints pertaining to future lives; by the second, those pertaining to the present life. Likewise, by the first, there is the inspiration of those without faith;
by the second, the further increase of those already inspired. Likewise, by the first, there is the endurance of the true Dhamma.

It should be understood that by the second [factor], there is assistance through the Vinaya. According to the method of the *Parivāra*, by the first [factor] there is the cutting off of the faction of monks with evil desires, and by the second, there is compassion for householders. For this has been said:
"The Tathāgata has laid down the training rules for his disciples based on two purposes: out of compassion for householders and [to restrain] those with evil desires."
“...for the cutting off of the wings. In the same way, an application should also be made by way of enmities, faults, and unwholesome states pertaining to the present life and the future life.

For this has been said: “Two purposes... [etc. ...it was laid down for the warding off of enmities pertaining to the present life and enmities pertaining to the future life,” and so forth. Furthermore, in this context, everything connected with an intimation that has not yet been performed—

That which is connected with the affliction of householders, and that which is connected with their confidence, the loss of their wealth, and its protection, is called "prescribed out of compassion for householders.
The eating in groups and the corrupting of families were prescribed to cut off the faction of those with evil desires.

All that is "worldly transgression" (lokavajja) is for the sake of warding off enmities and so forth pertaining to both this life and the future life; while "arranging [meals] with women" is for the sake of restraint regarding enmities and so forth pertaining to this life.
It should be understood as "a designation. Furthermore, here the exposition should be understood as being based solely on the performance of the ten advantages from the very beginning.
That which, through the transgression of the basis, would be exclusively unwholesome;
That [training rule] was laid down for the welfare of the Saṅgha because it is a world-transgression (*lokavajja*).
Regarding the offenses such as the *pārājika*, an offense occurs only through the knowledge of what has been prescribed, and not otherwise.
Whether for the sake of the stability of the Dhamma or for the purpose of increasing one's faith,
that which is connected with the teaching of the Dhamma and other training rules (*sekhiya*) constitutes what is called a "worldly offense" (*lokavajja*) arising from formal designation (*paññatti*).
This applies even in the absence of an actual object or a formal designation, when there is an intention to transgress what has been prohibited or to fail to do what is required.

Alternatively, when there is non-commissioning, with the exception of all those cases where an offense arises [for failing to commission], drinking fermented liquor should be understood as an offense of formal precept (*paṇṇattivajja*).

In that regard, there is a *pācittiya* for reopening a settled matter; furthermore, "whatever monk, having given his consent for legitimate legal acts, should subsequently fall into the state of grumbling, there is a *pācittiya*; whatever monk, during a discussion of a legal decision in the Saṅgha..."
“If a monk, having not given his consent while the formal act is being carried out, should rise from his seat and depart, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Furthermore, if a monk, after a robe has been given by a unanimous Saṅgha, should subsequently fall into a state of criticism... [etc. ...it is an offense of expiation.

Such rules as these were laid down for the sake of the Saṅgha’s comfort. “In the case of one who speaks otherwise or causes vexation, it is an offense of expiation; in the case of reviling with offenses such as pārājika, [it is an offense of expiation].”
The Saṅghādisesa rules and others are for the restraint of the wicked; the rules concerning encroachment, expulsion, and eavesdropping and others are for the comfortable dwelling of the virtuous;
all that is forbidden by the world is for the warding off of the taints pertaining to both the present life and the future life;
all that is forbidden by the formal rule (paṇṇatti) is for the restraint of those pertaining only to the present life. All that is connected with householders—
It is for the purpose of inspiring confidence in those who lack it, and for increasing the faith of those who already possess it.

Specifically, the training rule concerning the novice Ariṭṭha, as well as the general rules regarding the limits set upon the requisites, are connected to the endurance of the True Dhamma. The Suttas beginning with, “This Dhamma is for one of few desires;
this Dhamma is not for one of great desire,” serve here as proof. [In the case of] one who disparages the training rules and causes delusion...

It should be understood that the rule beginning with "an offense entailing expiation" (pācittiya) was laid down for the purpose of supporting the Vinaya. If one asks, "For what purpose was this rule, 'An offense entailing expiation for destroying a living plant' (bhūtagāma-pātabyatā), established?
it is for the sake of inspiring confidence in those without confidence and for increasing the faith of those who already have it. How so?
"A living plant is something endowed with life"—for one whose view is not perverted [in this regard]...
“With the perception that it is dead, there is faith in the Buddha’s disciples.
How could the faultless Sage, who perceives this as being devoid of life, feel anger?
For how could he be angry at the permission of fish and meat?”
Thus too:
"The disciples of the Buddha possess confidence because of their perception of his freedom from anger;
whereas these founders of other sects are not free from the company of living beings."
“For the sake of protecting the minds of the world, the Sage has abstained even from that.
Thus, for those with clear confidence, there is an increase in their faith.
[He maintains] a secluded dwelling, free from craving for its enjoyment, devoid of living beings, and well-guarded.
Avoiding both [the practice of] leaning toward meat-eating and its opposite,
the Buddha prescribed a training rule therein regarding the consumption of even lifeless meat by a monk.
Seeing people censuring him, he renounced the class of living beings.
Regarding the permission for fish and meat, because it was pure in three respects,
the permission for meat was granted out of dependence on that purity, and out of fear of the attachment to views regarding ritual action.
Out of compassion for the world that lacks discernment, out of consideration for others,
out of a desire to avoid the destruction of living beings, and out of fear of the consequence of taking life—
the Blessed One permitted there a figurative expression, but he prohibited food prepared specifically for him, fearing it might lead to the sin of another.
Furthermore, it should be understood that he permitted a dwelling and a hut for his own use in order to demonstrate the absence of evil in the destruction of living plants.
It is called "the preparation of purposes" (*atthavasapakaraṇa*) because various specific purposes, which are designated as "benefits," are scattered therein.
The commentary on the Mahāvagga is finished.
The commentary on the first section of socializing (gāthāsaṅgaṇika);
the commentary on the training rules (sikkhāpada) prescribed in the seven cities.
335. Or the meaning is that it is a particle used in the sense of accepting what has been said. "Three hundred and fifty" means three hundred and fifty. "A human being" means a human person.
"Exceeding [ten days]" refers to an extra robe kept for more than ten days.
"Black" refers to the blackness described as "purely black. "Truth" refers to the declaration of truth. "Successive meal" refers to eating in succession.

by the giving of consent from one undergoing probation (*pārivāsika*), she may ordain a trainee nun (*sikkhamānā*). The four *pārājika* offenses for nuns are: [1] a hut built by solicitation (*saññācikā kuṭi*);

"And it is to be confessed. Regarding "exhortation": if a nun does not go for the purpose of exhortation or for communal residence, [she incurs an offense].
"The four pārājikas," etc., is a summary of what was prescribed in two cities.
This concludes the commentary on the four failures.
336. Regarding the thirty-one "heavy" offenses: there are eight *pārājikas* for both [monks and nuns], thirteen *saṅghādisesas* for monks, and ten *saṅghādisesas* for nuns.
