Why? Because it was said there as well: 'Give the method by distinguishing only the *Uposatha* and *Pavāraṇā*.
It should be understood that this is because it would follow that even offenses are settled by means of an illegal, incomplete, or other such formal act."

This should be investigated. "By two, by four, by three, and by one for a transaction" means: the legal issue of dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*) is settled by two; the legal issue of accusation (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*) by four;
the legal issue of offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) by three; and the legal issue of business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*) by one. This is the meaning.
[End of] the commentary on the offenses such as the *pārājika*.

339. "Nibbacanamattaṃ" means merely a synonym (*vevacanamattaṃ*). "The rest" (*sesa*) refers to those following the beginning, namely the middle sections. "A clause" (*pada*) means a training rule (*sikkhāpada*). "Saddhācittaṃ" means a mind of confidence;
the meaning is "a serene mind" (*pasannacittaṃ*), or alternatively, there is the reading "santācittaṃ. "Anāḷiyaṃ" means poverty.
Although this etymological explanation (*nibbacanaṃ*) is not found in the question beginning with "heavy or light," [it is relevant here]: "Come, let us hear the discourse."
It should be understood that this was spoken for the purpose of illustrating the meaning comprised by the words "these.
There is also a reading, "Space is the resort of birds," which is appropriate in terms of genus. "Of birds" (pakkhīnaṃ) refers to them directly.
The commentary on the first verse in the *Saṅgaṇikā* section is finished.
Commentary on the Classification of Legal Issues; Commentary on the Classification of Reopening, etc. 340.
To demonstrate the reopening of the methods of settlement through the reopening of legal issues, [the text states] that legal issues are settled by seven methods.
The intention is that by reopening those [cases] which have been settled, one is said to reopen the seven methods of settling (*satta samathā*). "It gives birth" means it originates.

Regarding the statement, "They are found in the legal question concerning accusations (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*) and so forth," it is said that because they are identical to [the categories of] "Dhamma and non-Dhamma" and so on, they are specifically found within those [seven methods].
"Not refuted" means by means of the Suttas and so forth. "Not adjudicated" means by means of [the determination of] "offense and non-offense" and so forth.
“In this regard, ten [methods] are stated: ‘one reopens a legal issue that has been settled by means of a Jātaka... up to... one reopens a settlement by covering over as with grass. It is written:
‘Because the *sammukhāvinaya*, *paṭiññātakaraṇa*, and *yebhuyyasikā* are not mentioned, they cannot be reopened; furthermore, there is no formal ritual procedure (*kammavācā*) for them.
Therefore, it is said that they cannot be reopened. This is according to the *Pāḷimuttakavinicchaya*.”
The meaning is: "by means of the mere teaching of the Dhamma alone, without the characteristics of the Vinaya. Or, by means of a Sutta brought from either the Khandhaka or the Parivāra.

They "persuade" or show [the matter]. The meaning is: having explained things such as "what is non-Dhamma is Dhamma" regarding a legal issue (adhikaraṇa) previously adjudicated according to the Dhamma and Vinaya for the sake of preceptors and others. Uneven bodily actions and so forth.
Because it is dependent, it is "dependent on what is uneven. The same applies to the remaining cases. 342–3.
Commentary on the Origin of Legal Issues (*adhikaraṇa-nidāna*):
"What equipment? means what requisites; here, *kiṃ* is an indeclinable used as a common gender marker. "A dispute previously arisen..."
The dispute that arises subsequently based on [the offense] is called the "source of dispute. Due to the legal issue of an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*), one incurs four types of offenses:
if a nun knowingly conceals a *pārājika* offense, it is a *pārājika*; if she conceals it while being in doubt, it is a *thullaccaya*;
if a monk conceals a *saṅghādisesa* offense, it is a *pācittiya*; and [concealing] a failure in conduct (*ācāravipatti*)...
To conceal it is a *dukkaṭa* offense. [This refers to] those duties that arise depending on a previously performed act such as *ukkhepaniya-kamma*.
Of what kind? By way of *samanubhāsanā* (formal admonition) and so forth. "That" (*taṃ*) refers to the legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*). 344.
To show by which legal issue among the legal issues they are settled, [it says]: "When they are settled by means of the legal issues..."

This was stated for the purpose of showing that at that time they settle [disputes] by means of a legal question (*adhikaraṇa*) alone, and not by other means; it is not for the purpose of showing that they settle them exclusively by means of a legal question. 348.
"The Saṅgha disputes regarding a legal question concerning an offense" means: "Is it an offense or is it not an offense? in this manner.
353. Because there is no formal origin (*samuṭṭhāna*) for it, the performance and non-performance of the legal act (*kamma*) in the *sammukhāvinaya* has not been analyzed;
rather, only the six origins of the *sativinaya* and so forth have been analyzed. Why is that?

It is because, due to the absence of a collective legal act, there is no such thing as "being a duty" for the *saṅgha-sammukhatā* and other factors, as there is for the *sativinaya* and the rest—this is the intended meaning.
The commentary on the analysis of the divisions of legal cases is finished.
The commentary on the second section, the collection of verses,
consisting of the questions and answers regarding the formal charges and so forth.

359. "Viggāhikakathaṃ" means a contentious discussion. "Nisāmaya" means examine. "Kāraya" is the reading [of the text]. Some say he is unskilled because he does not know what precedes and what follows; however, this refers to being unskilled in either of the two types of duties through any of the postures.
Commentary on the Section on Reprimand (Codanākaṇḍavaṇṇanā). Commentary on the Duties of an Investigator (Anuvijjakakiccavaṇṇanā).

360. In the inquiry by the investigator (*anuvijjaka*), failure regarding livelihood (*ājīva-vipatti*) was not asked about. Failure regarding conduct (*ācāra-vipatti*) was asked about by way of the five classes of offenses (*pañca-āpatti-kkhandha*). They say: "It is likewise for failure regarding livelihood, because it is included [within that inquiry]. The reading is "one who commits" (*ajjhāpajjanto*). 363.
Therefore, it should be connected with "and not depending on material things" (*na ca āmisaṃ nissāya*).
The Shorter Commentary on the Battle (*Cūḷa-saṅgāma-vaṇṇanā*).
Commentary on the Practice of the Examiner (Anuvijjaka): 365.
"Dependent upon standing, sitting, clothing, and so forth" means such things as "one should stand thus; one should sit thus.
"For the purpose of producing recognition" means for the purpose of recognizing [the person] thus: "One should be addressed in this way. "By being conformed to" refers to the mind.
The meaning is "while setting aside. Regarding the phrase "Is that indeed shame?": the intention is, "Is this assembly [the one characterized by] that shame?

Regarding "having had him recite the rules of formal questioning (*anuyogavatta*)": having asked, "Do you know the rules of formal questioning?", and having had him recite them by means of that very question.

"Ignorance" refers to the possibility of not knowing. Regarding the expression "through fear he goes out of fear": it is stated by way of cause as "through fear, for the sake of fear, he goes out of fear. Just as it is said, "But because of passion and because of hatred, he goes out of desire and out of aversion," so it is here.
The Description of the Great Battle;
the Description of What Should Be Known by One Speaking. 375.
"Color and non-color" refers to the white and unobstructed [light] spoken of both by way of colors such as blue and so forth, and by way of non-colors such as health and so forth.
402. *Bhūmipucchā*: "Earth," "the ground," and "the world"—all these are synonyms for the earth (*pathavī*).
[End of] the commentary on the classification of the *kathina*. [End of] the commentary on the state of being *kathina* and so forth.

It is said that [the action] occurs subsequently "having become immediate by way of the future" because the preliminary acts such as washing arise after the performance of the operation such as fetching water;

this is stated with reference to the act of washing and so forth, and because the operation is performed. However, in the case of the *purejāta-paccaya* (pre-arising condition), the meaning is that this is the "operation. Even a single dhamma...
It does not obtain because of the non-existence of what was previously born for itself.
412. Regarding the commentary on the classification of things to be known, such as the *kaṭhina* robe:

"In phenomena such as form" refers to the eightfold sets beginning with color and fragrance. Since it is stated, "the last month of the rainy season," it is established that it is permissible to spread [the *kaṭhina*] on any day whatsoever during that final month.
415. They say that because it was spoken by one who is "a kinsman of the Sun," it is the word of the Elder (Thera).
Commentary on the Discussion of the Questions and Answers Regarding Obstacles (Palibodha):
How is [the robe] formally relinquished (uddharīyati) outside the boundary (bahisīmā) by one who has reached a final decision (sanniṭṭhānantika)? A bhikkhu, taking up an unmade robe (akatacīvara)...
He departs with the intention, "I will not return. While he has yet to reach the boundary, the thought occurs to him, "I shall not have this robe made.
In this way, for one who has gone outside the boundary, the robe is forfeited. How [is it forfeited] within the boundary?
Taking up an unmade robe, he departs with the intention, "I will not return. Then, failing to find a comfortable dwelling there, he returns to that very same monastery.
For him, only the obstacle of the robe remains; and that [obstacle] is severed when the thought arises, "I will not have this robe made.
Therefore it is said, "It is relinquished within the boundary" (*sīmā*). The type based on final determination (*sanniṭṭhānantika*) is twofold:
having severed the obstacle of the residence by thinking, "I will not return," and then returning again to that same monastery, [thinking], "I will not..."

If one makes a formal determination, thinking, "I will have a robe made," and while standing outside the boundary, forms a mental resolve, thinking, "I will neither have this robe made nor return [to the monastery]," it is a case of "termination by resolution.
In the verse as well, the phrase "the two obstacles, neither before nor after," refers to this very point.
How is there "cutting off of hope" within the boundary? It is through that which is expected, [thinking], "You..."
It is written: "When one who had previously gone [to another monastery] with the thought, 'I will not return,' thinking, 'Pray for that very monastery;

I shall send someone,' has gone there having severed the impediment of the residence (*āvāsa-palibodha*), and is then sent back by that [monastery] with the words, 'I am unable to give [the robe],' [this is the case].
For it is said, "When there is a formal entrustment (*atthāra*), there is what is called 'sending back' (*uddhāra*). Thus, they do not obtain sending back without a formal entrustment; therefore—

It has been stated: "The first two" refers to the two modes of suspension of the *kathina* cloth mentioned in the context, "Two suspensions of the *kathina* arise together and cease together"—namely, the first mentioned, the suspension due to the interval within the rainy season (*antarabbhāsa-hu-uddhāra*).
It does not refer to the two beginning with the suspension due to departure (*pakkamanantika*). "They cease together" means they reach the state of being suspended simultaneously.
The commentary on the breaking of the *kathina* cloth is finished.
The commentary on the Chapter on Designations is finished.
The commentary on the Five Questions of Upāli.
The commentary on the Chapter on Non-Dependence.
419. "Bodily injury" means transgression by means of the body.
Commentary on the Chapter on Non-Subsiding: 420.
"One who causes oppression" means one who acts by oppressing and overpowering.
Commentary on the Vohāravagga 424.
A legal issue arising from dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*) originates based on the grounds for schism; thus it proceeds according to their respective order.

The legal issue arising from dispute has the twelve root-activities beginning with anger and enmity as its application, and likewise for the remaining [legal issues]. Regarding the nine [procedures] beginning with reinstatement (*osāraṇā*):
The performance of formal acts (*kamma*) by means of a motion (*ñatti*) in two instances:

in the two instances of formal acts consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiya*) and a motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha*). Since the two Vibhaṅgas are not included [in the *Parivāra*] according to the method stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, the connection is that what is stated in the *Kurundi-ṭīkā* should be accepted.
Commentary on the Chapter on the Manifestation of Views (Diṭṭhāvikammavagga) 425.

It is not permitted for three [monks] or more to confess an offense together. One who is of a different communion by way of formal act (*kamma*) is indeed one who is of a different communion by way of attainment (*laddhi*). The phrase “for one standing within the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsa-sīmā*)” is said, it is reported, with reference to the great boundary (*mahāsīma*).
433. The reading is “due to madness or mental derangement.”
Commentary on the Chapter on False Speech (Musāvādavagga): 444.
“To one who knows by way of a figurative expression” means: to anyone who knows, a false speech spoken by way of a figurative expression;
this is the meaning. 446. “No further questioning should be given” means: without taking what was said into account, one should remain silent; this is the meaning.
Commentary on the Chapter on Exhorting the Bhikkhunīs (Bhikkhunovādavagga):
454. Regarding "vohāra-nirutti" and "sadda-nirutti. There are nineteen [factors], beginning with the reviewing of the path (maggapaccavekkhaṇā).
Commentary on the Chapter on the Committee (Ubbāhikavagga).
455. *Pasāretā* and *mohetā*.
Commentary on the Chapter on the Settlement of Legal Issues (458):
“‘According to the time of dyeing’ refers to one who has not yet received full ordination,” so they say. “‘According to seniority’ refers to one who has received full ordination,” thus it is written.
Regarding the commentary on the section on the spreading of the *kathina*:
“*Ekāvatto*” is also read; its meaning, it is said, is one who is angry or overcome by anger.

Some also read it as “*ekavattho*,” meaning one who stands having removed his upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*). All of this is [explained] in the commentary according to the canonical text (*pāḷi*) cited therein.
"It is contradictory. For "one turn" has been extracted; therefore, it should not be accepted. "By the reason stated in between" means by the reason stated [in the text]:
"Because he was intent on his duties, failing to attend to the salutation, he might strike his forehead," and so forth.
The commentary on the five cases of Upāli is finished.
Commentary on the Origin of Offenses (Āpattisamuṭṭhānavaṇṇanā): 470.

“Only what was stated before” refers to those offenses involving formal rules (*paṇṇattivajja*), such as sharing a bed and so forth. “The other” refers to that which involves a conscious state of mind (*sacittaka*). “While teaching,” the intention is: having become dejected and having committed an offense by means of frightening others and so forth.
Commentary on the Second Verse on Socializing (Gāthāsaṅgaṇikavaṇṇanā).
474–5. Regarding the commentary on bodily and other offenses:
it is stated that "it includes all recitations of the Pātimokkha" because there is no other recitation apart from the recitation of the *nidāna* (the introductory section).
In the Vinaya, those [offenses] which are grave are called "grave in the Vinaya. Although this [term] appears in two of the verses, by others...
However, since they are stated by combining [the two], the distinction between them should be understood. "Kamma occurs in nine instances" means that there is a formal act (kammañatti).

"Speech" (vācā) refers to that which originates from speech. "One deficient in years" means one who is less than twenty years of age. "Moreover, 'herein' refers to the Kurundi tradition," so it is said.

"The forest-tree" (vanappati) refers to the "forest-tree" as it appears in the context of taking what is not given. "Relinquishment through release" (vissaṭṭhichaḍḍana) refers to the *sukkavissaṭṭhi* (dry relinquishment).

"An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) has been committed" means that an offense of wrong-doing is stated. For one who requests raw grain and then eats it, there is an offense of wrong-doing in the preliminary action;
upon swallowing, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya). This concludes the commentary on the offense entailing expiation.

476. It is said that the Mahāsāṅghikas cause even novices to confess an offense; therefore it is stated, "they should not be made to confess. However, in the case of such a gross transgression, disciplinary action (daṇḍakamma) must be performed against them.
Commentary on Persons Not to Be Venerated, etc. (Avandanīyapuggalādivaṇṇanā): 477.
"A thousand offenses" means one thousand offenses. "In this matter of discipline at Campā" refers to the Campeyyaka Khandhaka.
The meaning is that these four legal procedures—beginning with "proceeding contrary to the Dhamma" and so forth—were indeed spoken by the Blessed One.

It is not only offenses [that are settled]; rather, the six principles for settling disputes (*samatha*)... [as follows]... they are settled by means of resolution in the presence of the parties (*sammukhāvinaya*);

they reach a reconciliation, they reach an agreement through resolution in the presence of the parties; this is the meaning. Even without the [other] principles for settling disputes, it is settled; it attains the state of being a principle for settling disputes.
It proceeds. When the sense of negation is intended, "without the *samathas*" means "apart from the *samathas*.
478. Regarding the commentary on the sixteen formal acts (*kamma*) and so forth:
"not based on the Sutta" (*asuttaka*) means devoid of the Sutta; the intention is that there is no deviation from the Sutta (*usutta*) therein.
The commentary on the second verse regarding socializing is finished.
[Now begins] the commentary on the verses for wiping away sweat,
and the commentary on the question concerning non-separation.
479. *Tahiṃ* means in that person. *Akappiyasambhoga* (improper enjoyment) refers to sexual intercourse and so forth. It is stated in the *Garubhaṇḍavinicchaya* (Analysis of Precious Goods):

"It is permissible to use [an object] after having assigned it for the purpose of protecting excellent lodgings. Regarding the eleven who are not to be saluted (*anavaṇdiyā*), there are eleven beginning with the *paṇḍaka* (eunuch).
He approaches together with his retinue. He does not live because he is of a created form (*nimmitarūpa*). By the phrase, "I speak with my neck raised,"...
This illuminates the absence of sexual intercourse in the mouth. By the exclusion of "below the navel," it refers to the urinary passage and the anal passage.

"With reference to a nun who has entered the other bank of a river included within the village boundary" means that this was stated specifically with reference to the vicinity of the river on the opposite bank, which is not included within the village.
Therein, the village precinct on the opposite bank extends as far as the limit of the river, defined by the distance of a single stone's throw.

It is delimited; therefore, there is not even a space the size of a jewel on the opposite bank that is forest, and because it is concealed by grass and so forth, it renders that area devoid of the range of vision.

In that regard, there is no offense within one's own village. However, on the opposite bank, he places his foot right within the village precinct, which is defined as the distance of a single stone’s throw.
By way of the Abhidhamma, he thus passes through his own village, which has become "forest" [by that definition].
Therefore, it should be understood that there is a falling away from the community. Even at this point, one should accept [the teaching] after reflecting and being satisfied with it.
Five hundred women, headed by Mahāpajāpatī, received full ordination (*upasampadā*) in the presence of the monks.
For even Mahāpajāpatī is said to have received full ordination in the presence of the monks because she accepted the exhortation given by the Venerable Ānanda.
Commentary on the Questions on the Pārājika, etc., 480:
“With reference to a robe-shed” is said because it is possible to commit an offense [against the rule] while possessing a robe.
Since the acceptance [of the robe] is relinquished upon a change of gender, it is not permitted to take it up oneself and consume it. “Or like a crow’s nest” means by a crow...
Or, it is *ūhadanaṃ*. The phrase “having approached even three men” is a textual supplement (*pāṭhaseso*).
481. Commentary on the Questions regarding the *Pācittiya* rules:
“On account of sexual intercourse” means physical contact. By reason of that, it constitutes a preliminary stage to sexual intercourse.
“Or they strive for physical contact” refers to the fulfillment of the eight bases. “On account of enjoyment” means for the sake of enjoyment.
“Therefore” means because one incurs [the offense] on account of enjoyment; therefore, it occurs at the conclusion of the meal—this is the meaning.
In the ancient manuscripts, the reading is “tassā. They say, “The statement of the cause is excellent, as it demonstrates the delimitation of the meal.”
The commentary on the *Sedamocanagāthā* is finished.
[Now begins] the commentary on the *Pañcavagga* of the *Kammavagga*.
483. It is stated: “Having requested the formal authorization for one who is insane (*ummattaka-sammuti*) from an insane person, it is permissible to grant it even when they are not present.

In this regard, it does not fail [to be valid] even if [the requester] is seated [elsewhere], because there is no fixed rule [regarding presence]. To show that there is no fault in what is done in the absence [of the candidate], it is stated:

“What is done in the absence is well-done. However, in this case, ordination (*upasampadā*) by means of a messenger cannot be performed in the presence [of the candidate], because the nature of the ritual proclamation (*kammavācā*) requires diversity [in its delivery].
Actions such as overturning the bowl (pattanikkujjana) must be performed after removing [the person] from hand’s reach; therefore it is said, “What is done in their absence is well-done.
The meaning of the words “having asked, having accused, and having reminded, one should act; he acts without having asked, without having accused, and without having reminded” is as follows.
Excluding the month of Kattika, that is the month of Pavāraṇā, and the two full-moon days are for those who have entered the first and second rains-residence.
There are two *pavāraṇā* ceremonies on the full moon day.

485. The meaning is "or he abandons a word. In the five [consonant groups] beginning with the *ka*-group, "heavy" (*garuka*) refers to a long vowel and that which is followed by a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*).
In the phrase, "Of the Elder Buddharakkhita, for whom it is not pleasing," the *ta*-kāra and *ka*-kāra are followed by a consonant cluster. [This applies to] long vowels.
Regarding the phrase "it should be said that it is short": where it should have been said, "he should remain silent," the expression used is "so tuṇhi assa.
486. In the remaining commentaries (*ṭīkā*), the statement found in the *Kurundi* is made clear by saying, "they are unable to sit [in the assembly].

487–8. "Four bhikkhus of pure virtue" means those who have not committed a *pārājika* offense. "Neither their consent (*chanda*) nor their purity (*pārisuddhi*) goes [to the assembly]" means that when three or two [bhikkhus] are sitting [in the assembly], even if the consent and purity of one or two of them are brought forward, they are as if not brought at all.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Act of Notification (Apalokanakamma): 495–6.
"Physical enjoyment, communal living, receiving a shared bed, and so forth, constitute the grounds for this act of notification;
thus, in this way too, the act of notification proceeds"—this is the meaning. An action itself is the characteristic; hence, it is called the "characteristic of an action" (kammalakkhaṇa).

Just as acts such as reinstatement (*osāraṇa*), banishment (*nissāraṇa*), and the act of censure (*bhaṇḍukamma*) are both formal acts (*kamma*) and receive no other name, but are characterized solely as acts;

thus, the characteristic of an act is like a decisive support (*upanissaya*). For all specific conditions are subsumed therein, being free from the characteristics of the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*) and so forth.
It is for this reason that it is said: "It has the characteristic of an act. The characteristic of an act.
To demonstrate this, it was said: “for those whose robes have been stolen, whose robes are worn out, or whose robes are lost,” and so forth.

Regarding the statement, “One giving more than that must give after having obtained formal consent (apaloketvā),” the act of obtaining consent is itself the defining characteristic (lakkhaṇa) of the formal act (kamma). In all such cases, the defining characteristic should be understood in this way.
“And also the obstacle of debt”: if creditors should obstruct such a monk, [the gift] must come from funds appropriate for that purpose.

It is permissible to give it. "An intermediate assembly" refers to occasions such as the recitation of auspicious verses that occur between the great assemblies of the *Uposatha* and *Pavāraṇā*. "From what has been set aside" means from what was deposited for the sake of providing for the *Cetiya*.
"'Another agreement must be made' means that since these [trees] belong to others, an agreement different from the one previously made regarding those trees must be established. "If..."
In that context, by the previous statement, "Starting from now, divide [the goods] and eat," personal consumption was prohibited.
"Having gone along after them" means having followed behind them; the sense is: "expecting requisites from them.
"The root-portion" means having made it into a tenth part. In former times, it was done by making it a tenth part.
They gave [it], therefore it is called the "root portion. Or, "having made it a place where no one dwells" means by means of income that has arisen.

"It should not be forbidden even at the time of cultivation" means that once it has been cultivated, it should not be stopped when it is laden with flowers and fruit. "At the time of cultivation" means at the time when one has begun to cultivate.
"But as for the classification of the bases of formal acts consisting of a motion (ñattikamma)" refers to the different bases of the formal act consisting of a motion.
Now, here is some incidental matter: there is a formal act of the Saṅgha that the Saṅgha alone performs, neither a group nor an individual;
this should be understood as the other fourfold types of formal acts, setting aside one portion of the characteristics of a formal act belonging to the *apalokana* (informal) type.
There is a formal act of the Saṅgha that the Saṅgha performs, a group performs, and an individual performs; this [is as described] previously.
It has been set aside. For this has been said: "In whatever monastery two or three persons reside, what is performed by them sitting together is just as if it were performed by the Saṅgha.
But in whatever monastery there is only one bhikkhu, [it is performed] by that bhikkhu," and so forth.
There is a formal act of a group (gaṇakamma) which the Saṅgha performs, the group performs, and an individual performs; that is the Uposatha of pure confession (pārisuddhi-uposatha).
It is performed in the presence of others; it should be understood by way of that.

There is a *gaṇa*-action (*gaṇakamma*) which the *gaṇa* alone performs, neither the Saṅgha nor an individual; it should be understood by way of that *pārisuddhi-uposatha* which is performed through mutual announcement.
There is an individual-action (*puggalakamma*) which the individual alone performs, neither the Saṅgha nor the *gaṇa*.

This should be understood by way of the *adhiṭṭhāna-uposatha* (the observance day by formal resolution). Regarding a formal act performed by a group (*gaṇakamma*), one group performs it while another does not;
in that case, for an act requiring four [monks], only two perform it, not three. For an act requiring five, only three perform it, neither fewer nor more than that.
Commentary on the Chapter on What Was Not Laid Down and What Was Laid Down (Apaññattapaññattavagga): 500.

Indeed, it was only Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa who laid down the seven classes of offenses (āpattikkhandha). However, Vipassī and the others recited the Pātimokkha of exhortation; they did not lay down formal training rules (sikkhāpada).
Commentary on the Concluding Statement:
There exists for that Vinaya Piṭaka a teaching analyzed according to the Ubhatovibhaṅga, Khandhaka, and Parivāra;
its commentary, named *Samantapāsādikā*, has been completed—this is what he meant by saying "the commentary named *Samantapāsādikā* is finished.
In that regard, it was in the principal hall (*padhānaghara*). It was successful (*iddhā*) through the determination of meanings and other such qualities.
He has arisen rightly and has arisen fully; he has attained those qualities without difficulty, or he has arisen together with qualities of superior measure.

Because of that arising, the faith and other [faculties] produced by the mindfulness described as "examining the destinations of states that have gone" are called supremely purified, owing to their being protected by the [five] faculties. Thus, it is said to be accompanied by faith and the others.
This being so, regarding the fourfold virtue mentioned here, the virtue of restraint by the Pātimokkha is adorned by faith, for it has faith as its means of accomplishment.

It should be understood accordingly that the virtues of restraint of the sense faculties, purity of livelihood, and proper use of requisites are adorned by mindfulness, energy, and wisdom respectively.
Furthermore, faith devoid of understanding is not purified, because it is through understanding that faith becomes a cause for serene confidence.
However, through its power, the *buddhis* (intellects) become what is called "supremely pure. Wisdom (*paññā*) that is devoid of faith (*saddhā*) falls into the category of the miserly (*kerāṭika*);
only when conjoined with faith does it become pure. And energy (*vīriya*) that is lacking in concentration (*samādhi*) leads to agitation;
because it is said that energy is pure only when conjoined with concentration, concentration is also implied here. Thus, they are supremely pure.
It should be understood that faith and the other [faculties] also adorn the Pātimokkha. How so?
Without faith in the Teacher who points out the practice, in the practice itself, and in the fruit of the practice, it is impossible to undertake the precepts or to purify those already undertaken;
thus, faith adorns the Pātimokkha. In this regard, by means of the passage beginning, "Thus indeed is the Blessed One... [the faculty of faith is established].

And one is able to honor the Teacher. The development of faith regarding the visible and future fruits rooted in the failure and success of moral conduct within the practice should be understood in detail.

Having seen the danger and the benefit caused by the failure and success of moral conduct, as well as the means for abandoning the danger and accomplishing the benefit, the wisdom that proceeds accordingly brings about restraint according to the Pātimokkha.
“He adorns. By means of the passage beginning with “It is too cold,” one abandons the laziness that is unfit for practice;

then, following the instruction stated in “He who [endures] cold and heat,” one adorns the Pātimokkha by means of the energy that proceeds through the non-arising and abandoning of unarisen and arisen non-restraints, and the arising and increasing of restraints.
In this same manner, it should be applied to the restraint of the sense faculties and so forth as well.
Here, "conduct" (ācāra) should be understood as conduct that is in accordance with the four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu).

By the term "straightforwardness" (ajjava), the state of having a disposition free from greed is illustrated through the demonstration of being endowed with the quality of straightforwardness—the opposite of deceit (māyā) and fraud (sāṭheyya), which are crooked actions such as bodily misconduct committed for the sake of gain and honor.

By the term "gentleness" (maddava), [the state of having a disposition free from greed is illustrated] through the demonstration of being endowed with the quality of gentleness—such as loving-kindness (mettā)—which is the opposite of hostility (paṭigha) and other factors that produce harshness.

The inclinations toward what is beneficial (*hitajjhāsaya*) and so forth are illuminated. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the association with the qualities mentioned in such passages as "patience, gentleness, amiability, and hospitality" is indicated.

The virtues mentioned here, such as uprightness (*ajjava*) and mildness (*maddava*), are both causes for the perfection of virtue (*sīlasampatti*) and its fruit, because they bring that perfection about. "One's own assembly" (*sakasamaya*) refers to the fourfold assembly.

By this, the non-existence of suffering that shares in [the nature of] parts is indicated. Alternatively, "one's own system" (*sakasamaya*) refers to the Buddha’s own three baskets (*piṭakattaya*), for it is precisely one's own system because it is difficult to explain;
the "comprehension of one's own system" is the definitive conclusion regarding one's own system:
"Truth, a being, rebirth-linking, and the very mode of conditions."

"Four things are difficult to see, and they are very difficult to teach"—since this was said, just as the application of the phrase "grasping one's own system" was explained, so too is that for another system.

By the term "clarity of wisdom" (*paññāveyyattiya*), it refers to a wisdom whose intrinsic nature is like a sword sharpened on a whetstone, produced by this keen knowledge. Regarding that which is designated as the "Three Piṭakas"...
The classification of the *pariyatti* (the teaching) is the classification of the *pariyatti* consisting of the Three Piṭakas.
Within that classification, both the "threads" (*tantrī*) and the meaning of those threads are called the "Dispensation" (*sāsana*). Here, however, they say it is "only the threads.

Because there was an absence of the knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*) at the time when this commentary was completed, the phrase "by the power of unimpeded knowledge" is stated with reference to the knowledge consisting of what has been heard (*suta-maya*).

Because it is produced by the perfection of the grammatical instruments (*karaṇa*), it is "well-issued" (*sukhaviniggata*). Because it is well-issued, it should also be joined with the charm of speech that is sweet and noble;
such speech provides both pleasure to the ear and the pleasure of a perfect arrangement.

By saying "by a great grammarian" (*mahāveyyākaraṇena*) instead of simply "by a grammarian," it is indicated that his nature was characterized by a unique mastery of the system of Pāṇini, adorned with training in phonology, etymology, prosody, metrics, and so forth.

It is indicated. Regarding the phrase "one who speaks appropriately" (*yuttavādinā*) and so forth, the meaning is: by one who speaks what is fitting and appropriate, and who is endowed with the wisdom of the occasion (*ṭhānuppattiyapaññā*).

Even though there is a difference in their nutritive essence (*ojā*), due to the possession of capacities such as sustaining life and providing sustenance, or because of the greatness of the works composed by the Great Poet (*Mahākavi*), [the term applies] in these three places:
within the Dispensation (*sāsana*) through expressions such as "the analysis of the study of the Three Piṭakas," in the domain of logic (*hetuvisaya*), and in the field of sound (*sadda*).
By demonstrating the state of proficiency, he indicates the presence of his perfection of analytical wisdom (*venayika-buddhi-sampatti*).

Those individuals for whom the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) and so forth have been broken open are "those whose analytical knowledges and so forth are broken open" (*pabhinnapaṭisambhidādayo*); these are the phenomena (*dhammā*).

Surrounded by them, and without effecting a severance of the continuity (*santati*), that which is surrounded by the broken-open analytical knowledges is "surrounded by the broken-open analytical knowledges" (*pabhinnapaṭisambhidāparivāro*), by way of being established and increased within one’s own continuum (*santāna*). In that...
The meaning is: "in superhuman states accompanied by the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) that have been fully developed.

However, when one is adorned with qualities such as the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*) and the four analytical knowledges, the six direct knowledges themselves are indeed superhuman states. As for the four analytical knowledges, they consist only of a portion of the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*).
How can both of these, which are themselves included within the category of superhuman states, be [called] "superhuman states"?

Does it "adorn"? Just as flowers and other parts belonging to a tree adorn that tree, [the analytical knowledge] adorns those superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) of which it is itself a constituent part.

However, the analytical knowledge included within the dhammas of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), not being a constituent part of the superhuman states, adorns the superhuman state—just as an ornament that is not a constituent part of a person adorns that person.

...like a man. Alternatively, it adorns the sixfold supernormal knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*), the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), and other such qualities, which are the retinue of the analysis of the Dhamma pertaining to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).
Furthermore, the word "analytical knowledge" (*paṭisambhidā*) is used again with reference to the supramundane analytical knowledge (*lokuttara-paṭisambhidā*).

Having arisen within the Dispensation, it serves as an ornament for the Dispensation, or it serves as an ornament for the very lineage in which one has arisen. [This applies] to both the concise and the detailed [expositions].

It is the mutual clarification [of meaning], the production and increase of confidence in those who lack it and the further development of that which already exists, and the making profound what has been stated as profound yet obscure;
thus, by virtue of possessing these six qualities of a teacher, one is called "one of vast intelligence.
As for those who, in their excessive pursuit of investigating the Dhamma, grasp at various extremes such as annihilationism, or [think] "everything..."

If they grasp [the object] as being "merely a conventional designation" (paññatti) or "merely the ultimate reality" (paramattha), their intellect is called "defiled" because it has wrong view as its condition;
however, this person's intellect is called "pure" because it is free from the excessive running about of conceptualizing phenomena (dhammacintātidhāvana).
Therefore it is said: "by one of vast and pure intellect. By the teachers, [he is described] as "dear, venerable, and worthy of cultivation," and so forth.
By one endowed with the aforementioned qualities; by one who is a *thera* because he has attained stability through those qualities;

by one who possesses purity of virtue (*sīla-visuddhi*) through virtue or the purification of virtue; by one who is the eldest in the world because he was the first to be born after breaking open the eggshell of ignorance; or by one who is a *mahesi* because he seeks (*esi*) the great and profound aggregates of virtue and so forth of the world.
Up to this point [is the explanation] of the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā* known as the *Samantapāsādikā*, which consists of approximately twenty-seven thousand words.
Although the expansion of the knotty points has been accomplished here by condensing the various explanations found in all the sections, nevertheless,
one should thoroughly investigate what is written herein, taking note of both the Canon (Pāḷi) and the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā),
and observing those teachers who have perceived the great majesty of the Blessed Buddha and the diverse, profound meaning of the methods in the Vinaya Piṭaka.

Having paid homage at the feet of those who stood forth revealing the Vinaya Piṭaka solely for the sake of establishing the True Dhamma and out of a desire to benefit others— without destroying the path of the ancient teachings and setting aside their own opinions— I, being endowed with qualities such as patience and gentleness,
won their hearts through the perfection of my conduct, and requested them to explain the legal decisions (vinicchaya) that have come down through the lineage.
Having reflected, whatever is consistent with that [teaching] should be accepted, while the other should be discarded. Otherwise, one should remain silent.
One must certainly not act as a creator of confusion in the adjudication [of the Dhamma]. Why? Because it would be a cause for the destruction of the Dispensation. And there is a verse on this:
“The unawakened [person] regarding the Great Power of the Buddha...”
He who, being ignorant, would praise the Vinaya while [ignoring] the profound method and meaning of the Dhamma,
is difficult to see and is a cause for the destruction of the Teaching.
For he who, through lack of understanding, destroys the Pāli, its meaning,
and the method of the Aṭṭhakathās, and through lack of desire,
[misrepresents] what is certain as uncertain by means of others—
He leads [the assembly], preceded by them;
the monk who fancies himself wise is preceded in turn by the great multitude.
“Without entertaining doubt, as the unwise might,
he displays the graceful ease of a teacher before them.
Thus ends the *Gaṇṭhipadādhippāyappakāsanā* (The Elucidation of the Intent of the Glosses) on the *Samantapāsādikā*.
The Vajirabuddhiṭīkā is completed.
